PREFACE 

5/11/48 Frui

HIS study of Modern Corporation Finance is intended to review financial principles and practices in light of the pronounced changes which have occurred in recent years. Numerous re- 

Forms have been adopted which affect financial operations and, more important, temper the spirit of their motivation and direction. There has been a sharpening of the concept of public interest, and the introduction of active public regulation will exercise profound influence upon the activities of corporation finance. No analysis of the subject, today, would be complete without a recognition of these forces, and it is for this reason that the authors have injected these modern developments. 

In giving consideration to the changing financial pattern, there is equal need to appreciate the importance of the undergirding struc ture developed through years of experience. After all, financial practices and the forms of institutions may change, but the functions are likely to endure. This volume describes the structural background and considers the changing financing scene in relation to the cumulative and inherited past. It is not intended to declare the merits of the changing order so much as to recognize it objectively as a fact and to invite the free thought which is characteristic of a democracy. 

As this book goes to press, the pressures of great social movements seem to be brought into focus by the second World War. The struggle brings into relief even more sharply the question of public interest and makes governmental regulation and control a matter of dire necessity. Irrespective of the outcome of the conflict, there would seem to be little prospect of a quick subsidence of this governmental authority. For this reason, the reader can gain perspective in reviewing private financial practices by keeping in mind the larger inexorable forces of control.

While accepting full responsibility for the observations made, the authors wish to acknowledge the helpful suggestions and assistance of all who contributed to this volume. There is also a recognition due to students, friends, and members of the family who have contributed in numerous ways. Particular acknowledgment is due to 

Isabel Dockeray who served as stenographer and assisted in the production of the manuscript.

March, 1942 WILLIAM H. HUSBAND JAMES C. DOCKERAY

PART I ECONOMIC SETTING

CHAPTER I  Modern Corporation Finance and Its Setting 

HE financial catastrophe which was announced by the stockmarket collapse of 1929 did more than bring an abrupt ending to a spectacular decade of thriving business. Initially, it resulted in the usual economic chaos and disorder which always follow major crises. Ultimately, ordered thought gave rise to what may be considered the first comprehensive and critical survey of our business and financial system. Doubts about the economy were typified by such questions as the following: 

1. Did the system exist for the benefit of the few or the many? 

2. Were crises an inescapable and inherent part of the system? 

3. Was the control of business unduly concentrated? 

4. To what extent was economic progress limited or checked by financial manipulation? 

5. Did those in charge of the system render an adequate accounting of their trusteeship?

The diagnosis of business ills led to the passage of various legislative measures which have had a pronounced effect on financial institutions and practices. The depression, itself, also gave rise to conditions which were unusually conducive to change. It is fitting that the subject of corporation finance be studied in the light of these modern influences and developments. 

Review of Recent Business Conditions 

The nature and character of financial operation are determined in large measure by underlying business conditions. Prosperity naturally raises the tempo of financial activity and causes financial policy to resemble a campaign of strategic offense. Conversely, depression shifts the emphasis from extensive developments to intensive changes within the existing structure. There is less need for new funds, and the problems of finance are chiefly those of meeting internal stresses and strains. Prolonged and severe depression, especially, exercises great 3

influence upon traditional business and financial practices. It is for this reason that the study of corporation finance today must make due allowance for the strains of the past decade. Some may believe that the great depression of the thirties represents a passing, abnormal phase and that full prosperity is inevitable with the passage of time. Others may go to the opposite extreme and presage the beginning of an era of retrogression and gloom. For our purposes, little is to be gained by entertaining such long-term predictions; our primary objective will be to evaluate what has already happened and to note some of the effects on financial policies and practices. 

The sensitivity of financial affairs to business trends makes it desirable to refer briefly to conditions which have prevailed over the last ten years. During that period new and prominent salients appeared on the economic front which will affect business and financial policies for a long time to come. During 1932 and 1933, business volume shrank to astonishingly low levels which seemed to defy expected minimum standards of American living. Using the 1923-25 average as 100 per cent, industrial production declined to 64 per cent; factory employment to 66 per cent; factory payrolls to 47 per cent; and residential construction to 11 per cent. Since the bottom of the depression, some fitful bursts of expansion have occurred but never were they of sufficient intensity or duration to absorb the large amount of unemployment, which had appeared on the American scene for the first time, until the defense boom got under way in 1940. Such business conditions were bound to make their imprint on familiar patterns of financial practice as well as to have marked effect on the volume of financing.

Possibly more serious than the physical changes in the economic structure is the development of a widespread sense of insecurity. This feeling of uncertainty undermines confidence which is one of the main taproots of business financing. Investments are made primarily on the basis of future outlook either in the anticipation of an appreciation of capital values or in the expectancy of a reliable return where minimum risks are entailed. If these incentives are weakened materially, business is necessarily handicapped in raising funds for expansion or in attracting capital to discharge existing maturities. Some developments which give evidence of extreme caution may be noted. Individual and institutional investors show a marked preference for the obligations of government; business enterprise is compelled to use shorter maturities 1

for their indebtedness; and fields of enterprise which have greater risk find it difficult to raise capital at almost any price. 

Public Responsibilities of Business Enterprise 

Prior to the 1930's, private business was called upon to assume a minimum of public responsibility. The operations of private enterprise were assumed to be both automatic and beneficial to society at large. Under the circumstances, there developed a philosophy which seemed to place an obligation upon society in favor of business. Freedom of individual action was presumed to assure the maximum output, and government regulation was believed to be detrimental to the growth of industry. Difficulties did appear in the form of recurring depressions, but ensuing periods of recovery and prosperity always seemed to take up the slack and to point the way to further progress. 

It is not surprising that immediately following the crash of 1929, improvement was thought to be inevitable and that full recovery was believed to be "just around the corner." When the rising sun of recovery failed to appear after long years of unemployment and various forms of economic distress, there was no longer escape from widespread public inquiry as to the effectiveness of the private system. 

Many reasons have been advanced to account for the failure of full recovery to return as it has in past cyclical movements. Warm advocates of unbridled individual initiative place the blame on numerous measures of reform introduced by the federal government. Others with a more philosophical turn of mind look to more deep-rooted causes, such as a fundamental transition from an extensive to an intensive economy or to disturbances brought about by widespread social unrest. However, irrespective of cause, all agree that the effect on the business system is profound and that private interests may no longer regard their business as a form of preemptive right without regard to the public benefits. Instead, business is being faced with a challenge to provide full employment or to expect many innovations in traditional forms of operation. In many respects, there has been a virtual reversal of the line of responsibility so that private business is now being expected to assume many burdens of a public nature which were hitherto excluded under the more limited doctrine of private rights.

Because financial processes constitute the most convenient and effective medium to bring about changes in the business system, they

are vitally affected by the transition which is now underway. For instance: the cheap money policy of the government has a direct effect upon the cost of capital raised by private industry; increased taxes arising from the enlarged scope of governmental activity change the complexion of the profit and loss account; and foreign markets are affected by the chaotic conditions which exist throughout the world. 

All this vast overhang of disturbance and change must necessarily be reflected in financial policies and practices. 

The Nature of Corporation Finance 

With the increasing scale and complexity of business, finance tends to be shrouded with mysticism. Many people come to believe that it is susceptible of understanding only by the financial "four hundred." 

Limited knowledge has undoubtedly characterized numerous instances of financial practices. One holding company executive stated publicly that he did not personally know all the ramifications and relationships existing within his own affiliated companies. But this does not necessarily bespeak the desirability of the condition. By and large, simplicity in finance is to be preferred to complexity, and understanding by the public is more desirable than comprehension only by the controlling boards of directors.

Basically, corporation finance serves two important functions. First, it is a means of assembling the funds necessary to initiate or to undertake a new business; and second, it involves the financing and accompanying formulation of policy so essential to the proper co-ordination of the various productive elements after the business has become a going concern. As an important corollary, financial direction is also the gateway to control; in fact, this by-product is more frequently in the spotlight than the funds themselves or the means necessary for obtaining the funds. Abuses of control do not necessarily constitute prima facie evidence for the abandonment of the present financial process, but they do call for remedial action.

Social changes cause us to emphasize that the financing process is undoubtedly an essential and permanent part of our economic life. 

This is true because it furnishes the mechanism by which the necessary co-operation is achieved to make business possible. Moreover, the need for financing exists regardless of whether economic activity is operated on a capitalistic or collectivistic basis. The mode of control or the organizational forms will change as society evolves new sys-

tems, but the basic functions to be performed will be essentially the same. A collectivist society might replace the present stockholderdirector-manager line of authority with a state owned, politically controlled, system under a military type of organization. The methods of internal control and responsibility would change, but the basic functions would remain the same. It would still be necessary to raise funds, and some one or some agency would have to determine how much financing would be required and to develop facilities for raising capital. Lastly, the problems of production and distribution would continue to plague the management, whether it be public or private. 

This Book's Point of View 

The manifold activities of corporation finance affect diverse interests and groups, and it would be feasible to study financial policies and practices from the point of view of any one. Most textbooks give primary emphasis to the corporation since it is the party of origin and because finance is viewed chiefly as a function of business management. 

In this book, the basic position of the corporation is recognized, but in addition, it is intended to give adequate consideration to the interests of the public as a whole and to the rights of investors as a portion of the public whose interests in the corporation are more intimate. 

An attempt will be made to analyze the effects of financial policies and practices on public welfare as well as on the corporation itself. 

This social emphasis constitutes an entirely practical and necessary approach; this is a day of social awakening when business policies must be considered in the light of their effect upon the public-at-large. 

While the public interest in corporation finance cannot be overemphasized, there is need to recognize the representative character of the corporate structure. At the outset, the state issues a charter on the grounds that the corporation will be beneficial to the public; at the same time, it is felt that the many individual interests should also derive reasonable personal gains. Were it not for the latter incentives, there would obviously be little occasion for private groups to assume either the responsibilities or the risks of business venture. Hence, in adopting any approach which is intended to give cognizance to the rights of the public-at-large and of investors, it is still our purpose to maintain a balance of analysis which will also give due credit to the contributions and problems of management. 

Another observation which should clarify our perspective is to

recognize that the corporation all too frequently is regarded as an inlet for funds with insufficient attention being given to their outlet. 

It is significant, however, that the real test of business and financial policy is to be found in the second phase of activity. The use made of the funds is comparatively more important than their source. The raising of capital occurs largely as a result of promise and outlook, but the justification is found only in the later achievements. Moreover, proper recognition of the rights of the investor and the public demands adequate accounting for the results of operation. Investment is more than a mere commitment of capital since it represents a long time, continuing interest. It is the duty of the corporate management to recognize this condition and to respond in fitting manner. And it is equally a necessity for the investors to keep themselves informed. 

Viewing corporate policy as it affects public welfare also is believed to be consistent with the general trend of financial activities. Since the termination of World War I, the public has continued to enlarge its place in the corporate household. Growth was encouraged naturally by the expansion of business from 1922 to 1929, and then it persisted during the following period of severe depression. Stockholding lists grew in the face of declining profits. A most unusual picture, indeed, for in the background appeared innumerable stockholders firm in the belief that greater prosperity loomed ahead, while in the foreground the masses of unemployed gave evidence of the unhealthy state of business. Such a dramatic scene testifies to the faith of the public in American enterprise.

The existence of large public interest in corporate life places a great responsibility upon the shoulders of the managers of industry. 

Years ago it was common belief that corporations often deceived and mulcted the public, and judging from the Senate investigations of 1933 and 1934, some dubious practices continue to exist.¹ There is no justification for such betrayal of trust, and sound financial policy demands the elimination of these evils. Sustained corporate growth cannot be made at the expense of the public but can occur only simultaneously with the increased welfare of the latter. Leading corporations today are giving greater recognition to this fact. Increasingly, corporate and public interests are becoming synonymous, and the 

1 See Hearings before Senate Committee on Banking and Currency on "Stock Exchange

collective investment of small investors is of such importance as to command formal recognition.

In addition to the group having a direct investment, there is an even larger number with an indirect interest in the success of corporations. Representative of the latter are the millions of people holding life insurance policies in companies whose funds are invested in varying, but substantial, amounts in American corporations. The value of these insurance policies is influenced to a marked degree by the success or failure of corporate ventures as a whole. While the available statistics on the number of direct or indirect owners of American business are not satisfactory, it is safe to say that they make up a large portion of the American public. 

Relationship between the Fields of Investment and Corporation 

Finance

Because of our point of view, it is necessary to indicate clearly the line of demarcation between corporation finance and the commonly known subject of investments. In the latter, the end or goal is to be found in the individual or institutional investor, whereas in the former it is the corporation. From the investment point of view, the corporation is simply one outstanding agency for providing investment opportunities. Government securities, real estate mortgages, and other residues of value may also be utilized as outlets for funds. 

In the study of corporation finance, the corporation occupies the center of the stage, and its manifold financial operations become the object of attention. It is possible to view this mass of phenomena strictly from the angle of corporate officials. Under these circumstances, the approach is of necessity more narrow and technical. By viewing it also from the perspective of the layman, greater emphasis may be given to the wider economic aspects of the subject. 

While it is desirable to distinguish between investments and corporation finance, it is equally essential to acknowledge the connection between the two. The former is simply the outlet for the latter, and an understanding of corporation finance is one of the cornerstones of investment operations. Successful corporate financing implies satisfactory achievement in the following two channels: (1) proper promotion and selling of securities; (2) maintenance of a sound financial position after the securities are issued. The first feature is by its very nature allied with the field of investment, and it

is to this that corporate financing must cater. This is accomplished par excellence by obtaining satisfactory results in the second channel. 

New security issues may be sold more readily when the earlier offerings have been supported by adequate earnings and sound management.

Volume of Corporate Financing 

One of the most startling ways to reveal the scope of corporate financing is to present the volume of financing during the period 1926 to 1940. The data shown in Table 1 indicate the extent of corporate financing as well as its significance to the economic system. 

In 1926, which is frequently referred to as a normal year, the volume of financing amounted to more than $5,300,000,000. In 1929, security offerings had grown to the staggering total of $10,026,000,000, but by 1933, which was the bottom of the depression as measured by corporate financing, this figure had shrunk to $382,000,000.

Not only do these figures indicate the large scale of the capital financing done by corporations, but they also reflect the relationship existing between general business trends and corporate financing.

The accompanying statistics reporting the total volume of corporate financing (Table 1) and the importance of the individual unit (Table 2) should aid the reader to comprehend the scope of corporate finance in at least two ways. In the first place, the field of corporation finance as a whole may be visualized. Secondly, the importance of the individual unit in the financial process is indicated. 

It is important to bear this distinction in mind since it should assist the reader to interpret various financial policies and practices. Frequently, the act of a specific corporation is of significance as a revelation of general financial practice, rather than being restricted to the particular corporation. Again, general financial data may mean much to the individual enterprise. This is simply the old story of understanding the whole by analyzing the parts, and vice versa, comprehending the parts to better advantage by being conscious of the whole. Classification of a subject into its component parts lends greatly to its synthetic comprehension. Because of the dual significance, it is important to note the possible individual aspects as well as the scope of our subject,

New Capital and Refunding Financing 

In discussing the total financing of domestic and foreign companies, a distinction needs to be made between the two categories, refunding and new capital. The refunding classification represents securities issued to pay off outstanding obligations which have matured or are about to mature. It is essentially a means of replacing existing capital and does not add to the capital supply. In addition, the proceeds from refunding issues may be used to call and pay off existing issues prior to the maturity date when money market conditions are sufficiently favorable to permit the corporation to obtain funds at a lower rate of interest. In 1929, refunding issues amounted to $1,387,000,000, or approximately 13 per cent of the total flotations. 

Since 1932, refunding operations have continued to increase in scope because of the favorable opportunities for refinancing and because of the curtailment in the rate of economic expansion.

The second purpose of financing is to raise new capital for purposes of expansion. Practically all the individual companies cited above illustrate the need for such financing in times of prosperity.

It should be observed that the accretions to the capital account of these companies do not necessarily represent the total financing that was done. Over and above the gains reported would appear all other financing which was effected for refunding purposes. Table 3 shows the division of corporate financing according to the two main purposes.

Fields of Enterprise 

In its broadest sense, corporation finance applies not only to the industrial and trading enterprise but, in addition, includes railroad and public utility financing. Each field has distinctive operating features which affect the nature of its financing. Attention will be called to important variations which have an industry origin, but our chief purpose will be to develop general financial principles of broad applicability. Most financial dogma have a universality which cuts across business lines, and variations are more a matter of degree than a form of substantive difference. For instance, many basic principles of finance apply equally well to areas as divergent as government and private industry. Market operations do tend to segregate business in terms of industry categories, but the main basis of classification arises from characteristics of income and assets. It follows that financial activities are often classified along similar lines for purposes of convenience, but this in no way affects the universality of financial principle.

The Size of the Corporation 

Writers on corporation finance differ on the emphasis which should be given to the size of the corporation. Some favor considering only the large and prominent corporate enterprises, while others prefer to place greater emphasis on the smaller or more nearly average concerns. There is the advantage in the former approach that complete data are more readily available concerning large corporations, and their operations are far more important as measured by volume of business done, number of employees, capital investment, etc. The latter treatment has the advantage of dealing with the typical corporation as measured by number of enterprises. Moreover, the smaller enterprise is the type with which most students are likely to be associated in a management capacity.

It is our intention, in this book, to emphasize the social, or public policy, aspects of corporation finance. For this reason, our attention will be confined largely to listed corporations, which have a good range as to size, methods of financing, and fields of operations. Also, these are the corporations in which the public has the greatest interest through security holdings. By drawing examples from all sizes and types of corporate enterprise, the student will obtain a broader understanding of corporation finance as a body of principles and practices, rather than a narrow, particularized technique. 

Need for Perspective

Financial operations are an integral part of the larger economic system. The latter comprises a complex of activity, performing numerous interrelated tasks and functions. Many of the tasks are relatively minor individually but are important in the aggregate because they are feeder-jobs necessary to the satisfactory execution of larger functions. In a system composed of a myriad of separate enterprises, each working for its own end but simultaneously making a necessary contribution to the system as a whole, some force is necessary to bring about direction and co-ordination. Something must direct the flow of economic activity and promote smooth operation. Finance is the agent which produces this result. In a sense, it is the circulatory part of the economic body making possible the co-operation between the many units.

To avoid possible misunderstanding of this co-operative process a distinction must be made between the functions of finance and the symbol or measure of its operation, the pecuniary unit. The latter is primarily a measuring device and is chiefly the means to the end. 

As a common denominator, money facilitates the co-ordination of business, but it remains for the financial process to furnish the motivating force and the facilities necessary for organization. 

The functional contributions of finance are difficult to isolate from the rest of our economic order. The interlocking of the various activities is such as to preclude any accurate segregation of a precise area or to establish the exact working relationships of the component parts. Hence, it is not always clear just what part is played by finance and what part should be more properly classified under some other heading. The thread of finance is so woven into the business pattern that its identity is not easily apparent. Therefore, the unravelling of

this thread must be accomplished through general description and deductive reasoning. 

Finance, an Agent of Co-operation

Economic activity is nothing more nor less than the production and distribution of goods and services. There exists a continuous process of assembly and dispersal in which numerous focal or assembly points contribute to the flow of output. These are, of course, the business enterprises so characteristic of modern civilization. The reader might well visualize a flow chart in which the products of industry or trade are carried on a huge conveyor belt from producer to consumer.

The magic of this ceaseless march of trade tends to conceal many of the factors which are responsible for the procession. Particularly, is this true of the financial element. So intangible is its quality and so intermingled with all of the other factors of production and distribution, it is not easy to appreciate the part played by finance.

Yet in reality financial operations are a constant force of liaison both between and within the units of enterprise. 

Co-operation between Business Units 

Transactions between business enterprises are seldom on a cash. basis and, for this reason, need to be financed. First of all, this is true of the familiar manufacturer-wholesaler-retailer relationship which is facilitated often by dealings of long standing. The prompt dispatch of goods and service through this channel is indicative of the undertow of finance which makes exchange possible. In everyday language, the financial arrangements are commonly referred to as "terms of credit." They almost always precede the transaction and obviously pave the way for the actual transfer of the goods. Many of these financial relationships exist because one business unit or the other is unable to provide all its own capital. In some lines of business, the manufacturer is best able to arrange for financing; in others, it may be the wholesaler. However, even if every unit could easily provide its own capital, it would still be true that many, if not most, transactions would be on a credit basis because of the convenience of deferred payment and of numerous other advantages. 

A similar pattern is found in transactions between units of business within a like classification. In the broad field of manufacturing,

. 

relationships between producers of primary and accessory products are typical. Here, as in the basic distribution process, many types of credit transactions are to be found. Some represent, in effect, the provision of necessary capital by one business unit for the benefit of another. Others are purely of the facilitating, convenience type. But, whatever the immediate purpose, financing aids in bringing about co-operation and efficient dealings between business enterprises. 

Co-operation within the Individual Unit

Less obvious is the role played by finance within the confines of any one business organization. A trip through a modern manufacturing plant leaves behind a moving picture of the magic flow of goods from crude to finished form. The enchantment of this physical process is apt to preclude adequate appreciation of the motivating forces behind the scene. Diagnosis reveals that finance is one of the more important of the latter. Not only does it make possible the original assembly of the plant, but its stimulating force continues through the production of the goods. Enormous expenditures are required for wages and other operating costs, and these are usually made in advance of actual sale of the goods. Finance furnishes the "waiting power" which makes this possible.

Relationships between labor and management usually take form through financial arrangement. Wage increases and shorter working hours do not become living realities simply because of some agreement, but they must be financed the same as any other cost. 

This is equally true of improved working conditions and numerous other aspects of labor relations. 

Co-operation between Business and the Public

Finance plays its most important role in bringing together business and the public. Granting that these two identities are mutually dependent, they prosper or suffer according to the bonds which unite them. Greater business activity means improved public welfare, and, in turn, business can advance no faster than the demands made upon it. 

Until fairly recent times, finance was thought to be primarily an agency to aid production and to facilitate distribution only as between business units. Financing the final exchange between the last processor or retailer and the consumer was not widely practiced except in a rudimentary form in the financing of homes and in the use of

the so-called charge account. The automobile industry has done much to show the power of financing as a means of accommodating the consumer. The majority of the transactions in the sale of cars at retail are now financed through specialized institutions. More recently, arrangements for consumer financing have been extended to other durable goods, and some experimentation is being made with longer-term financing of the less durable consumer goods found under general merchandise classifications. This extension of financial accommodation has given rise to many economic and social problems, but it has resulted in many benefits to debtor and creditor alike. 

Business has gained by increased sales, and consumers have been able to enjoy many conveniences not otherwise possible. 

However, in this book, the chief interest is in the field of business finance, and attention will be confined to this area. The most outstanding earmark of modern production is the large scale on which it is conducted. To make this possible, it is necessary to accumulate pools of capital so immense that public participation is imperative. 

The corporation is peculiarly fitted for this task and the numerous advantages which it offers may now be observed.

CHAPTER II THE CORPORATION 

HE most important form of business organization today is the corporation. While it is exceeded in numbers by the sole proprietorship, the corporate form is responsible for more than 80 per cent of the total production of goods, laborers employed, and wage payments made. Possessing a distinct status in the eyes of the law, the corporate organization is constantly being extended to meet new conditions. It is used not only for purposes of business but is equally applicable to various other activities. Several of the federal government's agencies have been organized in the corporate form, usually under federal charter. It is a common form of organization for municipal governments. Although the principal use of the corporation is found in the operation of business for profit, the corporate form of organization is frequently adopted to conduct non-profit enterprises.

It is no exaggeration to say that the corporation has been one of the major agencies making possible the scale of economic progress which has characterized modern times. Because of this importance, as well as the fact that an appreciation of the nature of the corporate form is essential to any study of corporation finance, its advantages should be well understood. In summarized form, the corporation offers the following benefits: (1) a rècognized legal entity; (2) limited liability to its owners; (3) continuity of existence; (4) facilitation of large-scale production.

Recognized Legal Entity 

The separate and distinct personality of the corporation is both real and vital to the conduct of business. By having a legal entity, the corporation may conduct business in its own name, hold title to property, sue and be sued, and exercise many other rights of an individual. Not only does the existence of a separate entity permit the corporation to act in its own right, but it also contributes materially to the other advantages of the corporation. Especially does it facilitate the continuity of a business enterprise and make possible the limited liability of the shareholders. 20

THE CORPORATION 

21 It is important to recognize that this intangible person with nearly full personal rights may abuse its privilege. Acts which are not entirely advantageous to employees, customers, the public-at-large, and stockholders may be committed. Of course, the corporation may be held liable for damages, but the individuals who are really responsible are usually able to escape liability. It is this relative freedom from the consequences of actions taken by the corporation which may lead to abuses of the public interest. At the present time there is a tendency to limit the freedom of officers and to make them jointly responsible as individuals along with the corporation which they direct. 

One means of increasing the responsibilty of officers is found in a bill introduced in Congress by Senator O'Mahoney in 1937. The bill would make officers liable for a fine equal to twice the compensation received by them during the period of violation, plus a possible additional penalty of removal from office for a period of ninety days to life. In the past, any fines levied on a corporation for illegal acts have been paid out of the corporate treasury at the expense of the stockholders. Proper emphasis upon managerial responsibilty is undoubtedly warranted as a means of protecting those whose interests are at stake, but there is need that it be reasonable in character. Otherwise, penalties may become an undesirable restraint on business enterprise.

Limited Liability 

The corporation provides limited liability for its shareholders, although this is not inherent in the form of organization. Instead, the protection is conferred by specific statute. The statutes creating corporations could require unlimited liability or such other liability as may appear to be expedient. An illustration of the former is found in the earlier California corporation laws, which provided that the shareholders would be liable for their proportionate share of unpaid debts. Over a long period the shareholders of banks were quite generally held liable in an amount equal to twice the par value of their stock. Recently, the federal laws have been amended so that the stock of national banks is limited in liability to its par value. Some states have made similar amendments to the laws applicable to state chartered banks although others still retain the double liability feature. 

The total liability of the shareholder in a business corporation is usually restricted to the par value or initial purchase price of the

stock, but it should be noted that the corporation itself has unlimited liability. To make this clear, the following balance sheet may be. assumed: 

Assets 

$50,000,000 $50,000,000

Current liabilities 

Bonds outstanding

Capital stock Surplus 

. $10,000,000 10,000,000 10,000,000 20,000,000 $50,000,000 

In the event of failure, the liability of the corporation is not restricted to its capital stock of $10,000,000. As far as the corporation proper is concerned, there is no expressed limit of liability, and the creditors would have prior claim against the entire $50,000,000 of assets. Limitation of liability applies only to the shareholders of the corporation. 

In the foregoing illustration, their liability of $10,000,000 is discharged by the investment (assuming the stock to be fully paid), and they would not be liable for any assessments.

The limitation of liability is obviously a privilege which is intended to encourage the promotion of business enterprise and to aid the attraction of private investment in the form of venture capital. At the same time, special privilege may be justified only on the basis of its ultimate effects on the public welfare. Granting that shyster promoters may have taken advantage of this attribute of the corporation to escape personal liability, nevertheless it is believed that the larger benefits to the public greatly outweigh the abuses which have occurred by reason of restricted liability. Among the advantages to the public interest, the following may be cited. 

1. New enterprise is encouraged because of the greater freedom from risk, and the resulting expansion of business is expected to be of benefit to society. 

2. Limited liability encourages the use of ownership capital instead of borrowed funds. By enlarging the former, many of the hazards of debt may be avoided and thus contribute to the stability of our economic order. 

3. Protection may be afforded the many instead of the few be cause creditor participation is usually less than the amount of ownership capital. Also, the former usually has less public distribution than the latter.

THE CORPORATION 

23 

Continuity of Existence 

Continuity of existence is made possible by the privilege of the stockholder to transfer his shares. Transfer may be effected at the discretion of the shareholders alone without the advice of either the corporation or its officers. The corporation or its agent simply makes out a new certificate in the name of the new owner and cancels the old stock. The continuity of the corporation is made obvious by its contrast to the uncertain life of the partnership. In the event of the death of one of the partners, the organization is automatically dissolved. On the contrary, it is possible for all the stockholders of a corporation to die, and the corporation still retains its existence and identity.

The continuity of existence of a corporation may be limited by the laws of the state from which it obtained its charter. In the early period of corporate development, each corporation obtained its charter by special legislative enactment, and the charter usually provided for perpetual existence. Later, when the practice of special enactment became burdensome, the various states provided a standardized procedure for the granting of charters, but to retain a semblance of control, the laws frequently stipulated a definite period of years for the duration of the charter. However, upon expiration of the term, there is usually a renewal of the charter if its provisions are in accord with the laws existing at the time. This gives the state added control over the corporation by making it possible to require amendments to the charter at periodic intervals.

Facilitating Large-Scale Production 

The corporate form of organization greatly facilitates large-scale production because of its ability to obtain the large aggregation of capital necessary to conduct large-scale operations, and because it aids the establishment of an efficient management program. Management may be both subdivided and delegated to a great degree. In a partnership, assignment or allocation of authority is made difficult by the powers and rights which attach to the individual partners. Each partner is able to bind the partnership to the limit of its resources. and may encroach further upon the resources of the partners as individuals. In the case of corporations, the manager and officers have only the status of agents. Again, the board of directors is likely to be

more diversified and representative than the corresponding group of most other forms of organization. Corporations are also generally larger and, hence, able to obtain the best management talent available. 

The corporation is unexcelled as a medium for raising large amounts of capital. Both the limited liability feature and an efficient technique for acquiring capital through the issuance of stocks and bonds in varying-sized units serve to attract funds. This should be increasingly evident as the life and characteristics of a corporation are more completely explained. 

The Interrelationship between Finance and Organization 

The form of organization affects in pronounced manner the financing of business enterprise, particularly the important elements of risk, income, and control. In the.financing of all types of organization, these incidents of ownership are present in varying degrees. 

Any form of organization that affords greater flexibility of these elements of ownership facilitates the financial process. For example, if a form of organization permits the modification or lessening of the risk element to the investor, it is evident that capital may be more quickly attracted. Similarly, the ease with which control may be concentrated, or at least made more effective, should increase the efficiency of operations. This feature may be abused, but when employed legitimately, "controlled" control offers many benefits to both management and investor. Finally, the division and assignment of income on the basis of stipulated preference is a direct outgrowth of the form of organization and may be used to advantage in the attraction of capital funds.

The Corporation as a Medium of Financing 

Those qualities of the corporation which facilitate the financing of business may now be set forth more specifically. First of all, a wide variety of classes of investors, such as the ultra-conservative, the conservative, and the so-called speculative investor may be reached. 

This diversified appeal is possible because of the many classes of securities which a corporation may issue and sell. Bonds which are protected by specific pledge of assets and with sufficient coverage of interest requirements may be sold to meet the needs of high-grade investment. Again, bonds may be issued where the margin of principal protection is slightly less or specific pledge may be lacking, but

THE CORPORATION 

25 where interest requirements are comfortably earned. Such securities usually carry a higher yield and should appeal to those investors who are willing to accept a smaller degree of safety for the slightly greater return. Many of the debentures or unsecured bonds are in this classification. Upon occasions, the corporation may issue short-term notes to provide for temporary working capital needs, or to provide temporary financing until such time as it may be possible to borrow on a longterm basis at a lower rate of interest. 

The second general classification, stocks, represents the ownership element in the corporation. The purchaser of stocks makes what is intended to be a permanent investment in a business, and from which he may withdraw only through the sale of his stock to some other person. Stocks are of two general types: preferred and common. 

Preferred stock may be issued by a corporation to those investors who are willing to accept some of the risks of ownership in exchange for a more stable and definite return on their investment. Their stock is preferred in the sense that it is the first to receive earnings remaining after interest payments and the first to receive a return of any assets remaining after the satisfaction of creditor claims in the event of liquidation. Preferred stock enables the corporation to avoid the liability of fixed charges and, at the same time, raise capital to advantage.

Common stock, on the other hand, is issued by all corporations. 

Not only is common stock required by law and is necessary to the existence of the corporation, but it is now recognized for its possibilities as a sound investment. Securities of this type offer the best and possibly the only means of sharing in the appreciation of values growing out of the secular trend, as well as in any improvement in the earnings arising out of changing price levels or expanding volume of business. Because of these qualities, investors frequently buy common stocks to balance their portfolios and to secure a hedge against inflation.

It can be seen that the corporation is able not only to cater to a large variety of investment tastes, but its form permits the distribution of the incidents of ownership to meet the quantitative requirements of the many types existing within any class of investors. Because of the divisibility of the securities, the corporation can accommodate the needs of the small as well as the large investors. Stocks may be sold in lots of 10 shares, 100 shares, one share, or any number

of shares. Stocks may be quoted on the stock exchange at less than one dollar a share or at several hundred dollars per share. In either case, the investor has the opportunity to buy any number of shares, be it one or a thousand. Bonds are not as universally within reach of small investors, but they are sold in a number of denominations, in some cases as low as $20 per bond, and are usually available in any quantity.

Great Adaptability of the Corporate Form The powers of corporations are so wide and the structure so flexible that they may be adjusted to meet many diversified conditions. 

To illustrate the extremes to which the corporate form may be used, the closed corporation and the consolidation may be noted briefly. 

The former is a family affair, which usually adopts the corporate form in order to achieve a separation of business from personal affairs, or to facilitate the adminstration of the business. An example of the family corporation is the Ford Motor Company, which has assets of nearly three quarters of a billion dollars. All the stock is owned by members of the Ford family. By means of the corporate device, the members of the family may own property outside of the corporation, free from the risks involved in the manufacturing business.

In great contrast to the Ford Company, the same fundamental form of organization is employed to achieve the consolidation of en terprises. An example is the General Motors Corporation. A num ber of competing automobile companies have been brought into one concern to acquire the advantages of centralized financing, engineering, and management, as well as to obtain many accessories and other supplies from wholly owned or controlled subsidiaries. In this case, however, a rather large degree of rivalry has been maintained among the different units of production. Control The flexibility of the corporate form and its marked ability to raise large sums of capital endow the corporation with great power. 

Viewed in the aggregate, corporations occupy the greater part of our business economy, and there are numerous individual companies which operate on a nation-wide scale. Control of this vast business domain resides largely in the financial process and makes financial 3

THE CORPORATION 

27 operations a strategic factor in the direction of business activity. Because of this broad importance, the questions of who shall control the financial process and to what end have great significance as matters of public welfare. Just as a railroad system may prove to be a bottleneck limiting the geographical development of businesses dependent upon transportation, so it is that financial direction may become the crucial and deciding element in the operation of business generally. 

For this reason, it is necessary to analyze with care the character and nature of financial control and influence. 

Financial moves are often made for tactical advantage as a form of competitive strategy, or for personal gain, rather than for the sole purpose of promoting the larger interests of business enterprise. Such manipulative practices make the headlines because they are dramatic, but they are frequently misleading. There is a tendency to regard extreme concentrations of control as an example of smart management, especially when this control may be obtained with relatively small amounts of capital. It is a fascinating game, but it is beside the point as to the more basic economic purpose of financing which, as has been said, is to facilitate business operation. 

Aside from the personal or manipulative character of certain operations, financial policy, in the past, was for the most part developed strictly on a business basis. Policy was made more nearly from a purely commercial point of view. The basic test was the effect upon the profit-and-loss statement. If the net profit would be increased, the policy was regarded as desirable, otherwise not. Modern management is qualifying the strictly commercial viewpoint. To an increasing degree, management policy is tested in terms of other criteria in addition to the profit factor. As one prominent business leader has said, "No longer can industry plow a single furrow toward a strictly commercial objective; instead it must manage its affairs with due regard to the whole field of human relations."1 

This broader attitude on management problems has not been uniformly adopted because the guiding force of the corporation is its board of directors, which is made up of natural persons. For this reason, the corporation is subject to all the limitations of human nature. It may come under the domination of a single personality. Brilliant moves and bad mistakes are equally possible. Some corporations 

¹ Address by Edward R. Stettinius, Jr., Chairman of the Board of the United States Steel 

Corporation, at the annual convention of the Association of Life Insurance Presidents, 1939.

may drive forward and achieve tremendous success, while others disappear because of errors in judgment. Of course, there are other major influences and factors affecting corporations in addition to the limitations of human nature. The corporation must face the often serious effects of strictly external forces such as price changes, the business cycle, and the normal risks of competitive practices. In addition, there are the more serious and unpredictable forces such as war and the acts of governments. 

Business Mortality 

Giving consideration to the influences just described, it is not surprising to note that between 1930 and 1935 one out of every five new business enterprises failed each year.2 While conditions during that time were abnormal, they reveal the striking consequences of the dangers inherent in business activity. The causes of these failures are too numerous and complex to discuss at length at this point. Various errors in financial plans were important, but perhaps the extreme depth of the downward swing of the business cycle was the chief cause. Of course, financial weaknesses show up in business failures in good times and bad, but they appear more frequently in periods of depression. The depression serves to shake out many weak structures which might have been able to endure indefinitely if times had continued more normal. But whatever the extent and the causes of business failures, it is important to appreciate the relationship which exists between finance, the tool, and business activity, the machine. 

Balance Sheet Concept of Business 

The interdependency of finance and business may be made clear by visualizing a master balance sheet of the composite business structure. On one side would be listed all the assets classified as to liquidity. On the other side would be shown the equities or claims to those assets classified as to maturity, plus the residual equity as the balancing item. The latter, of course, is made up of the permanent or venture capital contributed by the owners of the business. In 'studying this picture of the business structure, the need for balance must be apparent. Any change in the total asset account must be balanced

29 by an equivalent change on the equity side. It needs to be emphasized that, generally speaking, no specific equity has a claim on a specific asset. Independent shifting within each classification is possible, and in a broad sense, each equity merely has a claim upon a given proportion of the asset values. Any inequality between total. assets and total equities would mean an impairment of capital, and if the condition persisted, insolvency would undoubtedly be the final result.

Since total assets must be offset by an equal amount of equities, it follows that the composition of the equities is important. Excessive short-term debt may be the cause of serious embarrassment if the amount and liquidity of the assets are not sufficient to meet the obligations. Exacting requirements for the liquidation of long-term debt may prove to be burdensome in the light of later unforeseen developments. Hence, for all practical purposes, the equities are often the ruling force in matters of management policy. The following three questions suggest the possible relations between financing (or the equity side of the balance sheet), and the operating structure which is represented by the assets. (1) Should the financial plan be set up in terms of the life expectancy of the assets? or, (2) Is it intended that the asset accounts be constantly administered to meet financial requirements? or, (3) Does the economic process compel adjustments on both sides?

It is difficult, if not impossible, to give categorical answers to these questions. Neither may the answers be determined by any empirical observations of day-to-day operations. Prevailing business practice represents an aggregation of varying policies based either upon sound, long-range planning or upon temporary and pressing financial expediency. It would be difficult to separate from this practice any conclusive answer to the questions or to earmark the exact part played by finance in any given situation. Rather, it is necessary to study in mass the functional responsibilities of finance and their relationship to the whole economic order. As has been said, the production and distribution of goods and services are the primary purposes of business operation, and financing is secondary. Financing simply provides the co-ordinating element that brings together the necessary facilities for the production and sale of goods and services. Changes are constantly occurring in business so that it is impossible to develop any accurate classification of the relationships which exist within bus-

iness, but if the financial plan is the secondary element, then it follows that it should be designed so as to facilitate general business activity. This means that the financial plan should, whenever possible, be related to the life-expectancy of the assets rather than have the asset accounts dependent upon financial requirements. 

In an abstract sense, it would seem that financial policy should arrange the equity pattern so as to accommodate a changed distribution of the asset classifications. However, there are many practical difficulties which retard such synchronization of financial accommodation with operating or asset needs. This may be illustrated by assuming the organization of a company whose assets and equities at the outset are as follows:

31 of some adjustment, the life of the business will be allowed to function in a normal way. However, serious difficulties may develop if too great a degree of rigidity is present in the equity account. 

Again referring to the new balance sheet, the extreme possibility that the "definite promises to pay" had a maturity of one year may be assumed. While the current assets total more than the promises to pay, any delay in the regular conversion of current assets represented in the form of accounts receivable and inventories into cash might result in forced liquidation or reorganization with their attendant sacrifice of values. Any refusal of the creditors to renew the obligation would force the company to liquidate its assets or to make arrangements for financing elsewhere. The latter alternative might be difficult and would be subject to all the variations brought on by money market and general business conditions. Tight money conditions might be the cause of upsetting an operating condition which would have proved entirely sound had the company obtained a greater period for development, or had it been able to refinance on satisfactory terms. For example, events since 1929 have put many corporations in a difficult position in meeting maturing obligations or in arranging new financing. As a result, a greater emphasis has been placed upon liquidity and flexibility, and many corporations now carry cash accounts much larger than are necessary to meet the requirements of normal business.

Relationship of Operating and Financial Elements 

The foregoing review serves to emphasize the vital relationship between the asset or operating area and the equity or financial area of the corporation. In turn, it points to the virtual impossibility of attaining the ideal wherein technical operation may be regarded as primary and controlling. On the contrary, the important element of control is usually found within the secondary process of finance. 

This accounts for the fact that much of the life-history of business is found in the evolution of the financial program. The relatively rigid composition of the financial structure may be the cause of much irritation and may unduly limit the physical operations. Under such circumstances, the plan of financing can easily become a burden rather than a tool.

The well-known railroad problem is an outstanding illustration of many of these points. Undoubtedly the appearance of new sources of

competition and the presence of a long period of depression served to lessen the amount of business done by the railroads. At the same time, the problem is made acute by the burdensome nature of the railroad financial structure. Fixed charges are inordinately high in relation to operating income, and maturities are largely the result of opportune financing undertaken in accordance with prevailing money market styles and with too little regard for future needs. As a consequence, there is little harmony between financial obligations and the supporting operating structure. To à considerable degree these conditions have developed because of the easy assumption that transportation is a public utility for which there is a permanent need. 

This attitude overlooks the ups and downs which must characterize the progress of any country and of any line of business. While transportation may be a service which is indispensable, this does not necessarily apply to any particular means of transportation. 

Fixed Charges 

Attention must also be directed to the pressure of other recurring fixed charges which accompany the regular operations of a business. 

Increasingly their control is getting beyond management influence. 

Examples of uncontrolled overhead and operating expenses are taxes and wages. Taxes are constantly increasing in amount and have priority over private claims. Wages are another important item in costs which are not fully controllable. Total wages are still subject to the control of management, but wage rates are not. Management is able to dictate within limits how many hours of work will be used, but it is not able to say in many industries how much shall be paid for each hour of work.3 This rigidity of wage rates is important in any study of financing and the management process. One cannot escape the observation that the area of fixed charges is increasing with equivalent contraction of the area within which management control can be exercised freely. Formerly, fixed charges were thought of chiefly in terms of interest on bonded indebtedness which was voluntary at the time of its inception; today a constantly increasing por- 

3 The Wages and Hours Act has restricted management's power by placing a floor under wages and a ceiling over hours in industries operating in interstate commerce. The wage limitation is below the prevailing wage rate in the bulk of American industry, and the hour limitation is on a weekly basis. Unionization of labor probably constitutes a greater brake upon management discretion than the law.

THE CORPORATION 

33 tion of business expenses is becoming fixed, involuntary, and continuous.

The reasons for the increasing importance of fixed charges are fairly obvious. Labor costs tend to be higher and less flexible through the development of collective bargaining which is an outgrowth of the increasing unionization of labor. To this should be added the increased social responsibilities now being assumed by management. 

Present-day financial policies of governments-federal, state, and local -call for more revenue, hence more taxes and higher fixed costs to business. Lastly, in an effort to avoid some of the higher labor costs imposed under unionization, managements have resorted to a greater use of labor-saving equipment, thus reducing the labor charge but increasing the financial and depreciation charges which accompany mechanization.

The Financial Plan 

As a means of meeting the new problems presented by large amounts of fixed charges, many believe the financing of the future must include more ownership capital, or what is sometimes termed "venture" capital. The simplicity of this plan is attractive but its practicality is uncertain. Ownership capital as represented by stock means the substitution of optional dividend charges for the fixed charges represented by interest on bonds. The change would, of course, have nothing to do with the other forms of fixed charges such as taxes and wages. Moreover, it is doubtful if optional dividend charges can furnish much in the way of permanent corrective relief. 

In the long run, return on the investment must be satisfactory, be it optional or otherwise, if new capital is to be attracted when needed. 

Financial convenience is not the same as economic justification; the former can effect temporary relief, but it is not sufficient to make the industry self-supporting. This again reflects the primary character of the business process as distinct from the secondary nature of the financial factor. Moreover, there is always the tendency for expediency to work at cross-purposes with basic economic objectives. This is especially true in the financial area where the appeal of the security issues in the market is often given more emphasis than how they may fit into the plan of the business. As a result, bonds with maturities entirely unrelated to the asset structure may be issued instead of stock which would impose less rigid demands upon management.

The ultimate outcome of pursuing a policy of expediency in financing may be to place certain portions of the financial structure of a corporation in a strategic position in times of distress. Investors naturally seek to preserve their own investment, and the favored security holders may be expected to resist any major adjustment or overhauling of the financial structure no matter how great the need to successful future operations. In many instances, this causes financial error to be pyramided on top of financial error only to make an unsatisfactory situation still worse. Operating management is then loaded with an overhead not justified in light of the earning power of the particular enterprise.

The source of capital, because of its strategic position, exercises tremendous influence upon the success of an enterprise, but it is only a part of the larger criterion of sound business operations. In the last analysis, this is determined by the self-supporting or self-sustaining character of any individual enterprise. The real question is whether its output is sufficient to replace or retire the investment as well as to cover the attendant current demands incident to operation. The latter consist of the usual operating expenses plus a fair return to those providing the capital. The financial plan must recognize and facilitate these more ultimate and controlling demands of business. Flexibility must be maintained at all times, and the need for financial readjustments must be faced realistically.

The financing of a new business is also affected by the prevailing financial styles and the accumulated financing pattern. The financial practices of the immediate past are reflected in this pattern, and it is difficult for a new concern to go too much against the grain no matter how sound its basic approach may be. The new concern is somewhat in the position of the mansion built in the slums. A single structure can do little or nothing to offset the accumulated deficiencies of the surroundings. Similarly, the new enterprise is affected by financial environment and it is not free to choose its own financial course. Its demand for capital must from necessity cater to the mode of the financial market; otherwise, it is compelled to pursue a costly course of justification for its own individuality. 

This reconciliation of the business process with financial patterns is to a great extent taken as a matter of course. In practice, it is assumed; only in the background of principle is it possible to take into account the deeper question of organic relationship. It is easy to prove

THE CORPORATION 

35 in the realm of logic the principle that business is primary and that finance is secondary, but this does not assure its application in dayto-day practice. By analogy, it may be noted that economists have long proved the merit of free trade, but the various forces of expediency have brought about wide adoption of the protective tariff system. 

Equally so, finance and business relationships are subject to the appeal of present gain as against a sounder, long-term policy offering the chance of profit only in the future.

Much the same forces bear upon the government in its financing. 

In a dictatorship, government would be free to follow what it deemed to be the wise course, although errors in judgment would still be entirely possible. But in a democracy where the state is presumably on a par with competing business enterprise, it is forced to fit into the business pattern as determined by market conditions.4 Thus, it is not uncommon for government to take advantage of the lower rate of interest in short-term financing even though the funds may be needed for long-term purposes. It is possible that the money market may not be acceptable to long-term financing, but, irrespective of the particular cause, the significant fact is that government, like private enterprise, will yield to prevailing market demand.

The dominating influence of the market raises the pointed query as to what can be done about it. Long-term planning of financing, for instance, may be an interesting item for the agendum, but unless it is accepted by the market, it is void of meaning. Actually, the answer is likely one of compromise. A balancing of short-term gains must be made against the longer-term implication of any given program. 

The advantage to the particular enterprise as against the effects on the larger, social order must be appraised. These alternatives only accentuate the responsibilities of management. As related earlier, it means that business management must "manage its affairs with due regard to the whole field of human relations." This is difficult because management is human, and human beings think too often in terms of the short run.

Summary of Problems 

In order that the reader may have the proper perspective, the main 4 In times of emergency, the government may determine that greater control is necessary to accomplish various objectives. Even here, it usually works through established market media instead of resorting to outright dictation.

problems which will be analyzed in the succeeding sections of this book are summarized. 

1. The instruments of corporation finance.-Securities furnish the primary basis of all corporate financing. Because of their importance, careful analysis will be made of the various types of securities, as well as their relationship to the whole financial structure. 

2. Promotion and organizing the corporation.-The initiation of a new enterprise involves an analysis of the motives behind the organization of a corporation and some of the factors which must be considered by the incorporators. 

3. Security distribution.-Having decided upon the basic plan for the organization of the corporation, it is necessary to determine the sources of capital funds and how to tap these sources. The most common way is through the sale of securities to the general public, represented by individual or institutional investors. 

4. Administration of income.-In order to appreciate the problems of management, it is necessary to study such internal problems as the flow of income, its use and distribution. 

5. Expansion. It is the normal expectancy for corporations to grow and to enlarge their operations under one control. The methods by which expansion is accomplished and some of the resulting problems are discussed in this section. 

6. Failure and reorganization.-Unfortunately, corporations often get into difficulties and require reorganization to avoid failure or to rebuild after failure. The problems involved here are important because of their effect upon society as a whole and the losses which are suffered by investors. 

7. Regulation and control.-Lastly, the problems of regulation and social control arising out of corporation finance and its relationship to the economic system will be discussed wherever immediately pertinent, as well as in a separate section dealing with regulation. 

The student may now turn to the specific analysis of the instruments of finance. Not only should the reader seek to understand their nature, but in addition, they should be fitted into the larger picture which has been outlined in this chapter. Do they facilitate the business process? 

What are the possible repercussions of their use upon the social order?

PART II INSTRUMENTS OF CORPORATION FINANCE

CHAPTER III 

HE ownership of a corporation may be represented by many types of stock which range from the certificate of residual ownership, known as common stock, to securities with various privileges and preferences, usually termed preferred stock. Both for legal and economic reasons, a corporation organized for profit cannot exist without common stock.¹ It is the first stock to be issued by a corporation and the last to be retired in the event of liquidation. The extremes of success or failure are the lot of common stock. In the case of unusual profits, it may be the beneficiary of extra or increased dividends, and in the event of failure, it will be the last to receive any return of capital. In other words, the common stock represents both the primary and residual equity underlying the corporation. 

The position of common stock may be illustrated by presenting in summary form a recent balance sheet of the General Motors Corporation:

The position of the common stock is far from desirable in the case of failure. Forced liquidation brings about marked shrinkage in book values, and the common stock may receive little or nothing. An experience of this type may be noted in the failure and reorganization of the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway Company. As a result of the reorganization plan completed in March, 1927, assessments were levied upon the common stock at the time of its exchange for new shares.³ Stockholders owning 150,000 shares of common stock failed to make the exchange, thereby losing their entire original investment. This sacrifice gives mute testimony of the position of the common stockholders in time of failure, and chills the more optimistic atmosphere which is found in time of prosperity. Obviously, the bright side of the picture predominates at times, while on other occasions a more gloomy scene is in evidence. This was well illustrated in the booming 1920's. In the peak year 1929, over $5,112,000,000 of new capital was raised through the sale of common stock, and, in addition, the volume of trading in common stock on the New York Stock Exchange exceeded all prior records. The story was not long in changing, and, beginning in 1930, the less colorful aspects of the residual position came to the fore. By 1932, sales of new common stock had shrunk to an insignificant $13,000,000. Total sales of common stock in the nine years, 1930 to 1938, amounted to less than half as much as was sold in the year 1929 alone. Clearly, when business profits decline, common stocks lose much of their attractiveness. 

Moreover, there is reason to believe that people tend to overemphasize the desirability of common stock in good times and to underrate its value as an investment in poor times.

In fairness to private management, it should be pointed out that the inopportunistic response on the part of the public creates several problems of policy. If management is to give first consideration to the long-term soundness of operation, it may often be necessary to act contrary to popular trends. At the same time, the adoption of such conservative policy may easily be misunderstood by the rank and file of stockholders who would naturally favor making hay while the sun shines. Advantageous hindsight now makes it clear that the unwise and rapid expansion of the late twenties was eventually the cause of much financial embarrassment and difficulty; at the time, however, the virtue of restricted operation was not so apparent. Under the circumstances, it is easy to call attention to the public responsibilities of private management, but the application of such policy is by no means simple and may easily lead to unfortunate misunderstanding. 

The reader is urged, therefore, to view the problems of corporation finance in broad perspective and make due allowance for the difficulties of private operation when passing judgment upon unfavorable developments. 

Further Evidence of the Variability of the Residual Position 

It has been observed that the position of the residual equity is extremely variable. This aspect is strikingly shown in the price quotations of common stocks on the Stock Exchange, which are influenced greatly by waves of overoptimism or extreme pessimism. For example, in 1929, the investing public believed General Motors stock to be worth as much as 913, but in 1932 the same stock was quoted as low as 7.
