Issuance of Common Stock by the Corporation 

When stock is sold either by the corporation or by transfer in trading, certificates are issued as evidence of the ownership rights.

These certificates indicate that the holder is the owner of a certain portion of the corporate net worth. Actually, the certificate is stated in terms of shares, the share being the unit of measurement and the certificate simply stating the right to the number of shares purchased. 

The relationship may be illustrated by reference to our monetary system. A ten dollar bill is the equivalent of ten one dollar units, but for the sake of convenience, the right is expressed on one piece of paper. In the same way, a stock certificate for fifty shares of stock permits the combining of various shares into one larger unit. 

The Meaning of Par Value 

Prior to 1912, all stock certificates carried a nominal value per share, $100 being commonly used. If a corporation were capitalized at $50,000, it probably meant that 500 shares of stock at $100 par were available for distribution. Moreover, in many states, the corpora- tion or its officers were not permitted to sell the stock for less than the par figure, i.e., they could not sell it at a discount. Where such was the 

The company still exists as a general manufacturing enterprise.

COMMON STOCK 

45 case, there was a tendency for the par value to be the equivalent of the actual worth of the stock at the time of beginning corporate activity, unless of course, the stock sold at a premium. 

This potential agreement of par value with exchange value would naturally endure only momentarily. Business is dynamic in character, and values are changing constantly in response to the gains and losses accruing to the business enterprise. Large and increasing profits tend to increase the value of common stock, and vice versa, operating losses and other shrinkage of values produce an unfavorable effect. Since par value is a constant figure, it must necessarily fail to register or reflect changing conditions.

Changed Values as Portrayed by the Books 

In order to reflect the changes accruing to the investment in a business enterprise, accounts are kept and the ultimate net gain or loss recorded. To be specific, let us again consider the foregoing assumed corporation which was capitalized at $50,000. If, at the end of the first year, $5,000 net profit has accrued, it is logical to assume that the individual shares would have a value of $50,000 plus $5,000 divided by the number of shares issued (500), or a unit value of $110. 

Stated generally, the book value of a share of stock may be calculated by the following formula: Assets less liabilities (and other claims preceding the common stock) divided by the number of shares outstanding equals the book value per share.

Since book value is based upon actual transactions as reflected in the accounting records, one may be inclined to believe that it represents the final and most realistic basis of valuation. On the contrary, rarely, if ever, do book values agree with market values, i.e., the price of each share of stock as quoted in the market is seldom in accord with the book figure.

The Meaning of Market Value 

In the same manner that an individual may have purchased a house with an actual outlay of cash for $15,000 and later finds that his property is worth only $10,000, the market may not accept the value of the corporation as expressed in its books. For the successful corporation the market value of its stock is often in excess of the book figure. Books of account fail to record either possible or actual appreciation of values, although the market is dealing constantly in

terms of the future outlook. For the unsuccessful corporation, the market price of its stock is apt to be less than the book value because of the failure of past operations to support or justify the investment. 

Concrete examples may more quickly illustrate the principles involved. In November, 1933, the book value of a share of common stock of the International Mercantile Marine Company amounted to $42, while its market value at that time was $3. At the same time, the General Motors Corporation had a book value per share of $15, and a market value of $28, and as of December, 1940, the book value had increased to $21 and the market value to approximately $50. 

Furthermore, a corporation may have a market value in excess of book value at a given time, only to have the condition reversed at another date. This may be caused by changes within the corporation itself, or by external conditions such as general business trends. The 

Jordan Motor Car Company whose sales decreased without exception from 1925 to 1929 inclusive is an outstanding example of internal decay. The decline from 1927 to 1928 was particularly prominent since that period was an unusually prosperous one for the automobile industry. Naturally, the market value of the stock fell along with the declining position of the company. 

The period from 1930 to 1932 illustrates the disturbing influence of adverse business trends. Few industries escaped the devastating effects of the business depression, and all automobile companies without exception reported declining sales. Stock prices tumbled in wild confusion and caused a marked change in the ratio of book to market value. During the late twenties, stock prices had increased with little regard to the book investment, causing market values to be greatly in excess of book figures. This was followed by a complete reversal with irrational trading and dumping of securities in reckless abandon. 

The action of the common stock of the General Motors Corporation is typical of many others. In 1929, the stock reached a high of 913 which compared with a book value of $17.58; in 1932, the market quotation dropped to a low of 71, while the book value was $14.27.

These pronounced variations emphasize the unreliability of any figure as an absolute measure of value and suggest the following general observations. 

1. Par value is a nominal figure and does not reflect the amount which a stockholder may actually realize either in the event of sale or in the case of liquidation of the company.

COMMON STOCK 

47 2. Book value registers the effects of transactions on a cost basis, but it cannot be accepted as a yardstick of true worth. 

3. Market value is the most reliable yardstick of the amount which a stockholder may realize upon his investment, but distinction should be made between short- and long-term movements. 

Liability Aspect of Par Value 

Although par value has little meaning for purposes of valuation, its interpretation is more precise when applied to calculate the liability of stockholders. To illustrate, if stock having a par value of $100 were purchased from the corporation for $65, the stockholder would be liable for a possible $35 assessment, either in the event of failure or if the corporation decided to expand and had need of extra funds. 

Since this liability is a feature of the stock issue, it is assumed by the new buyer in the event of later sale. Thus, if A had bought the stock from the corporation at $65 and later sold it to B for $110, B would assume the liability to the corporation for $35. 

This contingency of assessment becomes a serious deterrent to the use of common stock for raising capital where conditions prevent the sale of stock at par. Investors would naturally avoid the purchase of securities which carried a prospective liability. It is not surprising, therefore, that ways were found to circumvent the contingent liability arising from the sale of stocks at a discount. The first method to be developed was the donated stock device. 

Under this plan, the initial sale of stock is made to an individual friendly to the corporation or to an individual already having a large interest in the company. The stock may be paid for in cash, but services or other forms of property are the more likely means for payment because of greater leeway in their valuation. A piece of property worth $10,000 may be sold to the company for $25,000 in stock, with the understanding that the purchaser will donate $15,000 of this stock back to the company. Since the donated stock would be deemed to be paid in full, it would be legally non-assessable and could be sold to the public at any price which the company is able to obtain in keeping with market conditions. The use of this subterfuge entails the risk of stockholders' suits charging fraud or mismanagement and is a clumsy procedure in raising large amounts of capital.

A more satisfactory procedure for the avoidance of contingent

liability was found in the use of stock without par value, i.e., without any nominal value on its face. This type of stock first became available with the enactment of a New York statute in 1912, and today it is permitted in nearly every state. The use of no-par stock grew rapidly, and by 1929, 42 per cent of the stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange were of this type. Only a small portion of the stocks in the country are listed so it is possible that as many as twothirds of all stocks are no-par. Currently, there is a tendency to use low-par stocks, but until recent years, the majority of new stock issues were of no-par variety. 

Considerable controversy arose as to the propriety of the no-par feature, with reformers taking the position that it should be made illegal. Proponents stressed the following advantages of no-par stock. 

1. Avoidance of contingent liability.-No-par stock may be sold at any price, and the liability does not extend beyond this initial figure. 

However, some states set a minimum price below which no-par stock may not be sold. 

2. Increased marketability of stock issues.-Not only is the potential liability of further assessment avoided, but the corporation is enabled to sell the stock at any price. There is complete freedom to fix a price which harmonizes with conditions prevailing in the market, rather than being limited by an arbitrary and rigid par established by a statute of many years' standing. If there is a great demand for stock selling in the $60 bracket, such stock may be issued, or if stocks at a lower figure are more popular, then the price may be set to attract this demand. In general, no-par stock permits flexibility in the setting of price and gives relief from the more static requirements existing under laws requiring par stock. 

3. Avoidance of nominal value.-The use of no-par avoids any possible fiction of value resulting from the use of par. Investors frequently err in accepting par as a norm or yardstick of the worth of stocks. Actually, investment value is completely unrelated to the par figure which is purely nominal in character. 

4. Accounting for capital stock.-The no-par feature also permits greater flexibility in the treatment of the capital account. The net worth may be presented in the aggregate or may be apportioned between stock and surplus to reflect managerial policy. Similarly, • President of the New York Stock Exchange, Report (May 1, 1929), p. 85.

COMMON STOCK 

49 there is greater ease in adjusting the capital structure to recognize marked changes in the value of the assets. The laws of many states specify a minimum stated value for no-par stock. In most cases the minimum requirements are nominal in character and do not represent any important restriction on accounting policy. 

On the other hand, the advocates of par stock point out the following disadvantages of no-par stock to the interest of public welfare. 

1. Effect on credit.-The reduction of the liability of the stock holders is said to weaken the credit rating of the corporation because of the more limited protection to creditors. However, credit is usually granted on a going basis instead of expectancy of liquidation, and few par stocks carry any assessable liability. 

2. Aid to unscrupulous promotion.-The claim is made that nopar stock aids the unscrupulous promoter in selling securities because of the lessened liability, as well as in facilitating the transfer of stock for his services and other intangible items. On the other hand, nopar value is an invitation to the prospective investor to study the facts of the case, whereas par value often leads him to accept the value stated on the face of the certificate. 

3. Manipulation of accounts.-First, the absence of a standard of value (par) makes it easy to transfer no-par stock for promoters' services, because of the flexibility in setting up (evaluating) the capital account. Second, after operations are started, the surplus account may also be adjusted to conceal unfavorable conditions or to meet particularized motives of management. 

In general, the gist of the arguments against no-par value stock is the granting of excessive and dangerous flexibility to the promoter and financier. Abuse of investor and public interest is obviously possible, but the use of par value offers little in the way of substantive protection. Rather, fact-finding investigations and effective legal restraint are more essential to curb ill practices of promoters. Moreover, low par is just as convenient as no-par as a means of adjusting the capital structure. The recent tendency to change stock from a nopar to a par basis illustrates the impotency of a nominal value to curb undesirable adjustment of the capital structure. Indeed, this reversal of the previous trend is encouraged by the higher taxes which apply to the transfer of no-par stock, as well as by the convenience the change affords to adjust the stated value of the stock.

Stock Terminology 

Regardless of whether the stock is par or no-par, there are certain terms used in connection with stock issues with which the reader should be familiar. Authorized stock, issued or outstanding stock, treasury stock, and donated stock are terms that are common in any discussion of capital stock. Brief definitions covering these items follow.

Authorized stock.-This is the amount of stock that the corporation is permitted to issue according to the statement of its certificate of incorporation. The authorization may be for common stock alone, or for preferred stock in addition. 

Issued stock. The amount of authorized stock should be large enough to cover present and anticipated future needs. By this means, there will be sufficient stock to finance future expansion, to pay stock dividends, and for other purposes. Otherwise, the charter would have to be amended whenever additional stock was needed. The stock which has been sold is known as issued stock while the balance is classified as unissued. 

Treasury stock-In its largest sense, treasury stock includes any stock of the issuing corporation which is held in its treasury. Such holdings may originate through purchase, by donation as previously described, or by the existence of unissued stock. Usually, the term is intended to include only the stock which has been purchased by the corporation.

Donated stock.-The use of donated stock was mentioned briefly at a previous point. In general, any capital stock which is acquired other than through purchase is included in the donated category. A donation may have been with or without intent to use it as a subterfuge to avoid liability provisions. 

Advantage of Financing with Common Stock 

The advantages and disadvantages of holding common stock by the investor were referred to at the outset of this chapter. Analysis from the corporate point of view is equally important. In many ways, common stock constitutes an ideal source of funds for the corporation. The pertinent reasons for this may be summarized as follows: 

1. Absence of fixed charges.-Common stock is admirably adapted to meet changing business conditions. If business is depressed and the 

7 See p. 47.

COMMON STOCK 

51 earnings of a corporation are lowered materially, sound financial policy may require the passing of dividends. Default of interest on bonds would precipitate failure, but the omission of dividends has no such serious consequences. As a result, stocks provide a cushion of safety against temporary unfavorable developments. 

2. Improved credit standing.-Extensive use of common stock to raise capital also improves the credit position of the corporation. Automatically the enlargement of the residual equity increases the base of credit operation.

Overland Company in 1933. 

3. More economical financing.-On occasions it is cheaper to finance with common stock than with bonds. 

For instance, in 1929, widespread speculation in the stock market and the belief in a new era caused stock prices to reach an abnormally high level. Among the many common stocks offered, the following may be cited as examples:

Jordan Motor Car Company was able to sell common stock at $12 per share, although it was paying no dividends and had suffered a declining business since 1925.

Peerless Motor Car Company sold its common stock at $8, although paying no dividends.

Continental Can Company sold common stock at $60 per share while paying annual dividends of $2.50, thus giving a yield of 4.2 per cent.

General Gas and Electric Company sold common stock at $70, paying dividends (including extras) of $2, or an actual yield of 2.9 per cent. Evidently the market at this time regarded the extras as a permanent part of the dividend rate. 

Celotex Corporation sold common stock at $65 while paying dividends of $3, or a yield of 4.6 per cent.

B. F. Goodrich Company sold its common stock at $81, which at the dividend rate of $4 then being paid allowed approximately a 5 per cent yield. Its 6 per cent bonds were originally offered at $97 and interest to yield 6.75 per cent. Apparently the future outlook was so bright that people were willing to buy common stock on a 5 per cent basis rather than bonds on a 6.75 per cent basis. 

The advantages of common stock financing are so noteworthy as to suggest its exclusive use as a source of funds. The Pullman Company is an outstanding example where this policy has been pursued. However, there are many reasons why common stock may not be used as the sole medium to raise capital. In the first place, stocks are not always acceptable. There is a large element in the investing group which will not buy stocks either because of choice or of legal restriction. Also, stocks may be acceptable to local interests and investors

COMMON STOCK 

53 but may not be salable in other sections where the management is not known. Under these circumstances, a bond possessing the proper legal protective provisions is desirable. Second, bonds usually sell at lower rates than stock issues over a long period of time. Exceptions may occur as in 1928 and 1929, but these conditions are abnormal. 

Third, the issuance of common stock has a direct bearing upon control. This is an intangible but an important determinant in the selection of new securities. Fourth, the sale of more common stock increases the base over which any future appreciation in value, or increase in earnings, must be spread.

Rights of Common Stock 

With the issuance of common stock, the corporation assumes definite responsibilities and obligations to the holders of the stock. 

At the same time, it is essential to remember that the stockholders simply own the corporation, and the title to the property is lodged in the corporate name. Because of this breach between the stockholders and their ultimate property, it is necessary to provide them with sufficient rights and powers to afford adequate protection. This is achieved mainly through the following two channels: (1) the power of stockholders to elect those in control; (2) certain other rights which are either preemptive or provided by law. 

Power of Stockholders to Elect Those in Control 

Because the stockholders have the power to elect the board of directors, it is sometimes believed that they are fully protected against mismanagement, fraud, etc. While the importance of this right not be denied, its significance is not generally realized by the great mass of stockholders. The privilege is abused and neglected in much the same manner as political suffrage, i.e., by inaction and disinterest. 

Furthermore, except on a few occasions, the stimulus arising from party competition or other forms of opposing forces is lacking. These conditions combined with remoteness of many stockholders from the scene of operations create a tendency not to regard voting seriously. 

Again, the stockholder often contends he is uninformed of the technical operations of industry and is unable to vote intelligently. In reply, it should be pointed out that he is not voting upon operations, but rather upon the selection of personnel to supervise the activities of the company. Stockholders having few shares are especially in-

clined to believe that their voice would be of little significance and to refrain from exercising their privilege.

Under these circumstances, it is comparatively easy for the active few to secure complete control of a business enterprise. In fact, concentration of control is now generally recognized to be the modus operandi, particularly for large corporations. Occasional abuses of trust are given great publicity, but, nevertheless, the student of finance and corporate policy must be conscious of that great body of business enterprises functioning so efficiently that their merit is lost in silence. 

As a protection against the exceptional abuses, the right of the stockholder to vote may be a most potent weapon.

Non-Voting Classified Stock 

To avoid inconveniences of mass voting as well as to afford a ready and economical concentration of control, many corporations have issued common stock having no voting power. The usual practice has been to issue two classes of stock, designated as Class A and Class B common. The Class B stock is usually voting and Class A, non-voting. 

This is done because of the desire to concentrate control with the "insiders" and because of the tendency on the part of investors to believe that the A grade of anything is better than the B grade. Sometimes one class of stock is given the right to elect the majority of the board of directors while the other class may obtain control under certain contingencies. For example, the National Cash Register Company had outstanding as of December 31, 1929, 1,190,000 shares of

Class A and 400,000 shares of Class B stock. The "B" stock had the right to elect a majority of the directors unless the company failed to pay the preferential quarterly dividend of seventy-five cents on the 

Class A stock for two consecutive quarters, or if earnings failed to equal the annual dividend and were not made up in a later year. 

In either of these events, the stocks assumed equal voting power (share for share) which, of course, meant that the control would pass to the Class A stockholders.

The Bankruptcy Act requires equitable distribution of voting power in the reorganized company and prohibits non-voting common stocks. As a reflection of the prevailing governmental policy, the New York Stock Exchange has instructed its Listing Committee to give consideration to the question of voting control on all new applications for listing. As a result, any extension in the use of non-voting stocks has been checked for the present at least.

Other Rights of Common Stock 

In addition to the right to vote, which has been described above, the holders of common stock possess certain other prerogatives which are of value in protecting their equity. For instance, holders of stock issues with original voting power usually must be given the first option to buy new stock issues in proportion to their holdings.12 The objective of this requirement is clear, viz., to prevent particular interests from buying new stock unfairly for the purpose of obtaining control. From another point of view, the stockholder is given an opportunity, if he so desires and has the funds, to maintain his proportionate share in the control and in the earned surplus of the company. The last point may be fairly important. Let us assume a corporation having 1,000 shares of stock and an earned surplus of $50,000, or $50 per share. The decision is made to sell another 1,000 shares of no-par stock and to capitalize it on the balance sheet at an issuing price equal to the average selling price of the original shares. After this operation is completed, each share will have a proportionate interest in the surplus of only $25. Hence, the stockholder who does not participate proportionally in the new issue will lose half of his accumulated prior earnings. 

Stockholders also have the right to inspect the books of the corporation. Opportunity is thereby provided to prevent the inside forces from concealing the facts of operation. At the same time, it is quite possible to employ this privilege for ulterior reasons. For example, a competitor may buy stock expecting to exercise this right of the 12 Stockholders voluntarily may forfeit this right, or the corporate charter may provide that stockholders are not to have the right of prior subscription.

57 stockholder to inspect the books-for all practical purposes, a form of espionage. However, if it can be shown that a stockholder desires to examine the books for unscrupulous reasons, the right will undoubtedly be denied in a court of equity. In addition to these more specific rights of protection, stockholders have such general privileges as the right to transfer stock, the right to receive dividends, the right to share in the proceeds of dissolution, etc. In other words, the stockholder possesses most of the characteristics of owners of property. 

Founders' and Management Stock 

Although founders' shares and management stock are not popular in this country, it is well to understand their occasional use. The stock is designed to facilitate the concentration of control or to favor the management with additional dividends, or both. For example, the former Armour Leather Company13 was organized by Armour and Company as a means of acquiring all of the tanning and leather properties of the latter. Another type of security issued for control purposes is the certificate of beneficial interest. This certificate represents stock deposited with the trustee of a voting trust and gives the holder a proportionate interest in the earnings and assets of the issuing corporation without voting power. The trustees hold the voting rights to the deposited stock and are, therefore, able to exercise centralized control over one or many corporations. The control is relatively permanent because the trust is ordinarily for a long period of years, and the board of trustees is a self perpetuating body. 

The Great Northern Iron Ore Properties may be cited as an example of the trust form of organization for control purposes. This trust was organized in 1906 and is to continue for twenty years after the last survivor of eighteen named persons, the youngest of whom was born in the same year, 1906. In this case, the trust is a pure holding trust since it carries on no operations directly but controls

Special Classes of Stock under Present-Day Conditions 

Since 1933, there has been a decided change in the public attitude toward business corporations. Many of the regulatory measures undertaken are intended to increase the degree of democracy in the control of business. Corporations are required to give full and complete information about each issue of stock, its obligations, its rights, and its purposes. Founders' and management stock clearly does not harmonize with this trend to enlarge the public interest. As stated earlier, this type of stock has never been popular in this country and may be expected to disappear in the future. With the increasing demand for information put upon the corporation by regulatory bodies, there is likely to follow a simplification in capital structure. 

Classified stock will be more difficult to issue and will be replaced in most cases by a single class of common.

CHAPTER IV PREFERRED STOCK 

REFERRED stock is a type of security issue which illustrates in striking fashion how the corporate structure may be molded to meet differing investment needs. Many investors seek an outlet for their funds where they may avoid the final risk, but where the return is favorable. Preferred stock is intended to appeal to this group by combining some of the characteristics of creditor obligations. with certain features of common stock. In providing this compromise, several disadvantages are created. Usually there is no opportunity to share in unusual earnings or to derive major benefits from the appreciation in the value of the original corporate investment. And, unlike bonds, preferred stock does not have any contractual guaranty of income. Because of the hybrid nature of this security, the student of finance will be interested to learn its appeal both from the viewpoint of the corporation and the investor. 

Meaning of the Term "Preferred"

Preferred stock usually possesses a right of priority over common stock as to dividends and as to principal in the event of liquidation. 

The prior claim to dividends is a recurring right which is applicable to all income periods; that is, the preferred stock is entitled to receive dividends before any may be paid to the common stock. Often neither the common nor the preferred stock may receive any dividends, but if dividends are declared at all, they must be paid first to the preferred stock. To complete its priority over common stock, the preferred usually takes precedence in the event of liquidation. Under either voluntary or involuntary liquidation of the company, the preferred stock is entitled to be paid in full from the remaining assets before any payments may be made on the common stock. 

Preferred stock ordinarily does not have the right to vote on matters of general corporate policy; but it may have voting rights under certain circumstances, and a few issues of preferred stock have full voting rights. For example, in the reorganization of the Cleveland 

Discount Company, the general creditors received preferred stock in 61

the new company with power to elect two-thirds of the board of directors. The old 7 per cent cumulative prior preferred stock of the 

Virginia-Carolina Chemical Corporation provided that, as long as there was $10,000,000 of this stock outstanding, the preferred holders would have the right to elect a majority of the directors. The former 

7 per cent preferred issue of the McKesson and Robbins Company required that the exclusive control of the company was to pass to the preferred stock at any time arrears in dividends equalled four quarterly payments, with the control to continue until the deficiency was removed. An example of full voting rights is the 7 per cent cumulative preferred stock of the United States Steel Corporation. 

Other Protective Provisions 

Since preferred stock stands in a middle area between bonds and common stock and, ordinarily, has only restricted voting power to protect its interests, additional safeguards are necessary to prevent possible abuse of its position. Protective provisions and other attractive features may be enumerated as follows: (1) cumulative dividends, (2) redeemability of the principal, (3) creation of a sinking fund to facilitate the retirement of the stock, (4) convertibility of the stock, (5) participation in exceptional earnings, (6) protection against the issuance of additional securities, (7) voting privileges under certain circumstances, (8) stated rate of dividends.

Par Value 

While approximately one-half of the states permit the issuance of preferred stock without par value, the reasons for such use are by no means clear. Wherever a fixed rate of dividends is stipulated, the simple logic is to associate the stated rate with some given amount of principal. Thus, 7 per cent preferred stock would normally be related to a par value of $100. Where the preferred stock is without par value, the dividend is necessarily stated in terms of dollars instead of percentage; for example, there may be $3 preferred stock, $7 preferred stock, etc. A stock termed $3 preferred would ordinarily be associated with $50 par value and the larger amounts with the $100 par. As is true of common stock, the chief merit in the use of no-par preferred is the flexibility permitted in the balance sheet presentation. 

In practice, preferred stocks are usually on a par basis in the

PREFERRED STOCK 

63 industrial group, entirely so in the railroad field, and about one-half of the preferred stock issued by public utilities carries a specific par.¹ 

Approximately one-third of the preferred stock issued in recent years has been in the no-par category. It is interesting to note, however, that these stocks frequently include in their provisions an agreement to capitalize them on the balance sheet at some specific figure, such as $50 for a $3 preferred, or $100 for a $6 preferred. 

Cumulative and Non-Cumulative Dividends 

Dividends on preferred stock may either accumulate when not paid, or they may be non-cumulative and expire at the end of each dividend period. The reason for making dividends on preferred stock cumulative is best explained by describing what happens when they are non-cumulative. Under the latter plan, if the dividends are not paid during a given period, the stockholder is no longer entitled to receive them, assuming, of course, that the passing of the dividend is legal. Automatically the failure to pay a dividend on the preferred means that nothing may be paid on the common. 

Let us now assume that a corporation could earn in a given year only enough to cover the preferred dividend. By passing the preferred dividend, it may be further presumed that earnings are sufficient the following year to pay dividends on both the preferred and common stock. The simple expedient of omitting the preferred dividends thus makes possible the payment of a return on the common. This would hardly be termed an ethical procedure but probably could be defended in many cases as being legal. In any event, preferred stockholders would be called upon to use personal funds to protest the action in court, while the defense would be financed out of corporate money. 

However, such a practice would be impossible when the stock is on a cumulative basis, because dividends not previously paid are added to those currently due and the total obligation must be discharged before common stock may receive anything. Naturally, if there is bad faith in passing a dividend, or if the directors are unable to show financial justification, the courts would favor the non-cumulative stockholder by compelling the payment of the preferred dividend. 

The verdict of the Supreme Court of Michigan in the case of Dodge v. Ford Motor Company ordering the company to pay additional divi-

64 dends on the common stock is partial evidence of this legal support.2 

However, there are not many cases of this nature and directors do have a large degree of freedom in deciding whether or not dividends should be declared.

As a point of law, preferred stock is assumed to be cumulative, unless there is a statement to the contrary either in the charter or by-laws of the corporation. Notice of such restrictions must be printed on the back of each stock certificate. Prevailing legal interpretation gives the preferred stockholders all the rights of the common stockholders if there are no limitations to the contrary. Because of the extensive, implied powers inherent in preferred stock, most companies take great care to provide the necessary restrictions. The following extract from the certificate of the Tide Water Associated Oil Company may be quoted as an instance: " .... the holders of the preferred stock shall be entitled to receive, when and as declared by the Board of Directors, dividends from the surplus or net profits of the corporation, at the rate of six per cent (6) per annum and no more.... and shall be cumulative .... 

While the cumulative feature offers some protection, numerous weaknesses are revealed in its effectiveness. If a company gets only slightly or temporarily in arrears in the payment of preferred dividends, there is a reasonable expectation that the arrearage will be paid off in a later and more prosperous period. However, if the company suffers a long period of depressed earnings and is forced to pile up sizeable arrearages, a compromise agreement with the preferred stockholders will usually be made. New preferred stock is often issued in place of the old, and the stockholder is likely to receive in cash or other securities less than was originally due him. Two examples of such compromises may be given. 

The American Zinc, Lead, and Smelting Company, as of December 31, 1934, owed its preferred stockholders accumulated unpaid dividends of $75 per share. In July, 1935, the stockholders approved

Redeemable Preferred Stock 

The majority of preferred stock issues are callable at the option of the company. From the point of view of the corporation, the advantages of this feature are perfectly clear. Not only does optional redeemability permit a more flexible financing program, but it provides an opportunity to use periods of easy credit and low money rates to escape from onerous terms. Preferred stock has a relatively high dividend rate and other attractive features which may at times prove to be undesirable, if not unnecessarily deterring to the management. The redemption privilege offers a convenient means for the removal of these restrictions. Since the exercise of the option is at the discretion of the company, it may come at a time which is detrimental to the investors who hold the stock. As a result, the redemption price usually includes a premium and the stock is callable only at a figure above par, or above the original issue price in the case of no-par stock. For $100 par stock, the premiums may vary from $5 to as much as $20 per share in the event of call. 

The use of the call privilege varies considerably in the different fields of enterprise. Approximately three-fourths of general industrial

and public utility issues are callable. Among newer utility issues which are listed on the New York Curb Market, fully 90 per cent are callable; in the older railroad issues, less than half may be called at the option of the company. These differences are caused partly by the spread in the issuing dates, but the comparative freedom of management in the three fields is probably of greater influence. There is also less need for the redemption of railroad preferred stock because of the lower rate of dividends which usually characterizes this group. 

Sinking Fund 

In a number of instances, a sinking fund may be required to make redemption both more certain and more systematic. This may be done to make the preferred stock more attractive to a certain type of investor, or it may be included in the stock's protective privileges to conform to prevailing market conditions or styles.

Again, the reason for the issuance of the stock may explain the inclusion of the sinking fund provision. If preferred stock is issued to provide capital for special uses of limited duration, a sinking fund provides a means of orderly liquidation. Since the need for the capital is expected to be temporary, it is proper that the retirement of stock synchronize with the depreciation of the assets. As might be expected, the sinking fund requirement is found more frequently in the industrial field where temporary investment is more usual than in either the public utility or railroad fields.

Convertibility 

Convertibilty affords an opportunity for the retirement of preferred stock through its conversion into common stock at the option of the stockholders. The use of the privilege is naturally inviting when stock prices rise and loses its appeal under adverse price movements. 

However, the conversion option is often inserted in the preferred stock's rights in the hope that price movements will eventually result in complete retirement of the stock. To encourage early conversion, the terms of exchange usually become less attractive the longer the security holder delays the conversion, and the right may expire entirely a few years after the issuance of the preferred. The following cases are offered as examples of convertibility. 

Republic Steel Corporation 6 per cent preferred: on or before May 

1, 1932, conversion was permitted at the rate of share for share; thereafter and to May 1, 1937, 14 shares of preferred for each share of com-

PREFERRED STOCK 

67 mon; thereafter and before May 1, 1942, 14 shares of preferred stock for each share of common; and thereafter 12 shares of preferred for each share of common. 

Shell Union Oil Corporation 5 per cent preferred: convertible into common at the rate of one share of preferred for 33 shares of common on or before July 1, 1932, and thereafter to July 1, 1935, at the rate of one share of preferred for 2 shares of common. The privilege terminated at this later date. 

Warner Bros. Pictures, Incorporated, preferred: conversion was allowed only until September 1, 1930, at the rate of 215 shares of preferred stock for each share of common stock. 

Some question may be raised as to the fairness or necessity of attaching the provision of convertibility at all. Preference as to dividends exists from the beginning, and, in most cases, the stock has prior claim to the assets in the event of liquidation. Under these conditions, why should the holders of the stock be given protection in the early life of a corporation with an opportunity later to enjoy the results of its success? In answer to this question, it should be pointed out that, first, undoubtedly a higher price is paid for the stock than would otherwise be true if there were no opportunities for conversion. In other words, the privilege is not a gift, but is actually purchased by the security holders. Second, the attachment of the conversion feature makes the stock more marketable as well as bringing a higher price. 

Protection of the Conversion Privilege 

The conversion privilege is an option to buy common stock at a time to be selected by the preferred stockholder. Unless otherwise stated this means such stock as may exist at the time of conversion. 

But the common stock available may be quite different in value from that existing when the convertible preferred was issued. Additional stock may have been issued, the stock may have been split-up, a portion of the assets may have been distributed, a new prior lien security issued, or other actions taken reducing the value of the common stock. 

As protection against such action, the charter usually provides that in the event of any change affecting the value of the conversion privilege offsetting adjustments must be made in the conversion ratio. 

For example, if an issue of preferred stock was convertible share for share into common and a 100 per cent stock dividend should be paid on the common, then the conversion ratio would be changed to two shares of common for one share of preferred.

Participating Preferred The exercise of the conversion option means that the preferred stockholder sacrifices his privileged position and assumes the role of common stockholder. With participating preferred stock, it is possible in a sense "to have the cake and eat it too," because the holder retains his original position and, at the same time, may receive dividends over and above the stated rate. Sharing of additional dividends may be on either of the following bases: 

1. Unrestricted participation in which the participation would commence without necessarily waiting for the common stock to receive a stated amount. 

2. Restricted participation in which the receipt of extra dividends may be delayed or restricted in the following ways: (a) Participation not to begin until the common stock has received an amount equal to the stated amount of the preferred, after which both classes of stock share equally. (b) Same delay as provided in (a), but the participation is restricted to a fixed amount. (c) Same delay as provided in (a), but the participation is restricted to a certain percentage of the extra distribution.

Illustrative of these various types, a few selected cases may be noted. One well-known issue is the 7 per cent cumulative preferred stock of the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company. 

The stock has equal voting power with the common stock and receives dividends on the same basis as the common as soon as the latter has been paid 7 per cent. As a result of this privilege, the preferred stock has benefited by dividends in excess of the stated rate upon a number of occasions. From 1903 to 1907, extra dividends of 3 per cent annually were received; from 1920 to 1929, 2 per cent annually; in 

1930, the extra dividend amounted to 3 per cent, and in 1931, the extra dividend amounted to of 1 per cent. Cash extras were paid equal to 4 per cent in 1936, 5 per cent in 1937, and 2 per cent in 1940. In 1933 and 1935, the preferred stockholders were offered an opportunity to take R. C. A. stock in lieu of the regular dividend. 

Another extra took the form of a 10 per cent stock dividend declared in 1924.

The 6 per cent preferred stock of the Virginia-Carolina Chemical Corporation has participating rights similar to those of the Westinghouse Company. To date no benefits have been derived from the participating feature as the common stock has never received any

PREFERRED STOCK 

69 dividends. Irrespective of the dividend record, it is interesting to note that the preferred stock is redeemable at 105. In this respect, the stock differs from that of the Westinghouse Company which is not callable. 

Generally speaking, it would seem that the right of redemption is essential as a matter of equity to the common stockholders; otherwise, they carry all of the final risk but are deprived of the excess earnings to which their position entitles them. 

Prior to February, 1930, the 8 per cent preferred stock of the Midland Steel Products Company allowed not only participation in earnings but also in the assets in the event of liquidation. The latter feature stated that the preferred stock was to be paid $110 per share plus 80 per cent of the remaining assets. Likewise, its share in the distribution of earnings was 80 per cent after the common had been paid $4 for the current year. These liberal provisions probably account for the recapitalization occurring on February 11, 1930. At that time, the participating feature was removed as an attachment of the preferred stock. However, for all practical purposes, the participating feature was retained by the preferred stockholder, since he received one share of new 8 per cent cumulative preferred stock and two shares of new common stock for each old share of participating preferred. Common stockholders received one new share of $2 non-cumulative preferred stock and one share of new common stock for each old share of common stock. The case involves special circumstances which likely account for the unique provision that the $2 stock may not share in the distribution of assets in the event of liquidation. For this reason, it is shown at the nominal amount of ten cents per share in the balance sheet of the company. 

The right of participation is not a common feature and appears to be related to the purpose underlying the issuance of preferred stock. 

Stock which is issued to raise new capital is not likely to carry the participating provisions while stock issued in connection with the reorganization of a company may have the privilege attached for "sweetening" purposes. In the latter case, participation in possible future gains makes the new security appear more attractive to those investors who are forced to accept a junior security for their formerly "secured" holdings.

Protection against Issues Having Prior Claims 

Without protection against the issuance of additional securities in the future, the position of the preferred stock may be dangerously en-

croached upon. On the other hand, the imposition of too many restrictions upon corporate financing may prove embarrassing to the management. The problem is often settled by permitting the issuance of new securities, but only with the sanction of the preferred stockholders. The approval of two-thirds of the preferred stockholders is the most common requirement, although there are a number of instances where more or less than this majority may be required. 

Since it is frequently difficult to obtain a return of ballots from such a large majority of the preferred stockholders, some companies provide that action may be taken unless a certain percentage of the preferred stockholders object. Under the latter procedure, the required vote for objection is the complement to the percentage required for approval and is customarily one-fourth or one-third of the preferred stock. Where the preferred stock has the right to vote on all occasions, there is obviously less need for a specific vote of the preferred stockholders on any particular question. 

Although the provision for voting usually relates to the issuance of preferred stock or bonds with a prior position, it is not uncommon to find specific requirements for the issuance of additional amounts of the type outstanding. This, of course, affords further protection to the outstanding preferred stock, since added increments of the same stock or other prior lien securities might not always be issued on as favorable a basis as the original securities. As a result, continued payment of dividends on the original issue may be rendered uncertain by the new fixed dividend and interest requirements. The contingency is usually provided for by limiting the issuance of new stock or bonds to 75 per cent (or some other reasonable percentage) of the value of the property acquired, by requiring adequate coverage of the dividends, by requiring a liquid condition preliminary to the issuance of new securities, and by other devices conducive to maintaining the status of the preferred stock. 

Provisions for the protection of preferred stock against the issuance of additional securities are employed much more widely in the industrial field than in the public utility and railroad fields. Corporations in the latter groups have larger fixed capital requirements and there is less doubt of their continued operation over a long period of time. Moreover, they have enjoyed a more favorable investment rating and have, therefore, found it less necessary to include protective clauses in order to sell the stock,

PREFERRED STOCK STOCK 

71 

Voting Privilege

Preferred stock is a mixture of various privileges and rights obtained by the reservation of authority. Dividends are usually on a cumulative basis, the privilege of conversion may be found, and often the right is reserved to approve the issuance of new securities. Because of these conditions, the need of preferred stockholders to vote on all questions is not pronounced. Nevertheless, the majority of preferred stocks carry the right to vote in the event of failure to meet prescribed standards of operation.³ One circumstance which gives cause for voting is the omission of dividends. Numerous issues provide for the assumption of the right to vote as soon as two consecutive dividends are passed, while others may require as many as four. Because of a minority position, voting power may prove to be of little value unless it provides for the right to elect a specified proportion of the directors. 

The $5 cumulative preferred of General Motors Corporation is a case in point. This stock is entitled to elect one-fourth of the directors whenever the dividends are more than six months in arrears. 

Industrial and public utility issues usually provide limited voting rights, but the majority of the railroad issues have the voting privilege without restriction. Railroad preferred stocks are customarily noncumulative as to dividends and are not greatly removed from the common stock classification. Under the circumstances, it is fitting that railroad preferred and common stocks be given equal voting power. The peculiar character of railroad preferred stocks is largely the result of their origin-chiefly as a consequence of reorganization proceedings.

A $3 no-par stock sold and capitalized at $50 on the balance sheet is equivalent to a $50 par, 6 per cent stock, but the similarity would not exist if the no-par stock had been sold at $55. Reasons Why Preferred Stock May Be Issued 

Because of the comparatively high cost of obtaining capital through the channel of preferred stock, certain good reasons must exist to justify its use. The following appear to be cogent. 

1. Necessity-a substitute for bonds.-Financial conditions may preclude the issuance of high-grade bonds, but may be satisfactory for the sale of preferred stock. More specifically, the earnings of a particular company may not be sufficiently stable to meet the fixed charges on bonds, but the average return may justify the use of preferred stock. 

2. Reorganization issues.-Preferred stock, particularly of the noncumulative variety, has been utilized as a means of satisfying junior bondholders' demands in a reorganization program. Examples are found in the 5 per cent non-cumulative preferred of the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Pacific Railway Company, as well as the two preferred issues of the Chicago, Rock Island, and Pacific Railway Company which are partially non-cumulative. The latter company's 

7 per cent Class A preferred is cumulative to the extent of 5 per cent of dividend rate; and 1 per cent of the rate is preferred over the 6 per cent Class B preferred, which is also cumulative to the extent of 5 per cent of its dividend rate. In other words, only a portion of the dividend rate has the cumulative protection. The balance is speculative in the sense that it is non-cumulative and payable at the discretion 5 Data computed from tables in Moody's Manual of Industrials (1941), p, a43,

PREFERRED STOCK 

75 of the directors. However, the entire rate precedes the claims of the common stock to share in the earnings. 

3. Protection of control.-Preferred stock is not only a convenient alternative for the raising of capital, but it may also be favored for reasons of control. As discussed earlier, preferred stock usually has limited voting rights, but seldom has authority to vote on operating policies. By using stock of the preferred type, controlling interests may continue their positions without further investment. 

Even where the preferred stock has voting power, ultimate protection to those in control may be assured if the stock is redeemable. 

A famous illustration of this influence of the callable feature is the fight between Hill and Harriman in 1901 for the control of the Northern Pacific Railway Company. The capital structure of the company at that time was composed of $80,000,000 common stock and $75,- 000,000 preferred stock. In the scramble for the controlling position, Hill obtained common stock to the extent of $42,000,000 and preferred stock to the extent of $29,000,000. Harriman had common stock amounting to $37,000,000 and preferred stock of $42,000,000. 

It will be seen that Harriman had a majority of the existing voting control. On the other hand, Hill had a majority of the common stock, and since the preferred stock was redeemable, he simply started a rumor that it would be redeemed. By reason of his strategic position, Hill was able to reach his objective by ultimately co-operating with Harriman in the formation of a holding company which would exercise control. 

4. Market conditions. — Money-market conditions occasionally make it desirable to float preferred stock in preference to common stock. The statement of the volume of preferred and common stocks sold in the eleven-year period from 1929 to 1939 appearing earlier in this chapter reveals this principle. 

Miscellaneous Types of Preferred Stocks 

Other terms of nomenclature are sometimes applied to stock issues that are fundamentally preferred. One instance is the use at one time of debenture stock by the General Motors Corporation. 

Originally the company had outstanding 7 per cent and 6 per cent debenture stock issues. The 7 per cent issue was disposed of by exchanging it share for share for a new 7 per cent preferred stock which was a part of the simplification program inaugurated in 1924. It was

also hoped to eliminate the 6 per cent issue by offering one share of the new 7 per cent preferred for each share of the debenture stock plus $10. However, almost $2,000,000 of the 6 per cent debentures did not make the exchange. Later, all of the preferred issues were consolidated successfully into no-par preferred stock bearing an annual dividend rate of $5. Curiously enough the common stock bears a par value of $10 per share, while the preferred is no-par. 

In the same manner that common stock may be classified into A and B groupings, it is not uncommon to find a similar classification of preferred stocks. Usually, demarcation is simply for the convenience of distinction, especially for purposes of giving one of the issues priority. Again, as indicated in the preceding chapter, there is good reason to regard many so-called Class A common stocks as part of the preferred category. In fact, there is so much overlapping of security issues that it is virtually impossible to establish any perfect classification.

So-called prior lien stock is also a form of preferred security, achieving a position of priority by permission of the holders of other preferred stock issues which may be outstanding. On occasions, existing security holders may find it expedient to make such a sacrifice. 

Where new financing is difficult and the outstanding security issues are in jeopardy, the sacrifice of priority of claim because of improved prospects may be sound policy.

Guaranteed stock is sometimes thought of as being a form of preferred stock. Technically this is incorrect since any class of stock may be guaranteed. Guaranteed stock is created whenever a corporation other than the issuing corporation guarantees the payment of the dividends upon an issue of stock. The guaranteeing corporation must pay the dividend or face receivership as insolvent. The stockholder is placed in the position of being a creditor of the guaranteeing corporation while retaining all his rights in the issuing corporation. The guarantee usually arises through the lease of corporate property in its entirety, or as an aid from a parent corporation for the financing of a subsidiary.

Future Outlook 

Preferred stock has many features making it peculiarly adaptable to the new financing order which seems to be evolving. In the future it appears that the emphasis is to be upon stability of operation and

PREFERRED STOCK 

77 144 employment and upon the avoidance of forced liquidation. Preferred stock may facilitate this objective through the greater flexibility offered to financial management, through such features as the absence of a fixed maturity date for the payment of principal, the power to defer dividends without serious consequences, the ability to reorganize the capital structure to meet pronounced internal or external changes. 

Obviously, these rights may be abused by a management which lacks a proper conception of the public interest, but when exercised judiciously, they may be of real benefit to both the corporation and the investors. The losses usually attendant upon forced liquidation or readjustment may be avoided; and business situations which might prove disastrous under bond financing can be successfully weathered.

CHAPTER V  

N THE preceding two chapters, the ownership elements of a business corporation consisting of common stock and preferred stock were discussed. Another type of financial interest is the claim arising as a result of borrowing funds which creates an obligation on the part of the corporation in favor of the lender. The latter type is more frequently referred to as a liability, but it constitutes a valid claim on the assets of the company. In accounting and financial parlance, the two familiar categories of liabilities and proprietorship are thereby created. The corporation never promises to liquidate the stock issues because their extinction would destroy the corporate entity, but it is expected that the loan obligations will be retired at maturity. 

The second class of financial interest is made possible in a credit sense by the existence of the permanent investment of the stockholders. 

It would be impossible to borrow if it were not for the presence of the safety factor provided by the ownership equity. An appreciation of the part played by the stock equity may be obtained by citing a simple everyday occurrence in the public utility field. Public utility companies usually require that new customers make a deposit upon the installation of a meter, but the requirement is waived if the customer happens to be a property owner. Why the difference? Obviously under the latter conditions, the utility company issues the meter wit out a deposit because more than sufficient protection is found in sustaining equity of the property holder. There exists a definite value upon which the company may levy if necessary. hand, the renter lacks tangible security and is requir deposit as a guaranty for the payment of his bill. 

The principles underlying the simple requireme customers make an advance to assure their credit stan applicable to the corporation engaged in raising fun be borrowed only by having a sustaining equity as manence and good faith. To express the dependency upon the residual elements, the term "trading on the e monly employed. In essence, it means that the manager vantage of the permanent stock investment to borrow may not otherwise be available. Or, the manageme 79

the use of additional funds at a favorable rate of interest would add to the profits of the stockholders. In either event, borrowing is facilitated by the existence of capital stock which serves as a margin of protection against loss by the creditors. "Trading on a thin equity" would result whenever the borrowing was large in proportion to the capital stock, and, vice versa, "trading on a thick equity" would be a condition where the amount of funds borrowed was small in comparison with the amount raised by the sale of capital stock. Operating on a thin equity may mean excessive risk because large contractual obligations in the form of regular interest payments and principal maturities must be met. At the same time, failure to trade on the equity may mean that funds are not being obtained as cheaply as they might be. As a result, the stockholders may be deprived of profits which would otherwise be possible by obtaining capital through special channels at a lower cost. 

Before determining the line of demarcation between reasonable and unreasonable trading on the equity, reference may be made to its use in actual practice. A recent balance sheet of the Bethlehem 

Steel Corporation may be used for this purpose.

Restricting the analysis to long-time financing, attention may be directed first to the funded debt of the corporation. Why was the public willing to loan the Bethlehem Steel Corporation the large sum of $161,434,148? One reason, though by no means the only one, was the existence of an ownership equity of more than $414,000,000 in the form of common and preferred stock which served as a margin of safety for the loan. With this large equity as a buffer, the corporation was in a position to trade in relation to the stock, that is, to borrow additional funds.

The next point of interest relates to the benefits derived from trading on the equity. The most important advantage is the profitableness of the operation. For the year ended December 31, 1929, the 

Bethlehem Steel Corporation had net earnings of $53,460,160 (after allowing for depreciation but before interest). This amounted to 8.9 per cent of the total outstanding bonds, preferred stock, and common stock. However, the bonds received only $11,217,180 as their share and the preferred stock, $7,000,000. The balance was credited to the account of the common stock and afforded a net return of 11.2 per cent. Part of this balance available for the common stock was disbursed as dividends and the remainder was transferred to surplus. 

Stating the foregoing results generally, trading on the equity is profitable and desirable so long as the rate of earnings is in excess of the interest rate paid on account of borrowed capital. Whenever the former rate is less than the latter, then it is unprofitable to the common stock, and if carried too far, must ultimately mean failure. 

As an example of how trading on the equity may prove to be unprofitable, the results of operations of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation may be noted for the year, 1922. The net profits amounted to $13,294,524, which was 4.5 per cent of the capitalization (stock plus bonds). After allowing $8,689,193 for interest on the funded debt and $3,662,310 for preferred dividends, there was available for the common stock $943,021, or only 1.2 per cent on the investment. If all the capital had been raised by common stock instead of the fi-/ nancial set-up existing at the time, it is apparent that the rate of earnings on the common stock would have been 4.5 per cent instead

of 12 per cent actually realized. On other occasions, there may be a loss from operations before allowing for the fixed charges due on the funded debt. This was true of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation in the year 1932. Persistence of this condition over a number of years would have caused the company to fail. 

Case of Potomac Electric Company 

Another case which illustrates the benefits to be derived from trading on the equity is that of the Potomac Electric Power Company. 

Undoubtedly, the earnings results are primarily the result of the nature and location of this business, but the limited rate paid on the mortgage indebtedness and on the preferred stock has served to bolster the earnings applicable to the common stock. The case is also one which illustrates the tremendous earning power possible under a favorable business opportunity. Requirements for Trading on the Equity

Because losses may occur from time to time and may under certain circumstances continue for a number of successive years, it is essential that business organizations utilize bond issues with proper caution. 

A company whose earnings are reasonably stable may be justified in trading on a comparatively thin equity, but if earnings are subject to violent fluctuations, borrowings should be resorted to on a limited scale, if at all. The rigid, contractual demands of interest payments must be met regularly if failure is to be avoided. A company borrowing with a thick equity has a large ownership account in the business upon which there is no obligation to pay any return, thus leaving all of its earnings, if it has any, to pay interest on a relatively small amount of borrowing. Oppositely, the corporation with a large amount of borrowing is under constant pressure to earn a return sufficient to cover the average interest rate paid on its borrowed funds. 

A second feature which often favors trading on the equity is a. large investment in fixed assets. Large amounts of fixed assets consti tute a valuable adjunct for borrowing money since they give the lender

a feeling of security and an assurance that his security will not vanish over night. Frequently, stable earnings and large fixed assets accompany each other. For example, the public utilities borrow rather heavily, but they have stable earnings and a large amount of fixed assets.

A third requirement for satisfactory trading on the equity is that the field of enterprise be well established. The new and untried field should be financed with a plan that imposes as little hardship as possible and one that does not require the management to face the necessity of meeting heavy fixed charges on a given date. A good rule would be the avoidance of large-scale borrowing until at least one business depression has been weathered successfully, although this is a rule which is not always followed. 

Applying the foregoing observations, one would expect to find railroads and other public utilities engaged in trading on the equity much more extensively than industrials. This is confirmed in Table 9 showing the relative importance of the main types of securities as sources of capital.

Trading on the Equity-Railroads 

As one of the oldest fields of enterprise in this country, railroad companies have had long experience in applying the trading on the equity principle to their financial operations. Early in their history, bonds were used to attract foreign capital; and today bonds still constitute the largest single source of funds, despite the fact that railroads have been through many receiverships and reorganizations. Because of long and extensive use, many interesting arrangements of debt tructure are found in railroad finance. Table 10 reveals the extent to which some of the representative roads are securing their capital through borrowing operations. In only one case is there a dollar of

$105,099 74,360 191,442 151,107 562,333 140,648 658,388 To analyze the merit of this extensive trading on the equity, it is necessary to recognize the character of funded debt, or bonded indebtedness, in railroad financing. While any specific bond issue is usually of a terminating nature because of a definite maturity date, funded debt as a whole represents a permanent source of capital. 

Virtual perpetuity of debt in the aggregate is assured by the process of refunding matured obligations, i.e., by the replacement of old bonds with new securities. The history of railroad finance is replete with transactions of the refunding variety. Numerous financial critics have deplored the seemingly excessive use of bonded indebtedness, but undoubtedly the momentum of long experience will force continuance of the practice for many years to come. Proponents of extensive trading on the equity refer to the following economic factors which are innded to justify large borrowing: (1) the basic nature of transportation service; (2) the technical operating aspects of the railroads. 

Transportation is a basic public utility for which there is permanent need. Railroads have long played a prominent part in providing this service, but in recent years competition between different types of transportation has increased in scope and intensity. Nevertheless, many believe that the bulk of our transportation service will continue to be performed by the railroads, particularly for bulky and long distance shipments. Observers declare that the present financial difficulties of the railroads are caused by other factors, such as excessive regulation, internal inefficiency, poor financial practices, and the serious effects of the depression.

888 

In contrast to the relative permanence of the railroads, the life of most industrial companies seems to be less assured. New industrial enterprises come to the front with surprising frequency and disappear from the scene with equal rapidity. The new enterprises may also force older companies into a relatively inferior position or out of business entirely. This change of industrial enterprises does not necessarily affect the railroads adversely. In fact, an increase in the volume of traffic may result if the innovations enlarge the market, or they may mean simply a change in the type of goods carried. 

The large amount of fixed assets required for railroad operation is both a need and a basis for borrowing funds. Roadbed and equipment alike necessitate heavy expenditures, but at the same time, they constitute excellent security for the attraction of capital. In normal times, railroads have three to four dollars in capital investment for each dollar in annual gross revenue received. This relationship may be contrasted to mercantile establishments which frequently receive a dollar or more in gross revenue annually for each dollar invested.

In times of depression, both ratios will be much higher. Because of such large capital requirements, railroads have been forced to tap all possible sources of funds and have, as a natural consequence, traded on the equity rather extensively.

The extent to which railroads should indulge in borrowing capital may now be studied. This has been an issue of wide public interest in the last few years because of the serious decline in railroad income.

The result may, therefore, reflect the mistake of management, instead of being a criterion of the basic soundness of the industry.

Trading on the Equity-Public Utilities 

In discussing the extent to which public utilities may trade on the equity, it is necessary to bear in mind that there are various classes or types of utilities. These may be classified as electric light and power, gas, telephone, telegraph, water, and electric traction. With the exception of the electric traction group, all have shared generously in the prosperity of the nation. Illustrative of the growth, statistics taken from the Census of Electrical Industries, 1932, are presented in Table 13. The decline in salaries and wages paid between 1927 and 

1932 is a product partly of depression conditions as well as being affected by the considerable amount of electric traction lines retired during that period. The other utilities do not have as large labor outlays in proportion to their business as the traction companies. The most rapid growth in the utility industry has occurred since the World War I; and because of its shorter history, the industry until recently has not been accorded as high an investment rating as the railroads.

Their business constitutes a virtually indispensable service to the public and is usually conducted on a quasi-monopolistic basis. Earnings are stable from year to year and capital requirements are high, averaging about five dollars of invested capital for each dollar in annual gross revenue. This combination of steady earnings, large fixed assets, and quasi-monopoly puts the operating utilities in a position to make use of the trading on the equity principle in the extensive manner as indicated in Table 14.

Trading on the Equity--Industrials 

The industrial field is much less homogenous in character than either the railroad or the public utility fields. For this reason, general statements applying to industrials as a group are apt to be misleading. There is a tendency to engage in more extensive borrowing where large fixed investments are found, but there are many exceptions prevailing within the various branches of the industrials. Practice shows many variations and anomalous conditions. Companies doing a satisfactory business and showing good profit margins may do very little borrowing while weaker members have comparatively large funded debt. For instance, the automobile industry as a whole has been prosperous. Yet the largest and one of the most successful concerns, the General Motors Corporation, has no bonds outstanding; while Hudson and Studebaker, companies with a less favorable record, have a small bonded indebtedness. Significantly, the company that is in the best position to issue bonds is not doing so. Another instance of inconsistency is found in the tire and rubber industry which has been subjected to considerable fluctuation in volume and in profits. 

Nevertheless, funded debt represents an important source of capital for most of the tire and rubber companies. Other observations may be made by referring to Table 15.
