Per cent of protection. 1,000,000 200,000 20 The 5 per cent debentures of the former North American Edison Company may be cited as another example. The amount of bonds authorized was unlimited, provided the net income for twelve consecutive months out of fifteen preceding months was at least twice the interest requirements on the outstanding, plus proposed indebtedness, plus any interest payments guaranteed by the company. 

The principle underlying the open mortgage is sound and is of value to both the corporation and the investor if hedged with the proper restrictions, such as requiring adequate coverage of the fixed charges and the limitation of new issues to a fair percentage of the value of new property. However, it is realized all too seldom that restrictions designed to curb management authority may actually func-. tion to the detriment of the investor. Furthermore, there is an abundance of ways and means to avoid such restrictions. 

Open-End Mortgages 

The open-end mortgage is a combination of the open and closed types. It provides a definite limitation in the amount of issue as a protection for the investors, and an opportunity for the corporation to use a given lien as a basis for borrowing to the fullest extent. Under this arrangement, the corporation may have more bonds authorized than it needs at the time of original sale; but a definite limit is set beyond which bonds may not be issued. An illustration is the 5 per cent refunding and consolidated mortgage bonds of the former Northern California Power Company. The original authorization provided for $10,000,000, but only $5,000,000 was issued. The indenture provides that the remaining $5,000,000 may be issued if the net income (after allowing 15 per cent of gross income for depreciation and maintenance) is equal to two times the interest on all bonds outstanding. As in this case, a standard of operations is usually established as a requirement for additional issues whenever the open-end agreement is used.

Mortgages Classified according to the Scope of the Lien 

Not only is there a question as to whether or not the mortgage should cover property acquired in the future, but in addition a deci-

sion must be made as to what extent the mortgage may cover the prop erty currently owned. Shall the mortgage cover all or only a portion of the property? The answer to this question may be found in an analysis of the following factors and conditions: (1) the existence of other mortgages, (2) the size of the financing to be undertaken, (3) the field of enterprise.

If other mortgages are outstanding, the new mortgage must necessarily give consideration to the existing liens. As a consequence, the new mortgage may be a first lien on certain pieces of property combined with a junior lien on other parts, or numerous other potential combinations may be worked out as shown elsewhere in this chapter. 

The amount of the new financing is also a factor. A first lien on a large and valuable piece of property is not warranted for the sake of minor financing, and, oppositely, it is impossible to base a large financing program upon inadequate property protection. 

Finally, the field of enterprise exercises a broad influence. The property of an industrial plant is much more concentrated in character than that of most utility or railway companies. Railroad property, particularly, is diversified and extended over a wide area, and it is much easier to utilize the separate divisions as a basis for mortgage bonds. Security issues of this type are usually designated as divisional mortgage bonds. They offer an adequate security to the investor, provided, of course, the portion of property is an essential one to the company. In an industrial concern, the division of property is not feasible and has little appeal to investors.

Specific v. Blanket Mortgages 

Allowing for the diverse circumstances that are found in business, mortgages may be conveniently classified according to the scope of their lien into specific and blanket. A specific mortgage grants a lien on a particular piece of property only, while a blanket mortgage covers all the property of the corporation. The following two cases are representative of these two types. 

Specific. The Jamestown, Franklin, and Clearfield Railroad, a subsidiary of the New York Central, has 4 per cent gold bonds outstanding secured by a "first lien on 122.05 miles of line from Rose Siding, Pennsylvania, to the Pennsylvania-Ohio State Line."

Blanket. The Pacific Gas and Electric Company's former general and refunding mortgage gold 5's of 1942 were protected with “a lien on all the propcrties now owned by the company (and all extensions thereunto, as well as any

other property acquired by means of such bonds)." These bonds were callable and were retired in 1936.

An example of combining the blanket feature with an after-acquired clause is found in the Tennessee Coal, Iron, and Railroad Company, a subsidiary of the United States Steel Corporation. The 5 per cent general mortgage gold bonds of this company are secured by a "mortgage on all property now owned by the company or hereafter acquired by it," as well as certain other securities. The effects of such a far-reaching clause may at times be unduly restrictive to desirable expansion of a business corporation, and numerous loopholes have been discovered whereby it may be avoided.

Means of Avoiding the After-Acquired Clause 

Whenever the after-acquired clause is present in a closed mortgage, management is compelled to effect desired financing either on a junior lien basis or by evasion of the restrictions. While no universally applicable method of evasion exists, óne of the following methods is usually available: (1) creation of a subsidiary corporation, (2) merger or consolidation, (3) exercise of the call privilege, (4) use of the purchase-money mortgage, (5) by means of a lease. 

Creation of a Subsidiary Corporation 

If an after-acquired clause proves to be too burdensome for new financing, a new subsidiary company may be organized which is free and clear of the obligations of the parent company. Bonds issued by this newly organized corporation are obviously not subject to the liens or claims of any other corporation and the subsidiary company would be able to offer a first lien on any property acquired. First mortgage bonds of the subsidiary could be sold to finance the construction of a new factory building or any form of expansion, but operations would be under the direction of the parent company through common management or interlocking directorates. For all practical purposes, the original corporation would provide for its additional property needs without having been hampered by the afteracquired clause. 

While the formation of a subsidiary unit affords a clear, legal path for the issuance of bonds with a first lien, it is not always to the advantage of the parent corporation. The subsidiary will usually be small and, of course, not well known. For this reason, if no other,

its bond issues will not sell to the best advantage. Larger bond issues, that is, those in excess of $10,000,000, sell at a definitely more favorable interest rate than smaller flotations.2 Because of this cost factor, the parent corporation may find it more profitable to do its financing on a junior lien basis. 

Merger or Consolidation

Sometimes the after-acquired clause may be so drawn that the lien may be vitiated through the merger of one company with another. 

While the merging company would have to assume the bonds of the merged companies, it would not have to assume all of the restrictions of those bond issues. As a result, the merging company would be free to finance future expansion on a senior lien basis. This outlet will usually be a result of chance rather than deliberate foresight. 

Exercise of the Call Privilege 

The most practical means of eliminating the after-acquired clause is the exercise of the call privilege whenever the right exists. By calling the old bonds for redemption, the way is cleared for new financing. The new issue should be large enough to cover both the payment of the old bonds and the amount needed for expansion. Moreover, it is possible that the sale of the larger issue may be made at lower interest rates and thus offset the premium usually required for the exercise of the call privilege.

Use of the Purchase-Money Mortgage 

Another common, but somewhat limited detour around the afteracquired clause is the purchase-money mortgage. The method is most widely used in the financing of railroad equipment but more recently has been extended to various industrial needs. The corporation usually makes arrangements with a third party or trustee to purchase, or have constructed for the corporation, the required property. The trustee obtains the necessary funds through the sale of bonds or certificates of interest which are secured by a first mortgage upon the property which is to be purchased. The corporation then accepts delivery of the new property subject to the newly created lien and is able to thwart the priority of claims arising as a result of the after- 

2 J. B. Hubbard, "Industrial Bond and Preferred Stock Refundings, 1933-1939," Review of Economic Statistics, XX, 16.

acquired clause. Since the new mortgage was placed on the property before the corporation acquired title to it, the investors protected by the after-acquired clause will have to be content with a second lien on the additional property acquisition. 

By Means of a Lease 

The lease plan permits the use of property without the transfer of title, differing in this respect from the preceding method. To illustrate, if a railroad desires to add another line to its operations, it would find that an acquisition made through merger would be subject to the after-acquired clause. If the property were taken on a lease basis, the clause would have no effect because of the absence of title. The lessor corporation simply issues the necessary securities for extensions and improvements and then proceeds to lease the property to the lessee, the parent company. This procedure obviously entails the disadvantage and expense of continuing the life of the lessor corporation. However, in the case of railroads, such expense often may not be avoided since railroad companies frequently hold their rights-of-way only for the life of the originally chartered corporation. In such cases, the corporation does not own the right-ofway in fee simple, but instead the company has only a privilege of use or occupancy granted by the landowners. This right was granted for the life of the particular corporate entity for its exclusive use without any rights of succession. If this entity should be destroyed through merger or otherwise, the right-of-way would revert to the present owner of the land over which the right had been granted. 

Types of Bonds Secured by Real Property 

So far in this chapter the discussion has been concerned mainly with mortgages, but for financial purposes this document is incidental to the bond. Most of the powers and rights granted to a bond issue are incorporated in the mortgage and the accompanying indenture, but the bond is the means of direct contact between the corporation and the investing public. For this reason, it is essential to have clearly in mind the various types of bonds used. If bonds and their terminology were standarized, such a task would be simple; unfortunately, under existing practice it is especially difficult. It is one thing to state what the name of a bond should indicate, but the facts may not be in accordance with the title. The investor should always

investigate the security and other aspects of a bond issue and not place too much reliance upon the name.

Bonds secured by real property may be tentatively subdivided into the following:

First mortgage bonds.-As the name indicates, the security for this type of bond should consist of mortgages having first claim. An illustration is the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company's first mortgage 4 per cent and 5 per cent bonds. These bonds are secured by a direct first mortgage on 859.53 miles of line and by collateral which is itself secured by a first lien on another 798.09 miles of line. 

General mortgage bonds.-General mortgage bonds have as security a broad mortgage covering a large portion of the company's property. To be more accurate, the security probably consists of a number of mortgages with varying positions as to priority of claim. For example, the general mortgage 4 per cent bonds of the Atchison, Topeka, and Santa Fe Railway Company are secured by first and second liens. and indirectly through collateral liens. The Great Northern Railway 

Company's general mortgage, 33 per cent to 6 per cent bonds, series B-I, are secured by a first lien on 581.38 miles of line, a second lien on 4,855.19 miles, and by other junior liens on 1,910.44 miles.

In addition, there is further collateral security consisting of liens on 202.46 miles of line. Thus, it can be seen that a general mortgage bond usually means security partially represented by a first mortgage, but for the most part by liens of only junior standing. 

Refunding and general mortgage bonds.-This type of bond is issued mainly for refunding purposes with a general mortgage as security. An example is the refunding and general mortgage 6 per cent gold bonds of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. The security of these bonds is represented by a combination of first direct, second direct, second collateral, third direct, third collateral, fourth direct, fourth collateral, fifth direct, and fifth collateral liens.

Refunding and improvement bonds.-Bonds of this class are quite common and are usually issued for the dual purpose of refunding a maturing or called issue, and at the same time providing funds for expansion or improvement of the property. The refunding and improvement mortgage, 5 per cent, series of 1927 of the Erie Railroad, are representative of this type. Of the $50,000,000 in bonds issued, $40,- 

000,000 were used to replace former A and B series bonds, $5,104,000

were used to refund other liens, and $4,896,000 were used to reimburse the company for additions and betterments made to the property. 

The underlying security for this bond issue is made up chiefly of junior liens.

First and refunding bonds.-This type of bond should be secured partially by a first mortgage and partly by junior liens. Usually, they are issued to cover improvements and extensions, as well as to refund maturing obligations. These features are well illustrated in the first and refunding mortgage 5 per cent bonds, series A, of the Florida East Coast Railway. The bonds are secured by a first lien on 193.66 miles of road and a second lien on 436.85 miles of additional line, plus a general mortgage upon the entire property of the company not otherwise subject to specific first liens. The bonds were issued to cover improvements already made and to retire funded debt. 

Consolidated mortgage bonds.-These bonds are issued upon a mortgage or series of mortgages with a claim against the properties of a consolidation. For example, the first consolidated prior lien gold 

4's of the Erie Railroad were secured by liens ranging from the first to the fourth on various properties, as well as by a number of collateral liens.

First and consolidated mortgage bonds.-First and consolidated mortgage bonds should be secured in part by a first lien and the balance by a general mortgage on consolidated property. The first and consolidated, gold 6's, series A, of the Seaboard Air Line Railway Company are illustrative. These bonds were issued in connection with the consolidation of the old Seaboard Airline Railway (not company) and the Carolina, Atlantic, and Western Railway Company. The security consists of a first lien on 412.25 miles of line and a pledge of $65,915,000 of refunding mortgage 4 per cent bonds of the old Seaboard Airline Railway and other securities. Through these pledged bonds the issue now outstanding has a further first lien on 

218.38 miles of line and a second lien on 2,697.27 miles of other line.

First consolidated bonds.—Strictly interpreted, a first consolidated bond means the first consolidated issue sold by a company and does not necessarily imply that a first mortgage is offered as security. The first consolidated general lien gold 4's of the Erie Railroad are an example. These bonds were issued at the same time as the first consolidated prior lien gold 4's, but are junior in claim to the latter

bonds. Hence, not even a portion of their security is represented by a first lien.

Secured Bonds and Fields of Enterprise 

The reader probably has observed that most of the examples of mortgage bonds given in the foregoing sections were those of railroads. Varieties of bonds are more numerous in this field than any other because of, first, the greater development and longer history of the railroads, and, second, the railroad plant is more easily divided for purposes of mortgage security. Unfortunately, many railroads have issued mortgage bonds for reasons of necessity instead of choice. During the early life of the railroads, it was necessary to issue a well-protected security to attract foreign capital; while in more recent years, the use of capital stock as a means of financing the railroads has been retarded because of an impaired credit standing. Reduced earnings and burdensome overhead have served to weaken the position of junior equities. 

With the railroads as a whole unable to earn fixed charges in recent years, individual companies find it difficult to finance except on a well-secured mortgage basis. 

In the industrial field, the mortgage bond is not nearly so much in vogue. While there is some tradition against engaging in the practice, the reason is probably of a more inherent nature. Because of the competition prevalent in the industrial field, as well as other factors contributing to a relatively greater lack of stability, the plant investment does not always constitute an ideal security for a bond issue. 

Where the mortgage bond is used in the industrial field, a large fixed investment is usually present, such as is found in the iron and steel industry.

The public utility field offers an excellent basis for the issuance of mortgage bonds. This applicability is restricted more particularly to operating companies inasmuch as pure holding companies lack the direct ownership of real property which is necessary for the establishment of a lien. Variation is found also according to the major divisions of the industry. Electric light and power companies (operating) and water utility companies are inclined to use mortgage bonds more freely than the companies producing gas or furnishing telephone service. This is a reflection, in part, of the tradition prevailing within each industry and, in part, of the relative degree of permanence in the plant's operating assets.

3 One large utility system formerly took pride in the fact that it was able to finance its operations without utilizing a single mortgage. 

The capital requirements were met through the issuance of unsecured obligations of the holding company, i.e., some form of a debenture bond. This utility organization, as well as others, even went so far as to provide its own selling organization. The chief argument advanced for the use of unsecured financing on such an extensive scale is the claim that the security covers the property of the entire system. 

A further advantage, more especially from the standpoint of the corporation, is that the mortgage bond issues may be reserved to provide funds when market conditions are more stringent. In the words of one financier¹

The plan contemplates that under normal market conditions the capital required for the extension of the company's system and for the acquisition of additional properties to broaden its scope and business will be provided through the sale of debentures of the parent company, and should funds be required under adverse market conditions, as, for instance, in a period of panic, they can be made available through the sale of the mortgage secured obligations of any of the numerous constituent operating companies. 

Value of Specific Security to the Investor

As indicated at the beginning of this chapter, specific security does not automatically provide the investor with a cloak of armor against failure. Attention must also be given to the income position of a company. A sound and stable income supply provides continued economic buoyancy and solvency, but the security afforded by lien is of use only ultimately or under emergency conditions. The value of a senior lien in time of failure and reorganization has been demonstrated on more than one occasion. The secured holder is in a position to demand better treatment than the unsecured creditor, and cases are known where the security holders have actually benefited by a reorganization.

CHAPTER VIII SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

S STATED at another point, it is impossible to formulate a classification of bonds where the various types or categories are mutually exclusive. Indeed, it must now be clear that the combination of many features into a single issue necessarily creates overlapping and causes many securities to be distinctly hybrid in character. Thus, as illustrated in the previous chapter, it is not uncommon for issues to be secured by various degrees of lien priority and thereby making it impossible to classify them either as first or second mortgage bonds. Even the line of demarcation between secured and unsecured issues is by no means precise because it is possible to create a lien which may be extremely remote or deferred until other issues having priority are liquidated. This is true of income and adjustment bonds where the interest is paid only if earned. Nevertheless, these bonds are included in the present chapter on other secured bonds for the following reasons. 

1. Mortgage security may be achieved by virture of the liquidation of other bonds having prior lien. 

2. Some income bonds are issued on a mortgage basis at the outset, although the mortgage may occupy such a junior status as to possess little actual value.

Analysis of Income and Adjustment Bonds 

Income and adjustment bonds are the instruments of necessity rather than normal financial planning. The terms income and adjustment are used interchangeably or may be used in combination in designating issues of this type. These bonds are the outgrowth of failure and reorganization and are practically imposed upon the participating junior bondholders. The interest is paid only if earned, a feature accounting for the name, "income." The term adjustment is usually the result of the following features. 

1. The bonds are used for adjustment purposes. 

2. Frequently, during the first few years after the reorganization, the interest payment may be only a fraction of the stated rate, 133

However, the interest payments are generally increased and gradually adjusted to the nominal rate. 

The interest on income bonds may be cumulative or non-cumulative. The more common practice is to place the issue on a noncumulative basis during the first few years and later, when the achievement of a more stable position is anticipated, the bonds are put on a cumulative basis. This provision is true of such issues as the following:

The inclusion of the privilege of conversion has much merit by offering potential relief to the original sacrifices resulting from fail,

SECURED BONDS OTHER 

135 ure and reorganization. In the foregoing two instances, the opportunity for profitable conversion may be very remote. However, if profitable operation should occur, the bondholders affected by the reorganization and resulting adjustment would be able to share in the profits and reduce the losses suffered in the preceding reorganization.

The imposition of a sinking fund also strengthens the general standing of income bonds. Of the issues described previously, only that of the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Pacific Railroad has this feature, but the provision did not take effect until April 1, 1936, or more than eleven years after issuance. The question as to whether this class of bonds should feature a sinking fund more generally may be considered. The inclusion of this safeguard may be of much value to the investors called upon to accept these bond issues, but, on the other hand, there is doubt whether it is wise to saddle a financially embarrassed corporation with such a rigid requirement. The usual absence of the sinking-fund clause indicates that its inclusion is generally regarded as undesirable.

In rare instances, income bondholders may be given the right to vote, the privilege ceasing after the interest payments have been restored to a normal basis. To permit voting is not unlike the right accompanying many issues of preferred stock, where the right to vote is gained upon the failure to meet the dividend payments. At the same time, the income bondholder is essentially a creditor, and of course, retains his priority over the preferred and common stockholders in the event of liquidation.

Special Investor and Public Interest in Income Bonds 

In many respects, income and adjustment bonds are clothed with a peculiar investor and public interest which is not present in other types of bonds issued by normal, going concerns. The latter are purchased voluntarily in the open market and are on a strictly quid pro quo basis. In contrast, income bonds are obtained under conditions where only limited alternatives are present, and the discretion of the investor is affected by his losses arising from failure. Under these circumstances, the public interest may dictate that securities of the income and adjustment type contain provisions which would permit investors to share in future gains as a partial offset to past losses, In addition, there should be every assurance that other rights of in-

vestors, such as priority of position and a voice in control, should not be vitiated by the manipulations of insiders or of other selfish groups. Fortunately, there is now less opportunity for such abuse of investors in distress because laws have been enacted which require formal approval of reorganization plans by regulatory bodies.¹ 

Real and Personal Property Security 

Generally speaking, fixed property is preferable to personal property as security for a bond issue. Fixed property offers a definite and permanent basis of support, while personal property is so mobile that the specific property offered as security may easily disappear from among the assets of the corporation. Personal property is easily moved, has a temporary life, and is being converted constantly into the goods or services which the corporation sells. On the other hand, in time of failure, the ready movability of personal property may prove to be of advantage because it adds to the property's marketability. How to utilize the benefits accruing from the marketability of personal property and, at the same time, avoid its limitations as a form of security is a problem of financial arrangement which will now be discussed.

Equipment Obligations 

To be used as a basis for reasonably long-term credit, personal property must first have sufficient life to make a satisfactory lien possible. Inventories, receivables, and other current assets do not meet this qualification and are not adaptable as security for long-time corporate financing. The requirement is filled excellently by rolling stock of railroads. Possessing an average life of more than twenty years, and being indispensable to the railroad's operations, it offers a susbtantial basis for financing. Railroads have taken advantage of this condition and have issued equipment obligations, totaling in excess of four billion dollars.

An equipment obligation is a security issued with rolling stock or other equipment as collateral. It was practically unknown until introduced into railroad financing in the last of the nineteenth century as a subterfuge for the evasion of the after-acquired clause. 

Later, equipment obligations came to be recognized in their own right as an excellent means of obtaining low-cost financing. 

1 See chapter XXXVI for discussion.

SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

137 Equipment obligation may be divided into two main types: indirect and direct. Indirect obligations may be defined as those for which the railroad or other issuing corporation is not directly liable. The corporation's liability is ultimate and actual, but it is not direct. The absence of direct liability is intended to prevent the creation of possible prior claims against the equipment which is to be purchased. 

In order to escape the after-acquired clause, title to the property must not pass to the railroad, and at the same time the railroad must assume final responsibility. This is accomplished by selling the property to a third party, usually a trust company, which issues certificates of interest in the property instead of direct obligations of the railroad. To make the certificates more readily marketable, they are guaranteed by the railroad buying the equipment.

The indirect method is usually known as the Philadelphia or lease plan. Three parties participate in the transaction: the vendor of the equipment, the trustee, and the vendee, which is the railroad. 

When negotiations between the equipment manufacturer and the railroad are complete as to the details of the equipment, the manufacturer is instructed to sell the property to a properly designated trustee. In turn, the trustee leases the equipment to the railroad, and in consideration the railroad promises to pay an initial deposit plus annual rentals. 

With the title vested in the trustee, certificates of interest are issued and sold to the public. As a result, the holder of a certificate becomes a partial owner of the actual property, i.e., cars, locomotives, etc. The proceeds from the sale of the certificates plus the initial, deposit made by the railroad equal the purchase price of the equipment, and the funds are used to pay the equipment manufacturer. 

This permits the latter to drop out of the picture and only two parties remain: the railroad and the trustee as the agent for the certificate holders.

The annual rentals are sufficient to pay the interest on the outstanding certificates (known as equipment trust certificates) and to liquidate a part of the principal. Amortization of the principal is accomplished by making the certificates of serial maturity. These features, however, apply also to the direct obligations and may be discussed in common at a later point. 

Practically the same results are achieved with direct obligations, but by a slightly different technique. Again, the same three parties are involved, i.e., the vendor, the vendee, and the trustee. In this

case, the vendor sells the property directly to the railroad (and not to the trustee as in the Philadelphia plan), but on a conditional sale basis. The title does not pass to the railroad but remains with the vendor, the equipment manufacturer. The title is then assigned to the trustee in consideration of the purchase price, which in turn is raised by the initial deposit of the railroad and the sale of equipment obligations to the public. These equipment obligations, however, are the direct liability of the railroad; in short, they are equipment bonds, and not equipment trust certificates. The reason for making the securities direct in this case is because the equipment is sold to the railroad. To meet the purchase price of the equipment, the railroad advances its initial deposit in cash and the balance in long-time promissory notes, i.e., equipment bonds. The bonds have serial maturity and are secured by the equipment in the same manner as the equipment trust certificates. This method is commonly referred to as the 

New York plan.2 

To be strictly correct, the terms “equipment bond” or “equipment note" should be restricted to direct obligations. However, in actual practice the term "equipment trust certificate" is used broadly to cover the whole field of equipment obligations. 

Which of the two plans is more widely used? Why is this plan used in preference to the other? The answers to these questions disclose again the effect of the law upon corporate financing. Although one would expect to find the more simple and convenient New York plan in wide use, the facts are the opposite. This condition may be accounted for as follows: 

1. The lease plan is valid in all states, but the conditional sale plan is not legal in Pennsylvania, where the lease method must be used instead. 

2. The lease plan was the first to be adopted. 

3. Under the lease plan, the sale is made to the trustee and not to the railroad. As a result, no pretense is afforded for claiming that the title resides in the latter.

The fundamental differences which exist between the direct and the indirect methods are in a sense trivial; and were it not for a few legal conventionalities and niceties, the direct plan would most likely 2 A slight variation of the New York plan is found in a few cases using the chattel mortgage. In this arrangement, the equipment is sold to the railroad on the condition that it be deeded to the trustee as security for the equipment bonds,

SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

139 be employed almost universally. The convenience afforded by the direct method was recognized by the government in 1920, when it used this basis to settle for equipment turned over to the railways after the period of government operation. Fundamentally, the two plans achieve virtually the same results, and obligations issued under the two plans have the same elements of strength as well as other common characteristics. For this reason, no distinction is made between the two types in the following discussion of the security, income, and miscellaneous features of equipment obligations. 

Security Features 

The greatest source of strength of equipment securities lies in the fact that the title to the property does not vest in the railroad. 

To quote the words of an indenture, Until payment by the Railway to the vendor. . . . and to the holders of the notes hereinafter referred to, of the entire purchase price of said equipment, and of all installments and amounts as hereinafter specified, and until all of the obligations of the Railway hereunder shall have been duly complied with and performed, the title to the equipment aforesaid shall not pass or vest in the 

Railway, but shall remain in the said Vendor. . . . .

The practical application of this provision has been tested in many reorganizations, and equipment obligations have always escaped virtually unscathed. Usually, the holders of the equipment obligations have suffered only the inconvenience connected with a temporary default of the interest and principal payments. Both the legal security inherent in the equipment obligation and the ready marketability of the equipment place securities of this type in a key position in time of reorganization. 

In the case of default in the payment of interest or principal, "such default continuing for a period of 60 days.... the Trust Company shall be entitled to, and at its option, may repossess itself of the said equipment, and of every piece thereof, retaining all payments which up to that time may have been made on account of the said equipment." Because of the indispensability of equipment to railroad operations, it has seldom been necessary to make use of this power. 

Protecting the Obligations against Depreciation

Since railroad equipment is subject to unusually heavy wear and tear, a material diminution of value must occur. Two features are intended to protect the holders of equipment obligations on this ac

count: (1) The presence of an adequate original equity behind the issue. (2) Increasing the relative equity throughout the life of the issue. Examination of a number of equipment trust indentures reveals the fact that the initial deposit, or original equity, varies from 15 per cent to 25 per cent, with 20 per cent being common. This means that at the very beginning the outstanding obligations are equal to only 80 per cent of the value of the security. Throughout the life of the trust certificates, liquidation of principal proceeds at a rate faster than the depreciation of the equipment. Not only do the certificates mature serially, but their maximum maturity is less than the average life of the equipment. A conservative statement of the life of a railroad car is twenty years, while obligations seldom have maturities in excess of fifteen years.

Minor Security Provisions 

The trust indenture provides in numerous ways for the maintenance and protection of the equipment. First, the typical maintenance provision declares, "the company during the continuance of this lease, will maintain and keep all of the Trust Equipment in good order, and repair, at its own proper cost, and charge and will replace, at its own cost, any of the Trust Equipment that may be worn out.... 

Second, the equipment must be properly insured, "Each box car and each stock car and each refrigerator car shall be insured for not less than 50 per cent of the value thereof under the rules and regulations of the Master Car Builders' Association . . . . " Third, the railroad is usually required to render an annual report depicting the condition of the equipment, and in addition the trustee has the right to inspect the property. Fourth, adequate restrictions are incorporated in the agreement to prevent the railroad from selling or transferring the property, e.g., "The Railway agrees . . . . not to part with the possession or any of such equipment .... (except so far as is necessary in the usual interchange of traffic) or to be in any manner encumbered by or through the Railway." Fifth, each unit of equipment must bear a plate showing the true owner of the same, so that no doubt remains as to whom the title is vested in. · • 

Income Features 

Features of the income position of equipment trust certificates are in large measure a reflection of the security provisions. Default in

SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

141 the interest payments may be used as a basis to deprive the railroad of the right to use the equipment. An illustration of the general strength of the income position of equipment obligations is found in a certain railroad that was in the hands of the receivers for seven years. During the greater part of this period, interest was passed on practically all of the funded debt except the equipment trust certificates.

Miscellaneous Provisions 

Because of the interstate character of transportation, the railway agrees in the trust indenture to abide by the laws of the various states in which it operates. In addition, various minor items such as the following appear in the indenture: (1) stipulations regarding the form of the bonds or certificates; (2) arrangements for the delivery of the cash deposit and securities; and (3) detailed statement of the duties of the trustee, provision for his resignation, death, etc.

Collateral Trust Bonds 

Another type of obligation based upon personal property is the collateral trust bond, which is secured by stocks, bonds, or other forms of intangible property owned by the issuing corporation. It is possible for the security to take the following forms: (1) bonds of other corporations, (2) stocks of other corporations, (3) a combination of

bonds and stocks of other corporations, (4) other securities of the issuing corporation, (5) other intangibles such as patents, leases, etc. 

The question may be raised as to why securities of the same type, or even of a different type, may be used as a basis for other issues. 

In general, securities are used as collateral for two major reasons: first, to facilitate economical financing, and, second, for purposes of corporate control. At times, there may be a combination of these two reasons. In the ordinary course of business, corporations frequently come into possesssion of bonds and stocks of other companies. These securities may pay the owning corporation a return, but often the funds invested in the securities may be of more value if converted into operating or physical capital assets. This, the company is able to do through the collateral trust device. The securities are deposited with a trustee under suitable indenture, and bonds are issued against the pledged collateral. The company usually retains all the rights of the deposited collateral and receives any interest or dividends accruing while the securities are held in trust. Thus, where the collateral consists of sufficient stock, the control of a subsidiary may still be exercised without being deprived of the use of the funds. Irrespective of whether or not control is the chief objective, there is the additional · incentive of adding to income by this financial arrangement. Obviously, profits would be possible whenever the rate of return earned on the pledged securities was greater than the rate of interest paid on the collateral bonds.

Bonds Secured by Bonds of other Corporations 

Bonds are often used as collateral when it is desired to substitute an obligation of the parent company for that of the subsidiary. The parent company may make advances to subsidiary companies by purchasing their securities, and then replenish its own treasury by the sale of a bulk issue secured by the bonds of the subsidiaries. In this manner, advantage is taken of the more favorable rate which is possible under wholesale financing. Also, the larger parent company may be better known and be able to obtain better terms because of its prestige. The following examples are illustrative of collateral bonds secured by the bonds of subsidiaries. 

Illinois Central Railroad collateral trust gold 4's, due in 1952, are secured by the deposit of bonds of controlled lines which are operated by the Illinois 

Central Railroad.

SECURED BONDS—OTHER 

143 The Louisville and Nashville Railroad Company's secured gold 5's of 1941, now retired, were secured by 5 per cent first mortgage bonds of the Lexington and Eastern Railroad, 5 per cent general consolidated bonds of the South and North Alabama Railroad, and 4 per cent first mortgage bonds of the Knoxville and Cincinnati Division. 

Railroads make wide use of bonds as security for collateral issues because of the nature of their development. The early railroads were short lines, each under separate corporate organization. By a long process of evolution, these scattered units were welded into larger, co-ordinated systems by the lease of property, mergers, or purchase of controlling interests. Large amounts of bonds were bought by the parent organizations to assist the financing of the subsidiaries, or build up the leased properties. Later, as in the foregoing examples, the acquired securities were used as a basis to recover the capital for operating purposes, either through the issuance of collateral trust bonds or as part of the security for so-called mortgage bonds. 

Bonds Secured by Stocks of other Companies 

Corporations also purchase the stocks of other companies to obtain control or to get into a position to make favorable working agreements. When such action is taken, the parent company may find it advantageous to recover its funds for operating purposes. Collateral trust bonds offer a convenient way to make this recovery without loss of control. The stocks deposited with the trustee may still be voted by the parent company, which will also continue to receive all dividends paid on the pledged collateral. In this way, the issuing corporation maintains any desirable element of control and may be able to profit by paying a smaller amount in interest than it receives in dividends. 

In the last analysis, it is impossible to determine the basic purpose of a collateral bond without knowing the intent of the directors responsible for the issue. While there is always the presumption that collateral issues, secured by stocks, are ipso facto for control purposes, such is not necessarily the case. The stocks may have been acquired years before and the present bonds issued for general financing, expansion, etc. At other times, the bonds may be issued directly and immediately in connection with the actual acquisition of the collateral. In the latter instance, there can be little question of the purpose.

The following examples of collateral issues secured by stock are fairly representative of the type of issues that are to be found today. 

American Telephone and Telegraph Company's thirty-year collateral trust 5's of 1946 were issued on the security of stocks of subsidiary corporations. In view of the company's practice of financing its subsidiaries largely through issues of the parent company, it is likely that this bond was issued primarily for financial reasons. It was replaced in 1936 by a debenture carrying an interest rate of 34 per cent.

On the other hand, the Allegheny Corporation's fifteen-year and twenty-year collateral trust convertible 5's of 1944 and 1949 were issued as a means of obtaining control of the companies whose stocks served as collateral for the bond issue. The collateral includes stocks of the Chesapeake Corporation, itself a holding company, and several other companies of the Van Sweringen group.³ 

The General Water Works Corporation's first lien and collateral trust gold 

5's of 1943 constitute a first lien on all the outstanding stock of eight water companies as well as on bonds and notes of the same eight companies. The published purpose of this bond issue was to acquire these operating companies and to retire their funded debt. This indicates that the issue was partly for financial reasons as well as to obtain control of the companies. 

Missouri Pacific Railroad secured 5 per cent gold bonds, due serially to 1956, are secured by 121,460 shares of capital stock of the New Orleans, Texas, and Mexico Railroad Company, which is a subsidiary of the Missouri Pacific 

Railroad. 

Bonds Secured by the Stocks and Bonds of Other Corporations 

Cases are found where the collateral consists of both bonds and stocks: 

For example, the National Steel Corporation's first collateral mortgage bonds, 3's, due in 1965, are secured by a pledge of all the issued capital stock of the subsidiary companies and by a first lien on certain demand mortgage bonds issued by the subsidiaries. These include such well-known companies as the 

Wierton Steel Company and the Great Lakes Steel Corporation. 

The Sinclair Consolidated Oil Corporation's first lien collateral gold 6's and 7's, while no longer outstanding, are another example. In this case, the collateral consisted of first mortgage 7 per cent bonds of the subsidiaries and nearly all the capital stock of the companies owned by the Sinclair Consolidated 

Oil Corporation. 

The Western Union collateral trust 5's of 1938 were issued to acquire the outstanding securities of subsidiary companies which had been operated under lease and whose securities had previously been guaranteed by the Western Union.

Bonds Secured by Obligations of the Issuing Company 

Collateral trust bonds secured by obligations of the same corporation are not used widely. An example is the 6 per cent collateral trust issue of the New York, New Haven, and Hartford Railroad, which was issued to retire the extended 7 per cent European Loan Debentures. The pledged securities consist of first and refunding mortgage bonds of the same company. 

More recently, the New York Central ten-year secured sinking fund 33's of 1946, were issued to retire bank loans outstanding at 4 per cent interest. These bonds are secured by an equal amount of 

New York Central Railroad Company's refunding and improvement gold 5's, series C, plus various stocks of the subsidiary companies. 

New York Central also has fifteen-year convertible secured 3's issued for refunding purposes, which are secured by a pledge of New 

York Central Railroad Company's collateral 4's, series C of 1998. 

Bonds of this type are used because it is possible to align the terms of unissued securities with prevailing money-market conditions. 

The pledged securities may lack appeal because of undesirable features or may carry an unnecessarily high rate of interest. The new offerings may correct these deficiencies. There is the further advantage that a company having in its treasury small amounts of unissued or reacquired stocks and bonds of several different issues may consolidate the collateral as security for one large issue. The larger, collateral issues could then be sold more favorably than the smaller direct-lien and miscellaneous issues.

Bonds Secured by Other Intangibles 

Occasionally, the collateral trust principle is applied to security other than stocks and bonds. The pledged assets may consist of valuable franchises, leasehold interests, or various other forms of intangible personal property. Examples of bonds secured in this manner are the following:

Elk Horn Coal Corporation's collateral trust 4's of 1956 are secured by stock purchase warrants, leases of coal lands, and all shares of stocks, notes and other evidences of indebtedness owned by the company. In addition, any certificates. of interest, leases, or royalties received as dividends from the shares of stock held as collateral are to be added to the security.

The Eastern Gas and Fuel Association's first and collateral trust 4's of 1956 

are secured by a lien on all real estate and rights in real estate and upon all franchises, privileges, licenses, patents, etc., as well as by all stocks, bonds, and notes of subsidiaries with certain exceptions. 

Copley Press, Incorporated, collateral gold 5's, series A of 1943, are secured by all the capital stock of subsidiaries owning three newspapers in Illinois and one in California, plus the personal guarantee of the president of the company who, according to the indenture, must pledge in his will securities equal to the amount of collateral bonds outstanding. Similar examples may be found wherein a portion of the collateral is made up of life insurance policies upon the chief officers.

Mixed Bonds 

In recent years there has been some use of bonds with mixed forms of security. They are usually secured by a lien upon real property and by other types of collateral. Most of these bonds have been issued at rates of interest favorable to the corporation. The complaint was common during much of the recent depression that although interest rates were very low, capital could be obtained only on the basis of furnishing the best security as collateral. Evidently, this statement has some basis in fact, because many of the recent bond issues have combined a first mortgage on the company's real property with extensive collateral security. For example, Goodyear Tire and

Rubber Company's first and collateral 34's of 1958 were issued in 1938 to refund an issue of 5 per cent bonds then outstanding. The new issue is secured by a first mortgage upon the fixed property of the corporation now owned or hereafter acquired, upon all leasehold estates now held, and upon notes of other companies. The Koppers 

Company's first and collateral trust 4's, series A, of 1951, issued in 1936, are secured by a first lien on all property with certain specific exceptions, plus the pledge of the stock held in ten other companies. 

Substitution of Collateral Provision may be made to have the collateral fixed for the life of the bonds, or the privilege of substitution may be granted. Assuming a wise selection of pledged assets, the advantage of the first plan is pronounced, but it may not be sufficiently flexible to accommodate the numerous changes that may occur. Flexibility may be desired by management as a means of retaining control over the hypothecated securities. On the other hand, from the point of view of the bond-

SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

147 holders, changes in collateral requirement may make it possible to maintain the original relationship between the value of the collateral and the par value of the outstanding bonds. An excellent illustration is found in the three collateral trust issues of the Allegheny Corporation, where it is stipulated that a deficiency exists whenever the market value of the collateral is less than 150 per cent of the par value of the bonds. Correction may be made by one or more of the following methods: (1) deposit of additional collateral; (2) retirement of sufficient amount of the outstanding bonds to restore the ratio; (3) a sufficient increase in the value of the pledged securities. In the event the ratio is not restored by any of these means within thirty days, the income on the deposited collateral is retained by the trustee until the deficiency is eliminated. 

Provisions to maintain the value of collateral throughout the life of a bond are of real benefit to investors, but even so they may be inadequate to meet the exigencies of changing times. In the illustration cited above, beginning in 1931 the value of the collateral was frequently less than 150 per cent of the outstanding bonds. The application of the collateral provisions was of little value because of the condition of the company, and all three issues dropped to a small fraction of their face value. 

The Investment Value of Collateral Bonds 

A collateral trust bond frequently implies a sort of family relation ship, i.e., intercorporate activities of a friendly variety. Because of this background, it behooves the investor to investigate carefully the securities which underlie collateral trust bonds, as well as the provisions designed to provide security in the future. From the viewpoint of the corporation, this type of bond constitutes a legitimate means of financing if the collateral is of high caliber. This requirement is met when collateral trust bonds are used as a means of financing subsidiaries, with senior securities of the latter pledged as collateral.

When used primarily for purposes of control, these bonds are likely to be secured by collateral carrying greater risk. Because of these varying conditions, investors need to scrutinize carefully the purpose for which the bonds are issued. سار .. 

Another approach for the investor, in investigating the security behind a collateral trust bond, is to proceed as if he were considering the purchase of the collateral itself. All the factors relating to the financial

position of a company, liquidity, asset condition, etc., should be applied to the companies issuing the collateral. If any sizeable portion of the collateral seems dubious, the bonds should be purchased only if the general credit position of the company offering the collateral issue is above question, or if the diversification of the collateral offsets other weaknesses.

Quasi-Secured Bonds 

For the want of a better term, certain bonds may be designated as "quasi-secured." These bonds include guaranteed, assumed, and joint bonds. Often these bonds are secured ultimately by liens on real property, but that is not the basis underlying this classification. 

Instead, the predominating feature to be noted at this time is the existence of multi-liability. In other words, some party or parties other than the issuing corporation are also liable for the bonds. While the security is not in the form of property, it does give added protection to the bondholders. For this reason, these bonds are presented in this chapter instead of the following one on unsecured funded obligations.

Guaranteed and Joint Bonds 

Strictly speaking, a guaranteed bond is one which is guaranteed by a corporation other than the issuing corporation. The value of a guaranty depends primarily upon the comprehensiveness of its statement and the standing of the corporation making the indorsement. 

Ordinarily, the guaranty is made within the family, being used frequently to help finance subsidiary companies. It is just another method of injecting the credit position of the parent company into the subsidiary. 

In the case of joint bonds, two or more companies assume the guaranty of some undertaking having common interest to the participating guarantors. Usually a subsidiary is organized to undertake the necessary co-operative function and the bonds issued to finance the project are given market strength through the guaranty of larger better-known concerns.

Examples of guaranteed and joint bonds are quite numerous. For example, the Central Pacific Railway Company's thirty-five-year guaranteed 5's of 1940 are guaranteed as to principal and interest by the Southern Pacific Railway through the indorsement of the latter road.

SECURED BONDS-OTHER 

149 The Washington Terminal Company's first mortgage 34's and 4's of 1945 are guaranteed jointly by the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad and the Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington Railroad Company, a subsidiary of the Pennsylvania Railroad. The Cincinnati Union Terminal Company's first mortgage, series C and D, of 1957 and 1971, are guaranteed jointly by the eight railroads using the terminal. Monongahela Railway Company's first mortgage, series A, 4's of 1960, are guaranteed by the Baltimore and Ohio, the Pennsylvania Railroad, and the Pittsburgh and Lake Erie Railroad Companies. 

Assumed Bonds

While it is common to guarantee the bonds of a subsidiary company, a more direct acceptance of liability is necessary in the event of actual merger. This is accomplished by an outright assumption of the bonds of the company taken over. Often the guaranty precedes the assumption. Thus, the first gold 41's of the Cleveland Short Line

Railway were previously guaranteed by the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern Railroad. Upon the absorption of the latter by the 

New York Central Railroad, this company took over the guaranty and still later actually assumed direct liability for the bonds. Likewise, upon the merger of the Central New England Railway into the New York, New Haven, and Hartford, the latter assumed the first gold 4's of the merged company. To indicate the prevalence of assumed bonds in the railway field, it may be noted that practically half of the issues for which the New York Central Railroad is responsible are assumed. 

Since the assumption of bonds arises primarily from consolidation, it is not surprising to find these bonds among the public utilities. As an example, the Standard Electric Company of California first mortgage gold 5's of 1939 and the San Joaquin Light and Power Company's unification and refunding 6's of 1952 have both been assumed by the Pacific Gas and Electric Company, which absorbed these companies and dissolved their original corporate identities.

CHAPTER IX UNSECURED BONDS 

HE term "unsecured bonds" is of more significance as a classification than as a means of interpretation. No implication is intended as to the safety or investment merit of bonds which are placed in this group. For example, most government bonds are classified as unsecured, but this does not affect their investment position. Or, the unsecured bonds of one corporation may be safer than the secured obligations of another. The chief distinction between secured and unsecured bonds is primarily the directness or priority of claim. An unsecured bond is any bond in which there is an absence of a lien on specific property, real or intangible, and which is issued solely on the basis of the general credit of the corporation. 

Debenture Bonds 

The term "debenture" means "debt," and in this broad sense, it could be used in connection with mortgage bonds; that is, mortgage bonds could be designated as mortgage debentures. However, financial practice has restricted the meaning of debenture to include only those bonds which are not secured by any specific pledge of property. 

The debenture bond is a widely accepted mode of corporate financing. 

It appeals to the corporation because the absence of a specific lien gives greater freedom to management and permits the reservation of secured obligations for periods of emergency. In the event of default in interest or principal payments, the bondholders are unable to bring foreclosure proceedings and have the property sold by the court. 

Instead, the bondholders have recourse to equity proceedings wherein a receiver is appointed for the protection of the bondholders, but the corporation continues to operate under this receivership for the benefit of all interests.

From the point of view of the investor, the debenture bond has an appeal because in the last analysis the general credit rating or financial condition of the corporation constitutes one of the most valid forms of security. A debenture bond issued by a corporation with a sound credit position is more likely to be a safe and satisfactory invest- 152

UNSECURED BONDS 

153 ment than a mortgage bond issued by a company in poor standing. 

Values usually disappear rapidly in the process of liquidation, and even the first mortgage bondholders frequently are unable to recover all their investment in the event of foreclosure and forced liquidation. 

In addition to the soundness of present position, protection against future contingencies is also necessary to safeguard the rights and interests of investors. Various checks or limitations on operations are commonly provided in the bond indenture and ordinarily take one of the following two forms: 

1. Under the first plan, no limitation is placed upon future financing except that the company may not issue securities having prior lien to the debenture bonds. If mortgage bonds are issued, it is usually provided that the outstanding debentures must be included under the mortgage indenture on a basis at least equal to that of the new issue. 

This is illustrated by the 5 per cent debenture of the American Cyanamid Company where the company agrees not to create "any lien upon its property without first securing this issue equally and notably therewith." The agreement does not cover purchase money obligations or pledges created in the normal course of business as security for temporary loans or the performance of contracts. The exception is a customary one under this plan of investor protection. 

2. The second plan definitely affects the future financial policies of the company. The restriction may vary from the simple requirement of a certain coverage of fixed charges before additional bonds of the same class may be issued, to the more binding stipulation that the consent of the bondholders must be obtained before any secured bonds may be authorized. In addition, restrictions may be placed upon the payment of dividends, short-term borrowing, and other phases of operations. For example, the following provisions are incorporated in the indenture of the McKesson and Robbins Company's convertible debentures, gold 51's of 1950.¹ a) Neither the corporation nor any of its subsidiaries may pledge or mortgage its property (except for purchase money obligations or mortgages assumed in the acquisition of property) as long as any of the debentures are outstanding. b) Dividends may not be paid and further investment in fixed 1 This company failed in 1938. See chapter XVI for discussion. On May 15, 1941, the court approved a reorganization plan which provided for replacing the outstanding 5's of 

1950 with a new issue of 4's of 1956.

property is not permissible if it would result in reducing current assets to less than 3 times the current liabilities. c) Money may not be borrowed "so as to reduce consolidated current assets below an amount equivalent to 2 times consolidated current liabilities."

The effect of the control placed in the debenture bonds under the second principle may prove to be of vital concern to the interests of both the bondholders and the corporation. While designed to protect the position of the former, arbitrary limitation of action may work to their detriment. Sound management and wise expansion of the company are of benefit to the bondholders as well as to the stockholders. Curbing legitimate financing does not necessarily achieve ideal protection for the bondholders; instead, it may check the growth of the corporation or prevent changes necessary to meet competition. 

From the viewpoint of corporate management, restrictive clauses may place undue emphasis upon the current position at the expense of future opportunities. Since flexibility of financing and a substantial degree of freedom for management are desirable, protection of the first type would seem to be more satisfactory to both the corporation and the investor. Reasonable protection of the latter is found in the prohibition against the creation of a prior lien, and at the same time the corporation retains the desired freedom to undertake future financing whenever circumstances dictate. 

Substitution of Debenture Bonds for Preferred Stock 

Sometimes debenture bonds are used as a method of financing the retirement of preferred stock.2 Management may decide in favor of such a revision of financial structure in order to save the difference between the higher rate of dividends and the lower rate of interest which would be paid on bonds. At the same time, the risk is increased by the substitution of a fixed charge which must be met regularly for a contingent charge that may be avoided if the directors so elect. If future earnings prove to be inadequate, default in the interest may occur and cause the company to be placed into receivership. There is the further burden of a definite maturity date when the principal must be retired through one means or another, while 2 For example, the Standard Oil Company (New Jersey) debenture 3's, 1961, were sold to help finance the retirement of the 5 per cent preferred stock of a subsidiary, the Standard Oil Export Corporation. The Purity Bakeries Corporation sinking fund debenture 5's of 1938 were issued to retire the 7 per cent preferred stock and debt of subsidiaries.

UNSECURED BONDS 

155 the preferred stock may provide permanent financing without any fixed time limit.

The risks incurred in switching from preferred stock to debentures suggest caution in the adoption of this policy. The savings made possible by the rate differential does tend to strengthen the current position under normal operations but only at the sacrifice of longer-term security. Hence, there must be full assurance that careful consideration has been given to the latter both as to the prospects of stable earnings and the ability to discharge the indebtedness at maturity. Assuming these two important prerequisites, debentures may occasionally be substituted to advantage for preferred stock where a high rate exists, or where the creation of a sinking fund is required to retire the stock.

The exchange of preferred stock for debentures also suggests the need for increased recognition by management of the public welfare. 

Too frequently, temporary and spectacular gains are the goal of management instead of greater stability of earnings with its resulting soundness of position. As a result, the economy may be shocked by unnecessary failure and investors suffer a loss which may be damaging to their confidence. Giving weight to these larger criteria, it is apparent that the full burden of proof rests upon the management which elects to replace preferred stock with debt. 

Debentures Used to Retire Other Debt 

When debentures are used to retire other debt, a distinction must be made between floating, or short-time indebtedness, and permanent debt arising as the result of fixed capital outlays. The funding of floating debt is a practice to be avoided. If a corporation is unable to pay its current obligations or to provide its working capital with current financing, it will not likely be able to pay the fixed charges accompanying the debenture debt. Where used to retire debt which arose in connection with the expansion of the plant, the use of debentures is justified. For instance, the corporation may have temporarily available an unusually large amount of working capital. It may use this capital for expansion or improvement of the plant with the intention of selling a bond issue later to recover the funds. In doing this, interest charges may be saved during the construction of the plant and the period prior to the funding of the expenditures into a bond issue. At one time, debenture bonds were commonly

used for this purpose but more recently, especially in the case of industrial concerns, there has been some tendency for debenture bonds to be replaced by mixed bonds secured by a mortgage on property and by collateral.

Debentures as a Source of New Capital 

The use of debenture bonds to raise new capital is virtually the equivalent of the process just described. The difference is that when used to retire debt, the capital outlay has already been made, whereas in raising new funds the investment of the capital is delayed. 

Neither may the delay in putting the capital to work be extended unduly because earnings will not be forthcoming to cover the interest charges. Assuming a proper balancing between the investment or utilization of the funds and the financial arrangement, the debenture bond may be said to be a sound medium for raising funds to provide for fixed investments, but it should be used sparingly as a source of working capital.

The Debenture Bond and the Field of Enterprise 

The debenture bond is a common medium of financing in the industrial and public utility fields, but it finds only restricted use in railroad finance. Moreover, many of its characteristics reflect the nature of the field of activity in which it is used. Such features as the rate of interest and the maturity are incidences of the industry more than the type of issue. Likewise, the condition of the company and the state of the money market will exercise marked influence. The accompanying tables are based upon one hundred industrial debenture issues selected at random, upon nearly all the railroad debenture bonds now outstanding, and upon a large portion of the public utility debenture bond issues. It will be observed from a study of Table 20 that the rates of interest paid by the different fields vary materially. 

Most of the issues carry rates of interest equal to the lowest rate in each class interval. Thus, the prevalent industrial rates appear to be 4 per cent, 5 per cent, and 6 per cent. A number of years ago a similar study showed no bonds below 41 per cent, but there are signs that industrial corporations are taking advantage of the low money rates of recent years. A large amount of refunding has been done since 1932, and today a considerable number of issues paying 3 and 3 per cent are to be found. Many bonds have been called before maturity and replaced by issues of the same type at a lower rate.

Considering the fact that industrials are believed to have greater uncertainty as to future outlook, it is significant that they tend to have a lower rate of interest than either the utilities or the railroads. 

The advantage is largely the result of a greater amount of refunding during the period of low interest rates. The utilities have been hampered by governmental restrictions, and railroads have suffered from inability to earn fixed charges satisfactorily. In addition, both the utilities and railroads have many prior lien obligations which render the sale of debenture issues much more difficult. It should be kept in mind, however, that this table deals only with debenture bonds and that the utilities have been able to do considerable amounts of refunding at lower interest rates through the use of secured issues. 

In view of the marked preference for secured bonds for railroad financing, it seems remarkable that there are as many as forty-nine railroad debenture issues carrying rates of less than 5 per cent.

It is highly improbable that industrial assets have such a uniform life, or that industrial corporations will need added funds for so definite a period as fifteen years. Actually, the outstanding use of ten- or fifteen-year periods is an expression of a prevailing investment style in the money market resulting from the unsettled conditions of the 1930's. Hence, corporations borrowed for the maximum term possible during the period of low interest rates.

The debenture bonds of public utility companies tend to have longer maturities. The bonds having six- to ten-year terms were all issued in the 1930's when money conditions and business uncertainties compelled the use of shorter-term financing. Conversely, the brighter business outlook of the previous period made possible the use of extended maturities. All thirteen of the issues found in the fifty-one to one hundred years group (all actually have a life of one hundred years) were issued prior to 1931. Financial terms are naturally related to conditions which exist at the time of issue, but the wisdom of century maturities is open to question irrespectve of the contemporary markets. Technological improvements occur with such rapidity in the utility industry as to make such long-term financing hazardous for both the operating and the holding company.

UNSECURED BONDS 

159 Like the public utilities, many of the railroad issues have a long maturity. Again, there is grave question as to whether such remote maturities constitute sound financing. Railroad debentures occupy a junior position and are usually preceded in claim by a sizeable overhang of secured bonds. The practice of using well-secured bonds was established early in railroad history and debentures were usually issued only as a result of reorganizations. The position of the debentures is also made tenuous by the erratic record of railroad earnings. 

Both conditions invite careful analysis by prospective investors because the debentures may be an anomaly of high risk combined with limited return. In periods of prosperity, the return is necessarily limited to the stated rate and, in times of adversity, the security may be seriously affected by the existence of prior lien issues.

The debentures of two of the railroads illustrate also the functioning of the protective clause. Automatically, these issues became mortgage bonds when the corporation issued new secured bonds. Despite

this feature and others, debenture bonds may sometimes lack public appeal and some additional attraction may be attached. This is the reason for attaching the conversion feature which will now be discussed.

Nature of Convertible Bonds 

Convertible bonds give the holder the privilege of exchanging his holdings for securities of a different type, usually common stock. 

The conversion feature may be attached to any type of security other than common stock, but it is most commonly appended to the unsecured debenture. The conversion privilege is always of potential value to the bondholders but may never prove to be of actual value. 

It permits the holder of the bonds to obtain a position in corporate activities in the creditor group but later, upon his option, to transfer his lot to that of the residual, or ownership, group. It does not permit the bondholder to keep his original security and still share in the net profits as is true of participating preferred stock, but he is given an opportunity to be either a bondholder or a stockholder. 

Value of Conversion Privilege to the Corporation and the Investor

The conversion privilege appears to confer a great favor upon the bondholders without contributing equivalent benefits to the corporation. If the corporation does not succeed in making unusual profits, the convertible bondholders quite naturally retain their original position. On the other hand, if the enterprise is successful to a marked degree, the bondholder may convert and share in the exceptional returns to which the residual equity would be entitled. To have the option of a preferred position as a creditor in the time of adversity and, at the same time, be permitted to convert to the favorable position of the common stockholder in the event of success, makes the position of the convertible bondholder seem especially attractive. 

Actually, a convertible bond provides many compensating benefits to the issuing corporation. By attaching the conversion privilege, the corporation makes the bond more attractive and is usually able to obtain funds at a lower interest rate. Often, it is the equivalent of selling stocks at bond prices at a time when stocks would not be sufficiently attractive to be sold in adequate amounts. Moreover, if the corporation realizes satisfactory earnings, the convertible bond provides its own method of retirement.

UNSECURED BONDS 

161 

Terms of Conversion 

Conversion is a privilege which may prove to be of great value to the bondholders. At the same time, the exercise of the option dilutes the earnings which would be available to the old stockholders. 

To provide a proper balancing of the interest and rights of these two groups of security holders, the following limitations upon conversion are common: 

1. The time of conversion may be limited; that is, after a certain date, conversion may not be permitted at any price. Thus, the $120,- 

000,000, 5 per cent convertible bond issue, due in 1950, of the Cities Service Company restricted the option to the first five years of the bonds. The U.S. Radiator Corporation convertible debenture 5's of 

1946 are convertible for the first seven years of the ten-year life of the bond. 

2. Recent practice frequently makes the terms less favorable with the lapse of time. This principle may be illustrated by the Allis 

Chalmers Manufacturing Company sinking-fund debenture 4's of 1952. This bond is convertible into common stock at $75 per share on or before September 1, 1939; $80 per share on or before September 

1, 1941; $85 through September 1, 1943; $90 through September 1, 1945; and $95 per share to August 1, 1952. 

The Chicago Molded Products Corporation convertible debenture 

5's of 1949 apply the same principle through a different conversion. arrangement. Each $100 of principal amount is convertible into 13 shares of common through April 1, 1940; into 11 shares through 

April 1, 1941; 9 shares through April 1, 1942; 8 shares through April 

1, 1943; and 7 shares thereafter to maturity date. The common stock is $1 par and was originally issued at $6.25 per share. 

3. Sometimes the conversion price may be determined by a sliding scale based on the principal amounts converted. To illustrate: the first ten million dollars of principal amount of bonds converted might be in the ratio of $25 per share, the second ten million dollars in the ratio of $30 per share, and the third ten million dollars in the ratio of $35 per share, etc. The purpose of such a price progression is to encourage early conversion. On the other hand, there is the possible disadvantage that the arrangement may lead to increasing resistance on the part of the bondholders to convert. 

As is the case with convertible preferred stock, convertible bonds usually carry provision to protect the investor against dilution or loss

of the conversion privilege. This is usually accomplished through a clause in the indenture which provides a method for adjusting the terms of conversion in the event of stock dividends, split-ups, etc. If the conversion securities should be abolished through merger, the bonds are made convertible into equivalent securities of the new company.
