Conversion Possibilities 

Thus far, it has been assumed that the bonds are always converted into common stock. This is the most typical form of exchange, but the following conversion possibilities also exist: (1) conversion of bonds into securities having priority; (2) conversion of bonds into preferred stock; (3) conversion of bonds into a combination of preferred and common stocks.

The first form of conversion cannot be justified except when used to convert short-term obligations into longer term. The second offers little incentive to the investor unless the preferred stock is participating; otherwise, there would be no advantage in converting except possibly for a slightly higher yield. The third alternative is used only occasionally. 

When Should the Investor Convert?

One of the perplexing problems that always faces the convertible bondholder is when to convert. Not only is there a question of shifting from a creditor's to a stockholder's position, but at the same time the exchange should be made so as to obtain the greatest profit. The transition from creditor to stockholder is primarily a matter of investment policy and may be determined only in terms of individual investment needs. The profit possibilities are affected more by the market price of the stock and its effect on the price of the convertible bonds. For this reason, several concrete cases may be noted for the purpose of illustrating the inevitable interplay of influence between the price movements of bonds and the stock into which they may be converted.

Market Price of Convertibles

Because of the fact that convertible bonds may be exchanged for stock, their respective prices should show a high degree of correla-

tion. If the price of the bonds should lag, speculators or investors would buy the bonds for profit. Oppositely, a precipitous advance in the price of bonds may cause corrective liquidation. The facts presented in Table 22 reveal clearly the sympathetic movement of prices. 

In four of the six instances, the convertible bonds and stocks reached their high prices in the same month, and a similar condition is true of the low prices. However, the trend of the price of a convertible bond and the stock into which it is convertible conform only so long as the price of the stock is sufficiently high to make the exchange ratio attractive. For example, the convertible bonds of the 

American Beet Sugar Company were exchangeable into stock in 1929 on the basis of $50 per share of stock; in other words, a $1,000 bond could be exchanged for 20 shares of stock. At the time, the bonds sold as low as 75, and the stock as high as 20. To show that the conversion feature would have no effect under these conditions the purchase of a bond at its lowest price of 75 may be assumed, following which it is exchanged for stock. The results obtained would be: .$750

In other words, the upper limit of the price for bonds is determined by the price of the stock into which it is convertible. If, however, the stock price is below the conversion figure, the market price of the bond is determined in the same manner as other types of bonds by the yield and the credit standing of the company. Under these circumstances, the price of the bond may be above or below par, depending upon market conditions and the outlook for the particular bond. For example, the Allis Chalmers Company convertible 4's of 1952 were selling in the spring of 1940 at approximately 108 although the price of the stock was not high enough to have influence.

The foregoing principles make it clear that an immediate and almost precise relationship should exist between the price of a convertible bond and the stock for which it may be exchanged providing the market price of the stock is above the conversion price. In the case of the International Telephone and Telegraph Company, the convertible bonds reached their highest price in 1929 on exactly the same day as the stock. At that time, each bond was convertible into fifteen shares of stock, which for the purpose of conversion meant the stock had a nominal value of $663 (1000-15). In other words, the bond price should have been one and one-half (100 over

66) times the market price of the stock. Since the latter reached a high of $149, the bonds should have sold at $223.875. Actually, the bonds sold at $224, or almost in exact accordance with the determined price.

To What Extent Are Convertible Bonds Converted? 

To what extent do bondholders exercise the privilege to convert? 

To what extent do corporations realize upon the value of conversion as a means of debt liquidation? While these two questions are prompted by two entirely different approaches, the answers are of necessity contained in the same data. Unfortunately, this information may not now be assembled in any large quantity. Many convertible bonds were issued during 1928 and 1929 with conversion ratios based on the high stock prices prevailing at that time. The tremendous decline in stock prices since that time has discouraged, if not almost annihilated, the likelihood of early conversion. There are a few outstanding individual instances, however, where bonds have been largely liquidated by the conversion process. For example, the American 

Telephone and Telegraph Company put out a convertible bond issue of $150,000,000 in 1906; at the expiration of the conversion period, March 1, 1919, less than $3,000,000 of the bonds were still outstanding. 

The $50,000,000 convertible issue of the Anaconda Copper Company was fully converted during the 1929 stock market boom. 

Receivers' Certificates 

As suggested by the title, receivers' certificates are issued by receivers who have assumed active management of corporations that have failed. It is obviously impossible to accommodate a company in distress by means of normal financing, and special privileges are necessary if the receiver is to succeed in the task of rehabilitating the enterprise. Not only is this required because of the weak credit position of an insolvent organization, but the efficiency of the operating structure is also reduced to a low state. As a prelude to the fateful hour of failure, private management impoverishes the inventories and expends a minimum for the maintenance of plant. Consequently, one of the first tasks of a receiver is to place the business on a basis where it can operate normally. To do this, financial media must be created which will enable the receiver to raise funds despite the impoverished condition of the company.

UNSECURED BONDS 

167 To make it possible for the receiver to raise funds, a moratorium is placed upon the private obligations previously outstanding, and the receiver is given authority by the court to issue certificates with priority of claim over some or all of the outstanding liens. Such special dispensation is made possible legally by virtue of the fact that the title to all property rests, in a sense, in the court which may therefore order preferential treatment of holders of receivers' certificates. 

From a financial and business point of view, the priority of claim is equally necessary because of the impossiblity of raising funds by less drastic measures. Obtaining new funds is advantageous to the existing security holders, since added capital may be necessary if any of the existing investment is to be recouped. For this reason, receivers' certificates usually precede the issues in default and follow any issue which may still be current, or which appears certain to pull through unimpaired.

Receivers' certificates are usually issued for a short term because it is anticipated that they will either be liquidated or exchanged for new securities upon the successful reorganization of the company. 

A limited maturity is also in keeping with the types of expenditures usually made by the receivers, viz., for wages, materials, and for the maintenance of plant. Where capital expenditures of long life are essential to the rehabilitation, it may not be unreasonable to issue certificates having extended maturities. However, certificates are not issued often for capital expenditures other than for the completion of projects undertaken prior to the receivership. 

Because of the limited life and the priority of claim, receivers' certificates usually carry a high investment rating. The holders may not be paid off in cash, but they will usually receive senior securities in the reorganized company. The reorganization plan of the Wabash 

Railroad Company sets forth a typical treatment for receivers' certificates. In the plan of reorganization dated January 1, 1941,³ five issues of receivers' certificates are listed, four series are held by the R.F.C. and one by banks. The first series, second series, and serial certificates held by the R.F.C. are to receive 75 per cent of the principal in new thirty-year first 4 per cent bonds and 25 per cent in forty-year income A 4 per cent bonds. The series A (held by R.F.C.) and series B (held by banks) certificates are to receive 37.5 per cent of the principal 

8 Dated March 15, 1941, U. S. District Court, Eastern Division of Eastern District of 

Missouri.

in first 4's, 12.5 per cent in income A 4's, and 50 per cent in serial collateral notes bearing 1 per cent interest and maturing over a twelve-year period. Accrued interest on the receivers' certificates is to be paid in full in cash.

In contrast, the plan provides for paying the favorably located first mortgage bonds with new first 4's and with income A 4's, but in no case will the bondholders receive more than 17.6 per cent of their back interest in cash with the balance to be funded through new bond issues. Less favorably situated mortgage bonds are to receive even less. For example, the Des Moines Division first mortgage 4's are to receive 70 per cent in fifty-year income B 41's (following both the first 4's and the income A's) and 30 per cent in preferred stock. 

It appears evident that in this reorganization the receivers' certificates hold a privileged position.

The use of receivers' certificates also casts another ray of light upon the public interest in private corporations. Private management is presumed to deal equitably with the rights of investors as long as the corporation is operating normally, but in the event of failure, the court intervenes. It may be contended that this is caused solely by the possible conflict of rights which is more or less inevitable in time of distress, but this, in turn, means that such a conflict would affect the public interest. In addition, it is reasonable to believe that the public gains more by constructive rehabilitation where possible than by drastic liquidation, in which event, the public has an interest in promoting the former. To do this, receivers' certificates are given a right-of-way over other obligations.

PART III ORGANIZATION AND STRUCTURE

CHAPTER X PROMOTION 

HE instruments of finance which have been described in the preceding section are simply the raw materials-the lumber, brick, and mortar - with which to build the structure of finance. Unfortunately, there is a tendency to allow the complicated or diverse character of the former to conceal the more basic elements of the latter. The styles of securities do not change with the frequency of automobile models, but nevertheless they do appear in rhythmic procession to meet changing public moods. Such variations in security forms and types are the subject of much financial discussion, but this does not mean that the instruments constitute the essence of financial operation. The design of the securities is dictated by the problems of distribution or sale, but it does not constitute finance in the larger sense. 

If securities themselves do not constitute finance, what then is its meaning? More significant are the important organic relations which exist between financial administration and business operation. 

How well does the plan of financing accommodate the stresses and strains of never-ending business fluctuations? Is the financial program a drag or burden on operations, or does it serve as a girding member of the larger corporate structure? These are the questions which reflect the comprehensive nature of finance. In brief, the essence of finance is to be found in underlying policy more than in the superstructure of practical operations. For the most part, policy is developed by a small centralized group of officials whose position is made possible by the form of organization. An appreciation of the part played by the policy-making group will be aided by an analysis of the purposes and nature of business promotion. Here, the student may see the beginnings of corporate life and get an understanding of the motives which serve as a drive-shaft of business activity. 

Nature of Promotion

In the language of the dictionary, promotion is "an act of advancing or encouraging." Although the term is used in a more tech- 173

nical sense in the field of corporation finance, the common everyday connotation of the word is applicable. In other words, two of the major contributions of the promoter to business should be: 

1. The advancement of business enterprise. Ideally, any act of promotion should result in an improved way of doing business, or should introduce a product which lends itself to social progress. Practically, the promoter's objective is the attainment of a satisfactory profit. Such personal gain may seem to contradict the larger, social objective, but in reality it is intended as a practical incentive to stimulate action and to serve as a test on the soundness of proposed improvements. Indeed, if a loss appeared to be likely, the project would have little justification in terms of social desirability. 

2. Supplying the optimism necessary to overcome the many barriers and obstacles existing in the path of a newly conceived enterprise. The promoter must encourage his followers and those with whom he comes in contact, or otherwise the anticipated adventure may fail to survive.

Opportunities for the promotion of new enterprise are found principally in the introduction of a new product or service or in the improvement of existing business practices or products. Too often, the concept of promotion has been commonly limited to activity of the first type, but the present state of business development has naturally increased the importance of changes in products already in use. In either event, three essential elements are involved in the act of promotion: (1) discovery, (2) assembling the factors necessary for production and distribution, and (3) financing the project. 

Discovery 

When Columbus sailed westward in 1492, many would have said that he discovered a new continent upon first sighting land. Actually, the true discovery did not occur until after the party had landed and sufficient investigation had been undertaken to warrant the finding that they had really found land never before known to civilization. 

This principle is equally true of prospective business products and enterprises; they are not truly discovered until they have been investigated thoroughly. For the purpose of promotion, investigation is the essence of discovery.

The ultimate goal of investigation is to determine whether or not a prospective business enterprise would prove profitable in actual

PROMOTION 

175 operation. Possibly this criterion should be taken for granted in a capitalistic economy, but several developments in our national thought make it desirable to state its justification. It should be emphasized that reference is not made to the profitability arising from monopoly or other special privileges but to that which arises from the performance of a function under competitive conditions. In the latter light, profitability is an index of soundness which indicates whether or not any particular business venture is self-liquidating. In addition, the profit margin is intended to serve as a buffer against failure with its consequent shock upon the entire economy. Individual promoters may lack the sense of social responsibilty to be aware of this more ultimate test, but unless this be the result of their actions, there can be little defense of profits as a social phenomenon. Thus, the test of profitability is intended to serve not merely as a benefit and an incentive to the few, but it should contribute equally as an important safeguard to economic soundness and to the public welfare. 

The area and nature of investigation to be conducted by the promoter are indicated by the following questions: (1) What opportunities shall be investigated? (2) What factors shall be investigated?

What Opportunities Shall be Investigated? 

Often, the source of a business opportunity is an invention. However, the inventor usually knows little of business policies and practices and needs someone schooled in these affairs to determine whether or not the idea is practicable. Such an individual is the promoter. 

At times it is possible for a promoter to reject immediately certain inventions, knowing from long experience that the device would not sell. At other times careful investigation is necessary before a decision can be made.

Other business opportunities that may call for investigation by the promoter are: 

1. Proposed consolidations (discussed in detail at a later point). 

2. Establishment of a new concern in an existing field of business. 

3. Expansion of an old concern to produce a new product, where it may be desirable to organize a subsidiary company. Promotion may be undertaken by the company itself or by promoters employed for the assignment. 

4. Introduction of new services (as opposed to products) by either old or new companies.

Factors To Be Investigated 

If the investigation is deemed warranted after a preliminary consideration of the proposed venture, the problem arises immediately as to what factors should be analyzed. The objectives should be clearly outlined at the beginning or much time will be wasted. While these objectives will vary according to specific cases, there are a few aims which are general to all investigations. 

1. Is there a demand for the new product or could a demand be created? 

2. What is the state of competition? 

3. Is the new product properly protected by patent? 

4. What would be the cost of producing the product and how much profit may be anticipated? 

5. Could the necessary capital be raised to finance the project? 

The Demand Factor 

The extent to which the demand factor may be reduced to reliable estimates varies greatly according to the field of enterprise. In the public utility field, the forecast of demand is facilitated by the degree of standardization existing in this type of business and the greater likelihood of a comparable situation being found for estimating purposes. In the railroad field, the problem is slightly more difficult, `but again the existence of a comparable case is more than likely. In the industrial area, however, the projection of demand is not so simple. 

Complications arise because it is difficult to find projects operating under conditions similar to those of the proposed enterprise, and if found comprehensive operating statistics would probably be unavailable.

Within the industrial group, the problem of estimating the demand is also greatly affected by the type of product. Here, the chief consideration is found in the type of market in which the new product or service may be classified. Is the proposed product a substitute or an accessory? Is its market fairly independent? The answers to these questions are significant to any determination of the demand factor. If the product is intended mainly as a substitute for some other article, the calculation of demand is facilitated to some degree. 

At the same time, the question as to whether or not the market may accept the substitute product can never be truly answered until it is actually offered for sale. However, the limits of market appeal may

PROMOTION 

177 be measured more readily in relation to the existing product than where such a comparison is lacking. Thus, it should be easier to calculate the potential demand for nylon as a substitute for silk than it would for some innovation such as television. 

Where the product is to be used mainly in conjunction with another major article, the task of estimating demand is much easier. 

Under these conditions, reasonable statements of demand may be obtained from the producers of the primary commodity, with the added possibility of placing orders on a definite contractual basis. 

Even where fixed arrangements cannot be worked out in advance, the scope of the market for an accessory product is more easily perceived. By learning the total number of units of the major product in use, there is less difficulty in estimating the demand likely to appear. These conditions are well illustrated in the automobile accessory industry. Obviously, no more accessories can be sold than there are cars being produced or already produced and still in service. With this absolute limit visualized, a more accurate appraisal can be made of the demand likely to be realized. The objection may be raised that there may be competition by producers of the same article, but this may often be controlled by patent protection or by contractual commitment. In the absence of such protection, the difficulty of determining the extent of competition is no different from that of any other product.

If a product is intended to appeal to a fairly independent or undeveloped market, demand is more difficult to estimate. Such a situation calls for thorough and complete market analysis. This involves a careful study to determine the product's uses, the types of customers to be reached, and the geographical extent of the market. In addition to data directly related to the product, it will be necessary to ascertain the facts concerning all forms of competition. Can the proposed product compete with possible substitutes? Can it compete successfully against all other commodities for a share of the national income? 

Methods of Investigation 

Attention next needs to be given to the method of conducting the investigation. In other words, how will the information be obtained? First, the problem may be assigned to a market analyst, who specializes in this field. By careful research and the application of other readily available data, the market analyst is enabled to render an opinion as to the marketability of the product. His opinion may

not always be accurate, but it is generally worthy of careful consideration. Second, demand may be estimated by some sort of a trial-anderror method, i.e., by a sampling process. This method is not practical for all products but is feasible in many instances. Third, the promoter may elect to send a questionnaire to a number of people within the market area in which he expects to operate. While this method has been overworked or poorly applied, it may at times be used to good advantage.¹ In all these methods, the results obtained are of necessity purely an estimate, but the material is more than essential to a complete investigation.

State of Competition 

The second factor is often affected by the changing character of the first. Competition may be normal for a given period but may quickly be made intense by a change in public demand or by the vagaries of market action. An illustration is the aviation industry. Beginning with the last half of 1929 and during 1930 the sales volume declined precipitously because of general business conditions. This narrowing of the market quite naturally intensified the race to secure the remaining business. Oppositely, beginning in 1938, the world-wide armament program increased demand and eased competitive pressure. 

The entry of a company into a new field must be made with extreme caution. The potentialities of a new industry often appear to be so great that too many companies may be attracted. For example, few radio companies survived the early stampede to gain a foothold in this industry. The automobile industry is now well out of the infant stage, but competitive risks still continue, and during its beginnings the weeding-out process was strongly in evidence. Less than 10 per cent of the companies entering this field have survived. 

Not only is competition apt to be keen in entering an entirely new field, but it is one of the largest obstacles to overcome in entering an old established industry. Such a venture should be undertaken only if the promoter is assured of one or more of the following prospects: 

1. Evidence that the product can be produced more efficiently or more cheaply than is currently being done. This may be made possible through the discovery of new methods of production or other means of lowering cost. 

1 Recently, the widely recognized work of Dr. George Gallup of the American Institute of Public Opinion has done much to establish the validity of the questionnaire technique. 

Dr. Gallup's work has shown what can be done with a small, but carefully selected, sample.

PROMOTION 

179 2. Possession of abundant evidence that the concerns already in the field are lax in production methods or are generally inefficient. 

3. Acquisition of actual orders, preferably on a contract basis. 

Patents 

In entering a new field, the promoter frequently must ascertain whether or not the new product or device is adequately protected by the necessary patent rights.2 In order to eliminate all doubts about protection, it is more than likely that a reliable patent lawyer will be consulted. Legal proceedings are apt to have a deterring influence upon the morale of the organization as well as to cut into its profits. It should be recognized, however, that there is no sure escape from patent suits because competitors may initiate legal action solely for the purpose of using obstruction tactics.3

Patents also give rise to an interesting question of internal policy with respect to their valuation. Many patents are worth much more than their costs, while numerous others are not. Because cost is so futile a base for the valuation of patents, it is the general practice to rely upon the earnings as an index of their value. Many conservative and established companies go to the other extreme of carrying their patents at a very nominal figure in their financial statements. Even in those concerns where patents and other intangibles account for the bulk of the income, it is not unusual to find them shown at very reasonable amounts, or even omitted. The sum of $1 is often shown. Such practice indicates to the stockholders and the investors that the company has patents which it considers valuable, but for the sake of conservatism, no attempt is made to report their actual value. The promoter of the new enterprise could make no mistake by following a similar policy. Overvaluation of patents at the outset can do much more injury to a beginning enterprise than undervaluation. 

Costs and Profits

It should be observed that all the data assembled by the promoter are on an estimated basis. For this reason it may appear rather in- 

2 Currently, corporations obtain more than half of all patents issued. In 1938, 17.2 per cent of all patents were issued to corporations of $50,000,000 assets or over, 34.5 per cent to smaller corporations, 5.4 per cent to foreign corporations, and 42.9 per cent to individuals. 

T.N.E.C. Hearings, Part 3, Patents: Proposals for Changes in Law and Procedure, p. 1127.

congruous to calculate the costs of operations or to be optimistic enough to forecast the profits. This does not mean that any one cost schedule or profit figure will be found. Instead, a number of cost schedules should be prepared to allow for the following: 

1. Varying demand schedules. If 500 units are considered to be a reasonable daily production, cost estimates should also be prepared for production of 100, 250, 400, 750, 1,000, etc., per day. It is not intended here to specify in exact detail how many schedules should be prepared, since this will naturally be adjusted to meet the condition peculiar to the case. 

2. Varying prices for the major cost factors. Prices of raw materials especially may be subject to change, and such contingencies should be provided for on a schedule basis. The right to buy materials at a specified price through a long-term contract should not deter the promoter from making the schedules. Even though a specified price is guaranteed, any drop in the market price of the raw material would be adverse to the prospective company's cause. This development would give a definite advantage to new competitors, or to old companies who may be in a position to renew their contracts. 

3. Not only should allowance be made for the actual costs of production, but in addition adequate consideration must be given to numerous costs and sacrifices that are necessary to reach the state of a going concern. Examples of such costs are the initial taxes and legal fees upon undertaking a business, losses likely to be incurred in seasoning the business, and special advertising expenses. 

The preparation of these schedules will give a variety of profit figures, and, if the investigation is conducted honestly, losses should also be in evidence at times. Besides giving income results, the schedules may be used to help determine the amount of capital necessary to conduct operations. While anticipated income is a measure of the amount of capital the new company will be able to finance, the actual amount of capital required is determined more immediately by the expectations of output. Whenever the prospective income appears likely to be inadequate to carry the capital needs, the project should be dropped.

Is the Capital Available? 

If the investigation thus far warrants the organization of a new company, the promoter should next be assured of the capital necessary

PROMOTION 

181 to finance the project. Where the company is to be of small proportions the major sources of funds will most likely be from friends of the parties interested in the venture, or in any event, the funds will have to be raised by direct selling. If the organization is to be large in scope, the financing will have to be accomplished through some existing company or through resort to large capitalists, because most investment bankers will not handle securities for new enterprises except possibly in the public utility field. In either case, the promoter should be positive that the sources will produce the funds when needed. (At this time, the certainty of the funds is our only concern; the actual selling of the securities will be discussed later.) 

It is only after detailed investigation takes place that the project may be said to be truly discovered. The idea may have originated long before, but it cannot be considered ready for business adoption until it has been thoroughly tested. Investigation often leads to a negative conclusion but may be well worth the price. If the conclusion is favorable, the steps required to organize the company and to assemble the necessary means of production will be undertaken. Even this favorable conclusion is no guaranty of the success of the enterprise, a fact supported by an abundance of evidence. Assembling The next function of the promoter is to assemble the factors which are necessary to put the project in working order. The main tasks of assembly are the following: (1) selecting and acquiring the site of operations; (2) arranging for the construction of the plant and equipment; (3) organizing the corporation and determining the financial plan. 

Selecting the Site 

The power of the promoter to select a site for the location of the plant will depend usually upon the extent of his continuing interest in the enterprise. If the promoter is to become the operating executive, he will exert much influence, if not practically control the selection. On the other hand, if he is hired temporarily to take care of the details of promotion, the original backers of the venture will undoubtedly control plant location. 

To acquire the property it is necessary for the promoter to enter into many contractual obligations. There are a number of ways by

which arrangements may be made for the transfer of the property, e.g., by an option, outright sale, etc. Regardless of the method used, there are two points of outstanding significance to the parties involved: namely, the liability of the promoter, and whether or not he may profit by the transaction.

Liability of the Promoter 

From the standpoint of the proposed corporation, the status of a promoter is essentially that of an agent. This is true even though the corporation for which he is acting is not yet created. In his dealings with those interested in the project he has most of the rights and responsibilities of an agent. In this capacity he cannot take advantage of his principal by concealing either profits or information. Although he may purchase the property in his own name, he cannot conceal the price and sell it at a profit to the corporation unless the property were purchased prior to the period of promotion. It is possible, however, for him to accept a profit if he has revealed all the facts and if the approval of the board of directors has been officially secured. 

From the point of view of third parties, the promoter may be held personally liable unless he provides for an exception in his contracts. Where purchases of property are made in his own name, the promoter is held liable to the vendor if the corporation later fails to ratify the act. However, if he distinctly specifies that the vendor is to look to the proposed corporation for payment, he is released from this responsibility. Because of these and other risks, the promoter must be particularly careful in his dealings with third parties. He must have every assurance that the contracts he makes will be ratified by the corporation. At the same time, he must so protect himself as to prevent other interests from taking the fruits of his labor. 

Arranging for Construction of Plant Problems similar to the foregoing may arise in connection with the construction of the plant. If the formation of the corporation has not been completed, the promoter will take the same risks as in connection with the purchase of the site. Ordinarily, however, the organization of the corporation will have been completed and the funds made a certainty before construction of the plant is begun. This is necessary because large building jobs must usually be paid for as the work progresses. Landowners can sell their property under a contract

PROMOTION 

183 calling for future payment without undue risk to themselves, but contractors generally require partial payment as the work progresses. 

Organization of the Corporation 

During the last stages of gathering together the productive factors, the new corporation will be formally organized. This work may be done by the promoter, or legal specialists may be obtained to handle the technicalities involved in applying to the state for a charter. The request for incorporation implies that the capitalization has been determined at least as it relates to the amount of authorized capital stock. The problems involved in incorporation and in determining the capitalization are so important in themselves that their discussion is reserved for more complete analysis in the next chapters. 

Promoter's Profits

Promoter's profits have received considerable notoriety because they are believed to be excessive. Often this is the result of a misunderstanding of the exact nature of the compensation which promoters receive. Undoubtedly, promoter's profits are large where the enterprise is successful, but where ill fortune attends the venture, there will be numerous losses to be absorbed. Also, it is not uncommon to confuse the appreciation in value, which is available to all stockholders, with the gains received from promotion. This may be made clear by analyzing the character of the consideration given to the promoter for his services.

Although the promoter is reimbursed for his cash outlays, the major payment for his services consists of stock. Payment in stock is desirable because it conserves the cash of the corporation and reflects the faith of the promoter in the enterprise. At the same time, the nominal value of the stock is undoubtedly greater than the amount he would receive if he were paid in cash. Such a differential is by no means unusual and may be illustrated in the sale of a house. Suppose an individual has a house for sale and is asking a price of $10,000; it is probable that he would accept less in cash but would insist upon the $10,000 if paid on a time basis. The same principle applies to the promoter; if paid with stock where he has to wait for his returns, the amount is usually greater than if he were paid in cash. 

If the corporation proves to be successful, the stock appreciates in value and the promoter realizes an excellent profit. This is not the profit of promotion; instead, it is profit that accrues to all holders of

the stock. In reality, the profit or the compensation for the promoter's services consist of the value of the stock at the time it was received. To illustrate this principle, reference may be made to the promotion of the United States Steel Corporation. A few years after its organization the price of its stock was as low as $6 per share. In 

1929, the stock sold as high as $366 (adjusted price after allowing for 

40 per cent stock dividend). The appreciation in value of this stock may not reasonably be regarded as promoter's profits, but as a return that may be had by any stockholder holding for the same period of time.

Classification of Promoters 

Promoters may be classified into three types: occasional, professional, and a combination. Most promotions are performed by the occasional promoter, i.e., one who does not make it his life-work. 

For instance, most consolidations are of the occasional variety though there are a number of exceptions to the contrary. An instance of occasional promotion in the consolidation of companies was the attempt of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation to acquire the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company. Apparently, the officials of the Bethlehem Steel 

Corporation conversed with the officials of the latter company and agreed upon the terms to cover the exchange of stock. Failure to secure the ratification of the stockholders finally prevented the merger from being put into effect.4

Occasional promotions are more common, however, in the initiation of new enterprises and particularly for smaller companies. Groups of limited size are unable to finance the services of a professional promoter, and furthermore have only local attention. Under these conditions, bankers, lawyers, or leading business men usually assume the role of promoter. One outstanding example is the Ford Motor Corporation. While assistance and advice were rendered by other business men and financiers, the dynamic figure in the organization of the company was Ford himself. Similarly, many of our leading corporations today may trace their origin back to humble beginnings. 

A professional promoter specializes in organizing business ventures. 

This does not mean that this work is his sole task, although there are a few of this type. For the most part, however, the promotion function is fulfilled by concerns who engage in such activities as a side 4 * See chapter XXXIII for more complete discussion of this case.

PROMOTION 

185 line. This is especially true of certain investment banking houses and engineering firms.

Investment Banking Houses as Promoters 

Because of the connection of the investment banking house with the financing of most large corporate enterprises, it is necessary that the banking organization be interested in all of the details of promotion and organization. On occasions it may become more aggressive and actually try to initiate promotions. Promotional activity may not always be under the auspices of the banking house itself, in which event, the officers and agents serve as a front. Cyrus E. Eaton, formerly of Otis and Company, is a good example. Not only was he active in opposing the merger of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation and the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company, but in addition he was one of the leading figures in promoting the Republic Steel Corporation and was active in the organization of several investment trusts.

The transition of the Dodge Brothers Automobile Company and the National Cash Register Company from a closed to an open ownership basis is another example of promotion by a banking concern. 

Both cases were sponsored by Dillon, Read and Company which acted in the capacity of promoter and underwriter. A brief recital of the course of events in the Dodge Brothers deal may be used to typify transactions of this kind. First, the task of investigation was simplified because of the long and successful record of the company. Second, the existence of a going concern eliminated any need for assembly of plant. 

Third, the only remaining function consisted of raising the necessary capital.. Dodge Brothers proved willing to sell at a figure of $146,- 

000,000 but demanded cash as consideration. To obtain this amount, Dillon, Read and Company organized a new corporation for the purpose of raising the necessary funds through the sale of stocks and bonds to the general public.5

Engineering Firms 

Many utility companies, especially the smaller ones, have been promoted and organized by engineering and construction firms operating in the field. Rather than wait for orders for new jobs, these companies 

5 See Commercial and Financial Chronicle, Vol. 120, p. 1885, for financial details. • Stone and Webster, H. M. Byllesby and Company, and others.

have frequently initiated new enterprise to create a source of employment for their expensive staffs. 

Individual Professional Promoters 

Occasionally, there are individuals who devote practically their entire time to promotion activities. They may not be interested in the management of the companies formed; instead, their primary interest is in the initiating of new business ventures. An example of such a man is Charles M. Warner, who helped to promote the 

American Malting Company, the Corn Products Refining Company, the National Asphalt Company, the International Cotton Mills Corporation, and others." 

Most individual promoters are not known nationally although, unfortunately, too many make the headlines through various schemes intended to defraud the public. The Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Justice now have authority to curb many deceptive practices and they are rendering valuable service to investors by their constant policing of the financial front. The following summarized statements indicate some of the fraudulent schemes which they have uncovered:8 

Four individuals operated under the name of A. D. Lowe and Associates and represented themselves as a firm in business over 100 years. Actually, it was organized in 1937 as a means of enticing investors to switch out of securities into whiskey warehouse receipts. Representations were made that the latter could be disposed of at any time and that they would increase in value each month. As a matter of fact, the receipts were alleged to be worth one-third of what the investors paid.

A group organized the Colorado River Magnetic Black Sand Company whose securities were sold to the public. It was declared falsely that the company had a magnetic mining machine which had proved successful in extracting gold and other precious metals from black sand. At this writing, the United 

States District Court had issued a preliminary injunction enjoining "six companies and certain of their officers from violating the registration and fraud provisions of the Securities Act of 1933."

The stock of the Plymouth Cooperage Corporation of Plymouth, Michigan, was sold on statements made by the president of the company and a broker that whiskey and beer barrels were being produced at a profit of $1 per barrel.

The Place of the Promoter in Our Economic Order 

In many respects the promoter has been a favored son of our economic and social order. Of course, it is possible to point to certain laws which have been required in the organization and promotion of a corporation and to say that they are rigid and restrictive. 

Value received must be exchanged for stock, the corporation must have the approval of the proper state officials, annual reports must be filed, and a host of other demands may be noted. However, these requirements are more than offset by many attractions and privileges which are permitted. The limitation of liability made possible by the corporate form of organization, the introduction of no-par value stock, the broad statement of the purpose of a corporation, and numerous other favors all testify to the pedestal position of the promoter. 

Encouragement of worthy promotion is fully warranted as a contribution to the progress of civilization. Moreover, the risks of new enterprise require special incentives to attract capital as well as to invite the services of responsible and progressive individuals. Even today, certain well-known reformers of business are seeking ways and means to facilitate the raising of equity capital. The trail of business must be blazed by adventure and entails more than average. risk. Government may very properly offer sufficient inducements and incentives to spur business initiation and expansion. Fortunately, numerous individuals assume willingly the unusual risks found in promoting a new enterprise for the sake of possible realization of large returns. Legal restraint to the contrary, a certain element of the public will always be attracted by the glamour and thrill of promoting a new business structure. The unusual success of the few always looms as a possibility. The growth of the Ford Motor Company from the tiny acorn to the giant oak is still a source of inspira- Ition to those who commence a new business. 

In analyzing the place of the promoter in the economic order, several perplexing questions arise when classifying the function which

is performed. Classical economics provides for four productive factors: land, labor, capital, and the entrepreneur. The free lance nature of promotion makes it difficult to place it exclusively under any one of these headings. To the extent that the promoter receives direct compensation for his services, it would seem reasonable to place him in the labor category. On the other hand, many of his actions are of the entrepreneurial type, which consists of general guidance or direction of industry. The classical theory does treat the function of the entrepreneur as being continuous in nature and may seem to exclude the promoter because of the roving character of his activities. However, economic theory is formulated mostly on the basis of static conditions, thereby making it difficult to classify dynamic actions. 

Hence, if the function of the promoter were viewed realistically, it would seem proper to regard him as a special type of entrepreneur who exercises a distinct influence in the direction of business. 

The Promoter of the Future 

Recent trends and changes in our economy seem to foreshadow less notoriety and prominence in the part which individual and specialized promotion will play in the future. The individual inventor is giving way to the well-organized research laboratory which is usually a part of modern business organization. In turn, the latter will utilize its own research and analysis as the chief determinant of proposed expansion. Hence, more and more of the fuel of promotion will be quietly consumed by the going concern and not by some entirely new enterprise. This trend, however, should not cause us to regard invention and promotion as synonymous terms. The former is primarily a mechanical or technical process, whereas the latter discovers the business practicability of an idea. Outputs of the research laboratory must still be justified in terms of the economic market. 

Expansion and Promotion 

Formal or specialized promotion ceases when the organization of a new enterprise is completed. In many respects, however, much of the technique and spirit of promotional venture continues to be an important and, integral part of ensuing operations. Especially is this true of expansion which requires much the same analysis and procedure as initial promotion.

At a later point, the chief problems which arise in connection with

PROMOTION 

189 expansion will be analyzed more fully, but at this time it is necessary to recognize the nature of its germination. Active management departs from its functional duties and realizes the need for new ideas and methods. By means of such alertness, they are enabled to keep abreast of a rapidly changing social order and thus to maintain their share of the total business. The path of industry is strewn with the wrecks of those who simply tried to maintain the status quo; successful management must have its ear to the ground, and must be able to anticipate and to prepare for the future.

Profit Opportunities and Promotion 

Profits are commonly accepted as a popular symbol of private initiative and are believed to be of larger, social benefit as a means of stimulating business activity. In the conduct of normal operations, profits constitute a return comparable in functional character to wages, interest, and rent. There is less uniformity and regularity in the flow of profits than in other forms of income, and as a result they may appear to be excessive at times, as well as in the case of specific companies. Against such abnormal gains, however, allowance must be made for losses which appear in depression years and in various segments of industry intermittently. 

Particular attention must be given to the function of profits in the encouragement and development of new opportunities. It is here that there must be positive incentives and inducements if the risks of new and untried enterprise are to be assumed. Profits do not need to be guaranteed, and they need not be certain. But their possibility must exist if new ventures are to be undertaken. If profits are unduly restricted, private promotion will be seriously checked. In recent years, many reformers have emphasized abuses of the profit opportunity that have arisen as a result of monopoly and other forms of special privilege. Such perversions undoubtedly call for correction, but at the same time care must be taken to preserve the basic and cardinal virtues of the profit motive when used in connection with free enterprise.

In encouraging the development of business enterprise through the incentive to make profits, the 'state does have an obligation to protect investors and the public against fraudulent and deceptive practices. There is also need to curb promoters who take none of the risks but who place themselves in a position to get most of the profits. The dangers of such loose practices to the public interest are

readily apparent, and during the past decade legislation has been enacted to provide a safeguard against many abuses which appeared in the past. Some critics contend that these restrictions will seriously curb legitimate promotion and financing, but the question is mainly one of scope or degree. Today, business and government representatives alike recognize the need for reasonable regulation of investment operations.

The Place of the Promoter in Corporation Finance 

The work of the promoter is both unique and original, and without his services business enterprises could not be initiated. At the same time, it is possible to attach too much importance to his activities. The promotion of new companies is relatively minor compared to the activities of going concerns and financial policy necessarily takes form in the larger operations of corporations of long standing. 

Equally important, principles may be established only with practice which have been tested on the firing line of experience. For this reason, primary emphasis will be placed upon the operations of established companies.

CHAPTER XI  

INANCE may be likened in many ways to a great river. Both are fed by numerous tributaries and branches which add volume and swiftness to the stream, but in viewing the consummate result, it is easy to be unmindful of the river's remote and unimposing beginnings. To understand their nature and behavior, it is desirable to return to the origin. Thus in finance, the principles as well as the techniques involved in the initiation of a corporation need to be appreciated. In the first place, this permits a view of the corporation from the ground up. In the second place, it necessitates a comprehensive statement of corporate powers. Lastly, it reveals the power and position of the state in corporate life. 

The corporation has a recognized and separate entity only because this is granted to it by the state. The state grants a corporate charter under the general theory that corporations promote business activity, which contributes to the general welfare of the citizens and of the state. The charter is a contract between the state and the corporation wherein the corporation receives certain rights and powers, and the state imposes certain responsibilities. During the life of the charter, it may be amended only through the consent of both contracting parties, i.e., the state and the corporation. Charters were originally the result of specific legislative enactment based upon each individual application; but with the expansion of the corporate form of business organization, the states were soon forced to revise this cumbersome and awkward procedure. The solution took the form of general corporation laws which may be applied to all corporations desiring charters.¹ Under this program, application is made to the proper officer of the state (usually the Secretary of State) for incorporation. 

The essential steps to be taken in the organization of a corporation may be listed and discussed briefly: (1) preparation of the articles of incorporation, (2) petition to the state and payment of fees, (3) approval and filing, and (4) the organization meeting. 

1 Public utilities, railroads, financial institutions, and other specialized activities are generally provided for by means of a special statutory procedure involving different treatments from other forms of business. 193

Preparation of the Articles of Incorporation 

While the corporation is a creature of the state, its incorporators prepare their own articles of incorporation. The nature of the articles of incorporation may vary according to the type of business engaged in, but the following are common requirements: (1) the name of the corporation; (2) the location of the principal office; (3) the purpose or purposes; (4) the maximum of par or no-par shares which the corporation wishes authorization to issue; (5) the amount of capital required to begin business. Other statements of specification may be included, such as: (a) consideration for which shares are issued, (b) valuation of consideration accepted for the shares, (c) restriction of the scope of the corporation, stipulation of the shareholders' rights, etc. Some of the more salient points which arise in connection with the foregoing articles may be mentioned briefly. 

Name of the Corporation 

The name of the corporation may appear to be inconsequential to the layman, but its selection may actually be cause for considerable discussion. To a certain extent, it becomes the quintessence of all that the business may represent. As an earmark for public reference, the name takes on meaning as the corporation becomes known for its products and policies. Many corporate names are worth millions of dollars because they represent a long accumulation of valuable good-will or are peculiarly fitted to represent a particular type of business. An excellent illustration is the magazine Life which paid a large amount purely for the right to use the name, and the previous publication bearing this title went out of business. 

The choice of a corporate name is more a matter of art than of science, but it is not uncommon to select a title or appellation which (1) reflects the sponsorship of the person promoting and operating the enterprise, (2) gives ready reference to the product or service. being produced, or (3) conveys meaning as to the location of the plant or area of activity. The Ford Motor Company, Chrysler Corporation, Sears, Roebuck and Company, Westinghouse Electric and

Manufacturing Company, and many other companies of national standing illustrate the use of personal names. In general, enterprises whose chief market outlet is found in individual consumers tend to capitalize on the recognized standing of individual sponsors. Many department stores and other forms of retail business use the name of the personal owner for this reason.

Frequently the corporate name becomes a convenient abbreviation for the designation of products. In the gasoline and oil business, there are many such instances: Sun Oil Company-Sunoco; the earlier Lincoln Oil Company-Linco; Standard Oil Company of Ohio 

Sohio; Pure Oil Company-Purol, etc. Armco, a convenient label for steel products, is employed by the American Rolling Mill Company. Or, a name may be selected to convey a sense of quality, such as the connotation of "Pure" in the Pure Oil Company or of "Perfection" in the Perfection Stove Company.

As stated previously, a geographical title may be used to reflect either the scope of the market or the situs of production. The United 

States Steel Corporation, the International Harvester Company, the National Steel Corporation, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, and the United States Rubber Company all convey a sense of the national character of operations by these companies. Corporations, taking the name of the area in which the plant is located, are usually smaller than those with a national market, although later expansion may cause many exceptions. When this occurs, it may not be deemed wise to change the name because of public acceptance already gained. Examples of industrial companies with local names are the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company, Lima Locomotive 

Works, Bethlehem Steel Corporation, and the Pittsburgh Coal Com pany. Public utilities often take the name of the major community served, such as: Detroit Edison, Cincinnati Gas and Electric, Cleveland Electric Illuminating, and many others.

Legal requirements covering the choice of name are not specific but simply provide (1) that the name must not deceive the public in any way, and (2) that it must be easily distinguished from any other corporation authorized to do business in the state. New enterprises often attempt to adopt a name which is similar or identical to existing concerns in an effort to gain the benefit of a reputation already established. This is seldom possible in the case of two companies operating in the same state, but a local concern may succeed in doing this where a national organization may not have facilities in a given state. For instance, the United .... Company operating throughout most of the country did not have any units in Florida. Local promoters organized a United.... Company of Florida, taking advantage of the prestige of the national group. Later, the larger company saw fit to pay a substantial price to buy out the local company.

Deceptive names are also prohibited by state authorities to prevent possible misrepresentation to the public. Usually this question becomes most acute in the case of trade names and is subject to regulation by the Federal Trade Commission. To illustrate, the Commission has held that naphtha soap would be required to have naphtha as a component element to carry the name. Similarly, it would be reasonable to expect that a company like the Real Silk Hosiery Company would produce stockings of real silk; otherwise, unfair advantage would be taken of consumers who would presume a product. representative of the name.

Location of Principal Office 

As will be shown in the next chapter, large corporations frequently obtain their charter from a state other than that in which physical operation takes place. This is done to secure the benefit of the relatively greater freedom, or wider range of powers, which is possible under the laws of certain states, such as New Jersey and Delaware. 

However, most states require each corporation receiving a charter to establish an office in that state irrespective of the location of the plant. Where a state is selected for incorporation that is not also the state in which operations are conducted, it is common to appoint an agent instead of setting up complete home office facilities. It is not uncommon for a single individual or trust company to act as agent for many corporations. This agent will do little more than keep a duplicate list of stockholders and be authorized to accept or reply to legal processes served against the corporation.

Statement of Purpose 

In the early history of corporate enterprise, it was common practice to stress singleness of purpose. Corporations were not allowed to undertake varied and multiple operations but were expected to confine their activities to a stipulated and well-defined objective. However, the process of business evolution and the liberality of legal interpretation gradually gave rise to an enlargement of function, and most charters now create authority to act in a wide field. Later in this chapter, the wide scope of corporate powers will be discussed in more detail, but at this time the requisites for the statement in the articles of incorporation may be set forth. Briefly, the statement of purpose, or purposes, should possess the following characteristics:

1. Clarity-Clarity of statement is essential if later misunderstanding is to be avoided. Since the final test of this criterion will be found in the courts, it is customary to engage legal talent to draw the articles of incorporation. To the layman, the resulting language may appear to be verbose and confusing because of seeming repetition or overlapping; nevertheless, the expediency of the issues at stake usually require the sacrifice of informal, narrative presentation in favor of the technical, legal form. It would seem, at times, that the attempt to achieve clarity defeats itself because the effort to cover all possible contingencies gives rise to an involved and lengthy statement. To illustrate the type of language employed as well as the all-embracing character of a statement, the following partial recital of the powers of a federal agency to serve as a conservator or receiver may be cited: 

Provided, however, that the Board shall have power to make orders, rules, and regulations of general, limited, or special applicability, modifying, abrogating, restricting, or enlarging the rights, titles, powers, privileges, and duties herein otherwise provided for, or providing other rights, titles, powers, privileges, and duties, all or any one or more of which may be in addition to or in substitution for all or any one or more of the rights, titles, powers, privileges, and duties herein otherwise provided for. The provisions of this subsection (except the second sentence thereof) are, even as to the matters specifically dealt with in this subsection, cumulative and additional to, and not in limitation or derogation of, the powers now or hereafter otherwise vested in the Board, including without limitation those vested in it under section 26 .. 2 

2. Preciseness.-The statement of powers should be specific. From a practical, business point of view, it would seem that a corporation which wanted to be empowered to trade in various commodities could simply specify in its charter that it was incorporating to carry on a general merchandising business. However, legal prudence calls for a more precise and specific statement outlining each possible type of activity as the general authorization. For instance, the clause authorizing merchandising activity may be stated "to buy, sell, exchange, trade, and otherwise deal in any and all kinds of manufactured articles, raw materials, minerals, animal and plant products, "3 

2 Senate Bill 4095, June 4, 1940, p. 13, referring to the powers of the Federal Home Loan 

Bank Board. 

3 From the charter of the Atlas Corporation as quoted in J. C. Baker and D. W. Malott, Introduction to Corporate Finance (New York: McGraw-Hill Book Co., 1936), pp. 13-14,

Other portions of this charter will be quoted in this chapter. Reference should be made to this book for a more complete presentation of the charter as well as other valuable material in finance.

3. Scope.-In addition to being clear and specific about the powers desired, the charter should provide for all possible future developments which may result in different forms of business activity. The need for a broad statement of authority is caused, of course, by the limitation of corporate activity to the rights and privileges expressed in the articles of incorporation. Any departure from this delegation of powers requires a formal petition to the state for amendment of the charter. It is because of these requirements that corporations commonly seek a broad empowering clause in the statement of purpose, such as previously cited: " ... and otherwise deal in any and all kinds of manufactured articles, raw materials, minerals, animal and plant products, etc."

Amount of Capital 

Incorporators are also required to declare the amount and type of capital stock which they expect to issue. Because of the importance of this item as a regulator of size and future expansion, care must be taken that allowance be made for future contingencies. Usually no limitation is placed upon the amount of debt which a corporation may have; the charter or corporate statutes simply giving the corporation the general right to borrow funds. Analysis of the capital structure will be made at greater length in Chapter XIII. 

Consideration for Issuance of Shares

Most corporate statutes provide that shares may be issued only for adequate and equivalent consideration. In furtherance of this objective, shares must also be sold at a uniform price; otherwise, the measure of "equivalent consideration" would be destroyed, and favoritism of insiders would be facilitated. One of the chief difficulties encountered in determining the adequacy of consideration is found in the valuation of services rendered and the worth of intangible assets which are given in payment of shares. Outside investors invariably pay cash for their stock, which automatically precludes any dispute as to whether their stock was fully paid for. On the other hand, promoters and other insiders usually obtain at least a part of their stock for their personal services, or for various property items other than cash. Juggling of the values of physical assets is also possible by resorting to "convenience" or "ordered" appraisals at predetermined figures.

The following case may be cited to show how the property account may be adjusted to present a more favorable picture: the balance sheet of a newly organized manufacturing company set forth its fixed assets at a valuation of approximately $700,000. The properties in question had recently been acquired at a cost of $200,000 and were appraised, on the basis of reproduction cost new less depreciation, at approximately $1,200,- 000. For balance sheet purposes the company placed an arbitrary valuation of $700,000 on the properties, thus creating a “surplus" of approximately $500,- 000. The Commission instituted stop-order proceedings on the grounds that the balance sheet representations were misleading and that, in this instance, reproduction cost less depreciation did not constitute a criterion of value since the issuer had not demonstrated successful use of the properties warranting such valuation. As a result of the proceedings, the issuer amended its balance sheet to show the properties at cost, $200,000, thereby eliminating "surplus" of onehalf million dollars which appeared on the balance sheet as originally filed.* 

As stated above, the valuation of intangible property items is espe cially subject to abuse. To illustrate: 

A registration statement filed by a bottling company in connection with a proposed public offering of common stock contained a balance sheet of the issuer which included among its assets franchise rights at a stated valuation of $2,500,000. It appearing from information contained in the registration statement that the valuation ascribed to the franchise rights was excessive, the Commission proceeded to a hearing under Section 8 (e) of the Act. At this hearing, evidence was adduced to indicate that no basis existed for the valuation placed upon this intangible asset, whereupon stop-order proceedings were instituted under Section 8 (d) of the Act. Upon notice of hearing the registrant filed an amended balance sheet reducing the valuation of the franchise rights from $2,500,000 to $1.5

Investors are equally liable to deception and to the "milking" of assets by established companies seeking new capital. L. 

A mining company seeking to register an issue of its common stock, was required to amend its prospectus to disclose that it had been selling stock to the public for more than 20 years and that only a small percentage of receipts from such sales had been used in actual development of the properties, the balance having been used principally to pay salesmen's commissions, office expenses, and salaries. The company recently requested permission to withdraw its registration statement after a year's unsuccessful attempt to sell its securities by means of its amended prospectus. 

4 S.E.C., Third Annual Report, for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1937, p. 5. 

5 Ibid., pp. 4-5. 

S.E.C., First Annual Report, for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1935, pp. 27-28.

The initial status quo in which securities are fully supported by equivalent asset value may also be destroyed by later possible manipulation.

A Delaware corporation filed a registration statement covering 15,000 shares of $1.50 convertible preferred stock (par value $5) and 52,750 shares of common stock ($1 par). Under the charter provisions the preferred stock was entitled in liquidation to $25 per share and was proposed to be offered at $27.50 per share to net the company $25, of which $5 was to be allocated to capital and $20 to paid-in surplus. Under the Delaware statutes, corporations may pay dividends on any class of stock out of paid-in surplus. The registration statement and prospectus did not disclose the possibility that thus, under the laws of Delaware, the common stock holders might receive dividends out of surplus contributed by the preferred holders, thereby taking away the surplus contributed the preferred stock holders covering the excess of liquidating value over par value. Accordingly, the Commission required the registrant to include as a footnote to the preferred stock account in the balance sheet a statement of the aggregate amount to which the preferred stock would be entitled in liquidation, and an opinion of counsel for the company as to whether there was any legal restriction on surplus by reason of the fact that the amount to which preferred shareholders would be entitled in liquidation exceeded the par value of the stock. It was stated in the footnote that in the opinion of counsel there was no such restriction but that it was the present intention of the company to limit the payment of dividends to the amount of surplus in excess of $20 per share of preferred stock outstanding.

Since the effective date of the registration statement, the company has indicated its intention to remove from surplus and allocate to capital, by proper legal procedure, a sufficient amount of such surplus to cover the full liquidating value of the preferred stock.

The foregoing cases clearly illustrate the need for protecting investors against adroit diversion of assets. Obviously, legislation can do little more than establish the broad principle that security issues must be covered by accompanying asset value. Effective enforcement must rest primarily with the courts which decide specific cases, and with the administrative agencies concerned with the regulation of securities. Particular attention will be given to the Securities and

Exchange Commission in Chapters XXI and XXIII. 

Petition to the State and Payment of Fees

After the articles of incorporation have been drawn up in detail to cover all needs and possible contingencies, they are filed with the state, together with the required fees. The initial incorporation or
