Approval and Filing 

The articles are examined by the proper officials of the state. If the articles contain all the provisions required by law and no provision prohibited by law, they are approved and filed for purposes of public record. A copy of the articles is certified by the state official (usually the Secretary of State) and sent to the incorporators as evidence of their acceptance. The certified articles constitute the new corporation's charter. In many states, it is also necessary to file a certified copy of the articles with the clerk or recorder of the county in which the corporation is located. 

Organization Meeting 

Upon official acceptance, the incorporators call a meeting of all stockholders to meet various legal requirements which are preliminary to actual operation. In particular, the following must be provided for: (1) election of directors and officers, (2) adoption of bylaws to govern corporate activities.

Election of Directors and Officers 

One of the first requirements following incorporation is the election of a board of directors. Since at this point there is no wide distribution of stock, those who have acted in the capacity of trustees during the preliminary stages are usually elected. At ensuing annual meetings, the ultimate owners or stockholders are given an oppor-

tunity to express their choice. However, as has been noted elsewhere, the use of proxies and other devices makes it comparatively easy for the sponsors to retain their initial control.

The next step is the election of officers to have charge of the dayto-day operations. Such appointments are customarily made by the board of directors because election by the shareholders would be unwieldy as well as the source of possible friction. Corporation laws usually require as a minimum slate the following officers: president, secretary, and treasurer. In addition, the by-laws of the corporation may provide for such other officers as the following: chairman of the board of directors, various vice-presidents, assistant secretaries, assistant treasurers, etc. The exact number and type will depend for the most part on the size and nature of the business. Also, it is not unusual for a single individual to hold more than one office. 

By-Laws 

The major purpose of the by-laws is to provide regulations for the internal activities of the corporation. Third parties are not held for knowledge of these provisions, since the by-laws are intended for the guidance of the directors, as well as providing for the routine necessary to the conduct of a corporation. The general corporation act of the state of Ohio lists the following items which may be included: 

1. Provision for calling and conducting annual or special meetings. 

2. Place of holding shareholders' meetings. 

3. Requirements of a quorum for shareholders' meetings. 

4. Means of determining stockholders entitled to vote. 

5. Provision for the number and qualifications of directors as well as a statement of their duties. 

6. Stipulations governing directors, such as the place or places of holding meetings, requirements of a quorum, appointment of executive or other committees of the board, etc. 

7. Provision for the sale or transfer of shares. 

8. Any other statement of limitation or definition applicable to the scope of the corporation's activity, or of the directors' or shareholders' powers.

In short, it may noted that the by-laws are a means of liaison between the shareholders and the directors; in contrast, the charter or

articles of incorporation provide for the dealings of the corporation with third parties.

The powers of a corporation may be found in the following three sources: (1) rights and powers specified by statute, (2) rights specifically stated in the articles of incorporation, (3) implied rights. 

Rights and Powers Specified by Law 

Rights of general applicability to all corporations are usually enacted into broad statutes, thus serving both as a source of authority to corporate enterprise and of due notice to the public-at-large. Powers such as the following are commonly provided:8 (1) to make contracts as well as to sue or be sued; (2) to use a corporate seal; (3) to "purchase, acquire, hold, convey, lease, mortgage or dispose of property, real or personal, tangible or intangible;" (4) to borrow money and sell bonds or other evidences of indebtedness on either a secured or unsecured basis; (5) to acquire, guarantee, etc., bonds and other evidences of indebtedness of other corporations; (6) to perform such acts as are expedient to accomplish the stated purposes. 

It is ear from the foregoing that the corporation has practically all the rights of an individual, i.e., for operations within the state. 

However, it cannot freely enter another state and carry on operations without receiving permission or a special license, whereas the individual is not so restricted.

Rights Stated in the Articles of Incorporation 

The rights specified in the articles of incorporation should be specific in their statement as well as sufficiently broad to cover all types of activity which may reasonably be anticipated. An example would be the certificate of incorporation of the Standard Oil Company of California. Twenty-two specific statements are made to express the objectives or purposes, and one of these sufficiently general to allow for any further contingency. This statement may be quoted partially "To carry on any other lawful business whatsoever which may seem to the Corporation capable of being carried on in connection with the above, or calculated directly or indirectly to promote the interest of the Corporation... 

In the case of the Atlas Corporation, the charter powers included among others: (1) to manufacture, improve and work upon min- 

8 As expressed in the General Corporation Law of Ohio. 

---

erals, metals, wood, oils and other liquids, gases, chemicals, animal and plant products, etc.; (2) to manufacture, improve, repair, and work upon any and all kinds of machines, instruments, tools, implements, mechanical devices, etc.; (3) to own, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire lands and various enumerated rights in lands; (4) to plan, design, construct, alter, repair, remove, and otherwise engage in any work upon bridges, railroads, dams, canals, etc.; (5) to carry on the business of trucking, warehousing, and storage including the storage of all kinds of goods, wares, and merchandise, etc. 

In addition, the charter of the Atlas Corporation provided for the production and sale of electricity, gas, light, heat, refrigeration, ice, water, and power in all forms; the right to engage in real estate agency and brokerage business; and to deal in, discover and hold patents, etc. The various rights conclude with the statement, "The foregoing clauses shall be construed as objects, purposes and powers, and it is hereby expressly provided that the foregoing enumeration of specific powers shall not be held to limit or restrict in any manner the powers of the corporation."

To the layman, it would seem that the concluding statements in the foregoing example were all that were needed to give the corporation powers to engage in any kind of business whatsoever. However, in order to be specific and to avoid misinterpretation and ambiguity, the powers are stated in as much detail as possible. Often many of the objects stated are repetition of rights granted by law and, therefore, would be allowed without specific statement in the articles. Inclusion of these stipulations, however, is not entirely redundant but helps to make the statements of the corporation's objectives more complete and precise. This is beneficial to both the corporation and the public.

Implied Rights 

The corporation is deemed to have certain rights which may not be expressly stated in either its articles of incorporation or general corporation law. Such rights are those which are incidental to the operation of any business whether it be organized under the corporate form, or in any other way. Of the many instances of these rights, the following may be mentioned for the sake of examples: the right to buy and sell, the right to hire and discharge employees, and many other similar rights necessary to the operation of a business enterprise. 72

Ultra Vires Acts 

Those acts which are committed by a corporation outside of the scope of its authority are said to be ultra vires. While an act of this type is unauthorized to the corporation, it need not be illegal. The exact treatment of the parties involved will depend upon the circumstances as well as upon the knowledge of the parties. If the act is within the reasonable scope of the corporation's activities, the party dealing with the corporation will be able to enforce its claim against the corporation. On the other hand, if it is evident that the act is far removed from the scope of the corporation's normal activity and beyond the expectation of a reasonably prudent person, then any contract arising out of the ultra vires act could not be enforced against the corporation. If the situation arising out of an ultra vires act has not yet been carried out, i.e., the obligations imposed by the contract have not been fulfilled by either party, then either party may rescind the contract. However, when the contract has been executed by either party, the courts will ordinarily require proper payment by the other party.

The ultra vires principle may be applied to various aspects of corporate life. Its application in a financial manner may be illustrated. 

For instance, if a corporation issued bonds in violation of another bond indenture, the act is ultra vires. While it is not illegal for a corporation to issue bonds, it is without the scope of authority previously restricted by a specific contract. For this reason, the purchasers of such bonds are not devoid of rights, and a corporation would have to repair the damages to the bondholders. On the other hand, if bonds were issued contrary to the statutes permitting such, they would be illegal. Thus in some states public utilities may not issue bonds in excess of outstanding stock. If a company proceeded to violate this requirement, the bonds would be illegal. 

Types of Corporations 

Not only is it of interest to the reader to know just how a corporation is organized, but he also should be familiar with the many kinds of corporations. Restricting the classification to private corporations, the following types may exist: 

I. According to Profit 

A. Profit or stock 

B. Non-profit or non-stock

II. According to Field of Enterprise 

A. Public utilities-water, gas, telephone and telegraph, steam and hydroelectric, electric traction B. Railroads best classified on a geographical basis 

C. Industrial-iron and steel, automobile, oil, electrical equipment, etc. (see Appendix A for complete list)

III. According to Nature of Operation A. Operating 

B. Holding

C. Combination of A and B IV. According to Place of Incorporation A. Domestic 

B. Foreign

According to profit.-State laws provide for both profit and nonprofit corporations. Although corporation finance is mainly concerned with the former, it is of interest to note the latter. The nonprofit corporation is primarily for the convenience of co-operative or fraternal associations not interested in profits, but at the same time desirous of a separate entity for the purposes of conducting group activities. However, the mutual or co-operative plan of organization may possibly be used on a wider scale in the field of business in the future. Already, it has taken the place of private operators in many agricultural enterprises, and it has long held a position of preeminence in life insurance. The adoption of the co-operative principle as a basis of operation in private business would necessarily exercise tremendous influence on the financial pattern, but needless to say, the functions of finance would remain undisturbed. 

According to the fields of enterprise.-Classification according to the field of activity is used particularly in investment analysis, but it is also of interest to the student of corporation finance in the following ways: (1) as a means of reducing corporations to a more systematized and coherent basis; (2) as a means of acquainting the student with the more important corporations. In connection with the first reason, it has been implied at various times that financial policy is frequently attributable to the nature of the field in which a concern is operating, and the classification of corporations according to specific fields should help to make this more clear. In connection with the second reason, too often students and others lack familiarity with the leading American corporations. In order to

furnish the student with a convenient source for reference, a summarized but by no means exhaustive classification of American business corporations is given in Appendix A. 

According to the nature of operations.-From the standpoint of operations, corporations may be divided into operating companies, holding companies, and a combination of the two. An operating company is one which is actively engaged in the production of goods and services. Examples of such are numerous; in fact, most of the corporations listed in Appendix A are of this type. Broadly speaking, it might be said that active operation is the normal function of corporations and that any other function is more or less an adulteration of the true purpose of corporate activity. The holding company is a corporation organized for the express purpose of holding stocks of other corporations. It may be distinguished from an investment trust in that an investment trust is interested in holding stocks for their income and appreciation possibilities, whereas in the holding company the primary interest is the co-ordination and control of the subsidiary corporations. Absolute control is possible only when the holding company owns one share more than 50 per cent of the stock of the company it wishes to control. In practice, however, holding companies are able to exercise the desired influence with far less than 50 per cent of the voting stock. In recognition of this fact, the Holding Company Act of 1935 defined a holding company (for the electric power and natural gas industries) as being any company owning 10 per cent of the voting stock of a subsidiary, unless the company could show that in fact it exercised no such control. The law goes farther and states that any corporation exercising control of a subsidiary is a holding company even when it owns less than 10 per cent of the controlling stock.

On other occasions, a corporation may serve in a dual capacity, both as an operating and holding company. An excellent example is the American Telephone and Telegraph Company which is engaged in the actual operation of the long-distance service while the local services, as well as part of the long-distance service, is provided by the subsidiary companies. In the industrial field, General Motors 

Corporation may be regarded as representative of a combination of the two types. This type is also found in the railroad industry with the New York Central Railroad, Pennsylvania Railroad, and others constituting representative examples.

The holding company is a good example of what resources the promoter and/or active management may use to gain his end. Designed to avoid the legal interference connected with other means of intercorporate control, the holding company principle is widely accepted at the present time. In spite of its somewhat tainted conception, its use has proved a source of economical operation, as well as an easy way to achieve desired co-operation. Instead of being essentially a form of business organization, it has become a device for purposes of control. It occupies a large place in the field of corporation finance because of the close relationship existing between finance and control. At this time our desire is not to consider the holding company as used for consolidation purposes so much as to recognize the corporate principle underlying such a concern. 

According to place of incorporation.-If a corporation receives its charter from the state in which it operates, it is known as a domestic corporation. Corporations organized in other states are classed as foreign corporations by the states in which they do business. Of course, this latter condition refers to strictly intrastate business, as all corporations are free to engage in interstate business without restrictions on the part of the individual states. Included under foreign corporations are also those corporations incorporated in foreign countries. Some writers have chosen to designate this group as "aliens." 

The term has merit as a means of facilitating classification, but as treated in state laws this nomenclature is not applied.

CHAPTER XII  

FINAL step in the organization of a corporation is the selection of a domicile for incorporation. There are important variations in corporate laws which make it necessary to weigh the comparative advantages and disadvantages offered by the different states. Normally, a company should select the state where the bulk of its business will be done, but the specific application of this simple rule will depend upon: (1) whether operations are to be primarily intrastate in character; (2) the relative importance of interstate and intrastate commerce. 

Where Operations Are Primarily Intrastate 

It is seldom advisable for a concern engaged chiefly in intrastate activities to secure a charter outside of its home state. Other states may have more lenient and favorable laws of incorporation, but these charter rights are more than offset by numerous compensatory disadvantages. Unlike a natural person, a corporation does not have the right to do business within another state unless permission is granted by that state. Any organization which obtains its charter of existence from a state other than the one in which it operates is classed as a foreign corporation. Both the cost and inconvenience of this status are sufficient to justify, in most cases, operation on a domestic basis, i. e., to warrant obtaining the charter in the state where operations are to be carried on. 

Where Operations Are Primarily Interstate 

Where operations are primarily interstate, or where activities of the corporation are spread over a number of states, the problem is entirely different. Under these circumstances, the state conferring the broadest powers, at the lowest tax cost, is the one to be favored. 

Most holding companies are examples of corporations which find it desirable to choose a state allowing a wide range of powers. Where operations are both interstate and intrastate in character, it may be advantageous to incorporate on a large scale in one state and to set up smaller corporations in each of the other states where operations 210

are conducted. The American Telephone and Telegraph Company is an excellent example of this method of operation. The long-distance service is furnished by the parent company, while local service is supplied by subsidiary corporations organized to include only one state or a limited number of states. In some cases, the parent company has found it desirable to render intrastate long-distance service through corporations operating entirely within individual states. This has been done to secure tax advantages. 

The significance of selecting a state may be visualized more readily after comparing selected states with reference to some of the features of incorporation.

Capital Requirements 

Most states require a minimum initial capital which must be subscribed before the corporation may begin operations. The amount is usually so low as to be only nominal in character and of no real significance. In the state of Ohio, the minimum capital required is $5,000, while in the more popular states of New Jersey and Delaware, $1,000 is the minimum figure. Arizona has no requirement as to the amount, and the laws of Virginia and Maryland provide that the authorized capital shall be specified by the charter. Presumably, this would make possible a minimum capital of $1, although there should be no advantage from such a low minimum. Formerly, Minnesota had by comparison an unusually high minimum of $10,000, but has reduced this figure to the more usual $1,000. With the minimum requirements being so low, this factor can have little influence upon the selection of the state for purposes of incorporation. 

The nominal character of such minimum capital requirements means that the question of size is given little weight as a criterion for the granting of a charter. The individual with limited personal or family interests would appear to be just as eligible for incorporation as a larger organization raising funds from the public-at-large. In short, the corporate form is equally available for purposes of restricted personal convenience as it is for the mobilization of diversified public representation.

The present liberality in the granting of charters is usually justified on the grounds that encouragement of personal interest leads inevitably to the advancement of the social good. Indeed, numerous examples may be cited where small individual enterprises whose 1

operations were confined to a small locality have grown to become a significant source of employment for the public generally. At the same time, there are many cases where the corporate form has been used deliberately as a means of realizing large profits out of all proportion to the personal risks entailed. There are cases of corporations with capital stock of only $500 or $1,000 with liabilities ranging from $1,000,000 upward. It is apparent that the sponsoring interests assume little risk under such circumstances, but the opportunities for profit may be virtually unlimited.

Possibly size is not the only criterion by which to judge the propriety of incorporation, but it is important that steps be taken to avoid the use of the corporate form as a means of evading proper responsibility. After all, the corporation is a socially created institution and is by no means a natural right which takes root in the typical freedoms expected in any democracy. In brief, the corporate form is bestowed and is essentially a public trust. It is from this point of view that the safeguarding of the public interest warrants reasonable examination of the merits of any proposed charter. 

Requirements as to the Incorporators

The requirements specified for incorporators relate primarily to the following: (1) number required, (2) residence requirements, and (3) other qualifications. In most states at least three incorporators are necessary. This is true of such states as Delaware, New York, New 

Jersey, Virginia, Maine, Massachusetts, Minnesota, and California.

Arizona permits any number, but it is exceptional in this respect as well as in many other requirements for incorporation. 

Many states have no residence qualifications for incorporators, but others require that at least one must be from the state of incorporation. New York provides that at least one must be from the state and two-thirds residents of the United States. In Ohio, it is stipulated that the majority of incorporators must be citizens of the United States, but no residence requirement is enforced. Aside from these features, the other general requirement is that the incorporators shall be natural persons. Apparently, Nevada is the only exception to this rule. Since it makes no restrictions as to the incorporators, it may be presumed that corporations may act as incorporators. It should be mentioned that, as a matter of law, corporations may not become members in a partnership.

Qualification of Directors 

The requirements for qualification as directors are similar to those for incorporators and have much the same variety of treatment. The usual requisite is that there shall be three or more directors without any restrictions as to residence. 

Some states require that the directors must be stockholders in the corporation, presumably to stimulate greater personal interest in the company's welfare. As explained in a later chapter, there is much to be said for linking ownership and control, but customarily most states make no requirement as to the amount of stock that the direc tors must hold, thereby permitting qualification though the ownership of as little as one share. Frequently, in the case of a subsidiary corporation, this qualifying share may be furnished to the director without cost, with the understanding that it will be returned in the event the director resigns or is replaced. New Jersey has an interesting variation of the stock ownership requirement for directors. This state permits the election of a director who does not own stock provided he does own stock in a corporation which holds 25 per cent or more of the stock of the corporation which he is to direct. By this means, any stockholder in a holding company is eligible to serve as director in any of the subsidiaries. 

A few states provide that the directors need not be stockholders. 

Among these states are Delaware, Arizona, Minnesota, and California. 

The most usual arrangement appears to be the requirement that the by-laws of the corporation shall determine the qualifications for directors. A variation is that directors must be stockholders unless otherwise provided for in the by-laws and charter, Liabilities of Directors 

Most corporation laws include a statement of the liabilities of directors. The purpose of formally stating these responsibilities is perhaps twofold. In the first place, formal statement serves to remind the director of his obligations, and, second, it helps to prevent the corporation from exceeding its granted powers. In the General Corporation Act of Ohio, it is specifically stated that "the Articles [of incorporation] shall constitute an agreement by the directors and officers with the corporation to those acts which are authorized by the statement of purposes and within such limitations and restric-

tions as may be imposed by the articles." More specifically the liabilities of directors of Ohio corporations are: 

1. If any corporation begins business before the capital specified in the articles of incorporation has been paid in, the directors participating in the act are jointly and severally liable for the debts of the corporation up to the capital so stated. It should be understood that this does not relate to the authorized capital but only to the capital which must be paid in prior to the commencement of operations. 

2. Officers, employees, and others are liable for issuing fraudulent reports. 

3. If a loan advance is made to a director other than in the course of doing business, each officer approving the transaction is liable for the amount plus interest at 6 per cent. 

4. Directors are also liable for paying dividends contrary to law which usually means paying dividends out of capital instead of earnings.

Directors' liabilities vary from state to state, not only because of differences in the statutes but also because of their varied interpretations by the state courts. Until recent years, courts have been extremely reluctant to hold directors for acts other than extreme negligence and fraud. This philosophy resulted, at least in part, from the charitable conception that directors served without compensation and should not be held too rigidly for an accounting. Today the interpretation varies from the strict criterion that they should be held for the care that a reasonably prudent man should give to his own property to the more flexible view that they should be held only for action expected of a reasonably prudent director. Some people would hold that the element of trust would require that a reasonably prudent director give a greater degree of care to the property intrusted to him than if it were his own. Another group would tend to forgive the director for anything except the worst blunders in judgment. However, the former view is becoming more general, and the director's position is being treated as a fiduciary and his actions judged accordingly.

Illustrative of these principles, directors have been held for the following:1 (1) negligence in failing to attend meetings; (2) failure 

1 These instances among others are presented by the Securities and Exchange Commission in Report on the Study and Investigation of the Work, Activities, Personnel and Functions of Protective and Reorganization Committees, Part II, "Committees and Conflicts of Interest, 1936," pp. 22-31.

to inform associates of important information; (3) complacent acceptance of fraudulent action of officers; (4) allowing inefficient officers to remain in office; (5) failure to require a bond from an officer who later absconds; (6) actions without authority; (7) acceptance of secret profits arising by virtue of their position. Directors are not held for mistakes of judgment where reasonable investigation and study have preceded the decisions. 

Liability of Stockholders 

The liability of the individual shareholders is limited to the initial purchase price in the case of no-par stock and to the stated value in the case of par stock. This means that in the event of failure the stockholder is liable for any difference that may exist between the purchase price or par and the amount actually paid to the corporation. A few states, such as New York and Massachusetts, provide that stockholders shall also be liable for any debts to employees. 

As late as 1931 the laws of California were more rigid in attaching liability to the stockholders. In that state, it was specified that stockholders were liable for their proportionate share of the debts and liabilities of the corporation. To prevent the evasion of this law by incorporating in other states, it was stipulated that shareholders of foreign corporations doing business in California had a similar liability. The stockholders of Nebraska corporations may, through negligence of the officers, be subjected to even further liability than existed in California. Nebraska corporations are required to publish annually in the counties where business is conducted the total amount of all existing debts. Failure to do this renders the stockholders jointly and severally liable for all debts not covered by assets in the event of liquidation. 

Classes of Stocks

It is a customary feature of most corporation laws to permit any number of classes of stock, but it is necessary to specify in the charter the rights and privileges of the respective classes. Usually the corporation laws require a statement of the terms of redemption, dividend return, liquidation price, and the right to vote. In a few states the right to vote may not be removed from any issue, but in the majority it is permissible to centralize the voting in any class of stock. 

Centralization of the voting power has given rise to the use of classes of common stock, usually designated as Class A and Class B

common. As has been decribed at another point, the former has the privilege to vote only in the event of certain contingencies. This is not the place to discuss the merits of this plan, but it is obvious that the privilege may exercise a decided influence in selecting the state for incorporation whenever the incorporators are interested in obtaining absolute control with a minimum investment. To prevent the abuse of this right, it may be provided, as in Ohio, that no stock may be deprived of its right to vote on an issue which would relegate the outstanding stock to a more junior position. Further protection arises from the fact that regulatory agencies frown upon classified common stock. As a result, the present tendency is away from its use.

Cumulative Voting 

Under cumulative voting each shareholder is entitled to a number of votes equal to the number of shares he possesses times the number of directors to be elected. This arrangement permits the stockholders to spread their votes among various directors to be elected or to concentrate them upon a portion of the directors or even a single director. By mutual concentration, the minority element may thus be assured of representation on the board. Some states demand that this plan of voting be used exclusively. This is true of Arizona, Arkansas, Illinois, Michigan, and Pennsylvania. Such states as Delaware, New Jersey, New York, and Maryland specify that it is permissive, but not compulsory. This means that it may be included as one of the articles of incorporation or may be enacted as one of the by-laws. 

In Ohio, it is compulsory if any stockholder demands the cumulative voting privilege at least twenty-four hours before any meeting. In 

North Carolina, it is permissive but may be made compulsory by a vote of one-fourth of the capital stock.

Duration In the days of specific legislative enactment of corporate charters, corporations usually received perpetual life. Under the system of general incorporation laws prevailing today, the most frequent requirement relating to the life of a corporation is that it shall be either perpetual or term at the option of the corporation. Where a specified term is selected or required, provision for automatic extension of life is permitted in most cases. The state of Arizona allows only twenty-

Fees and Taxes

Corporations are subjected to two types of franchise taxes. One is the fee levied at the time of granting the charter and may be termed a tax levied for the privilege of existing as a corporation. The initial fee is sometimes referred to as a privilege tax "to be" and the annual tax as a privilege tax "to do."

The fees charged by the various states for granting charters to exist as a corporation vary widely. The degree of variation can be seen to best advantage by comparing the fees which would be charged by a number of the states for the incorporation of a company having 1,000,000 shares of no-par common stock. Only the organization tax is included in the comparison, and the miscellaneous filing fees and discretionary charges which usually accompany such proceedings are omitted. The organization tax for the assumed corporation would be as follows: Delaware Ohio Massachusetts 

New York 

$ 2,550 5,100 10,000 50,000

The difference between Delaware and New York is striking and, assuming other things were equally favorable, would constitute adequate reason for choosing Delaware over New York as the state for incorporating. Also those states having reasonably broad or favorable laws for incorporation generally have the lowest fees. 

It is more difficult to compare the annual tax levied on corporations because in many instances the tax is based upon a variable figure such as the volume of business done in the particular state, the value' of property, gross income, or some other measure. For example, in 

New York the tax is 6 per cent of the net income derived from assets segregated to that state. This means that if the foregoing corporation earned 8 per cent on its investment, assuming an investment of $100,- 000,000 in New York, its net income would be $8,000,000, and therefore its annual tax would be $480,000. In contrast, the annual tax if incorporated in Delaware would be $2,500.

·  

In Ohio, the annual tax is based upon a combination of the value of the property and the volume of business. The first step in determining the tax is to arrive at the value of the outstanding stock as measured by the total of the company's capital, surplus, undivided profits, and reserve accounts, excluding reasonable reserves for depreciation, depletion, and taxes applicable to the year of the report. 

Good-will may be excluded if it has been treated as an asset, as well as any additional amount by which the book value may be in excess of par value, provided proof of such existence can be made to the tax commission's satisfaction. The resulting figure is divided into two equal parts. One part is multiplied by a fraction, the numerator of which is the value of the corporation's property in Ohio and the denominator, the total value of all the corporation's property. The other is multiplied by a fraction whose numerator is the volume of business done by the corporation in the state and the denominator, the total volume of business done by the corporation for the year of the report. The two results are added and subjected to a tax of one-tenth of 1 per cent. This method applies to both foreign and domestic corporations. 

Which State?

It should be evident from the foregoing discussion that the problem of selecting a state for purposes of incorporation is a complicated one. 

The solution requires not only a knowledge of the various state laws but also the interpretation of these laws by the courts. States having corporation laws providing for a wide scope of operations and further supported by a well-defined and clear body of court decisions possess decided advantage over other states which do not have as broad laws or as definite interpretations. When one considers that corporate charters may be granted by forty-eight states, the District of Columbia, and the federal government, and that each of these jurisdictions has its own body of court interpretations, the great complexity of corporate law can be appreciated. 

Just as the law and its interpretation may make certain states popular for incorporation purposes, the same states may be affected adversely by any tightening of their laws or by other states offering greater advantages on a competitive basis. The former development may be illustrated by New Jersey, when, during the administration of Governor Woodrow Wilson, the laws favoring holding companies were abolished, only to be restored soon afterward because of the great

loss in tax income. At times, competing states may pass laws which offer greater advantages for incorporation either because of broad corporate powers or reduced fees and taxes. Delaware is prominent in this respect, and although the state is one of the smallest in the United States, it ranks high in the number of charters granted. Among some of the more important corporations receiving their charter from this state, as well as the date of issuing the charter, may be listed the following:

E. I. Du Pont de Nemours Company. 

General Motors Corporation.. 

Radio Corporation of America. 

General Foods Corporation. 

United Gas Company..

Commonwealth and Southern Corporation. 

United Gas Corporation... 

1915 1916 1919 . 1922 .1928 1929 .1930 1 In making the final decision upon the state for incorporation, the relative qualifications of the various states must be assembled and considered as a whole. Every state will have disadvantages as well as advantages for the particular corporation. With this in mind, the following criteria should be given adequate consideration. 

1. Do the laws of the state grant the powers desired? 

2. Do the corporation commissioners or other officials apply the laws liberally and consistently? 

3. Are the interpretations of the statutes by the courts favorable and consistent? 

4. Is the saving affected in fees sufficiently material to offset other disadvantages? 

5. What rights do foreign corporations have in the other states where it is planned to operate?

Often the last question may be of sufficient importance to offset favorable answers to the first four questions. In view of this, it is necessary to give brief consideration to the rights of foreign corporations operating in other states. 

The Right of Operating in Other States 

A corporation may not operate in other than its domicile unless permission is received from the proper officials in each of the other states. In this respect, the corporation differs from an ordinary citizen or natural person who is free to enter other states without formal as- 

Word.

sent. Instead, the corporation must make application for the privilege and pay the fees and taxes levied upon foreign corporations. The essential routine involved in gaining admission may be summarized: (1) filing certified copies of articles of incorporation; (2) appointment of a resident agent or giving a specified resident the power of attorney; (3) payment of filing fees as well as other fees; (4) payment of the annual franchise tax. 

Accompanying the certified copy of the articles of incorporation is the official form for petitioning the Secretary of State to do business within the state. The appointment of a resident agent is a simple matter in most states. Any person, a lawyer, or trust company may be chosen. However, New York and Massachusetts specify that the 

Secretary of State and the Commissioner of Corporations respectively shall serve as the corporation's agent or lawful attorney. The purpose of a resident agent is simply to provide means whereby legal notices may be served upon the corporation if necessary. New York and Massachusetts specify a government official merely to make it easier and more certain to locate the corporation's agent. 

The entrance or filing fees paid by foreign corporations vary widely from state to state. Delaware charges $10; Massachusetts and Ohio, $50; and New York, $100. Such amounts appear to be quite common among the states. In addition to the filing fee, many states impose initial and annual charges comparable to the organization and annual taxes of domestic corporations. Thus, in Ohio, a fee based on the shares reported in the state is charged as well as an annual tax computed in the same manner as for domestic corporations. In Ohio, the charges levied on foreign corporations are at the same rate as for domestic corporations, but in New York a higher rate is levied. Delaware and New Jersey, on the other hand, are examples of states operating on a reciprocal basis, meaning that the taxes levied are based upon the charges made by other states upon New Jersey corporations. In other words, if Arizona were to levy a heavier privilege tax on a New Jersey corporation than the New Jersey law required from a foreign corporation, then Arizona corporations operating in New Jersey would be taxed on the Arizona basis. 

What Constitutes Doing Business? 

Fundamental to the entire problem of foreign corporations is the determination of what constitutes doing business in a state. Although

it is almost impossible to state any prevailing rules that are universally applicable, in general it may be said that: 

1. Where the salesmen of a foreign corporation solicit business in a state, but shipment is made from outside of that state, such business is not intrastate business. 

2. If the shipment is made from a point within the state in which the sale is made, the transaction constitutes intrastate business. 

3. Delivery and collection by the foreign corporation's agent may not necessarily constitute intrastate business providing the shipment has come from without the state. 

4. The opening of an office may or may not constitute doing business depending upon the extent of the activities of the office. 

5. Performance of a single or isolated transaction is not usually considered doing business.

Although the conduct of interstate business by a foreign corporation is free of state interference and taxes, certain risks of operation are created. In addition to the great uncertainty as to what actually constitutes doing business, it may mean the sacrifice of the privilege of enforcing contracts through the medium of the state courts. Hence, if there is any doubt as to the nature of the business, corporations frequently qualify for intrastate operation to avoid possible complications. 

The existence of so many different corporation laws presents numerous complicated problems to both the states and the corporations. 

Some legal authorities are inclined to be optimistic enough to hope, if not believe, that eventually the various corporations laws will be standardized. A step in this direction was made by the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws when it drafted the Uniform Business Corporation Act in 1933. This was also approved by the American Bar Association. While this may prove to be a workable solution to the problem, it is not necessarily the ideal answer. 

Ultimately it would seem that the only real solution would be found in providing federal chartering for all corporations engaged in interstate business.

Federal Incorporation 

Under the interstate commerce clause of the Constitution, the federal government already has the right to grant charters to corporations engaged in interstate business. The Union Pacific and the Northern 

Pacific Railroad companies are examples of corporations receiving

their charters under this seldom used federal power. Acting under its currency powers, the federal government also grants charters to national banks and to federal savings and loan associations. However, such financial corporations do not belong to corporation finance as the field of study is defined. 

While there has never been any widespread or insistent demand for federal chartering of corporations, suggestions along this line are occasionally put forth. These may be to require all corporations in interstate commerce to apply for federal charters or they may provide for licensing such as is contained in the O'Mahoney Bill.2 Under the latter, corporations would obtain their charter from the various states, as is now the case; but before entering interstate commerce, they would have to obtain a Federal license which would be issued only if the corporation met certain prescribed conditions and which could be revoked for certain breaches of conduct. In this way, higher standards and greater uniformity could be enforced upon the corporations in interstate commerce, which would include the bulk of the business activity, though by no means the majority of individual corporations.

Federal charters appear to be a highly desirable step when viewed as a possible relief to the numerous and variegated laws and practices now in vogue among the states. The question may well be raised why any state should have the right to authorize a corporation to conduct interstate business involving the other states of the Union. For example, why should the state of Wisconsin have the right to give the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Pacific Railroad Company a charter to operate a railroad extending from the middle west to the Pacific Coast? Broad powers and loose restrictions granted in the charter of one state are difficult to limit by other states when it permits that foreign corporation to operate in its own territory. 

The conduct of interstate commerce by foreign corporations often becomes involved in questions of charter rights. Since many states attempt to restrict foreign corporations to rights no greater than those extended to domestic corporations, the foreign corporation may find itself forced to operate under many different requirements. What it may do legally in the home state may be illegal in much of the territory which it covers. Furthermore, much of the administration of the 

2 S. B. 3072, 75th Congress, 2d Session, 1937, Congressional Record, pp. 494-98; J. C. 

O'Mahoney, "Federal Charters and Licenses for Corporations," Journal National Education 

Association, Vol. 27, No. 1 (January, 1938), p. 27,

system is made difficult by many law suits. The respective rights of the state and the foreign corporation are constantly a matter of debate, and there is always the tendency for the state legislature to attempt the installation of discriminatory tax syste.ns in an effort to protect the home-state business.

The only practical solutions to this contradictory condition appear to be standardization of incorporation laws among the states, federal incorporation, or the adoption of a policy of local incorporation on the part of the corporation with interstate activity. Under the last plan, the parent corporation would become a holding company and would incorporate domestic subsidiary corporations in each and every state where it expected to do business. Since the first method is unlikely to occur and local incorporation would be expensive and cumbersome, it leaves only federal incorporation as a truly logical and satisfactory solution. Unfortunately, it may be many years before sufficient demand for federal chartering develops to bring about its adoption. In the meantime, the present unsatisfactory system will continue.

The State and Public Welfare 

The state plays an exceedingly important role in facilitating the organization of corporate enterprise. In playing this part, it is the duty of the state not only to provide the ways and means for an organization, but at the same time it must protect the public. The right to incorporate should not be granted too freely but should be permitted only after thorough analysis of the pertinent facts relating to the proposed undertaking. Clearly the state should exercise whatever caution is necessary to prevent the creation of fraudulent concerns. All too frequently the corporate form has been a convenient tool for the fake promoter to raise funds from the unsuspecting citizen. 

Safeguarding of the public welfare should demand that the state make these schemes virtually impossible, and probably it should also go so far as to afford some protection against corporations whose prospects appear hopeless.

Practice of the latter type is followed when considering applications to incorporate certain special types of business. It is not unusual for the state superintendent of banking or the comptroller of currency, in the case of national banks, to refuse to allow the organization of a new bank on the theory that the particular community does not need

further banking facilities. This is similarly true of railroads and other forms of public utilities.

Should the secretaries of the various states or commissioners of corporations be as free to act in this respect in considering the applications for the chartering of industrial and commercial enterprises? It is already their duty to give consideration to the exchange of securities for equivalent value, as well as to protect the public against other abuses of malicious nature. The question of the need of a new company is an equally important one. Should the general incorporation laws be enlarged so as to permit the denial of a request on the ground that the company is superfluous? Such action on the part of the public officials would, of course, be approaching the nature of a planned economy, and like so many phases of a planned economy it would seem entirely sound in the blue-print stage. In practice, however, it would introduce many difficult problems for the state authorities to meet and solve. There would be the question of determining the need for the new enterprise, which would call for analysis of the market and the outlook for continued development. There would also be other problems such as those dealing with techniques of production. Should a new enterprise be allowed to begin operations and introduce new techniques which would render existing organizations obsolete and unable to compete, or should the installation of new equipment be delayed until such time as existing capacities have been sufficiently depreciated? These would be difficult problems which could not be solved with any uniform degree of success, yet at the same time, it must be admitted that every year many new undertakings are begun which appear doomed to failure except to a few enthusiastic promoters and interested stockholders. A few of these ultimately succeed, but the majority fail; and in the long run the costs of failure must be borne by society at large. 

In 1925, Oklahoma attempted restrictive regulation by requiring the Corporation Commission to issue a license before any new ice business could be established. The law instructed the Commission to issue such licenses only upon competent proof that existing facilities were inadequate to supply the needs of the public.³ In a case decided in 1932, the United States Supreme Court held this statute to be an invalid regulation of a private business. While the practical problems 

3 Chapter 147, Section 3, Session Laws of 1925. 

A New State Ice Company v. Liebmann, 52 Supreme Court Reports, 371.

involved in securing fair, honest, non-political regulation of industry are considerable, there is a great deal of merit in the idea of requiring proof of reasonable need before a new enterprise is chartered in a competitive industry. 

The State and the Going Concern 

The relationship between the state and the corporation should be a continuing one throughout the corporation's existence. It is important that the corporation be made to feel a definite responsibility to the public as represented in the state. A going concern should be constantly called upon to defend its rights to existence in the same way that it justifies its creation. As it meets certain technical requirements to attain a charter, it should also furnish definite annual reports upon its ways of doing business. All too often, business depressions have brought to light various malpractices which should have been detected by responsible state authorities. Poor reports and still poorer supervision have been responsible for permitting dangerous financial situations to develop to the breaking point. The case of the Middle 

West Utilities Company is illustrative of this point. 

The immediate cause of the collapse of this public utility holding company, which occurred in April, 1932, was the withdrawal of the bank credit used to finance a portion of its operations; the ultimate cause, however, was unsound financial practices. The company had acquired control of many operating companies at absurdly high prices with funds obtained through the sale of various classes of securities and through bank loans. If the prosperity of the boom 20's had continued for a sufficient period, the capitalized values placed on the subsidiaries might have been justified, but if sound financial practices had been adopted and reasonable valuations placed on the company's assets even the severe depression of 1930 to 1936 could have been weathered successfully. This financial catastrophe was allowed to develop over a considerable period of time unchecked by the state authorities. It would seem that public officials should prevent the extremes of financial abuse. Proper regulation and supervision of industries is possible, but it will require high-caliber officials and adequate staffs serving on a permanent, rather than a political, basis. 

The state should not go so far as to guarantee the solvency of a company, but it ought to insure the honesty of the reports. For the attainment of this goal additional machinery and expense would be

required. This would mean a rather large direct cost, but it is doubtful if it would equal the enormous ultimate costs now borne by the public-at-large. One of the benefits which would arise from such state action would be corporation reports which more nearly represent the facts. Public officials would inspect all of the reports and, among other things, would challenge the statement of values appearing in the balance sheet. This would certainly be more logical than waiting for some unusual event, such as failure, to test the validity of the corporation values under the present mode of procedure. 

Nature of Present Supervision In contrast to the foregoing desired conditions, the state knows entirely too little about corporate affairs-both individually and as a body. Illustrative of this, a letter from the office of the secretary of one of the states may be quoted in part: "There are several thousand corporations incorporated under the laws of this state every year, of which number a large percentage go out of existence each year. 

Therefore, you will see it would be impossible to keep track of the exact number of active corporations." Again, “a numerical list of the companies incorporated in has never been kept, nor are the corporations classified.” 

The chief defense offered in support of this lack of corporate supervision is the cost and administrative routines which would be required. 

Without any question,.effective surveillance would constitute a mammoth undertaking, but it would assist materially in classifying the status of the corporate bodies. 

The reader must keep in mind that the foregoing discussion has dealt entirely with state supervision and regulation. The beginnings of much more effective and high quality regulation of corporate activity may be found in that conducted by the Securities and Exchange Commission beginning with 1934. The nature of this regulation will be discussed in a later chapter.

CHAPTER XIII CAPITALIZATION 

'N ordinary non-technical language, to capitalize means "to compute, appraise, or to estimate the present value of." The valuation of an income is computed on the basis of the duration and amount of the income at a given rate of interest per year. Thus, the capitalization of an annuity of $10,000 per year at 4 per cent interest would be $250,000. If the rate of interest used in computing the capitalized value were 5 per cent, the capitalization would be $200,000. 

The capitalized result ($200,000 in the latter case) constitutes an asset in favor of the owner and arises out of the existence of the annual income. There is need to distinguish clearly between this asset concept of capitalization and its classification as a liability when used in corporation finance.

The capitalization of a corporation is not found on the asset side but appears in the liability section of the balance sheet. It consists of the various media which are used to raise long-term capital. The presumption follows that the various media would normally be represented by equivalent assets, and for this reason capitalization is commonly regarded as a yardstick of value. In this sense, the basic and generic meaning of capitalization is usually implied when the term is used in finance to refer to the sources from which the capital was raised. 

The different meanings of capitalization are in large part the result of the approach used by, or the point of view of, the interested parties. Thus, if a group were negotiating for the purchase of a corporation, it could do so by obtaining title to the capital stock. Under the circumstances, the capitalization would be tested to determine whether it was representative of the value of the corporation. On the other hand, from the point of view of internal financial management, the question of value would be of indirect concern only. Instead, more attention would be given to the capital set-up for its adequacy as a plan of providing funds for the enterprise. 

In analyzing the financial structure of corporations, consideration will be given wherever appropriate to the dual nature of capitalization. 

Preliminary to this, the following connotations may be noted: 

1. The term may have reference to the capital authorized in the articles of incorporation. For example, if a corporation is permitted 228

CAPITALIZATION 

229 under its articles of incorporation to issue $100,000 of common stock and $50,000 of preferred stock, then its capitalization is said to be $150,000. This may be termed the "legal connotation." 

2. Occasionally the word "capitalization" may be used to refer to the amount of capital stock outstanding even though that amount may be less than the authorized capital. 

3. The more general financial usage of the term applies to the financial plan of the corporation, in other words, the financial structure by which capital is raised. In this use of the term, capitalization includes not only common stock and preferred stock, but also all forms of long-term debt. Broadly speaking, any media for obtaining capital for uses over an extended period of time would be included as a part of the capitalization.

Limitations of the Legal Concept 

These diverse definitions of capitalization may be clarified by noting their specific application. From the financial point of view, there are a number of limitations in the basic legal connotation of authorized capital. In the first place, it excludes funded debt and thus does not give a picture of the entire capital-raising media. The second difficulty arises out of the tendency to regard capitalization as a measure of the value of a business enterprise. This application is partially supported by the corporation laws themselves since they expressly provide that all stock issued by the corporation must be in exchange for assets or services of equivalent value. But the determination of equivalent value is subject to the vagaries of time and of personal opinion. Particularly is this true of stock subscriptions by insiders who often pay for their stock with intangible items whose value is both debatable and variable. The chance of error is further accentuated by personalities because the directors are passing upon a transaction which probably affects some of their own members. Even granting no shortcoming because of appraisal, the authorized capital can reflect value only momentarily. The first business transaction completed will begin a process of converting the cash into other assets which will make the actual value of the company more or less than its stated capitalization.

Limitations of the Financial Concept 

Similar elements of confusion are found in the financial connotation of capitalization. While book figures are used to determine

the amount of capitalization, they are historical in character rather than representative of current values. As a consequence, there will be a continuous disparity between the book capitalization of the enterprise and the actual or exchange value. At the point of initiation, when the assets are liquid, the two should be in approximate agreement, but beyond that there will be no necessary relationship. This will be demonstrated by numerous illustrations as the capital structure is analyzed in more detail. 

The value concept of capitalization is of less significance to financial policy than its meaning as a source of capital. When capitalization is thought of in the latter sense, it gives emphasis to one of the more important phases of corporation finance, namely, the financial plan. This concerns the vital question of how much capital is raised through the medium of funded debt, preferred stock, and common stock as well as the proper balance between the various sources. There remains the problem of the amount of capital to be raised. Practically speaking, this amount must be one that is capable of investment in equivalent values if investors are to be induced to intrust their funds in the enterprise. The relationship between source and amount can be seen to advantage by studying their applicability to both new and established enterprises.

One important difference needs to be emphasized in analyzing the capital structure of new and old companies. In the former, the approach is de novo, and the essential problem is to determine what the capitalization should be. At this stage, management or the controlling financial interests are relatively free to design the arrangement as it best fits the needs of the individual enterprise. The capitalization of an established company lacks this flexibility. Of course, it may be modified by write-down, the issuance of new securities, etc., but the net result is still a revision of an original plan. 

Capitalization of the New Enterprise 

In launching a new enterprise, reasonable provision must be made for future as well as for current needs. Hence, there arises the danger of either overcapitalizing or undercapitalizing the company. Both errors result in unfortunate consequences. In the event of overcapitalization, the burden usually falls upon innocent investors who discover too late the insufficiency of assets to cover their investment. Undercapitalization leads more to curtailment of opportunity than it does

CAPITALIZATION 

231 necessarily to the loss of capital; eventually, however, a capital shortage may lead to failure.

A new enterprise operates at great disadvantage in the raising of capital because there is no gauge of the risk entailed. Lacking the seasoning of an established company, promoters of a new company frequently become beggars instead of choosers of capital. As a result, they may be compelled to pay high rates, and their sources may be determined by expediency more than by judgment. The significance of capitalization as a measure of value is also weakened once the project is put into operation because the early stages are in many respects a discounting of future possibilities. 

To determine the amount of capitalization, two theories have been propounded. (1) The historical cost theory in which the capitalization is regarded as the equivalent of the cost actually incurred in setting up the corporation. (2) The earnings theory in which the probable earnings are forecast and capitalized at a representative rate of return.

The Cost Theory 

Under the cost theory, the amount of capitalization is based upon the original, out-of-pocket investment in plant, equipment, etc. Obviously, the use of initial cost facilitates the calculation of the amount of capital to be raised, but it may prove deficient as a formula for taking care of future needs. Under this plan, greater stress is placed upon current outlays than upon the requirements necessary to accommodate the transition to a going-concern basis. 

Upon first thought, the cost principle may appear to give assurance that the capitalization would at least be representative of the value of the enterprise. However, as indicated previously, this correlation would exist only momentarily. Original cost is static in character and would in no way reflect future changes. Not only is it possible for the capital equipment to become obsolete, but in addition true worth is dependent primarily upon earnings. 

The Earnings Theory 

Any business is worth what it will earn, and it would, therefore, appear that the earnings basis is the more sound for purposes of capitalization. Unfortunately, the earnings of new enterprises are unknown and it is necessary to resort to estimates. Moreover, from the very nature of promotion, there is a tendency to overestimate the

earnings with the possibility of giving rise to a situation which will be discussed later under watered stock. Because of this tendency, the uncertainty of predicting earnings, and the requirements of law, cost is usually favored as a basis in constructing the initial financial plan.

Under conditions of active competition, the two bases should be in approximate agreement. If competition is functioning, the profit levels of a business should be no higher than what would be regarded as a favorable return on the investment. Abnormally high profits in a line of enterprise would tend to encourage added investments in that business, which would in time reduce the profit yields to the competitive standard. On the other hand, if the profit yield failed to support a value on an earnings basis which was equal to cost, it would be expected that no new investment would be made in the field unless the cost of establishing a new enterprise could be reduced to harmonize with probable earnings.

Capitalization as a Source of Funds 

When used to mean the plan for raising capital, capitalization must vary according to the field of activity. Where the income is variable and uncertain, bonds must be avoided and stock used to raise the capital funds. If any doubt exists as to covering the preferred dividends adequately, then only common stock should be issued. In summary form, the following tentative principles may be expressed: 

Bonds.-Bonds should be issued only when the earnings outlook appears to be steady and certain. These features are prominent in the utilities field and are further accompanied by an excellent backing of fixed assets. 

Preferred Stock.—Preferred stock may be used by public utilities, railroads, and industrials. Issuance is warranted whenever it appears that the earnings over a period of time are sufficient to cover the dividends without causing undue curtailment of operations. The practice of issuing preferred stock to cover the investment and giving common stock as a bonus is open to question as a form of sound policy.

Common stock.-Common stock necessarily appears in all corporations and should be used as much as possible to provide the bulk of the financing. It should be used exclusively by all enterprises in-

CAPITALIZATION 

233 volving high risk, and quite extensively by all corporations as an evidence of belief in the project. The acceptance by investors of this residual risk is, of course, encouraged by the prospects of higher yields than are normally returned on bonds or preferred stock. 

Capitalization of the Established Company 

The established corporation shows in striking manner the deficiencies of capitalization as a measure of value. Here it is possible to apply other objective tests against the capitalized figures, particularly the following: (1) the value of the corporation as expressed in the securities market; (2) the value of the corporation on a capitalized earnings basis.

Economists have often said that the nearest approach to a perfect market is that of the New York Stock Exchange. This institution provides every facility for a ready expression of demand and supply, and the prices established over a period of time should therefore be representative. The fact that values determined in this market are so unlike those presented by the corporation's books calls for careful explanation. Market value is determined by multiplying the average of the high and low prices of the shares for 1929, 1934, and 1940 respectively by the number of shares outstanding. The process is the same for both preferred and common stock.

The discrepancy existing between book and market values is caused by numerous factors. One reason arises out of accepted accounting policy whereby cost or market, whichever is lower, is used as a basis for evaluating inventories. This may be justified as a means of encouraging conservatism, but it may under some circumstances be the source of a wide disparity between the book value and market value of a company. A more important reason for the difference is the failure to record changes in value of the asset accounts. Under standard accounting practice, fixed assets such as land and buildings are recorded at the cost figure, and no further changes are made except to accrue depreciation and to recognize actual transactions. As a result, considerable appreciation in the value of the fixed assets may take place without being a matter of record, and, conversely, there may be failure to recognize obsolescence or other causes of value depletion.

Furthermore, the fundamental nature of book and market values prevents any close correlation of the two figures. Market value is based primarily upon the anticipated future operations of the company, while the book value represents past transactions. Generally speaking, this causes market value to be less than the book figure when prospects are unfavorable. Value as Expressed by Capitalized Earnings 

A comparison of book value with capitalized earnings gives the results shown in Table 24. The computations have been made upon the basis of a 6 per cent capitalization rate. This rate may appear to be high when judged in the light of interest rate levels in recent years, but it should be satisfactory for comparative purposes. In this comparison, as in the former one, the book figures are too static to reflect the changing values which accompany variations in earnings. While the net results of operations are incorporated into the records, no change is ordinarily made in the initial capitalization as a result of changed earnings conditions. 

A word may be said concerning the comparability of capitalized earnings figures with market valuations. Analysis of Table 24 shows that there is slightly more similarity here than in comparison with book figures, but, at the same time, considerable discrepancy exists between the two. This is due, undoubtedly, to the fact that the capitalized value of earnings represents past achievements, while market valuations have a tendency to stress anticipated values arising from the future outlook.

Is Surplus a Part of Capitalization? 

Before deciding whether or not surplus should be regarded as a part of capitalization, it is essential to have clearly in mind the nature of the surplus account. Although many kinds of special surplus accounts may be created, usually they may be classified into the following two major categories: (1) some form of capital surplus; (2) some form of earned surplus. 

Capital Surplus 

Capital surplus arises from sources other than current operations. 

Perhaps the most typical sources of such surplus may be found in the sale of fixed assets at a profit or in the sale of stock at a price in 1

excess of par or stated value. In the sale of par stock, the excess is usually called capital surplus or premium on stock; in the case of no-par stock, the term "paid-in surplus" is common. Other sources are donations of stock and assets to the corporation, assessments upon outstanding stock, or reductions in capital stock. To these should be added surplus arising from mergers, the reorganization of insolvent concerns, and that due to an appreciation in the value of assets. 

While under certain circumstances and under some state laws, it may be possible to declare dividends out of capital surplus, such is not the normal expectation. Nor is it usually possible. Instead, surplus of this type will be held in the business as a means of facilitating long-time operations. Under these circumstances, it is an integral part of the long-time financial structure of the corporation and may logically be classified as a part of the capitalization. It should be recognized that this conclusion is applicable only in a financial or an accounting sense; when viewed in a legal light, capital surplus may not be so considered. 

Earned Surplus

Earned surplus is the accumulation of net earnings which are allowed to remain in the business. This means that its original source is to be found in the current operation of a business enterprise. Because the source of this surplus is in current activities, it does not necessarily follow that earned surplus may not be regarded as a part of the long-time financial program. A more satisfactory criterion for determining the classification of surplus would be found in the intentions of the management as to the disposal of the surplus. If the management plans to retain surplus in the business, it should be treated as a part of the capitalization just as much as common stock sold to the public. Both items (common stock and earned surplus) are simply means of raising capital and may well be placed in the same general category of capitalization.

To this argument, it may be replied that the surplus may be disposed of and used for dividend distribution. This may be true, but for the typical going concern, this would not be the usual practice applicable to the bulk of the surplus. The mere fact that surplus has been set up at the outset means that it is above the regular dividend distribution. Moreover, earned surplus is the usual basis for declaring stock dividends, which, in turn, are recognized universally

CAPITALIZATION 

237 as part of the capitalization upon completion of the formal issuance of the stock.

The point may be illustrated by the 40 per cent stock dividend of the United States Steel Corporation in 1927. The common stock was increased from $508,302,500 to $711,623,500, and the surplus account was reduced by the difference. From the legal point of view, such transposed surplus became an integral part of the capitalization, but from the standpoint of the long-time financial plan, little change was effected. It is more than likely that the original surplus was regarded as a permanent part of the financial structure, a conclusion which is supported by further analysis of the surplus account. From 1918 through 1929, the undivided surplus account was less than $400,000,000 in only the year 1927 when the stock dividend was declared. This means that over a long period of time one major source of capital funds was surplus earnings which were kept in the business. Under such a policy, it is entirely logical to regard earned surplus as a part of the capitalization.

The argument is even more convincing when applied to appropriated surplus. For many years, the United States Steel Corporation carried an account entitled "Appropriation for additions and construction." From 1926 to 1934 this account had amounted to $270,000,000, and beginning with 1918, it was never less than $110,000,000.¹ For a considerable period of time, the Bethlehem Steel Corporation had a similar account designated as appropriated surplus, but in 1931 it was merged with general surplus. Since the act of appropriation for specific uses destroys the availability of surplus for dividend purposes, the earmarked account really becomes a part of the long-time financial plan.

It is interesting to note in this connection the extent to which corporations are sometimes able to finance capital outlays from surplus and other internal sources. During the years, 1921-38, the United 

States Steel Corporation made capital outlays of $1,606,000,000 for plant and equipment and the retirement of debt. Of this large sum, 1 The account was closed out in 1935 through the transfer of $88,720,028 to the reserve for depreciation and depletion and the balance of $181,279,972 to the amortization reserve. 

These transfers did not withdraw capital from the business in any way. Capital stock could similarly be reduced in book value and the amount of the reduction transferred to valuation reserves.
