Watered Stock 

Watered stock has long been a subject for popular discussion. 

While it has been discussed pro and con (mostly the latter) for decades, the layman finds difficulty in giving a precise definition of watered stock. A colorful explanation may be obtained easily, but it is so general as to be almost meaningless. In the first place, the meaning of watered stock has been confused by the application of par value as a means of measurement. Quite frequently, any stock issued at a price less than par is deemed to be watered. This is not necessarily true in fact. The stock may be matched by equivalent assets in the form of cash and other consideration realized at the time of sale, and the discount is, of course, offset by the liability of the stockholders for an identical amount which may be collected by the corporation whenever deemed necessary. Secondly, the criterion of an absence of equivalent value representative of issued stock is true in its general outline, but too broad to define the term accurately. An understanding of watered stock may be obtained from the following specific applications: (1) watered stock as found in the new enterprise; (2) watered stock as a result of poor earnings; (3) watered stock as revealed by market operations.

Watered Stock and the New Enterprise 

According to the standards established by the general corporation laws of all states, stock may be issued only: (a) at a uniform price to all subscribers; (b) for value received. The first requirement is applicable only to a given series, which means that later issues may be sold at prices more adaptable to prevailing market conditions. The second requirement is the cause of the greatest trouble. Not only is it difficult to determine a universally acceptable value for fixed tangible property, but complications are applicable to the evaluation of both

239 tangible and intangible property items and of services. For example, stock may be issued in exchange for patent rights equivalent to the actual costs of developing and obtaining the patent rights. Thus far the transaction is apparently on a value received basis, but this by no means guarantees that the patented article will prove profitable. 

In the event of failure, the stock becomes, in effect, watered. 

Watered stock is believed to be created especially when used to recompense the promoter and his cohorts for their services, and undoubtedly this is often true. An equitable valuation of the promoter's services is a perplexing problem. Viewed at the time of promotion, the reward of the promoter may seem to be unduly high, but if the corporation is successful, it may be entirely justified. Any overstatement of the value of these services, however, must of necessity give rise to watered stock.

Another condition where the question of equivalent value may be raised occurs when converting a sole proprietorship or a partnership into a corporation. To make the transition, stock is exchanged for the property of the old enterprise. In turn, the stock may then be sold by the owners (usually through the medium of a banking house) to the public at prices in excess of recognized or previously admitted values. For instance, a corporation was organized in 1915 to take over a business which had existed under a personal form of organization for almost a century. Shares were not offered to the public until September, 1929, when 182,328 shares were sold at a price of $39.50 per share, giving the original holders of the stock a total of $7,201,956. Analysis of the earnings reveals that the corporation was worth approximately $10,000,000 by capitalizing the net earnings at 8 per cent. If this were divided by the number of shares outstanding, the value per share would be $25, leaving net "water" of $14.50 per share on the basis of capitalized earnings.

In another similar case, shares were sold privately at $23 per share. 

The actual book value per share at the end of the year of the financing was approximately $10, or $13 less than the sale price. Capitalization of the earnings at 8 per cent for that year, however, showed a valuation of $33 per share. From the standpoint of the books, the stock may be said to be watered, but in terms of earnings the stock was more than protected by equivalent value. 

Much perplexity arises because of the impossibility of reaching a final and absolute answer, but it is the nature of value to be variable in character. It changes with time, varies according to personal opinion, and shifts along with the basis of valuation which is used. Watered Stock the Result of Poor Earnings 

1 Again, in the sense that watered stock reflects an equivalent absence of actual values in the asset column, it may be noted that (1) stock of a going concern may attain a watered state as a result of poor earnings; (2) there are probably many more cases of watered stock arising out of poor earnings than where it is deliberately created. 

The following cases are typical of those arising out of poor earnings:

Advance-Rumely Company.-For the period from 1922 to 1929 inclusive, the company suffered an annual deficit without exception. 

In the meantime, its stock sold as low as 6 in 1924 and as high as 1047 in 1929. At either of these prices, the stock was in a watered condition from the earnings point of view. On the other hand, the book value per share of $100 par stock was $109, and the stock was legally fully paid and non-assessable. 

International Mercantile Marine Company.-This company had a deficit every year from 1921 to 1928 inclusive, but presented earnings of slightly over $4 per share for the year 1929. As of the latter year, it had a book value per share of $51, and sold as high as 391 per share as compared with a high of 27 during the earlier period. 

Was it watered from 1921 to 1928? Was it watered in 1929?

Watered Stock as Revealed by Market Operations 

It is difficult to determine any specific criterion for deciding whether or not a stock is watered when measured by its market price. For example, a stock may be selling considerably above both its book valuation and its value on the basis of its earnings (see General Motors Corporation in Tables 23 and 24), but at the same time this does not prove that the stock is overvalued or in a watered condition. The market quotation may be based primarily upon the future outlook, a feature which does not lend itself to specific 

7 Wall Street Journal (May 31, 1939), p. 5, or Opinion of S.E.C. on Newport Electric 

Corporation, rendered May 22, 1939.

diagnosis. Or, on the contrary, the market price of a stock may be less than its book value, and it would be preposterous to state that the fundamental condition of the stock was not watered. This is due to the important relationship between earnings and value. If earnings will not support book values over any considerable period of time, then the actual presence of these values may be seriously questioned. 

The case of Radio Corporation of America is particularly pertinent. During the year of 1929, the present stock sold as high as 

1143, and in the fall of 1935, a representative price was 7. Its earnings per share of common stock for the earlier period equaled only $1.58, and from 1930 to 1934, a deficit was suffered in every year except one. The book value per share in 1929 was approximately $7 and about $3 in the latter period. On the basis of these facts, may it be said that the stock was watered? The answer to the question lays emphasis upon the value of possible future developments. In this case, the difference between the book value of $7 and the market value of $1143 in 1929 and between the more recent values of $3 and $7 respectively may be regarded as the indicated present value of the future outlook.

Conclusions as to Watered Stock 

In summarizing this discussion of watered stock, the following principles may be offered.

CAPITALIZATION 

243 1. The comparison of par value with existing assets is at best only a superficial criterion of watered stock. It attempts a reconciliation of prevailing asset values with a more or less out of date statement of the value of the stock. 

2. A more intelligent approach is to study the problem through: (a) a comparison of market and book values; (b) a comparison of earnings and book values; (c) a comparison of earnings and market values. 

3. In both of the preceding principles, it will be recognized that the test of water is found in the matching of the book valuation of stock against the accepted value of the assets it represents. 

4. A less precise but perhaps more satisfactory criterion is to be found in the intent of the promoters or management. Do the latter act in good or bad faith? If there is a deliberate attempt to milk the stockholders, a watered condition is the inevitable result. On the contrary, if the disappearance of value is not accompanied by bad faith, it may reasonably be regarded as an incidence of economic uncertainty. 

Who Determines the Structure of the Capitalization? 

While the promoter formulates much of the groundwork underlying the corporate structure, the investment banker is largely responsible for the statement of the financial plan if the securities are to be sold through this channel. After all, a financial plan is a means of bringing the corporation and the investor together. To accomplish this successfully, consideration must be given to the desires of the public as well as to the financial principles which underlie the capitalization of a corporation. Hence, if the public is absorbing stocks as was true of the years 1928 and 1929, the banker will probably decide to issue equity securities in preference to bonds.

The banker is a specialist in serving as a liaison between the corporation and the public in raising of capital funds. His constant touch with the money market and his intimate knowledge of investor moods makes him peculiarly fitted to give advice in setting up the capital structure. For this reason, the promoter may well dispose of the task of formulating the financial plan to the more experienced bankers. The problems related to the distribution of se curities will be discussed in Chapters XVIII-XXIII.

CHAPTER XIV  

ESPITE the long-term character of the capital structure, it is not unusual to find remodeling taking place at various times. 

Just as the physical plant and equipment may become obsolete because of improvements and new inventions, the financial pattern may also be outmoded by changing conditions in the money market. 

Or, changes of an internal nature may suggest a revision of the securities structure. As stated at another point, synchronization of financial demands and operating performance is highly essential to successful operation, and this may entail at intervals an adjustment of the capitalization. Changes of this type arise spontaneously in the case of marked expansion, but at this time only those revisions which concern more especially the existing structure will be considered. 

Broadly speaking, revision of the financial structure may be caused by a state of financial embarrassment, by opportunities to improve the composition or arrangement of the capital structure, and by various conditions of expediency which affect the normal life of the corporation. Illustrative of these three major categories of influence upon the capitalization, the following specific examples of activity may be 

Financial embarrassment: (1) elimination of a deficit; (2) elimination of accumulated dividends on preferred stock; (3) adjustment for the purpose of recognizing changes in the value of assets. 

Opportunities to improve the financial structure: (1) to take advantage of money market conditions; (2) to provide a more effective way of reaching a larger number of investors; (3) to simplify the capital structure. 

Conditions of expediency: (1) to accomplish a transition from a closed to an open corporate status; (2) to meet legal requirements. 

Before discussing the changes in capitalization which occur as a result of these conditions, it is desirable to make reference to the use of terminology. Usually, the terms recapitalization and readjustment of the capital structure are considered to be the result mainly of a state of financial embarrassment, but as used here they will be em- 246

ployed generally to cover all changes irrespective of source. Also, the terms will be used interchangeably even though many writers draw a distinction between the two. Where this delineation is made, readjustment is considered to be a major transition and change in the composition of the financial plan, while recapitalization is interpreted as a simple amendment of the original plan, such as increasing the number of shares of stock or changing the amount of stated capitalization.

Practice shows, however, that the distinction between the two terms is mainly one of degree or personal opinion and that the same financial means may be used in either case. Thus, stock dividends would usually be regarded as a minor revision, but they may also be used to accomplish a fundamental change in financial policy. For example, a closed corporation may decide to open its ownership by increasing the amount of stock outstanding by the payment of a large stock dividend. Because of this difficulty in distinction, the terms will be used synonymously and the changes involved in readjustment and recapitalization will be thought of as one group, while those caused by actual failure will be considered in a later section dealing with major reorganization. 

Also, in considering changes in capitalization, it should be pointed out that attention is usually directed to revisions mainly of quantitative circumstance. Frequently, qualitative changes are of equal or greater significance; for example, real savings may be effected by refunding without affecting in any way the total amount of securities outstanding. Or, a shifting from bonds to stock of equal amount would bolster the financial soundness without affecting the total capital supply. Thus, the composition of the capital structure may be just as important as the amount, and indeed, in many instances, it becomes the marginal factor or balance between failure and continued operation.

Changes in Capitalization To Relieve Financial Embarrassment 

As a result of poor original planning or of changed economic conditions, the corporation may find itself in a condition which can best be referred to as one of financial embarrassment. The situation may be evidenced in various ways such as by an accumulated deficit, large dividend accruals on preferred stock, or by changed asset values due to changes in market conditions.

Birs

To eliminate a deficit.-Emphasizing, in a sense, the bookkeeping character of capitalization is the adjustment of the capital structure to eliminate a deficit. Bonds may not be changed without failure, and changes in the stated value of the stock usually require formal approval of the stockholders. However, the latter is not difficult to obtain under modern conditions of proxy voting, and, indeed, circumstances may exist where it may be the part of sound financial policy to reduce the stated value of the stock for the purpose of eliminating a deficit. For example, a corporation may have incurred a large deficit during some unfavorable period of operation, but the current operations have become profitable. Earnings are now satisfactory, the working capital position is sound, and funds are available to pay dividends. However, as long as the deficit exists, the company may not declare a dividend, even though it may be entirely warranted by the current condition of the company. In other words, the deficit may be so irrelevant at the time that it would be to the advantage of all concerned to eliminate it through an adjustment of the capital account.

A concrete example of the foregoing conditions is found in the 

Jewel Tea Company which in January, 1925, had 120,000 shares of $100 par stock outstanding. These were exchanged share for share for new no-par stock and the balance sheet was affected as follows: (1) common stock was reduced from $12,000,000 to $120,000; (2) good-will was reduced from $12,000,000 to $1,000,000; (3) the deficit existing at the close of the previous year was eliminated, although current earnings were of sufficient size to accomplish the same result. In 1928, good-will was further reduced to $1 in accordance with more conservative accounting practice. This later change had little effect upon the more permanent financial plan of the company as the charge was made against the net income earned in 1928. Also, in 1928, the company offered its stockholders 40,000 shares of common stock at a price of $100, which bears little relationship to the nominal figure of $1 carried on the books for the old stock. However, the concern paid $4 per share dividends in that year, and in 1929 the company paid a stock dividend of 75 per cent as well as $3 a share in cash. From 1929 to 1940, dividends fluctuated between $3 and $7.25 per share upon the basis of the 1929 stock outstanding.¹ In 

¹ On March 1, 1940, the stock was split 2 for 1. On the stock, dividends of $2.40 per share were paid, or the equivalent of $4.80 upon the former shares.

view of this record, the 1928 offering at $100 per share does not appear unreasonable. A more recent case of recapitalization to eliminate a deficit is the General Steel Castings Corporation. On the balance sheet for 

December 31, 1939, the company carried its no-par common stock at $13,772,430 and showed an accumulated deficit of $14,640,537. During 1940, the stated value of the common stock was reduced to $456,- 576 and the difference, together with certain reserves, used to eliminate the deficit.

To eliminate accumulated dividends.-Another common cause of recapitalization is the removal of the obligation to pay accumulated preferred dividends. The recapitalization of the International Mercantile Marine Company in June, 1929, succeeded in eliminating the accumulated dividends as well as a deficit. The former had accrued to the extent of $79.50 per share, while the deficit amounted to $28,- 

620,122 at the end of 1928. The back dividends were settled by paying $20 in cash per share of old preferred stock, and in turn the preferred stock was exchanged share for share of new no-par common stock. By the introduction of the no-par common stock as a substitute for the old common with a par of $100 per share, it was possible to reduce the value of the capital stock and thus to absorb a deficit. 

To dispose of the old common stock, one share of the new issue was given in exchange for every five shares of the old common. By eliminating the deficit and the accrued dividend obligations, the company became free to pay a cash dividend of $1 per share in February, 1930. However, the benefits of recapitalization were only temporary, and by December 31, 1940, the company had accumulated a new deficit of $27,049,068.

A similar case is that of the Central Leather Company which at the close of 1926 had accumulated preferred dividends of 36 per cent and a deficit of $19,647,077. A new company, the United States 

Leather Company, was organized, and both of these items were eliminated in the process of adjustment. To satisfy the claims of preferred stockholders, each old share of preferred was given $5 cash, $50 in par value of 7 per cent cumulative preferred stock, and threequarters of a share of participating and convertible Class A stock of the new company. The old common stock was exchanged share for share of new stock. The old common stock had carried a $100 par, and by making the new common a no-par security it was possi-

ble to absorb the deficit by reducing the stated value of the common stock. As a result, the common stock was carried at $3,970,103 after the adjustment as compared with $39,701,031 prior to the action. 

The funded debt was not specifically affected by the recapitalization but was retired in January, 1928. Thirteen years later, May 30, 1941, the new company had arrears on its preferred stock of $33.25. As of 

October 31, 1940, the common stock capitalization had been reduced to $1,566,279, and a new operating deficit of $1,620,666 had been accumulated.

A more unusual case is that of the American Agricultural Chemical Company. There were two companies of the same name, one being incorporated in Delaware and the other in Connecticut. The former held approximately two-thirds of the common and preferred stocks of the latter. Unpaid dividends on the preferred stock of the 

Connecticut company had accumulated to $58.50 (January, 1931), and "since no dividends could be legally paid until this deficiency had been wiped out," it was deemed wise to dissolve the company. This was accomplished by exchanging stock of the Delaware company for that of the Connecticut company.

To recognize changes in the value of assets. In the revaluation of corporate assets, it is possible to recognize either appreciation or depreciation. Conservative accounting practice seldom sanctions the former but is favorably inclined toward the latter. In either event, the financial plan is affected by the process. An illustrative case is that of the United States Industrial Alcohol Company. Early in 

1933, the stockholders approved the virtual writing off of the "land, buildings, and equipment" account by voting to carry the account at the nominal value of $1 in place of the previous valuation of $19,301,- 045. To absorb the charge a small amount was debited to earned surplus and the balance to capital surplus. The capital surplus had been created especially for this purpose by lowering the book value of the capital stock from $22,584,600 to $3,738,460. The announced purpose of the adjustment was to reduce fixed charges and to correct an overdeveloped capitalization.

The chief effect of such value adjustments is to eliminate depreciation charges and to introduce in their place a smaller charge for renewals and replacements whenever made. Because of this reduction in annual operating expenses, it is possible to show a higher operating return. Actually, no change of any fundamental importance is made

and any dividends paid thereafter require careful analysis to determine whether or not they are in fact being paid out of capital. This company has not repeated the write-off practice and, as of March 31, 1940, carried in its plant account an amount of $28,133,377 after depreciation. This was described as representing depreciated value of acquisitions to plant subsequent to January 1, 1933. 

A more common practice is to write off the value of good-will and other intangible values. For example, the P. Lorillard Company chose in 1933 to report the value of its "Brands, trade-marks, goodwill, etc." at $1 in comparison with the figure of $21,268,339 previously carried. This necessitated reducing the common stock from $44,519,255 at the close of 1932 to $18,878,620 the following year. 

In the two preceding cases no attempt is made to determine the current value of the property accounts, and their value is reduced to a nominal figure primarily to be conservative. Another basis of action is to have an appraisal of the property. The Pure Oil Company has resorted to this practice on at least two occasions, recognizing an appreciation of value in 1917 and a decrease in 1932. In the first instance, the adjustment was made by setting up a capital surplus account amounting to $39,540,621. In the latter year, the property account was written down by approximately $70,000,000, and not only was the capital surplus item eliminated, but in addition the common stock figure was necessarily adjusted. 

In terms of book figures the foregoing illustrations reflect major transitions in the capital structure. They also indicate the artificial nature of the bookkeeping processes. When the property account is reduced to a nominal or an appraised figure, it should be clear that existing values are not changed in any sense and similarly it does not affect earning power. Likewise, the market value of the stock is seldom affected by the change. The question may therefore be raised as to the significance of this form of recapitalization. No general rule can be stated because each case calls for special analysis. On occasions, the adjustment may be a legitimate revaluation to bring book values in line with estimated prevailing values. On other occasions, it may be a financial maneuver to make possible the showing of earnings and the paying of dividends. Again, such actions may be regarded as evidence of temporizing on the part of management without support of basic, financial principle.

Opportunities To Improve the Financial Structure 

To take advantage of money-market conditions.-The money market serves in many ways as a trading arena where advantage may be taken of lower interest rates or of other benefits which are possible through financial arrangement. By keeping in touch with the prevailing currents in the money market, management is enabled to secure more favorable financing. The financial plan may be adjusted to take advantage of money-market conditions by: (1) the substitution of one security for another of the same type, either for the purpose of lowering the fixed' or optional charges or of avoiding the burdensome terms of the old issue; (2) the substitution of a junior security for one possessing senior or underlying claims; (3) substitution of a senior for a junior security.

These transitions are usually made possible or at least facilitated by changing interest rates and business conditions which permit the individual corporation to change its capital structure to advantage. 

Often, important savings may be realized by issuing securities bearing lower rates or relief may be obtained by substituting securities carrying a contingent charge for those with a fixed obligation. During the years 1928 and 1929, common stock was greatly favored by the public, and corporations took advantage of the situation by issuing common stock to raise new capital or to replace securities having more rigid claims upon the corporation. In those years, a total of $6,219,000,000 in common stock was issued for new capital purposes and $937,000,- 000 for refunding.2 Between 1935 and 1940, corporations refunded their outstanding securities and raised new capital through the issuance of bonds at rates of interest which were highly favorable. 

There follows several practical illustrations which reveal clearly the gains to be derived.

The substitution of one security for another of the same type.- 

In 1929, the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company issued $60,000,000 of 6 per cent cumulative preferred stock for the following purposes: (1) to replace its 6 per cent and 7 per cent preferred issues then outstanding; (2) to retire the ten-year 6 per cent bonds of the Firestone

Park Land Company; and (3) to reimburse the company for expenditures made from working capital for permanent plant improvements. This refinancing was primarily a case of substitution of one security for another of the same class, but in addition, it accomplished 

2 Moody's Manual of Industrials (1941), pp. a42-3.

the retirement of certain funded debt and increased working capital. 

Savings in fixed charges and in dividends were also effected through the lower rate on the new issue. Management took advantage of money-market conditions which favored the use of equity securities, and, indeed, the question may be raised as to whether common stock could have been used in preference to preferred stock. 

A more common example of the substitution of one security for another of the same general type is found in the refunding of bonded indebtedness. No change in the basic outline of the financial plan is effected, but the revision may enable management to effect a substantial strengthening of financial position. Maturities may be extended and thereby undesirable pay-offs of principal indebtedness may be avoided and the cost of funds may be lowered so as to add to the net income account. In recent years, a number of companies have found it possible to retire existing bonds bearing relatively high rates of interest through the issuance of new bonds bearing lower rates and carrying other more favorable terms. For example, in 1938, the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company refunded an outstanding 5 per cent issue with first and collateral 3's of 1938. In 1940, the Dow Chemical 

Company retired its debenture 3's of 1951 (issued in 1936) and replaced them with an issue of ten-year 24 per cent debentures. The 

McCrory Stores Corporation retired $2,922,500 of debenture 5's through the issuance of debenture 3's. All of these operations required the payment of premiums on the retired issues. Thus, the 

Dow Chemical Company paid 102 for the bonds retired, or a premium of 2 to save per cent in interest for each of ten years.

McCrory Stores paid 104 for its 5's of 1951 in order to replace them with 34's of 1955, thus paying 4 points premium to save 1 per cent in interest for the remaining life of the original issue. 

The substitution of stocks for bonds.-The United States Steel Cor poration affords a good example of the policy of replacing senior with junior securities. In April, 1929, it increased the authorized common stock from $753,321,000 to $1,250,000,000 and had $856,087,- 600 actually outstanding a year later. During the same period, the authorized preferred stock and outstanding funded debt were reduced considerably. The amount of preferred stock authorized was reduced from $550,000,000 to $400,000,000 in April, 1929. During 1929, the funded debt was reduced from $456,602,415 to $112,257,978. This reduction was accomplished by the use of funds obtained from the

increased common stock, by the use of sinking funds, and from other sources of cash. The operation reduced fixed charges by $20,000,000 annually and was of material assistance in weathering the lean years of 1931-36. The policy of reducing the funded debt was reversed in 

1938 when the company issued $100,000,000 in 34 per cent ten-year bonds. These bonds were issued to repay bank loans of some $50,- 

000,000, and the balance was added to cash funds which were later used for plant expansion.3 

The wisdom of this flexible policy is apparent. Fixed charges were replaced in 1929 with those of a more optional nature and the general financial position of the company was strengthened. This action was facilitated by the prevailing market conditions which offered a ready sale for common stock. Conversely, in 1938, there was no great demand for equity issues, but low-interest rate bonds of leading corporations could be sold quite readily. To a certain extent the 1938 borrowing operation was made possible by the strengthening of the equity base in 1929.

Speaking more generally as to financial policy, it is sometimes stated that a corporation should keep its best securities (or a portion of them) for its last or emergency needs. While this policy constitutes a most conservative safeguard against future contingencies, it is not followed widely in actual practice. Securities issued when the money market is not favorable, or when the corporation is not in a satisfactory position for financing must of necessity be limited to a small number of cases. To carry the junior issues over a long period of time would mean imposing a considerable burden in the form of fixed charges upon the corporation, much of which could be avoided with the use of high-grade securities. A preferable policy would be for the corporation to arrange a financial pattern which would provide the lowest cost financing for normal operations, but at the same time attach the call privilege so that future action would be possible to take advantage of more favorable market conditions. 

The substitution of a senior security for a junior security.—It is usually regarded as unwise to replace a junior security with a senior security. Instances of the practice are rare, and for the most part this policy has been utilized only by a few of the larger companies, which were in excellent financial position and which had little rea- 8 The 3 per cent debentures issued in 1938 were retired in 1940 through the sale of serial debentures carrying an interest rate graduated from 0.625 per cent in 1941 to 2.65 per cent in 1955.

255. son to fear their future ability to pay the fixed charges. The case of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey is illustrative. In December, 1926, it issued $120,000,000 of 5 per cent gold debenture bonds* to obtain funds to assist in the retirement of the 7 per cent preferred stock then outstanding. As a result of the acceptance of a more rigid liability, the corporation was able to effect an annual saving of 2 per cent on $120,000,000.

An historical instance of this policy, and one involving many legal difficulties, is that of the United States Steel Corporation which, in 1902, substituted bonds for preferred stock on a rather extensive scale. It proposed to change the old capitalization, which consisted of approximately $300,000,000 in bonds, $500,000,000 in preferred stock, and $500,000,000 in common stock, by issuing $250,000,000 of additional bonds to raise funds for the retirement of preferred stock in the amount of $200,000,000 and the balance to provide additional cash. Certain stockholders objected strenuously to the plan and brought suit in the courts to restrict the action. Among other complaints it was pointed out that members of the underwriting syndicate were also members of the board of directors of the corporation, and that a contract which is to the personal advantage of any director is voidable. However, this contention was counteracted by the fact that the required majority of stockholders had formally approved the refinancing program. 

This substitution of bonds for preferred stock makes an interesting contrast to the more recent policy of the corporation. In 1902, the corporation was only in its second year of existence, yet it assumed the risk of replacing preferred stock and optional charges with bonds carrying fixed charges. In 1929, when the company had obtained a position of world-leadership and was in an excellent position to have bonds as part of its financial plan, it retired its funded. debt in favor of equity securities. Today, it is again resorting to the expedient of bond financing, but with more justification than was found in its earlier life.

To provide a more effective way of reaching the investors.-A corporation sometimes makes a minor recapitalization for the purpose of making it more responsive to the needs of its security holders and to This bond issue has since been refunded through the issuance of another issue bearing a lower rate of interest. 

W. Z. Ripley, Trusts, Pools, and Corporations (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1916), pp. 228-41.

the investors in general. If a stock is selling at a relatively high price, the market activity in the stock will be limited and the price will be subject to rather wide fluctuation. To remedy this condition, it is common to declare a stock dividend if the surplus account is sufficient or to split the existing shares into a larger number of units. The latter method achieves virtually the same results as the former but has no effect upon the surplus account. 

Examples of exceptionally high market prices and their later adjustment may be cited. In 1926, the common stock of Nash Motors 

Company reached a high of $645 per share. In that year, the company paid $13 per share in cash dividends and declared a stock dividend of 900 per cent. The marked increase in the number of shares outstanding lowered the price of the stock to approximately onetenth of its former figure. In 1922, the stock of the Eastman Kodak 

Company reached a high of $800 per share. In order to bring the market price to a more convenient level, the company called in the old stock and issued ten new shares of no-par stock for each old share of $10 par stock originally held. Nearly as extreme cases have occurred more recently. For instance, the price of Homestake Mining Company common, which had had a price range of 93-65 in 1929, reached a high of 544 in 1933 under the influence of the Treasury's gold-buying program. In June, 1937, the stock was split on an eight to one basis. The last day the old stock was traded it had a range of 382 to 378; the first day the new stock was traded, it was quoted from 48 to 473, or almost exactly one-eighth of the former price.

General Motors Corporation is an example of a company frequently adjusting its outstanding shares. In January, 1920, it exchanged ten shares of no-par stock for each old share of $100 par outstanding. This was followed by a reduction in the number of shares outstanding, in January, 1924, when one share of new no-par was issued in lieu of four shares of the old no-par stock. In September, 1927, two shares of $25 par stock were issued for each share of old no-par, and again, in December, 1928, two and one-half shares of $10 par stock were exchanged for each old share of $25 par stock. 

It is difficult to understand the nature of the policy underlying such rapid revision of the capital structure, but, regardless of the reasons, it is evident that the procedure would have a pronounced effect upon the market position of the stock.

A somewhat similar history may be reported for the common

stock of the Cities Service Company. In April, 1920, the par valuc of the stock was reduced from $100 to $20 and five shares of new stock were issued for each share of the old outstanding. In April, 1929, the stock was changed to no-par and four new shares were exchanged for each old $20 share outstanding. The stock of the Cities 

Service Company was one of the speculative favorites in the 1928–29 boom, but its value approached the zero point in the ensuing collapse of security prices. In 1938, the par was changed to $10 per share and one new share issued for each ten old shares, thus reducing the outstanding shares by 90 per cent and increasing the market price accordingly. At the same time, the common stock was reduced on the balance sheet from $185,718,850 to $37,040,668. The surplus was reduced from $78,876,072 to $12,872,259. The credits thus acquired were offset by a number of balance-sheet adjustments, the most important being the elimination of subsidiaries' surplus previously carried on the parent's balance sheet.

To simplify the capital structure.-A complex financial plan is not necessarily the best plan; in fact, there is good reason to believe that simplicity of capitalization is desirable. However, corporations often find themselves with a complicated capital structure as a result of rapid growth, combinations, or simply the lack of proper planning. 

Sometimes they assume the task of simplifying their capital structure. For example, at the close of 1923, the General Motors Corporation had the following issues of preferred stock outstanding: 

6 per cent preferred 

6 per cent debenture 

7 per cent preferred $16,183,400 60,801,000 32,931,600 In June, 1924, the stockholders ratified the proposal of the directors that the financial plan be simplified by (among other things) consolidating the foregoing preferred issues into a new 7 per cent preferred stock. To accomplish this, the old stock was made exchangeable for the new preferred on the following terms:

One share of old 6 per cent preferred plus $10 to be exchanged for one share of new 7 per cent preferred.

One share of old 6 per cent debenture to be exchanged on the same basis.

One share of old 7 per cent preferred to be exchanged for new 7 per cent preferred on a share-for-share basis. • During the week the change was made, the old no-par stock's range was 1-1 and the $10 par range was 101–94.

The extent to which the plan succeeded is revealed by a statement 

of the preferred stock outstanding at the close of 1924: 

6 per cent preferred 

6 per cent debenture 

New 7 per cent preferred.. 

Common Stock 

In 1930, further simplification was effected by offering new $5 no-par cumulative preferred stock in exchange for the three types outstanding, and where the exchange was not made, the old stocks were called for redemption. As a result, the financial plan now consists of only one class of preferred stock and one class of common stock.

The company placed no valuation on the individual issues. Instead, they were carried on the balance sheet in a lump sum designated as: .$100,443,433 111,188,522 33,627 119,665 55,847 97,042 101,386 59 48,617 6,805 25 10,980 3,842

The practice of presenting the value of securities in aggregate form is restricted primarily to combinations of the holding company type. In such cases the securities of the parent company have been exchanged for those of the subsidiary or for the property of the latter, and since they are usually transferred in toto, it is not thought necessary or desirable to present a distinct and separate valuation for each class. While it would be possible to work out reasonably satisfactory valuations for the property or securities to be acquired and to assign this value to the securities issued to pay for the property, holding companies have often elected not to do this. There is little that is favorable to say for such a policy. It represents undesirable secretiveness and offers an opportunity for manipulation and fraud. 

Conditions of Expediency 

Under this heading come the motives for recapitalization which are not dictated by financial necessity or by financial pressure. 

Instead, the reasons for adjustment are those arising out of internal policy such as the decision of insiders to retire from active management or permit outside participation. Or, the adjustment may be caused by governmental policy expressed through legal requirement. 

To accomplish a transition from a closed to an open corporation status. Whenever an enterprise is transformed from a closed or family affair to a state of open ownership, a complete revision of the financial plan is usually required. Where the selling par y wishes to retire definitely from the picture, cash will be demanded as the consideration. This is illustrated by the sale of the Dodge Brothers to 

Dillon, Read and Company in 1925.9 The latter, however, raised the necessary cash by selling securities to the general public. Almost overnight, a family enterprise was converted into a corporation featuring the usual financial trimmings. At the completion of the sale, the new company's capitalization consisted of: 

850,000 shares of preferred stock carried on the balance sheet at $1 per share but sold to the public at 100. 

1,500,000 shares of Class A common carried on the balance sheet at 

10 cents per share. 

500,000 shares Class B common, also carried at 10 cents per share. $75,000,000 in bonds.

Where the selling party is not anxious to relinquish actual con- 

See chapter X.

trol, the consideration will undoubtedly consist of stock. In the case of the National Cash Register Company, which was also changed from a closed to an open basis, the problem was solved by providing two classes of stock: Class A and Class B. The latter was given con trol as long as dividends were maintained on the former, and hence provided a ready medium for allowing the original owners to retain control and at the same time, to withdraw a portion of their original investment.10

It is clear that the transition from a closed to an open corporate status entails most of the problems found in connection with original capitalization. In fact, the record of tested operation should make it possible to design the financial pattern with an exactness not possible in a new, untried venture. The earnings record is known, and the valuation of assets may be determined on the basis of known facts. 

These objective tests do provide a more solid basis for the arrangement of the capital structure, but even here the hazards of business operation are not easily forecast. Thus, in the case of Dodge Brothers previously referred to, several questions were raised as to the accuracy of valuation, and it soon proved wise to arrange for a merger into the 

Chrysler Corporation. 

Legal provocation.-On some occasions, changes in capitalization may be compelled by virtue of legal requirement. Such change is inevitable in the case of failure and reorganization, but it is also possible for perfectly solvent corporations to be affected by abrupt or unusual changes in legal status. The most outstanding example in recent years is found in the Public Utility Holding Company Act which is discussed at length in a later chapter. However, at this point, it may be observed that the Act compels the dissolution of numerous companies holding stock in others as well as compelling the rearrangement of existing public utility systems. When the process is completed, considerable revamping of the capital structure of the remaining companies will be inevitable.

Along similar lines, the financial pattern of operating public utility companies and of railroads may be affected indirectly by regulation. This is achieved by virtue of the power of the regulatory

Class B stock was not listed; 37 per cent was given to company employees who had been in the profit-sharing plan prior to the reorganization. Apparently, the remainder of the B stock was retained by the president, Frederick B. Patterson, son of the companys founder. See

bodies to approve new security issues. In so doing, it is not unusual to find various conditions imposed which affect the entire capital structure. 

At other times, the change in capitalization as a result of legal influence may be purely voluntary on the part of corporate management, itself. For instance, it may prove advisable to change the state of incorporation for the purpose of obtaining rights or powers not possible in the original state. Whenever a corporation does shift in this manner, the effect upon the capitalization is usually of a minor nature. For the most part, it consists simply of the exchange of securities of the new for similar ones of the old corporation. 

Another condition which occasionally causes a corporation to shift from one state to another is the taxes imposed by the states concerned. 

At a previous point, the importance of taxation in connection with the original incorporation of a company was discussed and the application of the problem is somewhat similar here. The stimulus respensible for the reincorporation may possibly be caused by a change in tax rates, or one which may not be anticipated at the time of the initial capitalization.

The growth of a corporation may also make it desirable to select another state. The domestic state may offer sufficient powers for the purposes of the original limited operations but may prove entirely inadequate for the extended activities. While this case is not representative solely of legal peculiarities, the process of recapitalization is affected by the legal potentialities offered by the various states. 

Summary of Changes in Capitalization 

It has been shown that the capitalization of a corporation is the medium by which funds are provided for operations. Not only is it essential that a sufficient amount of capital be made available, but it is equally important that the supply synchronizes with changing operating needs. It is possible to have either too much or too little capital. The former may give to management a sense of freedom and independence, but at the same time a persistent redundance can prove to be a drain on income and be the source of embarrassment. On the other hand, a shortage of capital may prevent the adoption of promising opportunities, and at times be a contributing cause of failure. 

The essence of sound administration of the capital structure is, therefore, to be found in effecting a balance which is intended to ac-

commodate the changing needs of business operation. This balanced position means not only that the capitalization should harmonize with the asset structure, but in addition it means proper arrangement of the various securities or means which are used as a source of capital supply. Excessive funded debt can lead to ruinous fixed charges which result in failure; hence, it is exceedingly important that the capitalization be sufficiently flexible to permit revision. Both bonds and preferred stock should, wherever possible, contain the call feature so that management can have the necessary freedom to effect rearrangement. Common stock and surplus, by virtue of their residual position, are more readily adjusted and may even be reduced drastically without resulting in failure.

Despite the long-term function of capitalization, it is apparent that it is, nevertheless, changed at irregular intervals. Changes may occur automatically such as is found in the exchange of convertible bonds for common stock, or revisions may be planned deliberately to meet specific needs. The latter are more typical of financial activity and are of the type described in this chapter. All too often, however, these changes are haphazard or are the result of pressing emergency.

This is caused by the tendency to continue with the status quo as long as possible instead of using capitalization as a tool or moderator of business action. It is in this latter respect that the capital structure may serve as an important means of keeping an institution on even keel. Skilled management will anticipate needs by careful planning; less capable management too often waits for something to happen and then proceeds with abrupt adjustment.

CHAPTER XV  

R EFERENCE has been made to the fact that the ownership of a corporation is vested in its stockholders. It would be more accurate to say that the ownership resides primarily in the holders of common stock because of the many restrictions and qualifications usually attached to preferred stock. Moreover, the latter is often a means of temporary financing which invites investment interest more than ownership responsibility. The true residual equity is provided by the common stock. Because of the keystone position of common stock, it is important that proper recognition be given to the part which it plays in corporation finance. The following invite particular attention: (1) the use of common stock as a means of raising capital; (2) the nature and distribution of the ownership of common stock; (3) the effect of scattered ownership upon the control of the corporation.

The first of these problems was discussed earlier (chapter III) and the latter two will be analyzed in the present chapter. Beginning with the distribution of stock, the following forms or types of ownership may be noted: public participation or ownership, ownership by bankers and officers of the corporation, customer ownership, and employee ownership.

Ownership by General Public 

The increase in the number of stockholders of the leading corporations in the United States has been of startling proportions. Table 

26 shows the number of stockholders of selected corporations for certain years between 1900 and 1940. It will be observed that the increase varies from about one hundred per cent to several thousand per cent. This growth reflects, in part, the tremendous increase in size of American industries since 1900, but such expansion was made possible only by a wider participation of the public in corporate activity. Stock ownership has become a more or less commonplace practice for many people. 265

Difficulty of Establishing Absolute Proof of Increasing Public Participation 

The increases in shareholdings during the thirties are so surprising as to suggest some questioning of the results. First, it is necessary to distinguish between total shareholdings and the actual number of stockholders. They would be identical in the case of a single company, but because of multiple ownership, holders of record would obviously exceed the number of separate stockholders in a group of companies. Or, to state the condition conversely, a single individual or institution may own stock in more than one corporation. In an analysis of 1,710 corporations as of the year 1937, one study has shown an estimate of 5,000,000 different stockholders as representing 14,- 

000,000 "record shareholdings."

Second, changes in the number of shareholders may be more apparent than real, i.e., technical instead of genuine. Thus, during the period preceding 1929, there was considerable trading on the margin where the securities were retained by the brokerage house under what is known as a "Street Name." As a result, many different investors or speculators may have the real title to the stock, but the corporation records will show only the name of the brokerage house. One writer has suggested that following 1929 numerous small investors actually took over their stock because of the dwindling opportunities for speculative gain and a decision to hold the securities for an extended period of time. Under these conditions, there is no genuine increase in the number of shareholders and only a technical transition in title is effected.

It must be admitted that precise measurement of the actual number of stockholders is impossible and that appraisal of the nature of changes in ownership is partly a matter of rationalization. On the other hand, sufficient time has now elapsed to permit seasoned observation of what has taken place. It is more than a decade since the 

2 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 30, Survey of Shareholdings in 1,710 Corporations with Securi ties Listed on a National Securities Exchange (1941), p. 6. 

8 Lewis A. Froman, "The Increase in the Number of Stockholders in American Corpora tions since 1929," Journal of Political Economy (December, 1934), XLI, pp. 783-87.

debacle of 1929, and there is still no evidence of any slackening in the increasing number of shareholders. Moreover, the reality of participation by the general public is confirmed by the relative importance of the number of small shareholdings. Large institutions and wealthy individuals do not invest in small lots, and it may be reasonably assumed that the presence of limited holdings reflects a tendency toward diversified and distributed ownership. To be specific, a study of 1,572 corporations with total shareholdings of 11,432,992 showed that 9,884,962 (or 86.5 per cent of the total) were holdings of one hundred shares or less. The large number of small holdings do not represent a large portion of the total shares, because the 86.5 per cent of total holdings represented only 16.5 per cent of the total shares outstanding and 20.5 per cent of the total value of the shares as of December 31, 1937.4

It is not easy to appreciate the extent to which individuals will buy two or three shares to get a stake in American enterprise. However, it is a fact that these trusting, little shareholders are found in hamlets and villages throughout our entire country. And they have continued to invest from 1929 down to the present time. The General 

Motors Corporation had 198,600 shareholders at the close of 1929; at the end of 1940, there were 397,928. And, to show the mass significance of these "little interests," it is interesting to observe the following distribution of stockholders according to the size of holdings.5

Influence of Market Price per Share 

It is commonly believed the small shareholdings are concentrated in low-priced stocks. The analysis of 1,710 listed corporations found a contrary result for the corporations included in the study. Nearly twice as large a proportion of closely held stocks sold for less than $10 per share than was true of widely held stock. Stocks selling for $10 to $30 per share made up 20 per cent of the shareholdings in the closely held group and 31 per cent of the widely held stocks. Among the closely held issues 5 per cent were selling for $60 or more per share, while 12 per cent of the widely held issues were in that price class. The reasons for this distribution are not entirely clear. It may be due to the tendency of public interest to center in the leading corporations with national reputations. Such corporations issue stocks in the higher-price brackets. Again, the wider following and more active trading may influence the price.

Significance of the Foregoing Evidence to Financial Policy 

In view of the great expansion in stockholdings which has occurred, it seems fair to conclude that the depression was a period when the large holders of stock tended to liquidate their holdings, which were, in turn, absorbed by the public-at-large. This means that business risks are being assumed by the average citizen who is 

6 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 30, p. 41.

generally less able to bear the risks attendant upon business activity, or at least he usually lacks the reserves to bear the risks which have been typical of business in the past. In response to this manifestation of faith on the part of the public-at-large, management must more than ever adopt the public service point of view as well as provide complete accounting for the capital intrusted to its administration. To a great extent, recent governmental policies are directed to these ends, but at the same time many additional burdens are imposed upon private management. In many ways, the enlarged scope of governmental functions with their resulting tax burden make the problems of management more numerous and complex than ever before. In spite of this, the duty of management is clear. 

Response of the Corporation to Increased Number of Stockholders 

As the number of stockholders increases, the public obtains a constantly greater interest in the welfare of corporate activities. This creates a moral obligation on the part of the corporation to keep its stockholders and the public-at-large informed of its current operations and developments. Many corporations have already pointed their policies to meet the new conditions by making each individual stockholder feel that he is definitely a part of the organization, as well as to make him feel that the corporation is really his. In a sense, there is a tendency to tear down the entity of the corporation and to impress upon the stockholder his duties and responsibilities as part owner of the enterprise.

The Letter of Welcome 

A few corporations send a letter of welcome (as well as of information) to all new stockholders. Among corporations engaged in this practice may be mentioned: Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company, the Radio Corporation of America, the Chrysler Corporation, and the American Telephone and Telegraph Company. 

The following sample letter has been used by the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company:

It is a pleasure to welcome you as a stockholder of the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company.

The Management desires that those interested in the Company be informed of its operations in order that they may have a knowledge of the condition and progress of its business, and to that end you will receive quarterly a comparative "Statement of Operations," together with other information. 2

In the belief that you would like to be advised concerning the product manufactured by your Company and its subsidiaries, and to assist when opportunity presents in promoting the sale of those products, we set forth in the following pages of this letter, with other data, a list of our principal plants and products. 

It is always encouraging to those in charge of a corporation's affairs to hear from its stockholders, and, if you have any suggestions as to the business or management of your Company, we would be very glad to receive them. 

Other Means of Contact with the Stockholder 

Although many corporations do not employ a formal letter of welcome, they do keep the stockholders posted as to the progress and results of operations as well as to make known the various products of the corporation. The statement of the treasurer of one of our large corporations portrays in an excellent manner the relationship between the corporation and stockholders as well as the means of providing for this contact. To quote:

The information regarding "program to cultivate the interest of stockholders in corporate affairs," probably is included in the existence in the Executive Staff of a Vice President, having charge of personal relations with the public, the forwarding by the President of the Company to stockholders from time to time of letters regarding corporate activities; the providing annually to all stockholders of condensed statement of the financial condition of the . . . . Company and its principal associated companies; the providing upon stockholder's request of 

Annual Report of the Company to the stockholders as of the end of December in each year, and the addressing by the President to each new stockholder in the Company of a personal letter recognizing the stockholder's act in investing in the security of the company, and suggesting full cooperation of the stockholder's part in business activities enuring to the benefit of the Company. 

This statement is representative of the attitude of many other corporations, although not all go to this extent of furnishing inform tion. In summary form, it is fairly common for the leading corporations to supply the stockholders with one or more of the following: 

1. Quarterly reports of earnings as well as a letter from the president describing the status of operations. 

2. Annual reports that are much more voluminous than the quarterly reports. These reports present not only financial and profit-andloss statements, but also describe numerous other phases of corporate activity such as pension plans, a description of plant and equipment, statement of expansion, etc. 

3. Special booklets and pamphlets are frequently distributed. 

4. Accompanying the dividend check, or otherwise, letters of information concerning the products of the company are sometimes

sent.

Moreover, the stockholders are encouraged to favor these products. 

5. Many companies distribute their company magazine or house organ to the stockholders as well as to other interested parties. 

While it is true that the number of companies employing the foregoing tactics are entirely too few, still it is believed that a notable step has been made in the right direction. The practice of these policies indicates the existence of a sense of responsibility by corporate management to the stockholders, and reflects an underlying principle which is worthy of whole-hearted support. 

Response of the Stockholders 

A broad stockholder and public relations program is not a onesided affair, but its success depends upon the participation of all parties involved. Stockholders, in common with the citizens of the 

United States in general, are known for their laxness in exercising the privilege to vote. Cases are known where it has been difficult to secure enough stockholders or their proxies to have the quorum necessary for a stockholders' meeting. While the stockholder defends his position of indifference by a plea of lack of sufficient knowledge of the company's operations to vote intelligently, the contention is not sound. Ordinarily, he finds the time to inquire into the status of his investment if the company fails and he may well exercise a similar desire for knowledge in time of successful operation. He should be acquainted with the basic policies of his company; or at least, he should be familiar with the results of operations. 

Ownership by Banking Agencies and Officers 

The principles underlying stockholdings by officers of corporations were discussed in an earlier chapter. Such holdings may often constitute a majority of the outstanding stock in smaller companies but the amount of investment and the delicacy of public relations make such a condition unlikely in the case of very large companies. Thus, in the following two well-known enterprises, no stockholder owns as much as 1 per cent of the outstanding stock. It will be noted also that most of the largest stockholders are insurance companies, investment bankers, or investment trust companies.8
