The presence of the investment trust among the largest stockholders is a relatively new development in this country, which dates back less than twenty years. While these organizations are developed primarily to secure diversification of investment through the pooling of individual savings, they may acquire considerable influence in management policies due to their large holdings. They constitute an increasingly fruitful market for the sale of securities and may be an important source for obtaining capital funds.1º At the same time, the

size and intelligent administration of their holdings may enable them to play a distinct part in the control of management. This development has already occurred in more than one instance, and it gives rise to potential difficulties to both the corporation seeking funds and to the investment trust adopting such a policy. Recent legislation restricts the stockholdings of investment trusts to 10 per cent of the voting stock or 5 per cent of the assets of any one company. This and other provisions are intended to limit investment trusts primarily to investment rather than control purposes. 11 

Under the Securities Exchange Act, directors and officers of cor porations must now file with the Securities and Exchange Commission a report of their holdings. Any increase or decrease through purchase and sale or otherwise must also be reported to the Commission at the close of any month in which such transactions take place. 

In this way, the investment and speculative activities of insiders are made a matter of public record. While the information reaches the general public too late to afford any great value as a speculative guide, it is probable that the publicity may serve to restrict the speculative practices of officers and directors. 

Customer Ownership

The development of customer ownership is not equal in all fields, but it does offer special advantages to corporations where it may be utilized. For instance, many public utility companies have promoted direct selling campaigns for the purpose of enlisting their customers as stockholders. Industrial concerns do not have either the incentive or the opportunity to pursue a similar policy because of the shifting character of their market; instead, they have reversed the process by inviting their stockholders to become customers. 

Customer ownership gives rise to many questions of public policy, particularly as it relates to the public utilities. In many respects, the interests of customers and of stockholders are contradictory. The former naturally seek the lowest rate possible while the latter would favor a rate which would produce the largest amount of profit. Reconciliation of their diverse interests may, therefore, remove a possible source of friction and opposition and thereby simplify the task of management.

Even more important in this day when public relations and policies 

11 Investment Company Act of 1940.

are assuming greater importance, the alignment of customer and stockholder interests may prove to be of great value in creating goodwill. Various legislative measures are being enacted which seem to increase the conflict with private interests. It follows that sizeable customer and public representation in the list of stockholders may be of profound influence and serve as a bulwark against encroachment by government. Undoubtedly, this concern for future position was one of the compelling reasons causing the public utilities to seek the support of their customers. Oppositely, the dangers of pressure or group interests were recognized by the government in the case of public utility holding companies, and the house-to-house selling of securities by such companies was prohibited in Section 6 (c) (1) of the Public Utility Act of 1935. Current statistics on customer owner ship are lacking, but some idea of its extent may be obtained from the large number of stockholders of some of the leading public utilities listed in Tables 26 and 27. 

There are other advantages of customer ownership of a more immediate financial nature. This type of stockholder is apt to be a more permanent investor in the company irrespective of trends in security prices. As a consequence, customers may prove to be an excellent and reliable source of stable financing, as distinguished from the so-called "hot" money. Of less importance, customer stockholders constitute a means of expanding the companies' sales of goods and services. Occasionally, companies selling consumer goods arrange for periodic sales of the product directly to the stockholders of the company. An example of this is the policy of the National Dairy Corporation in offering each Christmas to its stockholders the opportunity to purchase gift packages of products manaufactured by one of the company's leading subsidiaries, the Kraft Cheese Company. Just how important this may be to the company's income is not known, but it is a clever advertising device and one which develops the personal interest of stockholders. 

Employee Ownership

Both labor leaders and financial interests are inclined generally to oppose employee ownership. Labor leaders see in it an attempt to break down or to prevent the development of a class spirit or class consciousness and thus to check unionization and the independent organization of labor. It is frequently regarded as a form of insidious paternalism. 

Some employers insist, on the other hand, that employee owners are

more seriously interested in their work and operate at a higher degree of efficiency than non-owner employees. There have been cases reported where this attitude has been successfully developed, but even in these cases the employee is still interested to a far greater extent in his wages than in his dividend income. At best, his dividends can amount to only 2 or 3 per cent of his annual income. 

Then, there is always the danger that in hard times dividends will have to be suspended, and employees will be inclined to doubt managements' decision as to the necessity of the action. Relatively few people understand fully the problems involved in financing and accounting, and not many of these would be found among the typical body of employees.

Many financial interests approach the problem from a different angle and look chiefly upon the efficiency of employee ownership as a means of raising capital. This group points out that it is a costly method as compared with syndicate selling and is a slow and uncertain source of capital. The ability of employees to invest in the company are related to employment and wage conditions which may not be good immediately preceding the time when additional funds are needed. Furthermore, the savings capacity of employees in general is not large and therefore cannot supply any considerable amount of capital funds.

Regardless of these facts, employee ownership is encouraged by many leading corporations. In many instances the plan is spoken of enthusiastically both by the employer and the employee. The plan is especially attractive when it is possible to offer securities to the employees at a price less than the prevailing market price. Whenever the market price falls below the employee's subscription price, the plan may be a source of misunderstanding. One such instance was counteracted by the generous attitude of the chief holders of the stock. The employees of the Simmons Company had at one time been offered stock at $101.50, but shortly afterward the stock broke in the market and was available at around $24 per share. To meet the situation, a group composed of the Simmons, Towne, and Vance families provided funds to cancel the subscriptions of the employees and to return the installments paid in, plus interest at 5 per cent. 

Relationship between Ownership and Control 

While the corporation has established itself as one of the most efficient means for raising capital, it has also been charged with all the

evils of absentee ownership.12 Stockholders are inclined to take no active part in the management of the company and to remain entirely indifferent to the corporation's policies so long as they receive a reasonably satisfactory return. Even if there were a desire on the part of stockholders to take an active part in the corporation's administration, it would be physically impossible for a majority of them to attend a stockholders' meeting. Because of this, their right to vote must be delegated to specific parties.

The practice of delegating others to exercise the stockholder's vote is widely used and tends to concentrate the control of the corporation into the hands of a few. Concentration may result in bad consequences, but it is the only practical means of achieving an efficient administration of large-scale enterprises. The remedy for any evils which may exist does not appear to lie in the abolition of concentrated control but rather in correcting or preventing some of the present abuses. Sometimes the control is concentrated in the hands of the minority through an active effort to obtain a situation wherein a small group of insiders can wield virtually absolute control over the policies of the corporation. Although these individuals are usually stockholders, they do not as a general rule hold a majority of the stock. Instead, they obtain their effective control through one or more of the following methods: (1) scattered ownership, (2) minority control, (3) non-voting stock, (4) classified voting, (5) voting trusts, (6) pyramiding of the corporate structure. 

Scattered Ownership

It is obvious that the scattering of ownership facilitates the concentration of control into the hands of a few active individuals. Not only does the scattering make it difficult for the stockholders to attend stockholders' meetings, but in addition it discourages any organized move to remove the controlling management. It would be an extremely hard task to organize a sufficient number of the 650,000 stockholders of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, each holding an average of 28 shares of stock, into a body with sufficient power and definiteness of purpose to wield much influence with the existing administration.

From the point of view of the stability of financing, it should be recognized that wide distribution of stock is desirable. Widely held 

12 Some of the social aspects of the problem will be discussed in chapter XVII. At this point, only the technique will be discussed.

stock in small quantities results in greater stability of market action which would not exist if the stock were held by a smaller number of individuals in larger blocks; and from the corporation's point of view, a stable market action is of importance in obtaining further distribution of securities. Wide distribution of stock does add to the initial cost of flotation, but usually it is achieved indirectly by means of later purchase in the securities market.

The dispersion of ownership necessarily means that financial interest in the form of stock investment is not required to effectuate control. Instead, power of direction is achieved through technique or organization whereby the votes of stockholders are marshaled into the hands of a small group. Usually, this controlling element is the operating management which automatically enjoys the right of selfperpetuation. Under the circumstances, there is a reversal of the normal, statutory flow of power so that the management directs and controls the stockholders instead of being selected by the stockholders with responsibility pointed to this end. Not only is this characteristic found in the operations of large stock companies, but it is equally a feature of large, mutual organizations, such as the mutual savings banks and life insurance companies. Hence, there is need to keep in mind that the concentration of control is likely more a characteristic of the size and nature of operation than it is the result of form of legal organization.

Minority Control 

On other occasions, the control center may be found in a minority financial interest instead of the operating management. In this instance, the latter is usually subject to the wishes of the former, and the minority's investment serves as a sort of balance favoring the stockholders' interest as against management. However, the pattern of organizing the control mechanism is essentially the same. This consists of a delegation of authority to a committee giving it the power to elect officers and to exercise all other powers of the shareholders at the annual meeting. Hence, those who name the members of this committee will automatically obtain control over the larger corporate body. The legal instrument which is used to create the power of attorney whereby a committee is authorized to act in behalf of the shareholders is a proxy. 

Stockholders' meetings are legal requirements and can be held only if a majority of the stock is legally present. It is not feasible and

would often be physically impossible for the stockholders to be present in person. The equivalent is accomplished legally by the use of the proxy, which is a legal document signed by the stockholder appointing certain individuals as his lawful attorneys to represent him at the meeting. The following copy of a proxy is illustrative of the process involved: 

Company,

KNOW ALL MEN BY THESE PRESENTS, that the undersigned stock holder of Company, does hereby constitute and appoint ..., attorneys and agents for the undersigned to vote at the Annual 

Meeting of the Stockholders of said and at any adjournment or adjournments thereof, the number of shares of stock which the undersigned would be entitled to vote if personally present at said meeting A majority of said attorneys and agents who shall be present at said meeting (or if one only shall be present then that one), shall have and may exercise all the powers of all said attorneys and agents. 

-- 
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the undersigned has executed this instrument day of April, 1942. the (L.S.) 

Signature of Stockholder 

As a result of the difficulty of stockholders being present, plus the lack of interest shown by them, the typical stockholders' meeting becomes largely a meeting of proxies. It is quite unusual for most of the large corporations to have more than one hundred individuals present, and usually it is a smaller number. In fact, there have been times when proxy committees have had great difficulty in obtaining a sufficient number of legal proxies to conduct a stockholders' meeting. A great many stockholders neglect to return the proxy sent to them by the officers, and as a result it is necessary to postpone the meetings. For example, during the month of April, 1937, fifteen companies having securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange were forced to adjourn their stockholders' meetings due to the lack of a legal quorum.13

Since the stockholders are present largely in proxy form, great power is conferred upon those persons appointed to vote, and it is apparent that they may easily achieve their desired ends. However, on occasions opposition develops, and there may be a mad scramble for proxies. This was true of a number of cases in 1929 and 1930. The fight between John D. Rockefeller, Jr., and R. Stewart for the control 

18 New York Times (April 25, 1937), p. Fl.

of the Standard Oil Company of Indiana is a pertinent illustration.14 

Similarly, the defeat of the Childs Brothers in the Childs Company not only affords an example of a scramble for proxies but illustrates in a pronounced manner the entity of the corporation; even though the 

Childs interests have been deposed from management, the name of the corporation still continues. 

Recognizing the potential abuse of the proxies, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 declared it unlawful to solicit proxies by mail or other channels of interstate commerce "in contravention of such rules and regulations as the Commission may prescribe." The latter were first issued in 1934. The chief provisions as amended in 1940 are: 

1. A clear statement must be made as to who is soliciting the proxy. Usually this will be the existing management, but it must be stated. Any other group desiring to solicit control must clear with the Commission before taking action. 

2. A copy of the proxy material must be filed with the S.E.C. 10 days before the solicitation begins. Copies must also be filed with cach Exchange upon which the stock may be listed. 

3. If auditors or a committee to select auditors is to be named at the meeting for which the proxy is solicited, the proxy must name the auditors or the nominees for the committee. 

4. If minority groups have indicated that they expect to raise certain matters of business at the proposed meeting, these matters must be described and the stockholder given an opportunity to indicate the action he wishes taken. 

5. Actions proposed by the management must be summarized in the proxy solicitation. 

6. Statement of costs being incurred in the solicitation must be given, as well as data on the stockholdings of the officers, directors, and members of the nominating committee.

An example of a proxy issued under the foregoing rules is that of 

General Motors Corporation for the April 30, 1940, meeting. The proxy statement was in essentially the same form as that given on page 281, except that the stockholder was given an opportunity 14 This was a fight between the operating management represented by Stewart and the minority financial interest of Rockefeller in which the former was ousted. For further details see A. A. Berle, Jr., and G. C. Means, The Modern Corporation and Private Property. 

(New York: Macmillan Company, 1933), pp. 82-84. Also see T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11,

Bureaucracy and Trusteeship in Large Corporations, p. 20, to the effect that the cost of obtaining proxies by Rockefeller amounted to about $300,000.

to vote on three issues. In each case the proxy stated that the com. mittee would vote the stock in a certain way unless the stockholder expressed himself otherwise. Thus, the stockholder could vote his stock for or against a proposed contributory retirement plan for executives, but if he failed to vote the committee would vote his stock in favor of the plan. In other words, the management still retained the position of maximum influence, but the stockholders were given a mechanism for playing a far greater part as an active policy-making force than was possible in the past.

Non-voting Stock 

The nature of non-voting stock has been indicated at a previous point, and two representative cases of its use may be cited at this time. The capitalization of the American Tobcaco Company is represented by: 

526,997 shares of preferred stock 

1,598,496 shares of common stock 

2,976,548 shares of common B stock

The right to vote is concentrated in the common stock while the preferred stock and B stock are without voting rights. 

The National Cash Register Company formerly had two classes of common stock outstanding, one of which had restricted voting powers. The Class B stock, represented by 400,000 shares, had the right to elect the majority of the board of directors, while the 1,190,000 shares of Class A stock elected the remainder. In the event of certain contingencies (passage of two consecutive dividends on Class A stock or failure to earn dividends), the Class B stock lost this privilege.

Although in this instance the Class A stock was not completely deprived of its voting rights, its power to control was nullified except under the contingencies specified.

Classified Voting 

Classified voting is similar to the foregoing but arises under different conditions. As an illustration, preferred stock may be given. the right to elect a majority of the directors. This is illustrated in the reorganization of the Cleveland Discount Company, which provided in its reorganization that the preferred stock would have the right to elect a majority of the directors. Again, in the Virginia- 

Carolina Chemical Company, the old 7 per cent cumulative prior

preferred stock was given the same right as long as there was more than $10,000,000 of the stock outstanding. The preferred stockholders of the Stanley Works elect three of the seventeen directors and acquire other voting rights if the stock should become eighteen months in arrears on its dividends. 

Voting Trusts

Voting trusts represent still greater concentration of control because final and absolute voting power is usually vested in a few individuals for a fixed period of time. Under this plan, stockholders deposit their stock with a depository in favor of the trustees and receive in return trust certificates. These may be bought and sold the same as any other stock certificates and are entitled to the dividends declared upon the deposited shares. The device is created under two sets of circumstances. 

1. It is used as a means of providing centralized and positive control for a period following reorganization. This is illustrated by the 

7 per cent cumulative prior preferred stock of the Virginia-Carolina Chemical Company referred to above, where a voting trust was created for a period of five years. Another instance is that of the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Pacific Railroad Company whose preferred and common stocks were deposited under a trust agreement at the time the reorganization plan was declared effective, December 31, 1927. 

The voting trust was to exist for three years, with the privilege of renewal upon a majority vote of the certificates outstanding. 

2. Voting trusts are also utilized by going concerns for the direct purpose of expediting control. The Pennroad Corporation was organized in Delaware in 1929 for the purpose of investing funds in other corporations but could not itself engage in active operations. 

All its common stock is held by a voting trust which has a specified life of ten years. All three voting trustees are directors of the Pennsylvania Railroad, which automatically permits common policy for the two corporations even though they are two distinct and separate entities. 

Pyramiding of the Corporate Structure 

Another device which is employed to accomplish the concentration of control is the pyramiding of one corporation on top of another in successive layers. By this means, the majority interest may be successively reduced in amount until it is readily financed by those seek-

ing control. To illustrate, a corporation with capital stock of $100,- 

000,000 would require one share more than $50,000,000 to assure positive control. If a second corporation were created with capital equal to this majority interest, it would then be possible to control the second corporation with one share more than $25,000,000. This process could conceivably be carried on ad infinitum until a relatively small amount would permit absolute control over a much larger superstructure. This method has been used extensively in the field of public utilities as described in Chapter XXXII.

Need for Concentration of Control 

The various devices which are used to effectuate the concentration of control are often considered to be tactics of evil and their very existence calls for condemnation. Actually, in any organization of large-scale operation, some form of orderly and centralizing procedure is essential to its proper functioning. Otherwise, disunity and various conflicts of interest would produce serious confusion and possible chaos. The primary test of its propriety, therefore, is whether or not it contributes to the best interests of the parties affected. If there is an unwarranted diversion of benefits from the many to the few insiders, then there is little justification for the concentration of control. 

On the other hand, if the delegation of authority by scattered owners of stock to a small group is exercised according to the real principles of true trusteeship, then both these owners and society-at-large may be the beneficiaries. 

15 See Berle and Means, op. cit., p. 94. The parenthetical comments are those of the authors.

In the case of small-scale enterprise, it is usually possible for the owner to exercise his authority directly. There need be little social concern for operations of this character because the responsibility is direct and absolute; in large-scale operation, it is the condition of absentee ownership which gives rise to many questions affecting the public interest. Society has long permitted great freedom in the exercise of rights which affect primarily the single individual, but where the action by a single person affects the rights of others, then some form of government is necessary. This general principle is applicable in a sense to the operations of big business because their internal structure is largely the result of a delegation of power. This larger social attribute will be discussed at greater length in a following chapter after the nature of the management function has been described.

CHAPTER XVI  

HE structural composition of the corporation consists of a financial framework superimposed upon a foundation of legal organization. But to understand the driving force of corporate activity it is necessary to look behind this outer shell and to observe its internal functioning and motivation. Just as a house is converted into a home by the process of living, so the corporation is transformed from an inanimate, technical creation into an animate, living force by its day-to-day operation. In a way similar to that of human beings, corporations develop personalities-strong or weak, attractive or repulsive, kind or cruel; all these features are molded into a single entity. The corporate life which is thereby generated reflects the expression of its inner force-management. 

In many respects, the study of corporation finance is an inquiry into the actions and policies of management. Methods of production, processes of selling, and various forms of administrative technique are usually adopted in the light of financial effect. The latter includes not only the relationship between sources of funds and these branches of business operation but also embraces the ultimate objectives of earnings results, and of sound and successful operation. In this larger sense, finance serves as a yardstick by which management makes decisions and determines underlying policies of operation. 

Who Constitutes Management?

The lack of preciseness and standardization of business and economic terminology makes it desirable to state who constitutes management. Commonly, management is interpreted to mean those in charge of the area of production, particularly the heads of operating departments and often excluding the selling and administrative groups. Actually, these individuals are only the agents of management and should be distinguished from the smaller central group 1 There is also another possible definition of management as a process or force which merges the various seemingly independent units into a common whole. 288

which determines the policies to be put into effect. Various supervisory heads may assume great dignity and create an imposing front by the exercise of authority, but they are still subordinate in their capacity. As in the army, numerous lieutenants, captains, and other officers are necessary to put the orders of headquarters into effect. 

But to understand the fundamental tactics employed in troop movements and the planning of major campaigns, one must look to the small general staff at the top. Equally so in business enterprise, the formulation and direction of basic policy is highly centralized. 

The management functions of the corporation are exercised by a small group of executive officers and the board of directors. Incorporating statutes prescribe that every corporation shall have a board of directors and usually, but not always, stipulate that the corporation shall have a president and a secretary. The actions of the executive group are directed normally by the president, although many exceptions are found in practice. In the performance of his office the chief executive officer works through operating departmental heads. and various staff officers who act in an advisory capacity. Irrespective of the terminology used to designate the executive head, his chief function is the direction of operations.

The duty of the board of directors is, on the other hand, the determination of basic policies. The operating head will necessarily make many recommendations involving questions of policy, but final decision is supposed to be the product of group thinking and deliberative meetings by the board. The law has recognized the importance of group thinking by the board of directors in the development of the legal rule that a decision of the individual directors-even an unanimous decision-is ordinarily not valid as action of the board or binding on the corporation if the decision of each director was given separately and without a meeting of the board. 

The general rule of law covering group action is stated in Fletcher, Cyclopedia of the Law of Private Corporations, as follows: 

By the overwhelming weight of authority, when the power to do particular acts, or general authority to manage the affairs of the corporation, is vested in the directors or trustees, it is vested in them, not individually, but as a board, and, as a general rule, they can act so as to bind the corporation only when they act as a board and at a legal meeting, unless the corporation has estopped itself, or has ratified the acts of the individual directors by receiving and accepting the 

2 Stevens on Corporations (1936), p. 640.

benefits of their acts adopted in such manner, and this rule applies to the meetings of the board of directors of banking corporations.³ 

The reasoning which underlies the rule is well stated by the court in the case of Ames v. Goldfield Merger Mines Company as follows:

The stockholders of a corporation have a right to expect from their directors a conscientious consideration of every proposition which is presented which involves any interest of the company, in conformity to the oath to which they have subscribed. They have a right to have the individual viewpoint of the several directors expressed at a conference, for the purpose of obtaining the exchange of view of the several persons in arriving at conclusions after deliberate consideration of any issue. It is fundamental that officers of boards can only act as such constituted boards when assembled as such, and by deliberate and concerted action dispose of the issue under consideration, and that they cannot act in an individual capacity outside of a formal meeting, and a majority of the individual expressions be the action of the board. The law believes that the greatest wisdom results from conference and exchange of individual views, and it is for that reason that the law requires the united wisdom of a majority of the several members of the board in determining the business of a corporation, The question may be raised as to the ability of part-time, nonexpert members of a board of directors to pass judgment on the many specific issues which require solution, and possibly the answer is more a matter of the arts than it is one of science. Full-time operating officials are apt to get so close to their problems that they often lack the objectivity and detachment which are necessary to screen out elements of weakness. Their subordinates frequently lack the moral courage to disagree with their superiors. To provide adequate checks and balances, much may be gained by requiring those responsible for operations to present their programs to an independent court, i.e., the board of directors. Many boards fail to render the service which is to be expected, but it is important to be aware of the peculiar contributions which a good board of directors may make. 

Nature of Responsibilities of Board of Directors Directors are the elected representatives of the body of stockholders, i. e., they represent the stockholders as a group and not the 

3 Fletcher, Cyclopedia of the Law of Private Corporations (Perm. Ed.), Vol. 2, Sec. 392. 

Application of the rule is illustrated by the case of Baldwin et al. v. Canfield, 26 Minn. 43 (1879) in which a conveyance of land belonging to a corporation was held ineffectual because it was executed in the name of the corporation by all directors acting separately and not as a board, and without previous authorization by the board. 

4227 Fed. 292,301 (1915).

individual holders of shares. It is true that their election is usually effected by minority interests which resort to various devices (particularly the proxy) to achieve control, but even so, the principle of representation underlies the whole process. Shareholders may be unable to vote intelligently or may fail to exercise their privilege at all, but it does not follow that directors are thereby relieved of the basic obligation to administer efficiently and to account properly for the funds committed to their care. Indeed, the acceptance of funds by the corporation from the public-at-large places the directors in a fiduciary position. Such utterances may sound platitudinous, but in the long run they are warranted in the light of cold business-like decision. Large-scale business of today is vitally dependent upon the flow of capital from millions of small investors whose continued investment will depend upon the treatment they are accorded. Abuses by the directors of their trust, imposition on the shareholders' rights of ownership, unwarranted assumption of power by the few, all serve to break the life-line of confidence which is essential to investor support.

The fiduciary position of the directors is also a reason why they should assume the responsibility for determining the basic policies of a corporation instead of the operating officials. The latter are appointed because of their technical or administrative ability to do a job in which their own professional or self-interest is necessarily paramount. Investor welfare is of secondary concern, it being presumed that the urge of operating heads to promote their own position will redound to the benefit of those who employ them. There is nothing fundamentally wrong in this assumption of derived benefit, but it is desirable that those with investments at stake be represented to counterbalance those whose interests are mainly of an operating nature. 

Moreover, elected directors should give expression to a financial point of view which would give greater security to business operations. 

Recognition of the fact that directors are representative of shareholders is more than a matter of economic desirability; it also has legal sanction. It is true that strict enforcement of legal liabilities has not been invoked,5 and, indeed, there is debate as to the extent to which penalities should be imposed for various forms of neglect of duty. The argument is advanced that capable and outstanding individuals are becoming increasingly reluctant to serve as directors 

5 See chapter XII. 

1

because the compensating benefits are not believed to offset the liabilities which are assumed. This attitude has become more prevalent in recent years as increased emphasis has been placed upon the rights of investors, particularly as formalized in the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.6 In answer to the objection raised, there is likely a need for more deliberate decision when considering the acceptance of office. All too frequently, directors have accepted appointment because of the honor of position or with the knowledge that they will serve in a dummy capacity for powerful interests seeking control. 

Granting that a sharpening of the responsibility of directors may increase the difficulties of finding capable appointees, it does not follow that the proper solution is to be found in the curtailment of duties or in the failure to enforce the liabilities designed to encourage conscientious performance of duty. Instead, the answer is probably one of creating sufficient incentives or benefits to offset the risks assumed. Consideration may now be given to the following possibilities: (1) restriction of directors to officers of the corporation, (2) requirement that directors be substantial holders of stock, (3) compensation for directors.

Restriction of Directors to the Officers of a Corporation Except in the case of closed corporations, it is unusual to find boards of directors composed exclusively of the operating officials. 

However, it is common to have the president and one or two other officers included, although there is usually no legal requirement which would compel membership. The chief point for discussion here is whether the use of corporation executives as directors should be encouraged on a large scale. Those who favor this plan contend that a board so constituted is more qualified to serve because of its greater knowledge of actual operations. Most directors, because of their parttime service, lack intimate familiarity with internal processes which full-time officials gain through their day-to-day contact. Hence, it is argued that greater use of dual-capacity officials should lead to more intelligent direction.

A second supporting point in favor of officers serving as directors is that their interest and attention are primary in character. Outside appointees are believed to have only indirect concern, accepting of- 

6 See chapters XXI and XXIII.

fice often because of the value of the contact for their more personal interests or other secondary reasons. They may be appointed for reasons of convenience as is recognized in the following court opinion: "The directors of the . . . . Company-men of prominence and probity in the community-were but nominal shareholders selected for their prestige, vulgarly called window dressing, proud to be financiers, and insensible of the part they were playing in the cupidity of others." 

In contrast, inside directors are said to have their own welfare at stake, and that in promoting their own gain they necessarily advance the larger interests of the corporation.

A board of directors composed mainly of operating officials is also said to afford greater continuity of operations. Under typical procedure of existing practice, board meetings are usually held on given dates without particular reference to the flow of business. The time of meeting is generally fixed in the by-laws and is, therefore, arbitrary in character rather than related to the needs or problems which are constantly arising. Full-time officials are said to be much more free to meet on call so that greater emphasis is given to need than to point of time.

It will be observed that most of the arguments which have been advanced are those of expediency, giving large weight to the shortterm point of view. Moreover, each is subject to rebuttal. Thus, while outside directors may serve to gain contacts of value to themselves, it is also likely that they become a source of new business for the corporation which they direct. In answer to the increased continuity of operations which is permitted by inside directors, it may be said that often much is gained by the seasoning of problems. "Make haste slowly" is probably good advice for business conduct as well as for purposes of individual living. Finally, the strongest argument in favor of independent, outside directors is their capacity to provide external check and balance. Experience has revealed on many occasions the value of unbiased observation from independent directors as well as the short-comings of introspection by full-time operating officials. Friendly and interested remoteness gives a perspective which is not possible under internal review and analysis. It would seem, Lynch v. Sapiro, 117 N. J. Eq. 485 (1935). 

8 Where the charter or by-laws of a corporation provide for regular meetings of the board, such meetings must be held at the time fixed. However, this does not prevent the directors from holding special meetings, whenever business of the corporation requires attention between the time of holding the regular meetings. Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 399.

therefore, that the problem of lackadaisical direction of business will not be solved to the best advantage by simply substituting inside officials for outside appointees. 

Requiring Directors To Be Substantial Holders of Stock 

Another proposal which is advanced to secure more effective administration of corporate affairs is that directors be required to own stock of the corporation. Before discussing the merits of a requirement that directors be shareholders, as well as the amount of stock which they may be compelled to hold, it will be helpful to examine briefly the legal status. The common law rule is that unless required by statute, the articles of incorporation, or the by-laws of the corporation, a director of a private corporation need not be a shareholder." 

It has been customary in the past for general incorporation statutes to stipulate that directors must be holders of stock,10 but revision of these statutes in recent years has often eliminated shareholding as a prerequisite to election to the board, except where the shareholders themselves impose such a requirement in their articles or by-laws.¹¹ 

Furthermore, where a requirement that directors must be shareholders does exist, its practical effectiveness has been weakened by the rule, followed by the overwhelming majority of the courts, that a person who holds the naked legal title to stock on the books of the corporation is qualified to act as a director, even though the beneficial ownership of the stock may actually be in another person.12 

Provisions specifying the amount of stock which must be held to qualify as a director are much less common, although such provisions do exist in the corporation statutes of some states. For example, in 

Kentucky the statute stipulates that a director must own in his own right at least three shares of capital stock.13 In Montana and South

A financial stake in a business would obviously create a keener and deeper interest than would otherwise be true. There are many instances where individuals have served capably and conscientiously without having personal investment in an enterprise, but this does not warrant the broad conclusion that the system is universally good. 

Usually, these individuals have been motivated by a fine sense of public service which ought to be cultivated and encouraged. If applied with moderation, the requirement of an investment to qualify as a director need not destroy the larger, moral values of altruistic endeavor.

The amount of investment which may be required for qualification would be a matter of personal opinion. Probably greater emphasis should be placed upon the relation of the investment to the personal wealth of the director than its relation to the capital structure of the corporation which is being served. Neither is it practical to establish any fixed requirements since more is to be gained by allowing considerable leeway in determining the reasonableness of the amount required. It can be said, however, that intent is the prime desideratum. 

Attention should also be called to some of the possible disadvantages of excessive personal investment. Instances are known where personal perspective has been substituted for the corporate point of view. High prices of the commodity or service being sold might be favored in the belief that greater profits would be available for dividends. Desirable ventures into new lines or markets may be discouraged because of the fear of personal loss. Under full competition, there is little need to attach much significance to these personal pressures, but where control of market or other forms of monopolistic practice are present, they do become a matter of concern. 

Compensation for Directors 

It is fundamental in our law that directors are not entitled to compensation for services rendered within the scope of their duties as directors.15 Compensation may be authorized by the articles, the bylaws, a vote of the shareholders, or by the directors acting under authority conferred upon them, but without some such special pro- 

14 Mont. Rev. Codes 1935, Sec. 5933; S. D. Code 1939, Sec. 11.0705. 

15 Stevens, op. cit., Sec. 157.

vision, remuneration for services as a director is not made. The rule is founded on the presumption that each director will have a stock interest sufficiently large to justify his devotion to the corporation without other reward.16

In practice, directors are usually paid a nominal amount for their services on an expense account or per diem basis. This fee is provided for in the by-laws and is payable for each meeting or each day the board is in session. There is little standardization in the rates paid to directors, but $20 per meeting is probably representative. At such compensation, it is apparent that the acceptance of directorships must be for reasons other than direct financial return. As already stated, these reasons consist of opportunities gained by inside connections, convenience for influential friends, and undoubtedly, often for the sake of rendering a public service. 

To give more substance to directorships, there is considerable merit in placing the directors on a fixed salary and possibly having them function full time. There is precedent for this form of organization, and experience to date has been largely favorable. Thus, the use of full-time city councilmen under the city manager system has demonstrated many benefits. In England, professional directors, who may serve many corporations, are properly compensated, and their relationship is on a strictly quid pro quo basis. While not on a full-time basis, the directors of the Johns-Manville Corporation may receive compensation up to $5000 per annum.17 To come to the heart of the issue, adequate remuneration means that directorships are given an out-and-out job status instead of being considered as some sort of honorary office.

There is increasing evidence of the likelihood of transformation of board operation along the lines suggested. Numerous public and private leaders are cognizant of the need for change and are now paving the way for the metamorphosis. A former member of the 

Securities and Exchange Commission has said:

Many of the deficiencies of our modern directorates result from the presence of so many inactive directors on so many of our larger boards. In many of our directorates there are business colonels of the honorary type-honorary colonels who are ornamental in parade but fairly useless in battle; men whose 

16 Navco Hardwood Co. v. Bass, 214 Ala. 553 (1925); Fox v. Arctic Placer Min. & Mill. 

Co., 229 N. Y. 124 (1920). 

17 Wall Street Journal (March 30, 1940), p. 4. For data on other companies' practices, sec, "Directors Who Direct," Business Week (February 15, 1941), p. 26.

fathers and uncles perhaps were generals but who themselves are qualified to command only by the virtue of the uniform they wear . . . . The term “paid director" may come as a novelty, but there is really nothing startling about the idea. Perhaps we might put it better by saying that we need more efficient directors and we can get them only by putting the position on a salaried basis.¹s 

The Nature of Active Board Management 

In the typical corporation, the board of directors is primarily a policy-making body which meets at relatively infrequent intervals to determine the guiding policies of operation. The president and other officers are responsible for putting these policies into effect and for handling the resulting operating problems. The question may be raised as to the nature of the relationship which would exist between operating management and a full-time board of the type previously suggested. The latter would naturally be in session more or less continuously, and a clear delineation of function would be essential to avoid friction with the operating personnel.

Analysis of the practice of several public administrative corporations reveals two patterns of organization. Under one plan, each board member is made responsible for the supervision of designated departments or areas of business. In this capacity, the individual member does not direct the actual operations but serves more in the role of an overseer or supervisor. By specializing in a limited area, he is able to report with expertness to the entire board the results of operations and to make suggestions as to policy changes. To a certain extent, this form of organization is similar to that where the board is composed of officers of the corporation. Aside from the source of appointment to office, the chief difference is that of providing a clear line of demarcation between operating administration and policy formation.

The other plan of organization is to have the board sit as a body for the disposition of all major problems. No single member is assigned a specific task. Each one is free to call in operating heads to discuss any questions which affect their departments. This, of course, causes a certain duplication of effort. However, compensating benefits appear later when the various issues are presented for board consideration and discussion. By expecting each member to be familiar 

18 Address of William O. Douglas, Chairman, Securities and Exchange Commission at a luncheon of the Fort Worth Clearing House Association, Fort Worth, Texas, January 9, 1939, pp. 1-6. god

with all operations, a much more adequate basis is laid for intelligent discussion. Experience has demonstrated on more than one occasion the value of the checks and balances provided under this system of operation.

Irrespective of the set-up which is employed, there are several values that a permanent operating board of recognized standing may contribute. Within the organization, it is an important factor in building employee morale and esprit de corps. Operating personnel find it easier to present their problems because a board by its very nature invites discussion while individual control is apt to create the impression of arbitrariness. It is more difficult under the latter system to divorce issues from personalities. Individual dominance in business enterprise may easily assume the semblance of dictatorship because decisions are made by a single person. Under board operation, there is necessarily an exchange of ideas; hence, it is more democratic in character.

Other internal benefits derived under full-time board administration are found in the more careful separation of the legislative, judicial, and executive types of activity. As in government, the conduct of business involves actions which are similar in type to these three familiar categories. There are also equally good reasons for their separation in business practice. While recognizing this threefold classification of functions, it is unnecessary to segregate them as distinctly as is done in government. The board of directors occupies a vantage point favorable to the exercise of legislative and judicial duties while the operating officials are better fitted to perform the executive functions. Included in the legislative group of activities would be found the various acts of policy formation; actions of a judicial nature would be required in settling interdepartmental disputes, disagreements between labor and operating management, etc.; finally, the executive functions would take form in the actual administration of operations. 

A full-time board could also give invaluable service in handling many problems of an external variety. The public relations of modern business are rapidly assuming an importance which will affect materially the success or failure of any enterprise. It is now appreciated as never before that adverse public sentiment can do much to undermine the solvency of any enterprise, be it a public utility or a so-called private business. On the positive side, there is increasing awareness that price, wage, dividend, and other policies must have general pub-

lic approbation. To meet these new conditions, many corporations have created a specialized public relations staff to build proper public understanding, but to be successful, this department needs to work closely and to be in tune at all times with the board of directors. 

Too often, operating officials are technicians who lack the perspective to appraise social and political movements which may exert great influence upon business trends. A board is usually less technical in character and reacts more readily to issues involving human relations. Moreover, its procedure through discussion lends itself to the treatment of broad problems without precedent for solution. It is necessary only to think of the confusing and complex conditions of recent years to visualize the many enigmas confronting business management. Labor disputes on an unprecedented scale, money-market conditions which give evidence of numerous cross-currents, irregular and uncertain commodity price movements-these, and many other far-reaching issues, force themselves on the agenda. It is expecting too much of a single individual to determine the course of action to take; much more logical is the determination of a policy through frank discussion around the board table. 

There are also certain disadvantages under full-time board direction. Whenever more than one individual is charged with responsibility, the speed of reaching decisions would be reduced and the flexibility of action lost. Under some business situations, this would. be undesirable and costly. On the other hand, it could be expected that a decision reached more slowly after proper deliberation and discussion among a larger number of individuals responsible would be a wiser and better decision. It will be recognized that unrestrained clearance of major issues may also be costly in the long run. In any event, full-time board operation should result in a greater sense of director responsibility.

Need for Accounting and Auditing 

Most of the previous discussion has been concerned with the composition of a board of directors. Some thought should now be given to what may be expected in the way of checks and balances upon management itself. The most important safeguard to the interests of stockholders, in this respect, is found in the adequate reporting of operations by independent and external authorities. The exigencies of business conditions of recent years have produced on their own account a distinct unsettling of the investor's mind. Heavy losses

in capital values have raised serious questions as to the adequacy of returns to offset assumed risk. More important to the continued success of business enterprise, the losses may have shaken the faith of the investing public in business management. Many losses during the early thirties were of a highly conjunctural character, which even the most shrewd and careful management could not have avoided. 

Under the circumstances, it would be unreasonable to hold management wholly responsible for the results. However, the reverses did serve to bring numerous shortcomings to light as well as to bring management responsibility into more prominent focus. 

Management commonly accepts credit for successful operation but is apt to disavow any real responsibility for unfavorable results. Losses are conveniently ascribed to business adversity, but gains are believed to reflect the glory of individual achievement irrespective of the uplifting influence of prosperous business conditions. Such psychology is human, but it is not too realistic. Especially is this true where the results of operations are used as a basis for the remuneration of executives. Here it would seem to follow that if improved earnings are to be used as a criterion for increased compensation on the upswing, later adjustments should be effected in response to losses or declining profits. The task of management is more difficult in times of depression, which undoubtedly is a potent argument in favor of adequate remuneration regardless of net profits. However, where the rule of relating executive compensation to earnings results is adopted, fairness demands its application in both directions. 

Adversities of recent times have placed unusual but desirable emphasis upon the adequacy of accounting. All too often, secrecy has concealed many pertinent points of operation about which the stockholders should be informed, but the information has been withheld on the grounds that its publicity would give an advantage to competitors. This explanation is frequently one of convenience more than it is a matter of substance. Actually, competitors are usually apprised of each other's business through informal get-togethers and formal channels of interchange of data under trade association auspices.

Reports to stockholders need revision both as to their completeness and their form of presentation. Earnings statements, particularly, have been inadequate, there being a tendency to omit them entirely, to resort to undesirable abbreviation, or to present net figures only.

Balance sheets are characterized more by their formality than the amount of information they reveal. To provide more adequate accounting, directors need to think more in terms of the stockholders who are invited to read the reports. From this point of view, the adoption of a narrative and informal style should prove to be of much assistance; and it should be added that there are now definite signs of progress in this direction. Meaning and color may also be sharpened by presenting comparative results. Absolute figures are limited as to their revelation and need to be related to other yardsticks if they are to afford any satisfactory interpretation. Comparison of year-to-year results and the measurement of earnings in terms of the capital structure are both convenient devices to achieve the desired objective.

The need for independent auditing is also being recognized on an increasing scale. Directors benefit from the fact that an independent audit affords them a degree of self-protection, and shareholders are entitled to it as a safeguard to their rights. Internal auditing procedure can do much to prevent collusion and other acts of dishonesty, but it lacks the objectivity necessary to pronounce final judgment. 

It functions under the board whose record is being audited, and discovery of improper action may involve a choice between the auditor's job or remaining silent. As a result, the stockholders are by no means assured of a thorough investigation free from any bias or pressure. 

In the case of an external, independent audit, the question immediately arises as to who shall be responsible for the selection of the auditing firm. Precedent has lodged this privilege in the board of directors, but there is now considerable discussion as to whether the right to choose should be placed in the hands of the stockholders. The practice is already a legal requirement in the state of Massachusetts and is commonly employed in England.19 Some difficulties are inherent in the plan, particularly the procedure to be adopted in selecting a group by the stockholders who will be charged with the responsibility of naming the auditors. Several alternatives seem to be available. A vote by the stockholders may be taken at the time of the annual election, but the limitations and unwieldy character of this pro- 

19 Section 49 of chapter 156 of the General Laws of Massachusetts provides: "Such audi tor shall be employed for each ensuing fiscal year by a committee of three stockholders who are not directors which shall be selected at each annual meeting of the stockholders, or, if there are not three stockholders other than directors able and willing to serve on such committee, he shall be employed by the directors; but no bookkeeper, treasurer or other officer of the corporation shall be appointed as such auditor."

posal are readily apparent. Another possibility is that of giving the power of selection to the larger stockholders, setting the minimum shareholdings large enough to prevent the group from becoming too large. Still a third plan would be to appoint a committee of three, consisting of a representative appointed by the directors, one by the stock exchange on which the securities are listed, and one by the 

Securities and Exchange Commission. 

Irrespective of the procedure adopted to provide for an external audit, there is need to stress the importance of its adoption in practice. 

The relationship that exists in a large corporation between the stockholders and the directors is so remote that little weight may be attached to the historical and friendly ties which were presumed to exist between the two groups. Facing realities, directors of large corporations are necessarily far removed from the vast body of scattered stockholders, and they are motivated chiefly by their own personal sense of responsibility. This is cited not for purposes of condemnation but to point out that shareholders need to pursue a course which will also assure the maximum protection to their interests. 

In setting up these checks upon management, the importance of high standards within the ranks of management should not be minimized. In fact, there is no better safeguard to investor interests than honest and capable executive personnel. It is not easy for auditors to detect the beginnings of dishonest practice, and, of course, discovery always occurs after a certain amount of damage is already done. 1 

The McKesson and Robbins case.-The McKesson and Robbins case is illustrative of much of the foregoing discussion relating to management responsibility and to proper accounting. In December, 1938, this company was placed in reorganization after it was reported that the assets had been overstated and the firm was probably insolvent. The company had a good reputation and did a large business manufacturing and wholesaling proprietary drug lines. It developed, however, that the crude drug department, which had been under the sole direction and control of the president, F. Donald Coster and the assistant-treasurer, George E. Dietrich, was in reality a huge blind for illicit trading purposes. Over $10,000,000 in inventories charged to this department as well as $9,000,000 in accounts receivable were non-existent. During prohibition, Coster and Dietrich had carried on a sizeable bootlegging business and later had sold munitions to Spain under the guise of crude drugs. The "crude drug" dealings had been

carried on for years with W. W. Smith and Company, an English partnership and with Manning and Company of Montreal, both of which proved to be mere shells.20 Investigation also established that 

Coster and Dietrich were in reality Phillip and George Musica and had been involved in fraudulent activities before. 

The disclosure resulted from the discovery by the Treasurer that there was no insurance on the crude drug inventories. He inquired about the lack of insurance from Coster and was told that such insurance had been placed with the W. W. Smith and Company. The 

Treasurer had seen in the company's files several Dun and Bradstreet reports describing W. W. Smith and Company as a world-wide trading concern. Inquiry at the Dun and Bradstreet offices revealed the fact that the reports had not been issued by that firm and were forgeries.21 The other concern with which Coster's department had had dealings, Manning and Company of Montreal, proved to be a small office with a single employee.

It is difficult to understand how such a fraud could be continued for years without discovery if there had been an alert and inquiring management. However, Coster had been a smooth individual. He had taken over the crude drug department from the beginning of his connection with the company, and he had kept this department as strictly his domain. The auditors had certified the crude-drug inventories on the basis of the certification of "responsible" officials. If the auditors had verified the inventories, or if the directors had acted on the one accusation leveled some years before, the fraud could have been terminated earlier.

In 1932, Wadell Catchings was appointed to head a special committee to study operations in an effort to bring about greater economies. He became convinced that the wholesaling operations were being managed properly, but he was unable to obtain any information whatsoever on the crude-drug operations. Convinced that something was wrong, Catchings wrote the directors to attend the April, 1934, meeting. Coster heard of his letter, hired a lawyer, and conducted a whispering campaign among the directors. As a result, the directors refused to act upon or investigate Catchings' report, and consequently the company was defrauded for another four years before the plot was discovered.22 In fairness to the auditors, Price, Waterhouse and 

20 Moody's Manual of Industrials (1939), p. 2002. 

21 Time (December 19, 1938), pp. 48, 50. 

22 Time (January 9, 1939), pp. 48, 52.

30+ 

Company, who had done the auditing for the firm for fourteen years, the audit was conducted in accordance with the authorization given. 

Also, the accounting practices followed were those used by a majority of the practicing public accountants. As a result of the revelations of the McKesson and Robbins fraud, the public accounting societies have recommended the adoption of more extensive auditing procedures dealing chiefly with inventories and receivables. In the future, it will be a necessary part of an audit to verify the physical existence of inventories and to check receivables by direct communication with the debtors. If, for any reason, these steps are omitted, the fact of their omission is to be stated in the balance sheet rendered by the auditors.23 

Business activity cannot run smoothly without confidence and truthfulness. A board of directors must have confidence in its officers but at the same time it is well to recognize the frailties of human nature. Every company should be so organized that all employees can be checked as to effectiveness and honesty. The auditors should not accept essential information year after year on the word of the officers concerned. And the board of directors should not permit extensive private operations on the part of its executive officers. Certainly no corporation president should operate any portion of a company's assets without adequate and regular accounting for the results. 

All of this is important not because of any abstract ideals of fair play, but as a matter of practical business. Corporations must raise capital through the sale of stocks and bonds or other methods of borrowing, and the various sources of capital will hesitate to commit funds to the enterprise unless management is thorough, honest, and intelligent. Equally important is the probability that over any long period of time the honestly and efficiently managed concern will also be the most profitable one.

CHAPTER XVII  OF CORPORATE MANAGEMENT 

HE discussion in the preceding chapter was concerned mainly with the structure and form of management. There is need, however, to look behind the organization framework to inquire as to the responsibilities of management. Not only is this prompted by the need for orderly study of function, but, in addition, the developments of recent years have made the obligations of management a social issue. Such questions as the following are not uncommon: To whom is management responsible? What is the nature of its responsibility? What are the penalties for the neglect of responsibility? In seeking to answer questions of this type, a sharp distinction must be made between the legal and social responsibilities because only the former have practical means of enforcement. Attention will first be given to the existing legal status of private management.

The Fiduciary Position of Corporate Management 

As stated in the previous chapter, management may be said to consist of those officials who are responsible for the formation of business policies, that is, the directors and key officers. As the elected representatives of stockholders, it is not surprising that the law regards directors as standing in a fiduciary capacity to the body of shareholders and their interests.¹ The Sixth United States Circuit Court of Appeals in the case of Ashman v. Miller2 commented upon the principle and its rationale as follows: 

1 The general legal principle is stated in Fletcher, Cyclopedia of the Law of Private Cor porations (Perm. Ed.), Vol. 3, Sec. 838 as follows: "Directors and other officers, while not trustees in the technical sense in which that term is used, occupy a fiduciary relation to the corporation and to the stockholders as a body." Commenting further it is stated: "But whether or not directors and other corporate officers are strictly trustees, there can be no doubt that their character is that of a fiduciary so far as the corporation and the stockholders as a body are concerned. In other words, it is unquestionably true that, as agents intrusted with the management of the corporation, for the benefit of the stockholders collectively, they occupy a fiduciary relation, and in this sense the relation is one of trust." 

2 101 F. (2d) 85, 90 (1939). 307

A director of a corporation occupies a fiduciary relation to it and its stockholders. His position is one of trust and he is frequently denominated a trustee and so held accountable in equity. The ordinary trust relationship of directors of a corporation and stockholders is not a matter of statutory or technical law. 

It springs from the fact that directors have the control and guidance of corporate business affairs and property and hence of the property interests of the stockholders. Equity recognizes that stockholders are the proprietors of the corporate interest and are ultimately the only beneficiaries thereof. Those interests are in virtue of the law intrusted through the corporation to the directors and from that condition arises the trusteeship of the directors with the concomitant fiduciary relationship.

Rooted in this fiduciary relationship are two broad standards of conduct to which the law holds directors in their management of the corporation. These standards are: (1) the highest fidelity to the interest of the corporation, and (2) the discharge of their duties with reasonable care and reasonable prudence.3

Fidelity to the Interests of the Corporation 

In applying the first of these broad standards of conduct to the decision of concrete cases, the courts have developed several wellsettled rules which define the directors' duties and responsibilities arising from their fiduciary position. These rules may be stated briefly as follows: first, directors (and other officers as well) must exercise the utmost honesty in all transactions touching their duties to the corporation and its property, and all their dealings with and for the corporation must show the highest degree of good faith and fair dealing; second, directors must act for the benefit of the corporation and not for their own gain-they may not, directly or indirectly, derive any personal advantage or profit which is not enjoyed in common by all the shareholders;5 and third, all secret profits made by directors in the transaction of the company's business or resulting from deal- 

3 A. A. Berle, Jr., and G. C. Means, in The Modern Corporation and Private Property, p. 221, state that the general rules of conduct which the law has developed are: “(1) a decent amount of attention to business; (2) fidelity to the interests of the corporation; (3) at least reasonable business prudence." 

4 Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 850 and cases there cited. Globe Woolen Company v. Utica Gas & Electric Co., 224 N. Y. 483 (1918); McMynn v. Richardson-Phenix Co., 186 Wis. 442 (1924). See also, "Legal Safeguards about Transactions between a Director and His Corporation," University of Pennsylvania Law Review, Vol. 83 (1934), p. 56. 

Jackson v. Ludeling, 21 Wall. (U. S.) 616 (1874); American Circular Loom Co., v. 

Wilson, 198 Mass. 182 (1908); Fletcher, op. cit., and cases cited there.

ings in which their interest and the corporate interest conflict must be accounted for to the corporations. 

The variety of instances in the adjudicated cases of a breach by the directors of the fiduciary obligation implicit in the foregoing rules is without limit. A few examples will serve to illustrate the significance of the rules in practice. In a suit by a director against his corporation on a contract entered into by the two, the effect of which was to bring royalties to himself rather than to the corporation, the court refused to enforce the contract. In another case the board of directors authorized a sale of corporate property to the owner of the majority of the stock for an amount less than could have been obtained from another; the sale was held voidable at the instance of the minority stockholders.8

The situation has several times occurred where directors have exercised their power of control so as to divert to themselves unissued shares for which they pay the corporation par value and then resell to the public at a profit. The courts have held in such cases that the directors may be required to account to the corporation for the profit made, or may be compelled to surrender up the shares for cancellation.10

Humes, 157 Pa. 278 (1893): “A director is a trustee for the entire body of stockholders, and both good morals and good law imperatively demand he shall manage all the business affairs of the company with a view to promote, not his own interests, but the common interests; and he cannot, directly or indirectly, derive any personal profit or advantage by reason of his position, distinct from his coshareholder. . . . And by assuming the office he undertakes to give his best judgment in the interests of the corporation in all matters in which he acts for it, untrammeled by any hostile interest in himself or others. There is an inherent obligation on his part that he will in no manner use his position to advance his own interest as an individual, as distinguished from that of the corporation. . . . And all secret profits derived by him in any dealings in regard to the corporate enterprise must be accounted for to the corporation, even though the transaction in which they were made also advantage the corporation of which he was director."

They cannot have or acquire any personal or pecuniary interest in conflict with their duty as such trustees."

Situations involving interlocking directors have caused the courts considerable difficulty for the reason that in such cases a director owes a double loyalty. The courts scrutinize contracts negotiated by corporations, the boards of directors of which have common members, as carefully as they scrutinize dealings between a director and his corporation. They generally hold, where the fairness of such a transaction is challenged, that the burden of proof is upon those who would maintain the transaction.11

Other circumstances where there may be a conflict of directors' interests are found where directors may use their knowledge of the corporation's condition and plans for the benefit of a rival business. 

Numerous cases are found which prevent a director from entering into such a competing business as would cripple or injure the corporation; and instruments or property which he has acquired for that purpose may be impounded for the benefit of the corporation.12 

A commonly recurring situation calling for the application of the rules discussed above is where a director (or other corporate officer) acquires a title or interest adverse to that of the corporation while acting for the corporation or when dealing individually with third persons. In a case involving the stock of the Du Pont Powder Company, the president who was the largest stockholder, before leaving for an extended absence, offered to sell to the company a large block of stock at a certain price with a view to its resale at the same price to important employees. The finance committee of the company rejected the proposal solely because it thought the price was too high and instructed the acting president so to inform the absent president. 

The stock rapidly advanced in price because of World War I, and the acting president by concealing important facts from the absent president and from the company (and while acting as a representative of the company), purchased the stock for himself and his associates. 

Funds and credit of the company were also used as an aid in financing the purchase, at a price considerably higher than that at which it was originally offered. The court held that the company had the right at its election to take over the stock purchased at the price paid and to require an accounting for all dividends received thereon. Among other things, it stated:13
