When a director attempts in violation of his duty to acquire interests adverse to the corporation in respect to any matter involved in the confidence which has been reposed in him, as to which equity imposes a disability upon. him to deal in his own behalf, the court will hold him as a trustee for the corporation, and he must account for the profits which otherwise would have accrued to the corporation.

Exercise of Reasonable Care and Reasonable Prudence 

The law in holding directors to the second broad standard of conduct imposed upon them as fiduciaries, namely, the discharge of their duties with reasonable care and reasonable prudence, has developed the rule that they shall exercise such diligent care and skill as ordinarily prudent men would exercise under similar circumstances in like positions,14 The rule was stated and its fiduciary content indicated by the New York Court of Appeals in the case of Hun v. Cary in the following words:15

When one deposits money in a savings bank, or takes stock in a corporation, thus divesting himself of the immediate control of his property, he expects, and has the right to expect, that the trustees or directors, who are chosen to take his place in the management and control of his property, will exercise ordinary care and prudence in the trusts committed to them-the same degree of care and prudence that men prompted by self-interest generally exercise in their own affairs.

Application of the rule does not, of course, preclude delegation of certain duties to subordinates since directors cannot be expected to supervise all the details of the corporate business. Yet the right to delegate does not exempt the directors from the duty to check the conduct of their subordinates, nor does it free them of the necessity for exercising proper care in their appointment.16

Toward Whom Does Management Stand in a Fiduciary Relation under Existing Legal Principles In the preceding discussion an attempt was made merely to indicate briefly something of both the legal content and the practical legal effect of the fiduciary obligation which is imposed upon corporate manage- 14 Stevens on Corporations (1936), Sec. 146; the rule as stated in the text is also the substance of Sec. 33 of the Uniform Business Corporation Act. 

15 82 N. Y. 65, 71 (1880). 

16 See Briggs v. Spaulding, 141 U. S. 132 (1891); for a general discussion of the law on the subject of the standard of care and skill required in corporate management, see Rhoads, "Personal Liability of Directors for Corporate Mismanagement," University of Pennsylvania 

Law Review, Vol. 65, p. 128.

ment.17 Next, it is necessary to examine with some precision the question of toward whom does the director stand in a fiduciary relation. In brief, it is the view of the majority of the courts that the fiduciary relationship exists only as between management and the corporation together with its body of shareholders as a corporate group and does not exist as between management and individual stockholders.18 This designation of the corporation as the primary beneficiary of the trust obligations which the law imposes upon corporate directors is predicated upon a conception of the corporation as a fictitious legal entity separate and apart from the individual shareholders. It is reasoned that the duty of management is to the corporation as the representative of the body of shareholders, and that consequently there can be no fiduciary duty to the individual shareholder. 

The question of whether directors stand in the same position of trust with respect to individual shareholders as they do to the corporation and the shareholders as a whole has most frequently arisen in connection with the purchase of shares by a director from a stockholder. The issue usually is whether or not the purchasing director is under a duty to disclose his inside information of corporate affairs in order to present to the stockholders facts and circumstances which may tend to increase the value of the corporation's shares. The courts in the large majority of the states in this country hold that a director is under no such duty.19 On the other hand, a comparatively small minority of courts, mostly in the agricultural states, hold that a director is under such a duty.20 

17 For a more adequate discussion from a legal standpoint of the responsibilities of a director as a fiduciary, see "The Director of a Corporation as a Fiduciary," Iowa Law Review, Vol. 20 (1935), p. 808. 

18 Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 848. 

19 Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 1168. Of course the director may not actively mislead the selling stockholder or perpetrate a fraud, see Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 1172. The majority rule was expressed by the Supreme Court of Tennessce in Shaw v. Cole Mfg. Co., 132 Tenn. 210 (1915) as follows: "While directors occupy a trust relation to the corporation which they direct, their duty does not apply to the stockholder in the sale and purchase of stock. Dealing in its own stock is not a corporate function. In buying or selling stock, directors may trade like an outsider, provided they do not affirmatively act or speak wrongfully, or intentionally conceal facts with reference to it." The rule has been followed in Arizona, California, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Utah, and Washington, and perhaps other states. 

20 The leading case expressing the minority view is Oliver v. Oliver, 118 Ga. 362 (1903). 

The minority rule is followed in Alabama, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, and Wisconsin, and perhaps one or two other states. Where a director purchases from a co-director or officer to whom the same information is available, the rule does not apply. Perry v. Pearson, 135 Ill. 218 (1890).

The fundamental question is whether "a director can be honest. and faithful with regard to the whole corporation at the same time that he is taking a hostile position towards an individual shareholder."21 The Supreme Court of Georgia, in the leading case22 of the minority view, answers the question firmly in the negative. In that case the man who was both president and director of the corporation secured an option to purchase stock from certain stockholders at $110 per share. At the time the option was taken a sale of the company's plant was contemplated at a price which would make the stock worth from $140 to $185 per share. This information was not disclosed to the selling stockholders and as soon as the sale of the plant was definitely completed, the director took up the option and made a substantial profit. The court allowed the stockholders who had sold him the stock to recover the profit made. The court, in the course of its opinion, commented as follows:

And this brings us to a consideration of the relation which a director bears to an individual stockholder. All the authorities agree that he is trustee for the company, and in his capacity as such he serves the interests of the entire body of stockholders, as well as those of the individual shareholder, who usually cannot sue in his own name for wrongs done the company by the officer But the fact that he is trustee for all is not to be perverted into holding that he is under no obligation to each. The fact that he must serve the company does not warrant him in becoming the active and successful opponent of an individual stockholder with reference to the latter's undivided interest in the very property committed to the director's care. That he is primarily trustee for the corporation is not intended to make the artificial entity a fetish to be worshiped in the sacrifice of those who in the last analysis are the real parties at interest. 

No process of reasoning and no amount of argument can destroy the fact that the director is, in a most important and legitimate sense, trustee for the stockholder.... Not a strict trustee, since he does not hold title to the shares, not even a strict trustee who is practically prohibited from dealing with his cestui que trust, but a quasi trustee as to the shareholder's interest in the shares. 

21 Berle and Means, op. cit., p. 222. 

22 Oliver v. Oliver, op. cit. and commenting further the court continued: 

It is conceded that the position which the director occupies prevents him. from making personal gains at the expense of the company, or of the whole. body of stockholders. But the rule that he is not trustee for the individual shareholders inevitably leads to the conclusion that, while a director is bound to serve stockholders en masse, he may antagonize them one by one; that he is an officer of the company, but may be the foe of each private in the ranks.

When it is admitted, as it must be, both from the very nature of his duty, and from the rulings of nearly all the cases, that he is trustee for the shareholder, how is it possible, in principle, to draw the line, and say that, while trustee for some purposes, he is not for others immediately connected therewith? That the incidents of the trust relation stop short at the very point where it is vitally important to the shareholder that they should become active? For it must not be forgotten that the right to good faith in dealings concerning the stock is one of the very few which the individual shareholder is in a position to assert in his own name. Except in a few other instances the company itself is the only proper party to enforce the obligation arising from the trust relation of the director. 

Courts adopting the majority view commonly assert that the minority view assumes a personal relationship between a purchasing director and a selling stockholder which does not in most cases exist. 

They urge in support of their position that the purchase and sale of securities are ordinarily impersonal affairs effected on stock exchanges through brokers; that neither the actual buyer nor the actual seller has any personal relation whatever; that each individually and without influence from the other determines his own course of action; that, therefore, it is absurd to insist that there is any such relationship, fiduciary or otherwise, between the parties as to justify an action by a stockholder against a director or officer based on failure to disclose facts which might have affected the value of the stock.23 

The Massachusetts court in the case of Goodwin v. Agassiz24 in refusing recovery by a suing stockholder expressed its view on this point as follows: 

Purchases and sales of stock dealt in on the stock exchange are commonly impersonal affairs. An honest director would be in a difficult situation if he could neither buy nor sell on the stock exchange shares of stock in his corporation without first seeking out the other actual ultimate party to the transaction and disclosing to him everything which a court or jury might later find that he then knew affecting the real or speculative value of such shares. Business of that nature is a matter to be governed by practical rules. Fiduciary obligations of directors ought not to be made so onerous that men of experience and ability will be deterred from accepting such office. Law in its sanctions is not coextensive with morality. 

23 This is the position regarding exchange transactions taken in Walker, "The Duty of 

Disclosure by a Director Purchasing Stock from his Stockholders," Yale Law Journal, Vol. 32 (1923), p. 637. 

24 283 Mass. 358 (1933).

Development in Recent Years of a More Positive Fiduciary Duty upon Directors

Legal development in recent years points to the imposition upon directors of an increasingly more exacting fiduciary duty. Although this tendency manifests itself with more force in legislation than in judicial decisions, the latter are not without some indication of the trend. In most cases where the question of a director's fiduciary capacity has arisen, the courts have simply imposed a standard of conduct which prohibits a director from obtaining personal gain from a transaction to the injury of the corporation-a negative type of duty.25 However, in the relatively recent case of Bodell v. General 

Gas & Electric Corporation, the court talked in its opinion of a more positive type of duty.26 In holding directors as trustees of unissued stock, the court declared that it was not always necessary for them to reap personal benefit "in order for their actions in performance of their quasi trust to be successfully questioned." The court even went so far as to say that the directors as trustees "owe not alone the duty to refrain from benefiting themselves at the expense of their beneficiaries," but also owe "the duty of saving their beneficiaries from loss." By beneficiaries the court was of course referring to the stockholders. Further evidence of the tightening of the fiduciary position of directors is found in the tendency of some courts, particularly in the western states where the law relating to trusts has been codified, to apply to directors the statutory rules governing ordinary trustees.27 

The tendency to hold directors liable for negligent mismanagement has also progressed in, recent years. 

Although, nominally, the standards of conduct enunciated by the courts in recent years are the same as they were a half century ago, it is evident from the decisions that the courts are, in fact, holding the directors accountable for a higher degree of care, diligence and judgment than did the courts which first announced the very rules which are being applied today. It is no longer possible for a director, who has been little more than a figurehead, to escape liability for the consequences of his negligence by pleading, when called to account for his dereliction, that he has acted honestly and in good faith.28 

25 See note, Iowa Law Review, Vol. 20 (1935), p. 808. 

26 15 Del. Ch. 119 (1926), aff'd 15 Del. Ch. 420 (1927). 

27 Fletcher, op. cit., Sec. 840; see e.g., North Confidence Mining & Development Co. v.

Fitch, 58 Cal. App. 329 (1922), in which the court stated: "Directors of a corporation are trustees thereof within the meaning of section 2230 (one of the provisions of the California 

Code applicable to technical trustees).” 

28 University of Pennsylvania Law Review, Vol. 82 (1934), p. 364, 368.

The trend toward enforcement of a more positive fiduciary duty upon directors has received its chief impetus, however, not from court decisions but from legislative enactments of the last few years. In fact, much of the impact of New Deal legislation in the field of corporation law appears to have fallen most heavily on corporate directors. 

This may be partly attributed to a rather substantial reaction against the prevalence of "directors who do not direct."29 This newer attitude has manifested itself primarily in a tendency to require of directors adequate knowledge of the affairs of the corporation which they direct and to hold them liable accordingly. 

The Securities Act of 1933, which is discussed at length in a later chapter, requires a director to establish, if he is to avoid liability for misstatements in a registration statement filed under the Act, that after a reasonable investigation he had adequate grounds to believe and did believe the statements made to be true. The standard of reasonableness applicable in this instance as set forth in the Act is that which would be expected of a prudent man in the management of his own property.30 Similarly, in the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (also discussed later) there is an imposition of liability on directors for misleading statements.31 In this instance, the standard of liability is less exacting than under the Securities Act.since lack of knowledge coupled with good faith is a defense. And, unlike the Securities Act which imposes liability on every director, the Securities Exchange Act holds liable only those directors responsible for the misstatements.

Not only has recent legislation imposed greater liabilities, but it has also subjected directors to new and greater disabilities. They are now required to disclose (a) their security holdings and security transactions;32 (b) their remuneration, including bonus and profitsharing arrangement;33 and (c) full particulars of the nature and extent of their interest in any property acquired, not in the ordinary course of business of the corporation, within two years preceding the 

29 Douglas, "Directors Who Do Not Direct," Harvard Law Review, Vol. 47 (1934), p. 1305. 

30 Section 11 (a), (b), (c) of the Securities Act. 

81 Section 18 (a) of the Securities Exchange Act. 

32 Schedule A (7) of the Securities Act; Section 12 (b) of the Securities Exchange Act. 

38 Schedule A (14) (24) of the Securities Act; Section 12 (b) of the Securities Exchange 

Act.

filing of a registration statement under the Securities Act, or proposed to be acquired at such date.34

Additional restrictions which go well beyond the standards of conduct required by prior statutory or case law are found in Section 

16 of the Securities Exchange Act. The provisions here bear most heavily upon the court decisions which were previously discussed relative to the purchase of shares by officers and directors. It is provided in subsection (b) that directors and officers (and substantial stockholders as well) of corporations, the securities of which are listed on any national exchange, may be held accountable for all profits realized by them in the purchase and sale (or vice versa) of securities of the corporation consummated within a period of less than six months. This limitation on speculative trading by insiders reflects the broader purpose of the provision to prevent "the unfair use of information which may have been obtained" by the officer or director (or substantial stockholder) "by reason of his relationship" to the corporation.

Also, Section 16 (c) contains an absolute prohibition of short selling by directors of any corporation the securities of which are listed for trading on a national securities exchange.

Reaction of Directors to Increased Legal Liability 

As the parties directly affected by the sharpening of responsibility, consideration may be given to the response of the directors themselves. Many have expressed formal commendation of recent trends, but others believe that the added restrictions constitute unwarranted curtailment of private rights and interests. The opponents say, in brief, that to make public trustees out of private directors is unrealistic and impractical. On the first count, they see little incentive or reason why private directors (let alone the legal right) should become public servants; in fact, they believe their most effective public service is to keep their own house in order. As to the second point of impracticability, they believe that the increased legal liability of a position as trustee would cause many outstanding people to refuse to serve as directors. Particularly is this true, it is contended, when directors now receive only nominal fees or minimum compensation. 

Also, it is believed that the part-time service of directors makes it 

34 Schedule A (22) of the Securities Act. 

1

impossible for them to have sufficient familiarity with operations to justify the greater responsibility.35

Legal Means of Preventing Increased Liability 

As evidence of the practical effects of increased directors' responsibility, a number of corporations have already taken legal steps to curtail the personal liability of directors. This is particularly the result of the Securities Act and the Securities Exchange Act which have previously been referred to. In brief, the limitation of liability is accomplished by a formal vote of the stockholders authorizing the company to reimburse the directors or officers for the costs and expenses of law suits arising by virtue of their position.36 The following is an example of such proposed action:37

Section 1. Each person who acts as a director or officer of the Company shall be indemnified by the Company against any costs and expenses which may be imposed upon or reasonably incurred by him in connection with any action, suit or proceeding in which he may be named as a party defendant by reason of his being or having been such director or officer, or by reason of any action alleged to have been taken or omitted by him in either such capacity, exclusive of any costs or expenses imposed upon or incurred by him in relation to matters as to which he shall be finally adjudged to be liable to the Company, and of any sum paid by him to the Company in settlement of an action, suit or proceeding based on his alleged dereliction of duty. 

Section 2. Each person (including a director or officer of the Company) who, at the request of the Company, acts as a director or officer of any other corporation in which the Company has an interest to protect as stockholder or creditor, may be indemnified by the Company, by resolution adopted by the Board of Directors and subject to limitations similar to those contained in Section 1 of this Article, against any costs and expenses which may be imposed upon or reasonably incurred by him in connection with any action, suit or proceeding in which he may be named as a party defendant by reason of his being or having been a director or officer of such other corporation, or by reason of any action alleged to have been taken or omitted by him in either such capacity.

Section 3. The right of indemnification in this Article provided shall inure to each director and officer referred to in Section 1 or Section 2 hereof, whether or not he is such director or officer at the time such costs or expenses are imposed 35 See chapter XVI for a consideration of the merits of a full-time board adequately compensated. 

38 See Business Week (February 15, 1941), p. 26, for the statement that "approximately 

100 large corporations last year obtained stockholder approval of such indemnification.” 

37 Proxy statement of Air Reduction Company, Inc., Annual Meeting of Stockholders, 

April 9, 1941. ....

or incurred, and whether or not the claim asserted against him is based on matters which antedate the adoption of this Article; and in the event of his death shall extend to his legal representatives. Each person who shall act as a director or officer either of the Company, or, pursuant to the provisions of Section 2 of this Article, of any other corporation, shall be deemed to be doing so in reliance upon such right of indemnification; and such right shall not be exclusive of any other right which he may have. 

Section 4. The Board of Directors of the Company, acting at a meeting at which a majority of the quorum is unaffected by self-interest (notwithstanding that other members of the quorum present but not voting may be so affected), shall determine the reasonableness and propriety of the expenses incurred by any person who claims indemnity under this Article, and such determination shall be final and conclusive. If, however, a majority of a quorum of the Board which is unaffected by self-interest and willing to act is not obtainable, the Board in its discretion may (a) appoint from among the stockholders who are not directors or officers of the Company a committee of two or more persons to consider and determine any such question, or (b) cause any such question to be submitted to arbitration in the manner provided by the laws of the State of New York for the arbitration of a controversy; and the determination of such committee, or the decision rendered upon such arbitration, shall be final and conclusive. 

Section 5. None of the provisions of this Article shall be construed as a limitation upon the right of the Company to exercise its general power to enter into a contract or undertaking of indemnity with a director or officer in any proper case not provided for herein.

This statement affording protection to directors against possible loss is presented for two reasons: (1) to indicate that few stockholders would understand it and (2) to show the blanket character of the release from liability which is effected. It shows also how the increased responsibilties of directors may be defeated by other legal means. Because of these possibilities of legal neutralization, it would seem that the only real hope for changing the pattern of limited responsibility on the part of directors can arise solely from vigorous action by the stockholders themselves. There may be despair of such action, but it can be forestalled only so long as there is avoidance of serious abuse of the principles of trusteeship.

Social Responsibility of Directors 

The control of social well-being exercised by business as a whole is to a great extent an inevitable part of its operations. Consumers are affected by the prices they pay, and wage-earners prosper or suffer according to the opportunities for employment. Irrespective of the means of control of business, the institution, the process would exert

large influence over our daily lives. Since such influence is inherent, one may be inclined to follow the sage advice of the old colored deacon who exhorted his followers to "make peace with the inevitable." Numerous questions, however, may be raised in regard to the administration of the control, and especially as it relates to big business. It is from this point of view that the observation may be made that the control of business institutions is highly concentrated. 

Evidence of Concentration of Control 

During the height of the 1927-29 boom, Mr. James W. Gerard, former ambassador to Germany, proclaimed that the real rulers of the United States, the so-called powers behind the throne, consisted of sixty-four outstanding business and financial leaders. More recently, another public personality has said that "a few men controlling a few banks control a majority of the corporate wealth of the Nation, if not a majority of the entire wealth of the Nation."88 In support of this contention, it was estimated that the total national wealth amounted to $320,000,000,000. The corporate wealth of non-financial institutions was reported to be $120,000,000,000 of which more than onehalf was owned by 175 institutions. In turn, it was shown that the control of the latter was in the hands of less than 2,000 active directors and officers. Finally, the connection of many of these directors with banking institutions seemed to indicate the final source of authority and control.

An analysis of 100 large corporations showed many interlocking directorates with the twenty-four largest banks. By industries, the results were as shown in Table 31. 

Quoting from the Congressional Record, the following observations were made:

First. There exists a definite community of interest and interlocking control between banks and industry.

Second. Of a total of 1,543 directorships in the 100 major corporations, there are 403 connections with the 24 banks through interlocking directorates. 

Third. Of a total of 488 directorships in the 24 leading banks, there are 403 connections with the 100 corporations through the interlocking directorates. 

Fourth. Of the 403 interlocking directorships between the 100 corporations and 24 banks, 230 are held by directors of 7 banks and 103 by directors of 2 banks.

Fifth. The 100 major corporate units having interlocking directorates represent concentration of wealth in their respective fields. 

Sixth. Interlocking control is represented by the men holding the 403 interlocking directorates. One hundred men of this group represent the more important interlocking directorates and the potential control of a large part of our wealth.89

Appraisal of Responsibility 

In presenting these data about the directorship, first, the main purpose is to establish the fact. Second, there is the question of responsibility which calls for the greatest objectivity of thinking. To many, such statistics are the equivalent of a red flag and stand self-condemned; all too few ask how such a condition came about and what the statistics mean. Again, there is need to reiterate that some form of absentee control is essential if there is to be large-scale business operation; alternatives exist only as to the means of control. If it can be shown that private interests have abused or taken undue advantage of this concentration of control, then, clearly, there is need for action by public authority. Moreover, aside from fraudulent and other illegal acts, too much blame should not be placed upon private interests for the crash of 1929. They may be held accountable, but not blamed. 

39 Ibid., pp. 5784-85.

Some reformers apply all sorts of mental prestidigitation to the debacle of 1929, but, studied on the basis of calm deliberation, it must be apparent that a broad, generalized answer is impossible. Such questions do invite, and quite properly, the formulation of reasonable and intelligent personal opinion, but one should be chary of reaching a final and absolute answer. World-conditions are changing too rapidly to justify such static thought. Our chief purpose, therefore, in raising the question is to suggest or to bring into focus the public responsibility of private business enterprise. Moreover, the public has a right to expect that business enterprise will contribute to the social good and that it will be conducted with due regard for the rights of all interests.

Unfortunately, the question of corporate responsibility in this larger sense was the product of a depression which gave rise to much. social distress. As a result, there is a personalization of blame which serves as a deterrent to free and open discussion of the underlying issues. It is for this reason that it should be said that the depression was not created wilfully by any interest. Certainly the business community should be held to account for the results, but there should be no impugning of the integrity of business leaders for what happened. 

Of course, there are some individuals who did violate even the accepted business code, but it would be unfair to castigate the whole system because of minority action.

It is generally recognized that responsibility may be effective only if those in control feel the effects of their administration. Hence, where control and responsibility have arisen from direct ownership, it was reasonable to assume that the incidence of the former would be limited by virtue of the effects on the latter. In short, it was felt that the possibilities of personal loss would serve as a means of stimulating the sober exercise of responsibility. However, where control is separated from ownership and is achieved by technical devices, the question immediately arises as to the means by which order and balance in the exercise of responsibility may be assured. This is the problem of today where giant corporations are controlled solely by legal technique and without need for any ownership. Some believe that the only solution if the public interest is to be protected is to be found in rigorous regulation of private industry by the government. Others believe that corporate officials should voluntarily assume a sense of public trusteeship which would regard the corporation as a social insti-

tution and not simply as a facility for making profits for stockholders. 

Admittedly, the responsibilities of such public trusteeship would lack the force of legal sanctions and would require a sense of public service which is not easily associated with private interests. 

Nature of Public Trusteeship of Corporate Management 

In applying this broader concept of trusteeship to corporate management, it must be recognized that much of the thinking at this stage is ideological in character. It is an objective which has social glamour but is not so easily put into practical operation. Being an intangible force, its strength is found more in intent and spirit than in prescribed rules of conduct and in specific tests of measurement. In many respects, the doctrine of trusteeship is intended to apply to the individual directors, but there is also a broader applicability as a force underlying the formulation of board and industry policies. 

While recognizing the intangibility of trusteeship, it must be apparent that its application to practical affairs must be specific. Only by this means can true substance be provided. The sharpening of the sense of trusteeship may come about as a result of enlightened business leadership or it may be compelled by the pressure of public opinion. Already, many business leaders are giving expression to the thought. The following comment reflects the expediency of its adoption irrespective of ethical considerations: "Our company needs a public utility philosophy; if it doesn't get one it will become a public utility."40 

A well-known business leader said as early as 1931: "It makes a great difference in my attitude toward my job . . . . whether I am a trustee of an institution or an attorney for the investor."41 Moreover, there was cold realism underlying this expression of attitude because he wanted his company to be able to attract the best laborers, to secure public preference for the company's products, and to command public confidence so that capital would be available when needed. 

Reflecting a larger cross-section of business opinion, the editors of a well-known business journal "contend that a fundamental change in attitude among businessmen has taken place in the last few years and that. many . . . . believe, accept and advocate social • • • 

40 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11, Bureaucracy and Trusteeship in Large Corporations, p. 109. 

41 Ibid., p. 109, and also see the source of original quotation, Fortune, III (March, 1931), 1 94.

responsibility."42 There is always danger of inaccuracy in reporting composite opinion, but there can be little doubt that the uncertainties and risks of the past decade have had a profound influence upon business thinking. Indeed, there is little escape from the issue of social responsibility because the public is demanding an answer. 

Influence of Public Opinion 

In addition to enlightened business leadership, a second factor which will help to mold and determine the qualitative nature of trusteeship is public opinion. As long as freedom of individual action was held in high public esteem, business was able to function with a minimum of public interference. A shift in public approbation will automatically compel social institutions to revise their code in order to comply with the public will. This force normally accumulates momentum slowly, but it can be surprisingly cataclysmic in action in periods of emergency. Thus, in the decade of the thirties, the severe depression of business activity produced a vigorous response in the way of public reaction. Even in normal periods, the power of community standing and prestige is well recognized as a governor of individual action. In this connection, the following comment made in 

1927 is of interest:

If the community gets this social point of view, if it rather questions mere money-making, if money-making without social standards is frowned upon, and if real social accomplishment is esteemed. . . . we shall get the real leaders in a sufficient number, because it is the approval of the tribe that determines the types of leadership exercised by its leaders.43

Practicability of Trusteeship Motive in Corporate Management 

The specific and practical enforcement of the responsibilities of trusteeship in its larger sense is no simple accomplishment. Enlightened business leadership and the power of public opinion will do much to establish it as an objective of business operation, but there is always the likelihood that actual performance will be something less than the ideological standard. Thus, one writer has observed 

42 Ibid., p. 120, as based upon an article entitled "Business and Government," Fortune, XXI (March, 1940), pp. 38-39. 

48 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11, p. 123, quoting from Wallace B. Donham, "The Professional Side of Business Training," in Business Management as a Profession, edited by 

Henry C. Metcalf (Chicago: A. W. Shaw, 1927), chap. XIII, pp. 228-29.

that “a critical examination of the nature of the legal principle involved-loyalty to stockholders-tends strongly to dispel any high degree of optimism with regard to the future."44 Similarly, it is contended that "the difficulty which we are discussing, of producing a strong emotional response to the law of fiduciary obligations, is not confined to corporate capitalism but is inherent in all large-scale enterprise, whether its form be capitalist, socialist or something else."45 

It will be noted that the observations cited above relate primarily to the incentive of "loyalty to stockholders" as a means of cultivating a more profound sense of trusteeship. There is admission that other larger incentives may be more effective, but it is held that "profitmaking for absentee owners must be the legal standard by which we measure their conduct (the directors) until some other legal standard has been evolved."46 In similar manner, Adam Smith said long ago: "The directors of such companies, however, being the managers rather of other people's money than of their own, it cannot well be expected that they should watch over it with the same anxious vigilance with which the partners in a private copartnery frequently watch over their "47 own.

Extreme pessimists see little opportunity for any widespread acceptance of the trusteeship principle until human nature is changed. This is indeed a familiar argument which is commonly applied against any form of social progress. Obviously, it is not subject to specific or empirical refutation. At the same time, contrary opinions rest on equally sound ground and may often be supported by long-term observation of the course of human affairs. For example, the subsidence of individual aggrandizement is often found in times of dire emergency. 

Recent bombings of large cities reflect the application of this thought to physical distress; analogously, the economic difficulties of the thirties may likewise serve as a stimulus to change in the form of the business system. 

44 E. M. Dodd, Jr., "Is Effective Enforcement of the Fiduciary Duties of Corporate Man agers Practicable?" University of Chicago Law Review, Vol. 2 (1935), p. 200.

Ownership and the Scope of Trusteeship 

It has been previously stated that ownership tends to function as a balancing influence on responsibility. Thus, in the case of small business enterprise, there is little likelihood of abuse of control because the ownership equity usually represents a large percentage of investment and is commonly held by individual or family interests. 

Moreover, the small size means that no one unit can have great influence upon the whole economy. However, in large-scale enterprise, the actions of a single company may have national repercussions, and the public interest is more extensively involved. Hence, irrespective of the concentration or distribution of ownership, there is a tendency to impose on corporate management a broad sense of public trusteeship.

It is here that ownership as the primary factor of control is fast losing the prestige which it had under the principles of a competitive economy. The conditions may be seen to advantage in the ensuing discussion of majority and minority ownership. 

Majority Ownership

In Chapter XV, it was pointed out that small shareholders usually constituted a great majority of the total number, irrespective of the size of the corporation. A more important factor responsible for this condition seemed to be listing on a securities exchange which provided a convenient avenue for public entry. At this point, it may be observed that small holdings by no means represent a majority of either the number of shares outstanding or of the total market value. 

Actually, a smaller number of holders have large blocks and account often for a majority of the outstanding stock. This is shown in the

The picture of such concentration of wealth is exciting to various malcontents, but screening and refining of the information is necessary to justify specific recommendation. Consider, for example, the prominent part of non-profit organizations which are usually held to be so endowed with the spirit of public welfare that they are generally exempt from taxation. Facetiously, it may be observed that colleges would benefit by having their graduates go into the oil business, but seriously speaking, it is apparent that pot-shot observations about concentrated stockholdings are apt to be misleading. Undoubtedly, these public institutions would vote their stock according to the wishes of their benefactor, but judgment of the propriety of such action must be weighed carefully on the scales of ultimate results. It must be kept in mind at all times that accumulations of wealth are absolutely essential as a factor in maintaining a high standard of living. There remain, of course, the vital questions of ownership and control, where the only practical alternatives are government and private. Government ownership inherently means a concentration of control which is presumed to be for the public good; unfortunately, and speaking generally, history does not speak too well for the presumption. One government may rule wisely and with justice, while a succeeding one may quickly bring a country to ruin. Under private ownership, it is conceivable that both the ownership and the control could be distributed, but it 50 As reported by the Hon. John M. Coffee from the records of the T.N.E.C., see Congressional Record, Appendix, April 2, 1941, pp. A1684-85,

is unlikely. Probably from the point of view of public welfare, the essential point is to keep out recognized abuses from both systems. 

In short, under either government or private auspices, there is need to cultivate a sense of trusteeship.

The point may be raised as to the applicability of the trusteeship principle where majority ownership exists. Here, control arises out of ownership and, aside from the usual obligations between majority and minority interests and other third parties, inquiry may be made as to why any form of trusteeship should exist beyond these relationships. 

In answer, and the authors are trying only to report objectively current thoughts and trends, it may be said that the test of trusteeship is becoming increasingly applicable by virtue of the pressure of public opinion. At this stage, the concept is more ethical than legal in character and enforcement of specific requirements by the law is quite limited. Moreover, no one can say how far the principle will be carried. The return of full prosperity would likely retard its development; depression and the continuance of unemployment would accelerate the trend.

Returning to the practical question of the specific corporation, it is obvious that the ownership of a majority of the stock will provide positive assurance of control. However, in the case of the larger corporations, it is seldom possible for a single individual to acquire such a large amount, both because of the enormous investment required and because of the interest of other individuals in the enterprise. Usually, several key individuals will participate and they are enabled to satisfy their desire for authority by having charge of an important segment of operations. Occasionally, conflicts occur within the inner circle, such as was true of the Ford Motor Corporation. In this instance, the Ford family succeeded in buying out the other interests and obtaining complete ownership of the company. At other times, there may be a fight for proxies to obtain control at the annual meeting. 

Minority Ownership

As used in this connection, the term minority ownership will include all forms of ownership which is less than a majority. Necessarily, there will be a wide range from considerable minority holdings where control is exercised by virtue of the predominance of financial position to widely scattered ownership where the control is mainly

the result of technique. The exact methods of control were described in a previous chapter,51 and at this time our chief interest is in the larger social aspects and the applicability of the trusteeship principle. 

By way of setting, it may be repeated that in a number of large corporations, no single interest will own as much as 1 per cent of the stock outstanding.52 Under the circumstances, it is impossible to establish control by means of ownership, and special devices are clearly necessary to centralize the authority. It may be granted that the average small stockholder fails to realize the significance of the power of attorney which he extends to a small committee and that he is little interested in the control of the corporation. With much the same attitude in making a savings deposit in his bank, he is motivated primarily by his wishes to make an investment. He probably would not understand the term "entrepreneur," and his relationship with the corporation is largely impersonal. 

The large gap which has developed between ownership and control brings into sharp focus the responsibility of corporate management. Created by means other than ownership, there is an inescapable delegation of power which creates many obligations in favor of those who are represented. One authority has said "that corporate managers have automatically, although not necessarily inescapably, assumed a fiduciary responsibility toward owners, their nominal masters" and that "the present diffusion of stock and weakness of effective stockholder control create a situation closely resembling that of the ordinary trustee and beneficiary.' "53 

Distinction between Legal and Social Trusteeship 

By way of convenient summary, and in order to assure clarity of understanding, it may be said that expression is now being given to trusteeship in two senses. The first is the legal connotation which holds that the fiduciary character of a director's position is limited to relationships between the directors and the corporation and the body of stockholders. As pointed out at greater length in this chapter, the liability arising because of this status is usually subject to minimum rather than maximum accountability. It should be stressed that this is the type of trusteeship which is applicable in business practice because it alone is subject to legal enforcement. 

51 See chapter XV. 

52 Berle and Means, op. cit., chap. V, "The Evolution of Control." 

33 See T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11, p. 107.

The second connotation of trusteeship is of a social nature which at this time lacks legal sanction on any broad scale. Indeed, it attaches a form of public responsibility to a directorship which may always lack the preciseness to permit legal exaction of penalities for its violation. There is also the danger that its enforcement may be the cause of substituting arbitrary review by an external body for the long-recognized right of a board of directors to make business decisions. Moreover, it may call for a sense of altruism which is unreasonable to expect in the conduct of practical business affairs. Its force, therefore, will likely always be found in the allurement of ideology, but gradually the march of progress will transfer portions to the area of practice. And, as this is done, legal recognition will be forthcoming.

PART IV SECURITY DISTRIBUTION

Ad

CHAPTER XVIII  

NE of the vital links in corporate activity is the provision of funds in sufficient amount and with appropriate timeliness. 

While the established corporation is able to add to its initial capital through profitable operation, the great bulk of its funds must of necessity be obtained from the money market or outside sources. 

The various financial instruments which are available for this purpose, such as common stock, preferred stock, and the numerous varieties of bonds, have been described. But these are simply the tools or the means to the end. More perplexing are such questions as: From whom will the capital be raised? How does the money market affect the availability of funds? By whom will the capital be raised?

In seeking to answer questions of the type, there is need to recognize that their roots reach out into the whole economic system and the state of national development. Thus, the United States was primarily a debtor nation until World War I. During this period, the savings within were supplemented materially by investments made in this country by foreigners. Today, the United States occupies the role of a creditor nation which changes completely the complexion of the problem. Under the circumstances, one would anticipate the existence of a surplus of capital; indeed, many of the familiar indices give evidence of this condition. Unfortunately, this has been caused until recently by the failure of business to absorb the capital which is available. Bank deposits of $65,000,000,000 exceed those of the boom year of 1929 by 20 per cent. The reported stock of money in circulation is currently about $9,300,000,000, which is more than $2,000,- 000,000 greater than at the previous peak of prosperity. Money rates have reached an all-time low. Table 34 on page 338 shows the recent trends in money rates:

With such indices of the apparent availability of capital, it would be reasonable to expect a high level of prosperity during most of this period, but pronounced recovery did not get under way until late 1940 when the nation embarked upon a gigantic defense program. 1 337

Many place the responsibility for the conditions prevailing in the 1930's upon a dearth of capital-not in the sense of total available supply, but rather because of its distribution. It is contended that capital was not flowing to the points of need. Unfortunately, economic problems may not be reduced to laboratory tests, but it is fitting that some thought be given to the general question of the availability of capital. Certainly, it constitutes one of the outstanding problems of corporation finance.

At the outset it is necessary to distinguish clearly between what is called "venture" capital and what may be termed "confidence" or "investment" capital. The commitment of the former is made with full knowledge that all the risks of residual ownership are being assumed. The risk is taken knowingly by enterprising individuals or institutions because of their expectation that income returns in excess of normal as well as capital appreciation will be their reward. 

In contrast, the investment of confidence capital is made with primary emphasis upon the safety of the principal and a contentment with a minimum, reasonably assured, rate of return. It is impossible to segregate the total capital supply according to these two basic types, but it must be apparent that their respective quantity and availability will exercise considerable influence upon the employment of capital.¹ 

Moreover, there will be considerable shifting between the two types

However, from the standpoint of the amount sold within a year following registration, the former succeeded in disposing of only 15.2 per cent of the registered amount and the latter, 39.9 per cent. in keeping with the changing economic outlook and the resulting revision of the appraisal of risk.

Attending political and social movements and trends of a major character also serve as a stimulant or depressant of the flow of capital. 

Troubled international relations and uncertainties, or serious disagreements as to the kind of economic system desired, cannot help but dampen the enthusiasm and vigor which are essential to prosperous business conditions. Reacting to these influences, capital goes into hiding or is made available only on terms which are suitable to meet the anticipated risks of enterprise. Thus, the investing public may be reluctant to make long-time commitments, or it may demand a form of security which is apt to curb the desired flexibility of management. These elements of caution are undoubtedly at work today. 

Investment in government obligations are favored over those of private industry because it is believed that government credit is the last line of security. Similarly, investments that can be promptly withdrawn are chosen in preference to those which do not offer ready availability. 

Because of these intangible but all important drawbacks, industry is confronted with the very definite problem of uncovering reliable sources of capital to meet its special needs. 

Not only does the question take form in the distinction between venture and confidence capital, but it is also pertinent as between small and big business. For the most part, small enterprise raises its necessary funds from an unorganized market. Even as a matter of normal policy, there is apt to be much more temporizing in its program of raising capital. Loans with insufficient maturities may be obtained from commercial banks mainly because of their immediate availability. Again, the reluctance of local management to share either control or profits with investors may encourage the acceptance of investments with terms which are out of harmony with the flow of business operations. In either event, credit which is intended to facilitate and aid business may become an impediment, and creditors may be forced to assume control of management. Neither is it unusual to find big business facing similar predicaments. It is not uncommon to observe banking and insurance institutions operating numerous business enterprises with a variety running all the way from farms to factories. Thus, it is not appropriate to say simply that there is an insufficiency of capital. More significant are the queries, "What kind of capital?" "At what terms?"

Unlike small business enterprise, large business institutions are more apt to follow well-established trails in their quest for capital. 

They have access to a well-organized money market and, for the most part, utilize the services of the specialists functioning in this market.2 Moreover, their size and scope of operations make them nationally known, and this adds to their investment appeal. The existence of this familiarity does much to break down the typical resistance of the investor to the unknown. Under normal conditions, therefore, large corporations find it comparatively easy to raise large pools of capital. The American Telephone and Telegraph Company with its nearly 650,000 stockholders is a case in point. However, it is significant to note that even this more select group was confined or limited in the scope of their financing from 1929 to 1939. This indicates the broad sweep of the difficulties which account for depressed business in the last decade. It is undoubtedly a period of social change, in which established patterns and procedures are undergoing new stresses and strains.

With this background more specific attention may be given to the component elements of the market to which business enterprise must turn for its capital supply. The discussion will be confined to an analysis of the external sources, reserving for later treatment the opportunities and problems which are found in obtaining capital through the retention of income. In brief, there are three main classes or types of external sources: private institutional investors, individual investors, and the government. These may be classified as follows: 

Private institutional investors-commercial banks, savings banks, life insurance companies, investment trusts, investment banks, and miscellaneous. 

Individual investors-those operating on their own account mainly on a longterm basis, those operating on their own account primarily on a speculative basis, and those operating as trustees in behalf of others. 

Public institutional investors-various governmental agencies engaged directly or indirectly in the financing of private enterprise. 

The potentialities of each of these as a source of long-term capital supply may be discussed in some detail. 

Commercial Banks

While there is little, express statutory limitation upon long-term lending, strictly commercial banks are presumed to engage in short- 

2 See chapter XX for a discussion of this mechanism.

term credit. Obtaining their own funds on a demand deposit basis, it is only logical that their investments be made so as to conform to the pattern of their liabilities. Actually there are few banks operating under the label of "commercial" which confine their operations to demand deposits on the one side or to short-term loans on the other side. Practically all have entered the savings field, and today they constitute one of the most important agencies in this area. Their increasing participation is shown in the accompanying table, Table 35, portraying the amount of savings deposits held by all member banks of the Federal Reserve System.

Statistics are lacking to measure accurately the part played by commercial banks as a source of long-term funds. It is known that many have made demand loans which have for all practical purposes served as a means of providing relatively permanent capital because of a tacit agreement not to exercise the demand privilege. At the same time, with the exception of a few states, there has been no segregation of a bank's assets as between those representing savings accounts and those offsetting demand deposits. Logically, the former should be utilized to accommodate the longer-term needs of industry while the latter are better adapted to provide for the short-term or commercial loans. This means that the commercial banks generally have not properly distinguished between the savings and investment functions. Savings are simply assembled as a source of new business for the banks as well as an accommodation to the community without giving due regard to the proper functional use of the funds so assembled. 

If one were to assume a clear distinction between the commercial and investment banking functions, the question might then be raised 

* See, Harold G. Moulton, The Formation of Capital (Washington, D. C.: Brookings 

Institution, 1935), pp. 93-99, for discussion of permanent financing through bank operations.

1

as to whether or not commercial banks could constitute a legitimate and efficient source of long-term capital. To make such a condition effective, numerous changes in banking practice would have to be made. Savers or investors would have to be informed of the lessened liquidity which would inevitably arise because of the use of their funds for investment in the fixed capital area. Offsetting this, it would be reasonable to anticipate that they should receive a higher rate of return than is now prevalent. At the present time, commercial banks are restricted by law to a rate on savings deposits not in excess of 21 per cent (those insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation). In many sections of the country, rates of 1 per cent and 13 per cent are common. In 1939, the state of New Jersey issued an order prohibiting either savings or commercial banks from paying a rate on savings deposits in excess of 1 per cent. 

While it is not within the province of this discussion to determine whether the withdrawal of funds from banks could be accelerated through some plan of shiftability, obviously much relief could be afforded through the creation of proper reserve banking facilities. 

Listed securities are given considerable liquidity of a secondary type by virtue of their marketability. It seems reasonable to believe that equivalent availability might be provided the small savers who place their funds in banks. Certainly this is necessary if further investments on their part are to be forthcoming. 

Viewing the question from the point of view of meeting the needs of business enterprise, the so-called commercial banks should be unusually well qualified to appraise capital needs. Not only do such banks constitute the major agency specializing in finance in many communities, but through their servicing of the current needs of industry, they should be especially familiar with the complete needs for capital. 

Obviously, if the function of furnishing industry with investment as well as commercial capital were assumed, it would require complete separation of banking officials from industry control. This would be essential if primary consideration were to be given to the fulfilment of function and to avoid a natural bias where personalities are involved. 

Once more, however, it needs to be reiterated that the assumption of this broader financial service by the commercial banking institutions means the abdication of numerous traditions and attitudes which have accompanied strictly commercial banking practice. The investment account would have to be separated from the commercial account

and the depositing clientele fully informed of their rights and obligations.

Many will dissent as to the wisdom of converting commercial banks into institutions which render complete financial service. To a great degree, this is a matter of the ability of communities to carry or support more specialized agencies. The larger, urban centers can be expected to have a volume sufficient to support specialized facilities, but this is out of the question in rural areas and the smaller cities. 

In the latter, there seems to be little choice as to the course of action if proper recognition is to be given to the more permanent needs for capital of industries in such localities. This is especially true of smaller business which in many respects operates on a catch-as-catchcan basis at the present time. 

Attention must also be called to the difference between the need for borrowed funds and the need for equity capital. Commercial banks clearly lack the qualities which are necessary to provide the latter. They raise funds on a promise-to-pay basis, either on a variable or fixed schedule; this creates an element of fixity unsuited to the risks adhering to the residual equity position. Here, undoubtedly, individuals will continue to furnish the bulk of the capital as they have in the past. Perhaps the machinery for the distribution of securities of this type may be improved, particularly for purposes of facilitating the inter-community flow and for the accommodation of small business. However, many irregularities should continue to appear as a result of the cyclical character of business activity as well as spasmodic developments of the new industry type. Because of the expected recurrence of depression it is likely that the government will attempt to provide measures which are specifically framed to cope with such adversity. The growth of such governmental agencies will be described later in this chapter. 

Savings Banks

Giving full credence to the meaning of the term "savings bank," one would expect to find an institution which is ideally organized for the purpose of providing investment credit. However, traditional savings-bank practice to date has restricted their lending operations to a more limited area. In the first place, funds from the investing public have been accepted on a deposit basis, and their investment is of necessity made in a manner which would permit reasonable ability

to pay on demand. Under abnormal conditions, thirty or even ninety days' notice may be required preliminary to actual withdrawal. Furthermore, banks of this type are more conscious of their savings function than of the accompanying investment responsibilities. In other words, the investment is regarded as an incidence of savings instead of placing the two on a parity. Funds are therefore invested mainly in marketable securities or in the financing of homes. With the exception of the latter, there is a minimum of direct investment in industry itself.

It should be emphasized that the foregoing observations are not made in any critical way but simply as a means of reviewing the possible sources of capital for industry. The keepers or trustees of the savings of the public quite naturally realize the trust and responsibility imposed in them and, for this reason, are in a sense compelled as a matter of prudent policy to invest in the known and established securities. In pursuit of this goal, it is logical to invest indirectly in seasoned issues which have demonstrated reliability in preference to direct investment in new issues which lack a record of performance over a period of years. Possibly the responsible boards of control are in a paradox: if they give emphasis to the investment function and make direct commitments in new issues, they may be accused of taking unwarranted risk with the funds placed in their care; but, if they pursue the traditional and more conservative course, they may be charged with failure to provide industry with the necessary capital. 

It should be noted that existing savings banks have certain other limitations which would prevent their serving industry on a national basis. As of June 30, 1938, there were only 562 such institutions of the mutual type (stock savings banks are of comparatively minor importance) with total assets of approximately $11,500,000,000. Moreover, they are found in only eighteen states, with 70 per cent of their assets being concentrated in the two states of New York and Massachusetts. In addition, there are the further restrictions which were noted in connection with savings deposits of commercial banks, viz., the question as to whether deposit funds should be utilized for furnishing equity capital.

Life insurance companies are one of the major sources of investment funds of the present day. This is readily apparent from data in

In many respects life insurance companies are the most peculiarly fitted of all to provide for the long-time capital needs of industry. 

While provisions are included which permit the policyholders to realize a cash surrender value in the event of premature cancellation, it is the normal expectancy that the bulk of the funds are placed with life insurance companies for extended periods of time. On this assurance, these institutions are in an ideal position to extend credit which synchronizes with their own liabilities. An analysis of their investment portfolio shows that they have gone a long way in meeting this objective. However, they are not intended to provide equity capital, and the laws of most states prohibit this type of investment. 

Life insurance companies also feel that the hazards of venture capital are unsuited to the requirements of trustee investment. A. New business ventures; yes.

A. It would not be, in our judgment, suitable for the funds of life insurance; in other words, it is not a trustees' investment.

A. I think when we look back over the past 10 years I have to say no.
