A. Yes, we have. 

Q. Can you tell us what you have done in that regard and what success you have had? A. I spoke of our having stationed in Chicago nearly a year and a half ago a man whose function it was to find, if possible, small industrial loans. We didn't want to go much below one hundred thousand, possibly fifty, and considered small industrial loans to be limited by the figure of a million dollars. Our hope was that we might make the loan as a mortgage loan, secured by a first mortgage, and write the necessary covenants on the paper. The expense of a small issue providing for a corporate trustee could not be borne. It would not be economical. The rate would be too high for the borrower. In a word we have had practically no success. 

Q. How many such loans have you made, sir? 

A. We have made exactly two.

Giving further consideration to the investment policy of insurance companies, it should be observed that like the commercial banks and savings banks, indirect investment is favored in the case of loans to industry. Direct commitments are made in favor of individual home owners, farmers, policyholders, and certain select institutions, but for the most part investment in the various branches of industry are in seasoned securities. The advantage of this practice to the insurance company is clear; numerous tests of measurement are present in the case of securities of record which are not available in new and untried issues. On the other hand, it does not close the gap which is found in obtaining funds for smaller companies, new industry, or the more

fluctuating branches of older industry. Similarly, the question reappears as to whether responsible management of life insurance companies is warranted in assuming risks of this character in the face of liabilities involving supreme trust. Certainly there is every reason. to lean in the direction of conservative investment in preference to a policy where considerably more chance is taken. 

Further analysis of the investment portfolio of insurance companies shows decidedly the influence of the extended depression and other uncertainties which have assailed our times since 1929. Today, the legal reserve companies have cash and United States government bonds of approximately $5,301,000,000, or 20.9 per cent of their total assets; ten years previously these figures were $504,861,000 and 3.5 per cent respectively. Such a pronounced shift is evidence of the curtailment of the normal flow of capital into industry. It needs to be stated that the restriction is obviously not the result of malicious intent, but simply the response of prudent management to safeguard their investments.

During the past few years, insurance companies have also instituted the practice on a modest scale of making direct commitments to industry. One of the largest transactions of the type is the recent placement of $114,500,000 of Commonwealth Edison Company 3 per cent bonds with fifteen life insurance companies. One estimate has been made that $2,000,000,000 has been so placed with insurance companies or other financial institutions since 1933. The same authority believes that, in 1938 alone, private offerings amounted to $600,000,- 000 as compared with public offerings of $1,400,000,000 for the same period.?

It is to be noted that private sales to date are for the most part those of companies which had access to the open market and whose securities stand high in public favor. In addition to the case previously cited, such well-known companies as the following have engaged in the practice: Standard Oil of New Jersey, Goodyear Tire and Rubber,

United States Rubber, Union Carbide and Carbon, Consolidated Oil, etc. The shift from the usual banking channels of distribution to direct placement at this time is more likely the result of expediency than a reflection of deliberate, long-term policy. First of all, it is undoubtedly prompted by prevailing conditions in the money market. 

6 New York Times (May 14, 1939), p. F1. 

7 Wall Street Journal (January 27, 1939), p. 1.

High-grade securities command such high premiums as to encour-. age institutional investors to depart from customary practice. Second," the selling corporation is relieved from certain expenses and potential liabilities to directors and officers which are the result of registration requirements set up by the Securities Act. Under the circumstances, it is difficult to state with any great assurance whether the practice will be continued in substantial volume. 

Investment Trusts

There are many varieties of investment trust organizations, but in general all have the common purpose of pooling the funds of individual investors and diversifying the resulting investment. Usually, stocks are the selected medium for investment instead of bonds, the reasons for which are not pertinent to this discussion. Because of this plan of operation, one might surmise that such institutions would constitute an ideal source of venture capital. Unfortunately there are certain features of their operation which militate against the realization of the goal. Because stocks are selected to obtain capital appreciation rather than the normal, recurring income return, any capital obtained from investment trusts is distinctly of the shifting variety. 

It is true that the diversity of opinion among such groups may well cause some other organization to replace the one which is selling out, but at the same time, the practice gives rise to a form of capital turnover which lends an element of instability. 

Investment trusts also limit their activity for the most part to listed securities. This does not mean that as a consequence they do not represent an important source of capital, but it does exclude them as a source of new capital. Their comparatively recent origin in this country makes it difficult to state with too much finality to what extent they will become an integral part of the capital-raising process. 

It should be noted that as of December 31, 1935, it was estimated that 1,500,000 individuals held their securities. Their total assets were reported to be $3,700,000,000 at the close of 1935, as compared with over $7,000,000,000 at the peak in 1929.8 

Investment Banks

Investment banks present the most formally organized machinery for the raising of capital funds. It is indeed their primary function, 8 Securities and Exchange Commission, Report on Investment Trusts and Investment Companies, 1938-1940, pp. 4, 5.

whereas as has been noted, it is mainly an incidental operation in the case of the other financial agencies described. In a sense, they are not a source of capital but serve mainly as a middleman between investment outlets and industry. Because of their importance and the leading role they have played in security distribution, a separate chapter is devoted solely to an analysis of their operations. 

Miscellaneous Institutions 

Such other institutions as fire insurance companies, universities, and eleemosynary groups also make a sizable contribution to the capital supply. Again their point of view is largely that of the investor which means that there is little deliberate attempt to furnish capital as such. Many of the comments made in connection with other institutions are equally pertinent here. 

Individual Investors Operating on Their Own Account 

Undoubtedly, one of the important sources of capital is to be found in the savings of individuals. The funds of insurance companies and savings banks represent the organized and institutionalized savings of individuals, but in addition there are the independently managed funds of individuals. These savings are privately invested, often in small amounts, in stocks, bonds, and notes, both listed and unlisted. 

It is difficult to measure the exact extent of the individual holdings, and particularly so in the case of small business. However, there can be little question relating to their importance as a source of capital. 

Unorganized, scattered geographically, and functioning without benefit of organized facilities, corporations would do well to foster the good-will of this group. The importance of their contribution is already well recognized by several leading corporations which have made it a point to develop vital links of contact. Some indication of the means utilized was shown in an earlier chapter. More and more, established corporations will take advantage of the ties which exist between their existing security holders and themselves to raise new funds.

Individuals Operating on a Speculative Basis 

Competition has been commonly referred to as the spice of trade, but it is probably hard pressed by the force of speculation for this titular honor. By speculation, it is not intended to refer to the various

manipulative practices which are commonly associated with it. Instead, the willingness of venturesome individuals to take reasonable chance for the purpose of realizing income above the normal return or to gain by capital appreciation is meant. And especially is reference made to those who are willing to risk their own funds instead of being bold with the funds of others. This group of individuals operate many businesses on their own account, but it is likely that those operating in the stock market take the headlines. 

Speculators are, of course, noted for the shiftable character of their activities-in and out of the market as decision and opportunities dictate the course of their action. Those who are inclined to reach for the Utopian goal of stabilized business may criticize this group as a retarding element. On the other hand, their contribution to the opening of new fields of endeavor and the expansion of existing business must be recognized as a means of adding to the public welfare. 

It is difficult to measure the extent of their participation, not only because of the absence of supporting statistics, but also because their significance is largely qualitative rather than quantitative. Some notion of the participation of these rovers of industry may be obtained from a consideration of the stockholders of the United States Steel Corporation, distinguishing between those which own the stock outright and the so-called "floating supply" (stock held in brokers' names). As of December 31, 1938, there were 8,703,252 shares of common stock outstanding. Out of this total 2,166,473 shares, or 

24.89 per cent, were in the hands of brokers.⁹

Individuals Operating in Behalf of Others 

In this category, reference is made mainly to that vast body of trustees appointed either under court auspices or voluntarily by individuals to administer estates placed in their care. There is no record of the volume to be found in this classification, but this does not belie their importance as a source of capital. It may be expected, however, that the great bulk of their investment will be in the less speculative area.

Government as a Source of Capital 

Turning from private sources of funds consideration may be given to a third agency for the provision of capital, namely, the government. Prior to the onslaught of the prolonged depression of the 

9 Wall Street Journal (January 23, 1939), P. 5.

thirties there was little occasion to give serious consideration to the government or its agencies as a source of capital. It was presumed that funds could readily be attracted in response to the opportunities of industry. Emphasis was therefore placed upon the risk innate in a given industry and the rate of return determined accordingly. Where the risk was high, prospects of compensating income were essential to attract capital; oppositely, established industry with less risk was able to raise funds at lower rates of dividends or interest. In this earlier period of national expansion and optimistic outlook, the major emphasis was placed upon industry as distinguished from business risk. The basic or secular trend of business was presumed to be favorable, and the chief determinant of capital diversion appeared in the segregation of the risks of individual industries. 

Today, increasing attention is given to general business conditions in their entirety, which, unfortunately for the past decade, have prevailed like a large storm area overhanging the various industrial sectors. Established organizations are affected in common with new and untried enterprise. Moreover, there are so many interferences exerting pressure upon the income differential as a means of directing the capital flow as to render it largely impotent. The psychological edge of income attraction is blunted by the popular thought that taxes leave little cushion to serve as an incentive for the voluntary assumption of risk. The staggering losses of recent years add an even more realistic touch. As a consequence, evidence of the stunted growth of private investment is to be found on every hand. Savings have reached unprecedented figures, but their utilization appears to be stymied by numerous obstacles to their expected and normal investment. 

The foregoing conditions were believed at first to constitute an emergency, but their prolongation led to the thought that they could not be corrected by the historical and simple formula of rebounding business. In any event, it was commonly believed that government intervention was essential to free the capital log-jam. Aside from various forms of relief which were extended to consumers partly in the hope that the force of their purchasing power would serve as a stimulant to business, facilities were also provided to furnish capital more directly. The following three sources or types of assistance are particularly deserving of attention: (1) the Reconstruction Finance

Corporation, (2) capital loans made directly to business by the Federal Reserve System, (3) the insurance of loans to business.

The Reconstruction Finance Corporation 

The Reconstruction Finance Corporation was created by an Act of Congress on January 22, 1932. Its purpose was "to provide emer gency financing facilities for financial institutions, to aid in financing agriculture, commerce and industry, and for other purposes." Capital stock in the amount of $500,000,000 was provided with authority to raise additional funds by the sale of notes, debentures, and other obligations up to three times the amount of capital subscribed.¹0 At the time of its creation, the Corporation was authorized to extend credit to borrowers for not to exceed three years with power to make extensions to five years. Numerous adjustments have given greater flexibility to these loan accommodation provisions.

It is not the purpose to analyze here the powers or the nature of the operations of this well-known governmental lending institution; the present interest is found rather in the R.F.C.'s activities in providing business with capital funds. Initially, it was intended primarily to extend help to sound but financially embarrassed companies. Illustrative of this is the extension of credit to banks and other financial institutions during the crisis of 1932 and 1933. Similarly, loans were made to railroads which were confronted with financial difficulties. 

Gradually the question of the availability of capital came to be recognized as an important criterion of loan approval. Whereas in the beginning the Corporation responded to meet a widespread need created by a general shortage of capital, today greater attention is given to the merits of the individual applicant. Thus there may exist an abundance of funds in the general market, but the question is whether or not they are available to individual industries or companies. This is of significance to small business enterprise since the traditional machinery of capital-raising is geared to accommodate the needs of big business. Specifically, for the seven years ending February 2, 1939, 37 per cent of the Corporation's loans to business enterprises were for $5,000 or less (49 per cent for the last year), 53 per cent for $10,000 or less, and 83 per cent for $50,000 or less.11

To railroads (including receivers and trustees).. $1,138,217,337 983,701,788 160,595,495 826,773,161 In discussing the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, it is common to give emphasis to the fact that it is a governmental agency. 

The question may be raised as to whether or not private business enterprise should be financed through the medium of governmental instrumentalities. This is for the most part a matter of public policy which can be answered only by public opinion. At the same time, the mechanism by which capital is raised is deserving of analysis as a matter of financial advantage, i.e., irrespective of whether the organism be operated by government or private enterprise. The mere fact that it constitutes a distinct break from established precedent and traditional practice should not prevent an analysis of its merits as a general plan of raising capital.

The private financial structure has long provided an adequate mechanism for the short-term needs of business. Formally organized institutions (especially the commercial banks) have assembled funds from various sources, in turn making loans to business. Here the lending institution operates in the role of principal and not as agent of those who provided the funds. For the most part, there are no similar accommodations for long-term lending. Instead, the agency principle has been employed whereby the intermediary organization simply attempts to bring the investor and the borrower together. In view of the circumstances, borrowers are compelled to resort to diverse and scattered sources. Under the system used by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, prospective borrowers have a focal point which is readily accessible. The question is most pertinent as to whether or not a similar system could be worked out under private auspices. 

12 Ibid., p. 22.

Another advantage of long-term lending institutions acting in the capacity of principal is to be found in the resulting diversification of risk. Not only does this provide a form of carrying power for the lending institution itself, but in addition it serves to dilute the risks of investors. This is, of course, the chief advantage of the investment trust to which reference has been made previously. However, in this particular instance, it operates in connection with the direct extension of loans to industry, whereas it will be recalled that investment trusts for the most part confine their operations to seasoned securities which have ready marketability.

A third favorable quality of a long-term lending institution, be it public or private, may be found in the possibilities of a lower cost of money to the borrower. Bulk distribution of the securities of the investment bank would obviously facilitate sale more than the smaller scale and divided marketing of the securities of the individual companies. Not only would this be warranted on a cost basis, but in addition, the reduction in the aggregate risk made possible by a specialized investment institution would likely have more market appeal than the more concentrated risk to be found in buying the securities of the individual borrowers.

It should be remembered that any proposed private investment institution of this type, as well as the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, would for the most part be compelled to furnish capital on a loan basis. It is questionable as to whether such a device could be used to raise equity capital. To attempt the latter would involve perplexing questions of management and control as well as the propriety of the risk assumption which would follow. In some respects, holding companies have operated in a manner which gives this result, but the experience to date has not been too satisfactory. Then again, if consideration is given to the basic desirability that private enterprise should be encouraged to carry the onus of economic activity, it would be reasonable to expect that the underlying and permanent equity funds should be raised by individuals who are willing to assume the risk. Where this is no longer possible, it is likely that a fundamentally different mode of economy will be found. 

Lending Operations of the Federal Reserve Banks

Reflecting further the efforts of the federal government to aid recovery, the Federal Reserve Act was amended in 1934 so as to permit the Federal Reserve banks to aid in furnishing working capital. Sec-

· • tion 13 (b) (a) provides in part that "In exceptional circumstances when it appears . . . . that an established industrial or commercial business is unable to obtain requisite financial assistance on a reasonable basis from the usual sources, the Federal Reserve bank may make loans to ... such business ... for the purpose of providing it with working capital, but no obligation shall be made hereunder with a maturity exceeding five years." Section 

13 (b) (b) gives the Federal Reserve banks authority to discount or purchase similar obligations which may arise from loans of the type made by various financial institutions. • ... There is little need to discuss the comparative merits of such industry accommodation as provided by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation with that of the Federal Reserve System. That is a separate problem which concerns itself more specifically with the question of government organization. But the purpose of the two seems to be common-an attempt to raise funds for industry when they may not be readily obtained in the open market. Also, as would be expected, the Federal Reserve operations are restricted to provide working capital.

The operations of both the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and the Federal Reserve System have indicated that the basic criterion underlying credit extension is that of risk. The question of availability is not sufficient. Instead, there is a recognition of the fact that credit, whether it be generated from public or private sources, must be substantiated by the paying power of the risk at stake. Under the circumstances, it is not surprising to find that the Federal Reserve banks have found it necessary to reject many applications. This is shown in Table 37 on page 356.

An analysis of Table 37 will show that slightly less than 30 per cent of the applications for loans were approved, and in terms of amount just under 50 per cent. This means that where government lending agencies make loans on a sound basis, it is necessary to reject many applications in common with private enterprise. The existence of need or the popular cry of capital shortage does not necessarily mean that the gap has failed to close because of some flaw in the machinery of capital distribution. Instead, it shows, that, short of subsidy, the credit is not granted because applicants fail to meet the standards which are deemed necessary. Included in the latter is, of course, the type of capital needed. Undoubtedly, the Federal Reserve

Further analysis of the table shows that the average loan requested amounted to $43,000. This is further evidence that the problem of capital shortage is most acute in the small industry group. It is here that the problem of raising equity funds is of paramount importance. 

Clearly the correction of this deficiency is beyond the intended scope of the commercial banking structure. Even with the additional authority given to the Federal Reserve banks and commercial banks to make term loans, it is significant to note that repayments reveal a rapid rate of liquidation. Little relief is provided in the form of long-term or equity capital.

Government Insurance of Loans to Business 

A more novel device for stimulating the flow of private capital is found in several proposals which provide for some form of government insurance of business loans. The most widely publicized plan is incorporated in a bill introduced in the Senate on May 8, 1939, by 

Senator Mead of New York. Specifically, it is entitled a "Bill to provide for insurance of loans to business, and for other purposes." 

Formal hearings were held by the Senate Banking and Currency Committee, but the bill was not reported on favorably. Nevertheless, in spite of this unfavorable action, there can be no question but that considerable sentiment prevails in favor of some program of government promotion of loans to business enterprise. 

Undoubtedly the Mead Bill was encouraged by the experience of government insurance of private loans by financial institutions to home owners under the direction of the Federal Housing Adminis-

tration. However, the latter program was intended not only as a means of stimulating business recovery, but in addition it was regarded as a means of promoting public welfare. Extensive home ownership has always been held to be a cornerstone of national solidarity and strength. Hence the appeal of any activity to stimulate home ownership and to improve housing conditions is believed to be within the prerogative of government in a democracy. Insurance of business loans seems to lack this social setting, although many are of the opinion that the encouragement of industry and the resulting increase of employment is equally a form of contributing to social welfare. But viewed more practically, there appears to be less justification in the light of the generally accepted philosophy of private operation of business enterprise. Moreover, the experience of the insured loans under the Federal Housing Administration has been too limited to permit conclusive judgment as to their long-term soundness and desirability.

Keeping in mind the innovating character of government insurance of business loans as well as the division of opinion which exists as to its soundness, attention may be directed to the more important provisions of the Mead Bill. They are: 

Insuring agency-the bill provides that the Reconstruction Finance Corporation will act as the insurer, thereby taking advantage of the Corporation's experience in making direct loans.

Insurance coverage-protection is extended only to losses in excess of 10 per cent of the loans made.

Insurance premium-not less than of 1 per cent per annum on the unpaid balance.

Terms of loan to be insured-eligibility .restricted to loans maturing in not less than one year nor more than ten years. 

Miscellaneous-loans are not eligible (a) where the borrower's insured indebtedness exceeds $1,000,000, (b) if the rate of interest on the loan is in excess of 4 per cent unless otherwise permitted by the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, (c) if servicing fees or commissions exceed of 1 per cent of the loan principal, and (d) if any officer, director, or stockholder owning more than 10 per cent of any class of stock of the borrower is also a director of the bank making the loan.

An analysis of the foregoing provisions reveals that the proposed insurance, in common with other related recovery stimulants, is intended primarily to accommodate small business. Thus, the maximum indebtedness of any single borrower is $1,000,000. It is pre-

sumed that big business has sufficient facilities to attract funds without benefit of government aid. No attempt is made to provide equity capital and loans are restricted to comparatively short maturities as is true of the direct loans which already may be made by either the 

Reconstruction Finance Corporation or the Federal Reserve banks.

Summary of Sources of Capital 

Irrespective of the source of capital, it must be clear that the response of investors to the needs of business enterprise must be conditioned upon the vagaries of opportunity. Promising business conditions have usually been found sufficient to attract private funds in sufficient volume, but the abnormal conditions of recent years have confused the business outlook. Under the circumstances, government has tried to bolster private facilities as well as resorting to more direct excursions of assistance in order to stimulate recovery. But the activity of government, also, must be conditioned over the long run upon the soundness of the purpose for which funds are desired as well as the worthiness of the applicant. How far the present trend toward government sponsorship and performance of lending operations to private enterprise may go remains an open question. The answer will likely be found in the more or less normal evolutionary change of society. Abnormal events, such as war, may in addition exert pronounced influence to swing the pendulum.

CHAPTER XIX  

NOTHER source of capital funds is found within the corporation itself, i.e., from the existing stockholders. This is accomplished through the issuance of stock rights permitting the stockholders to buy the new issue at a price which is usually below the prevailing market price. As a matter of fact, there is a general requirement of law that existing stockholders be given the first option to buy a new issue of common stock. Such a limitation is a matter of simple equity because it gives the shareholders an opportunity to maintain their relative position in the control of the corporation, as well as their share in the accumulated earnings.¹ The prior right of subscription is also in accordance with sound financial practice because it provides a relatively certain and low-cost method of raising additional funds. 

Favorable Corporate Conditions 

It is to be expected that proper cultivation of the corporate soil will precede the issuance of stock rights. In the first place, the corporation must be able to justify the need for the additional funds, both in terms of its past record and of prospective future operations. Of equal significance is the confidence imposed in the management by the stockholders. A record characterized by secrecy and disputes is obviously not conducive to new commitments of capital. In addition to these two fundamental factors, it is not unusual to find that a corporation seeking funds through the issuance of stock rights possesses a relatively large surplus account. This is actually neither a legal nor an accounting requirement. However, the condition broadens the base of the residual equity and is usually interpreted as evidence of prudent management in the past.

To illustrate the fact that surplus is not an absolute prerequisite, the balance sheet on page 362 may be assumed. 

1 The pre-emptive right of the stockholder to subscribe for new issues of stock in order to maintain his original control or equity may be nullified by providing for its elimination in the articles of incorporation. 361

BALANCE SHEET OF THE MAKUP CORPORATION EQUITIES 

.$ 4,000,000 

Capital stock (par $100).... 36,000,000 $40,000,000 $10,000,000 30,000,000 $40,000,000

No surplus appears, but the declaration of stock rights is readily possible. It may be assumed that the firm has had good earnings in the past but has disposed of them by liberal dividends and "write-offs" or by the reduction of questionable asset values against earnings. In view of these conditions, the stock may be selling at a high figure, let us assume 175. If rights were now extended to stockholders to buy stock at 100, it is clear they would have considerable value (varying according to the proportion of new to old stock). However, such conditions are unlikely, and most corporations that utilize stock rights possess a representative surplus account. The surplus is the evidence of past profits and may in itself indicate a need of funds for expansion purposes, i.e., the good earnings may be a barometer of profit opportunities which have not been fully developed. 

Favorable Market Conditions 

Not only must the corporate soil be fcrtile for rights, but conditions in the money market must be suitable. There must be an active demand for equity securities, and the immediate outlook of the market must be assured; otherwise, the stock rights will have little appeal unless they can be exercised at a price below the market for the stock. 

Mistaken judgment of the market was not uncommon in the fall of 1929 because of the extensive and sudden reaction in the stock market. 

One large corporation, the Cities Service Company, found it necessary to recall its rights, even after they had been traded on the market. 

Because of the dangers of market fluctuation, a sufficient spread between the market and subscription prices is of great importance as a means of protection to the new issue. Stock prices are so volatile that the unexpected happens frequently. Spreads that are normally deemed entirely sufficient may prove inadequate almost overnight. 

The North American Company declared rights in favor of stockholders of record, October 17, 1929, permitting new subscriptions at a price of 100. On October 8, 1929, its stock was selling around 160.

Before the termination of the rights privilege, the stock had sold as low as 77. Such embarrassment was experienced by a number of corporations.

Because of these contingencies, the issuance of rights is frequently underwritten by investment bankers. While in many instances the underwriting syndicate may not have to sell any securities, the price paid for the guaranty is intended to be a quid pro quo, being in the nature of an insurance premium. An instance is the underwriting by 

Morgan, Stanley, and Company, Inc., and others, of the new stock offered by the Eastman Kodak Company to its shareholders in 1939. 

Of the 225,092 shares authorized for sale, 221,162 shares, or 98.25 per cent of the total, were purchased by shareholders or those holding rights. Under the circumstances, the banking group found it necessary to purchase only 3,930 shares.

In cases of popular issues, the commission received by the underwriting syndicate may easily be excessive and virtually constitute a gift. Under other circumstances, the underwriters may be forced to take up a large portion of the new issue. A case in point is the $48,000,000 issue of convertible debentures offered by Bethlehem Steel Corporation to its stockholders in September, 1937. The offering carried a 33 per cent rate and subscriptions were to be at par on the basis of $15 in debentures for each share of stock held. Due to the conditions prevailing in the securities markets at the time, the issue was poorly received, and the underwriters were forced to take up more than $46,000,000 of the debentures. 

Distribution of Ownership

To employ stock rights successfully as a means of raising funds, it is usually desirable that the ownership of the stock be well distributed. 

The failure of a single large stockholder to co-operate would otherwise lead to failure. Furthermore, the presence of scattered ownership affords all the advantages and features of a large market. 

Calculating the Nominal Value of a Right 

To appreciate fully the nature of rights, it is necessary to understand how their value is calculated. In general terms, it may be stated that a right is the privilege a stockholder has to participate in new offerings; more specifically its value is expressed in terms of the right that attaches to one old share of stock to subscribe for the new.3 To make this clear, if the opportunity were offered to purchase one new 

2 Wall Street Journal (May 2, 1939), p. 1. * Such rights are called New York rights and are used almost exclusively. Another type, the Philadelphia rights, is based upon the new issue.

share of stock for each ten shares of old, the holder of ten shares of old stock would come into the possession of ten rights. In turn, it would require ten rights plus the subscription price to acquire one new share of stock. The reader must guard against the easy error of assuming that a single right gives one the privilege of subscribing for stock. 

The calculation of the nominal value of rights has been provided by a number of formulas, but perhaps the most common and satisfactory is the following:

M S = Value of a right

R+ 1 

M represents the market price of the old stock and S the subscription price of the new. Obviously, the difference between the two represents the margin gained by subscribing for the new stock. In turn this differential is not applicable to a single share of stock, but is divisible by the number of old shares required to buy a new share, plus the new share to be issued. Thus, R is the ratio of old stock to new stock.

This statement of the process by which the nominal value of rights may be calculated is illustrated to good advantage by the declaration of rights by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company to stockholders of record, May 23, 1930, in the ratio of one new share for six shares of old at a price of 100. Trading in the rights began as early as April 17, when the stock of the company closed with a market price of 2601. Applying these facts to the formula, the following would result: 

R(6) +1 260-100 6 +1 1601 = 22.9, par or nominal value of the right on April 17. 

Actually, the closing market price of the rights for that particular day was 223, or closely approximating the nominal value (especially if allowance is made for brokerage and other miscellaneous expenses). 

It should be borne in mind that this so-called par or nominal value of a right is true at a given moment only and must of necessity fluctuate in common with the market price of the stock itself. In turn, it is natural that the market price of the rights should approximate the nominal value because of the market operations of three

groups: (1) activities of old stockholders, (2) activities of new stockholders, (3) activities of speculators. 

To illustrate the possible action of these groups, the market price of the rights of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company may be assumed to have been 20 under the conditions outlined above; in other words, the rights are assumed to be under-priced by about $3.

It is apparent that the foregoing operations would automatically tend to eliminate possible arbitraging, and the advantage of buying rights would be eliminated. This would be specifically effected because: 

1. The action of the old stockholder would increase the floating supply of stock and thus depress its price. At the same time, the stimulated demand for rights would raise their price. 

2. The action of the new stockholder would increase the demand for rights and thus increase their price.

3. The action of the speculator would produce results similar to those of the old stockholders.

The price of the stock would tend to fall as a result of these operations, while the price of the rights would tend to rise. The movements would continue until normal equilibrium was restored. 

Rights at a Premium

Although rights do not sell as frequently at a premium, a number of instances are on record. The following two cases occurring in the fall of 1929 are illustrative:

Grigsby-Grunow Company.-Rights were declared in favor of the holders. of record, November 1, 1929, to terminate November 21, 1929. On October 2, 1929, the stock closed at 47%, and the rights at 2. Since the ratio of exchange was one new share for seven of the old, at a subscription price of 40 the nominal value of a right at that date should have been: 47 40 7 7 +1 8 

In other words, the market price of the right was more than double its true value for subscription purposes. Moreover, the situation later resolved itself. into a condition of virtual absurdity when the price of the stock actually went below the subscription price and the rights still continued to be traded in. This was true of the entire period from October 24 to November 18, 1929. On October 

24, the stock closed at 32 and the rights at 1; on November 18, the stock sold at 21, and the rights closed at 1. 159-100 10 + 1 North American Company.—Rights were announced in favor of holders of record, October 17, 1929, to terminate November 15, 1929. On October 8, the stock was selling at 159-well above the subscription price of 100. With the ratio of exchange being one share of new for ten shares of old, the nominal value of a right should have been: = .92 59 11 514 Actually, the closing price of the rights on October 9 was 51, or approximately equal to its nominal value. This normal state of equilibrium was suddenly disrupted by the market break. The stock sold as low as 78 on October 30, but closed at 94, or five points below the subscription price. Nevertheless, the rights on the same day closed with a price of 1.

How to account for the anomalous condition of rights commanding a price when the stock itself could have been bought at a price lower than the subscription price is difficult. Referring to the foregoing cases, why should anyone have paid 1 for rights to buy Grigsby-

Grunow stock at 40 when it could have been purchased at 32 in the market? Or why did the rights of the North American Company close at 1 on October 30 when the stock could have been purchased at 941, 51 points below the subscription price? This state of affairs is decidedly abnormal but may perhaps be accounted for in the following terms: (1) Market conditions were most unstable and encouraged unusual situations. (2) The rights were probably utilized as a convenient means of speculating or gambling, much akin to the practice of dealing in options. Here was an opportunity to stake a small amount in the rights for the opportunity of profiting from a later possible rise in the price of the stock above the subscription price. 

Stocks had broken badly and were expected to rebound. Rights had the appeal of a cheap entry to achieve quick profits. Normally, a right should not continue to sell at a price above par over a period of time as this should lead to the following actions: (1) The purchase of stock directly instead of through the medium of rights. This should cause a relative increase in the price of the stock as compared with the rights. (2) The high price of the rights would also encourage selling them and therefore cause their price to drop. Both events would tend to restore equilibrium. 

The "Rights-on" and "Ex-Rights" Periods

Attention must now be called to the fact that rights are issued to holders of record as of a stated date, and the stockholders appearing on the stock books of the corporation as of this date are the recipients of the rights. Prior to this date, any stock that is sold carries with it the privilege to share in the rights; after the date, the rights are separate and distinct and hence the stock is referred to as "ex-rights." 

All market transactions in rights during the "rights-on" period must of necessity be on a "when issued" basis, since the actual rights are issued only as of the record date specified. "Rights-on," "Ex-Rights," and the Market Price of the Stock

At the time that a stock goes "ex-rights," it is logical to expect the price of the stock to decline by the value of the right. One study showed that stock prices move downward as much as upward during the "rights-on" period, but that in the "ex-rights" period there is a tendency for the combined value of the stock plus the rights to increase slightly. However, in most studies of the problem, no allowance has been made for the general trend of the market during the interval, and to this extent the results should certainly be discounted.

Effect of Rights on the Book Value of Stock 

A casual reaction to the effect of rights upon the book value of the stock is that their issuance should cause the book value to decrease. 

This is not necessarily true. The change will depend specifically upon whether the subscription price of the new stock is above or below the book value of the old stock; if the former is true, then clearly the book value will be increased, and opposite results will appear under the latter condition. Effect of Rights on Stockholder 

Rights are regarded in financial circles as a favor, or at least a privilege, to the stockholder. The merit of this view may be ques-

tioned. While a right bestows a privilege upon, the stockholder, at the same time certain obligations or impositions occur. Actually, the stockholder is compelled to make a new investment or to relinquish his pro rata share of holdings in the company. Except for the few in control, the latter feature is not necessarily adverse to the welfare of the stockholder since it may be offset by the sale of rights; as to the former, it may actually prove desirable to make the investment. 

However, regardless of whether a new investment is made or the rights sold, the value of the privilege is in a sense nil. 

What advantage does the existing stockholder have over the outsider? The answer appears to be little, if any. This may be clarified by referring again to the rights of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company described above. Assume that Mr. X, a stockholder, held six shares as of the record date. On May 22, his stock was accordingly worth: 6 X 244 or $1,466 Omitting the gain in price which may be attributed to other causes (such as pool operations, market conditions, etc.) X's position may be calculated as of the close of May 23. Since X is to subscribe for one new share of stock, he will have on hand or due: 

7 shares at 2241 or $1,569 

Less new investment 100 

Net value $1,469 or approximately his previous net worth."

It is evident the stockholder did not make any profits and was simply afforded an opportunity for new investment. This is no particular advantage over prospective stockholders, since the latter may buy the stock (ex-rights) at the old market price less the value of the right (ignoring price changes accruing from other causes).8 

Similarly, it would follow that if the stockholder sold his rights, the proceeds would not constitute income, but instead would be primarily a return of principal. In this respect stock rights are regarded in much the same light as stock dividends. This treatment of stock

rights is followed by the Bureau of Internal Revenue in connection with the administration of the income tax law." Here it is recognized that the rights are not taxable income, although some gain or loss may arise through the sale of the rights. To determine the net effect, the proper proportion of the total cost (principal investment) is assigned to the rights and is deducted from the proceeds created by the sale. Gain or loss is thus determined in exactly the same manner as in the sale of the securities themselves.

While rights do not serve as a source of income to the stockholder, nevertheless they are a convenient means of corporate financing and may be justified on the basis of policy, especially in view of the following considerations: (1) They provide an economical and reliable source of capital funds for the corporation. (2) They offer an outlet for the investment of new funds on the part of the investor. On these terms, the rights simply represent a value for value transaction between the corporation and the investor. True, there is the privilege of prior subscription,10 but this does not necessarily imply the bequest of anything of value to the stockholder.

Relationship between Par Value of Stock and Stock Rights 

There is no fundamental economic relationship between stock rights and the par value of stock. Of course, if rights are issued offering stock at a price less than par, the stock is assessable in the same manner as any other new issue. It is therefore obvious that such an issue would normally be foregone.12 If the stock were no par, this difficulty would be avoided entirely, and the corporation would be free to set the price according to market conditions. 

To Whom Are Rights Offered?

Legally, it is required that rights to purchase new common stock must first of all be tendered to the residual equity elements of a corporation. While this usually means common stockholders only, occasionally preferred stockholders may be included in order to broaden the market or because of conversion privileges of the preferred. Rights To Subscribe to Bonds 

While rights are issued chiefly in connection with the sale of common stock, their use is not unknown as a means of selling bonds. 

In practice bond rights have usually been limited to the purchase of convertible bonds. The use of rights to buy convertible bonds is virtually a necessity due to the preemptive right of the common stockholders. If the bonds are convertible into common stock, the existing common stockholders will find their position in potential danger. 

Under favorable market conditions, most of the bonds would be converted, thus weakening the control of the original common stockholders and diluting their equity in the surplus. To protect the common stock against this contingency, or at least to give the common stockholders a chance to avoid the risk, rights must be issued to the common stock giving it the privilege to subscribe to the convertible bonds before outsiders are permitted to do so. 

The Value of a Right To Subscribe to a Bond Issue 

To determine the value of a right to subscribe to a new bond issue, the same general principles that underlie stock rights may be applied. One cause of difficulty, however, is found in the absence of an established market price of the bonds. Where new common stock is issued it has all of the rights of the old stock, and hence its market value is known. This is not true of the bonds as they constitute a distinct and separate issue. For convertible bonds, however, this obstacle is obviated by virtue of their conversion into stock, which makes possible a statement of the value of the bonds on the basis of their conversion value.14 Perhaps more significant is the value determined by trading on a "when issued" basis.

Future Outlook for Rights 

The use of rights in the past has been on a larger scale than is commonly appreciated, bu: there is reason to believe that they may be employed much more extensively as a financing medium in the future. In the first place, other new financing has been made more difficult, and in the second place, corporate families are large enough to afford an excellent market for additional financing. Under these circumstances, it would seem reasonable to expect financial management to cater more largely to its own shareholders. Finally, it is likely that a greater share of new funds will be raised by means of stock instead of bonds. If this is true, the existence of the pre-emptive rights will compel the corporation to offer the securities to their own stockholders. 

Obligations with Warrants

Where stock rights are used, the stockholder is compelled to exercise his option within a comparatively short period of time. 

Another method which may extend the privilege of subscription over an extended period of time is found in the use of warrants authorizing the purchase of stock at predetermined prices. For the most part, they have been used to make preferred stock and debenture bonds more attractive by providing an opportunity for participation at some future date. The holder has the delightful alternative of not investing if the conditions are not attractive or of investing in the 18 It would require 813 shares to secure $100 of bonds, since the terms allowed subscription for $1,200 bonds for every 100 shares of stock held.

stock if dividend returns or capital appreciation are favorable. Under the circumstances, the following restrictions are usually incorporated in the terms relating to the warrant privilege. (1) The terms of purchase of stock are made less favorable the longer the option is delayed. (2) There is a time limit after which the warrant may not be exercised. (3) Adjustment of the terms following stock dividends, split-ups, etc., is customarily provided. The following examples of debentures carrying purchase warrants illustrate many of these features.

Loew's Incorporated.-Warrants were originally attached to the debenture. 

6's and empowered the holder to buy 5 shares of stock at $55. Because of a later stock dividend, the terms were adjusted so that for each $1,000 bond, 6.25 shares could be purchased instead at the same price per share. The privilege expired April 2, 1931. 

North American Cement Corporation.-Warrants were issued with the debenture 6's due in 1940. To each $1,000 bond were attached warrants entitling the holder to purchase 20 shares of stock at $40 per share. 

Remington-Rand, Incorporated.-Warrants were issued with the debenture 

4's, due in 1956. The holder of each $1,000 bond is entitled to buy 15 shares of common stock at $25 per share on or before March 1, 1938; during the year ending March 1, 1939, 15 shares at $27.50 per share; each year following, the price of the stock increases $2.50 until the year ending March 1, 1944, when the warrants expire.

Warrants No Longer Used Extensively 

Warrants were particularly an outgrowth of the rampant market conditions which prevailed prior to 1929. New issues are no longer common, but trading in existing warrants is found occasionally on such markets as the New York Curb Market. As an illustration of their market activity in the past, the action of the warrants of the American and Foreign Power Company may be described. These warrants were issued late in 1927 and authorized the holder to purchase stock at $25. In less than two years, they sold at 174 while the stock was selling around 200, or approximately equal to the price of the warrant plus the subscription price. Under these conditions, the holder was free either to sell the warrants and realize a large profit or he could elect to buy stock at $25 per share and obtain an excellent position from a speculative point of view. 

From the point of view of sound financial operation, the use of warrants is open to question. An attractive option does expedite the

sale of the original issue, but at the same time the planning of financial policies is hampered. Indeed, the device resembles a lottery scheme in some respects. Whenever the price of stock is higher than the warrant price, the holders will begin to exercise their option. 

This may or may not coincide with the corporation's need for funds. 

Security prices tend to move together, and a bull movement in the stock market may lift the price of the corporation's stock above the warrant price without any accompanying internal justification for either the stock or warrant price. As a result, the warrants may be exercised and provide new capital at a time when it is not needed. 

It would seem, therefore, that the use of warrants represents a catering to temporary demands for "stylish" securities, or an effort on the part of management to reduce the present cost of funds at the expense of future policy.

CHAPTER XX  

SIDE from the retention of earnings, long-term capital is raised mainly through the issuance and sale of securities. 

Most of the major corporations transfer this task to investment banking houses. The actual procedure involved in security distribution is, therefore, fundamentally a part of the study of investment banking. At the same time, the process is so closely connected with corporate financing that it seems advisable to include a brief analysis of security distribution in anv general discussion of corporation finance. Consideration may first be given to the reasons why the task of selling securities is transferred to investment bankers. 

These are as follows: 

1. Economy. The corporation is chiefly concerned with the manufacture and sale of goods and services and has occasion to raise funds at relatively infrequent intervals. Investment bankers, on th other hand, are specialists in the business of floating corporation securities and are able to act upon well-established procedures and to use financial outlets of long standing. For this reason, in the long run the corporation is able to raise funds more cheaply by the assignment of the task to a specialized agency. 

2. Certainty. The financing of business needs normally requires planning months in advance and is dependent upon complete assurance that the funds will be forthcoming on schedule. If the corporation undertakes to sell its own securities, an extraneous risk is assumed which may serve to deter physical operations. Transfer of the security-selling function to the specialized investment banker avoids this risk and provides certainty that the funds will be available when needed. 

3. Advice. By engaging the service of an investment banker, the corporation receives the benefit of the advice of a specialist in the practical field of security distribution. Information may be given as to the timing of sale, as to the type of securities which can be distributed to the greatest advantage, and various other services may be rendered in clearing the numerous legal and technical problems. 379

Technical advice is particularly essential today in order to comply with the registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933 as well as with the regulations prescribed by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Not only may the banker act as a consultant for a particular issue, but friendly relations may exist between a corporation and the investment banker over long periods of time.¹ 

4. Prestige. By selling securities through established banking houses, prestige may be added to many corporate issues. Some houses have a public reputation of taking part in the distribution of only the better classes of securities. If such a banking house is engaged, the corporation may receive a better price for its issue. 

5. Market Protection.-New securities lack the seasoning and stability of older issues which have been tried and tested over a period of time. Some of the purchasers of a new issue may be speculators who buy to take advantage of the usually expected rise in price; others may be individuals and institutions who have bought on the spur of the moment and later come to doubt the advisability of their purchase. Both classes may be inclined to sell shortly after the issue has been fully distributed and be the cause of an unfavorable price reaction. When securities are marketed by investment bankers, an effort is made to support the market during and after the preliminary selling.2 Buying to support the market can do little to counteract major declining trends, but it may offset temporary irregularities. 

Where successful, the financial position and prestige of the corporation are enhanced, and the purchasers of bonds are more apt to become a stable source of funds.

Like most middlemen functions, there is often general failure to appreciate the productiveness of the services of investment bankers. 

These functions are of the utility and service type and do not lend themselves to the objectivity of measurement which is possible in production activities leading to a change in the form of substance or material. In retrospect, it is now apparent that the policies and practices of investment bankers have at times been deficient in contribut- 

1 See "New Money for Industry," Business Week (November 30, 1940), pp. 42-52, for an informal and revealing discussion of the relationships between investment bankers and corporate management. 

2 Support of the market may also take place under other conditions. See Release No.

ing to the public interest, but this probably is true, also, of other economic agencies. In any event, it is essential to keep in mind that the functions are a necessary part of the financial system and provide a service both to society as a whole and to the individual and institutional investor. Among the broader services to society, the following should be mentioned: 

1. The productive process is facilitated by the raising of capital funds. 

2. Through the process of investigation prior to the acceptance and handling of security issues the bankers eliminate many issues which lack in economic soundness. 

3. Furnishing recognized outlets for the surplus funds of investors is likewise a service to society. 

From the point of view of the investor, the following services are performed by the banker. 

1. Supplying the investor with information needed for investment purposes through advertisements, prospectuses, reporting services, and through occasional advisory letters. 

2. Advising the investor as to what investment is most adaptable to his particular needs. 

3. Performing much of the investigation required for intelligent investment which in most instances is not only too expensive for the individual investor, but also well beyond the scope of his experience. 

4. Furnishing miscellaneous services such as the safekeeping of security issues, collection of interest and dividends.

The Nature of an Investment Banking House 

While it is easy to state that an investment banking house is a business engaged in the buying and selling of securities, it is difficult to go out in the world of practice and say, "There is an investment banker just like the description in that book." Many institutions engage in operations other than investment banking and resemble the typical department store more than a specialized retail unit. For example, it was common in earlier years to find a mixture of commercial and investment banking functions. At the present time, the federal securities laws compel their separation. Another form of multiple activity is the combination of brokerage operations with investment banking. In many respects, the two types of business lend themselves to common sponsorship since the stock in trade is identical;

the chief difference is found in the relationship to the customer. The broker acts in the capacity of agent while the investment banker serves as a principal. 

The long depression of the thirties has also had a marked effect in changing investment banking practice, as well as in influencing their general reputation. In earlier years, it was possible for a prominent banking house to advertise that no clients had ever lost money through failure of the companies whose bonds it had sold. It is doubtful if a single banking concern could make such a statement today. Economic devastation combined with various legislative measures of reform have also caused many investment bankers to fail or to undergo drastic reorganization. A contributory cause to the failure of some houses was their effort to maintain the values of securities which they had sold through market support or outright redemption.

The diversity of operations makes it impossible to classify investment banking institutions too rigidly, but there is a tendency to find a grouping along the following lines: (1) wholesale investment bankers, (2) retail investment bankers, (3) a class of bankers which combine the wholesale and retail functions. 

Wholesale Investment Bankers

A few investment banking houses restrict their operations to large transactions only and seldom sell securities directly to the public. 

Instead, the securities are sold to smaller banking houses and to other agencies which accomplish the direct public distribution. Illustrative of the wholesale type are Kuhn, Loeb, and Company and Morgan, Stanley, and Company. The latter is a comparatively new institution which was organized in 1935 by interests formerly associated with the J. P. Morgan and Company when it was forced to separate its commercial and investment operations as a result of the Banking Act of 1933. J. P. Morgan and Company, proper, continued functioning until 1940 as a privately operated commercial bank accepting deposits and making business loans; in that year, it incorporated under a state charter to obtain more favorable tax rates and greater flexibility in its capitalization. 

Retail Investment Bankers

As the name implies, retail bankers sell directly to the public. 

Most of their stock in trade is purchased from the wholesale houses,

but occasionally they underwrite issues for smaller corporations. Many of the retail houses are purely local in character; others are of sufficient size to have a national reputation. Most representative of the group is the so-called bond house, although the term is now misleading because of the entry of many bond houses into the selling of stocks. Many of these institutions handle established securities in addition to participating in new issues. Their clientele consists of commercial banks, other financial institutions, and various institutional investors and individuals. 

Wholesale and Retail Bankers

There are a large number of investment banking houses which buy in wholesale quantities and also participate in the direct distribution process to the ultimate purchaser. Bonbright and Company, Inc.; First Boston Corporation; Brown, Harriman, and Company;

Halsey, Stuart, and Company; and others may be referred to as examples of this type of operation. 

Criteria of Acceptable Security Issues 

One of the primary functions of investment banking is to determine which issues are acceptable for public distribution. Ignoring for the present the details involved in obtaining the desired information, it may be said that at least the following items must be considered by the investment banker before acceptance of an issue: (1) 

What is the nature of the industry? (2) What is the standing of the corporation within the industry? (3) Are the securities adaptable to current demand in the investment market?

The Nature of the Industry 

The larger investment bankers generally refuse to handle the securities of speculative industry. They are interested primarily in the securities of industries which are well established and have a reasonably long and satisfactory history. For example: the bulk of the funds raised to finance the aviation industry was obtained by smaller investment houses selling directly to the public, instead of being underwritten by the larger investment banking houses with a national reputation. In many instances, the houses disposing of the securities were frank to state that they were offered as a speculation and not as an investment. Many houses delayed handling the securities of motion picture enterprises until recent years on the theory

that the industry was not sufficiently established to have desired stability.

Today, the potential liabilities arising under the Securities Act of 1933 give further assurances of truthful statement about future prospects and compel full disclosure of the facts. Indeed, it is not unusual to find a statement to the effect that a given security is an out-and-out speculation offering sizable returns in the event of success but at the same time acknowledging a high degree of risk. For example, the registration statement of a mining company was amended by the Securities and Exchange Commission to include the following statement of facts (among others):

The investor should bear in mind that this is a highly speculative proposition. 

It involves construction at investor's expense of a comparatively large custom mill in a district where suitable ore in substantial quantity has not been blocked out and is not known to exist (beyond an amount sufficient for about three months' operation of the mill at initial capacity), . . . .³

In general, the large banking house is unwilling to handle an issue of stocks or bonds unless the issuing company is in a field of industry which is well established, such as the railroads, public utilities, steel industry, and the larger well-known units of other industrial types having a national reputation. Furthermore, the industry should be one that will permit a reasonably stable income free from the effects of abrupt changes in demand. In other words, the outlook of the industry should be what the bankers call assured.

The Status of the Individual Company 

Not only must the industry be adaptable to the foregoing require、 ments, but the specific unit within the field must also possess the proper qualifications. In the past, most banking houses assembled comprehensive information relating to the financial position of the company to determine whether the proposed security offering met their standards. Most of the data were believed to be confidential in nature and were not given general circulation. Today, formal registration statements are required under the Securities Act of 1933 and are readily available for public inspection. By this means, investors may give careful scrutiny to the following types of information relating to any company offering a new security issue: · 3 S.E.C., Fourth Annual Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1938, p. 38.

d et al al 83 On

2. Description of its business

Is the Security Adaptable to Money-Market Conditions? 

One of the most practical contributions the investment banker is able to make is advice as to the type of security which is best suited for raising funds at the particular time. To obtain lowest cost financing, it is necessary to harmonize the security with prevailing moneymarket conditions. In periods of high interest rates, long-term bonds are usually undesirable and short-term obligations or stocks become the prevailing type of issue. Conversely, in periods of low interest rates, long-term bonds may be issued advantageously, and extensive refunding operations should be undertaken.

The desirable policy from the point of view of the cost of capital and the way a particular issue fits into a corporation's financial structure may not always be possible because of temporary, adverse market conditions. Where this is true, it may be preferable to issue a shortterm, rather than a long-term, security. Similarly, it may prove profitable at times to incorporate conversion or participating privileges in bonds and preferred stocks while at other times the market might show little interest in such features. In any event, the intimate association of the investment banker with money-market conditions puts him in a position to give valuable assistance to the corporation in preparing the type of security which would obtain capital at the best price.

Enterprises entailing high risk and the small companies in any field are seldom in a position to avail themselves of the services of
