Service Relationship between Investment Banker and Corporation 

There are three general plans or methods of contracting for the services of the bankers which are worthy of explanation. These are the bid plan, the commission plan, and the outright purchase plan. 

The Bid Plan 

Under the bid arrangement, the proposed security issue is offered for sale to all groups interested and is sold to the banking house or banking group which makes the most advantageous bid. In the past, competitive bidding has been limited chiefly to state and municipal bond issues and to railroad equipment trust obligations; more recently, it has been required by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the case of public utilities. There had been occasional use in the public utility field before this time, being required by law in Massachusetts for all first mortgage bond issues and in New Hampshire by order of the Public Service Commission.17 

In view of the wide acceptance of the competitive bid plan in the case of municipal financing, it appears strange that the plan should not be more widely used by private corporations. There is a certain appeal to the idea of offering goods to the highest bidder whenever there is adequate competition for the goods. Likewise, it would seem reasonable to expect that competitive bidding for security issues would tend to bring about lower cost financing for the corporation. However, there is widespread opposition to the use of the bid plan not only among the bankers who have an economic interest at stake, 15 lbid., Table 7, p. A25. 

18 Ibid., Table 6. 

17 New York Times (February 12, 1939), p. Fl.

but among industrial concerns as well. The reasons offered are various, but among the more important are the following: 

1. Lack of permanent relationship.-The bid plan is not conducive to the establishment of permanent relationships between banking houses and business corporations. Many people believe that a wellestablished connection with a prominent banking house is of material advantage to the business corporation. 

2. Lower Standards. It is commonly believed that the bid plan may result in favoring banking houses of lower standards and that emphasis would be placed unduly upon the price, or yield rate, of the security instead of upon its over-all qualitative features. Eventually, these weaknesses would mean greater losses to the investor. 

Those who advance these views believe that competitive bidding is incompatible with the quality and standards required to build the long-term confidences which are essential to adequate investment. 

3. Adaptability. While the bid plan may be applicable to certain supervised fields which are susceptible to governmental regulation, it is contended that the diversified character of the industrial field is such as to make the bid plan impractical. 

4. Expediency.-Conditions of expediency also tend to discourage the extension of competitive bidding. There exists a rather close community of interest among leading banking houses which results in a reduction of competitive spirit in submitting bids. In the second place, many large banking houses have obtained considerable business because of their representation upon many boards of directors. 

5. Regulation and investigation.-Banking houses naturally investigate a security issue quite thoroughly before undertaking its distribution or before bidding for the issue. While the corporation would be required to produce a great deal of information needed in making the analysis, the banking houses would still find it necessary to do considerable amounts of industrial research in order to determine the quality of the issue and the price they should pay. Under the permanent arrangement, duplication of investigation would be avoided, and it is claimed that the resulting savings would enable the corporation to finance at lower rates.

As stated previously, competitive bidding is now required by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the case of all public utility issues. Aside from the merits of the procedure, the Commission believes that some such requirement is necessary to comply with the

provisions of the Public Utility Act of 1935. Here, the principle of "arm's-length bargaining" is introduced as being essential to prevent the "restraint of free and independent competition."18 Initially, the

Commission adopted a rule (U-12F-2) prohibiting the payment of any fee to affiliated interests in the absence of competitive bidding except where the participation in the underwriting was not more than 5 per cent and the same as that paid to non-affiliated underwriters. Later, a blanket requirement calling for competitive bidding on all occasions was adopted.19

Most of the banking houses interposed violent objections to the adoption of open bidding, contending that it was not required by the Act and that the effects would be harmful to their business as well as to borrowing institutions. Possibly this burst of reaction was the usual exaggeration of anticipation in comparison with later reality, because there is increasing acceptance of the principle with accumulating experience.20 Several interesting problems have developed such as keeping the members of a syndicated group together in the face of open bidding and the treatment of members of losing groups. 

However, these difficulties are being worked out and, undoubtedly, increasing use of the practice will probably show need for concessions on both sides.

Competitive bidding is not yet used to any extent in the handling of industrial issues and some observers contend that the principle is not applicable in this field. It is pointed out that open bidding can be useful only where a certain amount of standardization exists and where the securities are very high grade. There is some merit in this position because the element of variety necessarily destroys the common denominator which is a basis for bidding by different groups.21 

For this reason, the wide range of risks and other varying qualities of the many segments of the industrial area may prevent any widespread use in this field. This would be especially true of the small and isolated companies without sufficient attraction to command the presence of banking houses at the bidding. Under the circumstances, small business institutions are compelled to hire special agents or to 

18 See Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, Section 1 b(2) and Section 12 (f). 

19 Rule U-50. Certain issues are, however, excepted: such as issuance or sale not in excess of $1,000,000; issuance or sale to existing holders pursuant to pre-emptive right or in connection with reorganization; and other cases of limited applicability. 

20 See New York Times (July 6, 1941), p. Fl. 

21 However, the Home Owners' Loan Corporation was successful in using the bid method in placing its fire insurance contract where many factors were involved.

make other arrangements which fit their particular needs. Where agents are hired, it is customary to adopt the commission plan which may now be described. 

The Commission Plan 

Under this plan, the banking house or other representative simply acts as an agent in the sale of the securities and is paid a commission upon the securities actually sold. Broadly speaking, corporations do not look with favor upon this arrangement because no assurance is provided that the necessary funds will actually be raised; hence, there is no real shifting of the responsibility for the financing to the banker. 

The Outright Purchase Plan 

Under the outright purchase plan the investment banking house assumes the role of a securities merchant and buys the securities outright from the corporation at an agreed price. The source of profit to the banking house is the differential between the purchase price and the price at which it sells the securities. Under the bid plan the securities are also bought outright, but the present method differs in that the relationship between the banking element and the business corporation is often on a permanent basis, and the terms of the transaction are arrived at through negotiation rather than competitive bidding. A friendly and fairly continuous relationship prevails both in times of normal business and in times of financial stress. Under these circumstances, when the corporation gets into difficulty, the banking house usually deems it part of its obligation to assist in any necessary financial reorganization, often regardless of its economic advisability. However, critics of investment banking practices contend that the real reason for banker participation in reorganization is to take advantage of the opportunity to gain control of the reorganized company and to realize various fees and profits. See Chapter 

XXXV for discussion of this point. 

Permanent ties between banking houses and the corporation raise several fundamental questions as to their propriety in terms of financial and investment principles. Can a corporation which has failed or fallen into a difficult financial condition offer really high-grade investments to the public? If it cannot do so, should the investment banker urge such issues upon the investing public? Of course, under some circumstances, the investment banker may personally carry a portion of the securities through a long period of uncertainty, and in most

cases the new issues put out by the reorganized corporation are primarily for exchange purposes. The old securities' holders usually receive new securities bearing a lower rate of interest or receive junior equities or stock in exchange for the original issues. Nevertheless, there is always the risk that the practice of banking houses handling securities of troubled corporations which they have financed over a period of years may result in the sale of issues of dubious value. The extent to which this may be possible has undoubtedly been reduced by the new security regulations, but the fact remains that issues have been distributed from time to time which would not have been underwritten if it were not for the implied obligation arising out of a permanent financial relationship.

Syndicate Organization under the Outright Purchase Plan 

Under the outright purchase plan the funds are advanced to the corporation before the securities are sold. This means not only the assumption of greater risk on the part of the investment banking house, but in addition it implies an obligation to advance the required capital funds. The risk factor is met by the organization of a syndicate composed of a number of banking houses. The necessary funds are provided by the members of the syndicate through borrowings from commercial banks upon collateral composed of the issue that is to be sold.

The Purchase Syndicate 

Three types of syndicates may be found in the distribution of the typical security issues: the purchase syndicate, the selling syndicate, and the underwriting syndicate. In general, a syndicate is a group of persons, in this case investment bankers, associated for the performance of a specific business project. In the distribution of securities, this principle is first applied to the purchasing of the securities from the issuing corporations. Not only are many issues too large for most banking houses to handle easily, but even if such action were possible, it would mean an undue concentration of risk. As a result, syndicates are formed to permit sharing in a large number of securities offerings and to diversify the risk. There is the additional advantage of providing each of the participants with a more representative portfolio, enabling him to offer a more diversified list to his clients. While all the risks are assumed by the group as a whole, the actual negotiations with the corporation are conducted by a single

20 ive ui ert od זn Se 1. 1. 5 banker, who is known as the manager of the syndicate. The usual procedure is to have negotiations carried out between an individual banker and the corporation desiring the funds. Upon arriving at an agreement as to the price and other details of the issue, the banker will close the deal with the positive assurance that other bankers of his circle will participate in the transaction.

In the original purchase syndicate the members are allotted, or agree to accept, a certain participation in the total issue to be sold. 

Although it is not unusual for the syndicate manager to have all plans formed for the disposal of the securities, the terms, prices, and other details will be discussed by the members. With this accomplished, it is the duty of each participant to arrange for the disposal of his quota through the many retail outlets with which each of the participants has established connections.

The Selling Syndicate 

The selling syndicate is more extensive and complex than the purchasing syndicate. In selling the securities, each of the participants in the purchase group communicates with numerous bond houses, brokerage houses, and other outlets that he may have for the distribution of securities. This communication may be by telephone, telegraph, or by mail. Where the market is assured and the details of the organization are well arranged, it is likely that these retail outlets will be offered a certain stated amount. On other occasions, they may be asked for the amount of desired participation. In either event, the limited time allowed for decision means it must be of the immediate rather than the deliberate type. In fact, the retailer may be called upon to decide the same day without opportunity to indulge in any real investigation. His decision must be based upon: 

1. The general appeal of the issue. Some corporations have an excellent public standing and little selling effort is required to dispose of their securities. In such cases, the selling commission almost partakes of the nature of a gift. 

2. The state of business and financial conditions in the particular locality. 

3. The banking house extending the offer. At times small retailers hesitate to refuse offerings because of the danger of injuring their future contacts with the wholesaler.

It will be observed that the factors underlying the decision of the

retailer have little to do with the merits of the particular issue. This may appear to be unfair to the retailer, but it is often a matter of expediency. In almost every case the retailer would lack the facilities for complete investigation, and if he should attempt any investigation, it would mean a duplication of the work of the offering syndicate. On the other hand, such blind acceptance of securities may lead to an inconsistent investment policy. Retailers usually consider themselves not only as distributors of securities but as investment advisors as well. Profit consideration may frequently force the retailers to place only a secondary emphasis upon their advisory capacities, and the investment programs of their customers will be sacrificed for the sake of disposing of the securities on hand. 

Profits of Syndicate Operations

In the same manner as the distribution of any commodity, the profits of both the wholesaler and retailer of security offerings are obtained by the mark-up process. The purchasing syndicate buys the securities from the corporation at a discount from the offering price and passes on a portion of this discount to the retailer. The amount of the discount from the offering price is determined by agreement between the purchasing syndicate and the corporation and varies with the size of the issue and its probable salability. Large issues can be handled at a smaller discount than smaller issues, and issues of the larger, better known corporations can be sold more easily than those of the relatively unfamiliar companies as was shown in the first part of this chapter.

Early in, 1939, the North American Company offered three series of debenture bonds carrying rates of interest of 31 per cent, 34 per cent, and 4 per cent. The total amount of the three series was $70,000,000, and in addition an issue of 5 per cent preferred stock was offered at the same time. The gross discount granted the purchasing syndicate was 12 per cent on the 3 per cent series, 2 per cent on the 32 per cent series, and 24 per cent on the 4 per cent series. 

The discount on the preferred stock was one dollar per share or approximately 2 per cent of the $52 issuing price. In July, 1939, the 

Shell Union Oil Company offered a $85,000,000 issue of fifteen year 21 per cent debentures. In this case the underwriting syndicate received a discount of 11 per cent, or a total of $1,275,000. The typical discount or spread appears to be about 2 per cent which is usually dis-

tributed among the various agencies involved in the following man ner: About of 1 per cent goes to the originating underwriter for services as syndicate manager, to cover the preparation of the issue and the handling of the details of the underwriting and selling; approximately of 1 per cent goes to the underwriters, that is, the purchase syndicate, as compensation for carrying the risk and for bearing the direct expense of handling the issue; and approximately of 1 per cent goes to the dealers making up the selling syndicate throughout the country.22 Out of the of 1 per cent selling commission, about of 1 per cent is usually made available to dealers and brokers who sell the securities but do not participate in the original allotments made to the selling group. Larger discounts will prevail in some cases, but in an effort to avoid excessive discounts, the Securities Act requires that the underwriting discounts be stated in the official prospectus and in the abstract of the prospectus which is usually published in the newspapers. 

The Financing of Syndicate Operations 

Thus far the assumption of risk by the syndicate members, as well as the process of selling, has been described, but there still remains the problem of raising the funds necessary to pay the issuing corporation. This is provided for in advance of the actual sale of the securities by borrowing funds from commercial banks. Either the syndicate head or each of the participants arranges with its commercial bankers for loans on the basis of the new securities as collateral, borrowing from 75 per cent to 90 per cent of the purchase price of the bonds. The balance is supplied by the participants, usually in proportion to their participations. Borrowing from commercial banks is a common feature of underwriting because the capital investment of most investment bankers is not large. This is caused by the nature of the business, which consists mainly of heavy turnover and temporary accommodation rather than long-term provision of capital. 

The pledge of the securities as collateral gives rise to another problem in the distribution of the securities, viz., how may the investment bankers sell these securities to the public and at the same time have them pledged as collateral. The technique to overcome this difficulty is found in the form of the interim certificate, which is a 

22 Franklin T. McClintock, Competitive Bidding for New Issues of Securities, 1939. (Privately published.)

temporary certificate issued pending the delivery of the actual or socalled definitive certificate.

Obligations of Syndicate Members 

Syndicates are handled on either a divided or undivided account basis. In a divided account (sometimes referred to as a limited liability account), the syndicate member is responsible only for the sale of his own quota. There is a further obligation to repurchase from the syndicate manager any portion of the original quota which the manager may find it necessary to buy in the market, in order to support the price during and immediately after distribution. In the undivided account plan (also referred to as unlimited liability plan), the syndicate member is responsible not only for his assigned quota but also for a proportionate share of the unsold securities. This means that if a member had agreed to take 10 per cent of an issue and successfully sold his share, he would still be required to take over the sale of 10 per cent of the unsold portion. If for any reason sales proved impossible, the member would have to finance the carrying of 10 per cent of the unsold securities.

The Selling Group 

Another method for selling securities is being used to an increasing degree. This is through the formation of a selling group. The plan differs from a syndicate in that no formal organization exists and no liability is assumed. The members of the selling group buy such securities from the purchase syndicate as they think can be resold. 

Their only obligation is to sell only at the agreed price during the selling period. The selling group makes possible the use of many small dealers who would be unable to assume the risks connected with regular syndicate organization. 

While as a rule security issues are handled with a substantial degree of success, occasions do arise when unexpected market conditions or errors in judgment cause a portion of the securities to remain unsold at the termination of the syndicate, and the various banking houses find it necessary to carry them until such time as they can be marketed to advantage.

Underwriting Syndicates 

The syndicates which have been discussed are almost universally referred to as underwriting syndicates. Although the word under-

1 writing is used in this broad sense, its exact and correct meaning should be understood. Fundamentally, it means the assumption of the risk involved in connection with certain contingencies. Thus, fire insurance companies underwrite the possible loss arising through fire; life insurance companies assume the financial losses arising as a result of death; and in the case of security offerings, the underwriters guarantee the raising of a specific amount of capital funds. 

In the strictest sense of the word an underwriting syndicate, in the case of securities offerings, would be one which assumes the risks arising out of the failure of a corporation to raise its capital funds through some other means, such as the issue of stock rights or the direct public offering of the securities by the corporation. However, in practice the term is rather loosely applied to both purchasing and selling syndicates and should be so understood.

Reappraisal of Syndicate Activities 

It is fitting that syndicate activities be examined in light of the repercussions of the recent depression. To what extent have they been a contributory factor in the depression, and to what extent have their practices called for revision?

The most important and fundamental function of syndicate operation is raising capital to accommodate business needs. A common criticism advanced on this score is that investment bankers have encouraged both excessive and needless security issues. Without doubt the flotation of securities has been encouraged at times primarily to afford business for the banking houses instead of giving major consideration to the capital needs of business enterprise. Not only has this been promoted by the control which bankers exercise over business, but the additional profits which arise from greater sales volume add to the pressure. It follows that the remedy is to be found in divorcing more completely the ties between financial interests and operating management.

The second criticism is that the charges levied for financial services have been too high. Here again this has been true in frequent instances. While it has been especially true of foreign issues, the same situation has prevailed to a degree in domestic financing. As a means of correcting this abuse, numerous critics urge wider use of the competitive bid plan for the sale of securities instead of relying upon the so-called friendly banking houses. As has been suggested earlier in this chapter, it remains to be seen whether or not competitive

bidding will result in any gain to the corporation or to the investor. 

The steps taken to require publicity of underwriting discounts and commissions may prove to be of more value. 

A third objection has been found in the multiple activities of investment banking houses, such as the conduct of commercial and investment operations. Legislative steps have been taken to remedy this situation, and the law now forbids the practice of both commercial and investment banking by the same organization. 

It is apparent that legislation was necessary for the protection of both the public and the investor. Some of the steps taken in the various federal enactments since 1933 have been indicated in the foregoing discussion, but more complete analysis will be found in Chapter XXI. More important, however, is the need for a sense of social consciousness and responsibility. Investment bankers hold a peculiar position of trust, and it is imperative that their activities be conducted with proper recognition of this criterion. Desirable financing must be determined not on the basis of volume of securities but with careful reference to basic business needs. Similarly, the success of financing cannot be measured solely in terms of the profits accruing from the particular security flotation. More to be desired is financing conducted for a reasonable charge and with sufficient consideration of the needs of the investor.

CHAPTER XXI REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 

NTIL recent years, business enterprise has enjoyed all the privileges and freedom usually bestowed upon the favored child. Government provided many facilities to foster commerce and trade and allowed great freedom in the conduct of business activity. Protective tariffs were introduced under the theory that they stimulated American business enterprise. The Federal 

Reserve Act was passed for "the accommodation of trade," and business was virtually unrestricted in seeking the cooperation of the public in the raising of capital. Under such a laissez faire setting numerous errors and abuses were bound to arise, and the practice of selling securities was no exception in this respect. The need for legislation designed to regulate the sale of securities became apparent. 

Extent and Purpose of State Laws 

Legislation relating to the sale of securities was first enacted by Kansas in 1911, and by 1923 all of the states except Delaware and Nevada had adopted such legislation. In 1931, Delaware enacted such a law, leaving Nevada the only state without some regulation of the sale of securities at the present time. Known generally as "blue-sky" laws,¹ they were quickly attacked as to their constitutionality and several state and lower federal courts held a series of such statutes unconstitutional. However, all questions as to their constitutionality under the federal constitution were put at rest by the Supreme Court of the United States when that court in three decisions handed down in 1917 held such laws to be a constitutional exercise of the state's police power to legislate for the general welfare of the people in the prevention of frauds.2 

1 "The name that is given to the law indicates the evil at which it is aimed, that is, to use the language of a cited case, 'speculative schemes which have no more basis than so many feet of blue sky'; or, as stated by counsel in another case, 'to stop the sale of stock in fly-bynight concerns, visionary oil wells, distant gold mines, and other like fraudulent exploitations.' (Italics added.) Hall v. Geiger-Jones Co., 242 U. S. 539, 550 (1917). 999 

2 Hall v. Geiger-Jones Co., 242 U. S. 539 (1917); Caldwell v. Sioux Falls Stock Yards 

Co., 242 U. S. 559 (1917); Merrick v. N. W. Halsey & Co., 242 U. S. 568 (1917). 402

REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 403 

Although the underlying purpose of the blue-sky laws of the various states is to protect the investing public in one way or another, they differ widely both in scope and detail. In some states the statute is designed only to prevent fraud, leaving it to the individual purchaser to determine, unhampered by fraud or misrepresentation, the wisdom of his purchase. In other states the statute is designed not only to prevent fraud in the sale of securities by requiring a full disclosure of all pertinent facts and establishing penalties for misrepresentation and deceit, but also to prevent the sale of securities which have been found to be unsound or of low quality according to standards specified in the statute or the sale of securities on terms not considered fair.

Nature of Requirements 

Reflecting the varying purposes or objectives of the various state laws, it is not surprising to find marked differences in their requirements relating to new security issues. The so-called "fraud” type of law exists in only four states and merely provides criminal penalties for fraudulent action. The attorney general or some other official of the state is given authority to investigate and, in his discretion, to institute court proceedings to restrain the distribution of issues which are believed to be fraudulent. Such statutes do not require either the licensing of dealers in securities or the qualification or registration of securities to be sold.

The second type, also existing in a small minority of states, provides only for the licensing of the securities dealer and does not require that the securities be registered or qualified. Such statutes usually declare, in effect, that no person shall engage in business in the state as a dealer in securities without being licensed to do so. 

Authority to refuse a license and to revoke for cause a license once issued is vested in some state official or regulatory body as a securities commission.

The third and most common type of blue-sky law requires both that the securities be qualified or registered and that dealers in securities be licensed. Qualification of new securities ordinarily consists of filing rather extensive information concerning the issuing corpora- 

8 These states are New York, New Jersey, Maryland, and Delaware. 

4 Examples of this type of law may be found in Connecticut, Maine, Pennsylvania, and 

Rhode Island.

tion, its properties and business, the details of the issue, and the payment of a filing or application fee. If the applicant corporation is a non-resident, designation of an agent in the state is necessary in order to facilitate the serving of court orders in actions arising out of violation of the law. The offering is then permitted only upon a finding by the public official or administrative body charged with administration of the securities law that the proposed sale would not constitute a fraud or work a fraud upon purchasers. In some states, as illustrated in the Alabama statute set forth below, such a finding may be based on the public official's conclusion that the security is sound or that the business of the issuer is of a sound and non-speculative character. 

The permit to sell is limited to a stipulated amount of securities and may be conditioned as to price or otherwise. In addition to the usual criminal penalties, blue-sky laws generally provide that sales made in violation of the law are voidable at the instance of the purchaser. 

Example of a Blue-Sky Law 

An example of a statute designed to protect investors against the sale of unsound securities is the Alabama blue-sky law. The Alabama

Securities Act provides that the state securities commission shall refuse to qualify securities and shall prohibit their sale in the state upon finding, among other things; (a) That the sale of such securities would work a fraud, deception or imposition upon the purchasers thereof, or that the proposed disposal of such securities is on unfair terms; or (b) That the articles of incorporation or association, declaration or trust, charter, constitution, by-laws, or other organization papers of the issuer are unfair, unjust, inequitable, illegal or oppressive; or (c) That the issuers or guarantors of such securities are insolvent, or are in failing circumstances, or are not trustworthy; or (d) That the issuer's plan of business is unfair, inequitable, dishonest, or fraudulent; or 5 In some states securities not exempt and thus subject to qualification are divided into two classes. In the first class are placed securities of corporations having an earnings record meeting certain minimum standards. Other securities are placed in the second or residual class. St. Ch. 121, Secs. 104, 105, 116)

(f) That the reasonable value of any property or assets of the issuer for which the issuer has issued or proposes to issue securities is less than the par or face value, or the issue price, as the case may be, of all of the securities of the issuer so issued or to be issued in payment therefor; or .... (h) That the sale of such securities is a mere scheme of either the issuer or the applicant to dispose of worthless securities of no real intrinsic value, at the expense of the purchasers of said securities; ....

The contrast between the duty of a state regulatory body under such a statute to pass on the quality of the security and the function of the Securities and Exchange Commission under the Securities Act should be noted. As will be observed in the discussion of the Securities Act later in this chapter, it is not the function of the Securities and Exchange Commission to pass upon the quality of the securities being offered. Its primary duty is only to assure a full disclosure of all material facts in the registration statement and to require that the prospectus meets the standards set forth in the Securities Act. 

Exemptions of State Laws 

Laws of the third type ordinarily contain generous exemptions both of securities and of transactions. The securities exempted are usually those where their safety or character are thought to be assured by the nature of the business of the issuer, by public regulation of the issuer, or by some other assuring factor. They ordinarily include, among others: securities issued or guaranteed by the United States government, by any state or any political subdivision of a state or by any foreign government; issues of banks or corporations supervised or controlled by the state or United States government; issues of public utility corporations supervised by the state or federal governments; securities of educational and eleemosynary institutions; securities listed and dealt in on the New York and other approved stock exchanges; and certain types of local securities about which there is presumed to be sufficient knowledge.

Transactions which provide a basis for the exemption of the securities affected usually include, among others: judicial sales, distribution of stock dividends to stockholders, and sales to those who are presumed to have enough knowledge to safeguard themselves, such as licensed dealers and banks.7 

7 For a good discussion of the usual content of state blue-sky laws and the general nature of their provisions, see Note, "Blue-Sky Legislation," Iowa Law Review, Vol. 23, p. 102.

Weaknesses of State Laws Unfortunately, legislative action by the individual states has proved. exceedingly inadequate to protect the investing public against the abuses and frauds arising in the issue and sale of new securities. The huge amount of estimated losses during the decade prior to 19338 in worthless securities was seemingly little reduced by the existence of blue-sky laws in practically every state in the Union. Various legal devices made successful evasion of state blue-sky laws relatively easy and the complex interstate character of most corporate financing meant that the blue-sky promoter could obtain almost complete immunity by the mere transfer of his operations to interstate commerce where both practical and constitutional limitations prevented effective state action.10

The Beginnings of a Federal Program 

Under the Mail Fraud Act¹¹ passed by Congress in 1909 there had been a form of federal regulation of sales of fraudulent securities through the use of the mails, but this legislation needed to be supplemented.12 A much more comprehensive federal program was obviously essential in order to secure effective regulation of new security sales. Ultimately, the catastrophic break in the stock market in 1929 and the ensuing business depression served as a spearhead to mobilize public opinion in favor of a federal program. 

In the political campaign of 1932 and thereafter, President Roosevelt constantly emphasized the need of protecting the small inves- 8 The total has been estimated at $25,000,000,000. tor. In place of the historic policy of caveat emptor, he advocated a doctrine of "let the seller also beware." He maintained the position that the financing process was largely of a fiduciary character. "What we seek is a return to a clear understanding of the ancient truth that those who manage banks, corporations, and other agencies handling and using other people's money are trustees acting for others." 

Under this principle those engaged in the process of financing corporations should be held strictly accountable for their "wares." This basic policy finally took shape in the following legislative measures: 

(1) the Securities Act of 1933;13 (2) the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

The first of these laws is designed primarily to regulate public offerings of new securities14 and a discussion of its main provisions will constitute the balance of this chapter. The Securities Exchange 

Act is concerned mainly with the regulation of the national stock exchanges and the listing of securities and is treated in a succeeding chapter. 

State Laws Still Applicable 

At the outset, it should be made clear that enactment of the Federal Securities Act did not foreclose state regulation of the sale of securities. Section 18 of the Act provides: "Nothing in this subchapter shall affect the jurisdiction of the securities commission (or any agency or office performing like functions) of any State or Territory of the United States, or the District of Columbia, over any security or any person." The court in Securities and Exchange Commission v. Timetrust, Inc.15 said that this section did not indicate an intention on the part of Congress to limit the Securities Act to activities in interstate commerce but, at most, merely gave concurrent jurisdiction in such cases to the Securities and Exchange Commission 18 Numerous amendments to the Securities Act of 1933 were made by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, principally in the exemption provisions and the civil liability provisions.

Basic Purpose of the Securities Act 

Intelligent consideration of particular provisions of the Securities

Act requires an initial survey of its fundamental purpose. The clear objective of the Act is to assure adequate publicity and disclosure of facts which will enable potential investors to form an intelligent judgment of the worth of newly issued securities. To this end the Act prohibits the use of the mails or of any means or instruments of transportation or communication in interstate commerce to offer, sell or deliver after sale any security,17 with certain exceptions, unless: (1) the issuer files a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission containing certain prescribed information about the security issue; and (2) distribution of the security to investors is accompanied or preceded by a prospectus containing in condensed form most of the information given upon registration. Also, irrespective of whether the security concerned must be registered under the Act, there is a prohibition against the use of mails or any means of interstate commerce for the sale of securities through false or misleading communications or by fraudulent methods.18 A seller who

violates either of these two prohibitions is subject to both civil liabilities (purchaser may sue for damages or, in certain cases, rescind his purchase and recover the consideration paid) and to criminal penalties if the violation is willful. 

Administration of the Act is in the hands of the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Securities Act, as originally passed, intrusted the administration of the Act to the Federal Trade Commission. Later, the Securities Exchange Act, passed in 1934, transferred administration of the Act to the more specialized Securities and Exchange Commission.

It must be understood that the Securities Act does not in any way guarantee either the quality of the security or the soundness of the business of the issuer. The absence of requirements covering the merits of new security issues has been emphasized by both the President¹9 and Congress.20 The registration statement simply places certain prescribed facts about the security on record, and the prospectus conveys these facts to potential investors in convenient form. Neither guarantees the quality of the security about which the facts are given nor states any conclusion as to the merits of the security. To show plainly the absence of certification as to merit, the Commission has required that "on the front page of every prospectus" over which it has control, there shall be placed "in conspicuous print" the following: 

THESE SECURITIES HAVE NOT BEEN APPROVED OR DISAPPROVED BY THE SECURITIES AND EXCHANGE COMMISSION. 

(insert name of issuer) has registered the securities by filing certain information with the Commission. The Commission has not passed on the merits of any securities registered with it. IT IS A CRIMINAL OFFENSE TO REPRESENT THAT THE COMMISSION HAS APPROVED THESE SECURITIES OR HAS MADE ANY FINDINGS THAT THE STATEMENTS IN THIS PROS- PECTUS OR IN THE REGISTRATION STATEMENT ARE Correct. (Rule 825, 

Rules and Regulations under the Securities Act.)

Under the Act, the Commission must register any security issued where the registration statement is not on its face incomplete or inaccurate. The highly speculative character of the business enterprise 

19 See Hearings H. R. 4314, op. cit., p. 1. 

20 See Hearings S. 875, op. cit., pp. 103-5.

in which the issuer is engaged is no ground for refusing use of the mails or the channels of interstate commerce.21 

As a matter of policy the investor should and under the Act will continue to carry the business risks inherent in the commitment of capital, and losses (without recovery) should still remain as a more or less normal feature of investment. That portion of risk arising from the lack of information or from misrepresentation should tend to be eliminated. This is the primary prupose of the Act, and it is not surprising that it has been referred to as the "Truth in Securities Act."

Provisions of the Act 

In the ensuing discussion of the provisions of the Act consideration will be given to the following topics: (1) securities and transactions exempted from the application of the Act; (2) registration requirements; (3) prospectus requirements; and (4) civil and criminal liabilities arising from false registration statements and prospectuses, and false and misleading communications.

Certain securities and transactions are exempted from the registration requirement and the consequent duty of sending a prospectus. 

The exemption afforded does not, however, extend either to the criminal provisions of the Act or to the prohibitions of the Act against fraudulent interstate transactions. Thus, even though a security is exempt, the seller is still liable for fraud or misrepresentation whenever there is use of the mails or any means of interstate commerce, and the purchaser may rescind the purchase and recover the consideration paid, or sue for damages.

Securities Exempted from Registration and Prospectus Require ments

In presenting the most important classes of securities which are exempted from registration, it is convenient to classify them according to the reasons which serve as a basis for their exclusion. The first

group consists of issues which are already subject to government influence either as a result of direct issue by a governmental body itself or as a result of existing supervision or regulation. In this category will be found: 

1. Government securities, including securities issued or guaranteed by the federal or state governments, or by their instrumentalities or political subdivisions. 

2. Securities issued by common carriers, the issuance of which is subject to the regulation and control of the Interstate Commerce Commission. 

3. Securities of national banks, state banking institutions which are under state supervision, and building and loan associations (meeting certain specified requirements).

The second basis for the exemption of securities arises more especially out of the nature of the transaction. For instance, instruments used in the financing of current operations do not normally find an outlet in the investment market but are usually handled by specialized financial institutions with adequate facilities of their own to obtain the necessary supporting information. Securities which are used in transactions which do not materially affect the status quo may be excluded by virtue of this restricted influence. The following types of exemption are illustrative of these principles: 

1. Drafts and other documents arising out of current transactions where the maturity does not exceed nine months. 

2. Securities exchanged for outstanding securities where no commissions or other remuneration is paid for soliciting the exchange. 

Similarly, broad exemptions are extended to securities issued as a result of reorganization. 

Securities are also exempted where the burden on the issuer is obviously disproportionate to the benefit to the public. On this basis, the size of the issue and the nature of the activities of the issuing body are the chief determining factors for exemption, and are illustrated by the following: 

1. Securities issued by non-profit organizations which are operated for religious, educational, benevolent, fraternal, or charitable purposes. 

2. Securities exempted because of size of issue by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Securities Act empowers the Commission to exempt securities from registration where it finds that registration is not necessary “in the public interest and for the pro-

tection of investors by reason of the small amount involved or the limited character of the public offering." This power of the Commission is limited to offerings not in excess of $100,000.22 

Transactions Exempted from Registration and Prospectus Require ments 1 After the initial or primary distribution of a security has been effected, ensuing transactions in the security become a form of trading rather than distribution. Trading transactions are covered mainly in the Securities Exchange Act, but the distinction between trading and distribution is pertinent here as a means of delimiting the scope of the Securities Act. To avoid unnecessary restriction of market activity, all transactions which are not a part of the primary distribution of a security are exempted. Thus, transactions by persons other than an issuer, underwriter, or dealer are exempted since they constitute trading in securities after their initial distribution. This exemption assures a market unfettered with registration and prospectus requirements for the sale and purchase of securities by the public, and this even though the original distribution of the security should be suspended by the Securities and Exchange Commission. 

Transactions by a dealer (including an underwriter who is no longer acting in an underwriting capacity with respect to the security involved in the transaction, and including a broker since the Act defines a dealer to include a broker) are also free from the registration and prospectus requirements where they occur more than one year after the date of original offering to the public. An exception to this rule is found where the transactions relate to securities which are part of an unsold allotment left over from the original distribution. Since the primary distribution of a security usually is completed within one year, the provision covering trading by dealers is consistent with the policy of the Act to regulate only the distribution of securities and to avoid unnecessary interference with open-market activities. Similarly, ordinary brokerage transactions which are executed after the initial sale upon the unsolicited orders of customers need not be accompanied or preceded by a prospectus and may be engaged in without incurring possible civil liability because of the security being non-exempt and unregistered. 

22 Pursuant to this provision of the Act the Commission has adopted regulations exempting various types of small issues of securities upon certain conditions. The regulations thus adopted fall into two classes: (a) regulations relating to securities designated as "fractional undivided interests in oil or gas rights," and (b) regulations relating to other securities.

An important exemption, and one which has had marked influence on the distribution of securities in recent years, is where no public offering is involved. This occurs when the issuing corporation itself disposes of a new issue by a private sale to one or only a few purchasers. Ordinarily, when an issue is disposed of by private negotiation the purchasers will be institutional or other large and experienced investors capable of protecting themselves. Particularly prominent are the life insurance companies which account for the entire bond financing of some corporations. 

The line of differentiation between a public and a private offering is not always easy to draw. There is the question of how many purchasers would constitute a public offering, and likewise, the point has been raised that even a single purchaser may later involve the public by redistribution. Another example is an offering to existing stockholders, and in one such instance a court has held this to be a public offering within the meaning of the Act if the number of existing shareholders is large enough.23

It will be observed that the Securities Act fails to make certain exemptions which are commonly found in the state blue-sky laws. 

Some of these are: (1) securities listed on the New York Stock Ex change and certain other national exchanges; (2) securities issued or guaranteed by foreign governments; (3) securities of public utilities which are supervised by state officers or other state regulatory bodies. 

Registration Requirements 

Schedule A of the Securities Act, which specifies the information which must be contained in the registration statement, contains thirtytwo paragraphs. This of itself indicates something of the extent and quantity of information required. The following are some of the more important matters which the registration statement must contain. 

1. A detailed balance sheet as of a date not more than ninety days prior to the date of the filing of the registration statement, and a profit-and-loss statement of the issuer for the latest fiscal year and each of the two preceding years. Forms are provided for each of these statements, and in addition most of the items must be sup-

Need for Registration 

Our discussion of the Securities Act was prefaced with emphasis of the fact that the fundamental purpose of the Act is disclosure of sufficient information to furnish purchasers of newly issued securities a basis for intelligent judgment of their worth. An important means of making this possible is the registration statement which assembles a complete financial picture of the company. It needs to be reiterated that no guaranty of value is intended, the sole objective being to provide investors with reliable and accessible information. 

In the past, too many investors have been innocent victims of misrepresentation of facts, or have been unable to get pertinent operating and financial statistics at all. Undoubtedly, many individuals do not and will not take advantage of the facilities provided, but failure

REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 415 

to apprise themselves of the facts will at least be their own responsibility.

There has been some disposition on the part of industry to regard registration as an additional burden in the form of unnecessary delay and extra expense. However, the existence of reliable and adequate information is obviously essential to ordinary investment as well as to continued financing by worthy business enterprise. As business becomes more accustomed to procedure under the Securities Act and adjusts its operations to the requirement of the Act, the costs of assembling the necessary information to comply with the Act should not prove too burdensome. Little objection of merit can be raised against the fundamental purpose of the registration requirement, and even those engaged in the security business have generally recognized the propriety of furnishing the public with comprehensive information.

Approval of Registration Statement by the Commission 

If the Securities and Exchange Commission raises no objection to a registration statement within a period of twenty days after its filing, it automatically becomes effective. On the other hand, if the statement is found to be on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect, the Commission may, after notice and opportunity for hearing, issue an order refusing to permit the statement to become effective until it has been properly amended. Even after the registration statement has become effective the Commission may at any time after fifteen days' notice, and opportunity for hearing, issue a "stop order" suspending its effectiveness. This subsequent suspension may arise if it appears to the Commission that the registration statement includes any untrue statement of material fact or omits any material fact required to be stated therein, the result of which is to make the statement misleading. The Commission, in order to determine in such a case whether a stop order should be issued, is empowered to undertake a complete investigation.

Right To Withdraw Registration Statement 

The right of the issuer to withdraw the registration statement after it is once filed has several times been the subject of litigation in the courts and of dispute before the Securities and Exchange Commission. The question is an important one, since if a registrant can

withdraw his registration statement at will, he can prevent an investigation by the Commission and thus prevent fraudulent or misleading statements which he has made from being brought to light. The 

Act provides that a registration statement may be withdrawn with the consent of the Commission "with due regard to the public interest and the protection of investors."

The question of the right to withdraw a registration statement first arose, and was passed upon by the Supreme Court of the United States, in Jones v. Securities and Exchange Commission.24 The Commission had notified the issuer of its intention to conduct an investigation to determine whether or not a stop order suspending the effectiveness of the registration statement should be issued. In that case the Supreme Court held that the Commission could not deny a registrant the right to withdraw his registration statement when no securities had been issued and the statement had not yet become effective. The court took the position that to permit an investigation under such circumstances would allow the Commission to exercise unconstitutional investigatory powers. The majority of the court, as opposed to the minority, apparently considered that the good which might result from an investigation in giving publicity to attempted fraud, or in preventing a recurrence of a similar statement from the same registrant, was not sufficiently strong to support the Commission's finding that it was in the public interest to deny permission to withdraw.

The decision obviously limits the scope of influence of the Commission in investigating and unmasking fraudulent registrants who try to seek protection in retreat. In a vigorous dissenting opinion, three judges criticized the holding of the majority of the court making, among others, the following comments:

There are dangers in spreading a belief that untruths and half truths, designed to be passed on for the guidance of confiding buyers, are to be ranked as peccadillos, or even perhaps as part of the amenities of business. When wrongs such as these have been committed or attempted, they must be dragged to light and pilloried. To permit an offending registrant to stifle an inquiry by precipitate retreat on the eve of his exposure is to give immunity to guilt; to encourage falsehood and evasion; to invite the cunning and unscrupulous to gamble with detection. If withdrawal without leave may check investigation before securities have been issued, it may do as much thereafter, unless indeed consistency be thrown to the winds, for by the teaching of the decision withdrawal without 24 4298 U. S. 1 (1936).

REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 417 

leave is equivalent to a stop order, with the result that forthwith there is nothing to investigate. The statute and its sanctions become the sport of clever knaves. 

Recent decisions have, fortunately, presented a more liberal interpretation of the investigatory functions of the Commission and its power to determine what is in the interest of the public and investors. Thus an order of the Commission refusing withdrawal of the registration statement after the effective date of the statement but before any shares were issued has been upheld by the courts.25 And one case has even gone so far as to uphold the jurisdiction of the Securities and Exchange Commission to conduct an investigation and hearing to determine whether a stop order should be issued after all of the securities comprising the issue have been sold to the public.26 The court pointed out that the registration statement is not only a condition precedent to the right of the issuer to use the mails and interstate commerce for the sale of the securities, but is also, even after their original distribution, a vehicle of information for the investing public. 

In the case just referred to, the court said among other things: 

We do not agree with the contention that when all the securities had been disposed of by the issuer and its dealers the purpose of the registration statement was fully served and hence there was no need for a stop order. It does not follow when the securities pass out of the hands of the issuer and the dealers that they cease to be the subject-matter of sales in interstate commerce, and that the mails and facilities of interstate commerce cease to be used to effectuate their sales. In fact, the opposite is obviously true. Furthermore, members of the investing public might acquire the information contained in the registration statement during the time the securities are being sold by the issuer and its dealers, and might place reliance thereon in purchasing such securities from third persons after they have all passed out of the hands of the issuer and its dealers. 

Obviously, so long as the securities are outstanding, purchases thereof will continue to be made in reliance on the registration statement, unless notice of its unreliability is given by a stop order. 

Such an attitude on the part of the courts bids fair to result in enforcing truthfulness in registration statements and in making them of real value as a continuing source of information beyond the period of original distribution.

Prospectus-A Source of Information for Investors While the registration statement is intended as a primary source of information for the investor, there are limitations on its usefulness because of its bulky character, as well as its comparative inaccessibility. 

To alleviate somewhat these shortcomings, the Securities and Exchange Commission has established public reference rooms at both their home and regional offices as well as making photostatic copies available. 

Even so, this does not provide a convenient or simple means for giving information to potential investors.

To assure wider disposition of the essential facts relating to new security issues the law stipulates that a prospectus be given to every person solicited, and to every purchaser either before or at the time of sale. The prospectus must contain in condensed form practically all of the information contained in the registration statement, except copies of counsel opinions, agreements, contracts, organization papers of the issuer, and the like. It is filed along with the registration statement so that it may be reviewed for adequacy and accuracy of content by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The Commission is, however, authorized to approve elimination from the prospectus of any information required in the registration statement which it feels to be unnecessary or inappropriate for the protection of the public or investors.

Liabilities-False Registration Statement or Failure To File 

The requirements which relate to the offering and sale of new security issues obviously call for some means of effective enforcement. 

This is provided by the establishment of civil and criminal liabilities, as well as by empowering the Commission to investigate possible violations, to institute court action to enjoin violations, and to seek a court order compelling compliance with the Act. Willful violation of any provision of the Act or rule of the Commission is made a penal offense subject to a maximum penalty of five years' imprisonment and a fine of $5,000. The civil liabilities are more complicated, more technical, and hence more difficult for the layman clearly to understand. Yet study of the Act would fall short of full understanding if attention were not given to the liabilities which attach to violation of its prohibitions or to failure to comply with its requirements. 

First, liability may arise because of the failure of the seller to file a registration statement or to send a prospectus. In this event,

REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 419 

there is established an unconditional liability to refund the purchase price or to pay damages, but it runs in favor of the immediate purchaser only.

Second, liability may arise where the registration statement omits or makes an untrue statement of a "material fact required to be stated therein or necessary to make the statements therein not misleading." 

Prior to the amendments to the Securities Act made by the Securities

Exchange Act of 1934, such a misstatement or omission gave rise to liability if the purchaser did not know of the untruth or omission at the time of the purchase. There was no need under the Act as passed in 1933 for the purchaser to prove that he relied on the misstatement or omission in making the purchase. The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 made a considerable concession to the critics of this feature by amending the Securities Act so as to limit the blanket character of the liability. In brief, it provided that where the issuer had published an earnings report covering a full year subsequent to the effective date of the registration statement, and if the purchaser had acquired his security after the earnings statement had been made so available, then he must prove that he acquired the security relying on the untrue statement or omission. That is the law as it exists today. 

A seller who sells when no registration statement has been filed as required by the Act, as was noted above, is liable only to the person purchasing the security from him and not to any subsequent purchaser. On the other hand, where a registration statement is in effect and the suit is based on a misstatement or omission therein a remedy is given to all persons acquiring the security, even though it was not obtained directly from the person being sued. The extent of such liability is startling to all at first impression and even studied thought emphasizes its broad coverage. Yet the continuing liability may be justified on the theory that information concerning a security given out at the time of flotation does not merely impress the immediate purchaser but has a profound influence on the general market opinion of the security.

Persons Liable 

One of the most remarkable features of the Act is the number and diverse character of persons who are made liable for a false or misleading registration statement. The remedy runs not only against signatories of the registration statement, but also against (2) every person who was a director of (or person performing similar

functions) or partner in, the issuer at the time of the filing of the part of the registration statement with respect to which his liability is asserted; (3) every person who, with his consent, is named in the registration statement as being or about to become a director, person performing similar functions, or partner; (4) every accountant, engineer, or appraiser, or any person whose profession gives authority to a statement made by him, who has with his consent been named as having prepared or certified any part of the registration statement, or as having prepared or certified any report or valuation which is used in connection with the registration statement, with respect to the statement in such registration statement, report, or valuation, which purports to have been prepared or certified by him; and (5) every underwriter with respect to such security. 

Liability is also imposed upon "every person who, by or through stock ownership, agency, or otherwise, or who, pursuant to or in connection with an agreement or understanding with one or more other persons by or through stock ownership, agency, or otherwise, controls" any of the persons enumerated above. Prior to the amendments made by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 the liability of controlling persons was judged by the same standards as the liability of persons controlled. However, the Securities Exchange Act added an amendment which provided that controlling persons are not liable if "the controlling person had no knowledge of or reasonable grounds to believe in the existence of the facts by reason of which the liability of the controlled person is alleged to exist." The effect of this amendment is to assure the controlling person reasonable safety from liability unless he colludes in the misrepresentation or omission. 

Avoidance of Liability 

The person being sued may avoid liability to the extent that he is able to prove that part or all of the depreciated value which caused a loss arose from causes other than the false statement or omission. 

Thus, the decline of security values as a result of adverse general market movements or losses reflecting the decline of a specific field of industry are not cause for liability. Moreover, even where there is a causal relationship between the defendant's loss and the misstatement or omission, the liability imposed is still not absolute, except as against the issuer. First, any one of the persons liable may avoid liability by showing that before the effective date of the registration statement he resigned from the office, capacity, or relationship in which he was described in the registration statement, and that he so notified the Commission. Second, if he can show that the part of

REGULATION OF THE SALE OF NEW SECURITY OFFERINGS 421 

the registration statement with respect to which his liability is asserted became effective without his knowledge, he may avoid liability if he can show that upon becoming aware of such fact he resigned, notified the Commission, and gave public notice. Finally, he may escape liability by proving that after reasonable investigation he had reasonable grounds to believe and did believe at the time the registration statement became effective that the statements therein were true and that there had been no failure to state any material facts. 

The Act prescribes that the test of reasonable investigation and reasonable grounds for belief in the accuracy of statement shall be: "the standard of reasonableness required of a prudent man in the management of his own property." Prior to the amendments made by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 the standard of reasonableness was defined to mean that “required of a person occupying a fiduciary relationship." Opposition to the imposition of a fiduciary standard forced the amendment.

Damages Recoverable for False Registration Statement 

The amount of damages which may be recovered is first of all limited to the price at which the security was originally offered to the public. Within this basic limitation, damages may be recovered as follows: (1) The difference between the amount paid and the value of the security at the time of suit; or (2) the difference between the amount paid and the price obtained for the security when disposed of in the market before the suit was brought; or (3) the difference between the amount paid and the price at which the security was disposed of after the suit (but before judgment was rendered), if the damages calculated in this manner are less than those determined under (1). 

Civil Liabilities for False or Misleading Communications in General 

Civil liability under the Act may arise other than from a false registration statement or a failure to file such a statement or to send a prospectus. Any person who sells a security by use of the mails or any other means of interstate commerce through the use of a prospectus or oral communication which includes an untrue statement of material fact or omits to state a material fact is liable unless either of the following two conditions exists: (1) the purchaser knew of the untruth or omission; (2) the person being sued can prove

that he did not know and in the exercise of reasonable care could not have known of the untruth or omission. 

The remedy for this liability is the same as for failure to file a registration statement or to send a prospectus at all, namely rescission of the sale and refund of the purchase price or damages if the purchaser no longer owns the security. And, as in the case of failure to file a registration statement or send a prospectus, suit may be brought only by the immediate purchaser. 

Value of Civil Liability Provisions 

There has been much criticism of the civil liability provisions of the Securities Act and considerable controversy as to their real value. 

During a period of approximately seven years after the enactment of the Act in May, 1933, the civil remedies provided for in the Act had been invoked in only sixteen instances, and recovery had been obtained in only three cases.27 But the worth of the civil liability features as an instrument of enforcement is probably not to be judged solely by the extent to which they have been utilized. They probably serve a more useful purpose as a deterrent to possible violations. Other means of enforcement are the investigatory powers of the Commission and its right to seek a court injunction against violation or to obtain a court order compelling compliance with the Act.
