CHAPTER XXII  

RGANIZED markets for securities do not serve as a direct medium for the distribution of securities, but they do furnish a means of appraisal and a guide to many of the phases of corporate financing. There is a mutual and causal relationship between the security exchanges and their activities, and the distribution of corporate securities. The organized markets play an important part in determining the nature of corporate security issues, and likewise the success and failure of corporations affect trading activities. 

The following contributions of securities exchanges to the financial system may be noted: (1) directing the flow of capital funds, (2) elevating corporate standards, (3) providing a market for investors, (4) facilitating the distribution of new security issues, (5) furnishing an index of corporate and business activity, (6) furnishing the means of publicity.

Directing the Flow of Capital 

While the exchanges are seldom, if ever, used directly to raise funds for corporations, they do exert great influence upon the channels through which funds flow. They function like a traffic signal, indicating a green light when certain fields offer the necessary inducement to attract capital and blazing a red light when the outlook for new investment is not attractive. Influence upon the flow of capital investment is accomplished by the prices established in the market for the individual securities and by their relative yields. Unfavorable or unprofitable conditions are the cause of lower prices while a promising outlook acts as a stimulus in raising security prices. Obviously, the resulting yields will bear an inverse relationship to the price. Unattractive fields are likely to have low-priced securities with high-income yields, or no yield at all. 

The established markets serve in many respects as a proving or testing ground for the issuance of new securities. The types of security issues which are in demand are indicated, and investor support or interest in the various fields of enterprise is recorded by the volume 425

and other characteristics of trading. In appraising market activity as a guide to the financing of new enterprises or of expansion of existing companies, there is need to distinguish between the yield on market price and that on book investment. Thus, a low market return may often be an indication of large profits on the actual capital outlay. Under the circumstances, concerns with this status may find it easier to raise additional funds than those whose securities afford a comparatively high yield on the basis of market price. The latter may seem to have the advantage of offering greater income, but usually this is more than offset by the risk differential. 

The markets are equally effective as a means of registering the influence of various social trends or acts of government which are likely to have an effect on business. Such basic movements or changes will influence the entire securities market, but the constituent elements of the market will be affected in varying degrees. The devaluation of the standard money may affect the market as a whole, but its influence will be greater in some quarters than others. For instance, gold mining companies will gain considerably, but corporations involved in the importation of foreign goods may be seriously handicapped.

The importance of the proper direction of funds has been stressed in recent years. Many people regard the automatic direction, described above, as inadequate and relatively inefficient and recommend increased planning of investment by some central agency. This is not the place to discuss the merits of a planned economy, but it should be observed that too often the use of capital funds in this way is not subjected to the true test of solvency, that is, the ability of the enterprise to earn an amount sufficient to cover all expenses including depreciation as well as to yield a normal return on the investment.

The markets not only serve as an indication of the fields needing funds, but they also reflect the relative appeal of the two fundamental sources of funds, namely, stocks and bonds. Generally speaking, bonds have greater favor in times of cheap money, and stocks appear to be more advantageous when money rates are high. Some criticism is leveled against financial management for pursuing the line of least resistance and issuing the type of securities for which there is the greatest market demand. It is contended that such policies are purely those of expediency and take undue advantage of innocent investors.

However, it would seem that such a criticism relates more to the economic system than to corporation finance practice. As long as market conditions are a reflection of the composite of individual consumer preferences, financial management cannot reasonably be blamed for taking advantage of favorable situations. At least, indictment seems inappropriate as long as representations to the public are kept entirely honest.

Elevation of Corporate Standards 

Security exchanges tend to raise the plane of financial practice. 

Efforts of exchange organizations do achieve such an end because standards of behavior tend to be raised in any type of organized activity. In the field of securities, as in the sports world, the creation of a league or conference results in the establishment of operating standards, and a mechanism is provided to deal with those parties who do not conform to the accepted practices. 

As a result of the depression, some proponents of public welfare questioned whether or not security exchanges were adequately fulfilling this function. These critics contended that an umpire, somebody independent of the exchanges themselves, was necessary for purposes of proper supervision. This was provided in 1934 in the form of the Securities and Exchange Commission which now regulates the exchanges and has established numerous requirements prerequisite to the listing of securities. In fairness to the private administration of exchanges, it should be said that much of the information now required for listing of securities was previously required and for the most part was made available to the public. As a former member of the Commission has said, "The Securities Exchange Act has been, perhaps, as much an experiment in the self-government of exchanges as an effort of governmental regulation."1 On the other hand, the creation of a public commission constitutes a more formal recognition of the public service characteristics of the security exchanges and should enhance the trust of the public-at-large in the activities of these organizations. Whether or not this condition will be fully realized will depend primarily on how successfully the Commission avoids political pressure, and upon the type of its personnel. 

1 Address of James M. Landis, member, Securities and Exchange Commission, before the 

Associated Stock Exchanges, St. Louis, Missouri, May 20, 1935.

Providing a Market for Investors

One of the chief services of securities exchanges in facilitating the financing of corporations is the provision of a place and means for trading in securities by the investors who wish to buy and sell. Of course, this is primarily a service to investors, but without such facilities, corporations would find considerable difficulty in making their financial programs effective. The initial sale of new security issues is not made in the open market, but banking syndicates and other agencies could dispose of new issues only with great effort if there were no ready market serving to establish later values and to provide facilities for investors to dispose of their holdings whenever they deem such action wise or necessary. 

Funds invested in business are necessarily congealed for a long period of time. In some instances, there is little expectation of their ever returning to a liquid state, and in most cases a rather long period of time would be required. Moreover, business enterprise is seldom conducted with the intention of liquidation at the end of a fixed period. The basic philosophy is that of a going concern having indefinite, if not perpetual, life. As a reward for the sacrifice of the immediate funds, it is expected that sufficient earnings will appear. 

The realization of this hope constitutes evidence of the success of the enterprise from an economic point of view, but it does not necessarily meet all the demands of the investor. At the end of a few years, he may have other needs for his funds, and unless he were able to shift his share in the original enterprise to some one else, his freedom of activity would be greatly curtailed. The security markets provide this element of shiftability and lend flexibility to a condition which in itself is quite rigid. Because of the presence of this ready market for securities, investors are, of course, more willing to make commitments, and the whole process of financing business enterprise is facilitated.

Some reference should be made to the so-called "over-the-counter" transactions wherein no fixed market place is established but where buyer and seller are brought together by means of dealers in securities. 

These dealers usually fall into the category of merchants since they have clear title to the securities they sell. They help to give marketability on a small scale, but it is not sufficiently open in character to constitute a basis on which funds may be attracted from broad areas. 

The over-the-counter transactions lack the essential characteristics necessary for a continuous market with many buyers and many

sellers and with a mechanism to keep all parties fully informed of the nature of the transactions.

Because of the deficiencies of the over-the-counter method of sale, the investor lacks complete assurance that he can buy or sell at the proper price, and the irregularity of transactions plus the unknown volume of sales make it difficult for him to act intelligently. The 

Securities and Exchange Commission has already recognized these basic defects and has provided more adequate facilities of organization. 

Such securities may not be bought on a margin basis, and definite steps are being taken to encourage listing many of these securities. 

At the same time, one cannot be unmindful of the part played by over-the-counter operations. There are 6,555 brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission to do business in the over-the-counter market.2

Facilitating the Distribution of New Security Issues 

As stated previously, new financing is seldom accomplished through open-market channels, but instead the corporation usually acts through a specialized selling medium. Large corporations usually sell outright to investment bankers who, in turn, sell to the public, while small businesses employ agents on a commission basis. 

In either event, the organized markets facilitate the task of sale to the ultimate investor in at least two ways: 

1. The fact that a security is listed encourages public participation. 

2. Listing aids the selling medium to carry the securities prior to their final sale to the public. Listed securities, especially those listed on the New York Stock Exchange, are much more acceptable as collateral than unlisted securities, and in the future the rights of bankers to accept unlisted securities as collateral for general business loans will be greatly limited. This is because listed securities have a known value and a ready market, but both of these qualities lacking for unlisted securities. are 

Furnishing an Index of Progress 

It has been shown that as an agency in directing the flow of capital, the securities market exercises considerable influence. Simultaneously it tends to serve as an indicator of business conditions. In analyzing the latter function, there is need to distinguish between the market purely as a measuring device and its use. 

The market's accuracy as a measuring device has long been a de- 

2 S.E.C., Sixth Annual Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1940, p. 113.

batable point. Many market observers believe that organized exchanges tend to carry movements too far in a given direction, probably because of the momentum gathered in the course of the movement. In periods of prosperity, it is contended that security prices go to unreasonably high levels and then crash as a result of the overextension. Likewise it is believed that when security prices decline, they drop to a level far below that warranted by business conditions. 

This is undoubtedly true if the market is regarded solely as an index of business activity. The market, however, reflects much more than business statistics and is, in reality, also affected by the psychological state of the nation. It reflects the exaggerated hopes of prosperity and the extreme pessimism which usually accompany a period of depression. While it is probably fair to state that the market is a fairly accurate index of business conditions as viewed by the country as a whole, this view is subject to qualification. The success of the stock markets in forecasting future business conditions has not been uniform, and there have been times when its action has been indecisive over periods of months' duration. It would be more accurate to regard the securities market as a barometer only in the limited sense which arises out of the market's ability of acquiring information before it is available to business in general. 

The question might be raised on this point as to what effect the regulation of the market by the Securities and Exchange Commission will have upon its accuracy as an index. Here as elsewhere a wide difference of opinion exists. Those who favor regulation contend that the exchanges will become more reliable indexes of the financial health of a nation. The main argument advanced in support of this position is that regulation stresses the publication of facts and tends to reduce the dangers of rumor and other forces of inside manipulation.3 Those on the other side of the question believe that regulation curtails the freedom of activity and thereby lessens the accuracy of the measuring device.

The correct answer is that much will depend upon the amount and kind of regulation. It will take time to gather sufficient experience 

8 For evidence of the efforts made by regulatory authorities to prevent manipulation see the Sixth Annual Report of the Securities and Exchange Commission for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1940, p. 92: ".... there is maintained at the Washington Office of the Commission a trained staff of specialists with practical experience in trading, as well as economists and technicians, whose sole responsibility it is to observe systematically by broad industrial categories the movements in both price and volume of all securities and to develop from such studies probable cases of manipulation.”

to render a reasonably accurate opinion on this question. Since 1933, the stock markets have displayed more erratic movements than was customary prior to that time. This has caused many people to conclude that regulation has created a thin and discontinuous market. 

While there may be an element of truth in this position, it must also be remembered that the years since 1933 have been among the most unusual in history. World economic and political conditions have been in a turmoil under the influence of forces which are not yet fully understood. For this reason, if for none other, it is difficult to draw conclusions as to the correct cause and effect relationship. 

Furnishing the Means of Publicity 

There is a close relationship between the publicity of corporate affairs and the elevation of corporate standards. Wide publicity tends to raise standards because only honesty and decency can stand up for long under widespread distribution of information. Organized exchanges constitute an important part in affording publicity to corporate information. It should be pointed out, however, that they do not gather nor guarantee the validity of news which is given out in connection with their operation. However, the exchanges do provide a centralization of trading in securities which directly facilitates the assembly and dissemination of news relating to the financial events of the day. In addition, the exchanges compel those companies whose securities are listed to publish periodical financial statements as well as certain other data which may be pertinent to the operation of these companies.

To what extent is the public entitled to knowledge of corporate affairs? The stockholders possess this right through their ownership; the bondholders are entitled to receive adequate reporting because of their investment; but the public has no such direct claim upon the corporation. On the other hand, the corporation is a social agency created by the state to advance the economic development of society. 

The corporation's form of organization and its rights are bestowed upon it rather than being inherent in its existence. Under these circumstances the corporation rightly has a debt to society as well as to its investors, which can best be met by giving wide publicity to corporate affairs of public interest. This can be done by the publication at regular intervals of financial statements as well as publishing from time to time other data of interest.

Financial statements offer the best source of corporate data, espe-

cially when they are published in the spirit of giving the public the news. Too often these statements have been issued merely to fulfill legal requirements of the state or demands of the exchanges and are inadequate as a source of information. Professor Ripley, in his wellknown book Main Street and Wall Street, classified reports into the following types. 

1. The pictorial which presents much in the form of pictures and other features but offers little actual information. 

2. The abbreviated type which is too short to convey information. 

Such reports are represented by those done on a single sheet of paper. 

3. The pompous but empty type where much is stated but little definite information is given. 

4. Those which depict general business conditions but fail to describe the welfare of the particular corporation itself. 

5. Reports characterized by information which is not essential and are lacking in pertinent data. 

6. The truly informative type of official report which is well represented by the reports of the United States Steel Corporation. 

Since the organization of the Securities and Exchange Commission with its attendant powers of regulation over the issuance and listing of corporation securities, there has been a decided improvement in the quality of the reports; but in the years prior to 1934, many corporations felt that it was unnecessary or improper to furnish information relating to their business. The exchanges, especially the New 

York Stock Exchange, played an important part in obtaining more satisfactory and usable information but lacked the power to compel compliance or to effect any large measure of uniformity.* 

An example of a recalcitrant corporation is found, surprisingly, as late as the early 1930's, when the Allied Chemical and Dye Corporation refused to publish adequate information at sufficiently frequent intervals to be of value. The sort of work done by the stock exchanges to raise the general level of corporate reporting, and hence indirectly corporate honesty, is well exemplified by the action taken by the New York Stock Exchange in this case, beginning in the summer of 1932. The problems involved may be best shown by quoting from the letters written to the corporation by the Stock Exchange 

Listing Committee.5

DEAR SIR:

Since writing you on March 22, 1932, in reference to complaint from a stockholder regarding the lack of adequate information in your annual reports, this Committee has received complaints from other stockholders believed to hold substantial amounts of your stock. 

These complaints appear to us to be well grounded. When a corporation voluntarily applies for the listing of its securities, it incurs an obligation to provide present and prospective investors with sufficient information upon which to base their actions. This is because it does not separate operating earnings from nonoperating earnings, does not indicate non-recurring items of income or expense, and lacks all specific detailed information. . . ....

We therefore request your assurance that you will give any inquiring stockholder the information above outlined and that your future reports will be published as above indicated, subject, of course, to such changes, if any, as may be agreed upon, should you desire a conference on the matter.

It is apparent from the foregoing that the corporation resented giving additional data and that the Stock Exchange had to exert considerable pressure to get results. The latter were finally forthcoming, an amicable agreement being reached between the two during the latter part of June, 1933.º

In addition to their financial statements, many corporations publish other pamphlets of interest to the public. These reports are frequently for the purpose of advertising, but in some instances specific information concerning the organization and operation of the company is given. As an illustration of the latter, certain reports made available to the public by the General Motors Corporation may be noted: "Decentralized Operations and Responsibilities with Coordinated Control," "Development of Installment Purchasing," "Export Organiza tion of General Motors," "Financial Control Policies of General Motors," "General Motors Acceptance Corporation," etc. 

Corporate Data Required for Listing

Under the Securities Exchange Act, all companies desiring permanent security registration must make application to the Commission. 

This application form calls for information similar in many respects to that previously required by the New York Stock Exchange; however, it is probable that the publicity given to these data will now be • The Securities and Exchange Commission reopened the case again in connection with the application of the company for permanent registration, particularly for purposes of obtaining a list of its marketable securities.

HANGES 

435 much more effective. Illustrating the importance and general nature of the material provided in an application for listing, the Listing 

Committee of the New York Stock Exchange evaluates the information for the purpose of ascertaining the following:8 

1. That the applicant is a successful going concern. This means that the company's business must be an established enterprise, yielding annual earnings of $500,000 or more, and having assets in excess of $5,000,000. Adjustment may be made in the two figures after con sideration by the Listing Committee. 

2. That the management has a good reputation and agrees to be bound by the Exchange's standards of responsibilities to security holders. The company must agree to submit an annual report to the stockholders at least fifteen days prior to their annual meeting and to publish periodic interim reports of earnings at intervals agreed upon with the Exchange. Moreover, the company must furnish the 

Exchange on demand with any information which it may reasonably require. 

3. That the company is legally organized, their securities validly authorized and issued, and that a purchaser receives a valid certificate. 

The Exchange's rules and regulations require the publication of engraved certificates approved by the Exchange, setting forth the important rights and preferences of the holders. Also, the company must furnish an independent registrar for its securities. 

4. That there is sufficient volume and distribution of the securities to warrant a national market. Security issues having a limited number of shares or which are so closely held as to make transfers only casual in nature will not be listed. 

5. That the company complies with the Exchange's requirements as to accounting, periodic reports, and disclosure of corporation reports for the protection of investors. The Exchange analyzes the reports as filed from time to time to see that they are comparable and in such a form as to disclose changes in volume or profitability of business. Among other things, the company must agree to disclose any important change in the nature of its business or in the acquisition or disposal of major assets or holdings in affiliates.

Advantages of Listing to the Corporation 

Inquiry may be made as to why a corporation would choose to go through the foregoing examination as well as to pay the expense of listing. As may be inferred from our earlier discussion, one excellent reason for so doing is because of the aid received in the process of raising capital. There is also the more important problem of maintaining a financial position. The issuance of securities is just the beginning, and investor following and support throughout the life of the business is essential to successful operation. In addition, certain other favorable incidences accrue in the corporation's favor. 

For instance, it is a means of indirect or general advertising and can very well lead to an increase in the sales of the firm's products. Goodwill may also be created inasmuch as a public following of specific corporations is not at all unusual. This improves the credit standing of the company and opens new avenues not only for long-time financing but also that of a short-time nature. 

Not all corporations, however, should list their stock on organized exchanges, or conditions may develop which make it advisable to withdraw listing. Two examples of delisting are the following:10 ... 

The Chicago Union Station Company 4 per cent guaranteed bonds due April 1, 1944 were delisted because, among other reasons, the amount of the bonds outstanding had been so reduced as to make further dealings in them on the exchange inadvisable.” 66 The Kingsbury Breweries Company was permitted to withdraw its $1 par common stock from both the New York Curb Exchange and the Chicago Stock Exchange. The following reasons were pertinent: (1) During the calendar year 1940, trading on the Curb Exchange amounted to only 3,700 shares and on the Chicago Exchange, 14,550 shares. Hence, the expense of continued listing was believed to be unwarranted. (2) The price range of the stock during 1940 was from a high of to a low of ; the last trade was at the latter figure. The declaration was then made that "the Company's stock 

9 The basic fees for listing securities are: for stocks, voting trust certificates, etc., 1.2 cents per share for no-par and par of $100 or less, and any fraction of 10,000 "over and above a multiple thereof, to be counted as 10,000 shares for this purpose"; for bonds, notes, etc., in denominations of not less than $100, $120 per million dollars principal or fraction thereof, with the minimum fee being $120.

quoted publicly at these prices impairs the distribution of its products to the detriment of the stockholders; that continued listing and registration is not in the public interest, and retards the recovery in equity values of the stockholders." (3) "The best interests of the stockholders will be served by making the stock available for trading in the overthe-counter market."

Disadvantages of Listing to the Corporation Attention should also be called to the possible disadvantages of listing. Regulation will likely reduce the force of these negative influences, but the possibility of their existence should be noted. Among others, the following may be mentioned: (1) dangers of manipulation, (2) circulation of false rumors, (3) emphasis of short-time, as opposed to long-time, policy. 

Stocks have frequently been manipulated without considering the possible effect upon the corporations involved. This practice was in considerable evidence during the year of 1929. As an instance, the stock of the Advance-Rumely Company was raised to a price in excess of 100, without any legitimate basis at all. The company was not making a profit, and its record over a period of time was far from satisfactory. It was not surprising that the stock broke rapidly, and the effect certainly did not produce any desirable advertising for the corporation. On other occasions the results may be more disastrous.

Rumors are occasionally a quick means to profits, and at times they may be intentionally false. Rumor of consolidation was an especially popular one to develop public following of stocks. Similarly, payment of "extras" or stock split-ups were anticipated many more times than they were actually effected. Although the United States 

Steel Corporation has paid only one stock dividend in its history, they have been rumored on numerous occasions. While most rumors are not pernicious in nature, the state of falsification may prove to be bad advertising for the companies involved.

Speculation is obviously conducted on a short-time basis, and because of this there is a temptation to base financial operations upon the more immediate outlook instead of giving the necessary consideration to the long-time program. For instance, many corporations tried to issue stocks on a rights' basis in 1929, but were foiled by

the crash which ensued. There is also the temptation to management to institute policies for the sake of their influence upon the price of the stock instead of their effect upon the ultimate earnings of the company. A wise management will devote itself to the problems of production and distribution of its goods or services with the greatest efficiency possible, rather than worrying about the price of its securities on the market.

Importance of Listing to the Public and the Investor Not only does listing provide a market for the investor, but also a number of protective services are added. The protective services do not exist to the extent of a guaranty, but they do assure the presence of good faith and reduce the possibility of fraud. Specifications are set forth as to the form and content of stocks, bonds, and other financial instruments, and even the quality of the paper used to issue the certificates is stipulated. Likewise, the requirement of a transfer agent and a registrar provides both service and safety to the investor. 

The transfer agent's chief duty is to cancel old and issue new stock, although he (usually a trust company) frequently renders such additional services as mailing dividends, distributing various corporate reports, etc. It is the duty of the registrar to check on the amount of stock issued and to insure its legitimacy.

The importance of safeguarding the rights of the investor is selfevident, but more recently, it has been given more formal recognition. 

Reference is made, of course, to the Securities Act and to the Securities Exchange Act, which are discussed separately. 

Statistics of Listed Securities

Listing the Key to Public Interest 

Listing constitutes an open invitation to the public to participate in business enterprise. As shown in the various statistics covering listed corporations, the appeal is by no means limited; it comes from the big and small corporation and from all branches of industry. As a result, millions of American families have a direct investment in businesses of all degrees and description. It is little wonder that eventually the government provided facilities to regulate and supervise this important public interest.

CHAPTER XXIII  AND OF  

EGISLATIVE measures adopted by the states and the federal government to regulate the sale of newly issued securities were discussed in Chapter XXI. A policy of adequate legislative protection of investors falls short of realization, however, if it goes no further than the regulation of new security offerings. New securities constitute only a fraction of the securities already outstanding, and continuous regulation of the latter is equally essential for effective and complete surveillance of the rights and interests of investors. 

Moreover, legislation pertaining to outstanding securities greatly affects the policies of corporate financing both because of its effects on current operations and its influence on the flotation of future security issues. It is for these reasons that a study may be made of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 which provides for the regulation of outstanding securities by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Need for Regulation of Outstanding Securities 

The Securities Act provides for adequate information in connection with the issuance of a new security by means of a registration statement. However, much of the data provided in the registration statement become obsolete in a relatively short time, and the Securities Act does not require that it be kept current. In addition, there are many securities already outstanding which are not subject to the provisions of the Securities Act since they were issued prior to its enactment. It is therefore necessary that current information be provided and that other pertinent facts besides those submitted in the registration statement be made available if investors are to act intelligently. Not only is there need for reports covering the current financial position of corporations, but in addition publicity and regulation of trading operations are equally necessary to protect the interests of both investor and issuing company. 

Manipulative practices may easily give a false impression of the volume of trading transactions and distort the merits of a security 444

1 1 just as much as the omission or false declaration of material facts in connection with the original distribution. Similarly, artificial or primed price changes may be the cause of undue influence and inspire the investor to act unwisely. The effects of such abuses are particularly significant because it is in the trading area that the important secondary distribution of securities to the public-at-large really begins. 

Initial purchasers frequently buy in large blocks, and often with the deliberate intention of early resale; hence the need for protection of investors may be greater at the time of secondary distribution than at the time of initial sale.

To eliminate the foregoing abuses as well as to provide surveillance of market operations generally, the Securities Exchange Act supplements the Securities Act in two principal ways: (1) by providing continuing publicity and reliable information about the current financial condition of the issuers of securities bought and sold on the principal stock exchanges in the United States; (2) by prohibiting certain practices which tend to create fictitious values for securities. 

Over-the-Counter Sales 

The title of the Act would indicate that its regulation is confined to securities listed on the exchanges and to the exchanges themselves, but the Act also grants authority to regulate over-the-counter sales.¹ 

The so-called Maloney Amendment, passed in 1938, provides for a program of co-operative self-regulation of the over-the-counter markets by the industry. Under its provisions voluntary associations of brokers and dealers may register under the Act and, subject to the supervision of the Commission, assume the major responsibility for the regulation of their members. Over-the-counter operations are not, however, as fully developed as the full-time organized exchanges of which there are twenty-six in the entire country. Accordingly, our discussion of the Act will be confined to the manner in which it affects the stock exchanges, and since the largest and best known is the New York Stock Exchange, our remarks will be based primarily upon this particular organization. 

Need for the Securities Exchange Act

Two of the more essential economic functions of stock exchanges are the establishment of security prices which are fair and represen- 

1. See chapter XXII for further discussion.

tative, and the provision of a mechanism to accommodate ever changing holdings of investments in industry.2 Both buyer and seller are able to judge the value of securities by means of the market price and their transactions are expedited by the organized facilities which are available to make security transfers effective. It follows that any practice or device which tends to hamper the effectiveness with which a stock exchange performs either of these two essential economic functions is detrimental not only to corporate financing but also to the public welfare. 

Mechanism of the Stock Exchange

While it would be desirable for buyer and seller to meet face to face, this is rendered impossible by the fact that trading is necessarily concentrated in a few large centers. Hence, the major part of trading in securities on the organized stock exchanges located in a few large cities is done through the medium of persons who are active members of the exchange. These members may be divided into four principal groups: 

1. The commission broker.-The commission broker is a member of the stock exchange who devotes his time and efforts to the execution of buying and selling orders for the brokerage firm which he represents. This brokerage firm, in turn, acts for a great many buyers and sellers distributed all over the country. The commission broker does not own the securities bought or sold; his function is strictly one of acting as an impartial medium to bring together the supply and demand. 

2. The odd-lot broker.—Since the standard unit of trading in stocks on the New York Stock Exchange is 100 shares, special facilities are necessary to take care of orders placed by small investors. This function is fulfilled by odd-lot dealers who have special brokers on the floor of the exchange to handle this business. 

3. The floor-trader. The floor-trader acts in the capacity of a principal, i.e., he deals for his own account. His position is essentially that of a securities' merchant since he owns the securities in which he deals, and his profits or losses arise out of changes in price levels of the securities which he owns or has promised to deliver at some later date. In general, he plays the market for quick turns and is seldom interested in any long-term developments and trends. Often 

2 See chapter XXII for a more complete statement of the functions of a stock exchange.

5 3 he buys his securities in the morning and sells at the end of the trading day so that he has no holdings to carry over night. 

4. The specialist.-The specialist is an individual who may combine both the trader and broker functions but concentrates his efforts upon only a few stocks in a given industry. He may, in the case of important issues, limit himself to trading in a single issue. His position arises out of the necessity of having some means for handling orders placed at specific prices other than the prevailing price. 

Orders placed to buy or sell at the market are handled promptly and with relatively simple problems of bookkeeping. However, orders placed at a definite price above or below market must be filed so that they will be executed whenever the market reaches the specified price. It the function of the specialist to keep a record of all such orders and to execute them as it becomes possible to do so. Possessing as he does wide information as to the state of the market, it is quite apparent that the function of the specialist is susceptible to abuse. 

This becomes especially true when it is remembered that he exercises both brokerage and trading functions, and is, therefore, in a position to buy or sell in his own name while conducting the brokerage business.

Summary of Purposes of the Act 

Preliminary to an analysis of particular provisions of the Securities Exchange Act, it is essential to understand its basic purposes. 

These may be briefly stated as follows: 

1. Prevention of manipulative devices and maintenance of an honestly conducted market. 

2. Limitation of excessive speculation in securities, primarily through regulation of the amount of credit which may flow into speculative channels. 

3. Publication of systematic and reliable information as to the management and financial condition of corporations whose securities are listed on an exchange. 

4. Restriction of trading on inside information by persons possessing such information. 

5. General regulation of exchanges and members, brokers and dealers for the protection of investors and in the public interest. 

Administration of the Act The Securities Exchange Act created the Securities and Exchange 

Commission to administer that Act and certain other federal laws

relating to the issue and sale of securities. The Commission is given broad power to regulate the securities markets and the activities of their members by its rules and regulations and has been given broad discretionary powers in other matters. As a result, its interpretations of the statutory provisions under which it operates, the nature of its rules and regulations, and the vigor of enforcement of these will determine the ultimate practical effect of the statutes which it administers. Considerable time could weli be devoted to a study of the organization and operating procedure which have been developed by the Commission. This will not be done, since our primary interest is in the influence of its activities upon the field of corporation finance. 

Registration of Exchanges 

Effective supervision and elevation of standards depend, first of all, upon the qualification and conduct of the front-line operating units. This is accomplished by requiring that all national security exchanges must be registered with, and approved by, the Securities and Exchange Commission. In applying for registration, the exchange must furnish “such data as to its organization, rules of procedure, and membership, and such other information as the Commission may by rules and regulations require as being necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors." 

This is a distinct innovation in the affairs of these organizations. 

Prior to the passage of this law the New York Stock Exchange, for example, had never given publicity to its financial statement. Now it, along with all other registered exchanges, is required to submit each year a balance sheet and income and expense statement for the year, although the Commission may use its judgment about releasing this information to the public.

Another prerequisite for registration is the existence of rules of the exchange which provide for the expulsion, suspension, or disciplining of members for conduct "inconsistent with just and equitable 3 In addition to the Securities Act and the Securities Exchange Act, the Commission administers the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, the Trust Indenture Act of 1939, the Investment Company Act of 1940, and has certain functions in connection with corporate reorganizations under the 1938 Amendment to the Federal Bankruptcy Act (the Chandler Act). 

4 The Act does not directly require such registration but indirectly compels it as a result of the prohibition in section 5 of the Act against use of the mails or the instrumentalities of interstate commerce by a dealer, broker, or exchange for the purpose of employing the facilities of a securities exchange, unless the exchange is registered as a national securities exchange, or by reason of the limited volume of transactions effected on it, is exempt from such registration.

3 principles of trade." Most exchanges have always had such rules, but to strengthen them the Act requires that they must also provide that failure to abide by the provisions of the Securities Exchange Act or any regulation of the Commission shall be regarded as an act of misconduct subject to the penalties upon which the rules provide for other violations. Upon becoming registered, an exchange must agree to comply with the provisions of the Act and any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder. In addition, it must agree to compel, so far as it is within its powers, its members to give the same compliance. 

The exchanges are also required to assist in carrying the expense entailed by registration and the ensuing supervision. The Act imposes upon all registered exchanges a yearly registration fee amounting to five one-hundredths of 1 per cent of the total volume of sales for that year. The bulk of this assessment falls upon the New York 

Stock Exchange because it is by far the largest single securities exchange in the country. For the year ending June 30, 1940, the total value of all transactions upon all registered exchanges was $13,469,- 385,000, and of this amount, $11,557,958,000 was reported by the New 

York Stock Exchange.5 Segregation of Broker and Dealer Functions-Arguments for and against

The Act defines a member of a stock exchange as any person who is permitted either to effect transactions on the exchange without the services of another person acting as broker, or to make use of the facilities of an exchange for transactions thereon without payment of a commission or fee or with the payment of a commission or fee which is less than that charged the general public, and includes any firm transacting a business as broker or dealer of which a member is a partner, and any partner of any such firm. 

Obviously this definition includes the four main classes of active exchange members described earlier in the chapter, and also includes the securities firms which they represent. Controversy over regulating the conduct of members has centered largely on the problem of segregating and limiting the practices and operations of brokers, specialists, and dealers. The major battles on this matter have for the most part found exchange members ranged on one side and repre- 

5 S.E.C., Sixth Annual Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1940, p. 276. • Sec. 3(a) (3).

sentatives of the government, either within or without Congress, on the other.

The Securities Exchange Act in the form in which it was originally introduced in Congress segregated dealer and broker functions both on the floor of the securities exchanges and off the floor with respect to outside brokers and dealers. All members, other than specialists, were prohibited from trading on their own accounts while on the floor of the exchange. Specialists were allowed to choose either to trade as dealers for their own account or to function as brokers but were required to register their choice and to confine their activities to their registered function. The bill required security houses acting off the floor of the exchange, both as dealers buying and selling for themselves and as brokers executing orders for others, to elect between functioning solely as brokers or functioning solely as dealers.

In the debate over the bill, advocates of segregation contended that the combination of broker and dealer functions in the same member involves a conflict of interest to the detriment of his customers when he is acting as a broker. It was contended that a customer coming to his broker with the intent of buying a certain security was likely to be persuaded by the broker to purchase a security which the broker was selling as a dealer and out of which he would make a profit larger than the usual broker's commission. Furthermore, non-segregation leads to the use by members, particularly by specialists, of "inside information" of existing orders received by them as brokers to guide their own activities as dealers in the same securities. This, the supporters of segregation asserted, not only interferes with effective fulfillment of the brokerage function but also results in a type of dealer activity which exercises an undue influence on prices and prevents the market from reflecting the fair value of the security.

Opponents of segregation responded with the contention that although the specialist, the floor-trader, and the odd-lot dealer are motivated by self-interest when trading for their own account, eir activities contribute to the stability of the market and are essential to satisfactory and continued market operations. They pointed out that a large percentage of the trading on the exchanges in any day is made up of transactions of specialists, odd-lot dealers, and floortraders for their own accounts, and this increases activity in the

market and prevents wide fluctuations in prices with the result that liquidity of listed securities is increased. They also maintained that any broker who, in trading for his own account, acted adversely to the interests of his customers over a period of time would soon lose them.

Segregation Provisions of the Act 

As passed, the Securities Exchange Act imposed no categorical segregation of dealer and broker functions either on or off the floor of the exchanges, but in large part referred the problem to the Commission. The Act empowers the Commission to prescribe such rules and regulations as it deems necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors, to regulate or prevent floortrading on the exchanges, and to prevent such excessive trading off the floor by exchange members for their own account as the Commission "may deem detrimental to the maintenance of a fair and orderly market." It is provided that such rules and regulations may exempt transactions by odd-lot dealers and specialists in accordance with the rules and regulations as the Commission may prescribe. 

When not in contravention of rules and regulations of the Commission, the rules of a national securities exchange may permit the exchange to register a member as an odd-lot dealer or a specialist. 

The Act expressly provides that 

It shall be unlawful for a specialist or specialist or an official of the exchange to disclose information in regard to orders placed with such specialist which is not available to all members of the exchange, to any person other than an official of the exchange, a representative of the Commission, or a specialist who may be acting for such specialist; but the Commission shall have power to require disclosure to all members of the exchange of all orders placed with specialists, under such rules and regulations as the Commission may prescribe as necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors. It shall also be unlawful for a specialist acting as a broker to effect on the exchange any transaction except upon a market or limited price order." 

To date the Commission has issued no regulations of its own as to segregation of dealer and broker functions in floor-trading. Perhaps the problem has been found too complex to permit any ready solution. 

The segregation provisions of the Securities Exchange Act, so far ? Sec. 11 (b).

as they relate to the activities of securities houses off the floor of the exchange, represent almost a total victory for the opponents of segregation. The Act neither prescribes segregation of dealer and broker functions for outside securities firms, nor does it permit the Commission to prescribe such segregation by rules and regulations. 

The provisions of the Act merely provide: 

1. That a broker-dealer may not extend credit to a customer on any security bought from him if such security was part of a new issue in the distribution of which he participated within a period of six months prior to the customer's purchase of the security. 

2. That a member who is both a broker and dealer must disclose to a customer, in writing, at or before the completion of the transaction, the capacity in which he is acting. 

The Commission was directed to "make a study of the feasibility and advisability of the complete segregation of the functions of broker and dealer." This study was submitted to Congress in June, 1936. 

With respect to the segregation of functions on the floor of the exchange the Commission reached the following two general conclusions:8 

1. That the combination of the broker and dealer functions in the same individual or firm involves a conflict of interest which is provocative of abuse of the fiduciary relationship inherent in the brokerage function; 

2. That the survey made by the Commission manifests the prevalence upon the exchanges of a type of dealer activity which exerts an undue influence on prices, incites public speculation, leads to disorderly markets and interferes with the effective fufillment of the brokerage function. 

However, the Commission stated that it did not believe complete segregation advisable at that time, and that further study of the subject would be necessary. The report then set forth a proposed program. 

With respect to the abuses of non-segregation of dealer and broker functions off the floor of the exchange the Commission's report was much less critical, and confined itself largely to proposals for restricting undue speculative trading.

Prevention of Manipulative Transactions 

It was observed earlier that one of the primary economic functions of a stock exchange is the determination of prices for listed securities. 

8 S.E.C. Report on "The Feasibility and Advisability for the Complete Segregation of the 

Functions of Dealer and Broker" (1936), p. 109.

The performance of this function free of practices which tend to create fictitious values is of paramount importance to both the protection of investors and to the continued flow of funds into corporate financing. Hence, it is not surprising to find certain provisions of the Securities Exchange Act directed either to the elimination or regulation of manipulation and speculation. 

Practices Prohibited 

One or another provision of the Act is directed at almost every manipulative device that critics of stock exchange practices have suggested. Absolutely prohibited are the following transactions or practices: (1) "wash sales" and "matched orders"; (2) pool operations; (3) the dissemination of information that the price of the security is likely to rise or fall by reasons of individual or pool activities; (4) the dissemination of false or misleading information or tips as to market operations.

Certain transactions are not prohibited by the terms of the Act itself but are made unlawful only if in contravention of any rules and regulations of the Commission. These transactions are: (1) operations for the pegging, fixing, and stabilizing of market prices; (2) trading in options or privileges, such as puts, calls, straddles, and the guaranteeing of such options; (3) short sales; (4) stop-loss orders; (5) the use of any manipulative or deceptive device in contravention of any rules of the Commission with respect to same. 

The Commission has to date adopted rules and regulations with respect to all of the foregoing transactions except those numbered (2) and (4).

Effect of Speculation on Credit 

Economists are by no means in agreement as to whether or not speculation deprives industry of credit. Irrespective of this, the point of view expressed in the Securities Exchange Act is clear, for it attempts to check excessive speculation and regulates the amount of credit which may flow into speculative securities transactions. This is done by correcting or limiting the two exchange practices which have been criticized as most encouraging to speculation, namely, short selling and margin trading.

Regulation of Short Selling 

As was pointed out in Chapter XVII, short selling is absolutely prohibited by directors, officers, and stockholders holding more than 10 per cent of the stock of the corporation in which they have an interest. Other persons, however, may engage in short selling under rules and regulations promulgated by the Commission. The latter now provide that short sales may not be effected on any exchange "(1) below the price at which the last sale thereof, regular way, was effected on such exchange, or (2) at such price unless such price is above the next preceding different price at which a sale of such security, regular way, was effected on such exchange." The regulations also require that every selling order on a national securities exchange must be marked either "long" or "short.",

Restrictions on Margin Trading 

Margin trading attracted much attention both in and out of Congress when the enactment of the Securities Exchange Act was under consideration. Some advocated complete prohibition of margin trading, but this was regarded as being too deflationary in character. 

There is little question but that such a drastic step would seriously restrict the securities market. The Act attempts to solve the problem through control over the extension of margin credit. This control is effected chiefly by two means: (1) limitation on the amount of credit which may be extended or maintained for the purpose of purchasing or carrying securities; (2) regulation of loans to brokers and of the agencies which make such loans.

The Act provides that credit may be extended in a margin transaction in an "amount not greater than whichever is the higher" of the following: (1) 55 per cent of the current market price of the security or (2) 100 per cent of the lowest price during the preceding 36 calendar months, but in no event to be in excess of 75 per cent of the current market price. In order to provide flexibility the Federal

Reserve Board is given the authority to prescribe lower margin requirements if it is deemed necessary or appropriate for the accommodation of commerce or industry, or higher margin requirements if deemed necessary to prevent excessive use of credit to finance securities transactions. The Federal Reserve Board, acting under this au- 

⁹ General rules and regulations under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 as amended to and including February 15, 1941, Rule X-10A-1.

thority, has reduced the margin requirements to 40 per cent of the current market price.10

The provisions designed to regulate loans to brokers and the agencies which grant such loans are several. Members of registered exchanges and other persons doing business with a member may not borrow from any source other than a member bank of the Federal Reserve System, or from a non-member bank which has filed an agreement with the Federal Reserve Board to comply with the provisions of the Act and the Board's rules and regulations relative to the use of credit in financing security transactions. A broker's total indebtedness to all other persons is restricted to such percentage of his net capital as the Commission may prescribe, and in any event to an amount not greater than twenty times his net capital. Restriction are also placed on the hypothecation by a broker of his customer's securities. 

Opposition to Publicity

While the major opposition to the Act has centered on other provisions, there has been considerable objection to the parts of the Act requiring adequate publicity and disclosure of corporate affairs. 

Opponents of the publicity features argue first of all that such provisions do not logically belong in an Act to regulate stock exchanges. 

However, as noted earlier in this chapter, two of the primary economic functions of a securities exchange are the evaluation of the worth of securities and the supplying of means whereby the savings of individuals may be invested in corporate securities. Obviously, complete disclosure and publicity of pertinent information about the corporations whose securities are listed on these exchanges should facilitate the performance of these functions.

Another objection made to the publicity requirements of the Act is that they encroach upon the domain and functions of private management. The answer to this objection lies in the nature of the modern corporation. The growing separation of ownership and control has increased the fiduciary obligation which corporate management owes to members of the investing public.11 From this larger point 

10 Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Regulation T, effective January 1, 1938, provides a maximum loan value on registered securities in general accounts of 60 per cent of their current market value. 

11 See discussion of the legal and social responsibilities of management in chapter XVII.

of view, one of the responsibilities of management must be to make available adequate information with respect to the condition of the companies under their control. 

Previous Conditions of Publicity 

Prior to the passage of the Securities Exchange Act the public received, with respect to many corporations, neither adequate information nor with sufficient timeliness to give it currency. Some of the leading corporations did not publish their financial statements more than once a year and even these would not be forthcoming until well after the close of the financial period reported. Some protection was afforded investors by the listing requirements of the stock exchanges, and the New York Stock Exchange particularly had accomplished much in setting higher standards as to the corporate information which should be available to the public.12 The Securities Act of 1933 required adequate information in connection with the issuance of a new security. But neither stock exchange listing requirements nor the Securities Act provided adequately for securities already issued and listed. It was the need for continuing information on already outstanding securities which the publicity features of the Securities Exchange Act were designed to meet. 

Registration Statement 

The Act requires that securities listed on exchanges or admitted to unlisted trading privileges be registered before they can be traded in on any exchange. Registration consists of filing by the issuer with the Commission and the exchange such information as the Commission may in its rules and regulations require as to the following 

(A) the organization, financial structure and nature of the business; (B) the terms, position, rights, and privileges of the different classes of securities outstanding; (C) the terms on which their securities are to be, and during the preceding three years have been, offered to the public or otherwise; (D) the directors, officers, and underwriters, and each security holder of record holding more than 10 per centum of any class of any equity security of the issuer (other than an exempted security), their remuncration and their interests in the securities of, and their material contracts with, the issuer and any 

12 For a discussion of the New York Stock Exchange listing requirements, see Twentieth Century Fund, Inc., The Security Markets (1935), pp. 235-37, 592-609. 

18.Sec, 12 (b) (1).

person directly or indirectly controlling or controlled by, or under direct or indirect common control with, the issuer; (E) remuneration to others than directors and officers exceeding $20,000 per annum; (F) bonus and profit-sharing arrangements; (G) management and service contracts; (H) options existing or to be created in respect to their securities; (I) balance sheets for not more than the three preceding fiscal years, certified if required by the rules and regulations of the Commission by independent public accountants; (J) profit and loss statements for not more than the three preceding fiscal years, certified if required by the rules and regulations of the Commission by independent public accountants; and (K) any further financial statements which the Commission may deem necessary or appropriate for the protection of investors. 

The issuer must also file such copies of articles of incorporation, by-laws, trust indentures, underwriting arrangements, voting trust agreements, and other similar documents as the Commission may "require as necessary or appropriate for the proper protection of investors and to insure fair dealing in the security."

Comparison with Registration Requirements of Securities Act 

It will be observed that the registration requirements of the Securities Exchange Act are in general similar to those of the Securities Act which were discussed in the preceding chapter. Because the latter deals only with new issues, a registration statement under the Securities Act naturally contains more detailed information relating to underwriters and promoters. On the other hand, the requirements of disclosure of stock interest and remuneration of officers, directors, and substantial stockholders are more drastic under the Securities 

Exchange Act. The Exchange Act requires that the officers, directors, and substantial stockholders must be named and the remuneration for each stated, and also the remuneration of others if more than $20,000 a year. Under the Securities Act, on the other hand, the remuneration of officers and other persons, except directors, may be stated in aggregate without allocation to individuals unless they receive an annual compensation of $25,000 or more. 

Periodic Reports 

The Act empowers the Commission to require every issuer of a listed security to file with the exchange, and with the Commission:

(1) such information and documents as the Commission may require to keep reasonably current the information and documents filed in or with the registration statement; (2) such annual reports certified by independent public accountants, if required by the rules and regulations of the Commission, and such quarterly reports as the Commission may prescribe. This is in line with the policy of the Act to secure continuing information on the corporations who are issuers of registered securities.

The Commission is given authority to prescribe the form in which required information shall be submitted, and in this connection to prescribe the system and methods of accounting to be used in the preparation of reports. It is hoped that this will result not only in standardization of reports but will also facilitate and tend to promote uniform accounting. The lack of standardized accounting terminology and the existence of marked variances in accounting theory have always been a deterrent to financial interpretation. The Commission is presented with an opportunity to solve personal disagreements as to accounting treatment and render a service of value to the accounting profession and financial interests alike. Allowance will have to be made for different industrial categories, but within any single group reasonable uniformity should eventually be achieved. 

Publication of Information Filed with the Commission Many corporations object to disclosure of the detailed facts about their business and financial condition required in the registration statement and periodic reports on the grounds that it results in damage and loss by providing their competitors and customers with information which they would not otherwise have. In recognition of this problem the Act gives to the Securities Exchange Commission the power to determine whether information filed with it may be withheld from the public. Any person may make objection to the public disclosure of any information contained in applications, reports, etc., filed by him, and in such case the Commission may make the information available to the public only when "in its judgment a disclosure of such information is in the public interest." 

The constitutionality of delegating to the Commission the power to publicize or to withhold information was attacked in the courts. in a case involving the American Sumatra Tobacco Corporation.14 

14 American Sumatra Tobacco Corporation v. Securities and Exchange Commission, 

110 F. 2d 117 (1939).

The Tobacco Corporation had asked the Commission to withhold publication of information in its registration statement showing the amount of gross sales and the cost of goods sold. It contended that disclosure of its gross profit margin, which was larger than that of most other corporations, would cause resentment on the part of customers and result in damage and loss by creating a buyers' strike. 

The Commission denied the Corporation's request, and the Court upheld the Commission's action. The tobacco firm had argued that 

Congress had delegated power to the Commission without setting any standard for the Commission's action, the words "public interest,' it was asserted, being too general for that purpose. To this contention the Court replied as follows: 

22 Petitioner says the words "public interest" are too general to be a proper safeguard, but we think this point is without merit. The main purpose of the 

Act is to insure the maintenance of fair and honest markets in transactions in securities on national exchanges. The Act requires the issuer of securities-the registrant to make disclosures in order to forestall unfair practices in the sale of securities and for the protection of investors. The "public interest" in this respect is just as definite as the "public interest" in transportation facilities. 

Powers of the Interstate Commerce Commission to make decisions, confined only by the latter standard, have been continually upheld. * * * we think the

Act provides a sufficient guide for administrative action whenever the commission is called upon to decide whether or not disclosure is in the public interest. 

Trading by Corporate Officials 

The Act requires each beneficial owner of more than 10 per cent of any class of a registered equity security and each director and officer of the issuing corporation to file a statement of his stockholdings and to report any changes at the end of each calendar month. 

The purpose of this reporting is to make such actions of directors and other corporate insiders a matter of public record. The Act also provides that if any such director, officer, or substantial shareholder buys an equity security and sells it within six months at a profit, the corporation of which they are a part may recover the profit. By this means, it is intended to prevent trading by such persons on “inside information" for personal gain.¹ 15 

Trading on Stock Exchange 

Trading on inside information is also likely to be indulged in by stock-exchange members while operating on the floor of the ex- 

15 See chapter XVII for discussion of legal responsibilities of management.

change. As already pointed out in the previous discussion of the combination of dealer and broker functions in exchange members, this is one of the principal arguments in favor of the segregation of these activities. And, as shown in that same connection, the Commission is given power to prevent possible abuse by the adoption of rules and regulations which govern the use of inside information. 

Solicitation of Proxies 

The Act makes it unlawful for any person to use the mails or the facilities of interstate commerce or a national securities exchange to solicit proxies with respect to listed securities except in accordance with rules and regulations of the Commission. It is also made unlawful for any exchange member, or any broker or dealer who operates through such a member, to give proxies for stock which he carries on account. The proxy regulations promulgated under the 

Securities and Exchange Commission define "solicitation," specify the transactions exempted from the proxy rules, and specify the information which must be furnished in the proxy statement submitted to the Commission.16 

Enforcement of the Act 

To secure effective enforcement of the Act, both criminal and civil liabilities are provided. Willful violation of any provision of the Act or properly issued rule or regulation is made subject to fine and imprisonment. Civil liability may arise from misleading statements in a variety of documents or from willful participation in prohibited manipulative practices. Liability arising out of false or misleading statements attaches to any person who makes or is responsible for making the statement. The liability runs in favor of any person who in reliance on the statement purchased or sold a security at a price which was affected by this statement. Any actual damages suffered by reason of such reliance may be recovered unless the person sued can prove that he acted in good faith and had no knowledge that the statement was false or misleading.

In addition to the criminal and civil liability features, the Act contains numerous other provisions designed to empower the Commission to enforce the Act. The Commission upon complaint or upon its own initiative may (1) investigate possible violations of 

18 See chapter XV.

the Act, (2) bring suit to enjoin threatened violations, and (3) seek a court order to compel compliance with the Act. For violation of any provision of the Act or any of the rules and regulations of the Commission, the Commission may (1) suspend or withdraw altogether the license of any exchange, (2) withdraw the registration statement of any security, or (3) suspend or expel from an exchange any member or officer thereof.

The Commission is authorized, if in its opinion the public interest so requires, to suspend trading in any registered security for not more than ten days and, with the approval of the President, to suspend trading on any exchange for not exceeding a period of ninety days. The Commission is given the power to request changes in the rules of an exchange, and if such changes are not made voluntarily, to alter or supplement the rules of the exchange for the "protection of investors or to insure fair dealing in securities traded in upon such exchange or to insure fair administration of such exchange." Every contract made in violation of the Act or any rule or regulation of the Commission, and contracts binding any person to waive compliance with the Act or rules and regulations issued under it, are made void.

Appraisal of the Securities Acts 

It is difficult at this time to foresee the ultimate effects of the 

Securities Act and the Securities Exchange Act upon our financial organization and even upon the nature of the whole business economy. 

Many opponents of the measures contend that they will seriously limit business programs and discourage the use of capital. Advocates of the measures argue that they will raise the standards of securities and securities markets, and ultimately assist in raising capital. Probably the two positions are not as contradictory as they may first appear. 

The present requirements covering the issuance of new securities call mainly for full and honest disclosure of the facts and hinder financing only to the extent that the public may misunderstand and misinterpret the facts. The regulation of the securities markets is intended chiefly to prevent manipulation and similar sharp practices. 

There can be little basic objection to these purposes and the major complaint raised by affected private interests is that the burden of regulation is unnecessary. However, over the years, the new rules will become old and will likely be accepted as the shock of innovation disappears. When this occurs, the evidence may well indicate that

the higher standards required have made possible the availability of large amounts of capital, and at lower rates because of the reduced risk. Any decision on the question is at best an opinion, and developments over the coming years will render the verdict.
