PART V INCOME AND CURRENT OPERATIONS

CHAPTER XXIV  

U P TO this point in our study of corporation finance, attention has been given mainly to activities which involved relationships between the corporation and its investors and other outside parties. For the most part, the questions were concerned with the long-term phases of operation or with the composition of the structure of finance. Now, the more dynamic side may be considered wherein the structure is put to work, and the elements of change and turnover become more prominent. Like a hydroelectric project, the dam and other plant facilities are first created and then put into use for the furnishing of power; similarly, the corporation is first organized and then is placed into active operation. 

Investors are obviously affected by the results of operation, but they have little active contact with this day-to-day functioning of the corporate enterprise. It is essentially the province of management under whose generalship the campaign of business battle is mapped. 

Individual stockholders with ownership rights have no voice because only the stockholders as a group can act. The latter elect a board of directors which, in turn, selects the chief executive officers to carry on the actual operations. Usually, the president is a member of the board of directors, and in this capacity, he sponsors and guides the policies which are necessary for the conduct of business. Moreover, there is often great delegation of power to operating heads so that they, in effect, become responsible for many, decisions which have material influence upon the success or failure of the corporation. 

The problems in this operating area are manifold, but generally speaking they may be classified into production, selling, and administration. Consideration will be given only to the last category and further confined to that portion which is financial in character. The following are the more important subjects calling for analysis: the general nature and administration of income; the provision of adequate working capital; the formulation of dividend policies; the establishment of sufficient reserves and surplus to provide a margin of safety; and because of increasing public interest, it is now desir- 467

able to include a discussion of the compensation of executives. Such issues as these have to do with current operations as distinguished from the problems of capital structure which have heretofore been studied. The analysis of current activities necessarily calls for greater emphasis upon the management point of view, but at the same time the relevancy of public and investor interest will be recognized where possible. 

Gross and Net Income

In order to evaluate the influence of management over income, it is necessary first of all to distinguish between the gross and net figures. Gross income may be considered as the equivalent of the total sales and net income as the difference between the latter and operating expenses.¹ Obviously, the two are closely interdependent, but the distinction is helpful in attempting to appraise the responsibility of management. The element of control is greater in the case of net income because there is opportunity to change the intervening expenses. On the other hand, gross income receives the first impact of fluctuating business conditions and is to a great extent a characteristic of the type of industry. It is true that different managements operating in the same field will have varying degrees of success, but any observations on this point are primarily a matter of individual case analysis. At the same time, it is important that allowances be made between different fields of industry. 

Stable Income Industries 

Many industries are characterized by a relatively stable flow of income. Here the tasks of management are greatly simplified because the element of stability greatly facilitates long-range planning and the budgeting of expenditures. Instead of dealing constantly with the unexpected, an orderly financial program may be arranged. The task of building a sound capital structure is made easier and problems in the operating area are considerably reduced. Desirable as stable income is, it is not achieved through the medium of managerial policy. 

Management may relieve the problem and it may take farsighted steps tending toward greater stability, but it cannot eliminate fluctuat- 1 In accounting practice, there is additional screening of the net income account. Broadly speaking, expression would be given to the following three net concepts: Net Profit from 

Operations; Net Income before Interest, Income Taxes, etc.; and Net Income after All Charges.

The term will be used in a broad sense here and the proper qualifications will be made where necessary for purposes of interpretation.

3 1 ing income at will. Some industries will naturally be variable in character while others offer a more constant rate of income. The determin. ing factors are found mainly in the type and in the nature of the products or services handled. In general, it will be found that the following characteristics tend to promote stability of gross income: (1) necessity goods and service, (2) retail trade, especially low-priced goods which appeal to an extremely wide market, e.g., five-and-ten cent stores.

Variable Income Industries 

Contrasting with the foregoing types of business, there is a large group of industries which is subjected to more or less severe variations in gross income. In these industries, years of small volume may be followed by years of large volume and gratifying earnings. They may be rich or poor, princes or paupers, and may sometimes be cardinal examples of the familiar maxim: from shirt sleeves to shirt sleeves in three generations. Contributing to variable income are the following: (1) production of goods and services of the novelty and nonessential type; (2) high price may contribute to variable demand in times of depression, e.g., automobiles, refrigerators, etc.; (3) production of heavy goods and raw materials. 

In periods of depression, people naturally restrict their purchases of the nonessential items, and conversely, in periods of prosperity, spend large proportions of their increase in income for so-called luxury goods and services. In the case of higher-priced and durable consumers' goods, they are likely to be used for a longer period of time than normal when economic circumstances require. For example, it may be customary to buy an automobile automobile every three years and to replace a mechanical refrigerator every eight or ten years, but repurchase may readily be deferred in times of depression. Fluctuating with even greater magnitude are those businesses engaged in the production of raw materials and durable capital goods. They are the farthest removed from the consumer and suffer the effects of a pyramiding of curtailment.

Comparison of Essential and Nonessential Goods Industries 

Goods of the essential type are obviously needed regardless of prevailing business conditions; it follows that the income of concerns engaged in this field should be relatively stable. Conversely, companies producing nonessential items will experience fluctuating income to a

much greater degree. It should be understood that the difference in classification between these two types of goods is largely a matter of social custom, and that necessities includes many things which are not absolutely essential in a physical sense. For example among the most stable fields of enterprise are to be found both the food products and the tobacco industries. The latter may well have greater stability of income than, for example, the manufacturers of wearing apparel or of department stores. To illustrate the point, the sales record of a selected company from each one of these groups is presented for a representative period of years in Table 41.

Comparison of Low- and High-Priced Goods 

High-priced goods are usually durable in character, and for this reason their purchase by the consumer may be postponed for a considerable period of time. To illustrate, the construction of new houses virtually ceased during 1932 and 1933 and only recently reached a

level equal to that of 1929.2 Being unable to finance a new home, the public simply got along with fewer conveniences and utilized less space by the process of doubling up. Similarly, there was a deferment in the purchase of automobiles and of house furnishings. 

This reaction on the part of the buying public necessarily had great effect on the income of companies operating in such fields. In great contrast, the demand for low-priced commodities tends to hold up in periods of slackened business activity, often despite the fact that some of these goods may be somewhat durable in character. An excellent example of this characteristic is found in five-and-ten cent stores which carry a sizable line of durable articles. These features may be seen in the sales records shown in Table 42.

Other Factors Affecting Fluctuation of Gross Income 

In the complex of business activity, there are undoubtedly other factors which have a bearing upon the fluctuation of income. The nature of the business is clearly the major determinant, but probably such lesser factors as management control and the size of the business unit also play a part. Neither of the latter is powerful enough to eliminate fluctuation, but they may act as moderating influences; moreover, segregation of the influence of any single factor is impossible. It must be apparent, however, that these changes must also affect net income, and at an accelerated rate. This is caused by the rigidity of many forms of expense, thereby causing the differential of net income to rise more rapidly than gross in periods of expanding business and to diminish at a faster rate in periods of recession. The Public and the Investor Look at the Profit-and-Loss Statement 

The profit-and-loss statement is not only a historical report of operations, but it also serves as a criterion or measure of success. The balance sheet is a momentary flash of the financial condition at a given moment of time; it is helpful in revealing where the corporation stands, but it does not tell the investor how it arrived there. Yet it has been the widespread practice of corporations not to provide the stockholders with detailed profit-and-loss statements; the information is presented to the public authorities where it can be obtained by the public, but it is seldom incorporated in the annual report. As an illustration, the General Motors Corporation presented a comprehensive document of eighty-three pages to constitute its thirtysecond annual report for the year ended December 31, 1940, yet scarcely more than one page was devoted to the income statement. The operating expenses were neither itemized nor reported in total. Briefly, the report consisted of a comparative statement of the net sales and the various net profit and net income figures.5 

" See Thirty-second Annual Report of General Motors Corporation Year Ended Decem ber 31, 1940, p. 72.

Possibly management feels that the average investor would not understand the profit-and-loss statement, but if so, this could be easily corrected by interpretation and narrative comment. Such treatment is now being given the balance sheet, and there is no real reason why it could not be extended to the earnings statement. Also, the pretext is given that the publication of a complete profit-and-loss statement would divulge valuable information to competitors. Needless to say, they are in a position to get it from public sources as well as elsewhere.

Failure to provide profit-and-loss statements is also partly the result of the lackadaisical attitude of investors who are content as long as they receive their dividends regularly. Little thought is given to the question as whether they should receive more or less. At least, the trusteeship described in a previous chapter is a living trust, and the investor is not devoid of responsibility on his own part. To this end, investors, either singly or in groups, should take steps to obtain profit-and-loss statements and to analyze them. The following types of analyses are suggested: (1) analysis of the various phases of operations, (2) analysis of the results of operations, (3) application of the results to the investment. These analyses are given added meaning by various forms of comparison. The results of a single year's operations may have meaning in an absolute sense, but detachment and objective appraisal are possible only by comparison with other periods or with other companies.

Although this comparison was favorable, 1930 was regarded as a poor year because of the downward trend of business and current results were judged in light of the long-term trend. There is always a great tendency to compare the results of operation with those of the preceding year only, and conclusions are drawn accordingly. While this procedure is commonly used in the preparation of many of the analyses issued for public consumption, the real student of finance must be careful to have the comparison sufficiently comprehensive. 

A five-year comparison is essential and even a ten-year study may prove desirable. The need for extensive and adequate analysis is vital because: 

1. It is advantageous to know the record of a concern over a long period of time for historical purposes and to have background as perspective for current analysis. 

2. Long-time analysis reflects the ability of the company to cope

1. 1 1 1 with fluctuating business conditions. No concern is definitely seasoned, nor has it proved its worth, until it has successfully weathered at least one major business depression. 

3. The progress of the company and its relationship with the industry at large may be presented more accurately. Such questions as 

Is the company expanding normally? How does its rate of growth compare with the secular trend? may be raised and answered. 

Analysis within the Income Statement 

One of the first objectives to seek from an interpretation of the income statement is an appraisal of the efficiency of operations. Two familiar tests applicable for this purpose are the following: (1) ratio of total operating expenses to gross operating income; (2) ratios of major expense items to gross operating income. The ratio of operating expenses to operating income is familiarly known as the operating ratio and is one of the most convenient and overall devices used to measure the results of operations. Those industries having a large amount of fixed capital usually have a relatively low operating ratio, and, vice versa, smaller fixed investments are accompanied by higher operating ratios. Broadly speaking, the following ratios have been regarded as being common in their respective fields: 

Industrials-above 85 per cent. 

Railroads-65 per cent to 75 per cent 

Public utilities-55 per cent to 65 per cent 6 Within the industrial group, the following ratios based upon profit and loss statements for the year 1938 are found:

OPERATING RATIO (PER CENT) 

90.3 93.6 86.6 89.2 99.8 98.6 94.2 84.5 91.8 98.6 96.0 93.3 88.3

The conclusion should not be drawn that the operating ratio is a simple and all-inclusive measure of financial soundness. As a matter of fact, it is mainly an incidence of the type of industry and this accounts for differences in the average rates shown for the three main fields of enterprise. On the face of things, one would be inclined to infer greater financial strength where a comparatively low-operating ratio exists. However, this is usually offset by financial and fixed charges which are not included as a part of the operating expenses. 

Thus, railroads and public utilities commonly have a larger proportion of fixed charges than the industrials. The larger amount in fixed charges results in a reduction in the proportion of gross revenues available for dividends, and as a consequence the percentage of gross remaining for the stockholders is more nearly uniform for the three fields than might be assumed from the operating ratios. The presence of non-operating income or expense may also greatly offset the validity of the operating ratio in certain instances, especially in the case of holding companies.

While the operating ratio may not be used as a common yardstick for inter-industry use, it is a convenient index of the operating efficiency of the single unit. In brief, it shows whether or not too much of the income is being absorbed by operating expenses. At the same time, it is not sufficiently specific to permit a thorough inspection or diagnosis of the total expense account. This may be done by preparing ratios to show the relation between each major expense item and gross income (sales). Among the ratios which may be used are the following: cost of goods sold to sales; selling, general, and administrative expense to sales; repairs and maintenance to sales; depreciation expense to sales; taxes to sales. 

Table 45 shows these ratios for selected industrial groups. They represent weighted averages for the listed corporations included in the study, and may be taken as norms for comparing any individual company within the same industrial group. However, ratios are of greatest value when used to compare different years' operations, since the results would reveal any departure from the normal or general trend and changes within the operating set-up of the company. The ratios have little value in comparing companies in different lines of enterprise.

As indicated above, the ultimate objective of the income statement is net income. However, the significance of net income varies according to the interests of the parties affected: 

Bondholders-the amount available to cover fixed charges. 

Preferred stockholders-the balance remaining after paying fixed charges.

Common stockholders-the net amount remaining after allowing for the two preceding items.

To reveal the position of the bondholding group, the two following ratios are significant: (1) number of times interest is earned, (2) factor of safety. The ratio of net income to interest is designed to reflect first, from the corporation's point of view, the adequacy of income to meet interest requirements as a whole, and second, from the point of view of the bondholders, the sufficiency and surety of net income to cover the net requirements of the particular issue. For high-grade bonds, the net income should seldom, if ever, be less than two times the fixed charges. At the same time, the conclusion should

not be drawn that the investment rating of bonds varies directly with the income coverage of interest requirements. Again, the field of enterprise is an important factor. Railroad and public utilities commonly show less coverage than industrials, because of their greater stability of income. Conversely, a higher "net income times interest" ratio is necessary for industrials to allow for their greater subjection to income variations.

The foregoing point of view may also be applied to the dividends of preferred stocks. Although preferred dividends do not constitute a fixed charge in the legal sense of the word, it is necessary to have them well protected for other reasons. Inability to meet these dividends reflects upon the credit of the company and generally confuses its financial position. Ultimately, such deficiency must lead to a financial readjustment of some sort.

The net income remaining after allowing for the foregoing items belongs to the common stockholder. This is of significance to stockholders in two ways: (1) the total applicable, (2) the distribution or disposal of this income. The latter phase is discussed in the following chapters, and the former may be analyzed briefly here. Because dividends payable on common stock are not a fixed obligation, the relationship between the income available for dividends and the amount paid is not as vital as net income to interest. Instead, the more accepted practice is to stress the earnings per share. Obviously, one index of the vitality of earnings is their sufficiency to cover dividends, but in addition much attention must be given to the trend of earnings per share over a period of time, and to the relation between per share earnings and the market price of the stock.

In order to emphasize the importance of earnings per share as such, it is necessary to objectify them apart from current dividend policy. This is well illustrated by the Aluminum Company of America. The present company paid no dividends on its common stock from re-incorporation in 1925 to 1939, although during that time the common stock had sold as high as 5391 per share. The major justification of this price was founded in the future outlook of the company and the earnings record at that time. does not immediately concern corporate financing. It is of significance, however, because the price-earnings ratio as determined on the stock market indicates investor appraisal of the company's future. In general, the stocks of higher-grade industrial enterprises tend to sell at a greater price-earnings ratio than companies of lesser standing. 

This makes it difficult to state any universal norm which may be used in interpreting the significance of the price-earnings ratio. Furthermore, this ratio varies according to the speculative moods prevalent in the markets at any given time.

In the early 1920's, a common rule-of-thumb was that a stock should normally be priced at ten times earnings or twenty times dividends. The relationship between earnings and dividends was based upon the practice of paying out approximately half of earnings as dividends. However, during the speculative boom of 1928 and 1929 many price-earnings ratios were far in excess of 10:1, and most previous ideas concerning security prices and earnings had to be abandoned. During 1932 and 1933, the extreme pessimism engendered by the depression resulted in stocks selling at extremely low prices. 

Many stocks were quoted at prices below the net current asset values as shown on the corporation's books. This was followed in the recovery of 1934 to 1937 by price-earnings ratio which were again, in many cases, in excess of the old rule of ten times earnings.

Another test of the earnings position is provided by relating income to investment. From a broad, economic point of view, the latter would be represented by the total assets, but for financial purposes, it is customary to view the investment represented on the equity side of the balance sheet. Actually, any differences would be largely a matter of definition of terms since the assets are necessarily matched by an equal amount of liabilities and equities. In presenting the accompanying table showing the distribution of net profits to dividends, there is no intention to convey the thought that the apportionment of the net profits between dividends and retention in the business is a matter of simple, mathematical formula. 

Usually, the distribution is worked out in each fiscal period and is 

2 Statistics of American Listed Corporations, Part I, pp. 46-47.

the result of balancing numerous factors. Part of these conditioning influences are personal in character because the policy is formulated by a small group of men, the board of directors. Some of these individuals will vote for dividends on the basis of the way they feel because they conceive themselves to be overlords of industry or will be influenced by their own personal investments in the company. 

Others will act more objectively and seek to relate the dividends to other relevant conditions both within the particular company and as to the larger forces which are entirely external in character. In addition, there exists in the background several indirect influences which give a setting for the establishment of dividend policy. These various conditioning factors may be seen in reviewing the effects of the following: business conditions, the policy of the individual management, the age of the specific company, and the type of industry. 

Effect of Business Conditions on Dividends 

A larger percentage of net income is paid out in dividends during the initial stages of a depression than during the height of prosperity. 

This is true in part because of the mathematical effect of a larger denominator caused by increased income during periods of prosperity, and in part by a desire to maintain a relatively uniform dividend rate. In addition, there is the fact that the momentum of an established dividend policy often carries beyond the point of discovery that a business depression has started. Eventually, the error is detected and the necessary correction made.

To illustrate this relationship between business activity and dividend policy, it may be noted that dividend rates were increased through the first quarter of 1930 over the rates prevailing in 1929. 

The peak rate of dividend disbursement was achieved in March, 1930, and the low was reached in June, 1933. A study of the dividend record of 600 stocks representing the different fields of business activity showed that dividend payments in 1930 would have amounted to $2,691,000,000 had the March rates prevailed throughout the year.³ 

The data for 1930 are shown in Table 50 together with the precipitate decline to the low point in 1933. 216 303 Business conditions also affect the thinking of the board of directors because a certain compunction to pay dividends is felt when the earnings are available. Indeed, a real burden of proof confronts any board which fails to pay adequate dividends when the company is in a prosperous state. In essence, it means that the board is electing to make new investments for the shareholders without their express consent. Such accretions may be justified to the point of protecting the initial investment, but beyond this, the directors may be exercising a power which is not consistent with the principles of a competitive economy. Under competition, the market is presumed to be the yardstick of business activity, and the payment of the market rate on capital would be regarded as a normal and expected cost of operation. Hence, where the directors elect to pass dividends and to retain all net profits for purposes of expansion, they are operating, in a sense, on the basis of a private subsidy without benefit of the usual checks provided by market action.

Individual Management and Dividends 

In noting the relationship between individual management and dividend policy, attention may be directed to the two possible extremes: those organizations which are niggardly in dividend payments and those which are more liberal. Typical of the former type are the Aluminum Company of America and the Radio Corporation of America. The present Aluminum Company, organized in 1925, did not pay a single cash dividend during the first fourteen years of its existence although it had enjoyed earnings in all but a single year. 

In 1928, the company did pay one share of Aluminum, Limited, stock for each three shares of Aluminum Company stock. Its first cash dividend was paid in 1939. The Radio Corporation of America was organized in 1919 and through the year 1940 had paid cash dividends of twenty cents in 1936, 1937, and 1940. Its record earnings per share amounted to $15.98 on the basis of the old stock, which was later split in the ratio five to one. 

The only reasonable explanation of the type of policy just described is that the management believed it wise to conserve cash and to make it available for expansion. On the other hand, it may be lacking in its failure to observe a sense of proper responsibility to the stockholders who invest for the purpose of realizing a return. Especially would this be true if investors were invited to participate without information to the effect that dividends would not be paid for an extended period of time. The declaration of such policy would at least have the merit of due notice, but failure to do so is a use of other people's money on the basis of quiet concealment. 

At the other extreme there are a number of corporations which are generous in dividend disbursements, without, of course, jeopardizing the financial soundness of the company. This policy is best illustrated in the more recent records of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and the Diamond Match Company. Throughout the depression of the thirties and ensuing years the telephone company maintained a dividend rate of $9 per share on common stock in spite of the fact that earnings covered the dividends in only four of the years from 1932 to 1940. Recognizing a sense of obligation to its many stockholders, the management believed that the stockholders were entitled to the established dividend rate as long as the financial condition reasonably permitted the fulfillment of this objective. It was maintained that the stockholders advanced capital to the corpora-

tion during more prosperous times both in the form of new commitments and earnings in excess of dividend payments which were retained in the business. Capital was no longer being utilized at the previous rate for purposes of broad expansion, and the strong cash position made possible the payment of the dividends. The existence of these more technical factors, however, should not cause one to overlook the more fundamental philosophy of a deep sense of responsibility the management has toward the stockholders. 

The Diamond Match Company announced in January, 1935, that all of the stated net earnings would be paid out to the stockholders and employees. The significance of the policy of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company lay in its acknowledgment of responsibility to stockholders, but the motivating force behind the plan of the Diamond Match Company was said to be an obligation to society. In the words of the management, the purpose was "to assist the Government of the United States in its fight for business recovery, the employment of workers, and a restoration of prosperity and national purchasing power." The plan resulted in declaring dividends in excess of earnings in 1935, but in 1937 and 1938 a more conservative policy was adopted and dividends represented approximately threefourths of the earnings.

Within these extremes, there are many variations of individual policy. In fact, standardization is an impossibility in a diverse business world with wide ranges as to the size of companies and as to the amount of risk incurred. Note, for example, the payment of dividends equal to 200 per cent and more of net profits in the case of forty-four companies which was previously reported. As pointed out in that connection, sixteen of these companies had assets of less than $3,000,- 000 which means that restricted personal interest was probably the controlling factor. Broadly speaking, there would undoubtedly exist a marked difference in dividend policy on the basis of size. Large corporations with scattered small holdings must necessarily recognize a sense of public responsibility which is not equally incumbent on smaller organizations where the relations are more personal and common understanding is more readily facilitated. 

In large corporations, the elimination of personal bias is particularly desirable. Valuable as personal opinion based upon wide experience may be, it still needs the support of factual analysis to meet the requirements of public trusteeship. Even here, marked variations

will continue as a characteristic of dividend policy among the various individual companies and fields of enterprise. 

Age of the Company and Dividends

Age in and of itself cannot determine dividend policy, but the maturity of a business enterprise is usually indicative of certain basic factors of strength. Otherwise, the particular company would have long since joined the vast army of failures. Seemingly, management would pay a smaller percentage of net income as dividends during the earlier life of a company than later when the organization was definitely established on a much firmer basis. Actually, dividends are not anticipated in this manner but are predicated more upon short-term expediency than upon long-term planning. Moreover, income fluctuations which are caused by changing business conditions tend to retard patterning of the dividend program. As shown in

For the most part, all the records are erratic with some indication that current profits are used less as a basis of dividends in a period of depression. 

Type of Industry and Dividend Policy 

A fourth conditioning influence on dividend policy is the type of industry. Obviously, industries which are featured by stability of income may formulate a more consistent policy as to dividends than those having an uneven flow of earnings. For example, public utilities are in a much better position to establish a relatively fixed dividend rate than various industrial groups. Mining companies may go through a long period of development before paying any return at all on the equity investment and then blossom forth with exceptional payments. Likewise, other new industrial developments which are promoted independently will experience both deferred and fluctuating earning power so as to prohibit the formulation of a clear-cut dividend program. In such instances, the chief item which is subject to policy formation is the extent to which earnings will be retained for plant improvement and expansion. 

In the last analysis, the amount and regularity of income are probably the most important basis of determining dividend declarations. Thus, many railroads have been forced to withgo the payment of dividends in recent years while established industrial companies were able to return to a dividend schedule following the curtailment of the early thirties. During the same period, the public utilities have had a fairly consistent record. 

Legal Basis of Dividends 

The foregoing aspects of dividend policy have dealt with questions relating mainly to individual management, but in addition there are certain basic principles that tend to be more static and are largely external in character. These are the legal and economic phases. In the eyes of the law, the corporation is created principally for the benefit of stockholders.4 In recent years there has been a decided tendency 

4 See Dodd, "For Whom Are Corporate Managers Trustees?" Harvard Law Rev., Vol. 45, pp. 1145, 1146 for the statement that "The directors and other agents are fiduciaries carrying on the business in the sole interest of the stockholders."

by public leaders to give a broader social implication to corporate matters, but by and large the criterion of legal action is still presumed to be rooted in the rights of the specific parties affected. Hence, the legal basis for the treatment of disputes concerning dividends is found almost entirely in an examination of the respective rights of the stockholders and of the directors.

In considering the rights of stockholders, it must be remembered that they in turn delegate to a board of directors the power to determine when dividends shall be paid. Not even a majority vote of the stockholders can interfere with the authority of the board in the conduct of the ordinary business of the corporation.5 Only under extreme circumstances or upon evidence of bad faith is the court likely to reverse the decision of the board of directors. The courts generally believe that their arbitrary ruling should not be substituted for the discretion of the directors. Even where a large surplus exists, stockholders would have little prospect of securing a court order to compel the payment of dividends. "The ultimate test is the good faith of the board and the reasonableness of their policy in retaining the surplus profits in the business.”7 One of the few cases where the court compelled the payment of additional dividends is that of Dodge v. Ford Motor Company. The company had capital stock of $2,000,000, an accumulated surplus of $112,000,000, and cash amounting to $52,000,000. Declaring that a business corporation was operated primarily for the profit of the stockholders, the court ordered the declaration of a dividend equal to one-half the "cash surplus." Clearly, however, the element of reasonableness played an important part in this instance, and it is apparent that the surplus was abnormally large in comparison with the capital stock. Except under extreme conditions, such as these, the court is not likely to overrule the decision of the directors.10 

5 Stevens on Corporations, chapter 16, Sec. 138. 

• Trimble v. American Sugar Refining Co., 61 N. J. Eq. 340, 48 A. 912. 

7 Stevens, op. cit., chapter 12, Sec. 99. 

8 204 Mich. 459.

Further evidence or the test of reasonableness is shown in Raynolds v. Diamond Mills 

Paper Co., 69 N. J. Eq. 299, 308, 60 A. 491, where it was declared that an equity court "is not without control where the directors roll their profits into their business year after year until the great snowball has been magnified twenty diameters." 

10 In Stevens v. United States Steel Corporation, 68 N. J. Eq. 373, 59 A. 905, the court would not compel the payment of dividends; here, the surplus was equal to only 6 per cent of the capital stock. Also see McNab v. McNab & Harlin Mfg. Co., 62 Hun. 18, 16 N. Y. S. 

448 affirmed 133 N. Y. 687, 31 N. E. 627; Lindgrove v. Schluter & Co., 256 N. Y. 439, 176 N. E. 832.

More frequently, the courts have overruled the payment of dividends because the question of the safety of the principal investment may be raised. Here, the court may feel compelled to conserve the assets in the interest of many parties; at the same time, the element of indiscretion on the part of the directors must be readily apparent.11 

By and large, therefore, "the shareholders' right to participate in corporate profits is contingent upon the decision of the directors to declare a dividend."12

Economic Basis of Dividends 

Beginning in the late twenties, many corporations deemed it sound policy to fortify their financial structure with a strongly intrenched cash position. Hence, they took advantage of the favorable equities market to raise additional funds and later, as shown previously in this chapter, curtailed the payment of dividends in the ensuing depression years. The result was the accumulation of cash which seemed extraordinarily large in proportion to the current liabilities, as shown in Table 52.

Such excellent cash positions as these have afforded much relief to the corporations (and ultimately to the stockholders) in periods of strain and prolonged depression, and they are generally cited as examples of sound financial policy. The decreased cash position shown in 1938 appears to have been due chiefly to an expanded volume of business over the earlier years resulting in increased liabilities and to the transfer of cash to inventories and other forms of assets. 

11 See Liebman v. Auto Strop Co., 241 N. Y. 427, 150 N. E. 505, where the court refused to restrain the declaration of a dividend. 

12 Stevens, op. cit., chapter 12, Sec. 99.

To these factors should be added, in 1940, the importance of increased liabilities due to marked increases in tax accruals. 

Some economists have questioned, however, the benefits to society of excessive accumulation of cash. They point out that this wholesale storage of cash reduces purchasing power and tends to destroy the balance between production and consumption. A wide acceptance of this theory would naturally have an important influence upon dividend policy. Less stress would be placed upon capital accumulation by business itself, and extra dividends would undoubtedly be a result. 

Thus, during the period from 1933 to 1939, large dividend disbursements were made because of the emphasis placed upon spending and were further stimulated by a special tax on undivided profits.13 

Another factor of influence which is difficult to appraise consists of various, broad social disturbances which gave wide acceptance to the thought that there was a basic lack of opportunity to use additional funds.

Dividends constitute a smaller and more variable percentage of the national income than is usually recognized. During 1929, dividend payments constituted 8.4 per cent of the national income. By 

1932, this figure had fallen to 7.1 per cent of a much smaller total income. If the peak year, 1929, is taken as a base, the 1932 index of dividend payments would be found to be 45.6, thus showing a greater reduction than any other type of income except rents and royalties.

Types of Dividends 

It should be noted that there are several types of dividends: (1) those paid in cash, (2) stock dividends, (3) dividends paid in scrip, (4) dividends paid in property. None of these dividends may be paid in excess of the current and accumulated earnings of the company because such payment would constitute a return of capital to the stockholders. Hence, the law generally prohibits the declaration of dividends from sources other than earnings so as to avoid deception of the shareholders and to maintain the equity underlying the indebtedness of a company. British practice differs to the extent of basing dividend declarations upon current earnings only. This means

In favor of basing dividends on current earnings only: 

1. Current returns are said to provide the best index of a company's ability to pay dividends. 

2. An accumulated deficit arising out of previous years is frequently eliminated by the process of recapitalization. In effect, this may be the cause of paying dividends before restoration of the original investment. 

3. Dividends based upon current earnings cause greater irregularity of payments and force the stockholder to pay more attention to corporate affairs.

In favor of basing dividends on current earnings and accumulated surplus: 

1. Greater regularity of dividends is permitted. 

2. This in turn cultivates an investment rather than speculative attitude toward stocks. 

3. The payment of smaller dividends in properous years permits. the accumulation of surplus which may prove to be a differential of safety in periods of ensuing depression. 

Cash Dividends

A cash dividend, as the name implies, is a dividend payable in cash. It represents, therefore, a diminution of the assets of the cor-

poration, and an increase of those of the stockholder. In a highly abstract sense, the increase of assets of the stockholder may not be regarded as genuine, since, to the extent he is apparently enriched, the value of his equity in the corporation is diminished. On the other hand, the payment of a cash dividend makes available to the stockholder what he previously could not touch. In any event, cash is, with few exceptions, the major form of dividend payment. 

In spite of the fact that the flow of income to the business enterprise is variable, it is desirable that cash dividends be reasonably stabilized, i.e., dividend payments should be as constant and uniform as possible rather than erratic and uneven in character.14 Even though the total distribution of irregular dividends over a period of years may be just as great, uncertainty and irregularity are not conducive to sound financial policy. Speculation is encouraged, and the credit of the corporation may be affected.

Some corporations have been able to establish dividend records of remarkable consistency (see Table 54), but in order to maintain their records they have found it necessary at times to delve into the surplus account. This was particularly in evidence in 1921 and again in the years 1932 to 1935 and in 1938. Frequently, earnings conditions necessitated more drastic measures than mere invasion of surplus, and many concerns were compelled to omit dividends entirely. In a few cases long-established records were interrupted. Outstanding among such 

14 This is particularly true of large corporations with scattered holdings.

companies may be mentioned Swift and Company, Western Union, Illinois Central Railroad, and New York Central Railroad. The chief danger inherent in the preservation of a dividend record is the possibility of sacrificing the ultimate financial standing of a corporation purely for the sake of pride or reputation. 

As a means of reviewing a dividend program over a long period of time, a brief summary may be made of the record of the United States Steel Corporation. Although the steel combination has never failed to pay on its preferred stock, it was forced in the period 1933 to 1935 to reduce the regular $7 dividend to $2.15 There have been many years in which the company has failed to pay on its common stock. The most noticeable feature of the common stock dividend record or policy is the absence of extremes either of the short or long type. For example, anything beyond what is considered the regular dividend is termed an extra dividend. From 1910 to 1914, the stock was on a 5 per cent basis, although only 41 per cent was paid in 1914 and nothing in 1915. Commencing with June, 1916, the stock was once more placed on a 5 per cent basis and continued so until March, 1926. During this same interval extras were also very numerous, for the last two years of the period being per cent quarterly. This meant that the stock was actually on a 7 per cent basis. At other times, quarterly extras were as high as 3 per cent, but this was due to the war rather than to normal business conditions. The maximum the corporation has ever paid in cash dividends to common stock in a single year is 16 per cent in the year 1917. From the year 1926 to 

1940 the maximum annual dividend was $8, and during the years 1932-40 dividends were omitted with the exception of $1 paid in 1937 and $3 in 1940.

There are many outstanding points in the dividend policy of the United States Steel Corporation. Among other features the following are significant. 

1. Dividends were paid but were not placed on a specified basis until the corporation was well established. 

2. Care has been taken to distinguish between normal and extra dividends. The latter in turn are changed into regular dividends only upon assurance that their payments are likely to be continued. 

15 All the arrearages on preferred dividends were paid off in 1936 and 1937, and the stock returned to its full rate in 1938.

3. In spite of the occasions when dividends were not paid, dividend payments have been more regular than sporadic. 

Such policies are primarily for the welfare of stockholders and not for the professional speculators who are favored by unusual and unexpected news and are dulled by the monotony of regular dividend declarations. The need for a stable dividend policy has been made all the more necessary today because of the extensive public ownership of corporations. The smail and casual stockholder is likely to have a greater need for a regular dividend, and, more important to the corporation, the small stockholders may not appreciate fully the reasons underlying the abrupt cessation of dividend payments. 

In contrast to the dividend record of the United States Steel Corporation and the other consistent dividend payers noted above, the records of the following companies may be noted for the sake of example. 

United States Rubber Company. From 1895 to 1940, dividends have been passed as follows: 1896, 1898, 1901–11, 1915–19, 1921–40. 

Bethlehem Steel Corporation.-Although organized in 1904, the initial dividend on common stock was paid in 1916 amounting to 30 per cent. Dividends continued until 1924 and were dropped until 1929, from which date they were paid until 1932. Dividends were paid again in 1936 and 1937, omitted in 1938, and paid in 1939 and 1940. 

Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company.-Dividends were paid on the common stock from 1899 to 1903 at a rate of 6 per cent and again from 1909 to 1914. From 1915 to the middle of 1920, 12 per cent was paid annually, followed by a 2 per cent quarterly dividend, September, 1920. None was paid from that date to August, 1929, when the stock was placed on $5 basis. In 

1931, the rate declined to $3.50, and to 25 cents in 1932. From 1933 to 1936 the company paid no dividends, but $2.50 was paid in 1937, 25 cents in 

1938, $1 in 1939, and $1.25 in 1940.

These irregular dividend payments are not necessarily open to condemnation, because in many instances the irregularity is the result of operations rather than policy. In general, stable dividends are most frequently maintained by: (1) corporations of long standing, (2) corporations producing goods and services of the necessity type. 

Stock Dividends 

Although the usual medium of distributing dividends is cash, payment in the form of stock is occasionally employed. The adoption of this plan as a fixed policy has provoked much discussion and is

deserving of careful consideration. The payment of dividends in stock regularly achieves: (1) conservation of cash for the company engaging in the practice; (2) in turn this constitutes a means of raising capital for the corporation; (3) stability of dividends is possible since the payment in stock does not constitute an immediate drain upon the corporation.

Three leading companies16 which have employed this practice are the Electric Bond and Share Company, the North American Com pany, and the Cities Service Company.17 The Electric Bond and 

Share Company has never paid above a 6 per cent stock dividend which was distributed on a quarterly basis, while the North American Company paid 10 per cent for a number of years. Although the latter appears to be unusually high, it should be remembered that this dividend was based on a par value of only $10 (since changed to no-par). 

The latest payments made by Cities Service Company consisted of a 

6 per cent stock dividend, supplemented with a cash dividend of 30 cents per share made in 1930 and 1931, and 3 per cent stock and 15 cents cash in 1929 and 1932.

The results of this policy are well illustrated in the case of the North American Company.18 Assuming an investment of 100 shares in 1923, the holdings of an investor would be increased to 199 shares in 1930 without necessitating any further cash outlay. To be exact, the accumulation on a 10 per cent basis would be as follows:

The president of the North American Company in defending the program cited the following advantages: 

1. Providing an automatic method of financing, with reasonable cost to the Company and without burden to the stockholder, part of the capital continuously necessary in the public utility business. 

2. Giving a satisfactory return to the stockholder and enabling him conveniently to choose the form of it each quarter either as immediate income or investment, the former by easily converting his dividend stock into cash, the latter by keeping his dividend stock and retaining his potential profit. Retention of the dividend stock has proved to be equivalent to employment of one's income profitably, without loss of time and without having to provide additional cash to make up a minimum investable amount. Thus the stockholder immediately puts his dividends to work, which is an important principle of wise investment.

It is evident that the first of these cited advantages helps to provide capital for any company expanding its operations. Capital is obtained in smaller, but more regular, lots whereas the use of stock rights raises funds in larger amounts at irregular intervals. Ultimately, both media give rise to an increase in the stock outstanding as shown in Table 55 comparing the North American Company with other utility organizations which used traditional methods of financing.

At this point, however, our interest is in the dividend policy rather than in the raising of capital. Regardless of whether stock dividends or stock rights are employed to raise capital, increased earnings are essential to support the expanded capitalization. The rights plan imposes a more immediate need for earnings to defray larger cash dividends and therefore is more apt to affect the cash position of the company. The stock dividend plan also increases the

demand upon earnings but not as suddenly; instead, it helps to preserve the cash position of the company for the time being. 

The effect of cash dividends from the standpoint of the investor has already been discussed, so our present remarks may be concentrated upon the manner in which regular stock dividends affect the stockholder. Stock dividends give the stockholders the choice between acquiring additional stock and obtaining cash through the sale of the dividend stock in the market. In other words, the stock dividend program permits the stockholder to choose between a current return and further capital investment. The advantage of doing the latter was shown earlier, and some of the features involved in electing the former option may now be noted. Continuing with the North 

American Company for purposes of illustration, it is apparent that the stockholder would receive a return of approximately 10 per cent of the prevailing market price if his stock were sold.19 Supposing Mr. 

X holds 40 shares of the North American Company, it is apparent that: 

1. At a market price of 120, his investment would have a market value of 40 X 120 or $4,800. Dividends of 10 per cent would amount to 4 shares or $480-a yield of 10 per cent. 

2. At a market price of 60, his investment would have a market value of $2,400, but his yield on the basis of the prevailing market price would still be 10 per cent.

The actual yield may be greater or less than these figures, depending upon the price paid for the stock. Thus, if the investor paid $40 per share and the stock were selling at 120, his yield would be 30 per cent. In other words, it may be said that: (1) On the basis of market or current price, the yield does not vary. (2) On the basis of initial investment, the yield varies directly with the market price paid.

While it is exceptional for cash dividends to be in excess of earnings, this condition has been quite common for stock dividends. 

For example, the stock of the North American Company had an average price (average of high and low) for 1929 of 126ğ, so that the 10 per cent dividend had an average market value of 12ğ. The earnings per share for the same period amounted to $5.03,20 or con- 

19 Actually, the stockholder receives somewhat less because of commissions and other minor expenses. He would receive a full 10 per cent return only if he retained the stock. 

20 Earnings per share on the average amount of stock outstanding.

siderably less than the market price of the dividend. Such a condition, however, is not the equivalent of paying dividends out of capital. On the books of the company, the dividend per share is 

10 per cent of stated book value ($10) or $1. Since the earnings per share were $5.03 for 1929, it is apparent the dividend was well covered. 

The potentialities of an annual stock dividend policy are so startling as to invite inquiry as to whether or not it could be conducted perpetually. Obviously, no cash would ever be paid to the shareholders by the corporation, and the only outlet for such realization would be through sale in the market. Hence, the ultimate test of the propriety or soundness of the policy would be found in market response. As long as the corporation continues to expand at a profitable rate,21 the policy may well receive support. Conversely, declining earnings and general business recession would serve to retard its acceptance. Broadly speaking, the continuance of stock dividends as a substitute for cash dividends beyond the stage of profitable expansion would prove fatal to both corporation and the stockholder. 

It cannot be emphasized too strongly that the policy of paying regular stock dividends instead of cash is purely temporary and cannot be considered as a permanent replacement. To focus the ultimate effect, suppose all corporations pursued this course. Any investor committing his funds largely to stocks of this class would of necessity have to sell his dividend stock to achieve a real income. As stated above, this would be feasible only as long as the market response was favorable. Stock dividends of this type are also fatal to the stockholder in the event of failure, since it means that he may lose not only his initial investment, but in addition dividends that he might otherwise have received in cash. Because of these unusual characteristics, the adoption of a policy-paying dividend in stock in lieu of cash is the decided exception.

In addition to stock dividends of the regular variety, larger and spasmodic distributions are also common. Two conspicuous illustrations are: United States Steel Corporation-40 per cent stock dividend paid in 1927; Standard Oil Company of New Jersey 400 per cent stock dividend paid in 1922. From the standpoint of the corporation, a stock dividend permits the permanent retention of capital of an equal amount in the business. Thus, as a result of the 40 per 

21 For example, while the stock of the North American Company increased 154.6 per cent in seven years, its net earnings increased 312.8 per cent.

cent stock dividend of the United States Steel Corporation, $203,321, 000, or an amount equal to two-fifths of the previous stock outstanding, was transferred from the surplus account to the capital stock account.

From the point of view of the shareholder, his holdings of shares were increased in proportion to the stock dividend declared. If a 40 per cent stock dividend is paid, a stockholder owning five shares originally would own 7 shares after the dividend. Because of this increase in the number of shares outstanding, it is obvious that the unit value per share must decrease. To reflect this, the market price of the security declines accordingly when the stock goes ex-dividend.

Closing price, old stock 

Closing price, new stock 194 39 Stock dividends are usually regarded in the speculative market as melons, i.e., the division of accumulated surplus. As indicated above, however, the stock dividend simply divides the same amount of wealth into a larger number of aliquot parts. No increment of wealth is added, nor is any distribution actually made to stockholders. In the face of these facts, stock dividends are accepted with enthusiasm because of the following considerations. 

1. A stock dividend is a public admission of a large accumulated surplus. 

2. It regarded as being probable that a higher pro rata rate of dividends will be declared on the new shares. 

3. The stock dividend lowers the price of the stock and consequently enlarges the market for the stock. For the more immediate reaction, it is found that stocks usually have a rapid rise prior to the declaration, with a tendency toward dullness after the dividend is issued. 

Scrip Dividends

A third type of dividends utilized by corporations is scrip, which is a form of promissory note promising to pay the holder at a specified later date. Such certificates are usually interest-bearing and are frequently acceptable as collateral. They may be utilized either

0 when a corporation is immediately short of cash, or when it desires to conserve its present cash holdings for other more pressing demands. 

As an instance of their use, the American Tobacco Company paid its dividends in this form for six quarters during 1919 and 1920. Later instead of liquidating these obligations in cash, it succeeded in retiring the scrip by exchanging common B stock. Ordinarily, a scrip dividend is a substitute for cash, but in this case it proved a temporary medium for stock dividends.

Property Dividends 

Finally, dividends may be in the form of property, or paid in some asset other than cash. These distributions are usually the result of exceptional conditions and are not apt to represent normal policy. 

The following conditions are illustrative of their past use. 

1. As breweries were ruled illegal through the application of the 

Volstead Act, the stocks of liquor on hand could not be disposed of through normal sales channels. Hence, they were used for distribution to the stockholders. 

2. After the war, many corporations and individuals held large amounts of Liberty bonds. In a few cases, the former distributed the bonds as dividends. 

3. In closed corporations, it is common for the owners to utilize the products produced if at all adaptable to family life. 

4. Corporations holding stocks of other corporations (usually subsidiary or having a common interest) sometimes distribute these shares to their stockholders as a means of avoiding actual or possible prosecution under the Sherman Anti-trust Act or for reasons not usually made public. Examples are: the distribution of stock of Electric Bond and 

Share by General Electric Company, of stock in Radio Corporation of America by General Electric Company and Westinghouse, of stock in the Mission Corporation by the Standard Oil Company of New 

Jersey, etc.

Liquidation and Income Dividends 

As a final classification of dividends, it is necessary to distinguish. between liquidation and income dividends. The latter are the normal expectancy of all going concerns and are presumably covered by current or at least accumulated earnings. Liquidation dividends represent the distribution of assets either as a result of failure or dissolution for other reasons.

Summary of Principles underlying Dividend Policy 

With the foregoing discussion in mind, certain principles underlying dividend policy may be set forth. 

1. Dividends should be regular in preference to irregular. This is desirable for the welfare of both the corporation and the stockholder. 

2. Regular stock dividends may be used where concerns are expanding and can profitably employ the capital retained. 

3. Large irregular stock dividends should be used only occasionally and even then with discretion. The purpose should be strictly to accomplish the permanent retention of capital in the business and not to influence speculative proceedings in any way. 

4. Extra dividend distributions should be designated as "extra" and care should be taken to avoid the impression that the regular dividend rate is being increased. 

5. If the earnings position is sound, but current conditions make it desirable to conserve cash, scrip dividends may be resorted to for purposes of meeting temporary conditions.

CHAPTER XXVI  

HE balance of net income remaining after the distribution of dividends to stockholders is ordinarily transferred to the surplus account. Contrary to popular belief, surplus is not the equivalent of cash; it is simply an equity of the stockholders which arises from their right to participate in the earnings. Surplus differs from the initial capital investment mainly in its availability for distribution to the shareholders. The directors may elect to retire the surplus at any time by the payment of dividends while the original capital stock is frozen until the final liquidation of the company. On the other hand, the surplus earnings may be retained in the business permanently, either formally through their conversion into capital stock by means of a stock dividend, or informally by allowing the earnings to be designated simply as surplus. 

There is need to reiterate that surplus is solely an equity of the stockholders and is not an asset in any sense of the word. Neither may the assets arising from this source be segregated or earmarked as being representative of the surplus account. Profits affect the business enterprise as a whole and the increment of assets which comes from successful operation is more or less automatically distributed among all the various asset accounts. It is true that earnings serve initially to increase the current assets (cash, accounts receivable, inventories, etc.), but there may be diversion also into plant and other long-term improvements by action of management. 

Such an understanding of surplus is essential for the proper formulation of financial policy. It means that surplus itself does not fully inform the directors of the financial position of the company, of the results of operation, or whether or not dividend payments are economically sound. Equally important, the state of the assets must also be given consideration. Although the accumulating surplus may have resulted in additional assets, they may not be available for immediate dividend payments. A change in the rate of the turnover of working capital may mean a reduction in cash and an increase in accounts receivable, inventories, or goods-in-process. Under these 510

circumstances, a more conservative dividend policy may be desirable. 

Moreover, it is necessary to consider the accounting methods employed before it is possible to say that the profits indicated have actually been realized. Calculated depreciation may be inadequate, and hidden losses may be contained in accounts receivable and in inventories.

It is not at all unusual for a corporation to fail with a reasonably large balance appearing in the surplus account. For example, at the end of 1928 the International Combustion Engineering Corporation had a surplus in excess of $5,400,000 as shown in the accompanying balance sheet. Despite the indicated surplus, the company went into the hands of receivers in 1929 because of a shortage of liquid assets, although the ultimate causes were probably more deep rooted than this.

41,052,364 5,432,828 $60,513,769 To repeat for the sake of emphasis, the following observations concerning the nature of surplus may be stated succinctly: 

1. The surplus account is not offset by any specific assets but simply represents a claim of the stockholders against the assets as a whole. 

2. A large surplus account may not necessarily mean a satisfactory financial position. 

3. A surplus account does not necessarily mean that assets are in excess of current needs as of a given year; primarily, it reflects the growth of the stockholders' equity. 

Need for Retaining Surplus

With this understanding of surplus, consideration may now be given to the various questions of corporate policy relating to the 1 Based upon the balance sheet presented in Poor's Manual of Industrials (1930), p. 2799.

retention of income. Why should corporations retain a portion of net income in the business rather than distribute the excess earnings to the stockholders? The general answer to this query is obvious, but much may be gained by answering it as completely as possible. 

The practice may be analyzed from at least three points of view: (1) corporate management, (2) the investor, and (3) social welfare. 

Surplus and the Corporation 

One of the basic aims of progressive management is to make the corporation as enduring as possible. It should be able to withstand seasonal reactions, the shock of business depressions, and the vicissitudes of broad, social movements. An important means of attaining this position is the accumulation of surplus. This is true because, first, the presence of a relatively large and sound surplus account adds greatly to the credit position. The growing surplus account is usually indicative of progress and automatically increases the amount of the residual equity which helps to make the company a good credit risk. 

Second, a stable dividend policy is facilitated by a large surplus because the company is less dependent upon the results of any one year (assuming a satisfactory asset and liability structure). The combination of a good credit rating and an established dividend record affords great relief against business depressions since an assured credit position aids in obtaining liquid funds to meet current financial needs while an established dividend policy adds general stability by enlisting the support of the stockholders. 

The surplus account is also a source of capital for expansion purposes, and its use is sometimes referred to as the plowing in of surplus. Normally, the earnings of any given period are ultimately realized in the form of cash or other relatively liquid funds. Management has a choice of paying out dividends to the extent of the earnings or of keeping a portion of the earnings in the business. 

While the retention of a portion of the earnings in the business may not represent any sizable amount of additional capital in a given year, the accumulation may be quite important over a longer period of time. Plowed-back surplus may under some circumstances provide more additional capital than is obtained through the sale of new securities. Also, funds raised in this manner may be used to retire bonded indebtedness to the end of having a company free of long-term debt.

Lacking the fanfare of a new security issue, the importance of surplus as a source of capital is not commonly appreciated. Yet it is not unusual to find the surplus account in excess of either preferred stock or funded debt. Again, many smaller enterprises rely almost entirely upon common stock and the retention of earnings as sources of long-term capital. Taking a broad cross-section of business enterprise, the various classifications of surplus were found to account for 21.8 per cent of the total assets of 1,741 companies as of the year 1937. 

The composition of the surplus account is shown in Table 56.

Brief attention should be called to the fact that all forms of surplus are included in Table 56. In measuring the accretions to capital coming from earnings only, it is obvious that capital surplus would be excluded.2 However, the classifications are not mutually exclusive, and it is possible under accounting practice to have capital surplus created by transfer from the earned surplus category. In addition, it is likely that the great bulk of unsegregated surplus and surplus reserves came from earnings. This means that the types of surplus shown reflect primarily accounting classification instead of measuring accurately the original source of the funds. 

Surplus and the Stockholder

Broadly speaking, anything that improves the position of the corporation must favorably affect the welfare of the stockholder. 

Exception may be taken to this statement because it is conceivable that inside interests could retain earnings to the point that dividend prospects would be extremely remote. Dividends would be deferred 

2 See chapter XIII for discussion of capital surplus and earned surplus.

beyond a reasonable waiting period, and stockholders in need of funds would be forced to liquidate their investment. However, such conditions are decidedly abnormal, and stockholders, themselves, usually favor a reasonable accumulation of surplus for the following reasons: (1) greater assurance is provided against failure; (2) frequently the investment proves to be very profitable. The retention of surplus by a corporation is an act of trust performance, i.e., in the social implications of the term. In the first place, the decision is made to retain earnings which may be otherwise distributed as dividends. Secondly, this should be done only if it makes the stockholders' position more secure, as well as to obtain reasonable profits upon the additional investment. Irrespective of the outcome, it is clear that the retention of earnings gives rise to a form of involuntary investment by the stockholders. This right of decision is usually accepted as an ordinary prerogative of management, and in addition it has the support of legal sanction. At the same time, there is danger in carrying this power to the point of an assumed privilege of management without proper regard for the effects on both investors and society. Certainly the stresses and strains of the past decade have made it clear that the investment of surplus earnings should be checked just as carefully as funds coming from the open market. 

In analyzing financial practices, there is an inclination to probe for the underlying principles of a more or less ideological character. 

Often, the facts run counter to these theoretical concepts-not because of the unsoundness of the latter, but because powerful forces of expediency compel their violation. It is true that surplus is accumulated to provide a cushion of safety and to take advantage of profitable investment, but probably more important, surplus is frequently the only convenient source of new capital. Irrespective of safety and profits, the momentum of a going concern requires the infusion of new funds to meet the fluctuations of business as well as for purposes of normal expansion. Also, smaller companies with less access to the open market will raise a larger proportion of their capital from surplus than larger companies which can attract capital by the sale of new securities.

Another illustration of the effect of expediency on financial practice is found in noting the relationship between funded debt and surplus. Reasoning deductively, it would be expected that companies which utilize funded debt liberally as a means of raising capital

would have a stronger surplus position than those without funded debt. Actually, a cross-section of industry shows the opposite condition and that companies with only common stock outstanding have made greater use of surplus. The size of the company, the field .of enterprise, and numerous other conditioning elements will obviously affect the results but these, in turn, reflect various pressures of expediency which determine in large measure the financial pattern. 

The conditions just described are readily apparent in Table 57 which shows the percentage of all surplus to the total assets for the various patterns of financial structure. These are facts that stockholders need to face realistically. They may be told that the surplus will make the company safer or that the reinvestment of earnings
