And, as stated earlier, the most important criterion by which to judge the policy of surplus accumulation is to be found in the results obtained from the investment of the funds, i.e., on the asset side. In many respects, the ratio of surplus to total capital or to the total assets is mainly a financial decoration but the realities are found only in cold-blooded analysis of the asset structure. 

Society and Corporate Surplus 

Not only are the corporation and its stockholders directly benefited by a sound surplus policy, but there is also a contribution to the welfare of society. It is an act of saving which facilitates the storing of

wealth necessary to social progress. This may not be the intent of corporate management, but such must be the result to justify the accumulation. Surplus should facilitate the improvement of plant and encourage the adoption of technical advances so that goods of better quality are produced at lower prices. By this means, societyat-large should be the beneficiary by an increased standard of living. 

The existence of a sound surplus position may also prove to be a social benefit by its absorption of the shocks of business depression. 

Where the account is not large enough to absorb losses, there is an impairment of the capital account which often leads to failure. The charging of losses to surplus is purely a bookkeeping transaction, but it may be of importance in avoiding legal and financial embarrassment. Without this cushion, banks and other financial institutions are taken over by supervisory authorities because of their impaired condition. Ordinary industrial companies with a deficit may continue to operate if they are still able to pay their debts, but there may be great difficulty in securing credit and in maintaining the good-will of the stockholders. Hence, by avoiding failure and other financial embarrassment, surplus is a factor in relieving society from possible confusion and disorganization. 

Consideration should be given to the theory that the enlargement of surplus tends to produce and intensify the baneful effects of a depression. It is contended that corporate savings generate a lack of balance between purchasing power and production by diminishing the former and increasing the latter. The validity of the arguments depends upon the interpretation of purchasing power. In the sense that it is the equivalent of the very goods and services produced, the argument is obviously fallacious. Others regard purchasing power as a separate phenomenon and the assumption of this connotation lends merit to the view that large corporate savings tend to produce a state of overproduction. At the same time, it does not dispose of one other significant aspect of the case, viz., that savings are essential to the growth of industry. It also follows that improvements of the standards of living must necessarily be dependent upon an increase in the supply of goods, which is forthcoming only through the enlargement and improvement of industrial plant and facilities. Thus, it would appear that corporate savings, at least at a reasonable rate of increase, tend in the long run to help society.

Extent to which Corporations Retain Surplus 

Corporations vary greatly in their practice of retaining surplus. 

Some are inclined to keep as large a portion in the business as possible while others are more liberal in their dividend payments. Although it is generally accepted as a desirable policy to provide for regular dividend payments irrespective of fluctuations in profits, some companies are unable to do this and pay dividends only as current profits permit. As a general statement of practice, it appears that there is a tendency for dividend payments to approximate two-thirds of earnings.3

An example of policy in the retention of surplus is General Motors Corporation which had retained from the date of its organization to the end of 1940 a total of $641,477,000 out of its net earnings. This compares with a total of $2,011,504,000 paid to the common stockholders in cash dividends. The dividend record is most impressive, the disbursements representing almost a fivefold return of the present amount of capital stock. At the same time, the importance of earnings as a source of capital must also be recognized because the earned surplus still on the books amounts to $446,443,000. This compares with common stock outstanding in the amount of $435,000,000 and preferred stock of $187,536,000.

Another example is General Electric Corporation. On December 

31, 1938, the company reported a total capital investment of $322,- 

739,000. Nearly half of this sum, or $142,452,000, was earnings that had been retained in the business. A similar picture is presented by the country's railroads. In the seventeen-year period, 1921-37, they invested over $10,000,000,000 for all purposes. Of this amount 72 per cent was obtained from income, 19 per cent from security sales, and 9 per cent from decreases in working capital.5 

Administration of the Income Retained 

Having retained income in the business, the question arises as to its use and disposal. It is necessary in this connection to keep in mind the relationship between surplus as an equity account and the various counterbalancing assets. From the point of view of the assets, it may be said that surplus earnings may be used either for the improvement & Wall Street Journal (December 29, 1939), p. 1, reports a Treasury investigation which concluded that the usual corporate practice was to pay out 70 per cent of earnings as dividends, 'T.N.E.C. Hearings Part 9, Savings and Investment, p. 3599. 

Op. cit., p. 3571.

of the working capital position or to increase the fixed investment. 

As previously emphasized, it is impossible to designate specific assets as coming from earnings, thereby making it difficult to determine whether surplus has been used to improve the working capital position or to add to the fixed investments. At the same time, it is possible to secure a degree of correlation between the asset outlet and the equity source by the use of appropriated surplus accounts, which are more generally referred to as reserve accounts. 

Unappropriated surplus is simply the total of the accumulated earnings allowed to remain in the business which are not designated for any particular purpose. Frequently, it is desirable to align surplus with some specific program, and a portion of the surplus is definitely tagged as being for that objective. This may be made clear by reference to the accompanying summary balance sheet of the United State Steel Corporation, which is an example of a company making rather extensive use of reserve accounts.

It should be understood that allocations from the surplus account proper to the reserve accounts do not necessarily affect the distribution of the assets except to assure

their retention in the business to a greater degree. However, the allocation of surplus for specific purposes should imply definite needs which would reduce the amount of surplus available for the declaration of dividends and serve to restrict the disbursement of cash necessary for this purpose.

Occasionally, companies establish separate funds at the same time they set up reserves. Although the term "funds" is used loosely in practice and may appear on the liability side in the sense of a reserve, it is more accurate to restrict the connotation to asset allocations. In this sense, there is usually an actual segregation of cash for definite uses. The creation of separate and special asset funds is not a common practice because of the greater convenience and profitability in keeping all funds available for general purposes. It is true that special funds which are created voluntarily may be discontinued at the discretion of the board of directors, but there is danger that such action may be interpreted by outsiders as a vacillating and unsatisfactory policy.

Even though reserve accounts (as distinguished from funds) do not directly isolate assets for the specific purposes designated, their function still remains. This may be seen by relating financial policy to the following main classifications or types of reserve accounts: (1) valuation reserve accounts, (2) proprietary reserve accounts, (3) liability reserve accounts. 

Valuation Reserve Accounts 

A valuation reserve is usually a contra account to some asset. It is best represented by the reserve for depreciation and by the reserve for bad debts. For example, if the plant account of the Makup 

Company is reported as $15,000,000 and the reserve for depreciation as $4,500,000, the present book value of the plant is computed as follows: 

Original cost of plant.. 

Less reserve for depreciation.. 

Present book value, . $15,000,000 4,500,000 . $10,500,000

It is apparent that the major purpose of such a reserve is to replace or supplant the value which is departing from the original investment. 

Certainly, before any business enterprise can say that it has a net ...

profit (in the ultimate sense of the term), it must provide for depreciation of its plant, equipment, and other wasting assets. 

In periods of depression, there is often a tendency to minimize the pertinency of depreciation cost; either the charge is reduced or, occasionally, it may be eliminated. The latter is technically accomplished by writing the value of the plant down to $1, and charging the surplus account (assuming the account is large enough to absorb the charge) for the write-off. An illustration of this is the Commercial Solvents Corporation which in 1931 reduced the value of its "land, equipment, and buildings after depreciation" from $1,236,988 to $1.

Where the fixed investment is written off, it is commonly assumed that prices may be lowered and competition more easily met because of the elimination of the depreciation charge. From the accounting point of view, much may be said in favor of this practice, but it is not as easily defended in terms of financial management. Viewed from the perspective of the latter, it may be said that one of the chief objectives of management is to preserve the enterprise as a going concern. In this light, it will be observed that to write off the value of the plant is simply an act of recognizing a loss and does not contribute to the permanency of the organization the management represents. 

The removal of any basis for a depreciation charge would increase the paper net profits which would be reported to the stockholders in the future, but at the same time it is clear that the gradual accumulation of assets normally resulting from the depreciation charge would be eliminated. Consequently, if management should pay out the bulk of the apparent profits as dividends, it may in reality be sacrificing the recurring nutrition of plant which is necessary to keep a business in vigorous condition. After a few years of this policy the assets would become exhausted and the company no longer able to operate. This could be avoided by a judicious surplus policy wherein surplus was increased each year by an amount equal to depreciation. 

However, this could be more readily achieved by systematically charging depreciation based upon the current value of the physical assets used in the business. In other words, it may be said that management may regard depreciation in terms of the replacement of values rather than merely accounting for the investment originally committed to its care. While this is the equivalent of new investment,

it is probable that the stockholders are much better protected by this method. 

As an illustration of these principles, some mention may be made of the railroad field where no depreciation charge is made to cover the plant (not including equipment). It is contended, and with much logic, that normal replacement and maintenance automatically preserve the original status of the investment. Through the continuous replacement of worn-out ties and track, it would seem that the road should retain its original capacity for operation. This theory, however, stresses unduly the engineering or technical aspects of depreciation and attaches too little significance to changes in value which arise from other sources. It does not provide for obsolescence or for changes which may be desirable to lower the cost of operation. This failure to charge depreciation looks too much in the direction of the past, and pays too little heed to what may possibly be ahead.

The nature of depreciation and other valuation reserves, such as the reserve for bad debts, differs fundamentally from the proprietary reserve accounts which are in reality elements of "tabbed" surplus. 

The former constitute a legitimate charge against operating income, whereas the latter are the outgrowth of net income and its later accumulation. This may be seen to better advantage by a consideration of the more representative types of proprietary reserves. 

Proprietary Reserve Accounts 

There are a multitude of proprietary reserve accounts, but consideration will be given only to those accounts which are common expressions of financial policy. The following may be analyzed in order: (1) reserve for improvements, (2) reserve for contingencies, (3) sinking fund reserves, (4) reserve for insurance, (5) reserve for dividends, (6) reserve for working capital.

Reserve for Improvements 

The purpose of the reserve for improvements is to tap the surplus account for a specified amount of improvements. It may also be designated as a reserve for additions and construction or other similar terminology. The following cases taken from the December 31, 1929, balance sheets are representative:

United States Steel Corporation.-"Earned Surplus-Appropriated for and invested in capital expenditures $270,000,000."

Bethlehem Steel Corporation.-"Surplus appropriated for addi tions to property and working capital $120,000,000." 

The United States Steel Corporation carried this account at the $270,000,000 figure from 1926 to 1935, in which year it was written off through transfers to the reserve for depreciation and depletion of $88,720,028 and to the amortization reserves, $181,279,972. The Bethlehem account was dropped in 1931 by transferring the balance to general surplus and is an excellent example of the book nature of proprietary reserves. The balance in the original account rose from $94,000,000 in 1925 to $129,000,000 in 1929, and decreased to $116,- 

262,396 at the time of the write-off.

The creation of the reserve for improvements is accomplished by transferring a similar amount from the surplus. No new assets are obtained by setting up the reserve, and hence it in no way assists in the immediate financing of construction activities. Indeed, it may be created after the means of making the improvements have actually been assembled. This may be made more concrete by the following assumed example:

In the establishment of this reserve for improvements account, the expansion actually occurred first, but the procedure may be reversed. 

The principles are essentially the same, however, because: (1) Á reserve for improvements would be created by reducing the general surplus account by a like amount. (2) Upon the actual construction of the new plant, fixed assets would be increased and the current assets decreased (assuming no new financing). 

Although the creation of a reserve for improvements does not immediately provide the means of constructing the new additions, it does provide for the funds in an ultimate sense. By setting up a reserve for improvements, that amount is no longer available for dividend declarations, and hence, in an indirect way, the retention of an equal amount of assets is assured automatically. Of course, the funds or assets could be retained by means of a general policy, but the existence of a separate reserve account assures the following: (1)

The permanent retention of assets on a legal as well as an economic basis. (2) By the establishment of the account, the stockholders are informed to a certain extent of the expansion program and the source of the funds for its financing the same. Because of these facts, it is desirable for concerns which are expanding through the medium of earnings to adopt some specific procedure rather than blindly accumulate the funds through the general surplus channel without mentioning the fact to the stockholder.

Reserve for Contingencies 

While a general surplus account is in itself a reserve for contingencies, conditions arise where it may prove desirable to set up a special reserve account. The following circumstances may make this desirable: 

1. If definite contingencies are anticipated, it is sound financial policy to provide for them in advance of the actual event. 

2. Transferring funds from the general surplus account prevents the use of such funds for dividend or other purposes. 

3. Finally, a separate reserve for contingencies (either of the remote or near type) is of value as a matter of information to the stockholders and the creditors of the corporation. 

In current practice, the reserve for contingencies is frequently combined with miscellaneous and other reserves in the actual balancesheet presentation. For example, on the United States Steel Corporation's balance sheet there is the account "Contingent and miscellaneous reserves, $39,247,061." When the contingency occurs, the reserve will be reduced by the amount of the loss. For this reason, the question arises as to whether the reserve for contingencies is an earmarked form of surplus or a provision to discharge a liability. 

If the contingency is reasonably certain, the latter view should prevail; otherwise, it may be considered a part of surplus. In either event, it is a part of surplus until the contingency actually takes place. 

Again the reserve for contingencies is a simple accounting entry, but it does much to advance the financial program. 

Sinking Fund Reserve 

Upon first thought, one is apt to think of the sinking fund reserve as a liability. Is it not required by a bond indenture and, therefore, in the nature of a liability? The confusion again arises from thinking of reserves in terms of specific assets. To reveal its true setting, the following balance sheet tracing the flow of the account may be studied:

Upon the retirement of the bonds, it is evident that the sinking fund reserve is no longer necessary and that the stockholders have provided funds out of earnings to supplant those originally obtained by the assumption of debt. To give recognition to this change, the sinking fund reserve may be transferred to the general surplus account with the extinction of the bond issue.

If specific funds are desired to retire the bonds, a fund instead of a reserve (or else the two in conjunction) should be employed. 

Assuming a sinking fund and a sinking fund reserve as well as the perfect maintenance and replacement of the fixed assets, the foregoing balance sheet at the end of the tenth year would be: $8,000,000 10,000,000 17,000,000 10,000,000 $45,000,000

When the bonds are retired, the fund would, of course, disappear, and the sinking fund reserve would be restored to the surplus account. 

The accounting entries would be to debit the bond account and credit the sinking fund account thereby reflecting the payment of the bonds with the accumulated sinking fund; and debit the sinking fund reserve and credit surplus to return the appropriated surplus to the general surplus account.

Reserve for Insurance 

The United States Steel Corporation presents in its balance sheet for December 31, 1940: insurance reserve, $47,740,079. In some respects, such a reserve partakes of the nature of a contingency reserve in that it provides for possible future losses. The differences between the two are: 

1. Insurance reserves are provided for items which may be estimated on an actuarial basis or where they fall into the category of normal or recurring business risks. 

2. Insurance reserves cover possibilities which are more likely to occur. Because of this greater certainty, the reserve for insurance is for all practical purposes a liability reserve. 

In the interest of sound financial administration, very few enterprises should carry their own insurance. Only the large concern with diversified and scattered properties may do so successfully. Even here, it may be well to supplement the self-insurance with a policy from an insurance company to cover abnormal and extreme risks. In either case, adequate insurance is most essential to protect fully the longtime investor. For this reason, all new enterprises should seldom attempt to insure themselves. This applies equally to a new, large concern since self-insurance would intensify the risk too greatly at the inception of the enterprise. 

Reserve for Dividends

In the preceding chapter, the merits of a stable dividend policy were discussed. This program may be assisted by establishing a reserve for dividends. It is not uncommon to find a reserve for preferred dividends, but this is generally the result of an indenture requirement. In addition, it may be equally good policy to provide for a reserve for dividends on common stock. Again, the creation of the reserve would not set aside specific funds for the purpose; this could be accomplished only by setting up a concomitant dividend fund. Such practice is rare because: (1) it is desired to have the funds available for general purposes; (2) the funds can generally be employed more profitably when used for business operations than when treated on a fund basis. 

Reserve for Working Capital 

The purpose of a reserve for working capital is to retain assets in the business for the express purpose of strengthening the current

position of the company. Its creation does not directly nor necessarily increase any specific current asset as much as it may lead to the increase of the current items as a whole. Or the improvement in the working capital position may be the direct outcome of a reduction of the current liabilities. In either event, the process is facilitated by the retention of assets assured by setting up a specific reserve for working capital. As an illustration of this type of reserve, the reader is referred to page 522 where it is shown in conjunction with "Surplus appropriated for additions to property and working capital, $120,000,000" in the case of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation. 

Liability Reserve Accounts 

Although liability reserve accounts are usually provided to care for liabilities arising as a result of current activities, they may also be established to cover emergency liabilities. The former are illustrated by the reserve for taxes and the reserve for interest accounts. The purpose of these reserves is to remove from the net income account an amount sufficient to provide for liabilities that will shortly materialize and are uncertain only as to the exact amounts due. Such reserves should ordinarily be provided from current income. 

In contrast, there is the type of liability reserve which arises from some specific and non-recurring event. An example would be a reserve for damages arising out of a law suit. Such a reserve could be established through an appropriation of surplus, or as a transfer from the contingency reserve. The law suit is a contingency which has occurred, but the claims have not yet been paid. 

Trustee Aspects of Retention of Earnings 

The retention of earnings in a business illustrates in a peculiar way some of the qualities of trusteeship which are now being associated with corporate management. This is true both from the viewpoint of investors and of the larger public interest. As to the former, present dividends of immediate certainty are sacrificed for possible later returns with all the risks of future prospects. There is no element of choice on the part of the investor as was true of his initial investment, but the management presumes to act for the investors' benefit. This delegation of authority is inescapable in our present business system, but it is important that management be conscious of its part in acting for the welfare of others. Too often, there is a tacit assumption that the earnings belong especially to the cor-

poration and are not comparable to the capital investment which is represented by formal certificates. Business integrity demands, however, an equal accounting for funds irrespective of their source and with due recognition of the shareholders' interests.

Some attention has also been given in recent years to the possible effects of the reinvestment of earnings upon society as a whole. Not only is the question raised because of the lag in current purchasing power, but doubts have been expressed about the distribution of new capital. It is contended that the automatic inbreeding of capital is without the full benefit of market influence and that the remoyal of these funds from the market deprives other industries of an opportunity to compete for the funds. It is not presumed to debate the merits of this larger economic issue, but in self-defense management would do well to give an adequate accounting for this internal use of funds.

NOTHER phase of the distribution of corporate income is deserving of attention and that is the share which goes to the executives and officers. The question may be raised as to why this item of expense should be singled out for special discussion since it amounts to only a small percentage of the gross income. It is true that the amount is relatively small, but in this respect it is no different than numerous other items of expense which are normally put under the microscope of financial analysis. This may be seen by noting, in

Another basis of comparison which is appropriate is the relationship between the dividends paid to the stockholders and the amount expended for executives' compensation. As the owners of an enterprise, the stockholders should have a real interest in all forms of expense, including salaries. There is the danger of being accused of rabble-rousing, but the authors are attempting no more than an analysis of the income account, and especially as viewed from the perspective of the stockholders. Thus, in the two cases in Table 58, it is of interest to note that the Remington Rand Company paid dividends amounting to $2,081,000 in the year 1938, while the United States Industrial Alcohol Company did not pay any. Obviously, no conclusions can be drawn from the operation of a single year, but where dividends are omitted over an extended period of time the 530

stockholders should lose no time in protecting their interests. An examination of executive salaries should be undertaken along with all other items of expense. The tragedy is that stockholders are usually so ineffectively organized as to be without real representation, or when organization is provided, the sponsors are also interested mainly in their own fees and personal gains.

Comparison of Officer and Owner Returns 

Rule-of-thumb standards are, of course, inadequate to determine the most desirable distribution of corporate income. As a basic principle, most observers would likely agree that the division should synchronize as nearly as possible with the contributions to the total output. However, measurement of the individual contributions is impossible, and executive salary schedules are usually fixed through individual bargaining or friendly negotiation with those in control. 

Remotely, the responsibility may be placed on the stockholders because of their right to elect directors, but there is little effective exercise of this power for reasons already discussed. In addition, the stockholders are usually contented so long as they receive a fair return on their investment.

Another factor which complicates appraisal of the division of income between executives and owners is the difficulty of drawing a distinct line between an executive and certain other employees, particularly where the latter are on a salary basis. Bonus plans vary greatly in the number of officials scheduled to receive a share in the extra compensation. The Bethlehem Steel Corporation favored only a few of their executives, ten in 1917 and fourteen in 1929. The 

United States Steel Corporation, on the other hand, spreads the benefits over a much greater number. In both cases, the intent is to pay those more especially responsible for the success of the company, but certainly the latter method is the more democratic of the two.

It is obviously impossible to devise any yardstick which would determine whether or not there is an equitable distribution of income between the owners and the executive group. At the same time, there are many questions of philosophy or of underlying principle which arise solely on the basis of capitalistic operation. There is no market in the true sense of the term for executives and their placement is mainly a matter of private negotiation. Under these circumstances, high officials are frequently in a position to demand the top price.

They may not be criticized for this because it is in keeping with our standards of human conduct. It is expected that each individual should normally look out for his own interests because no one else would assume the responsibility.

Seemingly, stockholders would act in a similar manner, but there are many restrictions in the corporate system which prevent vigorous or prompt action on their part. Acting through a legal process of delegated authority, they can, at best, move slowly to protect their interests. As a result, the capitalistic system has developed so that there may be great reward for those having heavy responsibility with little risk while the owners with little direct responsibility have minimum or restricted income return in the face of residual risk. Possibly this condition is in keeping with recent trends which show surprising shrinkage of the return on capital, but stockholders, for their own protection, need to apprise themselves of this development. At least, the salaries of executives are now a matter of public record, and the failure of stockholders to respond must be considered to be evidence of implied sanction.

Table 59 presents a comparison of dividends and the amount received by officers on a much more diversified basis giving the results as a percentage of net profits for a period of three years as well as by three major groupings of business enterprise. It is not easy to pass impartially on the fairness of this distribution, but perhaps the most outstanding feature of the table is the smaller percentage of net profits going to the officers in the utility and transportation fields. 

It also reflects the attempt to adhere to established levels at the outbreak of the depression, and as a result the percentages of net profits

received by both owners and officers are greater in 1930 than for either of the other two years.

The passing of judgment on the reasonableness of salaries is probably impossible on a generalized basis, but at the same time it is easy to pose numerous questions which reflect the lack of any standards. Thus, it is difficult to understand why the United States Steel 

Corporation found it necessary to pay in 1938 executive salaries amounting to only $1,019,000 with a sales volume of $766,674,000 while the Bethlehem Steel Corporation paid $1,676,000 with sales amounting to $266,000,000. Or, why should numerous smaller companies feel compelled to pay salaries in excess of that paid to the president of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company?

These are inconsistencies within the circle of private industry itself which in all fairness should be explained to the stockholders who are the real owners of the corporation. Large salaries have been attacked by various social reformers for the purpose of creating public unrest, but our concern here is only with financial merit and the most economical conduct of business operations. Fortunately, these salary schedules now have the benefit of publicity and may be more readily justified than when they were paid without proper reporting to the stockholders.

Relationship between Salary Schedules and Size of Company 

At various points, it has been shown that the size of operation has had a distinct effect upon the characteristics of business operation. Salaries and their relationship to income are no exception. In a study of fifty-one companies with assets of more than $100,000,000 and fifty-three companies with assets of less than $10,000,000, the latter were found to pay a much larger proportion of their income for salaries than the former group.¹ Comparing the years 1929 and 

1936, the median salary of these two groups was as follows: 

1929-In the large companies, the median salary amounted to 3 per cent of earnings; for the smaller companies, it was 11 per cent. 

1936-In the larger companies, the median salary was equal to 3.5 per cent of earnings; for the smaller companies, it was 16.1 per cent.

Stating the foregoing results in more narrative form, the salaries paid by the larger companies were more than five times greater than those paid by the smaller companies in 1929; at the same time, their earnings were eighteen times greater. In 1936, the ratios were six 

1 J. C. Baker, “Executive Compensation," Dun's Review (November, 1939), pp. 17-18.

times and thirty times respectively. Speaking generally, the following observations were made: 

1. Large companies pay their executives a larger amount in dollars. 

2. In the case of large companies, the percentage of executive salaries to sales and net earnings is much lower than for smaller companies. 

3. The larger companies distribute a higher percentage of their earnings to the shareholders. 

4. Larger companies usually had around 12 or 13 executives while the smaller companies had 5 or 6.

The size of the company also affects the amount which is paid to the individual executive. In 1929, the median salary of the highest paid executive of the large companies was $101,000 as compared with $31,000 for the smaller companies; in 1936, the figures were $93,000 and $25,000 respectively. Publicity naturally centers around the odd or exceptional type of news, and for this reason the very large salaries of the few attract more attention than the pattern of the entire group. 

Taking a cross-section of large and small companies, it will be seen that the average salary paid to all executives does not appear to be inordinately large. In 1929, the average salary paid to all executives was $40,000 in the case of large companies and $18,000 for the smaller concerns; in 1936, the figures were $35,000 and $13,000 respectively.2 

Qualitative Aspects of Executive Compensation 

The most significant criteria of executive salaries are not, however, found in their quantitative relationship to net income, dividends, and the various items of expense. These comparisons do afford a degree of objectivity, but the reasonableness of compensation to executives will always be judged on a qualitative or subjective basis. The public generally realize that compensation should vary with the amount of responsibility assumed, and there has seldom been any great outcry against salaries simply because they were large. The thought as to whether or not the compensation was fair has been much more predominant in public thinking. 

In the appraisal of responsibility, the distinction between policymaking and administrative direction, on the one hand, and technical performance, on the other hand, has been generally recognized. Most 

2 See ibid. for further discussion of these salaries. For a more detailed study of large corporations see, J. C. Baker, Executive Salaries and Bonus Plans (New York: McGraw-Hill 

Book Co.), 1938.

people believe that capable leadership is essential to successful operation and are willing to pay a price to attract the right kind of talent. 

Viewed in this light, it is important to distinguish between the operating and the financial life of a business unit. Obviously, financial results depend upon satisfactory operations, but it is equally true that successful operations are dependent upon sound financial policy. As a result a careful distinction must be made between technical efficiency in the engineering sense and financial achievement in the profit-andloss and income sense. Many ideas which would appeal to the engineer with his interest in technical performance and conservation of energy may prove too expensive to use when evaluated from the point of view of financing the project and earning a reasonable return. 

For example, electric locomotion offers many advantages over steam, but its cost is frequently too great to warrant its use. Production of synthetic gasoline and rubber is technically feasible, but the cost of production is still too high to make it economically possible. Thus technical arts must be sacrificed to financial expediency. 

One may be prone, therefore, to condemn financial policy as a limiting force upon the progress of civilization. On the contrary, it is intended to serve as a safety valve and to insure production at the lowest possible cost. It is true that at times the search for the lowest cost may result in what appears to be a rather nearsighted policy such as is evidenced in the waste of our natural resources, but it would be difficult to say that the future may not bring forth some method of production which would recover the apparent waste or introduce substitutes which would make existing products obsolete. Much responsibility is placed upon individuals who are called upon to make decisions along these lines, and one of the real problems of society is to find talent of sufficient capacity to do the job. It is not a question of getting men with technical skill, but one where men with executive leadership are sought-men with constructive ideas which put progress above the status quo. "The capable executive is the man who has ideas, who inspires others to help effectuate them, who is able to coordinate the work of his subordinates. A few outstanding ideas often mean the difference between the signal success of an enterprise, and mediocrity or even failure."s 

8 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11, Bureaucracy and Trusteeship in Large Corporations, p. 85.

See particularly chapter VIII, "Personnel Factors," for a discussion of the qualities of business leadership.

It is a common complaint that first-class executives are scarce. 

Even in the worst days of the last depression there was difficulty in filling the top jobs. College students may not easily appreciate this condition because many look forward to the day when they will be in positions of authority. But leaders are chosen and are not selfappointed. The observation that "power with people is more important than power over people" illustrates the type of leadership which is sought. To achieve this quality, long years of training and experience are usually necessary. Beyond this, there are numerous prerequisites which are not easily cultivated by training, such as character and personality.

Means of Attracting Executive Talent 

The shortage of executive talent has led to various ways and means to increase the incentive of the executive or official heads of the corporate family. One familiar device is to pay a salary sufficiently large to encourage managerial forces to render constantly their best services.

Hence, many industrial leaders contend that the key men should share according to the fruits of the enterprise. This is usually accomplished by the payment of a bonus when earnings exceed an established minimum standard. It is common to establish a fixed salary with the bonus to be paid in addition. The results may be seen in the following sample of individual compensation for the year 1929:

For example, in 1931, when Gerard B. Lambert became the president of the Gillette Safety Razor Company, he agreed to serve without salary. However, if the earnings per share of stock amounted to $5, he was to receive 20,000 shares of stock, and an additional 20,000 shares if the earnings equalled $6 per share. The directors reserved the right to decide his future salary. For all practical purposes, this principle is also illustrated in the case of Eugene Grace, president of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation, whose normal salary per year until recently was $12,000. For the period from 1925 to 1930 he received, in addition to his salary, aggregate bonus payments amounting to $5,431,684.

Some authorities believe that real leadership cannot be bought and that it is the result of an appeal to incentives other than financial return. There is a feeling that bonuses are unnecessary and that they may favor the self-seeking individual who places personal gain above the welfare of the corporate group. The following comments by executives illustrate this point of view: 

Enormous executive bonuses are utterly inexcusable. They were the "growing pains" of industry. They were paid at a time when everyone was trying to take all he could while the taking was good.

Bonuses are indefensible. Profits are not a reflection of managerial ability to any considerable extent; they are due to general conditions-high during prosperity and low during depression. But men have to work harder during the periods of depression.*

Little is to be gained by entering into a long debate about the merits of the bonus system, but it should be recognized that some form of bonus payment is a common feature of business operation. 

It is used as a means of compensating both the operating personnel and the executives. The concern here is only with the latter group because of their responsibility to the stockholders. The owners of the typical corporation commit their enterprise to a small group, and it is fitting that they be informed about the actions of their managers. 

4 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 11, p. 91.

It is with this stockholder interest in mind that the various types of bonus plans may now be discussed. 

Cash Bonus

The principle underlying the cash bonus is that the added compensation is paid in consideration of, or as a reward for, greater earnings obtained during a fiscal period. Managerial services are regarded as being of a current nature and the obligation is settled immediately through sharing a portion of the company's cash with the management. While seeming to rest on a quid pro quo basis, the cash settlement may give undue emphasis to possible fortuitous events, over which management has no control and no responsibility. For instance, in the late 1920's, many corporations enjoyed exceptional earnings which were not necessarily a reflection of managerial ability but were merely a result of the large volume of business which was common to most fields of activity. It may be said with some reason that these exceptional earnings arose in spite of, rather than because of, management. Nevertheless, the cash bonus has the advantage of being specific, and unlike the stock bonus, free from possible entangling speculative motives.

Stock Bonus 

When stock is paid as a bonus it is apparent that a longer-term view is placed upon management. A permanent investment is given to the executive in preference to an immediate cash settlement. In most cases the recipient is free to sell his shares but this simply transfers the investment equity to some other party. As far as the corporation is concerned, there is no immediate drain upon the cash account, although the ultimate and potential demands are increased because of the heavier dividend requirements. It is anticipated that the status as a stockholder which is given to management will result in an improvement of earning power to provide the funds necessary to meet this need. Unfortunately, phenomena over which management has no control frequently arise to prevent the realization of this simple formula. The depression of the 1930's would be a case in point. In addition, it should be recognized that often the dividend returns of the leading officers may be relatively small in com. parison with the basic salary.

Another variation of stock payment is to give the officers an option to purchase additional stock at specified prices, usually below

the prevailing market price. An example of such a plan is the arrangement made by Loew's, Inc., with its chief officials. Under a contract dated December 15, 1932, Loew's set aside 250,000 shares which were allotted: 100,000 shares to Irving Thalberg, and 50,000 shares each to Louis B. Mayer, David Bernstein, and J. R. Rubin.

These officers were permitted to purchase the allotted shares as follows: 27.78 per cent of the allotment from December 31, 1934, to

March 1, 1935, at $30 per share. 27.78 per cent of the allotment from 

December 31, 1936, to March 1, 1937, at $35 per share, and 44.44 per cent of the allotment from December 31, 1938, to March 1, 1939, at $40 per share. The only restriction on the stock so purchased was that it could not be sold for less than $15 above the option price. 

In addition, the officers were granted a share in the profits of the company. Bernstein, for example, was to receive $2,000 a week salary, plus his travel expenses, plus 1 per cent of the annual net profits remaining after deducting $2 per share on the common stock. 

In 1935, Bernstein's total remuneration under this contract was $182,- 712. The contract was extended in December 31, 1938, for another five-year period.

In January, 1938, new personal service contracts were arranged with eleven of the leading officials of Loew's, Inc. The largest amount was to be paid to Louis B. Mayer, executive in charge of production. His remuneration was set at $3,000 per week, plus 6.77 per cent of the net profits, and a continuation of the stock purchase agreement made in December, 1932, which was discussed above. The personal service contracts with the officers involved a distribution in excess of 17 per cent of the annual net profits.

Dividends during the period amounted to $6,485,000.

Estate were ordered to repay $527,802 for overpayment received under the purchase-sharing contracts. The decree represented court approval to the stockholders' suit which charged the executives with dissipating the company's assets through "excessive and unconscionable" compensation paid to themselves and others under so-called profit-sharing plans.5

P. Lorillard Company is another company which has allowed on a number of occasions the purchase of a stated number of shares at specified prices. In addition, in 1921, it established a program whereby 15 per cent of the net profits were to be set aside for extra dividends on stock held by officers and employees. Net profits were defined as the amount remaining after allowing for taxes, cost, depreciation, preferred dividends, etc., and 7 per cent on the net worth of the common stock.

Combination of Cash and Stock Bonus 

The settlement of a bonus obligation by a combination of cash and stock is intended to serve both as a reward for past performance and as a stimulus for future effort. There is an implied approbation of the current earnings record with the stock serving as an inducement for further achievement. The bonus plan of the United States Steel 

Corporation is illustrative of this arrangement. An impartial committee has the power to pay the bonus entirely in cash, or partly in cash with the balance in common or preferred stock. Stressing the desirability of permanent management, the committee has the power to withhold the stock for a period of five years. If an executive is 

5 Standard Corporation Records, February 10, 1939.

discharged or leaves for other reasons during the interim, the stock may be forfeited. Since the adoption of the plan, the distributions have been 60 per cent in cash and the balance invested in the common stock which is held in the name and interest of the beneficiaries. 

The stock reverts to the company in the event the beneficiary leaves within five years after the distribution for any reason whatsoever. 

The plan was set up in 1921 and no distributions were made in 1921 and 1922, or in the four years, 1931 to 1934 inclusive. The annual average distribution in the years 1923 to 1930 was $3,112,468, and the average number of participants was 2,457. The distributions have not been large as compared with some companies since the largest amount ever paid to a single individual was $42,572 in cash and $28,258 in stock. Of related interest are the extra distributions made to employee stockholders who have held their common stock for five years or longer. These distributions are made regardless of whether any dividend declaration is made upon the common stock held by the general public. For example, in 1936, employee stockholders received $2.15 a share although no general dividend declaration was made, and in 1937, they received $2.94 while the general stockholders received $1 per share.

Calculation of the Bonus 

The bonus should be computed in relation to net in preference to gross income. If it were based upon the latter, it is obvious that too little incentive would exist to bring expense items under control. 

Executives would be free to incur added sales expenses in order to obtain greater gross income, and the stockholders would be saddled with the disproportionately higher expense. Moreover, it appears equitable to require that a fair return be made on the investment before granting the bonus. This may be done by establishing either a flat minimum figure or by expressing the minimum as a stated percentage of the investment. Illustrative of the former, the Bethlehem Steel Corporation plan (in force from 1917 to 1931) provided for a bonus when net earnings exceeded $2,000,000 (after fixed charges but before depreciation). In the case of the United States Steel Corporation, bonus payments do not begin unless net earnings are in excess of $100,000,000. It should be noted, however, that the salary scale of the latter corporation was much more generous than the

former. Under the General Motors Corporation system, no bonus allowance is made until 7 per cent is earned on the capital invested. 

American Tobacco Company

The bonus plan of the American Tobacco Company originated in 1912. It was incorporated as a by-law (article XII) which provided that 

As soon as practicable after the end of year 1912 and of each year of the Company's operations thereafter, the Treasurer of the Company shall ascertain the net profits, as hereinafter defined, earned by the Company during such year, and if such net profits exceed the sum of $8,222,245.82, which is the estimated amount of such net profits earned during the year of 1910 by the businesses that now belong to the Company, the Treasurer shall pay an amount equal in the aggregate to ten per cent of such excess to the President and five Vice-Presidents of the company in the following proportions, to wit: One-fourth thereof, or 21 per cent of such amount, to the President; one-fifth of the remainder thereof, or 13 per cent of such amount, to each of the five Vice-Presidents as salary for the year, in addition to the fixed salary of each of said officers. 

Since the net earnings for the period from 1929 to 1933 inclusive averaged $36,000,000, it is evident that a good-sized melon was available for distribution to the six officers. In addition, the directors had provided a plan in 1929 for certain valuable stock rights in favor of the management; it is estimated that the value of the rights to the president alone amounted to $705,550 in 1929 and $1,169,280 in 1931.6

In the latter year, a complaining stockholder instituted legal proceedings against both the stock rights and the bonus payments. Action on the stock rights was disallowed on the grounds that it was outside the jurisdiction of the federal courts. The plaintiff was unsuccessful in his plea against the unreasonableness of the bonus payments before the Circuit Court of Appeals, but the Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision and remanded the case back to the District Court for further proceedings. 

Following the reversion to the District Court, an agreement was reached out of court which changed the terms of the bonus. In 1933, the officers were granted a bonus of 10 per cent of the earnings in excess of $13,000,000 (as compared with $8,222,245.82 under the • Washington, "The Corporation Executive's Living Wage," Harvard Law Rev., Vol. 54, pp. 733, 743. 1 7 Several years later, the sordid background of the settlement came to light. In proceedings which finally resulted in the disbarment of the attorney of the tobacco company, it was shown that the complaining stockholder had been paid more than $500,000. original agreement). In 1934, they were to receive 10 per cent of the excess over $14,250,000, and in 1935 and subsequent years, they were to receive 10 per cent of the excess over $15,500,000 and up to $32,500,000. From $32,500,000 to $35,000,000 a 9 per cent bonus was granted; from $35,000,000 to $37,500,000, 8 per cent; from $37,500,- 

000 to $40,000,000, 7 per cent; $40,000,000 to $42,500,000, 6 per cent; and 5 per cent of all income in excess of $42,500,000. Under this plan the five top executives received an aggregate of $313,477 in 1935.

In 1931, the company allocated 56,712 shares of common stock to 535 employees to be purchased at $25 per share. Of this amount, 13,440 shares were allocated to George W. Hill, president, and a total of 16,685 shares to the five vice-presidents. Since the 1931 market range of the stock was 128 to 602, this afforded substantial profits to the executives in question. The other eligible employees were rated on their value to the company and those rated 100 per cent were allotted an amount of stock equal to one-third of their 1930 compensation. Those rated less than 100 per cent were allotted a proportionately smaller amount of stock.

The president of the company later renounced his allotment in order to be free of any personal interest in defending the bonus principle. It is interesting to note his point of view in offering this stock privilege. The following quotation is taken from a letter of the president sent to each of the selected employees: "It is not given to you for services that have heretofore been rendered; it is not given to you in the nature of a bonus. The purpose of the allotment of stock is solely to urge upon you further interest in the development of your Company's affairs." In the agreement following the stockholders' suit in 1933, the directors provided that further allotments of stock will be made only upon the approval of a stockholders' meeting. 

General Motors Corporation Plan 

The General Motors Corporation provides a savings and investment plan to which all employees below the rank of executives are eligible and a bonus plan which is restricted to the executive group. 

Consideration will be given only to the latter. In common with all bonus plans, the announced purpose is to vitalize the incentive of those responsible for the success of the company. To quote from a letter addressed to the stockholders, "The safeguard to the capital of the

stockholders invested in the business of General Motors Corporation, as well as the earnings power of that capital, is absolutely dependent upon the intelligence and aggressiveness with which the organization deals with the very important problems that constantly arise." 

The plan provides that 10 per cent of the net profits in excess of 7 per cent on the invested capital is to be allocated to the executive group. As of 1934 this meant that it was necessary for the net profits to equal approximately $58,700,000 or $1.15 per share of common stock before the executives would receive additional compensation. 

The number participating in these excess distributions has ranged from 550 in 1922 to 10,400 in 1940. From 1923 to 1936, only 5 per cent was set aside for a bonus proper, and an additional 5 per cent was paid, in the years 1923 to 1929, to the Managers Securities Company, and in the years 1930 to 1936, to the General Motors Management Corporation in which only the senior executives have holdings. In other words, the specialized corporations were simply a device for paying larger amounts to the executives carrying the larger responsibility.

The plan may well be subjected to further critical analysis. As stated above, one-half of the total bonus allotment was paid to a formally organized corporation, the General Motors Management Corporation. The latter was organized under the laws of the state of 

Delaware in 1930, and was capitalized as follows: 

6 per cent debenture serial bonds.... 

Common stock-$10 par value..

Class B stock-$10 par value.... 

$50,000,000 500,000 5,000,000

The bonds and the common stock were given to the General Motors Corporation in exchange for 1,375,000 shares of its common stock at a price of $40 per share, or a total cost of $55,000,000. Of this, the bonds accounted for $50,000,000, and the $10 par common was exchanged at the rate of $100 per share, thus offsetting the remaining balance of $5,000,000. The Class B stock was to be reserved and used for dividend purposes as follows: 

The 5 per cent yearly earnings under the contract, after making provision for income taxes, accrues exclusively to the benefit of the Common Stock. Such net earnings are capitalized and paid to the Common Stockholders as a dividend in Class B stock, and there is allocated to the Class B stock as many shares of the General Motors Common Stock at the price specified by the Directors, so that each share of Class B stock outstanding shall have allocated to it a share of 

General Motors Common Stock.

Three sources of profit were open to the Management Corporation: dividends on its holdings of the common stock of the General 

Motors Corporation, its bonus share of the funds allotted by the General Motors Corporation, and appreciation of the value of the common stock held. By these means, it was anticipated that the debenture bonds could be retired in seven years. At the time the latest plan was promulgated in 1930, the trend of events was not anticipated, and an adjustment of the plan proved necessary in 1934. At this time, stockholders were asked to reduce the interest from 6 per cent to 5 per cent for the period from March 15, 1930, to March 15, 1934.

Future interest was to continue at 6 per cent except that it was "not to exceed the amount of dividends received by the Management Corporation on its General Motors Common Stock not paid for."

In 1937, all the indebtedness of the General Motors Management Corporation to the General Motors Corporation was liquidated. Late in 1938, the Management Corporation and the General Motors Securi ties Company were combined into the General Motors Shares, Inc. 

The shares of the latter company may be converted into common stock of the General Motors Corporation. 

The distribution of the General Motors bonus is rather vaguely described as being on the basis of the degree to which employees' services contributed to the success of the corporation. Under the original plan all salaried employees of one year's service or more were included. Later the plan was restricted to employees receiving $5,000 and over. This was next extended to employees receiving $4,200 or more, and in the last few years has been further extended to include all salaried employees receiving $2,400 or more.

The plan is featured by a number of other details, but perhaps the foregoing are sufficient to outline its major principles. Its chief objective is obviously the establishment of a bonus plan which clears through a separate corporation. One need not, therefore, register surprise at the readjustment which occurred in 1934 which ignored the separate entities of the operating and management corporations and held that, as members of a common family, the latter corporation should be relieved of its pressing legal liabilities. Neither may this be necessarily condemned inasmuch as it would not be logical to impose added liabilities upon the executives when the company is really trying to extend them a favor. However, the complexity of the plan may not be as easily extenuated. Why should the

operating company not have direct control over bonus distributions at all times? Does not the establishment of a separate company permit a convenient means for concealing certain facts relating to bonus payments? Is there assurance that an adjustment would be made if the executives received excessive compensation in the same manner that they were given relief under adversity? Finally, the very complexity of the set-up is open to condemnation. When it is necessary for the chairman to write the stockholders in connection with the revision of the plan in 1934 that "unfortunately, the subject is complicated," there is some question as to whether the plan was established on a proper basis.8

Legality of Bonus Payments 

In considering the legality of bonus distributions to executives, the chief emphasis is necessarily placed upon the respective rights of the parties involved. Do the directors have the right to stipulate large salaries without limit? Do the directors have the right to establish a bonus system for the benefit of the executive officials? As is true of most legal issues, no general answers may be reached on these questions, but perhaps certain principles do become established by the individual cases.

Usually most bonus plans are approved by formal vote of the stockholders. Some particular individual or committee may be given the power to work out the percentages of distribution, but it is customary to seek the consent of the stockholders as to the general principle of excess distribution. After all, net earnings belong peculiarly to the owners, the stockholders, and it would be necessary to obtain their sanction before any share of the same may be diverted to channels outside the corporation. Assuming that this is done, there still remains. the matter of the rights of the dissenting or minority stockholders. 

Both the American Tobacco Company and the Bethlehem Steel Corporation have had to contend with suits which were instituted on the basis that the returns of certain executives were excessive. Complaint was registered that the stockholders were deprived of their just share of income distribution. In addition, the stockholders possess the right to demand of their officers a proper accounting for funds, although at the same time they must substantiate their action 8 A suit is now pending in which the compensation policies of the General Motors Corporation are under attack.

with the necessary evidence of justification. If the latter is lacking, the court may dismiss the case as was true of the Bethlehem Steel Corporation incident. If the merits of the case are established, the following principles would appear applicable: 

1. The stockholders have a right to establish a by-law or make provisions for a bonus system. 

2. At the same time, these provisions may not be "used to justify payments so large as in substance and effect to amount to spoilation or waste of cooperative property. "9 

3. Standards of the reasonableness of compensation are lacking and the courts are compelled to look more to the abuse of power than to the existence of power by the directors to fix remuneration. Large compensation, in itself, affords practically no basis for action. 

The position of the courts is indicated by the following extract taken from decision of the judge in the case of McQuillen v. National 

Cash Register Company: 

It may be conceded that, prima facie, judged by appropriate standards of the worth of the services of any individual for any particular executive position, a salary of $100,000 a year appears to the average person, of average business experience and responsibilities, to be more than liberal compensation. 

However, courts are not permitted to be controlled by this test any more than by what the average judge, familiar with cases of the present kind, might himself conclude to be adequate compensation. We must distinguish between compensation that is actually wasteful and that which is merely excessive. The former is unlawful, the latter is not. The former is the result of a failure to relate the amount of compensation to the needs of the particular situation by any recognized business practices, honestly, even though unwisely adoptednamely, the result of bad faith, or of a total neglect of or indifference to such practices. Excessive compensation results from poor judgment, not necessarily anything else. If the rule were otherwise, the result would be destruction of autonomy in private enterprise to a degree that would render such enterprise no longer private; personal initiative and its just rewards would disappear, and this would undermine the very basis upon which our economic life, with its constitutional guaranties, is founded, and upon which our democratic form of government depends.10

Economic Basis of Bonus Payments 

An economic appraisal of the bonus principle is more difficult to establish with any degree of finality. The problem contains both 

See the ruling of the Supreme Court, Commercial and Financial Chronicle, Vol. 136 (June 3, 1933), p. 3818. 

10 27 F. Supp. at 653.

an internal and external setting. Reference has been made to the former, and the difficulties of trying to allocate to the various interests of a going concern their respective and just shares of the total output have been suggested. The external aspects are even more confusing and evasive. The essence of the matter may be put in the form of a question: What effect does the distribution of income or wealth have upon the prosperity of a nation? It is not within the confines of this study to answer this question, but its pertinency arises more especially through its relationship to corporate policy. Until the last few years, there would be little likelihood that such a matter would be found on the agenda for a director's meeting; today, there is little escape from this issue. The Securities and Exchange Commission is publishing salaries and security holdings of prominent corporate officials, and these matters are being scrutinized by the publicat-large. In times of universal prosperity, they would likely attract little attention, but in periods of depression they are regarded with much suspicion. Does not the receipt of large returns by certain favored individuals automatically mean less available for the masses? 

By and large, the question is so easily answered in the affirmative, that sentiment spreads rapidly against those companies engaged in the practice of favoring their executives with excessive returns. 

The day is probably past when business enterprise can confine its attention to matters of its own household. More than ever, the affairs of the nation will necessitate action on the part of corporate directors. 

In the past, business has tended to look in the direction of government for various favors and privileges, but if the tendencies of recent years continue, it is likely that the direction of the line will be reversed. Government will expect more of business both in the way of taxes and responsibility.

Is the president of a large life insurance company worth $250,000 per year? Is the president of a large steel corporation worth $1,000,- 

000 per year? Who shall be the judge of such questions? Formerly, these were matters of great privacy and were settled in hushed tones around the directors' table. Today, they are viewed as items of public policy, and it behooves the directors to give proper consideration to public reaction.

CHAPTER XXVIII WORKING CAPITAL 

I 'N OUR discussion of the financing of business enterprise, consideration has been given mainly to the relatively long-term or relatively permanent capital needs of the corporation. In addition, the corporation has many financial requirements relating to assets of a temporary nature. Assets of this type remain with the business only for a short period of time, but they are constantly being replaced with other assets similar in nature and in value. Often a large amount of these short-term needs demand permanent financing. Moreover, there is a vital relationship between the current and fixed assets since both are component and complementary parts of the complete business structure. A fixed asset may be virtually useless without sufficient short-term capital with which to work it. 

Hence, the working capital position of any enterprise may readily become its controlling nerve center as well as determine the scope and character of its operation. Because of the key position of working capital, its special problems merit attention both on their own account as well as their effect on the long-term financial position. 

Definitions of Capital 

As a prelude to any discussion of working capital, it is important to have in mind an understanding of the concept of capital in its broader sense. Unfortunately, the term may be defined in many ways. The economist defines "capital" as wealth used in further production and stresses physical facilities without regard to their money values. Contrariwise, the business man uses the word "capital" with special reference to the money or money values used in the business. In corporation finance, there is an adaptation of both connotations. For some purposes, capital is thought of as the face or book values depicting the stock and bond liabilities of the business; for other purposes, it is regarded as the asset values of the enterprise. Both meanings will be employed in this chapter: first, in the analysis of the asset or operating problem, and, second, in the discussion of the financial or source problem. 551

Classes of Capital 

In terms of assets, capital may be classified as fixed or permanent and working or circulating capital. The fixed capital is represented by buildings, land, machinery, and similar assets of a relatively permanent nature. These assets have a long life, and once funds are invested in them, adjustments become difficult. Working or circulating capital, on the other hand, consists of that portion of the assets of the business represented by such items as accounts receivable, inventories of raw materials and merchandise, notes or bills receivable, and cash. Assets of this type are temporary in their nature since the invested values are capable of being recovered, or of being changed in form within a short period of time. 

Excluding those few businesses which require no fixed capital, it must be recognized that both classes of capital are essential for the normal conduct of business. There is some tendency, however, to overemphasize the importance of the fixed capital instead of recognizing that the two categories of capital complement each other as integral parts of the business whole. Fixed capital often represents the larger proportion of the assets and requires much attention in the determination of such business policies as depreciation, maintenance, and the accounting for values. Yet the business decisions relating to fixed assets may be comparatively infrequent, while those involving working capital are daily in their occurrence. Decisions as to whether a factory should be enlarged or a new type of machinery purchased do not have to be made frequently, but the formation or interpretation of policies dealing with extension of credit, the purchase of supplies, or the payment of wages take place continuously. The strategic maneuvering of the working capital elements combined with their impermanent nature increase greatly the potential risk of loss. Not only is there the risk of actual loss of values, but in addition, there is the further risk of conversion of current assets into fixed capital, thus, tending to destroy the liquidity which is so essential to the maintenance of a sound business position. 

Working Capital Defined 

Like the broader concept of capital, there is no universally accepted definition of working capital. Some authorities define working capital as the difference between the current assets and the cur

Analysis of this comparative statement obviously indicates that A has a stronger position than B. Both companies have the same amount of gross working assets, but it is clear that A is on a more substantial basis. There is less danger of A losing its gross position by the pressing demand of current liabilities which must be discharged through payment in cash or some form of refinancing. In vestors whose primary interest is in financial soundness will, there fore, be wise in using the net figure as the best measure of the work ing capital position.

Gross and Net Concepts in Practice 

The chief difficulty of the net concept of working capital arises from the fact that it is impossible to increase working capital by current borrowings. If either of the foregoing companies were to borrow $1,000,000 on a ninety-day note, both the current assets and the current liabilities would be increased by the same amount, and the net working capital would remain unchanged. Yet, from the point of view of the funds available for management purposes, both companies would have had an increase of $1,000,000.

From the management's point of view, it is probable that greater attention is given to the gross working capital or current asset concept because this constitutes the total funds used for operating pur- 1 This is the definition used by most financial services, and by writers emphasizing the accounting phase of finance. See E. E. Lincoln, Applied Business Finance (New York: 

McGraw-Hill Book Co., 1929), p. 312; E. A. Saliers, Handbook of Corporate Management and Procedure (New York: McGraw-Hill Book Co., 1929), p. 347. 

2 For example, J. C. Baker and D. W. Malott, Introduction to Corporation Finance 

(New York: McGraw-Hill Book Co., 1936), p. 92.

poses. Thus, in both companies A and B, the operating managements have the same amount of funds at their disposal although there may be a difference in the length of time for which they are available. 

Despite the latter uncertainty, the quantitative concept of working capital provides a more objective basis for determining the type and amount of financing. Obviously, all assets must be financed in some way, and the net position can only be an index of financial soundness or margin of protection.

Major Types of Working Capital 

In accepting the gross concept of working capital, the individual characteristics of the important component elements should be recognized. For the same reason that proper balance between working and fixed capital is essential to sound operation, it is also true that the more closely drawn balance within the category of current assets may be a vital factor in sound operation. This may be seen in the brief analysis of the more important types of current assets. Cash

Cash, in many respects, is the most important item in business operation. It is both a means and an end of business enterprise. Return upon the investment takes form usually through the payment of cash dividends, and in the event of liquidation, cash becomes the final medium by which claims are discharged. Likewise, cash is one of the most important tools of day-to-day operation because it is a form of liquid capital which is available for assignment to any new use. Cash is often the determining factor deciding the course of business destiny. The decision to expand the business may be determined by the availability of cash, and the borrowing of funds will frequently be dictated by the cash position. 

Because of the key position of cash, it is not unusual for business management to formulate policies which relate solely to this one item. Often liberal cash reserves are maintained in times of depression, while greater risks may be taken in times of prosperity. As cvidence of this, it may be observed that many companies maintained stronger cash positions in the uncertain period following 1929 than in the prosperous years of 1922 to 1929. This may be shown by the life insurance companies in the United States which held, in 1940, cash and United States government securities amounting to $5,505,-

555 7 000,000, or 23 per cent of their assets; but in 1929, cash and United 

States government security holdings amounted to only $432,668,000 or 2.7 per cent of the assets.

Like the Biblical observation that the "rich shall be richer; and the poor, poorer," so companies of strong
