standing can afford the luxury of maintaining liberal cash reserves for the sake of security while those having a weaker position may be compelled to plan carefully their cash expenditures. This is caused by the fact that cash is a non-earning asset which can be carried only by those concerns with operations sufficiently profitable to absorb the loss of income resulting from idle assets, although a strong cash position may be facilitated by a capitalization which creates few fixed charges. 

Accounts Receivable 

Another important item in the working capital classification is accounts receivable. On first glance, it would seem that these accounts might be more accurately described as a form of potential cash rather than real capital. As soon as they are collected cash is provided which can be used in the business, but prior to their realization they represent the advance of capital to vendee firms receiving the benefit of the credit. However, accounts receivable arise from the need to finance sales in our highly integrated credit economy and are earning assets as much as machinery or inventories of goods-on-hands.

Accounts receivable may be used to clarify the confusion of terminology which applies to working capital. In the asset sense, accounts receivable are classified as a form of working capital since they represent an earning asset necessary to the average business. However, accounts receivable lack availability to the business except as they mature and are returned in the form of cash. It is equally clear that the accounts receivable must be accommodated or financed during the time they are outstanding. The means of this financing is found on the equity or liability side of the balance sheet and may arise from accounts payable, notes payable, or a portion of the permanent financing. Viewed in this complementary manner, it is clear that the two concepts of working capital which were previously set forth are for practical purposes two phases of the same problem. Net working capital reflects the source of funds while gross working capital indicates the use. Inventories

Inventories are a form of working capital which must necessarily reflect the nature of the industry for which they are assembled. Manufacturing companies will have stocks of raw materials, goods-in-proc-

WORKING CAPITAL 

557 ess, and finished products, while retail enterprises will have for the most part stocks of finished goods which are available for sale to the final consumer. Railroads, public utilities, and most other service industries will normally have a comparatively small portion of their assets in inventories. Hence, it may be said that inventories are a direct variant of the type and form of business. 

Where the inventory account occupies a prominent position in business operation, it may usually play a key role in deciding the success of the venture. Unwise stocking of raw materials can play havoc with the profit-and-loss account, while insufficient accumulation can seriously interfere with the normal flow of goods through the plant. Similarly, abrupt changes in the market price of inventory materials may have a pronounced effect upon the competitive position of any company. Because of this variable character of inventories, they may prove to be the vital weakness of large companies which on the surface appear to be successful and imposing business institutions. 

As illustrated at another point, the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company is an appropriate example showing how the inventory account may actually be the chief cause of failure.4 There are many problems which plague the development of a sound inventory position. One important problem is the control of the quality of raw materials constituting the inventory. Defective quality in the raw materials or deterioration can have a ruinous effect upon the finished goods. A second problem of consequence is that of price changes. The market prices of the finished goods tend to be established at the cost of reproduction of those goods, as computed at the time of sale. This means that, in the event of declining prices, the values of inventories held on hand must be reduced to conform to the current market quotations with a corresponding reduction or elimination in profit.

To guard against the foregoing hazards, modern enterprise usually sets up various technical testing facilities to catch imperfections in materials and engages market analysts to study price trends. Thus, it can be said that the inventory account is dynamic in character and embodies many risks which may have great influence upon successful operation. In contrast, cash and accounts receivable are static and their book figures may be considered as reliable indicators of their value in the conduct of the business.

Chapter XXXIV.

The Amount of Working Capital 

With this brief analysis of the three most important items of working capital, it must be apparent that each requires individual attention. 

At the same time, there are certain overall observations which may be made with respect to working capital as a whole. First, working capital requirements vary with the nature of the particular business. 

Important determining characteristics appear in the credit terms that the business needs to extend, the material inventories which are found desirable in relation to the volume of business done, and the amount of machinery and buildings necessary to carry on the business. These Railroads

Railroads. It is clear from this table that the proportionate amount of working capital is definitely a variant of the type of business. Rail-

WORKING CAPITAL 

559 roads, with their large fixed investment, appear to have the lowest re quirements for current assets. This does not mean that the problems of working capital may be minimized in this field of enterprise because ready funds are still essential to cover the disbursements for wages, interest on funded debt, the purchase of materials and supplies, etc. Indeed, under such conditions, the working capital position may become even more strategic in character because of its relation to, and control of, the large amount of fixed assets. Thus, one of the outstanding problems of railroad management in recent years has been the maintenance of a current position sufficiently strong to permit vigorous operation.

Public Utilities.-Public utilities, like the railroads, also have a large fixed investment which causes the current assets to constitute only a relatively small percentage of the total assets. There is a difference between operating and holding companies, but even so the funds required to cover current transactions are minor compared with those necessary to finance the long-term structure. 

Industrials.-Industrial concerns, generally, require a large amount of working capital, although this varies from business to business because of the lack of uniformity characterizing this field of enterprise. 

However, the underlying determinants of the amount are essentially the same as in the two previous groups. Where large amounts of fixed capital are required for operation, working assets may be expected to occupy a smaller niche in the asset structure. For similar reasons, a rapid turnover of capital (sales divided by total assets) will inevitably mean a larger proportion of current assets. Looking to the underlying causes of these relationships, the following may be noted: 

1. In the case of industries with large fixed investment, one of the primary uses of working capital is its conversion into operating plant structure. In turn, it is expected that the income realized from operations will normally replace such defections. This means that the flow of a portion of the working capital is circulated through fixed investment and that its recovery is dependent upon the income realized. 

2. Where the current assets are relatively more important, a rapid sales turnover is usually found. Often, as in the case of retail concerns, the specific working assets are themselves the object of sale, and the recovery is direct and immediate. In manufacturing enterprises, a large share of the working capital is more likely to be

changed in form by conversion into finished products, but even here, the potentiality of recovery is not delayed as long as in the case of public utilities and railroads.

A second factor resulting in variation in working capital is the business cycle. During marked upswings of activity, there is usually need for larger amounts of capital to cover the lag between collections and increased sales and in order to finance purchases of additional materials to support the larger amount of business being done. Moreover, during the recovery and prosperity phase of the business cycle, prices of raw materials and wages tend to rise and require additional funds to carry even the same physical volume of business. In the downswing of the cycle, there may be a brief period when collection difficulties and declining sales cause embarrassment by the resulting failure to replenish the cash account. Later, as the depression runs its course, the concern may find that it has a larger amount of working capital on hand than current business volume dictates. 

Importance of Correct Amount of Working Capital 

It is now apparent that the correct amount of capital is the product of many modifying factors. Of particular importance are the type of business and the stage of the business cycle. However, in the last analysis, the specific need can be formulated only in the light of the individual company. From this point of view, management can be plagued with too little working capital or be embarrassed by the difficulties of utilizing an excess amount. Where there is an inadequate working capital supply, management is necessarily limited in the acceptance of promising opportunities, and there is a general undermining of confidence. Too much attention may be concentrated upon meeting current obligations with an accompanying lack of attention to other business needs.

On the other hand, an excessive amount of working capital may also be a deterrent to successful operation because it may lead to waste and to dangerous overconfidence. In any event, the presence of idle capital must necessarily mean reduced earnings and the payment of a smaller return upon investment that would otherwise be possible. There is also the danger of encouraging side-line speculative activity instead of facing the more objective alternative of deliberate curtailment where the excess is more or less permanent in character.

WORKING CAPITAL 

561 

Need for Balance

The real answer, of course, is to be found in providing the correct amount of capital. There is no mathematical formula to make this determination, but intelligent management can aim at a condition of reasonable balance in the business structure. In general, such a condition means an ability to keep current in the payment of liabilities and in providing maximum earnings upon investment. In this respect, the business machine may be likened to most mechanisms -proper functioning occurs only when the component parts are in correct balance.

The Flow of Working Capital 

The desired state of balance which has just been referred to may be seen more readily by describing the normal flow of capital. Broadly speaking, the assets (and particularly the current assets) should be kept in a properly "fluid" state, not in the sense of always being able to exchange the current assets for cash, but fluid in the sense that each of the forms in which working capital has been invested is constantly flowing into the next proper classification. 

When a new concern is first organized and financed, the working capital will be principally, if not entirely, cash obtained from the original financing. Very soon a portion of the cash will be transferred into raw materials, wages, supplies, and a host of other current operating accounts. These expenditures will be reflected in the value of the goods-on-hand consisting of raw materials, goods-in-process, or finished product. The finished product will then be sold, and for the typical business, the value will be transferred to accounts receivable. If the sales have been made at a satisfactory price, the amount of the accounts receivable should be larger than the expenses incurred for raw materials and other items. Gradually, the accounts receivable will be collected and the working. capital will have returned to its original starting place, cash, from which the cycle will be repeated.

Actually, the working capital cycle is continuous and reflects the turnover of values from one account to another and back to the most liquid form-cash. Although continuous, the flow will not be regular because of fluctuations in the volume of sales and in the changing price-levels of raw material, labor, and other costs. Moreover, if plans are laid for expansion in the volume of business, addi-

tions may be made to the working capital fund through special financing, or it may be enlarged by leaving in the fund the profits made on sales. Even without expansion, a portion of the working capital fund may be withdrawn and diverted to the purchase of fixed assets in the form of building improvements or the acquisition of machinery. 

With proper budgeting or financial planning, it is perfectly proper to use existing current funds for plant construction with the intent of recovering the working capital funds later through a bond issue designed to replenish the working capital expended on the construction. This procedure has been by no means uncommon in recent years when a number of bond issues have been offered for sale with the express purpose of replenishing working capital expended in the acquisition of fixed assets. 

The Sources of Working Capital 

Up to this point, our chief attention has been devoted to the nature and use of working capital as an integral part of the operating area. 

An equally important problem is found in the means by which such capital can be raised. Unlike fixed assets, where values are frozen and the liquidation or conversion spread over a period of years, the problems of working capital financing relate to a highly variable and easily realized form of asset. The various asset items representing working capital change rapidly and are capable of relatively easy and frequent recovery. This fluid condition invites financial accommodation because of the potential recovery of the funds, but at the same time, the instability may prove detrimental to the attraction of long-term investment.

While a portion of the working capital requirements of the business should ordinarily be obtained through the sale of stocks in the original financing, it is unusual for all the working capital to be obtained in this way. Other sources will be used so that proper balance may be maintained between the expected period of the use of the funds and the retirement of the financial obligation. Thus, a sharp distinction may be drawn between the amount of working capital which is needed more or less permanently and that which is required for peak periods of operation. The former may quite properly be raised by the use of long-term financial media, or permanent financing, while the latter invite only short-term or current financing.

WORKING CAPITAL 

563 

Permanent Financing of Working Capital Requirements 

Stock.-A portion of working capital needs should be accommodated by the sale of stocks. This should be an amount equal to the normal working capital requirements anticipated at the time of organization. The use of stock to obtain initial working capital places the corporation on a sound basis and enables it to provide more adequately for later needs by other means. As stated previously, the elements of working capital are highly variable and there is difficulty in maintaining the proper flow of valuc: through the various accounts and in avoiding diversions to fixed capital uses. The portion of working capital obtained through the sale of stock provides important relief to management against these contingencies because there is no fixed maturity date which must be met nor any addition to interest charges which exist as obligations regardless of earnings. 

The greater flexibility provided by the use of common stock makes it very tempting to substitute this medium for current debt whenever the opportunity is present. Thus, when stocks were selling at an extremely high level in 1928 and 1929, many companies raised funds by new stock issues and paid off current indebtedness. As a result, a larger proportion of working capital at the present time is represented by stocks than was true prior to 1928. Evidence is found in the unusually large cash holdings of many corporations and in the large investments in securities which are carried in order to reduce the amount of idle funds. This condition emphasizes the fact that working capital should not be obtained through permanent financing unless the need can itself be regarded as reasonably permanent. 

Temporary expansions in working capital assets due to boom conditions should be financed on a current basis. 

Accumulated Surplus.-The common practice of retaining earnings in the business as accumulated surplus affords another proper method for obtaining working capital. Corporations ordinarily do not pay out all of their earnings as dividends over any period of years. This practice is followed because successful corporations constantly grow in size and volume and have constantly larger needs for capital. Rarely does a concern maintain static conditions for any long period of time.

As an example of surplus policy which is definitely related to working capital requirements, the National Dairy Products Corpora-

tion may be cited. In 1938, the company announced a reduction in its regular quarterly dividend rate from 30 cents to 20 cents a share for the express purpose of increasing working capital funds. Since the corporation had over six million shares of stock outstanding, this meant an annual addition to current funds of approximately $2,500,000. The funds thus obtained were used in part to finance the retirement of outstanding bank loans with its resulting savings in interest costs to the corporation.

Bonds. In comparison with stocks and surplus, bonds involve certain difficulties as a source of working capital funds. In the first place, bonds give rise to fixed charges which must be paid regardless of the condition of earnings. If a portion of the working capital should be idle, not only would earnings be lost but also it would be necessary to pay a penalty in the form of interest on the bonds. For this reason, it is doubly important to use bonds for working capital purposes only where the requirements are believed to be permanent, and never for any seasonal or temporary purpose. 

In the second place, bonds have a definite maturity. During the years immediately following the issuance of bonds, the due date may appear to be unimportant but the future contingencies are definitely increased. Like bonds, the various forms of current indebtedness also have due dates, but these are relatively small in amount and frequent in their occurrence. Management must pay such obligations more or less regularly and is under a constant discipline as a result. 

Because of the contingencies arising from the use of bonds, there is merit in financing normal working capital needs with common stock and temporary needs from current sources. This will reduce the risk of bond default and provide a degree of flexibility as well. 

Current Financing of Working Capital Requirements 

The sources from which the current or working funds of the corporation are obtained depend upon the original financial plan and the trade practices prevailing in the industry. Some sources are used more or less continuously; others are resorted to only when temporary needs are experienced. Our discussion will be restricted to the principal sources in common use.

Trade creditors.-Most business between industrial and mercantile establishments is conducted on a credit basis. The customary terms may vary from a few days to a few months and it is common prac-

WORKING CAPITAL 

565 tice to grant cash discounts for prompt payment. Corporations may therefore raise a part of their working capital by trade credit which is extended by the concerns from which raw materials and other supplies are purchased. Offset against trade creditors as a source of working capital is the volume of trade credit which must be extended to the concern's own customers. Where the corporation is buying on short terms and selling on long terms, the accounts receivable will necessarily exceed the accounts payable. In such a case, there is a differential against the company which must be financed by other sources. If, however, the reverse is true, the company may be able to obtain a considerable portion of its current financing from its trade creditors.

Another important factor relates to the cost of using trade creditors rather than other sources for current funds. It is a common practice in industry to offer trade terms of 2 per cent 10, net 30 days, although in some cases the cash discount periods may be longer. In the furniture industry for instance, the terms are frequently 2 per cent 30, net 60 days. In either case, the business has the problem of deciding whether to raise the necessary cash through some other form of financing such as borrowing from banks, or simply to regard the trade creditors as a logical source of funds for which the business incurs financial costs in the form of cash discounts not taken. 

Ordinarily, it is much more profitable to take advantage of cash discounts even though it may be necessary to borrow the funds from other agencies. The business, which is operating under 2 per cent 10, net 30 days terms and does not take its cash discount, is in effect paying 2 per cent for the use of the funds for 20 days or an interest rate of 36 per cent a year. As a consequence of this high rate of interest paid by the firms which do not take advantage of the discount, the credit standing of such firms may be impaired. 

Giving consideration to the cost of funds, the amount of working capital obtained from trade creditors may be said to be only the amount of money or value which is contained in accounts payable within the discount period. Even this may be in many cases a rather important sum. For example as of December 31, 1940, the American Smelting and Refining Company had accounts and drafts payable amounting to $13,002,635. At the same time, its current assets totaled $98,- 

138,060. Thus, the company was obtaining approximately 13.3 per cent of its gross working capital from trade creditors. As of the

same date, the company was financing customers to the extent of $12,138,099. The fact that accounts receivable were nearly as large as accounts payable does not detract from accounts payable as a source of working capital. Presumably, the company would have had to finance customers to this extent in order to achieve the desired volume of business. If no funds had been obtained from its trade creditors, then the entire $13,002,625 would have been acquired from some other source.

Occasionally, companies doing a strictly cash business are found which have virtually no accounts receivable but have considerable amounts in accounts payable. McCrory Stores Corporation, one of the more prominent variety chains, reported as of December 31, 1940, accounts receivable of $44,873; but its accounts payable amounted to $1,673,469. As of the same date, total current assets amounted to $11,115,409. In other words, the company was obtaining 15 per cent of its working capital from creditor sources. 

Commercial banks.-The corporation may make continuous use of the lending facilities of commercial banks. While bank borrowings should ordinarily be the source for a large portion of the extraordinary or temporary working capital needs, they may also be used for obtaining a portion of the ordinary current financing. This has the advantage of developing established financial connections for use in times of emergency or of having a ready means of reducing working capital during periods of extreme decline in the volume of business. If the company regularly obtains a portion of its normal working requirements from banks, the bank borrowings may be paid off in periods of business recession to reduce both the assets and liabilities of the business. If the funds are all represented by stockholders' equity or long-term debt, the company will necessarily have excess funds which invite extraneous use or they will be the cause of waste by remaining idle.

Prior to 1929, corporations regularly obtained a considerable portion of their working capital through bank borrowings. In fact, a considerable amount of permanent or long-term capital was supplied by commercial banks because of agreements to renew shortterm notes or through loans on demand notes made with the understanding that they would not be called. However, during the 1928 and 1929 boom, large amounts of common stock were sold to provide additional working funds, and as a consequence corporations have

WORKING CAPITAL 

567 not made as great use of the commercial banks as was formerly true. 

As of June 30, 1929, the member banks of the Federal Reserve System had loans outstanding in the amount of $26,150,000,000 and had security investments, chiefly governments, of $9,784,000,000. In 1940, these figures stood at $15,321,000,000 and $21,805,000,000, respectively. 

It is impossible to tell just how much of the reduction in loans was due to the reduced volume of business and how much was due to change in financing policy. In view of the large cash holdings of corporations as well as the large holdings of government bonds reported in 1940, the conclusion seems reasonable that the change in policy is an important cause.

Commercial paper houses.-When bank facilities are inadequate or it is thought more economical to finance on the open market, the corporation may resort to the use of the commercial paper house. 

The commercial paper house is in reality a middleman specializing in the purchase and sale of promissory notes of reputable corporations and businesses. It buys the promissory notes usually in the form of a series of notes in round amounts such as $1,000 or $2,500 and resells them to banks or other investors who have idle funds and wish to make temporary investments. The commercial paper house buys the notes only after the most careful investigation. While the notes are not indorsed, the fact that they are offered by a recognized institution is an index of quality and results in ready salability. 

This method of financing offers favorable interest rates and also serves to advertise the existence of the borrowing concern through the often widespread ownership of its notes. On the other hand, there is the disadvantage that the borrowing relationship is strictly impersonal, and the notes must be paid at maturity whereas a bank would be more likely to have an element of friendly interest and a willingness to extend the note if circumstances justified. Due to the unwillingness of the holders of commercial paper to renew the loans in times of extreme need, plus the low interest rates prevailing for bank loans in the past few years, commercial paper houses are no longer used to the extent that was once true. At the end of 1924, commercial paper outstanding amounted to $798,000,000. In 1930, this had decreased to $358,000,000, and in 1940 had decreased to $218,000,000.5 

5 Federal Reserve Board, Annual Report, 1937, Table 70; Federal Reserve Bulletin (April, 

1941), p. 339.

Finance companies.-Finance companies are engaged in the business of financing the credit sales of other concerns. The financing is usually accomplished through the discounting of accounts receivable or by the outright sale of customer's installment contracts. The first method is applicable to any type of business regardless of the size of its unit sale or the duration of its credit terms. The second method is used entirely for the types of business involving the sale of relatively durable and expensive equipment which would otherwise call for considerable outlays of cash on the part of the purchaser. 

The corporation which finds itself in need of additional funds may assign its accounts receivable to the finance company in exchange for a cash payment equal to the face amount of the accounts, less the agreed discount. The assignment may be made on either a notification or non-notification basis. Under the notification basis the selling company notifies its debtors that it has assigned their accounts to the finance company and that payment is to be made directly to the latter. This method is not popular because many debtors prefer to keep the transaction directly with the original vendor corporation. 

The non-notification basis avoids this difficulty. The debtors are not notified of the assignment; the selling corporation collects the accounts receivable as they mature and pays the funds directly to the finance company. The fact that the accounts have been assigned need never become an item of general information. 

While the assignment of accounts receivable is unpopular and frequently regarded as an indication of a weakened, current financial condition, no such restriction applies to customers' installment contracts. Corporations which manufacture and sell expensive items such as automobiles, refrigerators, and certain forms of industrial equipment find it necessary to sell much of their output on relatively long credit terms. If the manufacturing company had to finance all of its customers, it would require large additional amounts of funds. 

Such additional financing may be avoided easily by the prompt sale of the installment contracts to the specialized finance companies. Under these contracts, the purchaser of the merchandise pays directly or indirectly most of the financing costs. While the interest rate is relatively high, the selling companies prefer to concentrate their operations on manufacturing rather than in the financing of sales. As a consequence, they customarily sell the customers' accounts to such specialized agencies as the General Motors Acceptance Corporation

WORKING CAPITAL 

569 or the Commercial Credit Company. The finance companies in turn finance their own operations through the sale of stocks and bonds and through borrowings from commercial banks which are secured by the installment contracts as collateral purchased by the finance companies.

The Management of Working Capital 

Reference has been made to the relation between management policy and the amount of working capital. Strictly speaking, the management of working capital cannot be separated from the management of business in the broader sense. When the management keeps a close control on costs, maintains a careful inventory policy, extends credit with discretion, and follows up closely on collections, then it is also managing working capital. There are, however, some problems which are peculiarly related to working capital. 

The control of working capital demands careful planning as to the source and application of funds. A budget should be drawn up setting forth in detail the cash on hand, the amount which will be received in the future period, and the expenditure requirements for the same period. Management must know how much cash can be derived from collection of accounts receivable during the projected period as well as receipts from investments, rents, royalties, cash sales, and any other source. Against the anticipated receipts must be set estimates for the cash expenditures.

Prominent among the cash expenditures will be the regularly recurring outlays for materials, supplies, and labor. In addition, provision must be made for the important but more infrequent disbursements such as interest payments on borrowed funds, dividends to stockholders, and tax payments to the various governmental bodies. 

Taxes constitute an important working capital problem because technically they take precedence over all other expenses and in most cases the annual amount due must be paid in a small number of lump sums rather than weekly or monthly. Interest payments are important if receivership is to be avoided, and payment of cash dividends must be scheduled in advance. The fact that a profit is shown for the period is no assurance that dividends can be paid. Dividends may be declared on the strength of the earned surplus, but ability to make payments in cash depends upon proper management of the current funds. 

With careful planning of the flow of working capital, the con-

cern's cash needs will be controlled. The management problem then becomes one of securing a sufficient volume of business to furnish the anticipated cash receipts in order to meet the necessary expenditures. This again is not entirely separate from the working capital problem because the volume of business obtained may depend in part upon the cash appropriated for sales promotion. However, there will be non-working capital considerations measured largely in terms of management ideas and policies relating to the methods of production, construction, design, and sale. To this must be added the imponderables arising from general business fluctuations with which business managements are often powerless to cope.

CHAPTER XXIX  

success is influenced greatly by economic fluctua- Btions caused by forces which are external to the individual enterprise. The volume of general business activity is subject to major changes at irregular intervals and business management often has great difficulty in dealing with adverse trends. There may be great strain upon the capital structure, but the more immediate effects are found in the segment of current operations. Income may fluctuate sharply and the working capital position is particularly subject to pressure. Because of this direct relationship between current operations and general business conditions, it is desirable at this time to give consideration to the phenomena of business fluctuations. Management is unable to control these external pressures, but at the same time, it is highly important that it be familiar with the problems generating from this source. 

Types of Fluctuation 

The factors involved in the fluctuation of general business activity are complex and many of them are not yet understood. However, means of analysis have been developed which attempt to isolate the more important components of changing general business conditions. 

Statisticians generally divide business fluctuations into four distinct types: (1) periodic variations, (2) secular trend, (3) random fluctuations, (4) cyclical movements. 

Periodic or Seasonal Variations 

Periodic variations are regularly recurring fluctuations which affect the production and sales of particular concerns in a similar manner year after year. These variations are principally seasonal in nature. 

They are caused mainly by climatic changes, although variations in certain lines of business may be due to conventional seasons observed by a large part of the population as a result of social or business practices. In the former category may be listed Easter with its demands 572

for new clothes,¹ the wedding month of June with its requirements for accessories, and Christmas, which gives rise to extensive purchase of gifts by poor and rich alike. 

Recurring changes due to climatic conditions are numerous. Radio companies do a major part of their business during the fall and winter months when radio reception is good and there is a greater tendency for people to spend their evenings at home. Construction activity tends to be concentrated during the spring and summer months when weather conditions make such work more pleasant and more economical. This reacts in turn upon related industries such as the building and materials industry. 

The automobile industry is an example of a business where trade practices have greatly modified the effects of seasonal variations due to the weather. In the early days of the industry, the spring and summer months were the seasons of greatest activity, but with the introduction of closed cars and the development of better roads, the degree of this variation was modified. The current practice of introducing new models in the fall of the year has brought about a further reduction in what had come to be accepted as normal seasonal variations. Today, car sales in October and November show a peak of activity followed by another peak in the early spring after which production usually falls off until new models are introduced again the following September.

The foregoing illustrations are sufficient to indicate the nature of seasonal variations. Such recurring changes necessarily affect the financing of business enterprise but the problems which arise are usually subject to control by management. As recited above, the automobile industry met the issue by the introduction of new models in a season which was previously characterized by declining volume. 

Many concerns have been able to iron out these variations in production and sales by handling a diversified line of products with opposing seasonal periods. The formerly wide practice of combining retail coal and ice in one enterprise is a simple example of this. With the appearance of mechanical refrigeration many of the larger ice dealers have combined cold storage locker service with their coal business. 

General Motors Corporation is an illustration of a concern which has 1 The importance of Easter as a seasonal influence is shown by the fact that retail sales for the week ended March 30, 1940, were 20 per cent below the same week in 1939. This was the week after Easter in 1940 and the week before in 1939. Wall Street Journal (April 6, 1940), p. 1.

attempted to obtain greater stability in its total sales volume by combining the manufacture of automobiles, electric refrigeration, radios, and other products.

Another method of ironing out the effects of seasonality is the preparation of sales estimates for the coming season, thereby facilitating uniform production of goods throughout the year to meet the estimated sales volume. While this method is highly desirable in itself, it faces serious practical complications in some industries. Concerns engaged in manufacturing style goods find it difficult to take the risk of changing consumer whim, and companies manufacturing automobiles or mining coal find storage and handling expenses prohibitive. In addition, there is the financial risk involved in tying up working capital in large inventories subject to changing price conditions. Nevertheless, many concerns have succeeded in substantially reducing their production and sales variations during the year. As examples, the Dennison Manufacturing Company and Procter and

Gamble Company may be cited. The Dennison Company increased the regularity of its operations by expanding its line to include novelty goods for all seasons and holiday occasions as well as for general household use. The Procter and Gamble Company has achieved stable operations through controlling the distribution process. At one time, the Company sold through some 5,000 jobbers whose orders were correlated with volume of sales on an annual basis only. Today, the company sells directly to thousands of retailers and shipments are made in relation to a monthly sales quota. This permits regular production without the excessive fluctuations formerly in evidence.2 

In brief, the financial problems of reasonably regular periodic or seasonal fluctuation are not serious. Often, a balancing of operations may be accomplished by simple expedients, and in any event financial accommodation of these vagaries is not difficult. The regularity of change gives rise to a pattern of ebb and flow which permits the assumption of indebtedness during periods of slack with reasonable assurance that the ensuing expansion of volume will provide the necessary funds for its extinction. Other fluctuations, however, lack this quality of consistency, and the elements of uncertainty and irregularity complicate financial arrangement and accommodation. 

2 For more complete discussion, see Nations Business, Vol. 19 (April, 1931), p. 17.

Secular trend refers to the long-time tendency of any series to increase or decrease.3 Such a prolonged movement or trend is based upon basic changes in fundamental conditions, particularly the national welfare. Until recent years, the secular trend of business in general showed a persistent upward movement and was characterized by increasing productivity and rising standards of living. An important stimulant was the rate of growth in population. The mere fact that population increased at the rate of from 2 to 3 per cent a year stimulated business activity because of the necessity of feeding, clothing, and sheltering the growing population. This in turn called for more production of all kinds and offered new business opportunities. 

Obviously, single fields of enterprise or individual companies, irrespective of the nature of their business, may not necessarily keep pace with the general trend. Competitive conditions may limit the possible gains which would be afforded by general upward movement, or a shift in demand may react unfavorably on selected areas. For instance, despite a persistent rise in general business over a long period of time, interurban railroad transportation and the manufacture of horsedrawn carriages have suffered because of competition from the automobile. 

An important factor which will affect the future secular trend is the fact that our population is gradually reaching a static condition. 

No longer will there be a growing and more or less automatic increase in demand for various necessities, except to the extent that the economic system may permit a distribution of income in such a way that the less privileged portions of our population are able to acquire the essentials of a higher standard of living. Further growth will have to come through the intensive cultivation or development of a constant population rather than through the extensive cultivation of an expanding population. Moreover, a static condition will mean an older population which will result in changes in the nature of demands as well as in public attitudes. 

The cessation of growth in population must inevitably affect the volume and the financing of business enterprise. In the past, the management of individual companies was facilitated by the tremendous momentum of a favorable secular trend. Expanding business 

3 The statistical technique for measuring and removing the effects of secular trend in business data may be found in any good book on statistical methods.

. 

volume, although checked at intervals by periods of recession and depression, made it possible for business institutions to remedy strained financial positions and provided timely opportunity for improvement. 

In the future, however, there is prospect that the national growth will be more intensive than extensive, and more qualitative than quantitative. Such a change is bound to influence the financing of private enterprise. It is possible that funded debt may not be assumed with the assured position of safety that it had in the past because its liquidation may become more dependent upon recoveries of the initial investment than upon the returns of expanding volume. Hence, wise management may resort to greater use of equity financing in order to obtain a degree of freedom and flexibility which is not possible with the use of bonds. In short, management may no longer be able to float with a favorable national tide and be assured of success, and instead it may be confronted with the problems of maintaining a relative position in the business economy. 

Random Fluctuations

In statistical analysis, random fluctuations are the unexplained variations which remain after mathematically correcting for seasonal, secular, or cyclical factors. They are caused by unforeseen events, which are sometimes referred to as "acts of God"-such as war, floods, disastrous fires, and similar happenings. The nature of these fluctuations and the irregularity with which they occur prevent any sound forecast of their approach. Hence, the business manager can rarely prepare for them in advance except to shift the risk in so far as possible and to maintain as strong and flexible a financial position as circumstances will permit. Illustrative of the first type of protection is the use of insurance to cover potential losses from such hazards as fires, floods, tornadoes, etc. The second means of protection is mainly a matter of financial policy which provides for a strong reserve and surplus position so that unexpected losses may be absorbed without disastrous consequences.

Other potentialities of the random type are those arising from acts of government. These may be the result of changing political credos pertaining to internal affairs, or they may be a response to world-conditions. Thus, it is now apparent that the New Deal gave rise to profound changes in the business system. Recognition of collective bargaining, the establishment of wage and hour standards,

1 8 3 the exercise of control over security issues, and numerous other governmental policies have had repercussions on financial management. 

There is no intention here to declare whether the consequences are good or bad; there is simply a recognition of the impact of these developments on private enterprise. As one illustration of possible effect on financial practice, it is conceivable that the greater rigidity of wages may affect the issuance of securities. By adding to the area of fixed burden, management may have less freedom in issuing bonds with a binding interest commitment and may favor equity financing with its greater flexibility.

The response of government to foreign affairs may also have marked influence on business activities. For instance, the present defense program has the right-of-way, and all other economic considerations are greatly modified as a result. The objective of national defense is supreme and industrial activity is being directed to this single end. In some instances, priorities in favor of defense needs make it impossible for certain lines of industry to operate at all; in others, there is abrupt transition or conversion of plant facilities for the purpose of producing goods which are now needed. In any event, here is a random development which affects business destiny, both now and in the years to come. 

Cyclical Fluctuations

The most familiar type of variation in economic activity is the so-called cyclical movement. Over long years the ebb and flow of business volume assumed a pattern of recurring depression and prosperity. In the last decade, pronounced changes have occurred in the rhythm of this movement and the rebound of prosperity from depression has been characterized by great uncertainty. As a result, governmental credit has been used to stimulate recovery, whereas in the past the main reliance was placed upon revival growing out of the accumulation of need. Because of this development, many changes have occurred in the cyclical movement of business and these should be kept in mind in the ensuing discussion of this type of fluctuation. 

The most widely accepted definition of business cycles is that of Wesley C. Mitchell, who defines cyclical fluctuations as recurrences of rise and decline in activity, affecting most of the economic processes of communities with well-developed business organization, not divisible into waves of amplitudes nearly equal to their own, and averaging in com-

munities at different stages of economic development from about three to about six or seven years in duration.*

This definition suggests certain characteristics of business cycles which should be kept constantly in mind. First, they are recurrences of rises and declines which are constantly taking place in business activity. The various phases of each cycle always occur in the same sequence and no one phase may be said to be the beginning or ending of a cycle. Rather, it is in the nature of a never ending phenomenon. 

The main stages of the business cycle are commonly classified in the order of their occurrence as prosperity, recession, depression, and recovery.

Another element indicated in the definition is that cycles have varying periods of duration. In the case of minor recessions, the period may be less than a year, but the great depression beginning in 1930 shows that business may drag bottom for a number of years. Obviously, a depression combining severity with duration creates many serious problems for business enterprise. Management may be hard pressed to keep the business alive, and it may be compelled to resort to confining measures of economy as well as to terminate expansion programs. Such shift in policy is not always successful, and failure may ensue because of insufficient liquidity of assets or because of rigidity in the capital structure arising out of the previous policy of expansion. It may occur also because the qualities which made management successful in the promotion of an expansion are not necessarily the qualities required to carry a concern through a period of hardship.

In order to appreciate the nature and magnitude of the fluctuations which management may be called upon to meet, statistics relating to some of the more important characteristics of the business cycle will now be presented. 

The Price Level

One of the most important problems to the average concern is the cost of raw materials, labor and other elements going into the production process as well as the prices received for the finished product.

decline in prices which began in 1928 and lasted through 1932. While the reduction in price level in this period of five years was not as great in absolute points, it does represent approximately the same percentage decline as that experienced in the depression of 1920 and 1921. 

The effects of these price crumblings were international in character and few industries were left unscathed. Some industries were, of course, affected more seriously than others.

An outstanding example of the effect of the 1921 depression is found in the meat packing industry. This industry which had been supplying a world demand during World War I suddenly found itself with immense inventories and no market. The result was a

tremendous decline in the price of meat products. Packing companies were forced to absorb great inventory and operating losses thereby injuring the financial position of a number of concerns to such an extent that as late as 1930 they had not recovered fully. The loss of 

Armour and Company in 1921 approximated $31,000,000. Swift and 

Company, another leader in the packing industry, suffered losses of over $7,000,000.

Undoubtedly the lessons learned from this depression made it easier for the same packing companies to face more effectively the more serious depression which started early in 1930. As a result of the experience gained in the 1920-21 depression, a hand-to-mouth buying policy was adopted, and as a consequence the depression of the 1930's did not cause inventory losses to the same extent as in the earlier depression. Moreover, the decline took a number of years instead of a few months to complete its course, permitting internal adjustments to be made more easily. 

Price changes usually occur in different degrees depending upon the types of commodities affected. Raw material prices tend to be more sensitive to change and to show the greatest degree of variation, followed in order by wholesale prices, retail prices, and wages. 

Thus in periods of recovery and prosperity, raw material costs tend to increase at a faster rate than selling prices of the finished products. 

However, the more sluggish changes in wage costs, interest, and similar items coupled with the increased volume of business obtained during these periods usually allow business concerns to show good profits. In periods of recession and depression, raw material costs tend to fall faster than the sale prices of finished products, but this apparent opportunity for profits is usually offset by other factors. 

Demand for manufactured commodities falls off while overhead charges continue. Most companies have on hand inventories of raw material and finished products which were purchased or produced at the higher prices prevailing during the preceding period of prosperity. 

Hence, they are unable to benefit by the falling raw material prices for some time.

Production Cyclical movements also affect the physical volume of production in various lines of industry in different degrees. Concerns in those industries with products and services having stable demand are af-

Some branches of the motion picture industry also seem to belong in the depression-proof group. Examples of "depression-proof" concerns are R. J. Reynolds, American Tobacco,

Borden, Life-Savers Corporation, National Dairy Products, General 

Foods, American Telephone and Telegraph, and Loew's, Inc. Their operating records throughout the greater part of the depression of the 1930's showed profits almost without exception. This, of course, was made possible primarily by the continued volume of business these companies enjoyed. However, the concerns which are affected adversely by a depression far outnumber those in the foregoing category. 

It is in this group that management has its greatest problems, and it is here that the managers have ample opportunity to give proof of their ability to conduct their business successfully through periods of unfavorable business conditions. The difference in the extent to which these lines of activity fluctuate is striking. In the case of the companies in the depressionproof industries, it is evident that the main changes for management to combat are not cyclical. In the other lines, management must be constantly prepared to meet not only competitive forces, but also the adverse effects of cyclical movements, and in addition it must be ready to take advantage of cyclical upturns. One is as important as the other and each requires constant attention and systematic study and analysis on the part of management. The successful business will be the one with that additional amount of punch and preparedness not possessed by its competitors. Earnings

The vitality of business enterprise is found mainly in earnings, and needless to say the profits of most companies are greatly affected by the vagaries of price and the volume of production. During 1932, the low period of the great depression, losses were more common than profits. An analysis of the statements of 840 industrial companies showed a combined deficit for these companies of $15,349,000. Only one group, petroleum, showed an improvement over the preceding year of 1931. At the same time, it should be noted that the depressionproof industries again showed to advantage. The earnings of the tobacco group decreased only 7.7 per cent, while those of companies producing food products had a decrease of 27.7 per cent. The effect

The psychological reaction of management to profit results is also an interesting angle of cycle phenomena. Seldom does management have the courage to measure objectively its own responsibility for the results. The gains during the prosperity stage of the business cycle are looked upon as a matter of personal accomplishment while losses may be ascribed to the unavoidable effects of depression. Obviously, it is impossible to determine what the record would have been under other management, but it is certain that a proper degree of humility would be beneficial to management and shareholders alike. 

All too frequently management is guilty of unrestrained boasting with improving general business conditions and then dolefully complains when depression prevents satisfactory operation. The idea is not easily given wide acceptance, but as a matter of fact many of the acts of promotion now found in periods of prosperity should be saved for the day of depression. Instead, the signs now indicate that government will take up the slack of depression by virtue of the default of private interests.

Effects of Business Cycle on Financial Policy 

It has been stressed on numerous occasions that one of the primary objectives of corporate financing is the accommodation of operating needs. Because the latter are so vitally affected by cyclical movements, it follows that financial policy is similarly influenced. At the same time, rearrangement of the financial pattern may also be effected on its own account in order to make use of the favorable opportunities which are afforded by changing conditions in the money market. 

It is seldom possible to rearrange the financial structure to advantage in the early stages of depression, but upon the first signs of recovery, profitable refunding may be undertaken. The surplus of capital which is characteristic of this stage often enables companies of recognized standing to improve their position by calling high-rate securities and issuing new obligations on more favorable terms. Thus, during the past decade, there has been extensive refunding, and material improvements in the long-term capital structure have resulted. 

Unfortunately, such periods do not invite the sale of common stock and financial change is limited primarily to the area of funded debt.

Some of these characteristics are readily apparent in the ensuing discussion of interest rates and securities prices.

Interest Rates 

Capital is one of the important elements of business operation, and its cost and availability always have great significance to management. For this reason, the movements and trends of interest rates may now be studied. According to historical pattern, short-term interest rates, notably commercial paper rates, have tended to rise more slowly during recovery and prosperity than most other statistical series. On the cyclical downswing they have tended to remain higher longer than other series such as prices, sales, or production. In more recent years, the pattern is less distinct because a plethora of funds has produced a low level which is difficult to relate to business conditions. 

Some business cycle authorities believe that business recession may be attributed to the high cost of borrowing money during the last months of a prosperity period. Conversely, it is frequently believed that the appearance of low interest rates will reduce the cost of doing business to a sufficient degree to serve as a stimulus to recovery. 

However, it is difficult to align these explanations to facts of the past twenty years; in addition, the underlying motivation is open to question. In the first place, the cost of borrowing money for working capital purposes is a comparatively small proportion of total operating cost. In the second place, interest rates are a result of demand and supply conditions which undoubtedly have direct effect on business operation.

In order to observe the relation between the cost of money and the general business trend, Table 65 presents average interest rates together with the Federal Reserve Board's index of industrial production. It will be seen that interest rates rose a little after 1924, but the rise could not have been important in terms of operating costs. 

Conversely, the sharp drop in interest rates in 1930 which was continued through 1936 did not act as a stimulus to improving business; and when business improved in 1936 and 1937, it did not bring any appreciable change in interest rates. Of course, it might be contended that the interest rates between 1932 and 1936 were largely nominal in that few loans were made, but it can also be argued that there were few requests for loans except from hard-pressed and desperate concerns.

1919 1920 1921 1922 1923 Probably more important than the level of interest rates, itself, is its relation to other important conditioning factors of business activity. Thus, it is not the high cost of borrowing that causes business to cut down commitments, but rather the fear of binding obligations to make payments and the uncertainty that the banks will be willing to extend the necessary accommodation. as there is a possibility of profits and so long as they are able to secure necessary operating capital. During much of the depression of the 1930's, interest rates were low in comparison with previous levels, but borrowing was limited partly because of unwillingness to lend and partly because the prevailing uncertainties made profits seem impossible even at the low cost for capital.

The partial recovery in 1936 and 1937 was accompanied by a rise in interest rates on commercial paper. However, the marked recovery in industrial activity in 1939 and 1940 did not have any such effect. 

On the contrary the rates actually fell. There are a number of reasons for this. During the period, interest rates on bonds were relatively low and considerable financing was accomplished both for new capital and refunding purposes. A portion of these funds went into uses normally provided from commercial paper. In the second place, idle funds in corporate treasuries were sufficient to finance a considerable expansion in activity. Lastly, there is the fact that much of the expansion in production represented defense work for the federal government, and defense contracts were made acceptable as collateral for secured bank loans. This made recourse to the usual commercial paper market unnecessary for many firms.

Fixed Charges and the Business Cycle 

Fixed charges constitute a problem of much concern to corporate executives during depression periods. These charges include such items as depreciation, interest on bonded indebtedness, maintenance charges, executive and clerical salaries, property taxes, etc. They cannot be reduced to any appreciable extent, regardless of the volume of business being done. As a partial offset, an increase in the efficiency of management usually occurs in depression periods, generally resulting in a lower operating ratio. Fixed charges, however, tend to remain about the same from year to year and are often the cause of reduced earnings or actual losses.

The time to overcome the disastrous effects of these charges is during prosperity periods when excess earnings make possible larger than normal depreciation charges, the retirement of bonded indebtedness, and similar policies. Many companies fail to recognize this element until too late and find themselves confronted with receivership proceedings and the possibility of a reorganization. Others feel that they need the excess earnings of the prosperity periods to finance expansion, to furnish additional working capital, etc. However, no management should burden its company with fixed charges too great for the lean years through which it must pass. 

If the company is already so burdened every effort should be made to scale down these charges at the earliest opportunity.

Cyclical Action of Securities Markets 

As has been stated on other occasions, the price of a share of stock is considerably influenced by earnings. These, in turn, are greatly affected by cyclical movements and it is not surprising to find that stock prices fluctuate to an astonishing degree. Bond prices on the contrary do not respond so quickly to earnings but tend to reflect the basic factors of risk and prevailing rates of interest. 

With these elements in mind, it is easily understood why stock prices are high in periods of prosperity while bond prices show greater resistance in periods of depression. Corporate earnings are good in prosperous years, and the investing public is usually too optimistic with regard to future prospects. The average price for industrial stocks fell from its all-time high of 381.17 attained in 1929 to a low of 41.22 in 1932. While the low in 1929 was higher than the high of any subsequent year (except 1930), it should be noted that this low was only about half of the year's high. Wide changes in securities prices are the rule rather than the exception and create many problems for financial management. : Of what importance are these movements of security prices to the

financial managers of corporations? Primarily, they are indicative of the types of securities that will be most quickly absorbed by the investing public in the various stages of the business cycle. They function much as a weather vane and reflect the general attitude of the investor as well as revealing his more specific tastes. At times it will prove convenient to raise funds by issuing bonds; at others, the corporation may take advantage of a public demand for preferred or common stocks. On still other occasions, it may not be desirable to float either bonds or stocks, and capital may be raised by selling short-time notes. Cyclical moods may also dictate that the securities of a hybrid nature should be issued in preference to those of a more standard type. At times convertible bonds may prove to be a popular type of security to offer. The conversion option will appeal to those who wish to share in the future profits, and at the same time have the advantages of a fixed income security. 

The student should also be warned that it is much simpler to make these generalizations than it is to follow them in actual practice. It is no simple matter to determine the full significance (both as to length of time and intensity) of security price movements. One's perspective in looking back is obviously more certain than when peering in the opposite direction. Moreover, especial care is demanded by virtue of the fact that financing is essentially a long-time process and too much may not be staked upon particular conditions existing at any given moment. Failures

Every depression period is accompanied by a large number of failures. These failures may result from one or more of a number of causes among which should be mentioned: poor earnings, frozen assets with their accompanying inability to meet maturing debts, inventory losses arising out of declining prices, or generally poor management. The economic losses to investors and creditors resulting from failure reach tremendous proportions every year, but in depression years the loss is even greater. An appreciation of the number of failures and the economic consequences may be obtained through a study of Table 67.

It is evident that the socalled prosperity years were accompanied by a large number of business casualties. In 1930 to 1932, under the influence of a major depression, the number and size of business failures again increased markedly. Since 1932, however, the number of failures has declined to a level roughly approximating that prevailing in the early 1900's.. 

This is probably best explained by the fact that the recent depression

eliminated the weaker concerns which might have failed within a few years under any circumstances and the federal government has extended direct financial assistance in many cases. As a result, business mortality may be expected to be lower for some years, or until the next major depression. 

Dealing with Cyclical Fluctuations In this chapter emphasis has been placed upon the importance of preparedness as a tool in dealing with cyclical fluctuations. The management that is well prepared can often solve the difficulties presented by the business cycle and, in some cases, even profit through cyclical movements. The question may be raised, however, “How is management going to know of these movements far enough in advance to prepare for them?" No categorical answer may be given, but there are times when farsighted management can prepare and can save a great deal of trouble and money by taking the proper precautions.

Management should know thoroughly and constantly analyze the characteristics and peculiarities of its individual concern and of the industry in which it operates. Statistical study should be made of past sales, profits, and expenses, comparing them with similar figures for other concerns in the same industry, and attempting to discover the presence of any regularly recurring pattern. The relationship existing between cyclical movements of the industry in question and those of other industries may also be studied. It is highly possible that some relationship may be found which will serve as an indicator of developments in the business with which management is concerned. Or, some definite causal relationship may be established between certain economic and political happenings and their resulting effects upon the business. In other words, the manager can never know too much about his concern and its relation to its own industry and to other industries. However, in studying industrial relations, it is important that management forecast the future with great care. 

The past sequence of events may repeat itself in the future, but important political or economic happenings may intervene and make its repetition impossible. The statistical record is of value in forecasting the future only to the extent that it is modified to allow for changed circumstances.

PART VI CORPORATE EXPANSION

CHAPTER XXX EXPANSION 

: T IS the universal desire of mankind to grow because growth in some form is essential to existence. Advancement may be either intensive or extensive in character which means that it may assume the form of internal improvement or of external enlargement. 

In the case of the individual, the former may be cultural growth in the broadening of personality and understanding. In the case of an institution, such as a business, growth may take the form of improvement in techniques and products or of facilitating relationships, such as exist in connection with labor control and wage systems. While business firms may experience a sufficient amount of qualitative improvement to maintain their vitality without increasing their size, the most common form of growth takes the form of expansion or enlargement of operations in the physical and financial sense. In corporation finance, the chief concern is with the quantitative phases of expansion as they relate primarily to financial problems. 

Business firms in all lines of activity are constantly endeavoring to expand their operations. Fear has been expressed at times that corporations may grow to be too powerful in scope. It has been estimated that some two hundred corporations control over 50 per cent of the corporate wealth invested in non-banking institutions. Numerous questions of public interest have been raised concerning this concentration of control, but our chief interest at this point has to do with the enlargement of the business organization. 

Why should a business corporation desire to grow? Why should it not be satisfied with an established place in the business world and be content with fair profits? As related previously, the reasons are deep rooted and reflect an innate characteristic of progressive civilization. Moreover, the internal urge of individual business leaders is stimulated by various forces of a psychological and economic nature. 

Among these, the following may be mentioned. 

1. Competition encourages growth. Unless a business firm expands, it will frequently be surpassed by competing groups. Business is essentially dynamic and to stand still actually means a loss of position. 595

The concern which is unable to make progress at a rate comparable with that of the entire industry develops a deadening inertia which frequently leads to decline and failure. Conversely, the momentum developed by sound expansion is a source of vitality and vigor. 

2. The possibility of greater profits is equally stimulating. While net earnings may be increased by operating more efficiently on the existing scale, the opportunities are more limited than where there is an expansion of the field of activity. In addition, large-scale operations may permit economies and advantages not obtainable to the same degree on a smaller scale. 

3. Business enterprisers like to do the spectacular, either for the sake of personal satisfaction or for social recognition. To them business is a game and maintenance of operations on a large-scale offers satisfaction as well as possible profit. This individual trait was illustrated some years ago when Henry Ford refused an offer from a banking syndicate of one billion dollars for his business. Such an enormous sum would naturally have considerable financial appeal, but it was rejected primarily because Ford was having too much fun running the show. 

4. Finally, monopolistic ambitions may be the cause of expansion. 

There are autocrats or dictators in business as well as in the realm of politics, and they are not satisfied with anything less than control of the field in which they are operating. 

Expansion of American Industry 

Expansion has been typical of most of our leading business enterprises. The growth of many corporations down to 1929 was startling in extent, as is illustrated by the examples shown in Table 68. The ensuing depression brought severe curtailment of industry generally, and there is evidence that some fields of activity face prospects of further decline. At the same time, other branches of trade are expanding at a phenomenal rate, but this is not generally recognized because of the lack of vigor which characterized business as a whole following the abrupt decline in the early thirties. Such uneven growth gives a constantly changing complexion to American business life. The field of enterprise that is predominant today may be surpassed tomorrow. 

Thus, the General Motors Corporation has passed the United States Steel Corporation in volume of sales, an accomplishment which would have been deemed impossible two decades ago. New fields of activity come to the fore with surprising frequency, among those in recent
