Occasionally, corporate management becomes so engaged in the process of expansion that the proper internal balance which should prevail within the concern is destroyed. An excellent illustration is the failure of the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company in 1907. Sales reached a new high of some $33,000,- 

000 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1907, and, as of the same date, surplus amounted to $12,029,000, or nearly two and one-half times the amount which had existed on March 31, 1901. Yet the company was forced to apply for receivership in October, 1907, due to the inadequacy of working capital to meet current needs. 

Another question that arises out of expansion is the perplexing issue as to how large the business unit may be without losing its efficiency. Is there a limit to expansion? Is there not a point beyond which management loses its effectiveness? It is difficult to answer these questions with finality because of the impossibility of isolating the numerous variable factors involved. However, observations based upon research and experience tend to indicate that there is a right size for numerous businesses and that a specific organization may proceed beyond this stage and become too large. The factors of determination are related to the advantages of large-scale production and to the principle of diminishing returns.

The Advantages of Large-Scale Production 

Numerous advantages of large-scale production are commonly recognized, the most important of which are the following: 

1. Specialization.-The degree to which specialization and division of labor can be carried is greatly increased under larger-scale operations. In turn, extensive specialization reduces unit costs of production, assuming, of course, operation at a reasonably satisfactory volume of output in relation to capacity. 

2. Purchasing.-Large organizations have an advantage in buying materials and supplies because of the superior bargaining power that comes with size. Also, from the point of view of the supplying firm, numerous economies are possible when dealing in large quantities. 

3. By-products. Many industrial processes result in waste products which can be utilized or made profitable only if the scale of operation is large enough to warrant the establishment of the necessary organization. 

4. Pooling of patents and processes.-Expansion through the combination of previously independent concerns permits common usage of patents and processes, as well as of more or less secret production methods. Moreover, large concerns have the financial capacity to acquire patents and to carry on organized research for further development. 

5. Financing.-Large companies are usually able to obtain better terms of financing because of their national reputation and because large security issues can be sold at a lower cost than small issues. 

6. Management.-Large-scale enterprises have sufficient income and capital to obtain the best grade of management talent. 

Care must be taken not to draw the generalization that these advantages are always the incidence of size. Modifications necessarily occur according to the type of business, the capacity of individual management, and the state of general business conditions. Such limitations become effective for the most part in the application of the principle of diminishing returns.

The Law of Diminishing Returns 

Originating in the field of economic theory as an explanation for economic rent, the law of diminishing returns was restricted in its application for a long time to agricultural problems. However, it has come to be recognized that the law is clearly applicable to industrial

EXPANSION 

599. operations. Before discussing the nature of its industrial application, a statement of the law should be made. ... .. after a certain point has been reached in the exploitation of a productive factor of fixed amount, additional applications of other factors to its exploitation, though they will increase the total product, will not increase it in proportion to the increase of the variable factors. 

The law may be applied to industries under two sets of circumstances: (1) assuming a constant supply of fixed capital and a variable supply of working capital; (2) assuming a variable supply of both fixed and working capital.

Both assumptions represent oversimplification of the problems because, in reality, each type or kind of labor, raw material, machinery, buildings, or each source of capital should be regarded as a separate factor affecting production. In other words, the traditional factors of production-land, labor, capital, and the entrepreneur-may be subdivided so that the possible combinations of type and qualities are almost limitless.

Constant Fixed Capital and Variable Working Capital 

It scarcely needs to be demonstrated that with a constant amount of fixed capital, a point will be reached where further quantities of working capital may not be used to advantage. Mere physical crowding, if nothing else, will cause confusion within the plant (fixed capital) which will in turn cause inefficient production. Moreover, while it is possible, with adequate working capital, to expand production with existing plant facilities through the use of additional amounts of labor or by driving the machinery faster, offsetting costs are bound to appear. Machinery, like people, requires rest, and higher speed operations result in greater maintenance costs.

At the same time, a distinction must be made between relative and absolute changes in the results of production. At the outset when a few units of working capital are applied to the fixed capital, the output will be increased in greater proportion than the increase of added working capital units. Obviously, a minimum amount of working capital in the form of proper materials or of labor is necessary to get effective utilization of the fixed capital equipment. Just as an automobile engine will not operate at all if it is not fed at least a certain amount of gasoline, so also an industrial plant cannot produce unless

it has a certain number of men employed. Next a step is reached where the output, while increasing, does not do so in equal proportion to the increase in the variable units of working capital. In this stage, the auxiliary capital is augmented in relation to the base of fixed capital, causing an increase in output but at a rate which is less than the increments to working capital. Finally, a third stage is reached where the output actually decreases and no advantage is gained by adding further quantities of working capital. Beyond this point no industry will knowingly operate.

Of the three stages of increasing returns, diminishing returns, and decreasing total returns, the most profitable operation is found within the limits of the second, namely diminishing returns. In the first stage, the fixed investment is not being utilized to the fullest extent, while in the last stage it is being overworked and output actually decreases. 

The precise point of desired operation in the second stage is deter-mined by the relative cost of the current and fixed factors. It should be understood, of course, that this is viewing the problem strictly in terms of the productive factors. Peculiar and unusual demand conditions may be the cause of forcing actual operations to be otherwise. 

Similarly, it does not necessarily follow that the most efficient levels of production in a technical sense lead to the greatest profits. 

The relationship which exists between current and fixed costs is variable and will depend upon the fluctuation of business as well as upon the type of industry. Changing business conditions will produce more immediate effects on current than on fixed costs so that the ratio between the two may be considerably affected by prices and other disturbances. In those industries where the variable or current costs are of much greater significance than fixed costs the effects of depression may not be as serious as in those industries having the opposite cost relationships. In the latter, curtailed volume leads much more quickly to unprofitable operation than for industries where the variable expenses are a relatively large proportion of total expense. Illustrative of this principle it may be noted that the United States Steel Corporation would not likely earn anything on its common stock unless operating at a level of from 50 per cent to 55 per cent of its capacity. In contrast, it has been estimated that the United States Gypsum Company could earn dividends on the junior equity when operating in ex cess of 14 per cent of its capacity.' 

1J. C. Lloyd, "Beneficiary of Building Gains," Magazine of Wall Street (December 3, 

1938), p. 195.

601 

Variations in the Amount of Fixed and Working Capital 

Since variations in the volume of business are so serious to industries requiring large amounts of fixed capital, the question might be raised, Why not also adjust the fixed investment as circumstances dictate and thus maintain the proper ratio between the fixed and current factors? In the first place, quick adjustment is seldom possible in the actual operation of industry. Many industries are by their nature ideally adapted to a combination of large fixed investment as compared with the working capital required, while in others, opposite conditions are found. Moreover, once the fixed investment has been made, it is not subject to peremptory withdrawal and its recovery is effected mainly through the charge for depreciation against earnings. 

Oppositely, it may be difficult to increase the capital commitment with any marked rapidity in order to meet expansions in demand. 

In the second place, the ratio between the two factors of fixed and variable elements is not a simple, mathematical factor of determination. In addition, the size of the organization affects the administration of business operation. Little argument is necessary to show that the capacity of human management varies inversely with the size of the enterprise. Exceptional cases may be found, but certainly a line (variable and intangible though it may be) must exist above which the limitations of human management become apparent. Precise measurement of this line of maximum efficiency is difficult, but various empirical observations reveal that large units are not necessarily more efficient than small ones.

Relationship between Size and Expansion 

In visualizing the expansion of business enterprise, the reader is likely to have in mind a transition which is similar to the change in a human being going from the youth to the adult stage. A more accurate simile would be found in comparing business with the rest of the animal kingdom-many varieties and types and of all sizes. Many forms of business are predestined to remain small forever; they may expand within their orbit, but they will never achieve the stature of big, or even medium sized, concerns. A few have evolved from the status of small local units to large, nationally known enterprises; however, they are not representative of business as a whole. Many stories are written about such spectacular success, but they are of the headline type and are not ordinary news.

Still another analogy may be given to clarify the nature of business expansion because an accurate concept is essential to a proper understanding of the problem. There are many local governments in this country. They have grown as their communities have increased in population but most are still comparatively small. In great contrast, the federal government is big and has grown in spectacular fashionindeed, to many, its rapid growth is alarming. However, our federal government is known to all, while the local governments have comparatively limited appreciation. Similarly, a small number of big business enterprises take the public eye while the small concerns operate with little public notice. They grow in their sphere, but there is no major transformation.

Any classification of business according to size would be arbitrary although it may serve the purpose of orientation. Size, in turn, may be measured in various ways, such as by assets, by the number of employees, by the value of products, etc. Probably the most convenient basis is by assets. Using this test of size, one study has considered all corporations with assets of less than $250,000 to be small; from $250,- 

000 to $5,000,000 as intermediate; and those with assets of $5,000,000 and over as large. For the year 1936, it was found that 290,118 corporations were classified as follows:

It is here that the public is mainly represented. For similar reasons, this analysis of expansion may be limited more especially to the larger institutions. Again, there is the fact that pronounced increase in size never occurs in a large segment of industry. 

The question is frequently raised as to the relative profitableness of large and small business. Several studies in recent years seem to render a verdict in favor of big business but it is probable that the issue will always remain in doubt.3 There are too many doubtful and unknown quantities to permit accurate and final conclusions. Big business does have the advantage of bulk or brute strength while small business is presumed to have the offsetting quality of flexibility. 

Here is an argument that could continue ad infinitum. Under the circumstances, it is well to avoid the issue and confine our attention mainly to the expansion of the larger business units. In brief, the study is one of size within limits, or where the stages of change are at least reasonably comparable.

While expansion may be accomplished by the sale of new securities or by the reinvestment of earnings, the problem is brought into sharper focus in the case of consolidation of previously independent units. Here, there is a deliberate and sharp change in operation and the accomplishment of greater size in one fell swoop is the objective. 

There is a sort of declaration that size, and size alone, is the cardinal principle underlying the change. Because the size of operation is put under a real test under these conditions, most of our comments will be confined to consolidations or related techniques, whereby independent organizations are brought under common management. 

Effect of Consolidation on Profits 

Several years ago Dewing made a study of the effect of consolidation upon profits. The industrial combinations studied were organized almost entirely prior to 1903 when consolidations were mostly horizontal in form and the major emphasis was placed upon size. Since that time the type and form of consolidations have changed materially, but the study is still useful in showing the possible adverse results 3 For example, The National Bureau of Economic Research reported in their Bulletin, Vol. 55 (April 11, 1935), that the results of all taxable corporations for the years of 1931 and 

1932 showed earnings varying directly with size. 

4 A. S. Dewing, Financial Policy of Corporations (New York: Ronald Press Co., 1934), p. 748.

of abrupt consolidation. Of the thirty-five industrial combinations analyzed, it was found that: (1) The actual net earnings before consolidation were about 18 per cent greater than the earnings for the first year after consolidation. (2) The earnings for the entire tenyear period preceding consolidation were greater than the ensuing period by an amount of one-fifth to one-sixth. In this particular study, it is evident that the increased size did not produce greater earnings. At the same time, the analysis is comparatively limited in scope and does not necessarily reflect recent conditions. Moreover, the results may have been caused by well-known abuses of consolidation or other inefficiences which may be avoided under careful management.

Limitations of Profits Test of Success 

The profits test of success is convenient and widely accepted, but there is some question as to whether it constitutes a sufficiently broad basis for satisfactory judgment. From the point of view of society as a whole, the profits measurement must be recognized as an index which gives money changes instead of real changes. Under certain conditions there may be a marked increase in money profits without any appreciable increase in the goods or services which provide the standard of living so necessary for true social welfare. 

Profits are of social consequence only to the extent that they bring forth productive effort. If, as a result of consolidation or expansion, prices were lowered or quality improved, society would benefit even though the profits were less. It must be admitted that combination is not likely to cause lower prices than prevailed under the previous conditions of competition unless a fair degree of competition remains, or the elasticity of demand is such as to make lower prices more profitable. On the other hand, under some conditions the combination may result in lower costs, and these may be passed on in lower prices. The automobile industry is an example of an industry where a substantial measure of combination has apparently made possible improved quality, lowered costs and prices, and still permitted the payment of an adequate return. However, a substantial degree of competition continues to exist among the three larger pro ducing units, Ford Motor Company, General Motors Corporation, and Chrysler Corporation, thus encouraging the management to pass efficiencies along in the form of better values or lower prices. If

EXPANSION 

605 the "big three" should ever combine under one central control, one may wonder if this would still be true.

Neither would the profits test necessarily reflect the comparative efficiency of management under combination as compared with previous independent operation. In the first place, the results may be affected by changes in the price-level which would have a pronounced effect upon the money earnings. The data could be made more comparable by correcting the results through the use of price index numbers, but the price movements within a particular field rarely harmonize fully with general changes. Secondly, possible revision of expense items may have a decided effect upon profits. This contingency would be apt to arise in connection with salaries paid to the higher officials and in the amount of depreciation recognized. Offi the consolidated company would undoubtedly feel that they should receive higher salaries, and the apparent earnings may be affected to a considerable degree through the depreciation account. 

Other Factors Affecting Consolidation Not only is a comparison of the results of consolidation with those of the preceding independent operating units retarded by the physical impossibility of using identical test periods, but also numerous other factors are not subject to measurement. For instance, the very process of transition itself tends to disturb established operating processes. 

Rearrangement of plant space, the changing duties of personnel and various other innovations serve to disrupt the momentum of a going concern. Hence, in the change from independent to consolidated operation, a considerable period may be required for seasoning. 

Much is also dependent upon the uniformity of accounting methods used prior to and after consolidation. The importance of this variable is too seldom appreciated. To illustrate the distortion which may arise because of different accounting procedures, attention is called to the four possible ways of reporting earnings of the "big five" meat packing companies as shown in Table 69 on page 606. This table shows that the reported earnings of Swift and Company were $1.48 per share as compared with $1.08 for Wilson and Company. Yet, if Swift and 

Company had used the same basis for reporting its earnings as was used by Wilson and Company, the per share earnings would have been $2.99 instead of $1.48 as reported. Similar comparisons could be made among the other companies.

Finally, the measurement of the effectiveness of consolidation is impeded by the averaging effect of the aggregation of operating units. 

Consolidations are frequently motivated by desire for control instead of operating efficiency, and as a result many weak units are absorbed. 

The inclusion of the latter inevitably serves as a drag upon the operations of the consolidated enterprise. Similarly, blanket conclusions as to the desirability of consolidation fail to take into account the varying results which may appear in the different fields of enterprise. 

Actually, consolidation may prove effective in one branch of industry only to result in failure in another. As a result of these various modifying influences, it is virtually impossible to isolate consolidation per se, and the available statistics on consolidated operation fail to give a clue as to the specific desirability of enlarging the scale of operation.

Granting that it is difficult to determine from statistics the absolute answer as to the ultimate results of consolidation, the dominant position of big business in our economy is well known. Not only is this true in the naturally monopolistic field of the public utilities, but it is also typical of the manufacturing and distributing industries. 

Four manufacturers account for about 85 per cent of all cigarette sales; three automobile organizations make approximately 90 per cent of the passenger automobiles sold; a single company produces about 80 per cent of our yeast; 50 per cent of such a widely used product as soap is the output of a single producer. Even in the retailing area where many individual units are found, it is well known that giant

EXPANSION 

607 chains account for a large percentage of the sales. These impressive statistics of the dominance of a few companies in their respective fields could be multiplied many times. 

Large-Scale Enterprises and Public Opinion 

Aside from the purely business pros and cons on large-scale operation, it is also an attribute of business activity which easily assumes the qualities of a public issue. As a consequence, popular and political thought is likely to have pronounced influence in its acceptance or rejection. Since public opinion moves in cycles of moods, it is not surprising to find big business enjoying public favor at times, while at other periods it may be found in the well-known "dog-house." 

In the closing decade of the last century, distinct public aversion to monopolistic practices was crystallized in the form of legislation which was intended to outlaw undue curtailment of competition. Yet in the decade immediately following, the aggression of big business was commonly accepted. Again, when big business was often credited with the stimulation of the business boom in the twenties, the formation of supersize business units was popular. Its castigation was equally prominent in the severe depression which followed. 

While public opinion is one of the great factors in the control of destiny, it is seldom developed in any logical manner. The decision rendered by public opinion may be right by virtue of the diversification of mass judgment, but rarely is scientific diagnosis present. Instead, the presumption is that sufficient reasons will be found to substantiate the popular position. This accounts largely for the marked undulations of public opinion in its approval or disapproval of big business. When business activity is vigorous and prosperity abounds, the public cares little about the form of organization. Oppositely, when business is bad, somebody must be blamed. Consequently, dominance or control is presumed to carry the responsibility, and the onus is placed upon big business. 

General Economic Factors Relating to Consolidation. 

The popular attitude has the merit of simplicity, but it is not satisfying from the point of view of financial analysis. In this more critical light, the advantages and disadvantages (for both will exist) of each case of consolidation need to be weighed in the balance to determine the net advantage. Such variables as prevailing economic

conditions, the type of industry, the condition of the constituent companies, the phase of the business cycle, all must be taken into consideration.

Consider, for example, the possible influence of changing labor conditions, and as a concrete instance, how they may affect the rubber and tire industry. Here the business is dominated by the so-called "big four": Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company, United States 

Rubber Company, Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, and the B.

F. Goodrich Company. All of these with the exception of the United 

States Rubber Company have their main plants in Akron, Ohio. 

The industry is, therefore, an excellent illustration of geographical and company concentration. For an extended period of twenty years, the 

Akron companies operated under an open-shop basis experiencing little labor difficulty. Sit-down strikes made their appearance in 1934 with a shift in labor leadership from the A.F. of L. to the C.I.O. 

As a result of the labor agitation, labor rates have increased materially, it being estimated that hourly rates in Akron are from 30 cents to 35 cents higher than in many other areas. It is not surprising to find that these conditions are causing the larger companies to decentralize their operations as well as giving a competitive advantage to smaller companies already in existence. It is estimated that the Akron companies now account for approximately one-third of the total tire production as compared with 55 to 60 per cent in earlier years. 

Not only may later development destroy advantages which existed at the time of consolidation, but the nature of its promotion tends to contain the germs of decay. Because some form of consolidation is often regarded as a corrective measure, it is often invoked as a means of eliminating weak units by their absorption. Not infrequently, companies which are on the down grade offer vigorous price competition in a desperate attempt to enlarge their share of the total business. 

Because of this practice, they develop a form of nuisance value which is utilized to good advantage in the bargaining which attends consolidation. The inevitable result is to saddle a consolidation with dead wood at its very inception. 

It also stands to reason that inefficient units are more susceptible to the lure of consolidation than the more progressive and stronger companies. Quite naturally, the latter are reluctant to dispose of the fruits of their accomplishment and take too much pride in their endeavor to dispose of their business readily. Oppositely, the weaker

EXPANSION 

609 1 1 1 ! enterprise is more willing to accept an opportunity to sell out to advantage. As a consequence, a consolidation may be compelled to pay top prices for both weak and strong units. 

Another characteristic which retards a favorable showing by consolidations is the tendency for them to be initiated in times of prosperity, especially so when business has been whirled into boom proportions. Such conditions readily spur promoters into the spirit of doing bigger and better things. Needless to say, because of their creation in boom periods, the consolidated companies are immediately burdened with a heavier capitalization than existed previously for constituent companies in their independent status.5 It is easy to see that in the ensuing periods of depression the consolidated structure will feel keenly the pressure of falling prices, reduced volume, and many other pressures generated under such conditions. 

Factors Accounting for Consolidation 

In addition to the lure of profits, numerous other factors encourage the enlargement of business organizations. Among the more important are the following: (1) the natural process of elimination which follows the initial stage of most industries; (2) public favor of trademarked or standardized commodities; (3) the ability of big business to attract capable management; (4) difficulties in eliminating large, established businesses.

Elimination Following the Initial Stage 

Any new industry is likely to attract more units than it is capable of supporting because the opportunities of a new field tend to create a ground-floor complex. Enterprising individuals yield to the temptation to get an early start and to share in the appreciation which often accompanies the transition from the initial stage to the more stable position of a mature industry. But many of these producing units disappear either through failure or as a result of their absorption by the more successful companies. Many start with inadequate capital and are receptive to any promising opportunity for retirement. Their interest may have been that of quick speculative profits as distinguished from longer-term operating profits. 

5 E. Jones, The Trust Problem in the United States (New York: Macmillan Co., 1921), p. 269, states that "generally speaking, the capitalization of the trusts was twice as large as the value under competitive conditions of the properties and businesses that they acquired."

The development of this natural tendency toward curtailment of the number of enterprises is influenced in large measure by the type and nature of the industry. Where a substantial capital investment is a prerequisite, there is apt to be less early mushroom expansion than where small units are adapted to the needs of the industry. While the tobacco industry is no longer new, it illustrates in an excellent way the significance and influence of the capital element. In 1935, there were twenty-nine cigarette companies with an output value of $806,- 

690,000, while for the same year there were 746 cigar establishments represented with an output of $151,265,000. It is obvious that entry into the highly mechanized field of the former would be much more difficult than trying to get started in the latter which operates on a comparatively small scale. This condition is sometimes referred to as a capital monopoly in that, while the industry may be free from restrictions as to patents or franchises, the very size of the capital requirements for initiating the new enterprise makes it extremely difficult for any competition to enter the field. 

Patented or intricate processes also serve as a check upon the easy entry of new companies into a field. To illustrate, the Census of 

Manufacturers for 1935 shows that there were thirty-two establishments engaged in producing rayon yarns and similar products for that year as compared with the same number for 1931 and twentynine in 1929. Here the influence of patented processes is coupled with rather large capital requirements to organize a single producing unit. In contrast, the producers of signs and advertising novelties numbered in excess of one thousand in 1935. In this case, there are rather small capital requirements and few, if any, restrictions upon the nature of the production.

Artificial stimulation also appears to accentuate consolidation in the initial stages of industry through the ever present promotion activities of the security houses and numerous enterprising individuals who are constantly on the lookout for quick profits. Trade association gatherings further contribute to a sense of industrial consciousness which often paves the way for group action, and finally for combination. In such an atmosphere, the virtues of competition are usually forgotten and the paper advantages of consolidated effort are magnified. Thus, the ground is laid for the formal consolidation of companies.

EXPANSION 

611 

Public Favor of Standardized Commodities 

Irrespective of operating efficiency, the ultimate test of business operations is to be found in the successful marketing of goods and services. Marketing methods vary of necessity according to the peculiarities of the products sold, but it is well known that price and quality are two common elements which facilitate sale. Emphasis upon price alone places tremendous pressure upon the cost of production; in addition, such a policy is likely to lead to a rapid turnover of customer clientele. Under the circumstances it is not surprising that established companies should attempt to build up prestige by stressing the quality of their product. To do this, it is convenient to standardize the main lines of goods and to give them a label or trade-mark which may be cultivated on a national basis. Obviously, the applicability of the principle will depend upon the type of market which is being served. Thus, it is more serviceable in the case of consumer goods with wide distribution than with the products of heavy industries which encounter more selective buying. 

Once a trade name is clearly established on a national basis the demand for the product not only tends to increase, but it also tends to become stabilized, providing, of course, advertising continues on its original scale and no marked changes in competitive conditions occur. The extensive advertising campaigns which are so necessary for the development of patented or trade-marked goods can be conducted on a lower cost per unit basis if handled on a national scale. 

As a result, the branding of goods tends to encourage large-scale operation. In the first place, volume is virtually synonymous with large-scale production. Secondly, the stability of demand is a force which facilitates the carrying of overhead so commonly found in the large-scale organization. 

One striking disadvantage of large-scale operations is found in the greater inflexibility of expenses. This arises out of the fact that the overhead expenses constitute a relatively large proportion of total expenses. Large-scale industry ordinarily results in a substitution of overhead expenses for direct and variable expenses, or in other words a substitution of machines for men. This will result in a more economical operation only if the scale of operations can be kept in proper relation to the capacity. When volume diminishes for any reason, the large-scale concern finds that many of its expenses continue irrespective of the reduction in volume, whereas the smaller concern 1

is better able to reduce its expenses to conform to its income. To offset the burden of fixed overhead expense, a large and diversified national market may offer substantial relief. 

Because of the benefits of a trade name it has become common policy to mold expansion programs around this convenient fiction. 

A railroad appeals to its market by telling travelers that they will "sleep like a kitten"; moreover, the cat is given a name so as to give it popular currency. Long corporate nomenclature is too clumsy and forbidding for purposes of consumer use; hence the adoption of more human and convenient symbols. Similarly, products ranging from foods to automobiles are known by their trade names rather than the company which makes them. 

Ability of Big Business To Attract Capable Management 

It is frequently observed that the success of any business, big or small, is determined by the quality of its management. This is a truth which is not readily demonstrated by statistics because intangible values are not subject to empirical treatment. Moreover, the observation is made all too often from hindsight instead of more profitable foresight. Nonetheless, in spite of such remote measurement of the management factor, its importance is commonly recognized. 

Broadly speaking, big business has an advantage in the search for managerial talent. Not only do larger salaries serve as a practical lure, but the greater prestige of connections with large companies also acts as a powerful psychological appeal. Executives of big business are often national figures, but it is the exception for capable managers of small enterprises to achieve similar standing. In short, and perhaps unfortunately so, society attaches more prominence to positions with large companies than with smaller ones. 

While recognizing the advantage which big business has in attracting capable management, it needs also to be said that the problems and complexities of large-scale organization demand the most efficient direction. There are difficulties of organization and personnel administration which are not equally present in small-scale enterprise. Instead of the direct supervision which is possible in the latter, authority is necessarily delegated in a degree directly proportional to the size of the operation. And delegated authority is seldom administered with the dispatch and exactness which accompany direct and immediate responsibility.

EXPANSION 

613 1 1 2 1 Another difficulty which seems to plague the managerial element of big business is that of providing for the perpetuation of good administration. This is caused by the fact that high-quality performance is due more to the qualities of the individuals who direct than to the pattern of organization. Many large corporations have instituted training programs in an attempt to provide for replacements, but often there exists some key individual or individuals who furnish qualities of morale, inspiration, and genius which are not easily developed by training methods. 

In view of these obstacles, the reader may well raise the question as to whether or not the ability of big business to attract capable management is after all a net advantage. The thought may be advanced that the attraction may be more than offset by the demands and pressures accompanying larger-scale organization. There is much merit in this contention, and to a great degree it precludes ready generalization as to this point. However, this is a question of the relative efficiency of the size of the organization, whereas our inquiry is directed to the persistency of the movement in favor of increasing the scale of operation. From this point of view, outstanding leaders naturally seek the more challenging tasks of big business for reasons previously set forth.

Difficulties in Eliminating Big Business 

Once big business is established, it is not easily eliminated. This is caused by the widespread character of its ownership which creates more extensive public interest than is true of smaller business units. 

As a consequence, when a large corporation gets into difficulties, it is usually reorganized. In contrast, small companies are more apt to be liquidated. Their public following is limited, and their demise does not disturb the investment market or arouse public opinion. As a convenient illustration, when small banks failed by the hundreds during the decade of the twenties little was done to afford positive relief. But when the larger banks started to fail in the early thirties, drastic steps were taken by the federal government to provide protection to the public-at-large. This went so far as to bring about the creation of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 1933 to insure the deposits of banks, both large and small. 

This quality of survival by big business is not necessarily of longterm benefit to the whole economy. The situation may simply mean the

perpetuation of business enterprise on an unsound basis. Because of this favoritism, for such it is, the increasing government influence upon and control of corporate reorganization is not surprising. The nature and extent of this government regulation will be described more fully in a later chapter.

CHAPTER XXXI  

B EFORE discussing the history and types of consolidation, a clarification of terminology may be helpful. Technically speaking, consolidation has been considered to be the creation of a new corporation for the purpose of taking over existing corporations. When an existing corporation is enlarged by the absorption of other companies, a merger is said to be effected. Later, there will be occasion to illustrate the application of these two methods (the difference is largely legal in character rather than economic), but for the most part the term consolidation will be used in a general way to include all forms of uniting or joining previously independent business organizations. The term combination is given an identical meaning and will be used synonymously for the sake of greater freedom of expression. There is some advantage in the use of the restricted definition, but the terms are used loosely and in a broad way in general business practice. The dictionary also gives virtually identical meanings. Under the circumstances, little is to be gained by creating a halo of restricted application when the terms are not so used in everyday language.

In reviewing the historical background and analyzing the possible types of consolidation, the special public interest in such financial activities should be kept in mind. In the first place, the combination of separate and independent companies is contrary to the accepted principles of a capitalistic economy, at least, to the extent that it serves to create monopolistic conditions. It may be that capitalism could exist on either a competitive or a monopolistic basis, but there would be important differences in the rules of the game. Under competition, virtually unlimited freedom of individual endeavor may be assumed because of the constant checks and control provided by unbridled market action. By this means, there is presumed to be an automatic safeguard of the public interest. Where monopoly in some degree is substituted for free competition, then the direction of economic activity is shifted from an impersonal and objective basis to one which is more or less personal and subjective in character. Auto- 616

matically, there is an assumption of authority by the few, and there can be no escape from the accompanying responsibility. The public, in its own interest, must accordingly look to those in control instead of relying upon the usual regulating effects of free market action. 

It is in this sense that the trusteeship character of corporate management has been pointed out previously. 

Not only does the sense of public interest in big business arise from its effects upon the common welfare, but in addition, millions of people have a direct financial investment. True, the representation is larger in the number of shareholders than in the amount invested, but the principles of trusteeship are equally rigid irrespective of amount. Moreover, these small shareholders have been invited to be partners in large-scale enterprise, and there can be no escape from a recognition of their rights. Either this consciousness of responsibility will take form voluntarily by action of management, itself, or it will likely be done by compulsion under some means of public authority. 

Indeed, the trends of recent years already reflect governmental action to protect the interests of investors; how much farther it will go will depend mainly on the response of management. 

It is from this larger perspective that attention may be given to the consolidation of corporations. The technique, itself, becomes fascinating and may easily become the focus of attraction, but it is simply the means and not the end. Hence, as the history of the combination of companies is unfolded and as the methods of joining independent units are examined, the reader would do well to keep before him the sense of the ultimate. To shake the spell and charm of brilliantly executed financial maneuvering, such questions as the following may be asked: What do gigantic consolidations of business enterprise mean in their ultimate effects upon the economic system? How will they affect the freedom of individual endeavor? Will there be continued opportunities for the initiation of small business enterprise? Moreover, these are questions which spring inevitably from the development of business on its own account and are not the result of enlarged governmental function. 

Historical Background 

There is a real and exciting history behind the majority of industrial combinations. They may start in a small, inconspicuous way; then burst forth almost overnight and appear as extensive new organizations in the business world. The next chapter may find them curbed

or broken up by the courts. Under the principles of common law, restraint of trade is recognized to be an illegal act. Similarly, it has been the intent of numerous statutory enactments to restrict corporate consolidation, at least to the extent of preserving a degree of competition. However, there is a large element of uncertainty concerning the interpretation of restraint of trade and as to the conditions under which legal action may be taken by public authority. Consequently, legal restrictions have not greatly inhibited the promotion of various types of corporate "get-togethers." Always some more or less effective method is found which conveniently fits the law, and just as frequently it is changed as the law catches up with existing practice. 

While many consolidations of independent companies are initiated to effect economies in manufacturing and distribution, there are others which are undertaken primarily for purposes of control. The latter serve to restrict freedom of competition which is so essential to the normal working of that important governor of business activity -price. As a consequence, markets may not reflect basic trends at any particular moment of time, but instead bias and restraint appear because of the control imposed by a few organizations. This is not the place to discuss the merits of free and open competition as compared to various degrees of control, but as stated previously consolidation does affect the public interest. In this country, there appears to have been three periods of active development, separated by intervals of relative inactivity. The periods of development date approximately as follows: (1) 1885-93, (2) 1897-1903, (3) 1919-29. 

The First Period of Development, 1885-93 

The problem of industrial combinations took form with the organization of the Standard Oil Trust in 1885. Minor consolidations had occurred before this time, but they were not sufficiently outstanding to attract public attention. Two years later, the American Sugar 

Refining Company was organized by combining a number of existing concerns, and this, along with the oil trust, tended to make the problem a public question and a political issue. Popular reaction was such that the Congress enacted the now well-known Sherman Antitrust Law of 1890. Despite this legislation, other trusts were organized such as the National Lead Company in 1890, and the General Electric Company and the United States Rubber Company in 1892. Many combinations organized at this time are still operating today although

in somewhat modified form. Whether this is purely coincidence or the result of economic and other advantages acquired through combination cannot be stated with accuracy. Probably various factors consisting of the type of product, skill of management, efficiencies of operation, and influence on market outlet account for this outstanding record of performance. 

The vigorous expression of general opinion at this time is a significant commentary on the interest of the public in business affairs. 

The consolidations then occurring are dwarfed in comparison with those of the present day, but the ideal of free enterprise was sufficient to serve as a call to arms. Many developments, both of a political and economic nature, have occurred since that time to weaken our zeal for the freedom of the business seas, and there is a tendency to substitute security for the rigors of individual action. This changing philosophy must inevitably affect the character of our business system. Indeed, it is possible that large-scale operation may become the accepted mode of business conduct, but in this event it may be expected that the government as the spokesman of public interest will change its traditional role from that of umpire to one of an active participant.

The Second Period of Development, 1897-1903 

In the second period many combinations were formed simply because it was the vogue. The "combine" came to be accepted as a panacea for business ills, and with such indiscriminate use many of the new organizations did not survive. However, it may be said that the real combination movement began at this time. It has been estimated that in the year 1899 alone there were some 259 industrial combinations formed having a capitalization in excess of $1,000,000.¹ 

In the three years 1898 to 1900, there were organized 149 combinations with a capitalization totaling $3,128,650,000.2

Third Period of Development, 1919-29 

The landmark twenties heralded a new day in the development of big business. The theme of expansion was common with that at the turn of the century, but the scale and pace were more phenomenal. 

Unfortunately, giant enterprises were created too often more by the spur of quick profits from promotion than they were evolved from promising, business opportunity. And the period of reckoning took the form of the most severe and prolonged depression our country has ever known.

It is not surprising, therefore, that many combinations occurred purely for their own sake in response to the momentum of the movement and because of their sponsorship by well-known financial interests. Combination became the thing to do and promoters were seeking more actively than usual for such opportunities as a source of profits. Undoubtedly, the stimulus for combination arose more often from financial sources without than from managerial influence within the companies involved. 

As a result, many combinations were effected primarily for purposes of financial strategy and manipulation, and to provide a supply of new security issues to be sold to the unwitting investor. Internal operating efficiency as measured by costs per unit was too frequently ignored. 

The basic merits of consolidation were also overlooked and greater emphasis was placed upon the development of organizational forms for purposes of control than for the actual production of goods. 

The Ensuing Depression and Future Outlook 

The trend of events in the twenties caught the public imagination and many believed that it was the dawn of a new era. Unfortunately, the groundwork was not solid and a combination of emotional instability and economic unbalance ushered in a violent and sudden crash which was, in turn, followed by a long and serious depression. In despair, business institutions openly appealed to the federal government for relief. This was forthcoming and the presence of the government in business today may prove to be one of the chief determinants of the future business pattern. There is now violent debate between those who want to keep the government in and those who want to get it out.

'Recognizing the fact that the government is now playing a prominent part in determining the course of business destiny, it may be expected that it will have marked influence upon the size of business units. An outstanding characteristic of governmental action is organization-some call it regimentation while others believe it to be merely the process of systemization. In any event, the government could conceivably encourage further consolidation of business enterprise as a means of facilitating administration. Yet, this pattern of business structure is not inevitable. It is only necessary to look to the organization and control which is now being exercised over agriculture to realize that it is possible to function with small individual units as a basis. At this time, only the possibilities may be suggested; the historian of the future will be in a much better position to speak more certainly.

The types of combination harmonize with the historical development and new patterns are evolved to meet changing conditions and times. The earlier forms of organization used to bring about the effects of combination were informal and simple in character. 

Gentlemen's Agreement 

The first methods of general application consisted of an ordinary gentlemen's understanding in which the interested parties merely agreed orally not to cut prices or promised to restrict activity in keeping with the terms of the agreement. This arrangement, however, had neither legal sanction nor administrative organization for purposes of enforcement. As a result, the participants were prone to violate the agreements whenever it was to their profit to do so. Pools In order to secure a more definite and comprehensive program on the part of the participating concerns, the pool was developed. 

This was ordinarily a written agreement providing for a co-operation of effort in exploiting the available markets. There were many kinds of pools, such as pools for the common distribution of profits, pools where the production was assigned on a predetermined equitable basis, pools in which all the members sold their output to a common agency for resale to the markets, and patent pools in which the members mutually used all patents.

The pool was formally organized and usually had a central administrative agency to which all the members reported. In the event any of the members violated their agreement, a penalty was imposed and collected by the central office. Such supervision served to make the pool slightly more effective than the gentlemen's agreement, but at the same time no legal means of enforcement were available because the agreements were illegally in restraint of trade. As a result, individual members were likely to desert whenever they had an opportunity to make unusual profits. A number of such recurrences would usually cause the complete dissolution of the group. 

Another cause which tended to destroy the pool was the policy of raising prices to an excessive degree whenever the market was controlled, with the result that new competitors were encouraged to come in and take advantage of the abnormally high-profit margins. Moreover, the various pools rarely included all the productive capacity and usually found it difficult to control the market influence of small companies not included. The Wire Nail Association of 1895 and 1896 is an example of the usual course of events whenever a pool was formed. 

The manufacture of wire nails had increased very rapidly between 1880 and 1895, during which period production rose from twenty thousand kegs in 1880 to six hundred thousand in 1895. As a result, the price fell from $10 per keg in 1880 to $1.60 in 1894. Productive capacity was well in excess of market needs, and the price structure of the industry was such that some of the larger and more common sized nails were being sold for less than the cost of the raw material used. In 1895, a group of wire-nail manufacturers formed an association or pool which fixed production quotas for each month and assigned the quotas to the various producing regions. All profits above cost prices were paid into the pool, and the balance in the pool after paying expenses was divided among the companies giving consideration to three factors-sales for the three months before the formation of the association, production in one of those three months, and capacity as measured by the number of machines. To provide further control, machinery manufacturers were paid to restrict the production of wire-making machines, and small-nail manufacturers not included in the association were paid to refrain from production. 

Illustrative of the effect of the pool, the price per keg of 8-penny wire nails was advanced by successive stages from $1.45, which prevailed in May, 1895, at the formation of the group, to a high of $3.15,

in May, 1896. This price remained constant until about the first of 

November when the pool broke under the pressure of outside competition and the unwillingness of hardware jobbers to continue the high-rate schedule prevailing. By the end of the month, the price had fallen to $1.70 and by the end of the year to $1.55.5 Trusts

The next form of business organization developed to effect a combination of existing enterprises was the trust. Properly speaking, the trust refers to a form of legal relationship (or fiduciary arrangement) and does not necessarily mean the existence of a monopoly or the presence of a combination of companies. However, some of the largest combinations to be organized, and those which held the position of attention at the close of the last century, adopted the trust form of organization. As a result, it is not uncommon to find monopolies or quasi-monopolies referred to as "trusts." 

Under the trust form, the stockholders of the constituent concerns turn in their stock to a board of trustees and receive in exchange trust certificates evidencing the receipt of shares. These trust certificates can then be bought and sold just like the original stock certificates. They have all the rights, privileges, and values of stock certificates except that of voting power. The board of trustees has complete control inasmuch as it holds all the stock, or at least a working majority of the stock of the constituent companies with its voting power. This gives formal, legal control to the central organization and offers none of the loopholes in the pool plan. 

The method was used effectively to organize a number of large and powerful groups which exercised substantial control over their markets, but its effectiveness was soon limited by the Sherman Antitrust Law of 1890 which declared combinations in restraint of trade to be illegal. Following this Act it became necessary to devise some plan embodying practically the same features in so far as control was concerned, but at the same time, a plan which would be legal. This was the objective of the holding company which was the next step in the evolution of forms of combination. 

Holding Companies

The essential difference between the trust plan and the holding company is the directness of control. Under the former, a board of 

5 W. Z. Ripley, Trusts, Pools and Corporations (Boston: Ginn & Co., 1905), pp. 46-71.

trustees has the express and exclusive right to vote the stock held in trust and is able to run the member businesses without restriction or influence from the stockholders. This board of trustees has the relationship to the stockholders which usually prevails between a trustee and his principal. On the other hand, the holding company is a separate corporate structure which has the same rights, but the control of the holding company itself needs to be guarded. Practically, the holding company retains all the effectiveness of the trust plan and at the same time occupies a better legal position. 

The legality of the holding company was first tested in the Northern Securities Case of 1904 where a company had been organized for the specific purpose of acquiring the stocks of two competing railroads, the Great Northern and the Northern Pacific. The courts held that this was action in restraint of trade and hence contrary to the Anti-trust Law of 1890. The case raised doubt as to the legal status of the holding company, but did not eliminate the device as a means of effecting combinations. Admittedly, holding companies may cause restraint of trade in a greater or less degree, but the attitude of the courts has been modified to insist only that the restraint shall not be unreasonable.

The holding company is not only subject to possible legal attack, but it may at times become cumbersome and uneconomical in its organization. Hundreds of subsidiaries may be acquired and holding companies are sometimes formed for the purpose of holding the stock of other holding companies. Even in the comparatively simple holding company organizations, the method results in the duplication of overhead expenses in the form of corporate franchise taxes and other items. To avoid these various difficulties, the companies affected may be completely absorbed into a single organization. 

Outright Absorption of Separate Corporations The molding of separate companies into a common and single organization may be accomplished either by the enlargement of an existing concern or by the creation of a new corporation. Under the first plan, one existing company expands its capitalization, obtains the outstanding securities of the other companies by giving its own in exchange, and then usually arranges for the dissolution of the corporate identities of the merged companies. Under the second arrangement, a new corporation is organized to take over all the individual concerns involved, following which the process of ex-

1 changing securities and the dissolution of the separate corporate entities are about the same as the other procedure. It can be seen that either method avoids the burden of carrying the separate corporate organizations necessitated by the holding company plan. Nevertheless, all three of these forms of accomplishing combinations are actually used at the present time and each has its particular advantages under different situations. 

Illustrative of the plan where a new corporation is formed is the Republic Steel Corporation which was organized in 1930. This company absorbed the following companies: Republic Iron and Steel 

Company, Central Alloy Steel Corporation, Donner Steel Company,

Inc., Bourne-Fuller Company, and the Berger Manufacturing Company. The merged companies have lost their separate identities and are simply an integral part of the new company which was created to accomplish the consolidation.

The merging of other companies into an existing organization is well illustrated by the General Motors Corporation. Many of the companies bought have been absorbed by General Motors Corporation and do not retain their original entities. As a result, General Motors is primarily an operating concern owning the plants, properties, and other assets involved in its manufacturing operations. Operations are carried on by the Chevrolet Motor Division, Buick Motor Division, and other divisions producing cars or other manufactured products, but the divisions have no separate legal existence apart from the General Motors Corporation. In addition, the General Motors Corporation is a holding company having stock interests in the Yellow Truck and Manufacturing Company, Delco Light Company, and a number of others.

An excellent example of the holding company in the industrial field is the United States Steel Corporation. Contrary to popular notion, this concern manufactures no steel, but it controls directly more than one hundred other corporations engaged in the manufacture of pig iron, steel metal, and other related products. In turn, many of the direct subsidiaries own other companies. 

Brief reference should also be made to other methods of bringing about a combination of existing organizations. • Among the more important manufacturing subsidiaries of the United States Steel Corporation are Carnegie-Illinois Steel Corporation, National Tube Company, American Steel and Wire Company, Universal Atlas Cement Company, and Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company.

The Lease Plan 

Under the lease arrangement, a rental agreement is effected whereby the operating company pays a rent as a consideration for the right to use the physical properties of the owning company or companies. 

The leases are frequently arranged for long terms and are usually renewable. This plan is used widely in the railroad field because the owning corporation retains its legal identity. As a result, it is not necessary to carry out any new financing as would be the case in an outright consolidation or merger. Moreover, many small railroads have favorable charters which could not be transferred to any successive corporation. An outstanding example of the use of the lease method is the New York Central Railroad Company. As of December 

31, 1939, this company operated 11,008 miles of first track, 7,295 or 66 per cent of which was on a lease or contract basis. 

Community of Interest

An informal, although often effective, method of achieving some of the benefits of consolidation is through a community of interest. 

A community of interest occurs whenever a small group of persons, members of a family or close acquaintances, own the controlling interest in several corporations. The owning group is then able to manage the separate companies so as to be mutually beneficial without there being any general public knowledge of the arrangement. 

Two disadvantages appear for this method of co-ordinating business policy. From the viewpoint of the corporations, it is a loose organization depending upon personal relationships rather than legal obligations for its effectiveness. In this respect, it is similar to the earlier "gentlemen's agreements." From the social viewpoint, the community of interest may represent a legal method of accomplishing an illegal consolidation for some purpose such as the restriction of competition. 

Interlocking Directorates

A more tangible method of securing common action among corporations without actual consolidation is through the use of interlocking directorates. Whenever the boards of directors of two or more corporations have members common to each board, an interlocking directorate exists. While the common members may never carry con-

fidential information between the various boards, they are able to influence the corporation's policy toward united or co-operative action. 

Unlike the community of interest, interlocking directorates cannot be concealed and, as a result, can be regulated by law. The 

Clayton Act prohibits interlocking directorates in large national banks (deposits and net worth of more than $5,000,000) or in industrial corporations of over $1,000,000 net worth which have been or are competitors of each other. Similarly, the Banking Act of 1933 separating investment and commercial banking prohibits common directors between Federal Reserve member banks and investment banks. On the permissive side, railroads may have interlocking directors only with the approval of the Interstate Commerce Commission; registered public utility holding companies may have common directors with banks subject to the rules of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Classification According to Products Controlled 

Another basis for the classification of combinations is in terms of the similarity or relationship of the products of the constituent companies. On this basis, the following groupings are found: (1) combination of companies producing like products; (2) combination of companies producing in the same major industry; (3) combination of the integration variety; (4) combination of companies producing nonrelated products.

Combination of Companies Producing Like Products 

The most frequent type of consolidation is that wherein two or more companies producing the same kind of goods combine their operations under one management. This is often referred to as horizontal combination since it represents a merging of concerns operating on the same plane. The usual reason for such linking of common activity is to secure benefits believed to inhere in operation on a larger and more closely integrated scale. In some instances, the chief purpose, veiled though it may be, is to obtain greater dominance or control in the field of enterprise. The combined group will constitute a larger portion of the total supply and may attain certain quasimonopolistic advantages in the markets. Greater diversification may also result because of the increase in the size of the market and because of geographical differences in the area of distribution. Selected

from the large number of such combinations the following may be regarded as illustrative:

Various Most horizontal combinations are of the specific type, that is, they are organized entirely in light of the existing situation and are completed in a single stage. At other times, the process of combination is more or less continuing in character, such as the case of two of the companies cited above where there has been an almost continuous program of buying out companies in the same general field. Thus, during 1928 and 1929, the Continental Can Company bought in each year eight other can or allied companies and merged their operations with the original concern. The expansion of the National Dairy 

Products Company was exceptionally rapid during the late 1920's due to the absorption of local concerns engaged in the dairy products business. The sales of this company in 1924 amounted to about $20,- 

180,000 and, by 1929, had grown to a little more than $300,000,000, an increase of nearly 1400 per cent. While more units have been acquired since that date, lower prices and the effects of the depression have checked the rapid growth as measured by dollar volume of sales. 

In 1940, sales were approximately $347,410,000. 

Combination of Companies Producing Complementary Products 

Another variation in the combination of companies on a product basis is the uniting of companies having complementary or related lines. The following illustrative examples may be cited: American 

Radiator and Standard Sanitary Corporation, General Foods Cor poration, Gold Dust Corporation, Remington-Rand, Incorporated, Standard Brands, Incorporated, Underwood-Elliott-Fisher Company. 

Combinations of the strictly horizontal type are effected primarily for the sake of operating efficiencies in terms of production cost or for the control of the market. In the case of complementary organization, greater stress is placed upon possible economies in distribution and administration. To be specific, the organization of the General

Foods Corporation as such did not necessitate an increase in size of the productive units. It is possible, however, that greater productive capacity may be necessary because a larger and more powerful organization may increase the sales of the individual units. Instead, the immediate result was simply that common and uniform administrative sales policies could be applied. The companies taken over by the 

General Foods Corporation would indicate the extent to which this statement is true: The Jell-O Company, Inc., Minute Tapioca Company, Inc., Walter Baker and Company, Ltd., Richard Hellman, Inc., The Log Cabin Products Company, Cheek-Neal Company, La France 

Manufacturing Company, Calumet Baking Powder Company, Certo

Corporation, Frosted Foods Corporation, Diamond Crystal Salt Com pany, etc. Obviously, after such a combination, separate operating units with different production problems still remain. At the same time, it will be observed that common marketing and administrative policies may be applied to advantage. Similar conditions should also be found in the Gold Dust and Standard Brand combinations.7 

Again, in the combination of the American Radiator and the Standard Sanitary Companies, the major economy to be achieved was in the process of distribution. Since both companies manufacture products for the building trade, it was quite convenient to offer customers sanitary equipment as well as heating apparatus. Also on the production side, savings may be realized by the purchase of common metals on a larger scale or by introducing common methods of administration. For similar reasons, the Remington-Rand Corporation and the 

Underwood-Elliott-Fisher Company should be able to offer their cus tomers a well-rounded line of office equipment instead of a single major appliance. Typewriters, adding machines, bookkeeping machines, and similar equipment require specialized, educated salesmen and trained service men. Hence, it is undoubtedly cheaper to sell and service this type of equipment on a complete-line basis instead of concentrating on a single product. Integration Quite frequently the term integration is used generally to cover both the horizontal and vertical types of combinations. Horizontal 

7 Occasionally, two competing organizations will combine certain common phases of operation to procure the benefits of large-scale operation. Illustrative of this, Richard Hellman, Inc., controlled by General Foods Corporation, was united with Best Foods, Inc., a subsidiary of Gold Dust Corporation. The combination made the concern the largest producer of salad dressing in the United States,

combinations as discussed above are those arising out of merging operations of concerns having similar products. Vertical combination, on the other hand, is a form of organization which brings together under common management various companies which produce goods having a supplementary relationship. Properly speaking, integration means a co-ordination, fitting together, or summation of effort. Similarly, when used in a business sense, integration means a linking of successive steps or products which are found necessary in the production of goods or services. The process of combination involved here may function in two ways: (1) The post-extension of activities where the initiating company endeavors to get nearer to the consumer, and (2) the ante-extension of operations wherein the activities are extended backwards toward the source of raw materials. 

In the first of these plans, the company may wish to attain more effective control of the steps between itself and the ultimate consumption of its product. Manufacturers often find that when selling through independent distributors or manufacturers who carry on further processes, there is no assurance of maximum development of the interests of the original producer. Indeed, it is likely that middlemen will give first consideration to their own immediate benefits. 

Or it might be considered a form of profitable expansion to grow in a vertical instead of a horizontal manner. Consequently, there have been a number of consolidations where companies absorbed other companies that existed next in the channels of distribution of commodities to the ultimate consumer. For example, Anaconda Copper 

Mining Company absorbed the American Brass Company, and Kennecott Copper Corporation acquired the Pacific Brass Company. In both these cases, it seems apparent that the main objective of the initiating companies was to achieve greater control over the outlet of their products. Instead of stopping with the refining of copper, the next phase of operations, the production of brass and brass products, is entered into.

A few companies have extended their operations even further, reaching down to the final retail transaction made with the consumer. 

Examples are Richman Clothing Company, Singer Sewing Machine 

Company, Real Silk Hosiery Products Company, and the big office appliance concerns which sell both through their own retail outlets and through local retailers.

Integration of the ante-extension type provides greater control

over the supply of raw material, the processes of production and the means of transporting the products. Prominent examples of this form of integration are United States Steel Corporation, General 

Motors Corporation, Ford Motor Company, and United States Rub ber Company. Thus, the United States Steel Corporation has extensive holdings of iron ore reserves; large coal and coke properties; several railroad and water transportation companies engaged in the transportation of raw materials to the mills; a large number of plants engaged in the production of steel in nearly all its forms (pig iron, steel ingots, wire, tubes, pipe, structural steel, etc.); natural gas properties; and others.

Combination of Companies Producing Unlike Products 

On occasions there may be combinations of companies producing unlike articles. In many respects this is well illustrated by the General Motors Corporation. In addition to its major products of automobiles and automobile parts and accessories, it produces electric refrigerators, radios, farm lighting systems, diesel engines, etc. There is little basic connection between these products, and perhaps their combination has been made possible only because of the decentralized type of management used by General Motors Corporation, wherein great responsibility is placed upon each unit. As a general rule, combination of unlike units is unsound because it fails to permit the usual advantages offered by large-scale operation. The advantages of specialization are reduced and management effort is spread too thinly over too varied a group of problems. 

Relation of Consolidation to the Field of Enterprise 

At various times, consolidations have been in favor in all three of the major fields of enterprise. In the railway field, an attempt was made through the Transportation Act of 1920 to force consolidation. This policy was abandoned in 1933, largely due to its complexity and to the unwillingness of strong railroads to consolidate with weaker units.

The movement was especially vigorous in the industrial domain during the boom period of the twenties, but perhaps the most interesting and socially important combination movement is found in the public utility field. It is here that the holding company has been utilized most fully, and through this medium a large number of units are combined under common managerial policy. The scope of

the problem is so far reaching that it constitutes the subject of the next chapter.
