There are many reasons why larger companies have a greater proportion of funded debt in their capital structure, but there can be little dissent from the view that size is one of the factors. As we have shown on previous occasions, larger companies undoubtedly have greater access to money markets than smaller concerns. It should be emphasized that the large companies frequently do not take advantage of this greater opportunity to resort to funded debt, but this is mainly the result of deliberate policy rather than lack of opportunity. 

A review of past consolidations shows the expected variety of results. Some immediately resort to the use of funded debt; others make little change from the prevailing types of securities found in the constituent companies; and there are instances where funded debt has been eliminated. For the sake of illustration, bonds played a prominent part in the initial financing of the United States Steel Corporation; in exact opposite, the merger of Dodge Brothers into the Chrysler Corporation brought about the retirement of the bonded indebtedness of the former within seven years. The National Dairy 

Products Corporation, which pursued a policy of consolidation over a long period of years, has made the use of bonds a regular part of its financial program. 

It cannot be said with certainty that consolidation per se causes the use of funded debt, but it may be reasonably granted that the enlargement of operations arising from consolidation does facilitate its use. Actual resort to the use of bonds will always depend upon specific policy and will likewise be affected by such other factors as: the need for additional capital; the relative cost of different forms of financing; the state of business conditions, etc. With allowance for such variables as these, it may be said that consolidation as a form of organization does tend to exert influence as a financial factor. 

The qualitative results of consolidated operation as compared with those of independent operation are difficult to evaluate. This has been shown in a previous chapter and needs only to be reiterated here. Some consolidations have achieved signal success; others have failed miserably. The financial side probably assumes undue proportions because of its spectacular character and because it is the means of giving expression to the changes which occur. In the end, however,

large-scale consolidation will be judged in the light of the larger, ultimate objectives. Such conditions as the centralization of business authority, the concentration of industry and numerous other social aspects may be expected to exert the usual inexorable pressures of long-term development. Indeed, there are signs that the decentralization of industry may already be under way.

PART VII FAILURE AND REORGANIZATION

CHAPTER XXXIV  

HIS chapter and the three following chapters deal with a less happy phase of corporate life, namely, the breakdown and overhauling of the business machine. Frequently, the need for change comes as a distinct shock to the public, but actually it is logical to expect that the business unit should occasionally need repairs, that at times it should be torn down and rebuilt, and sometimes that it should be completely junked. While this statement is applicable in both the physical and financial sense, the present analy- Isis will be limited to the latter. However, it is important not to overlook the inevitable relationship between physical and financial factors. 

Physical or operating difficulties are often the cause of financial adjustment, and vice versa, financial complications may lead to a serious derangement of the physical machine. For instance, the sudden obsolescence of a factory unit or a physical accident, such as fire or flood, might force financial readjustments in order to obtain funds for the replacement of the property. On the other hand, financial pressure may lead to deferred maintenance or be the cause of postponing the purchase of necessary machinery. Either practice may result in a serious disorganization of the physical side of the business unit. 

Effect of Failure on Economic Welfare 

In considering business failure, it is desirable to distinguish at the outset between the effects on the individual company and on the whole economy. As to the former, there is usually a response on the part of the individual interests affected to avoid liquidation at all costs. In short, it is felt that failure should be avoided like a plague. 

People lose their jobs and investors are likely to suffer loss; it is not surprising, therefore, that desperate efforts are made to extend the life of the enterprise. This response is perfectly human and natural, but it has all the weakness of subjective judgment and friendly interest.

Obviously, any economic system in a democratic society must give proper recognition to human welfare, but at the same time the 685

welfare of the whole must always take precedence over individual interests. Viewed in this larger perspective, it is conceivable that failure may contribute to the social good by eliminating inefficient business units. True, losses would be suffered by the particular interests affected, but offsetting gains in the form of lower prices and improved quality of product should be passed along to the general public. Moreover, the investors suffering loss would at least have the benefit and certainty of realistic accounting instead of having their funds tied up without return for an extended period of time. 

Those were the harsh virtues of competition which were presumed to function in behalf of the public welfare. 

In taking stock of the possible social benefits of failure, there is no intention to convey the thought that failure, per se, is good. Much depends upon the causes of failure and whether or not it can be avoided by sound means. Liquidation is usually destructive of economic morale, and where it can be prevented on a sound basis, there is avoidance of the destructive loss of public confidence. Indeed, failure on a large scale may lead to crises which decimate the standard of living and jar the foundations of social law and order. Such was the case in the early thirties when widespread unemployment made it impossible for large segments of our population to make a living. 

Also, the wholesale closing of banks stifled the flow of money and credit which is so essential to the conduct of business. As a result, there was an appeal to the federal government by consumer and business interests alike to relieve the distress. 

Results of the Early Thirties

The distress of the early thirties brought sharply into relief the public interest in the business system. There was common recognition of the fact that the latter must provide for the orderly process of day-to-day living. Hence, when business failed to recover sufficiently to provide full employment, drastic measures of relief by the federal government were introduced. The scope of this broad program of governmental assistance is beyond the confines of this volume, but it is pertinent to note at this time that much was done to relieve financial failure. The Home Owners' Loan Corporation was organized to refinance distressed home owners, and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation came to the rescue of financial and business institutions.1 

1 See chapter XVIII for discussion of the activities of the latter.

The governmental lending agencies, for the most part, did not proceed to eliminate all liquidation; instead, the liquidation of business concerns in an incurable state was facilitated. At the same time, loans and other assistance were extended to institutions which were deemed to be sound and which had reasonable prospects of recovery. 

These underlying criteria apply equally to operations under private management; in short, liquidation should be undertaken realistically where the existing set-up is basically unsound, but constructive measures should be adopted to prevent unnecessary failure. With this larger background in mind, attention may now be given to the specific conditions and causes of business failure. 

The Problems of Failure 

The path to business success is not an easy one and as a result failures of business units are common. While the student of finance is primarily interested in the financial aspects of the going concern, there is much to be learned by studying business failures. Failures may be studied to advantage from three angles: (1) the causes of failures and the obstacles which hinder financial success; (2) the means of preventing or of relieving these obstacles; (3) the process of actually liquidating or of reorganizing a corporation which has failed.

The first two of these problems will be considered in this chapter to be followed by a discussion of the more technical process of reorganization in the next chapters. It should be stressed that the present emphasis is upon the phenomena causing failure or creating the financial difficulties for the business enterprise and not upon the state of failure itself. Viewed from this angle, the following discussion should be equally pertinent to the operation of the solvent, going concern. 

Definition of Failure 

In a broad sense, failure is the opposite of success, and a concern which has not been successful has failed. Such a concept is too vague to be of practical significance because of the obvious fact that there can be gradations in the degree of failure and because of the need for determining when failure has occurred. Thus, a student may be failing a course throughout the entire term of study, but he is not officially charged with failure until his grade is reported. Failure is frequently viewed in a similar light in the field of business so that

the concern which does not make a profit is not necessarily regarded as failing. Instead, the official or publicly accepted test of failure is whether or not a company can pay its debts. Whenever a company is unable to do so, failure must be recognized, but of course the condition of failure has usually existed for some time prior to the acknowledgment of the fact. Another test which is used to determine whether or not a formal state of failure exists is that of the relationship between the assets and liabilities. Whenever the assets are insufficient to meet all liabilities, a condition of insolvency has developed, and proper legal action may be invoked to bring about a state of official failure.

Causes of Failure 

It is not easy to isolate with exactness the causes of failure in any individual instance. Frequently, a combinatiion of circumstances has persisted over an extended period of time, which makes it difficult to separate the immediate from the ultimate, or the superficial from the fundamental causes. Effects are also often misinterpreted as causes. Thus, a shortage of capital is commonly cited as a cause of failure, but actually this may be simply the result of more deep-seated conditions. Certain causes stand out, however, and are of sufficient importance to discuss individually. In summarized form the causes of failure (or the obstacles to success) may be said to consist of: (1) competition, (2) the business cycle, (3) changing public demand, (4) acts of God, (5) acts of government, (6) deficient management. Competition

In terms of business philosophy, competition is often regarded as a spur to success, the life of trade, and as a source of rivalry which adds to the vitality of business conduct. It is presumed that sound and progressive management should be able to compete successfully for a fair share of the available business. Such is the general dogma which is advanced in the abstract, but it is often denied in concrete and specific application. Indeed, it is not uncommon for the practical business man to ascribe failure to relentless competitive pressure and to explain that he was "forced out of business." 1 Although competition is thus cited as a cause of failure, its influence is usually more incidental than fundamental. Poor management, inadequate or improper financing, and other more deep-seated

factors are likely to be the real causes which put the concern in the position of being unable to compete successfully. Of course, it is possible to conceive of cases where competition has been carried beyond the bounds of reason, and disastrous results are the outcome. 

The spectacular struggle between railroads in the latter part of the nineteenth century is an instance of this. Rates between competitive points were cut with little regard to costs, while unreasonably high rates were charged at non-competitive points in an effort to recoup the losses. But even here, the cutthroat competition of the railroads was actuated by an overexpansion in transportation facilities, and the results were affected by the operation of the law of decreasing costs. 

Bearing in mind that normal competition is an immediate rather than an ultimate cause of failure, a more realistic picture of the operation of this force upon business enterprise may be constructed. 

In general, there are two ways for a business concern to solve the problem of competition. One is through consolidation, thereby avoiding the conflict of business battle, and the other is by actually trying to meet it. Stated in modernistic terms, the choice seems to lie between some form of appeasement and rigorous pursuit of aggressive action.

The first of these methods is well illustrated in the absorption of the Auto-strop Safety Razor Company by the Gillette Safety Razor 

Company. The Gillette Company had been first on the business scene with a safety razor well protected by basic patents. The company enjoyed a rapid growth and a high return upon investment because of its monopolistic position. About the time the Gillette patents expired, the Auto-strop Company entered the market with a new product which was highly salable, protected by patents, and as a result constituted a definite obstacle to the future life of the Gillette Company. In addition, the Auto-strop Company developed a patented process for making superior blades for the Gillette razor. The success of the Auto-strop razor as well as its process for making blades for the Gillette Razor is demonstrated by the reported earnings. During the nine months ended September, 1930, the Auto-strop

Safety Razor Company earned $16.13 per share of Class A stock which compared with $8.68 for a similar period during the preceding year. On the other hand, the Gillette Safety Razor Company earned only $4.42 per share in 1929 and $3.46 per share for all of 1930. 

Under the circumstances, it is apparent that the Gillette Com-

pany had to meet the problem of competition, and in view of the patent protection held by the Auto-strop Company, the former adopted the peaceful process of buying out the competitor. At the same time, it was compelled to favor its competitor in the merger process by exchanging convertible preferred stock on a share for share basis for both the Class A and Class B stocks of Auto-strop. This exchange gave the stockholders of the latter company a priority over the Gillette stockholders, and at the same time permitted them to convert their holdings into common stock in the event the merger proved successful. 

Since this merger was effected at the beginning of a major depression, it is difficult to determine the degree of its success. None of the preferred stock has ever been converted into common, and since 1930 the earnings of the merged company have never been as much as $2 per share of common stock. In 1940, for example, the earnings amounted to only $0.55 a share. The present Gillette capitalization is represented by approximately 2,000,000 shares of common and by 300,000 shares of $5 convertible preferred. The preferred dividend requirements are $1,500,000 annually. This means that the common stock would have an additional $0.75 per share of earnings available for dividends if there were no preferred stock and if earnings would be as great without the assets acquired through the issuance of the preferred stock. Therefore, it seems probable that the present low level of Gillette earnings is due to the presence of other competitors manufacturing razors and blades and to the introduction of the electric shaver.

In the event competition is actually met, it is not uncommon for a number of failures to appear among the weaker firms. Illustrations of this are abundant. As mentioned earlier, only about 10 per cent of the automobile companies which have been organized in the history of the industry are still actively engaged in operations. The disappearance of the remaining 90 per cent should not be entirely attributed to competition, although this has been a factor. In recent years, competition has been keen in the rubber and tire industry and earnings of all the companies in this field have been materially affected. 

The death toll of competition is particularly apparent in the retail field. Here conditions for entry into business are not as exacting. Only small capital investments are required, and almost anyone with a small amount of money can attempt to go into business for himself. As a result, numerous incompetents appear in the field,

and the number of failures is large. However, it should be emphasized that these failures are only partially due to competition and that ability, or rather lack of it, plays the greater part. In fact, there is a direct relationship between the ease of entering a business and the number of failures among the new enterprisers. 

The Business Cycle 

The nature of the business cycle was discussed in a preceding chapter, and statistics were given as to the extent of business failures. 

Business fatalities occur in surprising numbers every year, but are aggravated by recurring depressions. The conditions generated by a general business depression test the best of firms, although the actual undermining of financial soundness usually commences during some preceding phase of the cycle. Loose credit policies during the upswing, unwise stocking of inventories, undue expansion, etc., all tend to result in a financial state that may prove fatal. 

Analysis of cyclical influence shows marked variation in its effect on different types of industry. Individual industries are affected frequently by factors which are peculiar to themselves and which are not necessarily related to the business cycle. The flour milling business necessarily is influenced by the wheat market where climatic and numerous other phenomena determine the trend. The same is true of the container industry, although the extended diversification prevailing in this field has tended to give considerable relief. This diversification is true both as to the type of products for which containers are produced, as well as the geographical distribution of plants. 

Turning to areas which do not relate to agriculture, both the oil and copper industries have been bothered with overproduction which is more especially an industry rather a cyclical attendant. The rubber and tire industry is even more illustrative of isolated disruptions. In addition to the keen competition prevailing, the price of rubber has fluctuated considerably during the past two decades: for instance, it went from $1.04 per pound in November, 1925, to $0.16 in December, 1929. Consequently, while most other business concerns were enjoying the business boom of 1929, the rubber and tire companies were suffering declining earnings or actual losses. A reversal of this trend was witnessed when the price reached a high of $0.15 per pound in August, 1934, to give an average 1934 price of $0.129, in contrast with $0.059, the average price in 1933.

The potency of the business cycle as a cause of failure is modified further by the type of product. It is much more significant for concerns engaged in the production of raw materials than those dealing in finished products. Concerns having to carry large inventories subject to great price fluctuations are more adversely affected than companies engaged in an industry where small stocks are necessary. 

Necessity goods and services show greater resistance to depression than the so-called luxury category. 

How suddenly a firm may be engulfed by the business cycle is well illustrated by the failure of the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company in 1920. For the preceding twelve consecutive years, the volume of the company's business had shown a consistent increase, and in addition the company had not suffered a deficit since 1903. Yet, in the short space of a few months in 1920, the company was reduced to a state of failure. The story is graphically told in the words of the 

For the first six months of the period the volume of business was running 59 per cent greater than for the same period the year before, with the demand upon us for product beyond our ability to supply. This entailed financial requirements far beyond normal and your Directors decided to offer to stockholders two shares of preferred and one of common at par, selling thereby $27,794,700. 

At the time it was anticipated that this would afford the necessary relief to carry on our business successfully, but by Midsummer the buying demand fell off sharply, and with the accumulation of raw materials and finished product, our financial position became acute, necessitating an arrangement for some temporary financing, which was accomplished by providing in new money and extension of bank paper $28,800,000 maturing February 15th, 1921, with the expectation that permanent financing would be accomplished prior to said maturity which program is now being worked out. 

The process of readjustment and deflation affecting all lines of industry has been especially severe to the rubber industry, the raw materials-both rubber and fabric-having in a few months dropped in value over 50 per cent; and as inventories have been written down by the auditors to adjust to that condition, not only is our former surplus absorbed, but a deficit of $15,647,653.56 is shown. 

Future contracts have not been taken into consideration in this statement. 

Imagine one of the large companies in the United States with a surplus of $33,332,666 as of October, 1920, and at the end of the following year reporting a deficit of $15,647,634! This represents a loss of $48,980,300 in the fourteen months' period. The change was so drastic and sudden that it is almost unbelievable. In the later reor- 

2 Annual Report for Year Ended October 31, 1920.

ganization, the deficit was eliminated and since that time the concern has failed to show a net profit in only one year. It had a loss of $850,000 in 1932, but reported a net profit of over $4,000,000 in 1933, and of nearly $11,000,000 in 1936. 

The Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company was but one of many affected by the business depression commencing in 1920. Although 

Montgomery Ward and Company did not fail, it did prove wise to effect certain changes in the capitalization as a result of the depression. 

The company had shown increasing net earnings for an extended period, but a slight decline appeared in 1919. This was followed by losses in both 1920 and 1921. The bulk of the loss in the former year was mainly the result of a depreciation of $5,174,435 in the value of inventories. These losses had the effect of eliminating a surplus of approximately $12,000,000 that existed at the end of 1919, and causing a deficit of about $7,700,000 to appear as of December 31, 1921. This deficit was erased early in 1922 by means of a change in the plan of capitalization drastically lowering the stated value of the common stock and creating a capital surplus. 

Business enterprise is so vitally affected by the business cycle that possible preventive measures must be reviewed carefully. In the preceding discussion it was pointed out that the trouble really develops in the period of prosperity instead of depression. Hence, primary relief is to be found in enforcing the necessary restrictions during this period of boom. Sound purchasing policies, careful granting of credit, engaging in only legitimate and conservative expansion-these and similar policies achieve the desired protection. Most of these practices will characterize good management because of constant and careful analysis of current business conditions, thereby permitting intelligent forecasts of developments.

In addition to this major relief program, the development of a strong surplus or proprietary position is needed. Instead of disposing of the greater share of earnings realized in the prosperity stage by increased dividend disbursements, advantage will be taken of the opportunity to improve materially the net worth position. Not only does such action facilitate later borrowing, but it also provides a cushion to absorb the losses of depression. Because fluctuation of inventory values often seriously affects earnings, some concerns establish a reserve to cover this contingency. All of these various methods serve to illustrate that the best way to prepare for a business depression is to get ready in the period of prosperity.

Changing Public Demand 

When the demand of the public for the commodity of a particular company changes, it may usually be attributed to competition or to the business cycle. On other occasions, the change in demand may be the outcome of a definite shift or change in public preferences. It is not uncommon to find products occupying the pinnacle of public favor at one moment, only to be relegated to a forgotten or "has-been" state within a comparatively short time. The latter type of change in demand constitutes a serious problem for business management, and frequently is fatal to the business enterprise. While advertising may be invoked as a relief, this expedient usually proves to be totally inadequate if the demand has definitely shifted. It is true that advertising has a decided influence upon the types of products consumed, but it cannot successfully restore a product which the public does not want. Instead, it is generally necessary to change or to improve the product, or in some instances it may actually prove wise to abandon the field. On other occasions, relief may be sought by adding additional products.

In this connection the case of the Victor Talking Machine Company may be reviewed briefly. This company had a record of long standing, and its success was notable. A summary of its dividend disbursements provides convenient evidence of the company's record: 

1901-11, inclusive, 6 per cent annually 1912-14, inclusive, 10 per cent annually 1915-19, inclusive, 20 per cent annually 

January-April, 1920, 5 per cent quarterly 

July, 1920-January, 1921, inclusive, 15 per cent quarterly 

April, 1921-October, 1922, inclusive, 10 per cent quarterly 

January, 1923-April, 1925, inclusive, 2 per cent quarterly

In addition to these regular cash dividends numerous extras were paid, and in November, 1922, a 600 per cent stock dividend was paid. 

Allowing for this adjustment, dividends from January, 1923, to April, 1925, were equivalent to 12 per cent quarterly on the old stock. Dividends were then discontinued in 1925. 

The termination of this long and notable dividend record is well worth analysis. In 1924, the gross sales of the company declined approximately $7,000,000 as compared with the previous year. In 1925, the reduction was even more severe, total sales being less than onehalf of the sales for 1923. These declines were undoubtedly the result

of the introduction of the radio and the lack of marked phonograph improvements. To meet these circumstances, the company introduced its orthophonic Victrola and Electrola in the latter part of 1925, and the orthophonic Victor record in the fall of 1926. Favorable results were almost immediate, as is indicated by the fact that the sales of the company more than doubled in 1926, and probably were the greatest in the history of the company. Again in 1927, a slight increase appeared in the sales volume, and dividend payments were resumed with an initial declaration of 8 per cent. In January, 1929, the company was taken over by the Radio Corporation of America.

The locomotive industry is another segment of business which has experienced shifting demand. Not only has the serviceability of locomotives been considerably extended by improved construction, but the railroads themselves have developed extensive shop facilities which prolong the life of the locomotives for many years. Highway competition has also reduced the amount of business done by the railroads and consequently their need for locomotives. As a result, the specialized manufacturers of locomotives have been affected quite adversely. Lima Locomotive Works, Incorporated, made profits in only four of the fourteen years between 1927 and 1940. The American Locomotive Company's earnings fluctuated considerably between 1926 and 1940, with large deficits being experienced from 1931 to 1935 and again in 1938 and 1939. Baldwin Locomotive Works had a deficit in every year from 1928 to 1940 except in 1930, 1937, and 1939, when small profits were reported, and 1940 when earnings of $1.75 per share were realized. 

The adoption of a policy favoring greater diversification in product by the Lima Locomotive Works may also be noted as an example of a company which attempts to get relief from changing demand. In the words of the chairman of its board of directors the management has for some time considered the advisability of diversifying its product and to this end acquired during the year the management and ownership of the Ohio Power Shovel Company. The Company is now manufacturing power shovels, cranes, draglines, etc., which are being marketed through the Ohio Power Shovel Company, a subsidiary, under the trade name, the Lima 101.

While this policy was not adopted as the result of a change in public demand, it does represent an effort to meet the consequences of a change in a more specialized market.

The change in demand is so often fatal to the business enterprise that careful attention should be given to the remedies which may be available. If the nature of future trends is appreciated, the company may be able to take steps which will result in at least partial relief. 

Conversely, the appearance of an unexpected condition will usually prove disastrous. Assuming that the management does see the trend of future events, it may liquidate progressively as sales volume tapers off, or it may seek relief by: (1) improving the old product sufficiently to restore its favor; (2) substituting an entirely new line; (3) producing additional products.

Improving the Product 

Frequently, a product may be restored to favor by improving the quality or lowering the price; on the other hand, this may simply prolong the day of reckoning. These tactics were markedly successful in the case of the Victor Talking Machine Company when its phonograph was given a new lease on life by the introduction of the orthophonic principle. Eventually, a more permanent solution was found in combining the phonograph with the radio. However, it is not always possible to improve the product so as to restore its original position. No amount of improvement of the bicycle could have restored the status originally held in the early 1900's, because the introduction of the automobile eliminated much of the need for the bicycle, and a number of bicycle manufacturers failed, as did most buggy manufacturers. To be sure, recent years have seen bicycle unit sales again equal to, or in excess of, those prevailing about 1900, but the bicycle's relation to the total business economy is no longer important. 

Substituting a New Line

Improvement of the product is undoubtedly the first and most logical way to attempt to secure relief from changing public demand because the complete substitution of one line of products for another is a difficult transition. Manufacturing plants are usually so specialized that an abrupt change in product is expensive if not practically impossible. The heavier the industry and the more specialized the machinery, the more difficult it is to make the change. Lighter manufacturing industries using standard machinery and tools are in a better position to convert to another product. However, a new line

should be introduced only after a most careful investigation of the field as well as an exploration of the possible ways of improving the sales of the old product.

An example of a complete change in production, although not for purposes of avoiding failure may be cited. Several years ago Tinnerman Products, Incorporated, was engaged in the business of making stoves. As a means of reducing the cost of assembly and speeding up production, the company evolved a spring-steel stamping which could be used to replace both the usual type of nut and the accompanying lock-washer. The new "speed nut" was so successful and the concern had so many demands for the invention that it finally abandoned the manufacture of stoves and concentrated on making various forms of spring nuts for other manufacturers. Presumably, the profit results have been much more favorable than in the manufacture of · stoves.

Producing Additional Commodities 

Relief is sometimes sought by adding new products and thus securing some of the advantages of greater diversification. This was illustrated by the case of the Lima Locomotive Works just described. 

The value of this plan of relief usually depends upon the relation between the original or major line and the new products added, as well as the market prospects for the latter. It is one of the most attractive means of improving the prospects of the company, but it should be investigated carefully before being adopted. 

The method has been successfully used to reduce the effects of seasonal forces and to obtain greater stability of income from year to year. Recently, the Corn Products Refining Company announced the development of a new plastic, Mazein, derived as a by-product of the corn processing industry. The company stated in its announcement that the product had been developed specifically for the purpose of providing a means of reducing the price of cornstarch in order to meet foreign competition more successfully.³ 

Acts of God 

In the process of business operation there are various obstacles which may not be normally forecasted or even provided for in some instances. These barriers are usually found outside of the economic 

8 Wall Street Journal (March 28, 1940), p. 1.

structure and generally consist of such phenomena as fires, cyclones, earthquakes, etc. In legal terminology, these phenomena have been termed "acts of God." The loss accruing from these disasters is usually sudden and frequently fatal to the enterprise. Because of this, it is essential to give due consideration to the preventive means at hand. 

The most common source of relief from these non-business contingencies is found in insurance, whereby the specific risk is transferred to a community of risks. By this means, the uncertainty of the former is brought under control by pooling the risks so as to ascertain average probabilities. A second channel of relief from various forms of property risk is found in the proper construction and protection of the plant. Buildings may be designed so as to resist the devastating effects of earthquakes, fires, etc. Again, in the case of fire, fire-fighting equipment may prove to be of great assistance. Plants which are engaged in the manufacture of a product which is particularly inflammable may provide special apparatus as a precaution against fire hazards. A third source of protection is provided by the establishment of contingency reserves. Additional assets are thereby automatically retained in the business to provide a greater fund of protection. On the other hand, unless the assets are distributed, they may prove to be of little avail in counteracting the disastrous effects of "acts of God." Instead, it is apparent they may simply add to the total loss.

Acts of Government 

The corporation receives its birthright from the state; in a few instances, some governmental act may spell its death knell. Prohibitive taxation imposed by a government is frequently blamed for business failure. A number of the failures which occurred during the war as well as during the later business depression of 1920 and 1921 were blamed upon heavy federal taxation prevailing throughout this period. While too much stress was probably attached to this contention in many instances, it is true that corporations were deprived of much liquid capital which would otherwise have been available for business purposes. The influence of this factor is probably greatest in the case of those enterprises which are in a marginal position. 

Another policy of government which is likely to have pronounced effect upon business is that relating to tariff revision. Some believe that the long and delayed discussion of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff- Act of 1930 had a reactionary influence upon business because of the

uncertainty it produced. Others are inclined to believe that this act fostered the depression of the 1930's because its unusually high duties reduced foreign trade. There is no question that certain industries and individual enterprises within each industry are greatly affected by tariff changes. Those industries which have considerable foreign competition and which do not enjoy much export business are affected favorably by tariff increases. The dye industry, steel industry, and industries engaged in the production of optical goods and precision instruments are examples of these. On the other hand, concerns which have little or no foreign competition or which are interested in exporting a considerable portion of their products are adversely affected by tariff increases. Tariffs reduce the ability of foreign countries to sell, and to a similar degree they reduce the ability of the foreign country to buy. For this reason, industries, such as the automobile industry, with a large export market and with little foreign competition are inclined to favor low tariffs. 

The effect of court decisions may also be significant. Reinterpretations of existing laws may greatly change the cost of doing business, and other court actions may actually dissolve business enterprises. Examples of the latter are the Supreme Court decrees compelling the dissolution of the Northern Securities Corporation, the Standard Oil Company, and the American Tobacco Company. Decisions of the type which influence the costs or ways of doing business are those dealing with patent cases, trade associations, labor relations, and taxation.

The last few years have brought forth many new and important government reforms for industry. One of the first and perhaps the most important of these was the National Industrial Recovery Act. 

This Act was intended to facilitate industrial recovery, but it is well known that certain industries were affected adversely. Costs were increased on contracts already let with attendant losses to the producing companies. Freedom of management was curtailed and a period of indecision introduced in the business world. The effort to codify industrial relations was especially detrimental to the smaller companies which had previously achieved success primarily through flexibility.

One of the more recent examples of a governmental act of considerable importance to business is the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, better known as the Wages and Hours Act. This law establishes

a maximum number of hours per week and a minimum wage per hour for workers in industries in interstate commerce. While the bulk of American labor is already receiving wages in excess of the minimum prescribed by law and working hours approximating the maximum permitted, the law does introduce certain complications to management in the form of compulsory overtime pay, special reports, and uncertainties of interpretation. Time will probably show a few companies so close to the border line as to be unable to bear added labor costs or any added expenses connected with the adminstration of the law.

Deficient Management 

In a broad sense it may be contended that deficient management is the true cause of all business failures. May not the pitfalls of the business cycle be avoided by conservative and efficient management? 

May not the change in public demand be met sufficiently by management with vision? Is not efficient management well able to meet competition? These questions may easily be answered in the affirmative, and yet such a broad answer imposes a tremendous burden upon the shoulders of management. In fact, it must be admitted that to so charge management is well beyond the bounds of reason. Management is human and subject to error.

Careful analysis of management responsibility calls for distinction between ignorant and negligent management. Both types may be held responsible for poor administration, but there are occasions where it may be unreasonable to expect management to avoid certain business pitfalls. Business is dynamic and forecasting is difficult at best. A review of the forecasts made at the outset of 1930 by specialists in the field would give abundant evidence of the fallibility of man to forecast business conditions. Investors and society in general should therefore hold management responsible only under the following circumstances: (1) where it is negligent in its attempts to find the facts or in its endeavors to attack the problems; (2) where management is ignorant and no effort is made to obtain the desired knowledge.

Management is probably one of the most important factors in successful business operation, but at the same time it is perhaps the most difficult to evaluate or to measure its achievements in any precise fashion. Undoubtedly, many business failures are the result of poor

management but are attributed to other conditions. A shortage of capital is often advanced as a cause of failure, although careful study of the case generally reveals that this deficiency is usually precipitated by more fundamental causes. Often, the failure occurs because the management has unwisely invested the available capital, or because it failed to budget properly the available funds. At other times, a severe decline in inventory prices is set forth as the cause of failure; it is equally evident that shrewd management should be prepared for this emergency.

The degree with which management may be charged with failure is largely a matter of opinion. The most usual test applied to measure the performance of management is results of past operations. 

Where this record is both long and satisfactory, the management is generally admitted to be capable. On the other hand, conditions change so rapidly that ability which had been demonstrated as capable of meeting past events may prove totally inadequate for new and more complex conditions. In view of the many uncertainties and the lack of specific means of measurement, management will probably continue to be excused for many of its deficiencies. 

There is one type of managerial deficiency, however, which is universally subject to condemnation-the commitment of frauduent acts. It is difficult to appraise the relative significance of this factor as a cause of failure, but it is probably more important than is commonly realized. The defalcations of lesser employees are usually too small to provoke failure, but those of key officials may be sufficiently large as to cause trouble. Especially is the latter true of smaller companies where the fraudulent act may mean the discharge of the entire management in addition to the loss of a large proportion of the assets. Occasionally, large companies with nation-wide dealings may also fail on this account, a recent example being the 

McKesson-Robbins Company.

CHAPTER XXXV EARLIER REORGANIZATION AND SOME QUESTIONS AS TO PRACTICES 

F EVER security holders display an active interest in the corporation of which they may be owners or creditors, it is during a period of reorganization. When a corporation is operating successfully and is meeting its interest and dividend requirements promptly, the attention of its security holders is frequently lost in the haze of contentment. Reorganization is generally sufficient to restore consciousness, although not altogether of the orderly variety. 

The security holder is bewildered by his new predicament. His faith is changed to doubt, and he may wonder whether or not he should agree to proposed organization plans. In fact, he may have difficulty in understanding all of the many details involved. Under these conditions, it is most essential that order and confidence be restored. 

This is usually accomplished by the appointment of a trustee or receiver by a court of law to operate the company, and at the same time by allowing the proper machinery of reorganization to get into action.

Justification for Reorganization 

When a corporation fails, its reorganization should not be taken for granted. There are numerous cases where concerns should be allowed to pass out of existence. Errors are made in promoting business enterprises the same as in any walk of life, and it is wise to eliminate them as promptly and efficiently as possible. Under what conditions should a company in a state of failure be reorganized instead of being exterminated? In general, restorative proceedings are warranted whenever the following conditions exist: (1) There is a continued need for the product or service of the company. (2) 

Operation of the company on an efficient and profitable basis is thought to be possible.

In the case of public service enterprises, there is some danger of minimizing the importance of the second factor and of giving consideration only to the first requirement. Once established, utility 704

EARLIER REORGANIZATION 

705 projects are generally deemed to be necessary for the public welfare, and ways and means are provided to permit or to force their continued existence. However, in the strictly private enterprise category, the accepted method for determining need is the ability of the enterprise to obtain a cost-covering price for its services. If this is impossible to do with good management, the need is deemed to be insufficient and the service should be discontinued. 

The reorganization of a company is further encouraged by the apparent economy it affords. The liquidation of a company which has failed reduces its values to a minimum, and the sacrifices required are apt to be burdensome for the creditors and owners. As a result, the various claimants are likely to go the limit in favor of reorganization. The extent to which such claimants will go depends primarily upon the sacrifice they would suffer in the event of liquidation. From an economic point of view, there may be further loss arising from the destruction of intangible items such as good-will and going-concern value. The establishment of a company as a functioning enterprise involves much time, effort, and expense, and its abolition should be done only after careful study.

Anticipation of Failure Neither is the failure of an enterprise as abrupt or sudden as the investor sometimes believes. The investor is apt to register greater surprise at the news of discontinued interest payments or other evidences of failure, but this is because he has neglected to follow the company when it is working smoothly. On the contrary, the management usually sees the storm coming and is able to time its fury accordingly. The banker is consulted, and other things are put in order in preparation for the coming period of convalescence or ultimate demise.

The procedure of reorganization is rather technical in character, much of it being burdened with legal procedure and details. In analyzing this reorganization process, our primary interest is not in the technique involved. That is the work of the specialist and does not concern the general student of corporation finance. At the same time, it must be remembered that the operation of this legal machinery has great influence upon the investor and the public generally. 

For this reason, it is necessary to acquire an understanding of the reorganization process.

Nature of Reorganization Process prior to 1933 In recent years, there has been considerable revamping of the reorganization procedure, but the basic changes may be comprehended only by having an understanding of the earlier system. Moreover, much of the original pattern is still in vogue, and the revisions have significance more particularly in their effects on the powers of parties in interest and in the greater scope of supervision by the courts and the Securities and Exchange Commission. In essence, reorganizations prior to 1933 were effected through an equity receivership where the properties of the distressed company were transferred to a new corporation by a foreclosure sale. The equity receivership is still legal, but it is no longer in common use as a vehicle of reorganization. 

Appointment of the Receiver Failure gives rise to numerous conflicts of interest among the various creditors and owners, and creates a situation where it is highly important that the company be placed in the hands of some nonpartisan but competent party. Under the old receivership plan, such independent administration was obtained by the appointment of a receiver by the proper court.¹ The receiver is endowed with special authority permitting various priorities and privileges which are intended to aid in the rehabilitation of operations. For example, he may raise capital by issuing receivers' certificates having prior lien over all other obligations, or at least those in default. Again, the claims of the old creditors of the company may be relegated to a junior position, thereby permitting the receiver to buy new materials and supplies more favorably. The receiver, however, has no functional responsibility in working out a plan of reorganization. His job is mainly one of placing the firm on an efficient operating basis and of preserving the property of the company for the various claimants. 

Protective Committees 

As the name suggests, protective committees are intended to represent and to protect the rights and interests of the various groups of security holders. Recent reforms have greatly affected the powers and practices of these committees, but under the old system they played a vital and active role in determining the plan of reorganization. 

These committees, by means of formal agreements with creditor and 1 Federal courts were favored when the enterprise was engaged in interstate commerce.

EARLIER REORGANIZATION 

707 investor interests, had virtually all the rights of a true security holder. 

This may be seen in the following typical statement of their broad powers of attorney:

Each and every Depositor for himself and not for any other, does hereby, and by the deposit of Bonds hereunder shall be deemed to sell, assign, transfer and deliver to the Committee as from time to time, constituted, its successor and assigns, absolutely, each and every Bond deposited hereunder by him, and all his right, title and interest, at law or in equity, in and to the same, and also all his right, title, interest property and claim at law or in equity by virtue of said Bonds or the Indenture or other instrument securing the same or otherwise, in and to the property and assets of the Railway Company . . . .² 2 The organization of protective committees is largely the result of self-interest, and any group of investors is free to act. Since the committees are not officially appointed by the corporation or by reason of legal requirement, it would seem that some stimulus is necessary to secure prompt action. Actually, the necessary initiative is usually provided by large security holders with sufficient amounts at stake to warrant an expenditure of money to protect their existing investment. Also bankers who have previously underwritten the defaulted issues or who are in search of new business readily assume the task of committee organization. As a result of such sponsorship, select groups or other inside interests are usually in a position to control the plan of reorganization under equity receivership proceedings. 

Reorganization Committees 

As the term protective committee implies, its major objective is to protect rather than to reorganize the company. Of course, the protection may be achieved through reorganization, but there are usually too many committees to accomplish this easily or successfully. It is necessary to concentrate the work of reorganization, and this is accomplished by the creation of a reorganization committee frequently consisting of representatives selected from each of the leading protective committees. By this process differences in opinion and of interest on the part of holders of the various security issues are ironed out before the formulation of the reorganization plan. Closely allied with the activities of this committee are the bankers who will underwrite 

2 Bondholders' Protective Agreement of the Seaboard Air Line Railway Company dated 

January 31, 1931.

the new securities to be floated in connection with the reorganization. 

Occasionally, the bankers may be appointed as reorganization managers and allowed to conduct the arbitrations and other details necessary to the formation of a reorganization plan. While banker interest is necessary for a successful reorganization, extreme domination may operate to the detriment of the investors.

Making the Plan of Reorganization Effective 

The final step under the old equity receivership plan was to make the plan of reorganization effective. This called for court approval of the fairness of the plan and usually required a foreclosure sale for the purpose of transferring the property from the old to the newly organized company. The sale of the corporate property under foreclosure was usually a matter of formality because new and independent interests were practically estopped by the heavy cash requirements for purchase. On the other hand, those in control of the reorganization were able to settle largely in the form of securities of the old corporation. Dissenting interests were paid in cash, but they were necessarily in the minority, or otherwise the plan of reorganization could not be considered successful. 

Investigation of Reorganization Practices The domination of inside interests under the equity receivership plan of reorganization is readily apparent, and it was inevitable that the entire arrangement should come under the scrutiny of the sweeping reform movement which began in the early thirties. No attempt is made here to pass judgment on the merits of the old system, but at the same time, there is need to observe its workings and especially in the light of the official investigations which were made. As background for our observations, the reports of the Securities and Exchange Commission covering the activities of protective and reorganization committees offer voluminous and illuminating facts. These studies of the Commission were made pursuant to Section 211 of the Securities Act as amended by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. Through hearings, various persons had an opportunity to relate the facts pertaining to specific cases as well as to express their opinion as to the propriety of the actions taken. By this means, a moving and realistic 8 S.E.C.

, Report on the Study and Investigation of the Work, Activities, Personnel and 

Functions of Protective and Reorganization Committees, Parts I-VII, 1936–39.

EARLIER REORGANIZATION 

709 picture of the internal structure of reorganization is painted. As a result, an unusual opportunity is afforded to check principles in the light of practice, and vice versa.

Analysis of Reorganization Practices 

To bring the area of investigation into focus, a brief summary of the more important practices which are found in corporate reorganizations may be noted. These may be grouped into the following categories: (1) development of committee support, (2) remuneration of committee and reorganization officials, (3) "making the market," (4) activities to preserve old management, (5) promotion of banker interests.

Development of Committee Support 

To be successful, protective committees must first marshal the support of the holders of securities they wish to represent. Attention has already been called to the fact that anyone is free to organize a protective committee whether he is a security holder or not, but the influence of any group is necessarily determined by its backing. This explains the urgency of sanction and of delegation of authority by security holders. Organization and various tactics play a large part in accomplishing this indorsement. Under the circumstances, professional groups with experience have a decided advantage over lessorganized and inexperienced minority interests. 

Contact with security holders may be attempted through advertising, but this is slow, expensive, and uncertain. A much more effective medium is by means of prepared lists. The preparation of such a schedule is comparatively simple as to stockholders since, for the most part, they are of record. Moreover, in most states, stockholders have access to the records of a corporation by express right. It is more difficult to construct an accurate and comprehensive list of the bondholders. Identification of ownership is readily available in the case of registered bonds, but these usually represent only a small fraction of the total outstanding. Various sources are combed to obtain a list of the holders of coupon bonds, particular use being made of information held by paying agents and selling groups. Under regulations of the Bureau of Internal Revenue, certificates of ownership must be filed when interest coupons are presented for payment, thereby enabling agents of disbursement to compile a list, It is not accurate in

every respect because banks, brokers, and other collecting agencies may appear as the owners instead of the individuals for whom the coupons are cashed.

Availability of Lists of Security Holders 

Another question is the availability of these lists for general distribution. It is contended that authority to direct the release of the lists rests with the principal, i.e., the company issuing the securities. 

Under these conditions, it is obvious that committees representing management interests would have a decided advantage over outside or minority groups. The following testimony taken from the hearings conducted by the Securities and Exchange Commission express the opinions of several witnesses which are of interest: A. may suggest there that the method of advertising for the bondholders' names is highly expensive and unsatisfactory. I do not think any bondholders' committee can obtain the best results or best protect the interests of the bondholders unless it is able to obtain such a list of names. 

Q. Wouldn't you, from your experience in this field, Mr. Coyle, know that the so-called independent committee was pretty much at the mercy of the person who had possession of the bondholders' list? 

A. Yes, sir. Its work is seriously handicapped unless it obtains that list.*

A counsel of a financial institution which had refused to furnish an independent committee with a list testified as follows:

Q. Wouldn't you consider it extremely essential to the constitution of a Committee to have access to a bondholders' list in an issue like this? 

A. I should consider it helpful. 

Q. Wouldn't you consider it a great disadvantage if it did not have a list, if it had to rely upon newspaper advertising? 

A. In competition with another Committee, yes, sir." 

Deposit of Securities

The preparation of a list of security holders is but the first step in the enlistment of their support. The vital link is to be found in the deposit of the securities so that full proxy powers may be established in favor of the committee. Earlier in this chapter, it was pointed out 

4 S.E.C., Report on the Study and Investigation of the Work Activities, Personnel and Functions of Protective and Reorganization Committees, Part I, "Strategy and Techniques ol 

Protective and Reorganization Committees,” p. 410. 

Ibid., p. 410,

EARLIER REORGANIZATION 

711 that deposit agreements usually endow the committee with virtually all the rights of the original owner. It is for this reason that campaigns with much of the pressure of community chest drives take place. Unfortunately, few investors appreciate the force, and often irrevocable character, of deposit agreements. A signature on the dotted line accomplishes ready acquiescence on their part, but withdrawal from the contract is not so easily achieved. In many instances, drastic penalties serve as a barrier to withdrawal, while in other cases it may be a legal impossibility.

In the reorganization of the Cuba Cane Sugar Corporation in 192930, the assent of the security holders was sought in support of a voluntary plan in order to avoid a receivership. However, "depositing security holders were not permitted to withdraw their securities when the receivership was instituted." This refusal stands in great contrast to the spirit of the appeal for committee support, as shown in the following statements from various circulars which were sent out: 

Prompt and practically unanimous assent to the Plan is essential to avoid receivership.

Bondholders who prefer the Plan to a long and expensive receivership must DEPOSIT NOW. 

If, however, receivership is to be avoided, security holders must, with substantial unanimity, promptly assent to the Plan. .. 

If receivership is to be averted, you must act promptly. You are strongly urged in your own interest to execute immediately the enclosed Proxy, Agreement and Consent 

State of Mind of Investors

Security holders are naturally quite perplexed as to what course of action to pursue. Refusal to deposit may place them in the position. of being outcasts without anyone to champion their cause or to act in behalf of their rights. On the other hand, indorsement of a particular protective committee has many of the earmarks of signing a blank check. With such conflicting emotions, the uncertainty often leads to a state of indifference or inertia on the part of investors. It seems to be a case of tweedledee or tweedledum. To overcome the * Ibid., pp. 318-19,

indecision, committees resort to various enticements to attract support. 

Typical arguments used may be classified as follows:7 

1. Services rendered.-Emphasis is placed upon activities in behalf of depositors which are not available to non-depositors, such as filing proof of claim, protection of investors' rights, etc. 

2. Threats and discriminations.-Attention is called to potential losses which may be caused by failure to deposit or to possible refusal to pay interest coupons except on bonds which are deposited as well as to use various other pressure tactics. Where voluntary reorganization is anticipated, the potential losses usually associated with receivership are given prominence. 

3. Marketability of certificates of deposit.-At times, committees move to effect the delisting of the primary obligations and to arrange for the listing of the certificates of deposit. In one case, the cost of more than $5,000 for listing the certificates of deposit was allowed by the court, necessarily forcing the non-depositors to share this burden. 

4. Time limits for deposits. It is customary to limit the period during which deposits may be made. Security holders are then impressed with the urgency of deposit if they are to participate in the benefits made available by committee action.

Committee Representation 

Of vital interest to the security holders is the question of committee representation. It is likely the key in developing investor confidence and committee following. Ideally, bona fide and representative security holders would seem to have first call, but there are difficulties in putting this into practice. This may be noted in the following testimony in the hearings held by the Commission: 

Q. Do you feel that the actual owners of a security should be the members of the committee wherever possible? A. I think it very important that as large a representation of actual owners should actually serve on the committee as can be found willing to give the time and attention to it. However, it is not always true that those actual owners have the technical knowledge or financial experience to enable them to function successfully in working out a reorganization plan without legal and banking assistance. 

7 Ibid., pp. 506-65.

EARLIER REORGANIZATION 

713 Q. In other words, protective committees are for the purpose of protecting actual owners, and as such they should wherever possible be formed by or composed of actual owners of the securities. Would you subscribe to that?

A. Yes, I would subscribe to it, with the possible qualification that the issuing house ought to accept their share of the responsibility for the working out of the situation. 

Q. But only where the stockholders want them to? 

A. Absolutely.Ⓡ

The following facts based upon questionnaires sent by the Commission to committees representing 1,284 issues reveal more pointedly the composition of committee personnel. In 295 issues, or 22.9 per cent of the total, neither individual nor institutional security holders were represented. Of the remaining 989 issues, the representation of security holders consisted of less than a majority in 353 cases. If "only persons directly owning the securities are counted, committees for 782 issues, or 60.9 per cent, did not include a single security holder."

Amount and Fairness of Compensation for Committee Officials 

In analyzing the compensation paid for various services rendered incident to reorganization, probably the chief criteria are the amount and the fairness. Often the total may appear small in comparison with the size of the company but an individual item in favor of a specific advisory firm may appear to be excessive. Particularly is this true of counsel fees which frequently amount to the largest single item. In two cases upon which the Commission held hearings, the fees for legal counsel exceed all of the other items combined. In the Paramount 

Publix Corporation reorganization attorney fees amounted to approximately $870,000; in R. Hoe and Company, Inc., to about $131,000.10 

Because of the prominence of counsel fees in many reorganizations, the question has stirred discussion almost to the point of public issue. 

Condemning the service and attitude of the legal profession, the following statement may be quoted: 

8 Ibid., p. 373. 

9 Ibid., p. 374. 

10 Ibid., p. 211,

The depression with its consequent wave of security defaults presented the legal profession with an unsurpassed opportunity to render genuine public service in the rehabilitation of corporate enterprises in the interests of investors. 

Yet, though there are, of course, exceptions, the profession by and large has

not evidenced a desire to promote reorganization expeditiously, economically, and solely in the interests of investors. On the contrary, it has evidenced ability and ingenuity in furthering the interests of those who utilize the reorganization processes to serve selfish ends.11

Taking issue with this indictment, one of the witnesses appearing in Commission hearings testified: 

When it comes to the general basis on which compensation should be allowed to outside counsel appointed for a receiver, I am frank to say that I am in quite diametric opposition to the views you suggested this morning, to wit, that such receiver and their counsel should be considered as in the nature of having a public office, and I analyze the situation this way: If a man is a public officer, desires to have that position, he goes into it broadly, with a view that there is an amount of distinction attached to the position and an amount of honor attached to the position that will compensate for lack of a monetary return which he might otherwise have gotten in private work. He may also be a man who is altruistically minded, and therefore desires for altruistic reasons to give society the benefit of his service at less than those services might command if he stayed in private work. Such a person, therefore, goes into an office for reasons sufficient to himself, knowing that the compensations are perhaps inadequate, and voluntarily seeking them out and accepting them." 

Difficulties of Determining Fairness of Compensation 

It is not easy to lay down a final dictum in settlement of the ques tion. Lay interests are not apt to appreciate the quid pro quo for advisory service; its intangibility makes it difficult to visualize the concrete benefits which may be derived. Moreover, "hours of time spent, while an element to be considered, are not controlling, and sometimes of very little importance."18 On the other hand, the very courts which determine the fairness of fees are themselves, in a sense, a segment of the profession upon which judgment is being passed. Judges with years of practice in rendering legal service are likely to be sympathetic with generous fees. Often they have had occasion to render similar charges on their own account in previous private practice. There may also exist the smug but deceiving aura of professionalism which leads to the thought that it is impossible for the outsider to appreciate the peculiar values and qualities of legal advice. Some courts, however, show no hesitancy in reducing fees where they appear to be excessive.

Cost of Depositaries 

Another item of expense which appears prominently in most reorganizations is that covering various services rendered by depositaries. 

Agencies of this type perform many duties of a technical and miscellaneous nature, but their principal functions are to provide escrow facilities for securities placed in favor of protective committees and to issue certificates of deposit in exchange. A percentage fee or a fixed price per piece of paper handled (50 cents is typical) is frequently used as a basis for determining the total charge. Of the total expenses of $1,071,052.24 in the reorganization of the Cuba Cane Sugar Corporation, three depositary groups received $114,125.34. One of the members of the reorganization committee testified as to the unreasonableness of this charge as follows:

Q. Do you think that $114,000 is a large sum of money to pay for such services? 

A. I have, ever since I have been down there, been trying to persuade the trust companies that they should work for less than they thought the service justified, but I have never been successful in doing so. When you look at the expense they are put to and the enormous amount of mechanical labor 

14 Ibid., p. 226,

that is involved, it is very hard to handle it on a given job, and the total charge is large. However, the number of pieces handled is large also. I have been as I have said, for a number of years, trying to persuade the institutions to give me a cheaper price.15

Compensation of Receiver 

Usually the most lucrative position of all is that of the receiver. 

Operating under the jurisdiction of a court, a receiver becomes the executive officer with virtually plenipotentiary powers with respect to normal operations. Under the circumstances, it is not surprising to find salaries which are typical of the executive grade being paid. To illustrate, the following compensation was paid to various receivers and trustees in the receivership and reorganization of the Paramount Publix Corporation covering a period from January, 1933, to July, 1935:16 one receiver-$20,000 for a period of less than three months; one receiver-$7,500 for a period of less than three months; three trustees during bankruptcy-$97,299.99 for a period of approximately fourteen months; three trustees during 77B proceedings-$155,000 for a period of approximately one year. It may be observed that in this instance, the court was requested to approve remuneration of $333,000. 

Extent to which Compensation Is Provided

The committee is a popular feature of the democratic process which is frequently used in various types of social institutions as well as in business organization. A disputable problem is usually referred to a committee for consideration and report. Service on a committee is commonly incidental to one's major activity, and there is no specific compensation or it is only minor in amount. But in reorganization proceedings, the various protective and reorganization committees are units with a functional responsibility; in short, they are usually in a position of control. In addition, it is not uncommon for the various members to be reimbursed for their time and service. 

An analysis by the Securities and Exchange Commission of 846 deposit agreements showed that 632 had provisions covering compensation to committee members; in 59 cases, it was specified that there would be no compensation; in the remaining 155 cases, there was no statement relating to compensation, or its payment was possible only

All of the foregoing facts reveal forcefully that the reorganization process finds the pressure for individual or group advantage which is typical of going business. It means that the investor must continue to be on the alert to protect his investment and that he should not assume that a protective committee will function altruistically in behalf of the broader, investor interests. In short, the investor may find that receivership and reorganization give further emphasis to the rule of caveat emptor, instead of creating a period of convalescence in which the status quo is maintained. Also from the point of view of the public interest, there is license to inquire whether these overhauling programs function to revive distressed business units as a means of strengthening the whole economic structure or as a device of strategy to shift group positions.

Making the Market-Nature of Market Action at Time of Failure 

Announcement of failure necessarily throws the market for the securities of victim companies into a state of confusion. Dumping of holdings is not uncommon and may be reminiscent of a run on a bank. There results an erratic movement of price which reflects the fears of investors more than it expresses the underlying values at stake. Often public demand disappears, and it becomes necessary literally to "make a market." By this, it is meant that some group will 

17 Ibid., p. 196.

declare itself ready to accept offerings. Naturally, the price paid is one at which the group anticipates a profit by waiting through the uncertain period of reorganization. Occasionally, there may be evidence of greater generosity if the securities are desired for purposes of control. 

In either event, the security holder is virtually at the mercy of the limited circle of the dominating group. 

Securities with wide distribution which are listed may continue to be traded in the open market, but again the market is limited in scope. Normal buying by institutional investors is definitely curtailed by legal restriction or operating policy, and individual purchasers are likely to be bargain hunters. Transactions in listed securities which are in default do have at least the merit of trading at a published price; in contrast, much of the activity relating to unlisted securities is private and secretive. 

An illustration of the procedure followed where securities are not listed is found in the reorganization of the Celotex Company. The following letter was written by the Secretary of the organization committee to a vice-president of an interested financial group: Dear. ...

I have just had a firm offering made of $1,500 of the first mortgage Celotex bonds at 55 net to you. The same party said he would try and give me a firm offer in the morning on two thousand debentures at 334. 

Will you please wire me upon receipt of this letter whether or not you are interested in these offerings.18

Later the same vice-president apparently recognized the questionable position of the secretary of a reorganization committee working in such close relationship with an interested party; he wrote as follows:

I doubt whether it is wise for you as an independent secretary of the Reorganization Committee to be at any time representing directly. 

We have a broker in Chicago who is buying bonds for us on a basis of point commission, not a point and a half. The name of the broker is Kneeland and Company, Board of Trade Building. I would suggest that if you have any inquiries regarding these bonds that you refer them to this company or to Distributors Group in New York.19 

18 Ibid., p. 121. 

19 Ibid., p. 122.
