The foregoing presentation is by no means a complete summary of events, but it does indicate a little of the chaos, strife, and confusion which arise in the reorganization of a company. With such a setting, it is little wonder that a rather extended period of time is required to effect the reorganization of a company. 

As stated above, another departure from previous practice is to be found in the sponsorship of plans of reorganization. Previously, the plan usually emanated from a specialized reorganization committee, but the present law makes the following provisions: (1) Plans may be submitted on behalf of not less than 10 per cent of the amount of any class of creditors or stockholders. (2) The Interstate Commerce 

Commission, itself, shall approve a plan which may or may not be the same as any recommended.

Such features as the foregoing reflect in marked fashion the substitution of equity for legal right and of public policy for individual or group welfare. For example, one would normally expect the stockholders to have little voice in time of reorganization. In terms of property rights, the stockholders' investment frequently vanishes with failure, and to encourage this group to submit a plan of reorganization is distinctly a matter of equity. In turn, the requirement that the Commission shall formally announce a plan of its own is undoubtedly intended to introduce the element of public welfare. To quote from the law on this matter: "the Commission shall render a report and

REORGANIZATION-RAILROADS 

759 order in which it shall approve a plan, which may be different from and will be compatible with the any which has been proposed. public interest.” 

Confirmation of Plan of Reorganization 

Upon approval of a plan by the Commission, it is so certified and presented to the court. The latter gives proper notice to the interested parties and affords the opportunity to file any objections. If a hearing proves necessary, the court will give due consideration to the arguments of the opposition, after which the plan may be given final approval if the court is satisfied that: 

1. Provision is made to eliminate the previous causes of failure without unfair infringement upon the rights of the various classes of claimants. 

2. There is full disclosure of the costs and expenses of reorganization as well as the amounts to be paid by the debtor corporation or other corporations which may acquire the assets of the debtor. 

3. Provision is made for the payment or disposal of the costs stipulated in (2).

After court approval, a certified copy of the order and opinion is sent to the Commission, which proceeds to notify all interested parties in order that they may express their acceptance or rejection. Subject to the consent of the court, the Commission has the power to omit the approval of any class of stockholders under the following conditions: (1) if the corporation is insolvent at the time of the finding and the equity of the stockholders has no value; (2) if the stockholders will not be adversely or vitally affected by the plan; (3) if the stockholders are bound by the plan by virtue of "authorized corporate action."

Similar authority is given the Commission in the treatment of creditors, although the occasion for its use would be less likely in this instance. Assuming notification, all classes of claimants are required to express their acceptance or rejection in writing, and the Commission will then report the results to the court. 

Finally, the court announces its confirmation of the plan, "if satisfied that it has been accepted by or on behalf of creditors of each class . holding more than two-thirds in amount of the total of the allowed claims" plus a similar vote of approval from the stockholding classes. In the event these terms of approval are not met, the 

---

court has the power to declare the plan operative if it is of the opinion that the plan is fair and provides for the equitable treatment of the various claimants. Specifically, the law declares: 

Upon confirmation by the judge, the provisions of the plan and of the order of confirmation shall, subject to the right of judicial review, be binding upon the debtor, all stockholders thereof, including those who have not, as well as those who have, accepted it, and all creditors secured or unsecured, whether or not adversely affected by the plan, and whether or not their claims shall have been filed, and, if filed, whether or not approved, including creditors who have not, as well as those who have, accepted it. 

Other Features of the Law 

There are numerous other provisions set forth in the law, but the foregoing are the more important ones which affect corporate financing. The other sections deal with such matters as treatment of damage claims, staying of pending suits, power of trustees or the court to affect wages and working conditions, penalties for violation of the law, etc. However, there are a few pertinent points which may be presented in summarized form: 

1. The court may require the trustees to keep records and accounts which would allow the presentation of earnings and expenses according to various parts or divisions of the property. Such knowledge would naturally allow more intelligent treatment of secured creditors, lessors of property, etc. 

2. If there is undue delay in effecting reorganization, the judge may dismiss the proceedings. 

3. If it is necessary to determine the value of any property, the law states that this shall be the duty of the Commission and that proper consideration shall be given to "the earning power of the property, past, present and prospective, and all other relevant facts." 

4. Solicitation of proxies and of the right in general to represent stockholders and creditors may be engaged in only with the approval of the Commission. It is not intended that this shall deny any claimant of his right to protect his own interests, and groups up to twentyfive individual holders may function without interference. 

The Purpose of Reorganization 

With the foregoing discussion of reorganization proceedings in mind, it is important to stress that their importance is not to be

REORGANIZATION-RAILROADS 

761 found in their technique. The intricacy of legal arrangement easily gives the impression that it is the final objective, but actually the real purpose of reorganization is to restore to a sound condition a company which has failed. In effecting this transformation, it is important that due regard be given to the rights of the interested parties, but the desire to avoid loss by investors should not be permitted to interfere with the sacrifices which are necessary to bring about sound reconstruction. The nature of these sacrifices and the general effects of reorganization may be seen to advantage by their application to a specific case.

The Chicago Great Western Railroad 

With almost one-third of the railway mileage in the country in receivership or bankruptcy, it is not difficult to find a railroad for purposes of illustration. Most of them have complex financial structures and call for so much individual analysis that attention is easily diverted from the more important basic principles. Since the capital structure of the Chicago Great Western Railroad is relatively simple, it may be selected as a convenient example. Comments on Plan of Reorganization 

It will be seen from the brief summary of the treatment of security holders in the accompanying table that the capitalization of the Chicago Great Western is reduced virtually by one-half. 763 qualitative changes are even more significant and are indicated by such features as the following: 

1. Reduction of interest-bearing debt.-The plan reduces interestbearing obligations from more than $40,000,000 to a figure slightly under $20,000,000. 

2. Reduction of fixed charges.-As a result of (1), the drain of fixed charges on income is materially lessened. Under the old capitalization the fixed annual charges were about $1,900,000 and are reduced to approximately $875,000 under the new set-up. Included in the latter, there is roughly $275,000 applicable to the general mortgage income bonds which is contingent upon earnings. 

3. Creation of various sinking and capital funds. Additional safeguards to protect the future financial position are found in the requirements set up in the plan of reorganization to establish the following fund accounts: a) A sinking fund which is to be created at the rate of one-half of 1 per cent of first mortgage bonds for the retirement of these bonds. The charge is imposed after the payment of fixed charges and may be imposed only if the net income is available. b) A sinking fund with similar provisions for the retirement of the general mortgage bonds at the rate of one-fourth of 1 per cent per year. c) A capital fund for the purpose of facilitating the purchase of equipment and for other property improvements is provided by an annual charge equal to 2 per cent of the annual operating revenue. 

This charge has priority over the interest on the general mortgage income bonds, but when the fund accumulates to $1,500,000, thereafter allocations are necessary only to keep the fund at this figure. 

4. Treatment of unsecured claims. All such claims arising on or prior to February 28, 1935 (designated by the court as class 14) were left to the reorganized company for whatever disposition it saw fit, but without any priority because of the reorganization proceedings. 

Both the preferred and common stocks have equal share voting rights which means that the old first-mortgage bondholders would have control of the new company. In view of the heavy sacrifices imposed on these bondholders, the assumption of control by this group is undoubtedly justified. As shown above, the old common stockholders were completely eliminated because their equity had vanished, while the preferred stockholders were given some hope of

future recovery by exchanging one old share of $100 stock for onehalf share of new stock with a par of $50. However, even such drastic reorganization still leaves a company with sizeable risk, a fact which is reflected in the following recent market prices of the several securities.4

Indeed, as stated on another occasion, there are many times when actual liquidation should occur or the physical properties may be merged with more successful companies. In the present instance, there are several economic factors which are a deterrent to successful independent operation. Such basic conditions as the following are of the type referred to: (1) only 30 per cent of the freight traffic is initiated on the company's own lines; (2) present terminal facilities are inadequate; and (3) the company has few advantages to meet the competition of other lines operating in the same area. Whether or not the financial reorganization will be adequate to meet such basic economic obstacles remains to be seen. 

Priority of Position of Security Holders 

The foregoing case shows clearly the severe losses which investors may suffer as a result of failure and reorganization. These sacrifices invite sympathetic consideration of the plight of the investor, but they should not be permitted to interfere with genuine and thorough reorganization of a company which has failed. Vigorous pruning of the old set-up is usually necessary to restore soundness of financial position and, in the long run, is likely to prove more satisfactory to the investor. The main questions are the extent of the sacrifice and the distribution of the burden among the various classes of security holders. Since these incidents of reorganization are common to all fields of enterprise, the following discussion is also applicable to industrial and public utility companies.

This means that secured creditors must be satisfied first, following which recognition is given in order to the unsecured creditors, the preferred stockholders, and the common stockholders. Where there is insufficient value to indicate any real equity of the common stock, it may be completely eliminated as was done in the case of the 

Chicago Great Western Railroad.

Bond issues are not always readily put into airtight compartments; instead, there may be much overlapping and interdependency. To the extent, however, that priority of lien may be determined, its importance cannot be denied. One case is known where a first mortgage bond on the main line of a railroad has been through three separate reorganizations and has not been affected in its position." 

The financial structure of industrial companies is seldom as complex as that of railroads, but the principle of priority of claim is equally applicable. This may be illustrated by the treatment of the security holders of the Studebaker Corporation, and its subsidiary the Rockne Corporation, which failed in 1933. Under the ensuing reorganization, a new corporation was organized, and in 1935 took over the assets of the original companies except the investment of the old Studebaker Company in the stock of the White Motor Company. The reorganization plan made the following arrangements: 

Creditors of Studebaker received for each $100 in principal amount of claims and interest allowed, 2.64 shares of White stock, 4 shares of common stock in the new company, and the right to purchase debentures" and additional stock. 

Creditors of Rockne received for each $100 principal and interest, $25 in cash, $50 in debentures, shares of White stock, one share of new common, and the right to subscribe to debentures and stock. 

Preferred stockholders received for each share held 14 shares of new common and the right to subscribe for a unit consisting of $15 in debentures and 23 shares of common for $15 cash. 

Common stockholders received for each share held only the right to subscribe for a unit consisting of $2.25 in debentures and share of common stock for $2.25 cash. Creditors could subscribe on the same basis for such additional units as were not taken by the old common stockholders. 

Legal Status of Priority 

The treatment of security holders according to their position of priority is well established by legal sanctions. Court decisions have long placed emphasis on the subordinate position of the stock equity.

also the question of compelling minority interests to accede to a plan approved by the majority. On its face, it appears to be an outright deprivation of contractual rights. But this does not necessarily mean that the law establishing this authority is unconstitutional. True, the Constitution does provide that the states may not enact laws which impair the validity of contracts, but the Congress of the United States is not so confined. For instance, in the case of Hepburn v. Griswold, the Court said:

Congress has express power to enact bankrupt laws, and we do not say that a law made in the execution of any other express power which, incidentally only, impairs the obligation of a contract can be held unconstitutional for that reason. But we think it clear that those who framed and those who adopted the Constitution intended that the spirit of this prohibition should pervade the entire body of legislation and that the justice which the Constitution was ordained to establish was not thought by them to be compatible with legislation of an opposite tendency. In other words, we cannot doubt that a law not made in pursuance of an express power, which necessarily and in its direct operation impairs the obligation of contracts is inconsistent with the spirit of the constitution.¹ 12 Moreover, much may be said in favor of the restriction of minority interests from the point of view of business expediency. Altogether too often, minority actions are instituted for the sake of personal gain at the expense of the whole, and again, they are initiated frequently for nuisance purposes solely. Also, the law provides for hearings at various points along the reorganization process which should offer adequate opportunity for legitimate interests to present their case. 

Preservation of Junior Position by New Investment 

It is apparent from the foregoing that stockholders may not preserve their interest at the expense of creditors. The participation of the former in a plan of reorganization on the basis of existing investment is wholly dependent on the value of their equity. Of course, it is not uncommon for stockholders to invest additional funds in the securities of the reorganized company, and some future recovery of past losses may be possible by this means. However, such investment is purely voluntary, and the preservation of interest is the result of new funds rather than past equity. 

It should also be pointed out that claims having priority need not 

12 75 U. S. 603, 639 (1870).

REORGANIZATION-RAILROADS 

769 be settled in cash. Settlement is usually effected in terms of new securities, but it is required that the value of such securities be equal in value to the claims against the old company. If it is discovered that the claims of the creditors were not fully met, the new company may still be held liable for the old debts.13 Nevertheless, the use of securities to settle the obligations of the old company makes it easier for junior interests to participate because of the difference between values established for a going concern and those for purposes of cash liquidation. Also, reorganization managers seek to retain the support of old stockholders both as a means of retaining their support as well as to seek new cash by the sale of securities of the reorganized company.

Purpose of Chapter XV of the Bankruptcy Act 

The provisions of Section 77 are intended to accommodate the more serious cases of railroads with financial difficulties. In the summer of 1939, it was seen fit to provide for those railroads where voluntary adjustment appeared to be a feasible and practical solution. The covering legislation is also known as the Chandler Act, but more officially, it constitutes Chapter XV of the National Bankruptcy Act.14 It should also be noted that the procedure set forth in the Act is apparently not regarded as permanent in character since no authority is given to initiate action under the law after July 31, 1940. It, therefore, appears to be a form of special enactment which was passed to meet the requirements of a few cases which existed at the time.

Provisions of Chapter XV 

Irrespective of the limited applicability of the Act, it is desirable to note its main provision as an example of the many forms of technique which may be utilized to remove financial embarrassment. Recourse to the procedure created by the Act was confined to railroads which had not undergone reorganization under Section 77 or had not been in equity receivership for a period of ten years prior to the filing of their application. The petition was required to be supported by the following evidence: 

1. A plan of adjustment with assurance of acceptance from at least 

18 Northern Pacific Ry. v. Boyd, 228 U. S. 482 (1913). 

14 Commercial and Financial Chronicle, Vol. 149 (August 26, 1939), pp. 1235-37.

25 per cent of the amount of claims of creditors affected by the plan. 

2. An order from the Interstate Commerce Commission approving the issuance of the new securities proposed as well as certification that the railroad would not need financial reorganization of the type provided in Section 77, that the difficulties were of a temporary character only, that future earnings were likely to be adequate to meet future needs, etc. 

3. Assents to the plan of adjustment "by creditors holding more than two-thirds of the aggregate amount of the claims affected by said plan, which two-thirds shall include at least a majority of the aggregate amount of the claims of each affected class." 

A special court of three judges with "all the powers of a district court sitting in equity and all the powers as a court of bankruptcy necessary to carry out the intent and provisions" of the Act passed upon all proceedings. One noteworthy exception to the court's exercise of bankruptcy powers was its lack of authority to appoint trustees; instead the property remained in the hands of the existing, operating management. However, it was provided that the court should hold a hearing where parties of interest could register any objections or opinions. Ultimately, the final confirmation of the plan was to be declared if the petition had met several technical requirements and if it had been accepted by creditors "affected by such plan holding more than three-fourths of the aggregate amount of claims affected by said plan, including at least three-fifths of the aggregate amount of the claims of each affected class." 

Taking cognizance of the temporary character of the financial difficulties, it was declared that confirmation of the plan of adjustment must be effected within one year from the date of filing the petition, unless the court determined that its effectuation was "in immediate prospect." Specific protection was also established in favor of equipment trust obligations, since title to rolling stock could not be disturbed, and the rights of owners to take possession of such property were retained.

PART VIII

CHAPTER XXXVIII  

T ONE time, business enterprise was operated principally to the end of maximizing profits for the owners. This approach may have been entirely reasonable during an earlier period, but it is no longer the case in view of the present-day developments in economic and social institutions. It is now necessary to recognize the existence of at least three groups having both common and diverse interests in business, namely, the investors or owners; the employees; and a third group which includes both the foregoing -the public. One of the most promising features of the present day is the growing recognition by business itself that management policies must be shaped with proper regard for the public interest. 

Throughout our discussion, the nature of the public interest has been pointed out with reference to related topics. Public interest requires definition and expression through some form of compulsion before it can be effective. Compulsion may be limited to education or moral suasion, may take the form of legislative action, or may be attained through tax policies. Attention has been given to the first two ways of making public policy effective, and public policy as such will be discussed in the following two chapters; in this chapter consideration will be given to taxation as a tool of public policy. 

Reasons for Interest in Taxation

Taxation is today attracting wider attention and more careful study than has usually been true in the past. This is the result of a constantly increasing burden of taxation placed upon our economy through an almost continuous expansion of governmental functions. 

At one time the functions of government were limited principally to the maintenance of law and order within the country and protection against foreign powers. To these should be added a limited number of services which for one reason or another were assumed by government rather than by private enterprise. Gradually, however, the duties of government have been expanded to include public roads, free public education, and more recently a host of so-called social 775

services such as poor relief, work relief, unemployment compensation, and old-age pensions. Upon the cost of these and similar functions must be superimposed the enormous costs of a defense program in a day of advanced military technology. It should not be inferred that all of the services or functions named represent added costs to the economy. Roads and schools were once furnished by private enterprisers who sold their services. Today, they are furnished by government which makes no direct charge in the form of prices but levies taxes to cover the costs. 

In search for more revenue to pay for the added functions, corporations have received full attention from the legislative bodies. As corporations have grown in size and profitability, they have afforded a convenient basis for special tax treatment. This arises partly because the taxation of corporations is politically feasible and partly because of economic circumstances. From the political point of view, it is much easier to tax some 529,000 corporations rather than the millions of private enterprisers. From the economic point of view, special taxation is necessary because corporations as a group obtain the vast bulk of the gross receipts and net profits accruing to business enterprise.

It will not be possible to discuss fully the tax system applicable to incorporated business in this book. However, the student of corporation finance should have an appreciation of the influence of taxes on private business policies and operation, and the ensuing discussion will highlight some of the implications relating to taxation and public policy.

Effect of Taxation Upon Business Policy 

Before proceeding to a discussion of taxation as an instrument of public policy, it would be well to recognize briefly some of the effects of taxation upon business policy. The normal objective of management is to operate a business with the lowest costs possible to the end of securing a maximum of net profits. This search for profits is often affected by the complex structure of federal, state, and local tax systems which may present corporate managements with opportunities to make choices permitting lower taxes. As mentioned in 

Chapter XII, the selection of a state for obtaining a charter may be influenced by taxation. Organization tax rates vary from 100 of 

1 per cent to of 1 per cent of authorized capital stock. Frequently,

the rate structures applied in granting a corporation charter are regressive, the rate decreasing as the size of the corporation increases. 

In addition to organization and franchise taxes, states vary in the burden placed upon incorporated business through special taxes upon property, income, or the nature of business done. Ordinarily there are other economic factors more important than taxes in selecting the state for incorporation, but the relative tax burden among states is an important consideration.

Method of Conducting Business 

Special corporation taxes may have a material influence both on the form of organization and upon the mode of conducting business. 

A relatively heavier tax burden upon incorporated enterprise as com pared to unincorporated may easily be the marginal factor which determines whether a business should incorporate at all. While incorporation carries the advantages of limited liability and continuity of existence-to name two features which have been discussed elsewhere -these benefits are partly offset by special costs. As a consequence, many small enterprises which might like to incorporate for the sake of limited liability may find it more profitable to assume the unlimited risks attendant upon the proprietorship or partnership forms of organization. That corporations bear higher taxes is evidenced by the tendency of many small corporations to dissolve in recent years and to return to the private form of organization. Such dissolution is often for the avowed purpose of avoiding special taxation. 

An excellent example of special taxes is found in many states in their tax treatment of chain stores. The taxes are usually progressive and are based upon the number of unit stores operated in the individual chain. Most, if not all, chain-store organizations are incorporated. 

They are singled out for special tax treatment, partly as a productive source for tax revenue and partly because of a desire to impose punitive taxes upon a politically unpopular form of organization. As a result of such taxes, chain-store corporations have been forced to adopt business policies which hold the taxes to a minimum. One method is to lease the separate units to the managers who thus become private enterprisers and are technically in the position of customers of the parent organization. This has been done by some of the large oil companies for their operations in chain-store-tax states. Grocery chains have tended to adopt the policy of greatly reducing the number of

units operated and increasing their size. What are popularly referred to as super-markets are opened, and all existing smaller units in the same neighborhood are closed. This has served to reduce greatly the base for chain-store taxes and has also proved to furnish a powerful promotional device for getting more business. 

Methods of Financing 

Existing tax systems tend to place a premium upon one form of corporate financing as compared with another. Existing income-tax laws allow the deduction of all interest paid upon outstanding bonds or other forms of debt, thus making it relatively more profitable for corporations to use bonds rather than stocks for financing the business. Also, the usual arrangement for state franchise taxes is to base the tax upon a percentage of authorized or outstanding capital stock. 

This percentage is not high in most states, but it does lend encouragement to hold authorizations or issuances of stock to a minimum and to use bonds as a source of funds. 

Taxation as an Instrument of Public Policy 

"The power to tax is the power to define our economic system. 

Through taxation it would conceivably be possible to force incorporation of all business units, and conversely it would be possible to make the costs of incorporating virtually prohibitive. The latter practice would undoubtedly make business as it is known today practically impossible. However, as the tax laws are drawn favoring one method of operation or type of enterprise against another, so business initiative constantly seeks the alternatives which appear to offer the greatest opportunity for profitable operation. As a consequence, those interested in or charged with the responsibility of determining public policy may use tax laws to influence materially the course of business activity. "1 Taxation is not usually regarded as a means of shaping the business pattern, but this must necessarily be the effect, at least to a degree. 

Other alternative means of governmental direction would be the more outright methods of regulation and of government ownership. Under the former, some government commission would establish rules and regulations and the broad outlines of policy within which the 

T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 9, p. x.

regulated businesses would be expected to operate. Government ownership would furnish direct control, and there would be no question of regulation. Taxation as a regulatory device would operate through the imposition of heavy burdens upon the undesirable activities and little or no burdens upon the desired forms of practice. 

Presumably, taxation would not directly prohibit any practice and would therefore leave considerable areas for business initiative and discretion to function. Policies could probably be enforced through taxation with smaller administrative personnel and fewer arbitrary decisions than would be true through direct control of commerce by regulation.

At a time when taxation is taking constantly greater proportions of the national income, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to levy taxes which would have no effect upon the direction of business enterprise. Therefore, it is important to consider carefully the influence of taxation upon business and also to consider the possibilities of using taxation directly as an instrument of public policy in achieving a better economic system. This implies the need for definite objectives or standards of measurement toward which taxation should direct the system. There is, of course, no definite agreement as to the type of system which should be developed nor as to the objectives of the taxes to be imposed. However, certain objectives involving corporation taxation may be presented here, not in any sense of completeness but simply to point out some of the problems which may be approached through taxation or considered in designing tax laws: (1) the active circulation of economic income; (2) limitation of monopolistic or excess profits; (3) discouragement of excessive corporate integration; (4) encouragement of equity investment. 

Obviously, no one tax could result in achieving these objectives, just as full agreement on their desirability could not be obtained. 

However, they should be considered in designing and administering the tax structure.

Federal taxes are best adapted to control purposes because of their nation-wide effects. States are severely limited in their ability to impose regulatory taxes because of interstate competition. If a state imposes heavy taxes upon business activity as compared with other states, there would be a tendency for the business capable of doing so to move their operations to other states. The foregoing policy

points may now be examined with special reference to certain federal taxes.

The Circulation of Economic Income 

During the decade of depression which began in 1930, the economic system was subjected to much critical analysis. One of the conclusions reached during this period was that a contributory cause for this and preceding depressions was a lack of balance between savings and spending. The classical doctrine of balance between supply and demand was held to apply only if all the economic income was immediately spent for consumption goods or directly for investment. 

If, however, a considerable portion of income was withheld, then an unbalanced condition developed which if carried far enough, or complicated by other factors, would result in a depression. This viewpoint held that there had been oversavings and that much of it was the result of retention of earnings by corporations. During the late 

20's corporations as a whole had retained about 40 per cent of their annual earnings in the surplus account. While this was a boom period, and therefore unusual, it must be noted that corporations usually follow the practice of retaining on the average about 30 per cent of their earnings.2 

Failure to distribute earnings was criticized by many because often the earnings were not invested immediately and were withheld from active circulation. To a degree, there was a substitution of personal for economic motive because large and controlling stockholders sought to avoid the high surtaxes which would have been applicable upon their incomes if dividends had been paid. Instead of receiving the income, they preferred to have their ownership equity increased until such time as the funds were needed or lower taxes might prevail. 

At the same time, thousands of small stockholders were denied dividend income which they might have spent upon consumption goods or reinvested in other enterprises according to their judgment, and with the consequent stimulation of the flow of national income. 

The Undistributed Profits Tax 

In March, 1936, the President requested Congress to consider the adoption of a tax upon undistributed profits of corporations. This 

2 Revenue Act of 1936, Hearings, p. 18, Senate Committee on Finance, 74th Congress, 2d Session.

tax was to be accompanied by the repeal of all other corporate taxes based upon or related to profits, namely, the normal tax upon corporate income, the capital stock tax, and the excess profits tax. The purpose of the proposed tax was to put a penalty upon the retention of corporate earnings as surplus and to force earnings into the hands of individuals where it would be subject to the highly progressive personal income tax, thus serving to encourage the active circulation of one form of economic income. The further advantage was claimed that the taxation of undistributed profits would treat all business more equitably regardless of the form of organization." 

The Revenue Act of 1936 established a corporate normal tax graduated from 8 to 15 per cent and imposed an undistributed profits tax graduated from 7 per cent to 27 per cent. In other words, the law was a compromise and the undistributed profits tax was in addition. to existing taxes rather than a replacement tax as previously intended.

From the point of view of the distribution of tax burden, the undistributed profits tax was sound in principle. Taxation according to ability to pay is generally agreed to be sound but can be applied only in relation to individuals. Taxation according to ability means that large incomes are taxed at higher rates than small incomes. Largeincome receivers have a greater surplus above necessary living expenses and are in a position to pay a larger proportion of the excess without harm to themselves than would be true of the individuals receiving a smaller income. Taxation according to ability to pay is usually scheduled at what are known as progressive rates-rates which become higher upon additional increments of income. When corporate net income is taxed at a flat 24 per cent it constitutes what amounts to a proportional tax upon both the very large and very small stockholder. Proportional taxation is not taxing according to ability.

When earnings are paid out in dividends to the various individual stockholders, they must pay personal income taxes upon the amounts received. A person with a large personal income may have to pay 

50 per cent or more of the dividends received in the form of income taxes. The small income receiver may have a sufficiently small-sized income as to be required to pay no taxes and could receive corporate income tax free. Other individuals may have to pay only the basic 

10 per cent personal income tax. Due to the progressive tax rates, large stockholders may have much to gain by the avoidance of personal taxes through retaining a large proportion of the earnings in the business. On the other hand, if stockholders were taxed upon the proportionate share of corporate income whether divided in dividends, or undivided and retained in surplus, this phase of individual inequity would disappear. Such is the present practice in the taxation of partnerships where each partner pays taxes upon his share of the partnership profits whether retained in the business or withdrawn for personal use. 

4 The Revenue Act of 1941 established a 4 per cent normal tax applicable to all taxable income, plus a surtax schedule beginning at 6 per cent for the first $2,000 of taxable net income. In 1936, the normal tax on individual incomes was 4 per cent and the surtax did not apply to the first $4,000 in taxable income.

Objections to the Undistributed Profits Tax 

During its brief life, the undistributed profits tax was sharply criticized by business interests. Many arguments were presented against the tax, a few of which may be presented here. 

One objection was that the tax ignored the importance of surplus and reserves in corporate finance. It was contended that too little attention was given to financial stability or the ability to withstand economic shocks which arises from a general strengthening of the owner's equity in the corporation. If earnings are retained in the business, protection is acquired against unexpected losses arising from business conditions or any other cause. Not only does the stockholder acquire a margin of protection for his investment, but also a protection is given to the company's creditors and to the economic system. Failures can often be avoided when concerns have made adequate reserve provisions during good times to meet the exigencies of depressions which are likely to follow; and society gains to the extent that unnecessary failures are avoided.

A second objection was that the law did not make provision for previous deficits. If a concern has had a number of years of operating deficits as would be especially likely to occur in a new company, there is good argument for permitting it to retain part or all of later income to absorb the accumulated deficit and to restore the capital to its original position. In fact, most state laws prohibit the payment of dividends so long as invested capital is impaired. Yet, under the original undistributed profits tax no credit for previous deficits was permitted.

A third and widely publicized objection was the lack of recognition given to the financial problems of small corporations. Small corporations must rely upon internal sources for expansion capital to a far greater degree than is true of large corporations. The latter are in a position to issue bonds in amounts of sufficient size to appear attractive to investment bankers and to be marketed with a minimum of expense. Small concerns, on the other hand, find it difficult and expensive to issue new securities.5 They must rely upon stock sales to friends and insiders and upon retained earnings for expansion purposes. The undistributed profits tax appeared, therefore, to place an undue burden upon the small and expanding corporation. 

In terms of basic economic principle, it should be mentioned that 

5 See chapter XX for discussion of costs of distribution of small issues.

2 

the retention of earnings permits the investment of new capital without benefit of the checks and balances of market action. In the years 1935 to 1937, American business concerns invested $17,400,000,- 000 for plant expansion of which 92 per cent came from internal sources. Only 8 per cent or $1,400,000,000 was obtained through recourse to the investment markets of the country. It would be interesting to know how much of the remaining large sum obtained from internal sources could have been raised by the sale of securities in the open market.

If corporate control were truly democratic and it were possible for stockholders to take an active part, there would be less criticism of wholesale financing out of earnings. However, democratic control seldom exists and corporate management has become largely a self-perpetuating affair maintained through proxy committees and the lack of stockholder interest. Broadly speaking, funds should be retained in the business only to furnish a buffer for hard times or when expansion will definitely prove profitable. Actually, earnings are used as a primary source of capital mainly for reasons of expediency and it is likely that funds are sometimes retained and expansions financed when added capital could not be obtained through security issues.

Corporate Practice under the Undistributed Profits Tax 

As might be expected, the effect of the tax upon corporate dividend policy was not uniform. Some corporations avoided the tax and retained earnings by paying dividends in preferred stock upon common stock which, under the ruling of Koshland v. Helvering, were held to constitute a payment of earnings by the corporation and a receipt of taxable income by the stockholder. However, the most common form of dividends is cash and, undoubtedly, some corporations paid more dividends as a result of the tax. One study of 42 corporations showed an increase of dividend disbursements from 64.6 per cent of earnings in 1935 to 79.5 per cent in 1936.9 The sample is too small to

be conclusive, but it may be taken as an indication of the practice. followed by relatively large corporations. 

The tax yielded $145,000,000 in 1936 and $176,000,000 in 1937. 

Viewed as a whole, the tax was not prohibitive since the highest effective rate, if all earnings had been retained, was 20 per cent or a total rate including the normal income tax prevailing in that year of about 33 per cent.10

Economic Effects of the Undistributed Profits Tax 

The economic effects of the law may not be established conclusively because of the short time it was in force and the intense opposition it received. Taking all the corporations as a whole, the available evidence indicates that in 1937, the tax varied inversely according to the size of corporations, that is, the large corporations as a group paid relatively less than small corporations.11 In part, this was probably due to a tendency of the large corporations in that year to pay larger dividends. When the data are broken down by industries the relationship is not quite so clear. Apparently small and medium-sized concerns paid about the same surtax while large concerns clearly paid smaller amounts. From a profits point of view, the concerns earning the highest rates of return appeared to pay the largest tax, which indicates that profitable companies retain a larger proportion of earnings in surplus.

The tax was so unpopular with business that it was necessary to make concessions to the critics. In 1938, the law was extensively amended to exempt all corporations with net income under $25,000, more extensive reductions for debt requirements were permitted, the idea of a carry-over for previous years' losses was introduced, and the rate cut to a flat 24 per cent instead of the graduated 7 to 27 per cent. The tax was repealed in 1940 and a policy adopted which may have the opposite effect upon dividend payments.12

Limitation of Monopoly or Excess Profits 

Under the capitalistic system it is the function of profits to bring forth productive effort. Theoretically, excess profits stimulate competition, and it is presumed that profits out of proportion to the effort or the risk will result in the establishment of new business units and that the increased capacity will result in lower prices and lower profits. 

However, it must be recognized that in practice competition works all too imperfectly. Profits in excess of the amount necessary to maintain activity in a line of enterprise are a common occurrence and are to be found in any size or type of business. 

Excess profits are often associated with monopoly, but, in popular thought, monopoly is usually believed to be represented only by large enterprise. In reality, monopolistic profit may arise from a small enterprise which is favorably situated, as far as competitive pressures are concerned. In the strictest sense, monopoly or excess profits may exist in the eating place which has become the traditional hang-out for the college student, just as well as in the huge industrial combination which dominates some field of manufacturing activity. Because of our ability to notice big things more readily than small, there is a tendency to exaggerate the evil of the large rate of return in the big business and ignore the economic facts concerning the large rate of return in the small business. Actually, the latter situation may occur with sufficient frequency to be quite important in the aggregate and worthy of consideration in the design of an excess profits tax. 

Excess Profits Tax 

In an economic sense, excess profits may be regarded as any return above that necessary to bring forth productive effort; for purposes of taxation, excess profits constitute the amount in excess of whatever the law arbitrarily defines as normal profits. The first excess profits tax was enacted in 1917 and was revised again in 1918 before it went into effect. The 1918 law defined normal returns as 

8 per cent on invested capital and levied a special tax upon all amounts in excess of this rate. The tax was 30 per cent of earnings in excess of 

8 per cent but less than 20 per cent of invested capital and 65 per cent of all earnings in excess of 20 per cent of invested capital. The excess profits tax was in addition to the regular income tax which was, however, allowed as a credit before computing the excess profits. 

A special war profits tax was also in effect during 1918. The

war profits tax was 80 per cent of the amount above the average earnings for the years 1911 through 1913 with an adjustment allowed in the form of 10 per cent of the change in capital investment used in the business in 1918 as compared with the base period. The two taxes constituted alternative methods of computing the taxes due, and the corporation paid under the method resulting in the highest tax payment. The excess profits tax system was very productive to the government and was borne by the corporations without complaint due to war-time psychology and the abnormally high returns resulting from the war boom. With the return of peace, there was a demand for its repeal and this was finally accomplished in 1921. 

In 1933, a new form of excess profits tax was introduced which was entirely unlike the tax of the World War I period. The tax actually was intended to police the capital stock tax which was enacted at the same time. The capital stock tax was levied at the rate of $1 per thousand dollars of adjusted declared value of capital stock. Corporations were required to declare the value of their capital stock and were permitted in practice to choose any value they wished. The tax of 5 per cent was levied upon all profits in excess of 12 per cent of the declared capitalization. In 1936, the rates were changed and the corporation became subject to 6 per cent and 12 per cent excess profits' taxes upon the earnings which were in excess of 10 per cent and 15 per cent respectively of declared capital.13 

The chief problem for the corporation was to estimate what its future earnings were likely to be. If little or no earnings were expected, then the total taxes could be minimized by declaring the capital stock at a very low figure. If, however, good returns were expected, it would pay the corporation to declare a higher value for the capital stock. Taxes were minimized under the 1936 rates if the value of the capital stock was declared at a figure approximately ten times its expected earnings for the coming year. In this way, it was presumed that the two taxes would be self-administering. 

The Present Form of Excess Profits Tax 

The Second Revenue Act of 1940 introduced an entirely different conception of excess profits taxation and tax rates than had existed during World War I or existed since 1933 in connection with the 18 The 1941 law increased the capital stock tax to $1.25 per $1,000 of declared value and the declared value excess profits tax to 6.6 per cent and 13.2 per cent.

capital stock tax.14 Under the 1940 law excess profits are determined as the amount in excess of either (a) 8 per cent of invested capital, plus $3,000, plus certain carry-over adjustments, or (b) 95 per cent of the average profits for the years 1936 to 1939. Each corporation is permitted to select the basis for determining its excess profits and, logically, will choose the basis which would result in the lowest tax payments. Corporations having a relatively large amount of capital in relation to the volume of business done will favor the percentage of invested capital basis. Concerns earning a high rate of return will gain by using the average earnings basis unless earnings for the 1936 to 1939 period were unduly low. 

Invested capital is defined in part as "the aggregate of the daily invested capital of each day of such taxable year, divided by the number of days in such year." Under the formula, not only is paidin original capital included in the exemption base, but also current earnings invested in the business. Thus, 8 per cent of each dollar in added investment is exempt from the excess profits tax. Cases may arise where this will prove sufficient encouragement to retain earnings which might otherwise be distributed. Intentionally or otherwise, a policy has been adopted which constitutes, to a degree, a reversal from that prevailing under the undistributed profits tax.

This rate schedule has the effect of creating a tax which contains an element of taxation upon size as such as well as upon excessive returns. A large corporation earning 9 per cent upon its capital investment might have far more than $500,000 in adjusted excess profits on which it would be required to pay 50 per cent in adjusted profits 14 The 1940 tax is now known as the excess profits tax, while the tax introduced in 1933 is referred to as the declared value excess profits tax. Both taxes are now in force, each is computed and paid separately, and neither is allowed as a deduction before computing the other.

tax. A small corporation earning the same rate of return might have all of its excess in the first or 25 per cent bracket. This does not constitute the taxation of excess profits in the truest economic sense but must be regarded as the taxation of large corporations as a practical means of obtaining necessary governmental revenue coupled with a discrimination against size.

In the Revenue Act of 1941, approved September 20, 1941, the rates are increased by 10 per cent in each of the foregoing brackets. 

In addition, the invested capital credit is changed from the flat 8 per cent of invested capital as under the 1940 law to 8 per cent of the first $5,000,000 and 7 per cent of the balance. Here, again, is evidence of placing a further burden upon size rather than using excess earnings alone as a yardstick to determine the basis of taxation. 

The 1941 law also made a technical change of considerable importance in the treatment of normal and excess profits taxes. Instead of permitting normal income taxes paid to be taken as deductions in computing the excess profits tax, the excess profits tax is now permitted as a deduction in figuring the normal tax. Thus, after the corporation has computed its net profits subject to the corporate income tax and has taken the prescribed normal credits, it is then required to compute its excess profits tax at the increased rates. The excess profits tax may then be deducted from the original net income before computing the normal income tax.

From an economic point of view, an excess profits tax is entirely sound if levied upon excessive rates of return upon investment. The chief difficulties with such a tax are administrative. Two difficult problems must be met if such a tax is to be applied with fairness: (1) What is a reasonable return? (2) What constitutes capital value?

The question of reasonable return is not simple because two important variations exist among different types of enterprise. One is the degree of risk attendant upon the particular line of activity. The other is the variation in regularity of earnings. If the risk is great, high returns must be expected at intervals to offset the possibilities of unusual loss of investment. If the risk is low and returns are reasonably certain, the yield on investment may be smaller in amount and still bring forth business activity. Some businesses enjoy stable operations from year to year and have rather small percentage returns. 

Others have widely fluctuating earnings from year to year with deficits in some years and very high returns in the profitable years. It

would be difficult but not impossible to determine a fair method of adjusting for such fluctuations.

The question of determining the capital value or the invested capital upon which normal earnings should be allowed would also be difficult to solve. This is primarily an accounting problem and one which could not be solved to the satisfaction of all interests. 

Many questions would arise relative to such problems as true v. nominal values, the proper allowances for depreciation and depletion, and whether or not book values were in fact represented by assets used in the business. However, it is likely that an adminstratively practicable method for calculating capital value could be developed, so that a true excess profits tax could be installed if public policy should be so determined.

The Corporate Income Tax and the Restriction of Integration 

If it should appear desirable to tax business according to size, that is, to discourage big business and to favor small, then the corporate income tax is a better device for this purpose than the excess profits tax. The latter should be restricted to what its name implies -a tax upon excess profits. To be sure, either tax may be used to restrict the large corporation and favor the small. But certain advantages may be derived from using the excess profits tax to recapture monopoly profits and the income tax to limit size. Excessive profits arise from the imperfect functioning of competition in the economic system. At least a portion of the excess could be recaptured through taxation for general use without checking productive effort. 

Progressive corporate income taxes, on the other hand, place a restriction on the size of the business unit since there is no necessary relationship between the amount of income and the rates of return. 

Thus, there are two different factors in the income situation which should receive separate treatment whenever this is indicated by considerations of public policy. Neither practice has ever been followed in any important degree although both have been present in the tax laws at various times. 

Prior to 1936, the income tax was always a proportional tax ranging from 1 per cent in 1913 to 13 per cent during the 1932 to 1935 period. The tax applied to net income remaining after the deduction of business expenses such as the costs of materials and supplies; compensation of officers; rent; repairs; bad debts; interest; taxes; contri-

butions or gifts; losses from fire, theft, and other casualty; depreciation and depletion; and net losses for prior years. In addition, at the present time, 85 per cent of intercorporate dividends are exempt from taxation.

From 1918 to 1931, a small element of progression existed due to a specific credit of $2,000 or $3,000 which was granted in most tax years only to the companies with net incomes of less than $25,000. 

This made the effective rates upon small corporate incomes slightly less than the basic tax rate. In 1935, a system of truly progressive rates was introduced applicable to incomes of that year. The degree of progression was increased in succeeding tax laws, but it was always small until the rate schedule introduced under the Revenue Act of 1941. The corporate tax schedule introduced in this Act is as follows: 

15 per cent on the first $5,000 of net income 17 per cent on the next $15,000 of net income 19 per cent on the next $5,000 of net income 24 per cent on all over $25,000 of net income The 1941 Law also introduces for the first time in corporate income taxation a surtax of 6 per cent on the first $25,000 of net income and 7 per cent on the remainder. This makes the actual income tax rate upon 1941 incomes range from 21 per cent to 31 per cent depending upon the amount of income. Here, as in the excess profits tax, the tax is made to bear more heavily upon the large corporation. The difference is not prohibitive under the present rate structure, but if progression were carried to sufficient length, the tax could make large business units relatively unprofitable and thereby restrict their development. The progressive element in corporate income taxation was adopted to compensate for some of the supposed advantages possessed by large corporations.15 

While special advantages are inherent in large corporations, it is true that the advantages should result in larger net income subject to taxes. If it is admitted that taxation according to ability can be thought of only in terms of individuals, then progressive taxation of corporate income will have a most unequal effect for the small stockholder in the large corporation will pay a higher percentage of his share of the net earnings in taxes than if he had the same share of net earnings in a small concern. However, if it is desired to restrict 

15 T.N.E.C. Monograph No. 9, p. 26. ..

large-scale enterprise, such a tax may have this effect and investors may be encouraged to place their investments in small concerns where a smaller proportion of earnings will be taken for taxation.

Consolidated Returns 

A policy was followed during 1921-34 which tended to favor integrated corporate systems through permitting such corporations to file consolidated returns covering the parent company and the controlled subsidiaries. In 1932, a small charge of three-fourths of 1 per cent additional tax was imposed for the privilege of filing a consolidated return and in 1933 this was increased to 1 per cent. In general, a consolidated return was favorable to the tax-paying corporation because it permitted offsetting losses in some units against profits in others. From the tax point of view, there is the advantage that it treated business units as operating units rather than as artificially separate corporate entities.

In the period 1928 to 1931, at least half of all federal taxes upon corporate income were reported on consolidated returns.16 The abolition of the privilege of consolidated returns may have little effect upon future income tax yields, because under the present progressive tax system the tendency will be for corporate systems to attempt to break their income down into as many reporting units as possible. Under present tax laws with progressions based on size of taxable income, corporations may find it advantageous tax-wise to create as many separate corporations for tax reporting purposes as operating conditions will permit. It would appear that if the government really wishes to prevent large aggregations of corporate power under one effective management, it must couple a progressive rate structure with a required consolidation of tax returns.

Encouraging the Use of Equity Capital 

In a study made for the years 1934 to 1937, it was found that corporations having a large amount of equity capital paid relatively more income taxes as a percentage of net profit than was true of corporations using a greater proportion of credit capital. In another study of 609 corporations for 1937, similar though by no means uniform results were found; namely, the use of creditor capital tended to reduce income tax payments expressed as a percentage of net 

16 Ibid., p. 45.

I

profits before interest.17 It is evident, therefore, that taxation may have definite effects upon the form or method of capitalization of corporations. What is more important, the effects appear to have been the reverse of certain other governmental policies intended to encourage the use of equity capital. 

Taxation of Equity v. Creditor Capital 

The Federal Income Tax is a tax upon net income remaining after deducting typical business expenses including interest on borrowed capital. While it is constitutionally possible to devise a tax system which would differentiate between various forms or levels of income, the present law attempts to reach only net income available for the ownership interests represented by the various forms of stock and frequently referred to as equity capital. Interest paid upon the borrowed or creditor capital is deductible as a business expense before the tax is computed. The effect is to encourage corporate financing through the use of borrowed funds represented mainly by bonds. 

There are many angles to the problem, but from the point of view of public policy and sound business operation, important advantages arise in a greater use of venture or equity capital. Economic stability is increased, and the danger of forced liquidation and of receivership operation is reduced or avoided in hard times. The benefits to the stockholders arising from trading on the equity are limited, but so are the risks.

Prior to 1918, the income tax law did restrict the amount of interest which could be deducted. In the first income tax law of 1913, interest could not be deducted on an amount of indebtedness greater than one-half the total indebtedness plus the capital stock.18 The 

Revenue Act of 1916 relaxed this limitation with the provision that interest could be deducted whenever the indebtedness on which the interest was paid did not exceed "the sum of (a) the entire amount of the paid-up capital stock and (b) one-half of its interest bearing indebtedness then outstanding." Beginning with the 1918 law, all interest has been fully deductible except on debt which was incurred for the purpose of carrying tax-exempt securities. 

There is some evidence that the foregoing tax treatment of interest on indebtedness has had an effect on the capital structures of cor- 

17 Ibid., Charts 28 and 29 following p. 92. 

18 Ibid., p. 92.

porations. In 1917, gross receipts of all corporations amounted to $84,700,000,000 out of which interest was paid to the extent of $2,200,- 000,000. Gross income increased to $161,200,000,000 in 1929 and total interest payments to $4,900,000,000 in the same year. Beginning in 1930, interest payments for all reporting corporations declined to $3,000,000,000 paid in 1937.19 The large decrease in interest payments after 1930 is due to the large volume of refunding operations to obtain lower rates of interest rather than any large shift to equity financing. 

Encouraging the use of equity capital would result in a greater degree of business stability in good times and bad. In terms of fiscal yield, a tax based upon operating income, i.e., income before the payment of interest and dividends, would also have advantages. It would broaden the base and reduce greatly the fluctuations in yield of the income tax from year to year. Moreover, it would represent the taxation of income with regard to its economic nature rather than its legal existence. Strictly speaking, economic profits do not accrue to the stockholders' equity until a return is earned greater than the average market rates of interest on borrowed funds under the terms for risks involved. Thinking only in terms of the economic relationships, an income tax levied upon operating income (i.e., income before interest and dividends) and graduated to tax the profit or excess return element would be sound. It would produce revenue with greater uniformity than is now the case, and would place the burden upon those lines of enterprise with the greatest relative ability to pay; namely, the enterprise enjoying the highest returns. From the management angle, however, it would undoubtedly result in a trend toward equity financing because debt financing would no longer result in reduced income taxes.

CHAPTER XXXIX  Economic Progress 

PROMINENT economist wrote recently on the challenging subject "Must There be an End to Progress?" The query warrants the most searching analysis, but it equally suggests the existence of a popular mood of defeatism and bewilderment. Needless to say, the complete solution of economic problems relating to progress will not be found solely within the confines of the corporate and financial area. At the same time, it is apparent that there must exist a vital interdependence between social progress, as registered in the form of a secular trend of business, and corporate development. It is not easy to resolve these elements into primary and secondary classifications; likely there is an interchange of position, each serving as cause and effect. Despite this difficulty of delineation, it is desirable to note developments of recent years as well as to attempt some earmarking of responsibility. 120 It is commonly recognized that the results of business operation for the past decade have been inadequate to provide fully for accepted social needs. The most forceful index of this failure is to be found in the unemployment which continued until the inauguration of the current defense program. Not only does enforced idleness produce a form of overhead which serves as a burden on the remaining economy, but in addition, its prevalence breeds a form of unsettling discontent. Under the circumstances, widespread and persistent unemployment must be eliminated if any particular form of economy is to survive. This is more than a question of desirability; it is a necessity. 

Equally important, it is a matter of concern for all groups-employed and unemployed, capital and labor, agricultural and industrial. Too often, the problem is envisaged as one which concerns only those who are unemployed, but actually it also has an enervating effect upon the employed. This is caused both by the burden which the latter are compelled to bear and the absence of opportunities which attend full prosperity.
