It is here that the classical economic doctrine which pronounces there can be no general overproduction offers sound and needed guidance. The structure have crumbled because it lacked balance of the component parts, may but this may mean the existence of certain deficiencies as well as excesses. Unfortunately, popular political and economic thought give emphasis to the abuses of the twenties, and as a consequence there develops a fear complex which retards progress at the present time. 

The failure of business activity to regain previously established levels is made even more serious by the ever increasing demands being made on the economy. On the technological side, both the main-

tenance and expansion of the existing plant is an order of the first magnitude. In terms of human welfare, there is need to provide for an increasing population as well as to accommodate its changing composition. The percentage of youth to the total population is slowly diminishing, while conversely, adults are increasing. This means that the opportunities for employment should increase in greater proportion than the growth of population. To the extent that this does not take place, there is little alternative to the exercise of more or less arbitrary governmental action to take care of the various social needs which develop. Simultaneously, this imposes a greater, as well as a non-productive, burden upon the area of production-be it labor, management, or capital. In short, the nation is confronted today with the task of providing an economy which must meet even greater needs, and at the same time be self-carrying. 

Whose Responsibility? 

In retrospect, the word "responsibility" frequently connotes blame. 

This would not be true if the purpose were to ascertain those who were to be accredited with successful operation. But success is usually taken for granted and inquiry is more commonly instigated in the event of failure, hence, the more unsavory connotation of responsibility, meaning the source of error or mistaken judgment. There shall be little occasion to use responsibility in this sense because our objective is to look to the future. Our inquiry concerns the course of action which will assure maximum production as well as its distribution to accommodate a standard of living which is justified in the light of our resources. From this point of view, responsibility may be interpreted by posing the question: Who will be charged with the task of producing sound prosperity, meaning the development of maximum, social welfare. 

If it were simply a matter of finding jobs for all, extremists might well advocate the creation of some form of dictatorial government. 

On this basis, employment would be ordered in mass instead of individually sought. Already, it is known from the experience of other nations how quickly unemployment may be ended by arbitrary state control. However, the cost of this totalitarian process is yet to be determined. Aside from the effect upon personal liberties, there is no guaranty that forced employment will assure higher wages or an im-

1 1 1 proved standard of living; on the contrary, there is the possibility that living standards will be lowered.

The problem which confronts us is especially perplexing in a democracy where maximum emphasis is placed upon individual initiative and enterprise. Under such a system it is felt that the promotion of individual efforts on a wide front must of necessity produce the greatest social good. Unrestricted individual activity seems to afford. the advantage of the vigor and diversified strength of spontaneous response as distinct from the less stimulating character of directed action. The limited character of our discussion precludes a full analysis of the many developments which have served to curb the free working of a competitive system, but it should be noted that various limiting factors in the form of monopolistic practices and other elements of rigidity have become parasitic attachments to the body economic over a long period of years. Finally, the notorious business depression of the thirties struck with a fury and intensity which. seemed to put free enterprise into a panicky rout. 

Participation by Government 

Under the burden and extreme despair occasioned by depression, free enterprise voluntarily turned to government for succor. Possibly the response of state authority was greater than anticipated. In any event, it is important to recognize that government is now a real and component part of the business system. It may be that in many quarters government is no longer regarded as the invited guest but is viewed as the relative who has overstayed his welcome. But nostalgic sentiment must not be permitted to blind us to the realitie For better or worse, government is wedded to business enterprise by ties which are bound to exist irrespective of the political party which may be in power. A debt has been created which will require taxes for its servicing for decades to come. Business will be called upon to shoulder a heavy share. Direct loans have been made which automatically give the government a voice in operating policies. Indeed, in certain instances, terms of agreement relating to the loans give express authority to the government's lending agency to change management personnel. Viewed in a philosophical vein, such controlling relationships may come as a rude shock to those who worship at the shrine of a century of virtually free and unbridled enterprise. 

But the answer cannot come so simply from fond recollection; instead,

it can emerge only from a frank realization and consideration of the facts as they exist.

Because government participation is no longer a matter of free alternative, at least to the extent of its present encroachment, it follows that the formulation of future business policy must provide for adequate representation of the public interest. It is easy to deride this observation as a form of socialism, but such ready dismissal overlooks the incidences of control arising from dollars and cents investment previously cited. No attempt is being made here to advance individual preference as to the form of our economy; rather it is the hope to prognosticate in the light of facts which already exist. 

The common interests of both government and business will undoubtedly compel some form of co-operative effort.2 This will necessarily produce various changes from the old business process as well as modify incentives which have stimulated business activity in the past. 

For instance, there is already evidence that individuals of both low and high standing are attaching more significance to the wages or salary received from a job than to the profits which characterized business opportunities of the past. Fears may be expressed about this lessening of the profit motive, but disaster is not necessarily the inevitable outcome. Instead, other forms of organization are likely to evolve with reasonable opportunity for individual participation and initiative. 

As a possibility, it may be that greater use will be made of mutual organization, a basis upon which life insurance companies have already made an enviable record.

Another compelling force which is likely to give emphasis to greater participation by government is the uncertainty and instability of our times. One need not be a gloomy prophet to entertain the existence of this contingency. The wars which are now in process throughout the world are certain to leave provoking and far-reaching social problems in their wake. Paradoxical as it may seem, war appears to act as a business stimulant while the ensuing peace seems to produce a sort of business stalemate. This is not surprising when one recognizes the disturbance which is caused by numerous shifts 

2 Charles E. Wilson, president of the General Electric Company, comments in Total 

Security-A Challenge, p. 10, as follows: “. . . I present no thought of arm's-length cooperation, over-shadowed by suspicion between government and business. Instead, I seek armin-arm concord and co-ordinated effort in the common good-the kind of concord and effort which can, in my judgment, eliminate the causes of conflict, competition, and confusion between government and business."

and adjustments within the economy which are caused by the transition. Moreover, experience has now shown that business itself will likely turn to government for assistance. 

What the precise pattern of organization will be is not now apparent. It will likely unfold as the problems present themselves and solutions are attempted. That there will be room for both government and relatively free private institutions seems to be a reasonable assurance in our own country at the moment. Much will depend upon the extent to which business corporations recognize and provide for broad, social responsibilities which have previously been regarded as extraneous to their operation. In short, it appears that there will be joint responsibility and our discussion may now turn to an analysis of the respective parts to be played by the two parties. 

Corporate Responsibility 

Corporations have generally pursued a policy of isolationism. They were deemed to be distinct entities seeking to advance their own restricted interests; simultaneously, it was believed that this self-advancement automatically contributed to the welfare of the entire society. 

Largely as a result of thriving business over a long period of years, this developed into a sort of tradition. But events of recent years have tended to break through this shell of corporate identity and cause several questions to be raised about the responsibility of business toward the whole economy.

On a number of occasions it has been indicated that the corporation owes its birthright to the state, and for this reason it may be held to have a definite obligation to the public as well as to the more specific owners of the enterprise. However, like so many bestowed rights, it is easy to take them for granted once they become a common privilege. 

Similarly, incorporation has come to be regarded as being available for the asking rather than being granted upon proof of service to be rendered. To remove this bias of established practice, it is desirable to recall the character of the corporation's origin. 

In earlier years, incorporation was a matter of legislative enactment where each individual application was given special consideration as a matter of public policy. It is true that political abuses and increased demand for the corporate form led to the passage of general incorporation statutes, but it is important not to overlook the original classification of the corporation as an instrument of limited availability. In

principle, the grant of charter was to facilitate the "fulfillment of some public purpose. Nor was the advancement of private interests deemed a sufficient justification for the grant of such privileges as perpetual succession, limited liability, and delegation of power to designated individuals to act for the group." 

Reference to this early aversion to the granting of broad powers to private corporations may appear inopportune because of the remoteness of time. To a great degree, rights are evolutionary in character and are necessarily attuned to the conditions which prevail at any given moment. In this light, the march of business over the past century is bound to be a conditioning factor of first rank. It may well be cause for changing public policies in granting charters. However, this type of reasoning must apply equally to the new set of conditions which have developed over the past decade. In short, for the same reason that expanding business of prior decades may have justified more liberal treatment of corporations, the retrogression of the thirties may be held to be sufficient cause for curtailment now. 

Another feature of the present corporate structure which lends emphasis to the public interest is the separation of ownership from control. Legally, the stockholders have the power to elect directors, but the difficulties of exercising this privilege intelligently are well known. In any event, there is created a condition where the interests of the many are placed in the hands of the few. While it may be recognized that this delegation of authority is a most necessary requisite of orderly management, at the same time the character of the responsibility which is created is equally one of a broad, trustee nature. In fact, the representation takes on a form of public interest. 

If, then, the responsibility of the corporation toward the social economy be admitted, what is its precise character? Rather than offer any final pronouncement in answer, it is fitting to give consideration to the opinions which have general circulation. Here increasing attention is being paid to the accountability of the corporation for matters within its household as well as to the various obligations outside of the field of its immediate operations. Broadly speaking, therefore, the responsibilities of a corporation may be classified into (1) those of an internal nature, and (2) those of an external nature. 

3 Lyon, Watkins, and Abramson, Government and Economic Life, Vol. I, p. 49, Publication No. 79 of the Institute of Economics of the Brookings Institution.

Corporate Responsibility-Internal 

To a great extent, recognition of corporate internal responsibility may be taken for granted. The only possible dispute concerns its character-narrow or broad, spontaneous or coerced, restricted or comprehensive. In short, is the broad purpose of corporate policy one of advancing and accounting for investor interests, or is it primarily designed to favor special interests? Many instances are on record where the few on the inside capitalized on their favored position at the expense of the larger group which furnished the capital and carried the real risk. As a result, there is today a profound public consciousness of the need for proper corporate accounting. 

There follows the question as to the situs of the responsibility for the provision of proper accounting and adequate protection of all the various interests. It may be contended that investors already have the necessary legal rights to defend their interests, as well as having access to the courts. However, the expense of litigation and the practical obstacles which prevent joint action preclude prompt and effective response on their part. Under the circumstances, there is need to correct the impotency of scattered investors if their existing rights are to be exercised. Thus, there has developed a marked tendency to designate government as a sort of indenture trustee to act in behalf of those having investment in business enterprise. 

The enlargement of the supervisory powers of government is usually the cause for surprise and shock in the business community. But careful examination shows that often no new rights are created; instead, there is simply an empowering of governmental agencies to enforce rights already in existence. The immobilized state of investors had largely prevented giving effect to the numerous powers whereas the mobilized force of government is more apt to induce their application. Of course, it is important that the objective of supervision by government be kept in mind. Where it is used for punitive or arbitrary purposes, there exists a form of abuse just as if special, private interests had vitiated their trust. 

Where private management holds its trust in high regard there should be little occasion for governmental interference. Often, however, there is a tendency for management to develop a form, of vested interest. Particularized motives may supplant the larger, corporate interest. Peculiar rights are believed to accrue in favor of management or controlling groups by virtue of their record or long associa-

tion with an enterprise. Like lords of ancient feudal estates, there are assumed prerogatives by inside interests with reference to their industrial domain. As a consequence, there is failure to recognize the true, legal relationship which exists between management and owner. Overlooked is the basic premise that "other people's money" is being used to conduct business enterprise.

In large-scale business today, management is a delegated function. 

The delegation is underwritten by powers of attorney or other legal means, but at the same time the very franchise of authority carries definite and implied obligations of responsibility. Especially does this mean complete accounting by management for its activities. The real issue is, therefore, who will determine the adequacy of the accounting. 

Ardent advocates of individualism naturally declare this to be solely within the province of the private owners. Others believe that government has a moral obligation to assure full and complete accounting. Emphasis is placed upon the fact that the charter is a form of special privilege granted by the state and that its continuance depends upon the character in which the privilege is exercised. 

Much of the conflict between these two philosophies could be eliminated if their representatives would place less stress on the means and always keep in focus the common objective. Either course utilizes the agency principle, the choice being whether widely scattered investors shall be represented by private parties or by agencies of government. American tradition undoubtedly favors the former and recourse to authoritarian procedure should be a last resort. It is only where serious abuse develops under private representation that government should proceed to take action. The danger today is that the introduction of governmental authority to correct admitted abuses may cause the agencies of government to go beyond the point of correction. 

History records in no uncertain terms that the momentum of unleashed governmental action often carries beyond the role of umpire into that of active participant. For this reason there is real need to think through various reforms, with full recognition of the ultimate as well as the immediate effects. 

The expansion of the regulatory power of government does seem inconsistent with the emphasis placed upon private rights throughout the development of our country. It was assumed that the cultivation of private interests automatically contributed to the larger, public interest. Now there is a marked tendency to advance the thought that

the two interests are in conflict. In an address to the Federal Bar 

Association, an attorney general of the United States stated that "a respected private bar is engaged in the work of moulding the law slowly but steadily in the private interest." He then urged the Federal Bar composed of lawyers working for governmental agencies to "guide the processes of our courts in the direction of the public in- 99 terests.

A newspaper commentator took issue with the suggested antithesis between the advancement of private rights and its effect upon the public interest. He called attention to our historical foundations and observed that neither the Declaration of Independence nor "the Constitution made mention of 'the public interest,' but the Constitution had much to say on the point of personal rights." He raises the question as to whether the creation of a distinct and separate "public interest" has been effected "to meet the need of a modern philosophy which sinks the individual and his personal rights in society." 

Probably the concept of a public interest evolved in response to numerous conditions utterly unlike those which existed at the time of this nation's founding. In our early history, ownership and control were essentially bilateral, and agriculture represented the larger part of our economy. Today, there is marked separation between ownership and control, and large industry, with its attendant urban life, creates an entirely different economic framework. Call it "public interest," or devise other terminology, there has come into being a new set of problems which have seemed to halt the onward march of "private interest." In fact, these private interests turned to government on their own accord for assistance. Because of this combination of circumstances a fait accompli must now be recognized, viz., a common and pronounced recognition of broad, public rights. 

As has been observed, the public interest has become cause for intrusion within long-recognized private reservations. Our chief hope for the preservation of the vitality and virtues of private interest cannot come from simple reverence for the past; rather, private industry must deal with the facts at hand and prove its superiority. By this means, the chief support of private enterprise, public opinion, will come to its defense. 

Thomas F. Woodlock, "Thinking It Over," Wall Street Journal (February 5, 1940), p. 4.

Corporate Responsibility-External 

Consideration may now be given to corporate responsibility, if any, toward the entire economy. More specifically, does the individual corporation have an obligation to improve general business conditions? Naturally, it will seek at all times to promote its own interests, but these are affected by such broad phenomena as unemployment, depressed agricultural conditions, currency and credit inflation, etc. 

Should the individual unit take action to modify these larger influences, which are, in a sense, foreign to its own specific operation? 

Under a truly competitive economy, there would appear to be little occasion to embark on such ventures, but all of us are aware of the many compromises with vigorous competition. Moreover, public opinion and governmental policy play a large part in determining the answer. Recent trends of thought show that attention is being directed, particularly, to two types of corporate responsibility: (1) the stabilization of business and (2) provision for social security. 

The Stabilization of Business 

In the opinion of many, the stabilization of business is both desirable and necessary to solve existing problems. At this point, it is not necessary to consider the merits of this proposition, but our comments may be confined to the question of the responsibility of corporations to make it effective. Heretofore, the business cycle was virtually taken for granted, and the main task of business enterprise was to adapt itself to the changes. Today, business is being held liable for the cycle and is being told that it must assume its share of the leadership in disposing of the phenomenon. It is declared that wage policies, dividend policies, programs of expansion and other aspects of corporate activity affect social welfare and must be established with due consideration of their effect upon the activity of the whole. 

The validity of the foregoing philosophy is, of course, open to question. Is not the corporation's chief concern the preservation of funds committed to it by stockholders, bondholders, and various other claimants? Does it not partake of the nature of an ordinary trustee in which its first duty is to provide for the protection of the trustor's rights? Clearly, these are questions not simply of finance, but they involve the very essence of our whole economic system. Nevertheless, it will be observed that the answers will take form largely

in financial language. In the first place, the earnings of business enterprise would be vitally affected by any attempt on the part of individual business units to iron out extreme fluctuations. Secondly, these changes would be transmitted to the various equities, and their values affected as a result.

Some business leaders believe that stabilization would be an aid to earnings by virtue of the elimination of numerous uncertainties which play havoc with both gross and net income. Testifying before the Temporary National Economic Committee, the president of the Anaconda Copper Mining Corporation suggested a program of industry co-operation under governmental supervision.5 In essence, the various companies of a particualr industry would be permitted to formulate a specific agreement to control prices and pro ction. The agreements would be open for public inspection and subject to review by the federal courts. Unlike the ill-fated program provided under the National Industrial Recovery Act, the rapprochement of competing business units would be voluntary. It is proposed that the federal government scrutinize these industrial agreements, but review of this character would not be carried to the point of active regulation. 

Obviously, revision of the anti-trust laws would be necessary to permit industry co-operation of the type proposed. 

In a similar vein, it is reported "that the choice we have been facing for many years is not between pioneer individualism and state socialism, but is a choice between self-government in industry, under a limited but necessary governmental supervision, and a complete political control of industry." Here it will be noted that some form of control is taken for granted-the alternative being one of private or political sponsorship. Confronted with such proposals, the broader questions of policy become apparent. Under competition, there is little occasion for governmental interference since price and output are determined by market action. But under any system of control, there appears the query of the right by which it may be assumed by private sources. Can it be assumed that private incentive will function to public advantage when no longer subject to competitive pressure?

Verbatim Record of Proceedings of the Temporary National Economic Committee, 

January 15-February 17, 1940, p. 79. • Address of Donald R. Richberg before National Automobile Dealers' Association, Congressional Record, Appendix, February 7, 1940, p. 1859.

Stabilization too often becomes a fetish with its own brand of self-righteousness, but there are dangers of inflexibility which may prove costly in the long run. Moreover, it may easily degenerate into a form of special interest favoritism at the expense of the more important and broader, public interest. Most proponents of selfgoverned industry control recognize the need for some degree of governmental supervision, but it is usually of a passive variety. 

There is also need to question both the desirability and the feasibility of stabilization. At what level? May adjustment be effected to meet changing needs? Questions of this type suggest many difficulties which are inherent in programs of control. What, then, is the solution? As far as the writers are concerned, this opportunity may be taken to express their belief in competition. Admittedly, this may be a minority point of view and held in disfavor by many governmental and business leaders, but it is possible that the competitive system has been abandoned all too readily. Occasionally, one hears a "declaration of faith" in competition, such as:

I don't know anything better. . . . . I don't find that the countries which have abandoned competition are satisfied with their condition. Competition is the driving force in economy. I can't help but feel that some part of our failure to use our greater resources is due to the decline of competition. I would like to see, as a matter of experiment, a realistic attempt to put some of our basic industries on a competitive basis by withdrawing some of the sources of their monopolistic power.

Also, in the message of the President of the United States in April, 1938, to the Congress which finally led to the creation of the Temporary National Economic Committee, there is noteworthy recognition of the principles of competition. Speaking of events abroad, the following "two simple truths about the liberty of a democratic people" were set forth: (1) The first simple truth is that the liberty of a democracy is not safe if the people tolerate the growth of private power to the point where it becomes stronger than their democratic state itself. That, in essence, is a fascismownership of government by an individual, by a group, or by any other controlling private power. 

7 Statement of Leon Henderson, as reported in the Commercial and Financial Chronicle, Vol. 149 (December 30, 1939), p. 4110.

The second truth is that the liberty of a democracy is not safe if its business system does not provide employment and produce and distribute goods in such a way as to sustain an acceptable standard of living. 

Because of these dangers, the President recommended "a thorough study of the concentration of economic power in American industry and the effect of that concentration upon the decline of competition." 

Speaking further of the program to investigate the concentration of business, the following quotations from this address reflect the values of competition: 

It is a program whose basic thesis is not that the system of free private enterprise for profit has failed in this generation, but that it has not yet been tried. ... · 

It is a program to preserve private enterprise for profit by keeping it free enough to be able to utilize all our resources of capital and labor at a profit. 

It is a program whose basic purpose is to stop the progress of collectivism in business and turn business back to the democratic competitive order. 1 Competition imparts a vigor to the national economy which is not found under control programs. Under the latter, privilege and favoritism are bound to appear, with resulting inbreeding of weakness. There is a perpetuation of the status quo where survival is determined by sanction of authority. In marked contrast, competition forces continuous weeding out of the unfit and places a premium on the ruggedness of each separate unit. And individual solvency is prerequisite to the solvency of the whole. This emphasis upon the single business unit may accentuate the adoption of conservative business policies in periods of depression, but assuming effective competition, unwise expansion should be curbed in periods of boom. In large measure, the competitive process accepts the business cycle as inevitable but provides its own corrective agent in the form of price changes. However, viewing current political and economic thought, there appears to be little prospect for the return of free competition in the near future.

Provision for Social Security 

Another response to the uncertainties of business is found in the increasing demand for social security. Unfortunately, its underlying doctrine is often predicated upon a curtailment of individual oppor- 8 Hearings before the Temporary National Economic Committee, Congress of the United 

States, 75th Congress, 3d Session, Part I, Economic Prologue, December 1-3, 1938, pp. 185, 189, and 191.

tunity and freedom. It is not always the intent to limit the scope of free enterprise, but the taxes and legal restrictions which are a part of the social security program serve to restrain business activity in many ways. Indeed, social security tends to become the supreme objective rather than permitting the degree of security to be determined by the capacity of business to support it. In a similar vein, numerous proponents of various social security devices are inclined to regard them as a means of creating prosperity. 

There is now little question that business enterprise must participate in providing for the various contingencies which give rise to insecurity. Unemployment insurance, provision for old age, and various forms of compensation insurance are already in common use, being financed by business directly, or through joint action of government and private enterprise. Thus, in the case of the federal social security program a tax is paid by the individual workers, but is collected through the employer. When the present program is in full operation, this tax will amount to 6 per cent of the payroll-3 per cent to be borne by the employees and 3 per cent by the employers. 

It is inopportune to discuss in this volume the many ramifications of social security, our chief interest being confined to the character of the corporate responsibility for this social burden. Action already taken bespeaks its formal recognition and the main issue which remains is the extent to which business corporations will be called upon to finance the various aids to security. In the last analysis, public opinion will decide the question, and the actual realization of the security benefits will depend upon the ability of the business economy to carry the load.

Government Responsibility 

Under a competitive system, it may appear that little room is left for action by government. On the contrary, there is imposed upon government and its agencies the most dignified and essential task of all, that of supervising or officiating competition. Because of the rivalry which it stimulates, there is need for an umpire who will enforce the rules of fair conduct as well as require the observance of minimum standards. The government is peculiarly fitted to play this role as well as to take steps to raise the plane or level upon which the game of business is being staged. Consideration may be given to the relationships which exist between business and government

during the three possible stages of corporate life: (1) the promotion of business enterprise, (2) the operation of business enterprise, (3) the failure and reorganization of business enterprise. 

Promotion and the Government's Responsibility 

Until recent years, it was not unusual to consider losses by investors as a legitimate and normal cost of promotion. It was expected that investors would carry the usual business risks and, in return, be entitled to the profits of appreciation and normal operating earnings. 

In performing this function, investors have every right to expect protection against fraud and other forms of deceit. The facilities which are required to render this protective service are essentially of a policing character which logically fall within the realm of governmental activity. Therefore, governmental supervision of promoting ventures is proper and should be so effective that wildcat or fly-by-night attractions should be almost an impossibility. Reference has already been made to the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 which are serving to reduce the numerous unfair and deceptive practices so prevalent prior to recent years. 

The patrol of promotional activities has for the most part been confined to the issuance of securities. The effectiveness of this surveillance, however, is vitally affected by the fact that corporate charters are granted by the individual states. To have the powers of the corporation emanate from one source and regulation from another obviously lessen the potency of governmental influence. Giving consideration particularly to interstate commerce, the arguments in favor of federal incorporation are clear and forceful. The usual arguments are advanced against this further centralization of power, but it should afford many advantages to both government and business. 

To the former, it should bring about much needed co-ordination of supervisory practice; to the latter, benefits would accrue through increased uniformity and certainty of requirements to be met. 

The lessening of competition has served not only to remove many familiar checks on business, but, equally significant, it has destroyed many of the incentives to promote new business. There is a bare possibility that government eventually may find it necessary to offer inducements to initiate new enterprise. Pointing in this direction is the insurance of loan risks described in Chapter XVIII, and in other instances the government has assumed the role of investor. Con-

ceivably, such aid may take the form of outright subsidies, or to go still further, the state may assume the role of entrepreneur. Again, let it be said, that the writers are not expressing their personal preference, but are simply trying to interpret the developments of recent years.

Government and the Operation of Business Enterprise 

The government, either state or federal, has long played a direct and prominent part during the inception and termination of a corporation. Throughout the active and operating life of an enterprise, there was little interference as long as any organization did not run afoul of the law. Business has been compelled to live up to various requirements in the way of industrial insurance, taxes, sanitary and working standards, etc., but at the same time, management has been allowed a comparatively free hand. For the most part, the state played a negative part and did little along positive and aggressive lines.

Recent tendencies give some indication that the state may assume in the future a more important voice in the policies of various industries, if not of the individual companies. The National Industrial 

Recovery Act, more familiarly known as the N.I.R.A., was distinctly a step in this direction. Minimum wages were established, prices were controlled, output was regulated, and various other forms of standardization were required; individual management was distinctly limited in the exercise of independent judgment. The Supreme Court declared the Act to be unconstitutional, but numerous other legislative measures have served in less blanket fashion to affect corporate policy. The tax on undistributed profits, no longer in effect, had material influence upon dividend policies, and the existing laws decreeing minimum wages and maximum hours necessarily affect the decisions of private management. 

This increasing control is undoubtedly the result of public opinion but it is also a quid pro quo-the assumption of a voice by government in exchange for aid often requested by industry itself. Purely on the basis of logic, business must expect continued exercise of gov ernmental influence if it continues to receive public funds. Bankers have long made control an incidence of investment, and it should not occasion surprise to have government respond in a similar manner. 

At the same time, fairness demands that government accept the risks

813. on a par with comparable owners of private rights. Business men may charge that "Government control of business masquerading under the term 'regulation' is stifling private enterprise and genuine recovery," but private business must demonstrate an ability to operate on its own if it is to avoid government interference. 

Government and the Failure of Business Enterprise The government takes the role of either the family doctor or the undertaker when the business unit gets into difficulties. Thus, receivers or trustees may be appointed by the court either for purposes of reorganization or bankruptcy proceedings. Modification of the bankruptcy laws was prompted no doubt because of the wreckage resulting from the depression, but in addition it also reflects a growing recognition of the rights of small investors. Government clearly has a moral obligation to assure fair and equitable treatment of claimants against companies in default. The sharpening of this governmental responsibilty in recent years should contribute materially toward safeguarding private rights and promoting the public interest. 

In earlier chapters, the various steps which have been taken to facilitate the process of reorganization and bankruptcy have been discussed. Judged in the light of earlier standards, there appears to be some weakening of minority rights. Plans of reorganization may be forced upon recalcitrant participants where the court deems the overhauling to be beneficial to the larger group. It is hazardous to formulate a broad generalization about the ultimate effects of this curtailment of individual prerogatives, but it may be observed that clear recognition of property rights is essential to an orderly business process.

Investment represents a long-term commitment which rests upon an undergirding structure of confidence. In turn, this confidence is developed in large measure on the basis of reasonable expectation that adequate facilities are assured for the protection of the rights of the obligee against the obligor. The measures which have been adopted to safeguard the vast army of small investors should serve to stimulate confidence. More questionable is the tendency toward weakening of the rights which accrue through priority of lien. It is difficult to forecast the ultimate repercussions of the involuntary modification of contractual rights. Much of the expected reaction to date has been prevented by easy money conditions as well as hidden by the greater magnitude of pressing, social problems.

CHAPTER XL THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 

INCE our primary interest in this volume is found in the financing of corporations, it is fitting that some observations be made about the possible impact of social change on financial policies and practices. Prior to the recent depression, corporate financing was deemed to be essentially a private affair, but it must now be apparent that considerable modification of this assumed prerogative has already taken place. It will be our purpose in this concluding chapter to review the effects on corporation finance and to appraise the possibilties of further change.

Limitations Placed upon Use of Corporate Form 

Because of the interrelationships between organization and finance, attention may first be directed to the limitations which are being placed upon the use of the corporate form of organization. Often, in the past, the corporation was used solely as a control mechanism while its original and primary purpose was ignored. Used in this manner, the corporation became essentially a restricted private facility, and less emphasis was placed upon its value as an instrument designed to promote the public welfare. As a result, the present vast corporate system is a far cry from the original intended limitation of the corporate unit to a single business purpose. 

In specialized fields of business enterprise, government has long exercised control over the creation of new corporations. Thus, the organization of new railways and public utilities was restricted because of the monopolistic character of the business. Similarly, restraint was placed upon the chartering of banks and other financial institutions for the purpose of avoiding overcrowding in this field as well as to prevent unnecessary failures. As a specific example of such limitation, the following standards which are imposed by law for the chartering of federal savings and loan associations may be noted: 

No charter shall be granted except to persons of good character and responsibility, nor unless in the judgment of the Board a necessity exists for such an institution in the community to be served, nor unless there is a reasonable prob- 816

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 817 

ability of its usefulness and success, nor unless the same can be established without undue injury to properly conducted existing local thrift and homefinancing institutions.¹

In all these instances, the curbing of new charters arose primarily as a result of the nature of the business. Competition was presumed to be harmful if carried beyond a certain point, and hence regulation was deemed to be essential as a means of protecting the public interest. Recent developments, however, take root more especially in the form of organization as distinct from the nature of the business. 

Thus, the holding company with its network of control is condemned not simply because of its use in connection with the operation of public utilities, but, instead, stress is placed upon the deterring effects of structural arrangement. In addition, it is of interest to note that in many recent reforms, the cause for action is to be found in the interests of investors as much as the effects upon consumers. 

Whether the limitations upon the activities of holding companies will be confined to the public utilities or extended to blanket the entire area of financial and business operation is purely a question of conjecture. The trend of thought in recent years would indicate that the industrial area may also be affected or that its exclusion will depend upon the moderation of corporate interrelationships. For the most part, few industrial systems in the past developed beyond the second degree of control, and the entire organization of corporate arrangement was much more simple than was true of the public utilities. As a result, industrial companies escaped the stringent reforms which were adopted with reference to the latter. 

Relationship between Size and the Corporate Structure 

As stated previously, the chief criterion of public interest in the past was deemed to be the nature of the business. Thus, the various types of public utilities and most forms of financial institutions were commonly thought to be subject to some degree of regulation and supervision. In marked contrast, the industrial and commercial area was held free from such interference because it was presumed that competition would function to protect the public interest. However, the many compromises which have been effected with competitive principles suggest that, in the future, the modus operandi of the in- 

1 Home Owners' Loan Act of 1933 as amended, Section 5 (e).

dustrial group may be revised. As a criterion for such action, there is some indication that size may be the determining factor of classification.

It is well known that one, or at most a few companies, account for a large share of the output of many familiar products. In such instances, competition may not have been entirely stifled, but at the same time, it is necessarily modified or even controlled.2 As a result, there is increasing reference to size as an element of business operation affecting public welfare. Moreover, this is true entirely aside from the question of abuse of privilege by private interests; instead, there is simply a recognition of the fact that the action of the few may have great influence upon the many. In several industries, as few as four companies will account for a great majority of the total employment; for example, in the manufacture of motor vehicles, four companies account for more than 85 per cent of the total employment.3 

Another indication of the concentration of business is found in the large proportion of the total assets which is owned by a limited number of companies. The dominance of the large company is more pronounced in the public utility and transportation fields than in the case of the manufacturing area, but the latter is by no means typified by the small enterprise. This may be seen in the following summary which shows the percentage of total assets (less depreciation and taxable investments) held by the largest corporations:4

As long as business conditions were reasonably prosperous, few questions were raised about this concentration of ownership. It was inevitable, however, that the question of responsibility was raised in the severe depression of the thirties and this concentration of control simplified the attack. Where there is a diffusion of responsibility, it is not easy to establish particular accountability; but a state of con- 

2 See chapters X and XXX. 

3 National Resources Committee, The Structure of the American Economy, Part I (Wash ington: Government Printing Office, 1939), p. 112. ▲ Ibid., p. 106.

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 819 

centration highlights the few into a position of prominence. And in so many words those in control are called upon to perform or to subject themselves to changes which will provide full employment and acceptable living standards. Thus far, some business leaders have ignored the challenge and seek cover under the shield of traditional private rights; others have acknowledged their responsibility and suggest necessary reforms of the business system.5 In any event, it would seem that the large corporation has no escape from a measure of accountability not previously held in consonance with private operation.

There can be little quarrel with the broad principle that the corporate fiction is created solely for the benefit of society, and it must equally follow that pronounced social change will inevitably affect the corporate structure. Hence, little surprise should be occasioned if the large corporation of tomorrow is subjected to increased governmental regulation and supervision. This statement should not be interpreted as advocating such a course but simply as an attempt to read the signs of the times and to anticipate the march of movements already under way. In essence, it would seem that to retain freedom of private enterprise, the size of operation may become an increasing mark of distinction. The small corporation with its limited orbit of operation would be deemed to have such minor effect on the public interest that public regulation would be unnecessary; oppositely, large corporations because of their influence on employment, prices, and other factors affecting the social welfare would be brought within the purview of government. 

The Principle of Representation in the Large Corporation In a previous chapter, the nature of management was discussed at some length; here, there is need only to observe the possible impact of social change. Under the capitalistic system, the election of directors has so long been founded in the rights of ownership that it is not easy to anticipate its abandonment. In reality, however, it is well known that outright stock ownership has little influence on the election of directors for large corporations. The right is preserved in legal form, but its effectiveness has been largely destroyed by the 

5 See Total Security-A Challenge, by Charles E. Wilson, President of the General Elec tric Company, before the midwinter convention of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, January 29, 1941.

proxy system. Moreover, the latter is an absolute necessity both because of the size of many corporations as well as the scattered character of ownership. Under the Securities Exchange Act, an attempt is made to give the proxy a greater effectiveness as a representation of the stockholders' interests, but it is open to question as to whether this can be accomplished in light of the structural character of the modern corporation. Stockholders cannot be compelled to vote, and their lack of understanding plus their geographical dispersion may not be readily overcome by the simple expedient of orderly process. 

Despite this wide breach between management and stockholder, their relationship must necessarily be founded upon some principle which has legal and public acceptance. From the beginnings of the corporate system, the latter has been that of representation by the directors of the stockholder interests. In brief, the director was elected not to represent his own interests but to act entirely in behalf of the stockholding body as a group. The courts went so far as to recognize the hostility of personal gain by directors when such gain was derived at the expense of the corporation. Stated more positively, the fiduciary character of the director's position was generally recognized and charged with many of the duties of the ordinary trustee. 

Deficiences of the Principle of Representation Despite the high ethical rating of the principle of representation as a form of democratic process, it has become more of a ritual than a living expression of delegated authority. With the loss of personal contact between stockholders and directors, there is little to inspire and to motivate the latter. Some contend that the innate desire of the directors to better themselves must automatically redound to be the benefit of the stockholders, but this view fails to allow for possible conflicts of interest. Others feel that the position of a director needs further recognition as a form of public service and that directors should be imbued with a deep sense of social responsibility. This second appeal has the weakness of expecting men to assume considerable liability without expectation of compensating monetary reward.

In addition to these weaknesses of motivation, the system of election is perfunctory instead of functional. There is neither provision for the creation of a diversified board nor arrangement for the representation of different stock interests. A few companies have been

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 821 

1 farsighted enough to select directors with varied experience and training, but the most common practice is to choose men who will repre- 1 sent the controlling financial or management interest. To remedy this condition, much could be done by prescribing the composition of the board of directors. Obviously, there is no standard formula to accomplish this, but the practice of many of the government corporations indicates the possibilties. For example, the directors of the 

Federal Reserve Banks are divided into three classes, two of which are intended to represent ownership interests while the other is appointed to represent the public interest. By this means, men with diversified experience in finance, business, agriculture, and public service may be chosen.

Another example of the perfunctory character of corporate election systems is their failure to assure representation of minority or different stock interests. Some states do require the use of cumulative voting, but corporate management, itself, has been slow in advocating a program which would cause the board to represent a cross-section of the ownership interests. Again, the practices of government corporations with private stockholdings may be cited as an example of what can be done. In both the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Home Loan Bank System, the stockholders of the regional banks have been classified according to size groups, thereby assuring the representation of small as well as the large institutions. 

In similar manner, private industry, if it wanted to, could devise a system which would permit small stockholders to have their own special representatives.

The Outlook for More Adequate Representation It is difficult at this time to predict whether private corporations will of their own volition provide for more adequate representation of the stockholding interests. In any event, such a transformation would not likely be abrupt but would evolve in response to numerous social pressures. The most important of these is the Securities and 

Exchange Commission which serves as the champion of the rights of investors. Here is an agency combining both the force of government sponsorship and important rights of investors which have long remained inert for want of organization. Already it has been responsible for many changes in financial practice, and no one can predict the final outcome.

A more indirect force at the present time is the defense program which is necessarily bringing about a closer liaison between government and private industry. As a result, government is not only exercising greater control over business operations, but in addition, business leaders are becoming public servants in the management of their own institutions as well as in actual service in governmental departments. It is possible that this experience may be converted to private use after the existing emergency.

The Existing Multiplicity of Types of Securities in the Capital Structure 

Like the habiliment of American youth, the financial dress of our business enterprise has been varied and colorful. Bonds with varied degrees of priority of lien and other individual traits too numerous to mention, preferred stocks with various combinations of rights and privileges, even common stock with different shades of control and rights to dividends, all these are reflected in the capital structure of American business. Indeed, there is such overlapping of the three basic types of securities-bonds, preferred stock, and common stockthat satisfactory classification, even along these lines, is impossible. 

The kaleidoscopic character of the financial pattern is typical of our general mode of living, but its benefits to financial management and investors alike may be questioned. The former may become the victim of restrictions or privileges which they helped to originate while the latter become confused by the complexity of non-uniformity. 

It is true that special features are attached to new security issues for purposes of sales appeal, but this often results in placing undesirable emphasis upon the individual security instead of the general credit position. Of course it may be said that investment demands vary considerably and run the gamut from a willingness to assume the primary risk to that which insist. upon gilt-edged security, but, nonetheless, the diversity of security issues may be carried too far. There may easily be overemphasis of special privilege at the expense of analysis of the overall credit position.

Possibilities of Standardization 

The standardization of the types of securities, and indeed of the security forms as well, offers numerous advantages. Not only would there be simplification of the financial pattern with its resulting sav-

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 823 

ings, but in addition, there should be an upbuilding of investor confidence. All too frequently, the wizardry of finance assumes more prominence than the soundness of financial position, and investors become suspicious of financial transactions. The standardization of securities would permit the investor to ignore the dangers of special limitations and to concentrate upon the essential factors of investment merit.

Arbitrary control of the types of securities as well as the form in which they are issued would now likely be considered as an unwarranted curtailment of individual rights, but at the same time its adoption should not be too surprising in view of the magnitude of recent social change. Already the securities of railroads and public utilities must have the approval of regulatory bodies, and it would be reasonable to expect some standardization of pattern as a result of this common administration. As stated at another point, the Securities and Exchange Commission seems to look with favor upon greater uniformity of securities, and the provisions of the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 seem to point in this direction. 

It may be argued that the standardization of securities may restrict the flow of capital to industry although this is by no means an assured conclusion. Such institutions as banks and savings and loan associations are now limited in the type of investment or savings media which may be employed. By concentrating upon fewer types, it has been possible to attract a larger public following. Similarly, if other fields of enterprise would place greater stress upon operating record and soundness of business position, it is possible that the added financial accessories would be unnecessary. 

The Demand for Greater Publicity 

In the past, too many corporations were open as to ownership, but they were not equally open as to information. Annual reports were largely messages of good cheer, and the real problems of operation were veiled in secrecy. It was not considered good public relations to report anything which was unfavorable because of the fear of disrupting public confidence. Now, there is increasing recognition of the fact that a public which hears only good news is not properly conditioned for the shock of bad news. Hence, it is not surprising that in the early thirties the succession of failures and other unfavorable developments produced a public crisis. 

One of the encouraging notes in these troubled times is the de-

mand to hear the truth. Not only is this true with respect to public affairs, but it is becoming increasingly true with respect to business institutions. One of the evidences of this new state of mind is the earlier reference to the Securities Act of 1933 as the "Truth in Securities Bill." In this Act, as well as the Securities Exchange Act, provision is made for dissemination of facts which were previously considered to be highly confidential. Consider, for example, the reporting of the following: officers' salaries and bonus arrangements, the security holdings of leading officers and directors, trading in securities by officers and directors, etc.

Many improvements in reporting have come about as a result of legislation, but the greatest opportunity for proper reporting is to be found in voluntary action by management. To this end, financial statements and annual reports should become true chronicles of business operations. Management should attempt to report accurately the true state of affairs without attempting to color the results one way or the other. As the owners of the enterprise, the stockholders are entitled to know exactly what happened, and management which deliberately conceals the pertinent facts of operation is assuming a power which is not consistent with sound corporate organization. 

Suggested Nature of Financial Statements 

Aside from the larger opportunities which are provided by the annual report as a whole, the more specialized financial statements should be given particular attention. Balance sheets should reflect trends by using comparative figures and should be put into narrative form as far as possible. These features have been discussed elsewhere but they are reiterated at this point to suggest their significance in promoting sound public policy and as a response to changing social conditions. For similar reasons, it is highly desirable that stockholders be provided with profit-and-loss statements which are reasonably complete. The common practice of omitting the sales figure and the failure to report the operating expenses in some detail are not easily justified on the basis of reporting to the owners of the enterprise. The reluctance to furnish such information is usually ascribed to the need for withholding it from competitors, but this objection would be eliminated if all companies were required to report; at least, accounting by all would make the results available both ways.

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 825 

C 1 The Securities and Exchange Commission has already required public filing of complete financial statements, but this is simply the fulfillment of a function by public authority which should be done by management itself. Stockholders, as the owners of an enterprise, should naturally expect management to render an accounting for the results of operation. The gap between ownership and control does create the impression that management, itself, is the terminal facility, but this it utterly inconsistent with the basic relationships which are created by virtue of the corporate structure. Under the latter, the stockholders constitute the final court of authority and it is only by various legal devices that they have been deprived of this position for all practical purposes. And, undoubtedly, abuses of the type have been responsible in large measure for many of the pressures which are now influencing the conduct of private management. 

The Effects of Social Change on the Flow of Income 

The impact of social change will necessarily have great effect upon the flow of corporate income. In earlier years, management found its greatest challenge in meeting the ebb and flow of cyclical variation; today, there is the added problem of making adjustments to meet increasing social responsibility. When the latter is put into the form of prescribed law, management has no option in the matter but must necessarily provide for the absorption of the resulting cost. 

Moreover, the requirements of the state usually have a priority over strictly private obligations and the successful meeting of the former is a first test of solvency.

Indicating the increased scope of government control and influence, one writer has observed that "There are, roughly speaking, three major aspects of corporate management-and all three are under attack. 

They are the setting of prices, the purchase and supervision of labor, and the direction of financial policies affecting capital structure, depreciation reserves, dividend payments, and so on." Without attempting to appraise the nature of the motivation of these trends, it may be said that there can be little doubt about the fact of increased governmental voice in private business. And, as has been stated on previous occasions, the area of management control has necessarily been reduced as a result. 

See "The Trend Toward Regimentation of Business Gathers Momentum," Commercial and Financial Chronicle, Vol. 152 (March 1, 1941), pp. 1334-35.

The exact influence of enlarged government function on the flow of business income is entirely a matter of conjecture, but at the same time it may not be ignored by private management. Indeed, government policies and actions may easily become the balancing factor between successful and unsuccessful operations. Already, the defense program gives evidence of the potentialities in the restriction and closing of businesses not engaged in the production of defense materials. Admittedly, this is the result of a condition of national emergency, but it illustrates the possible magnitude of governmental power.

Under more normal circumstances, the advocates of increased government supervision of private business anticipate that the flow of income will be smoothed out and that this greater certainty of income return will offset and make possible the assumption of increased fixed expense by private industry. It is expected that expenditures by government will diminish in times of prosperity and increase to fill the gap in periods of recession. The logic of this argument is quite appealing and is worthy in many respects, but the application of such a program in the decade of the thirties gives practical evidence of numerous deficiencies.

Suggested Action by Private Management Itself 

The flow of income is one of those familiar economic paradoxes where it is virtually impossible to separate cause from effect. Thus, corporate activities affect and are affected by the trends of national income. Seldom, however, has private management given serious consideration to its position as a causal factor, and it has been customary to take advantage of prosperity and to more or less wait out a period of depression. While a reversal of this attitude would be unlikely in the case of small business enterprise, there are increasing signs that large-scale business is becoming more aware of the opportunities which would emanate from more aggressive action in times of depression. Conversely, business interests now seem to be more conscious of the dangers of price inflation and of other characteristics of a business boom than was true at the time of the last war. 

Most of the suggested programs of control under private auspices contemplate some form of central administration (see preceding chapter) where quotas of production, price schedules, etc., are formulated. 

Clearly, however, the adoption of such private facilities of planning

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 827 

would require some form of governmental supervision or regulation. 

Possibly, it is Utopian to expect individual management to function independently for the purpose of stabilizing income, but only on this basis could government be reasonably excluded. Any form of controlled or group action is contrary to the principles of a competitive economy and would call for means other than market action to protect the public interest. 

If private management did on its own account seek to curb the evils of extreme fluctuation, it would not necessarily do so for altruistic reasons. Actually, as a matter of sound business principle, it is usually profitable in the long run to adopt policies which seem to be contrary to the popular state of mind. For example, under many circumstances it would be advantageous to undertake expansion programs during depression periods when costs are likely to be lower. 

Similarly, there is good argument for the adoption of dividend and surplus policies which would permit resistance to undesirable general business trends. Specifically surplus accumulation would be accelerated in times of prosperity while at the same time there would be moderation in the payment of dividends; conversely, a depression would call for opposite action.

The Need for Promotion in Times of Marked Social Change 

Another economic paradox is found in the relationships between the promotion of new enterprise and the pressures of changing times. 

The risks of the latter quite naturally discourage the assumption of the liabilities of the former, but at the same time the lifting influence of new ventures are needed more than ever to counteract the contraction of many segments of industry. In earlier years, this problem was not so acute because of the opportunties of extensive development within our own nation, but today improvements are largely intensive in character and become all the more important. 

Financial reforms in recent years have undoubtedly done much to protect the rights of investors, but there is the danger that in the anxiety to safeguard existing rights there has been unnecessary discouragement of future opportunities. It is hard to believe that the requirements of registration as to the omission or the truth of material statements would have the effect of retarding legitimate enterprise, but of course there is always the question of what constitutes truth or omission. In addition, business men are so con-

stituted as to be chary of lawsuits with their attendant expense and publicity. Probably more important than the securities legislation, however, are the added burdens of fixed costs, and particularly taxes. 

As a result, it should not be surprising if the responsible man or institution of means would hesitate to risk unduly present availability and certainty of funds on hand for the sake of an uncertain and limited return in the future. When the government takes half or more of the profits in taxes but assumes none of the losses, investors naturally look for greater certainty of return than would be the case otherwise.

Means of Encouraging New Enterprise 

With the increasing hazards of profit-making, it is possible that the future may see government lending positive encouragement to the initiation of business enterprise. Already, numerous states have granted temporary exemption from property taxation and other favors as an inducement for corporations to move into their territory. Similarly, the federal government may conceivably deem it to be in the public interest to accord special treatment to new ventures. In the past, patents were intended to afford protection to the fruits of inventive genius, but this protection has less significance at the present time because of increased risks and higher taxes. 

Attention should also be called to the possible opposite reaction to higher taxes in the case of established business enterprise. Here, the increased burden may serve as a stimulus to research for the purpose of finding new technique and new products as a means of bolstering the income account. This does not mean that taxes could be increased ad infinitum because the law of diminishing returns would be applicable here as in other phases of business operation. 

The past decade has revealed the difficulties of raising venture capital. The government has developed numerous financial facilities which provide capital through the assumption of indebtedness by the borrower, but only rarely has the government assumed the risks of the residual owner. One of the few exceptions is found in the investment by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation in the shares of savings and loan associations where the justification took root in the assistance which was given to home owners more than in the encouragement of a form of business enterprise. For the most part, however, the financing of new ventures is still highly uncertain, and

THE IMPACT OF SOCIAL CHANGE ON FINANCIAL POLICY 829 

the cost of raising capital is greatly in excess of that for established enterprise.

Realistic but Constructive Disposition of Failures Probably it is fair to state that recent years have seen a much more realistic facing of the problem of business failure. In the past, there was a marked tendency to temporize with the conditions of failure, and the sacrifices of investors were conveniently held to a minimum. Always, there was the hope that business recovery would fill the breach, and as a result, drastic reorganization was avoided wherever possible. Today, the agencies of government which are concerned with business failures seem more intent upon effecting a revision of the capital structure and adopting other remedies which will more likely insure ensuing sound operation. Capital is written down to absorb existing losses, responsible management is discharged where necessary and the entire operation is tested in the light of its ability to carry itself.

In adopting this more realistic attitude toward failure, there has been at the same time a recognition of the need for rehabilitating business companies which are in trouble. Familiar minority rights have been sacrificed in favor of the welfare of the business as a whole, and loans have been extended where capital was not readily available from the open market. Government has also taken steps to see that the rights of all investors are fully represented and that plans of reorganization are not conveniently adopted for the advancement of special interests. 

Thus, the specialized Securities and Exchange Commission now has the authority to pass upon the merits of plans of reorganization and to advise the courts with respect to the final disposition of reorganization cases.

Summary 

The foregoing review indicates briefly some of the changes which are taking place in the financial system as a result of recent reforms. 

Heretofore, changes in the financial order seldom affected the basic philosophy but were mainly restricted to modifications of the technique. There was a reluctance to tamper with financial institutions because of the fear of upsetting public confidence, and as a result financial procedure became frozen and the power of the money changers was

absolute and final. But the spell has now been broken, and government is exercising a definite voice in determining the course of financial affairs. Many still bespeak that dire consequences will result while others hail the dawn of a new day. In either event, enlarged government function is now an established fact and that is the essential point for purposes of present-day financial policy. 

Conclusion 

The reader may wonder why broad, economic questions should be included in a treatise on corporation finance. This has been done because it is believed that the financial sector is the gateway to economic reform. Corporation finance, in the broadest sense of the term, is not simply a phase of business activity, but instead, it underlies or constitutes the foundation for the whole business structure. 

It is a bell-wether which measures success or failure and is the important control tower which guides economic activity. Rates charged by public service corporations reflect in large measure the decision of those in financial control; similarly, prices of other products and services are, in part, a reflection of underlying, financial conditions. 

In short, corporation finance is a focus from which there radiates important influence and control of the entire economic order.
